# TO THE READER

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut headpiece consisting of a horizontal band of repeating floral and scrollwork motifs, including fleur-de-lis and stylized leaves.</image-desc>

Our Treatises on **Harmony** <note>original: "Harmonie"</note> would have been imperfect had I not taken the time and patience necessary for such a work, in which I would have included the finest musical compositions from France, Italy, and Germany—where this Art flourishes most—if the ordinary printers had possessed the musical type. The lack of these fonts allowed me only to include the examples seen in the preceding books and those that follow, namely in the 5th book, which contains the practice of **figured counterpoint** <term>Counterpoint: the art of combining different melodic lines; "figured" refers to a more ornate or rhythmic style compared to simple note-against-note writing</term>. Those who find the examples of the practice of **consonances** and **dissonances** <term>Consonances: intervals that sound stable; Dissonances: intervals that sound unstable and require resolution</term> insufficient may wait for the many examples, both good and bad, for 2, 3, 4, 5, or more parts, from the practitioners who will write after us. Although the 4-part example found in Proposition 5 should satisfy the most curious—particularly regarding the practice of the **fourth** <term>Quarte: the interval between four scale degrees; historically, its treatment as a dissonance or consonance was a subject of much debate</term> and of dissonances in all their forms—I will provide the score to anyone who asks me for it. The 12 Duos in the first Proposition also demonstrate the practice of both consonances and dissonances. Furthermore, it was not necessary to include a greater number of examples, since the shops of all the music printers are full of them, and practitioners produce more than one could ever want.

As for the 6th book, which teaches the method of singing and embellishing songs, it should be noted that the examples of embellishments are found in Proposition 28, and whoever can sing them correctly will sing to perfection. But because the printers were unable to set the characters that signify the **trills** <term>tremblemens: rapid alternations between two adjacent notes</term> that should be performed on the notes where they occur, I have added them by hand in my own copy, which those who wish to mark them in their own books may consult. And if they wish to receive more profit and satisfaction from reading this book and the others, it is necessary that they correct the errors marked and corrected at the end or beginning of each treatise. It is not necessary to state that this 6th book contains four different treatises, as I have spoken of it enough at the beginning of the 6th book, nor that one may see there the manner of singing the verses of **Pindar** and **Horace** <note>Ancient Greek and Roman poets; their meters were often used as rhythmic exercises in Renaissance and Baroque music</note> in Propositions 23 and 29, since the simple opening of the book suffices. I add only that the method of singing without **mutations** <term>nuances/muances: the complex traditional system of switching between overlapping six-note scales (hexachords)</term> by means of the 7th syllable *BI, CI, DI, NI, SI, BA,* or *ZA*—which seems to have been invented or put into practice by several people at the same time—has been practiced in France by Mr. Gilles Granjan, Master Scribe in the city of Sens. His method consists simply of always taking *UT* at **C-sol-ut-fa** <term>C-sol-ut-fa: the pitch C; the name derives from the medieval Guidonian Hand system</term>, whether ascending or descending, when the song is in **B-natural** <term>Bquarre: the 'hard' hexachord using B-natural</term>, in which there is always a whole tone from **A-mi-la-re** to **B-fa-b-mi** <term>A to B-natural</term>; so that whenever there is no **flat** <term>Bmol: B-flat</term> marked at the beginning of the staves or the musical lines after the clefs, one must always take *UT* at **C-sol-ut** <term>the pitch C</term>, and consequently *FA* at **F-ut-fa** <term>the pitch F</term>, and *MI* at **b-fa-b-mi** <term>the pitch B</term>; and when the flat is marked after the clefs, one must always take *UT* at **F-ut-fa**, so as to sing *FA* at **B-fa-b-mi** <term>singing B-flat</term>. From this it happens that in descending an octave lower than **F-ut-fa**, one says *ut, mi, la, sol, fa, mi, re, ut*, just as when the song is in B-natural, in descending an octave lower than **C-sol-ut**, such that *mi* always follows *ut* in descending, as the same *ut* always fol-

<summary>In this preface, the author explains the limitations of current music printing, provides guidance on using the book's musical examples, and introduces a simplified seven-syllable solmization system to replace the traditional medieval hexachord mutations.</summary>

## To the Reader.

...always placed the **MI** in ascending, and that there is no other difficulty in starting the tone than to see if the **flat** <note>original: "bmol"</note> is at the beginning of the Music. This serves as a key and a sign to know that the **VT** <term>VT: The original syllable for the first note of the scale, now commonly known as "Do"</term> must only be placed on **F** <note>original: "Fvt"</note>, and consequently the **FA** on **B-flat** <note>original: "Bfa"</note>. Similarly, when the **flat** is not there, its absence signifies that the **VT** is taken only on **C** <note>original: "Cvt"</note>, and consequently the **FA** on **F** <note>original: "Ffavt"</note>, and the **MI** on **B-natural** <note>original: "bmi"</note>. By this, one sees that the "key of Nature" <note>The "Natural" hexachord starting on C</note> is banished from Music, as I have shown in the 19th Proposition of the 3rd book of *Musical Genres*.

But those who always begin **VT** in the same position, namely in **C** or **F**, use for this purpose the new syllable of which I spoke in the same place, and in the 2nd Proposition of the 6th book following, in order to have 7 entirely different syllables within the Octave; and others use 8, so that the **flat** <note>original: "bmol"</note> and the **natural** <note>original: "bquarre"</note> each have their own syllable. It is for this reason that Father **Adrian Banchieri** <note>An influential Italian composer and theorist (1568–1634)</note>, a Monk of Olivet, added to his music in the year 1614 the two syllables **BA** and **BI**. The latter is taken from the same text of the hymn, *So that your servants may* <note>original: "Ut queant laxis"; the hymn to St. John the Baptist used to name the notes of the scale</note>, from which **Aretin** <note>Guido d'Arezzo, the 11th-century monk credited with inventing the formal system of solmization</note> took the **LA**. Thus, he sings in his *Cartella* <note>Banchieri's work, "L'organo suonarino" or "La cartella musicale"</note> by always taking **VT** on **C**, whether by **flat** or by **natural**. When it is by **flat**, he sings **vt, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ba, vt** ascending; and descending **vt, ba, la, sol, fa, mi, re, vt**. By **natural**, he sings **vt, re, mi, fa, sol, la, bi, vt**, and the reverse when descending. If one wishes to sing the **natural** and the **flat** all together, one must say **vt, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ba, bi, vt**, which he asserts the Musicians of Rome have greatly approved.

He notes that it is appropriate to read the excellent Treatise by Master *Augustin Pise* <note>Agostino Pisa, an author who wrote on the technique of conducting</note> on the manner of leading and beating time, which was printed in Rome under the title *Musical Beatings* <note>original: "Battuta Musicali"</note>, etc. Those who desire to learn to sing at sight all kinds of Counterpoint, both simple and figured, will benefit from reading the book by the aforementioned **Banchieri**, where he explains several techniques with examples, in order to teach how one must sound all types of intervals. He also gives examples of slurs <note>original: "liaisons"</note> and diminutions for cadences, and calls them *Little Flowers* <note>original: "Floretti"; musical ornaments</note> on page 50 of his book; and up to page 60 he shows the manner of singing the 6 voices or syllables of Music in Duos. Finally, he gives one hundred examples of passages and several diminutions for final cadences, so that one can find in this Author everything that serves the practice; there, he calls the simple song *memory* <note>original: "memoria"</note> and its diminution *passage* <note>original: "passaggio"</note>.

# FIFTH BOOK
## ON THE COMPOSITION
### OF MUSIC.

---

*In this fifth book, we shall treat figurative counterpoint and the principal matters that may serve this subject, so that nothing further might be desired in this work. This we shall do so briefly and clearly that this book shall be neither obscure nor tedious, as will be seen by the propositions that follow.*

#### FIRST PROPOSITION.

*To explain that which belongs to figurative counterpoint, with 12 examples for the twelve modes.*

The preceding rules of simple counterpoint <term>simple counterpoint: A style of composition where notes are set against each other in equal duration, often called "note-against-note"</term> serve for the "diminished" kind, which is called "figurative" because it makes use of notes of different values, and because one part often plays 2, 4, 8, or 16 notes against a single note of the other part. In this way, the first notes of lesser value correspond to the first part of those of greater value, and the last to the second; from this, syncopations <note>original: "syncopes"</note> have taken their name. Without these syncopations, the art of composing would be deprived of many beautiful features that wonderfully embellish counterpoint, and which grant the freedom to use dissonances and mix them so appropriately with consonances <term>consonances: Intervals that sound stable and pleasing to the ear, such as the fifth or the octave, as opposed to "dissonant" intervals like the second or seventh</term> that the harmonies appear much better for it. 

But since it is not my design to copy Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), an influential Italian theorist whose "Le Istitutioni harmoniche" was the standard text for Renaissance counterpoint</note>—from whom Du Caurroy <note>Eustache du Caurroy (1549–1609), a prominent French composer of the late Renaissance</note> and all others, mediately or immediately, have drawn everything they know of practice—and as Nicola Vicentino and Cerone <note>Domenico Pietro Cerone (1566–1625), author of a massive treatise on musical theory</note> have given a great many rules and examples of all sorts of compositions, I place here only the 12 modes <term>modes: The precursor to modern major and minor scales, used to categorize the melodic structure of music</term> in two parts. These were composed by Master Racquet <note>Charles Racquet (c. 1597–1664), a celebrated organist at Notre-Dame de Paris</note>, Organist of Notre Dame in Paris, who is held to be one of the best masters of counterpoint of this time; for these suffice to show the true practice of dissonances in accordance with their cadences, their chords, and their nature. For this subject, I have chosen Psalm 146 in 12 verses, composed by Monsieur Habert, Abbot of Cerisé—namely, *Praise the Lord, for the psalm is good* <note>original Latin: "Laudate dominum quoniam bonus est psalmus"</note>—which I had already given at the end of the second book of the *Treatise on Universal Harmony* <note>original: "l’Harmonie vniuerselle"</note>.

<summary>This page introduces the fifth book on musical composition, defining "figurative counterpoint" and announcing a series of twelve musical examples composed by the organist Charles Racquet based on Psalm 146.</summary>

<header>On Composition,</header>

If one takes the trouble to analyze the examples of the 12 modes seen on the preceding pages, in order to observe the sequence of consonances, the mixing of dissonances with the said consonances, the <term>syncopations<note>In this period, "syncopation" often referred to suspensions, where a note is held over from a stable beat to a restricted one to create a temporary dissonance.</note></term>, and everything practiced therein, one could derive as many rules from them, because there is nothing there that is not permitted and practiced by the great Masters: or, if one prefers to take a copy of my musical score, I will freely provide it for this purpose.

As for the number of modes, there are properly only six natural ones, for the <term>plagal modes<note>Plagal modes are the "lower" versions of the standard (authentic) modes, sharing the same final note but having a lower range.</note></term>—namely the 2nd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 10th, and 12th—do not differ essentially from the other six, since they possess the same species of Fourth and Fifth: though one could count seven natural ones, namely the seven species of Octaves that I explained in the 3rd Book.

One may see the long Treatise that Girolamo Mei <note>original: "Hierofme Mey." Mei (1519–1594) was a Florentine humanist whose research into Ancient Greek music deeply influenced the development of early opera and Baroque theory.</note>, a Florentine, wrote regarding the modes of the Ancients. He begins them on B-natural <note>original: "♮mi"</note>, that is to say, on the string called the <term>lowest of the low<note>original: "hypate-hypaton." This was the lowest note of the Ancient Greek Greater Perfect System.</note></term>, to complete it at the other B-natural an octave above; that is to say, at the <term>next-to-the-middle<note>original: "paramese." In Greek theory, the note B above middle C.</note></term> string. He maintains that this is the <term>Mixolydian of Ptolemy</term>; and then he has the Lydian begin on C <note>original: "Cfaut"</note>, which goes from the <term>next-to-the-lowest of the low<note>original: "parhypate-hypaton," the note C.</note></term> to the <term>third of the disjunct<note>original: "trite diezeugmenon," the note C an octave higher.</note></term>; just as the Phrygian begins on D <note>original: "Drefol"</note>, the Dorian on E <note>original: "Emila"</note>, and so on for the others. To this he adds that the <term>Middle<note>original: "Mese."</note></term>, or the middle string of each mode, is the fourth note which forms a Fourth with the first, because it is indeed the middle string of the two <term>conjunct tetrachords<note>A tetrachord is a series of four notes; "conjunct" means the top note of the first is the bottom note of the second.</note></term>, although we now take the 5th note of each authentic mode for the <term>mediant</term> or middle.

## PROPOSITION II.

### *Explaining the Practice of Dissonances.*

To understand this practice of dissonances, one must assume that the note of a measure, which is ordinarily called a <term>semibreve<note>A whole note.</note></term>, has two equal parts, one of which begins on the beat, or lowering the hand, and the other on the upbeat; and that the two <term>minims<note>Half notes.</note></term>, which are sung at the same time by another part, must both form consonances against the semibreve: namely one against the downbeat, and the other against the upbeat. But when one places four <term>crotchets<note>original: "noires" (blacks). These are quarter notes.</note></term> against a semibreve, the 1st and the 3rd must form consonances, and the 2nd and 4th may be dissonances, provided they proceed by <term>conjunct degrees<note>Stepwise motion (e.g., C to D to E).</note></term>, since it suffices that one hears a consonance against the first part of the downbeat, and another against the first part of the upbeat of the semibreve. From this, it is easy to conclude that one must divide the note in the imagination into as many parts as there are notes of lesser value against it, in order to understand the score; and consequently, if the subject has four crotchets in the measure, the 2nd and 4th notes of the measure in another part may be dissonant, because they strike the ear so fleetingly that it is not offended by them. Indeed, the ear finds the consonances all the more agreeable afterward, just as it happens with the eye and all other senses, which receive more pleasure from what is most pleasing to them after they have felt some contrast. This will be more easily understood by the example of the preceding Modes than by a longer discourse. It is only necessary to note that I observe the ordinary order of musical modes, beginning the first on C <note>original: "Csolvfa"</note>, which some call <term>Lydian</term>, others <term>Ionian</term>, and the...

# On Composition.

others call them *Dorian*, though it matters not at all by what name they are called, provided that one understands their nature and their properties, from which more suitable—or at least more intelligible—names could be derived than the preceding ones. Be that as it may, if one prefers to follow the order of the Church Tones, as <term>Glarean<note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563) was a Swiss theorist who expanded the system of eight church modes to twelve in his book *Dodecachordon*.</note></term> has done, one will begin the first on D <note>original: "Drefol," the solmization name for the note D.</note>; and if one begins the first tone with the first <term>Tetrachord<note>A scale of four notes used in Ancient Greek music theory.</note></term> of the Greeks, one will place it on E <note>original: "Emila," the note E.</note>. If one named each mode by the location of its root, it would suffice to say the mode of C, of D, etc. <note>original: "Csol, de Drefol."</note>

Regarding their number, it seems they can be limited by the <term>Senary<note>The "Senario" is the set of numbers 1 through 6, which the theorist Zarlino argued were the source of all musical consonances.</note></term>, following the primary species of the Octave; from this comes the fact that many only place these six among the natural modes. However, I have discussed this so particularly and so amply in the 14th, 15th, 16th, and 17th Propositions of the preceding book—where I showed and marked the <term>cadences<note>A melodic or harmonic configuration that creates a sense of resolution or "closing" in a piece of music.</note></term> of each mode—that it is difficult to add more, particularly if one includes the Table of Modes on page 183. In that table, one sees in the blink of an eye all the cadences that suit and link together agreeably, and those that are "enemies." Thus, if the mind followed the eye in this matter, one could learn to compose music in the same amount of time it would take to look at the said Table.

As for those who believe that the tones and modes of the ancient Greeks were not similar to ours, and that the *Dorian* tone, for example, was one tone lower than the *Phrygian*, and the *Lydian* one tone lower than the *Phrygian*, etc., I do not prevent them from following that opinion. According to this view, one can imagine that the voice is always higher, and consequently the string more slender, shorter, or more tightly stretched for each tone; since each tone has a melodic structure <note>original: "deduction de sa melodie"</note> different from another tone, it follows that the mode changes. Now, this thought corresponds to the idea of the *Mese* <note>original: "Mese," the central or "middle" note of the Ancient Greek system.</note> of the system: namely, that it is the seat, or the place of the most vigorous and natural voice of all those that anyone can make, both above and below it, from which one can descend and ascend one Octave. From this it follows that the *Mese* of one person is the *Proslambanomene* <note>original: "Proslambanomene," the lowest note in the Ancient Greek "Greater Perfect System."</note> of another, depending on the low or high pitch of different voices.

Monsieur Doni <note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), an Italian scholar who attempted to reconstruct ancient music.</note>, of whom I spoke very amply in the 30th Proposition of the book on the Organ, explains several differences between our tones and modes and those of the ancients. He believes that the interval of the semitone for some was different from that of others; the same can also be said of the whole tones. One can see this diversity of semitones in the different divisions of the Greek Tetrachord, of which I spoke very amply in the 2nd book on Instruments, and in the book on the Genres. To this he adds that different ways of carrying the voice, diminutions <note>Rapid melodic ornaments.</note>, rhythmic movements, and accents could have created the difference in tones and modes. He notes that the most ancient Greeks did not establish their tones or modes as our <term>Practitioners<note>Working musicians and composers, as opposed to purely theoretical "speculative" writers.</note></term> do now, who follow the authority of <term>Gaffurius</term>, Glarean, <term>Zarlino</term>, and <term>Salinas</term>. For the ancients did not speak of the <term>mediation<note>original: "medieté." This refers to the mathematical division of the octave (Arithmetic or Harmonic) to determine the "final" and "dominant" notes of a mode.</note></term> or Arithmetic and Harmonic division upon which modern authors establish their twelve modes, as I showed in the 3rd book on the Genres and elsewhere. Rather, the most ancient writers, who only recognized seven modes (as many as there are species of Octave), gave them no other names than "first sound," "second sound," etc. <note>original: "premier & second son... ἦχος [echos]"</note>. And when they added the names of *Dorian*, *Phrygian*, etc., they placed them

4. towards the high <note>original: "l’aigu," referring to the higher pitch register.</note>, beginning with the highest, which is to say, with the **Hypermixolydian**, and ending at the **Dorian**, which they made the first of their four <term>Plagal modes<note>Plagal modes are "secondary" versions of the authentic modes, positioned a fourth lower.</note></term>. This was not always consistent among them, as they followed various opinions; from this comes the fact that they reduced them all to two species: namely, the four lowest to the **Dorian** harmony, and the highest to the **Phrygian**. It is from this that the proverb seems to have taken its origin: *to pass from the Dorian to the Phrygian*, used to describe changing the subject of conversation inappropriately. Now, there is a strong appearance that they began naming these tones based on the number of strings used on the instruments of <term>Terpander<note>A Greek poet and musician of the 7th century BCE, credited with increasing the number of strings on the lyre from four to seven.</note></term> and others. This first Lyre, which had seven strings, gave the beginning to the modes that I explain in the 17th Proposition of the 3rd book. In that book, two words must be corrected on page 186, lines 27 and 31: namely, **Hyperdorian** and **Hyperphrygian**; one should read **Hypodorian** and **Hypoliphrygian**, as these were not included in the <term>Errata<note>A list of corrected printing errors.</note></term>.

One can therefore assert that the <term>Aristoxenians<note>Followers of Aristoxenus, a Greek philosopher who emphasized the human ear's perception over mathematical ratios in music.</note></term> and many others only distinguished their modes, or tones, according to the different locations within their system. Thus, the **Hypodorian** is the tone of **A-re** <note>The note A.</note>, the **Hypophrygian** is that of **B-mi** <note>The note B.</note>, and so on for the others. Consequently, it was not permitted to start a mode higher at one time than at another. For example, if the first sound of the Dorian mode was made by a string three feet long, which made 40 vibrations in one second of a minute—or by a voice in unison with that string, such as my lowest or deepest voice—it was not permitted to begin that tone or mode with a voice deeper or higher, even though one used the same species of Octave. From this comes the fact that their modes were named <term>tropoi<note>original Greek: τρόποι; meaning "ways" or "manners."</note></term> and <term>ethē<note>original Greek: ἤθη; meaning "characters" or "dispositions."</note></term>, because they used them to change the passions and the morals of men. They called the lowest part of their system <term>hypatoeidē<note>original Greek: ὑπατοειδή; the "highest" in string position but "lowest" in pitch.</note></term> and destined it for tragic subjects, just as the middle <term>mesoeidē<note>original Greek: μεσοειδή; the middle register.</note></term> was for <term>dithyrambs<note>Wild, choral hymns dedicated to Dionysus.</note></term>, and the high or highest <term>nētoeidē<note>original Greek: νητοειδή; the highest pitch register.</note></term> was for <term>Nomical Poems<note>Ancient Greek hymns or legalistic songs performed to the flute or lyre.</note></term>.

Or rather, if it were permitted to start each mode at whatever pitch of voice one wished (which is more believable, since all voices cannot begin in the same place or on the same string, and experience shows that the same mode is always observed—for example, the first of **C-sol-ut-fa** <note>The note C.</note>, whether one begins it one or two tones higher or lower), and yet they nonetheless established a certain sound for the true or imaginary beginning of said mode, one can say that those who began this mode one tone lower (that is, in **D-re-sol** <note>The note D.</note>) sang the mode of C at the pitch of the mode of D, or the **Lydian mode** according to the opinion of <term>Monsieur Doni<note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), a contemporary of Mersenne who studied ancient music theory.</note></term>, in the Phrygian tone. Be that as it may, the systems I explain in the 4th Proposition of the 3rd book on Genders, up to the 9th, are very suitable for placing the modes and tones of the ancients according to one's design, as are the keyboards of the **Spinet** and the **Organs** that I explain in the 3rd and 6th books on Instruments. For one can do nothing more exact and easier on this subject, unless one prefers to use the division of the Octave into 12 equal semi-tones, following the demonstration in the 14th Proposition of the first book, the 9th of the 2nd and 4th, and the 15th of the 6th book on Instruments. And if one wishes to use the Octave divided into 24 enharmonic <term>dieses<note>Small musical intervals, specifically quarter-tones in this context.</note></term>, or quarter tones—which are easily found for marking on the neck of the **Lute** and other instruments by means of the 23 mean proportional lines, the invention of which I provided in the 7th Proposition of the 2nd book on Instruments—one finds...

practice through the ordinary notes in the 12th Proposition of the 3rd book on Genres, which will serve equally for the three <term>Genres<note>The three genera of Greek music: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note></term> and for all the modes, regardless of the tone in which one wishes to begin them, without ever needing to work further upon them or imagine something new.

This being established, I come to the **Practice of Dissonances**, about which I have already written an entire book; for they produce nearly the same effect among chords as vices do among virtues. From this, theologians conclude that God permits sins and rejects no one except to make His grace and goodness appear with more brilliance and splendor within the virtues and upon the predestined, following the doctrine of Saint Paul in the 9th chapter of the **Epistle to the Romans** <note>original: "l'Epistre aux Romains." Mersenne refers to the theological concept of "God’s Sovereignty in Election."</note>. This may provide an occasion for Preachers to demonstrate the use of all sins—of which **Saint Thomas** treats in his *Prima Secundae* and *Secunda Secundae* <note>original: "premiere Seconde, & dans la Seconde Seconde." These are the two parts of the second volume of Thomas Aquinas's *Summa Theologiae*, which deals with human acts, virtues, and vices.</note>—by comparing them to the use of Dissonances which enrich harmony. This is so that good people may draw all the advantages from the sins that are committed, just as Musicians draw from discords, in order to imitate God, who draws great good from great evils.

Now, all dissonances can be reduced to **three**, just like the Consonances: namely, to the **Second**, the **Tritone**, and the **Seventh**. For the **Ninth**, the **Sixteenth**, and the **Twenty-third**; the **Eleventh**, the **Eighteenth**, and the augmented **Twenty-fifth**; and the **Fourteenth**, the **Twenty-first**, and the **Twenty-eighth**, are merely <term>replications<note>In music theory, these are "compound intervals," which are simply the basic intervals (2nd, 4th, 7th) expanded by one or more octaves.</note></term> of the preceding ones, which must be judged according to the rules we shall set for the three aforementioned Dissonances. As for the **false Fifth** <note>The diminished fifth.</note>, it is so little different from the **Tritone** in the perfect system—specifically by a **minor comma**, as I have shown in the 7th, 8th, and 9th Propositions of the book on Dissonances—that it is almost impossible for the ear to distinguish them. And if one uses equal tones and semitones, they are one and the same thing; that is why one may speak only of the Tritone if one wishes, although I provide specific examples here of the **false Fifth** for the sake of Practitioners who are accustomed to distinguishing it.

It must therefore first be noted that the practice of Dissonances is considered almost as much in multi-part Composition as that of Consonances. It is for this reason that such high esteem is held for **Caurroy** <note>Eustache du Caurroy (1549–1609), an influential French composer of the late Renaissance.</note> and other Masters, who make one taste the goodness and agreeableness of chords by means of discords. These serve the overly great sweetness of Music just as <term>ragouts<note>A highly seasoned French stew, used here as a metaphor for "zest" or "spice."</note></term>, vinegar, and things that stimulate the appetite serve in sauces that are too sweet; or as shadows serve colors, making them appear more beautiful.

In the second place, discords must be **saved** <note>original: "sauuez." In music, this means "resolved," moving from a dissonant chord to a consonant one to release tension.</note>, and as if excused, by the preceding chords and by those that follow. But because one can always encounter new ways to practice them—particularly if one uses the three Genres and all their species and degrees seen in the second book on Instruments—I will put here only examples of the most common practice, to which everyone may add as many others as they wish.

I say then, in the third place, that the **Second** and other Dissonances can be made against a single part; for example, against the **Bass**, when it holds firm on the same note. From this, it happens that everything sung against the <term>drones<note>original: "bourdons." The continuous low humming notes of certain instruments.</note></term> of **Hurdy-gurdies** and **Bagpipes** <note>original: "Vielles & des Musettes."</note> seems good. The first example shows

The second example shows it between the major Third and the <term>Unison<note>The same pitch played by two voices simultaneously.</note></term>; the 3rd shows the <term>Ninth<note>An interval of nine notes, which is an octave plus a second.</note></term>, that is to say, its replica <note>Mersenne considers wider intervals like the ninth to be "replicas" of their smaller counterparts, like the second.</note>, between the minor <term>Tenth<note>An interval of ten notes, an octave plus a third.</note></term> and the <term>Fifth<note>A stable consonant interval spanning five scale degrees.</note></term>: it is also found between the major Tenth and the Fifth at the end of the 4th example: and finally, the Second appears between the two Thirds in the last example, in which the <term>Seventh<note>A dissonant interval spanning seven degrees.</note></term> is also found between the <term>Octave<note>The interval of eight notes, where the pitch doubles in frequency.</note></term> and the major <term>Sixth<note>An interval spanning six degrees.</note></term>; so that these two musical staves contain nearly all the <term>Dissonances<note>Combinations of notes that sound unstable or "harsh" and typically require resolution to a consonant chord.</note></term>, for the <term>Tritone<note>An interval of three whole tones (augmented fourth), famously known as the "Devil in Music" for its extreme instability.</note></term> is at the end of the first example between the major Third and the minor Sixth, which usually "saves" it <note>That is, provides a resolution to the tension.</note>. As for the Fourth, it is in the same example between the two Thirds; and between the minor Tenth and the Fifth in the 4th example. I will give other particular examples after having explained a notable difficulty proper to Music, because it is encountered in the preceding examples and in others that we will provide.

## PROPOSITION III.

->*Explaining in what manner one can understand the Harmonic Syncope, which is used in Figurate Counterpoint.*<-

Since the <term>Syncope<note>Known today as syncopation or a suspension; a rhythmic device where a note is held across a beat or "divided" against the pulse.</note></term> is one of the greatest ornaments of Harmony, it is reasonable to explain it: however, it is not understood here as it is by the Grammarians, where it signifies the absence of a letter or a syllable in a word—such as when one says *compostus* <note>original: "compoſtus"</note> and *virûm* <note>original: "virûm"</note> instead of *compositus* <note>original: "compositus"</note> and *virorum* <note>original: "virorum"</note>—nor as it is in Medicine, where it signifies a failure of the heart [fainting]; but rather (at least sometimes) for the division of a note, for example of a <term>Semibreve<note>A whole note.</note></term>, into 2, 4, or 8 parts, such that it would be better named a <term>Diaeresis<note>From the Greek word for "division."</note></term> than a Syncope, though I do not wish to innovate anything in this matter, no more than in others, where it is only a question of terms that signify whatever one wishes.

I say, then, that the Syncope taken in this sense consists of the mental division one makes of a note into two or several parts, so that two or several notes of one part correspond to a single note of the other part, as is seen in the preceding examples, and particularly in the first and the last; for the 2nd and 3rd <term>Minims<note>Half notes.</note></term> of the <term>Bass<note>The lowest voice part.</note></term> correspond to the second note of the <term>Treble<note>The highest voice part, or 'dessus'.</note></term>, which they divide in such a way that the 2nd note, that is to say,

# On Composition.

The <term>E<note>original: *mi* of *Emi*</note></term> corresponds to the first part of the <term>semibreve<note>A note value equivalent to a modern whole note.</note></term> in the *Treble*, which is to say, to the <term>D<note>original: *re* of *Gre*</note></term>, against which it forms a <term>minor Third</term>. The third <term>minim<note>A note value equivalent to a modern half note.</note></term> of the *Bass*—the <term>F<note>original: *fa* of *Ffa*</note></term>—corresponds to its other half, against which it forms a <term>Second</term> or a whole tone. In this sense, the first semibreve of the *Treble* is syncopated. This occurs similarly in the semibreve that follows, against which the fourth and fifth minims strike—namely, the <term>D</term> and the <term>C</term>—which form the <term>Fourth</term> and the <term>Third</term> against the <term>F</term> of the semibreve. Now, if one wished to reduce these <term>syncopations<note>In 17th-century music, "syncope" or syncopation often refers to a suspension, where a note is held over from a previous chord to create a temporary dissonance.</note></term> into simple notes, they would have to be written like this:

<image-desc>Two systems of musical notation on five-line staves. The first system shows a series of notes in the upper and lower staves, with vertical lines indicating alignment. The second system similarly shows musical notes aligned between upper and lower parts, representing the reduction of syncopation mentioned in the text.</image-desc>

This is done so that each note of the Bass strikes against each note of the *Treble*. However, this is not usually done because syncopated notes have more grace and "save" <note>That is, they resolve or justify the discord.</note> the <term>Dissonances</term> better than those that do not syncopate and instead strike together. But the syncopations in the second and other examples are taken according to ordinary practice; for the first part of the first semibreve of the *Treble* corresponds to the second minim of the *Bass*, and its second part strikes against the first part of the first semibreve of the *Bass*, whose second part strikes against the second minim of the *Treble*. In this way, there are two syncopations in this example due to the two syncopated semibreves, which is very pleasing and full of artifice in Music—particularly when the entire composition is so syncopated that there is almost no measure without a syncopation. Now, the Practitioners recognize only this manner as syncopation, and not the preceding one. One can see the same kinds of syncopations in the third and fourth examples, in which the <term>dot<note>Referring to a dotted note, which extends the duration of a pitch across the beat.</note></term> of the *Treble* strikes against the third part of the second semibreve of the *Bass*, and the <term>crotchet<note>original: *noire*, a quarter note.</note></term> strikes against its fourth or last part. I will pass over the fifth example, where the dot and the three following crotchets strike against the first semibreve of the *Treble*, which they consequently divide into four parts, just as eight <term>quavers<note>original: *crochuës*, eighth notes.</note></term> would divide it into eight equal parts. In this manner, the <term>diminution<note>The division of long notes into many shorter, faster notes.</note></term> that one part makes against another is a species of syncopation, though different from that of the Practitioners, as I shall explain after having clarified the practice of the other Dissonances.

## PROPOSITION V.

->*To provide examples of the practice of Dissonances in Trios, and in other Compositions for 4 or more parts, and all the ways in which the Fourth can be employed in Music.*<-

**T**he examples that follow for three voices will further help to make understood the practice of <term>discords<note>original: *discords*; a synonym for dissonances.</note></term> among the chords, and will show how the <term>Treble<note>original: *Dessus*; the highest voice part in a composition.</note></term>, or the middle part, employs Dissonances in Harmony: upon which there is no need to discourse, since the numbers that are seen show the places where the dissonances are encountered, and which consonances they are followed by; for the 2 signifies Seconds; the 4' the <term>Tritons<note>An augmented fourth interval, consisting of three whole tones.</note></term>; the 5' the <term>false Fifths<note>original: *fauces Quintes*; also known as the diminished fifth or semidiapente.</note></term>, and the 7 the Sevenths, as in the preceding Proposition. One must only remark that these numbers being placed above the Treble signify that it is that part which creates the Dissonances against the Bass, and being above the <term>Tenor<note>original: *Taille*; the middle voice part.</note></term>, they signify that it is that part which creates the discords with the said Bass, against which they must be considered more particularly than against the middle parts, because it is the foundation of Music, for which we have given the reasons in the 3rd Proposition of the 4th book on Composition.

# On Composition.

Now, after having given all these examples, it is necessary to show all the ways in which the <term>Fourth<note>original: *Quarte*; the interval spanning four notes of the scale (e.g., C to F).</note></term> can be used in two, three, and four parts. Some theorists place it among the <term>Dissonances<note>Intervals that sound "unstable" or "clashing" to the ear.</note></term>, though without much justification. Be that as it may, the <term>Fantaisie<note>A musical composition that follows the composer’s imagination rather than a strict formal structure.</note></term> that follows—which was composed by the <term>Sieur de Cousu<note>Jean de Cousu (c. 1570–1648), a singer and composer in the French royal chapel.</note></term> in honor of the Fourth—will demonstrate every way one can employ the <term>Diatessaron<note>The Greek term for the interval of a Fourth.</note></term>, both in <term>syncopation<note>original: *syncope*; a rhythmic device where a note is started on a weak beat and held over a strong beat, often creating a suspension.</note></term> and outside of it. Truly, nothing more could be desired after this piece of music, as it places the Fourth at the end, in the middle, and at the beginning of the <term>ternary measure<note>original: *mesure ternaire*; triple time or triple meter, where the beat is divided into three.</note></term>, and even after a rest.

He maintains that the Fourth has never before been practiced in several of the ways he employs it here; yet they are all excellent, both to the ear and by logic. No musician could find anything to criticize in them, and the ear itself does not even notice the use of many of these methods, so that they are more to be admired than corrected. This is because the Fourth is placed there with all the necessary observations and in its natural place, as those who understand the principles of music will easily judge. Furthermore, it always enters in relation to the <term>consonances<note>Stable, pleasant-sounding intervals like thirds or fifths.</note></term> that naturally surround it. To make it more pleasing to the taste, it is preceded by one or several parts forming a melody which it then imitates in the same <term>fugue<note>A technique where a melody is introduced in one part and then taken up by others.</note></term> or <term>counter-fugue<note>An imitation where the original melody is inverted (turned upside down).</note></term>.

If by chance someone finds it a bit harsh in certain places, they will judge it to be very good once they have accustomed their ear to it. The same thing will happen to them as happened to the disciples of <term>Pythagoras<note>Ancient Greek philosopher whose theories formed the basis of Western music intervals.</note></term>, who refused to approve of <term>Thirds and Sixths<note>In early medieval theory, only octaves, fifths, and fourths were considered perfect; thirds and sixths were only accepted later as "imperfect" consonances.</note></term> until time and the practice of them, founded on reason, made them recognize the excellence of these Consonances. In the same way, the reader will judge that the Fourth is an excellent chord. Nevertheless, this does not mean that everyone is permitted to use it in all these ways, unless they know how to apply the same precautions and the same reasoning as the one who first practiced them.

This *Fantaisie* will also serve several other purposes necessary for this book, for <term>Counterpoint<note>The art of combining different melodic lines.</note></term> is observed very strictly within it, with the required order of all the Consonances. One can also see the <term>Tritone<note>An augmented fourth, often called the "Devil in Music" for its harsh sound.</note></term> and the <term>false Fifth<note>A diminished fifth.</note></term> practiced in as many ways as one could desire, along with the <term>Second<note>An interval of two notes (e.g., C to D).</note></term>, the <term>Seventh<note>An interval of seven notes (e.g., C to B).</note></term>, and their <term>octave equivalents<note>original: *repliques*; the same intervals expanded by an octave (like a ninth or fourteenth).</note></term>, which appear in almost every possible fashion. Furthermore, one can see how to create and use <term>suppositions<note>A technique involving passing tones or non-harmonic notes that "substitute" for a consonant note.</note></term> and fugues, both in the standard way and in reverse, how one part imitates another in counter-fugue, and how fugues are redoubled. Moreover, it serves to give confidence to many in singing their part, particularly in triple meter; for whoever masters all the parts of this *Fantaisie* will be able to sing anything in any kind of music, no matter how difficult. Indeed, no one can sing it properly without having studied it beforehand—not because of any extravagant intervals, since the melodies are quite pleasant and very singable in all parts, but because one does not usually see such <term>diminution<note>Breaking long notes into many shorter, faster notes.</note></term> and such variation in triple meter, even though there is nothing extraordinary about it.

# Book Five

It must also be observed that there is not a single false relation <note>original: *fausse relation*; a musical term, often called a "tritone clash," where two notes in different voices create a harsh, discordant interval that was strictly avoided in Renaissance and Baroque counterpoint.</note>, however small it may be, not even among the middle parts. This gave no small amount of trouble to its author, who composed this piece for a purpose he will declare elsewhere. Furthermore, one will notice in which parts of the ternary measure <term>ternary measure: a time signature based on three beats, similar to modern 3/4 or 3/2 time</term> one ought to place syncopations to allow for Dissonances. For he corrects the error of those who place them in the 3rd part of the measure; syncopations that carry Dissonances should only be in the first and second part of the measure, and not in the third. That is to say, if one uses perfect time <note>original: *temps parfait*; a system of measurement where a breve is divided into three semibreves, symbolizing the Holy Trinity.</note>, making three semibreves <note>equivalent to modern whole notes</note> to the measure as he does in this Fantasia, the syncopated breve <note>equivalent to a double-whole note</note> must begin on the upbeat or the downbeat <note>original: *en levant ou en frappant*; literally "in lifting or in striking," referring to the conductor's hand movements.</note>, so that the Dissonances occur in the first or second part of the ternary measure, and not in the third. However, it is permitted in this perfect time to syncopate every semibreve in each part of the measure to pass the Dissonances found in the second part of said syncopated semibreve, which can be syncopated at the start of the ternary measure by means of a minim <note>half-note</note>, or by its rest or equivalent value. Finally, one will see in this piece how one should treat a Mode with all its cadences, and several other very useful and necessary things that can be considered therein, without it being necessary to explain them in more specific detail.

### COROLLARY OF HARMONIC SYNCOPATIONS.

->*Showing the manner in which Practitioners use Syncopations, and*<-
->*at the same time the employment of Dissonances.*<-

Although I defined Syncopation <note>original: *Syncope*; the rhythmic technique of shifting the emphasis from a strong beat to a weak beat, often used to create tension through dissonance.</note> in the third Proposition as the real or mental division of a note into two, four, or several equal (or, if one prefers, unequal) parts, practitioners <note>original: *Praticiens*; performing musicians or composers as opposed to abstract theorists.</note> nevertheless do not call this practice *Syncopation*. For they maintain that it occurs only when the note of one part is so opposed to the other that the first part of one corresponds to the second part of the other, or vice versa. For example, when the Soprano <note>original: *Dessus*; the highest voice part.</note> sings *re, mi, fa* in the first example, and the Bass <note>original: *Basse*</note> sings *ut, re*. The second half of the minim of this Bass corresponds to the first part of the minim of the Soprano, and the second half of the minim of the Soprano corresponds to the first half of the minim of the Bass. Thus, the Syncopation is a kind of binding of a note in one part with two notes in the other, which can be expressed to some extent with the ordinary solmization syllables *ut, re, mi*, etc. For if the *mi* of one part—for example, the Bass—is so arranged that its second letter or syllable corresponds to the first syllable of the Soprano's *la*, and the second syllable of this *la* to the first syllable or letter of the Soprano’s second note *re*; this mutual interlocking and engaged correspondence will create the syncopation in this manner: <insert>L A</insert> but the examples of the notes that follow clarify the <insert>MI RE</insert> Syncopation better than any sort of discourse.

<summary>The author explains the technical rules for syncopation and dissonance used in the preceding Fantasia, specifically criticizing the placement of syncopations on the third beat of triple meter. He also defines syncopation from the perspective of performing musicians as an interlocking of notes between different voice parts.</summary>

# On Composition.

### Examples of Syncopations.

<note>The musical notation shows eight examples of syncopated figures. The numbers above and below the staves indicate the intervals (distances between notes) and the rhythmic placement.</note>

For the first 4 examples show what I have explained previously, and demonstrate that the half of the <term>semibreve</term><note>A whole note in modern notation.</note> of the Bass corresponds to the first half of the semibreve of the <term>Treble</term><note>original: "Dessus"; the highest vocal or instrumental part.</note>, of which the last half corresponds to the first <term>minim</term><note>A half note.</note> of the Bass. Here it must be noted that this syncopation always begins on the upbeat when it occurs between semibreves, although many hold that it is a matter of indifference whether they are made on the downbeat or the upbeat. One can also create syncopation on the second and the last quarter of a note, and in a thousand other ways that can be invented: which I leave to the exercise of the Practitioners.

As for the Dissonances which are employed by favor of the said Syncopations, it is easy to discern them, for the numbers above mark the Consonances and the Dissonances, following our ordinary method; that is why I shall add nothing further to this Proposition, except for this small example from <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), an influential Italian music theorist of the Renaissance.</note>Zarlino.

### Example of fifteen measures of Syncopations by Zarlino.

<note>The notation illustrates fifteen measures of continuous syncopation, showing how dissonances are prepared and resolved according to Zarlino's rules.</note>

As for the dot, which is called the dot of *augmentation*<note>The modern "dotted note," which increases a note's value by half.</note>, which is always worth half of the note that immediately precedes it, and is worth as much as the note that follows, it must always be consonant with the notes of the other parts; and if it is sometimes dissonant, or if one creates a Fourth against it, one must always descend by a <term>conjunct degree</term><note>Moving to the very next note in the scale (a step) rather than skipping.</note> after having made the said dot, if one wishes the Compositions to have good grace.

The said Zarlino says that <term>Syncopation</term><note>A rhythmic effect where the accent is shifted from a strong beat to a weak beat.</note> is a transposition of a note that is tied to another note, and that it continues until it encounters a similar note that is not tied, in order to make it re-enter the measure from which it departed: and that when the semibreve is sung on the upbeat, it is said to be *syncopated*. But he forbids syncopating the measures themselves, for fear of confusing the <term>Cantors</term><note>Singers, particularly those in a church choir.</note>, and of breaking the measure and the time, which falls naturally on the beginning of each note, although many Practitioners now break the measure very often, and put one of their most...

-># Book Five<-

...great skill in this manner of syncopation. Now it must be remarked once and for all that many Composers do not place a <term>sharp</term><note>original: "dieſe"; an accidental raising a pitch by a semitone.</note> before the penultimate note which makes the cadence, even though it should only form a semitone with the preceding note, as occurs in the previous example from <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the preeminent music theorist of the late Renaissance.</note>Zarlino. They omit it because they say that this sharp must always be understood there, by reason of the general rule which requires one to make a <term>Major Sixth</term> before the <term>Octave</term>, toward which one moves by contrary motion; this is why I have not marked any sharp there.

It must also be noted that Syncopations are of great use when one finds several notes on the same pitch of the subject, and it is necessary for the Counterpoint to proceed by interval, because one cannot continue the variety of <term>Consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and pleasant to the ear, such as the third, fifth, or octave.</note> for long without difficulty unless one uses several syncopated notes; for example, the <term>semibreve</term> and the <term>minim</term> with the dot, always changing the pitches, as Zarlino teaches in the 57th chapter. This counterpoint is called *tied* <note>original: "lié"; referring to the way notes are suspended or connected across beats.</note>, and is better and more pleasing than that in which Syncopations are not practiced. For this reason, the semibreve of the subject should not fall entirely upon the <term>downbeat</term><note>original: "frapper"; the downward stroke of the hand used to keep time.</note> of the counterpoint's note, but upon the half, as happens when it falls upon the dot of the minim. He also calls it *tied* when the subject holds its note while the Counterpoint proceeds through various pitches. Regarding this, it is good to advise that the <term>unison</term> may be made on the second part of the semibreve, provided that the subject and the Counterpoint do not sound it at the same time—whether on the downbeat or the <term>upbeat</term><note>original: "leuant"; the upward motion of the hand in timekeeping.</note>—for it is not perceived as strongly on the second part of a note as on the first. This is why one may use it on the dot of the semibreve and the minim when the part is <term>diminished</term><note>Divided into smaller, faster note values.</note> and the music is set for several voices.

Now it is certain that the Masters may use several licenses against the ordinary rules when they are constrained to do so to make each part "sing" well; for example, they may place a <term>Fifth</term> after a Major Sixth placed on the second part of a syncopated semibreve, provided that one of the parts holds its note. For since <term>Seconds</term> and <term>Sevenths</term><note>Dissonant intervals usually requiring careful resolution.</note> are permitted by favor of the syncopation, it is certain that the Major Sixth may also pass there—although many find it difficult to pass from a minor interval to an Octave, because it is further away than the Major Sixth is from the Fifth. This is allowed unless one moves to the Octave with a "black note" <note>A shorter note value, like a crotchet (quarter note).</note> by stepwise and contrary motion, where even dissonances are permitted. These should not ordinarily be practiced on <term>chromatic pitches</term>, that is to say, those with sharps, since the sharp and the <term>flat</term><note>original: "bmol".</note> were only invented to create Consonances. In favor of these, <term>Singers</term><note>original: "Chantres".</note> must always supply the sharps even if they are not marked, as happens when it is necessary to make a Major Third or Sixth instead of a minor one. However, one must use these accidentals as little as possible for fear of changing the <term>mode</term><note>The melodic system or scale upon which the piece is built.</note>, and avoid them particularly at the first or second note of the song; for instead of beginning the modulation in the third mode, for example, it would begin in the ninth. And if the *sharp* <note>original: "dieſis".</note> is placed between G and A <note>original: "Gre & Ami"; pitches in the Guidonian hexachord system.</note>, this modulation is neither <term>diatonic</term> nor <term>chromatic</term>, because one cannot arrange the pitches of the <term>Treble</term> and the <term>Bass</term> in such a way that they remain diatonic.

### PROPOSITION VI.

*To explain the practice of Consonances, and the sequence they can maintain among themselves to create pleasing Compositions; that is to say, how one must move from one Consonance to another.*

Since there are only eight <term>Consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and harmonious, such as the third or fifth.</note>—namely the <term>Unison</term>, the two Thirds, the Fourth, the Fifth, the two Sixths, and the Octave—of which the Tenths, the Eleventh, the Twelfth, the Thirteenths, and other <term>replicates</term><note>Intervals larger than an octave that function similarly to their smaller counterparts (e.g., a tenth is a third plus an octave).</note> observe the same laws, we shall fully satisfy this Proposition by providing all the good passages that can be made in Compositions for two voices, from the unison to every other consonance, and from every consonance to the unison. Now, it is certain that everything done in two parts can, with even greater justification, be done in three or more parts, which are capable of greater liberties; hence it follows that not everything forbidden in two parts is forbidden in six or seven parts. However, because it would take too long to speak of all the permitted passages for four, five, and six, or any other number of parts, it suffices to explain what is good in two, as the model of the most precise <term>Counterpoint</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines.</note> one could desire. For this purpose, we shall begin with the Unison, from which one moves to the minor Third and to the other Consonances in the following manner. In this, the numbers between the notes are arranged such that the first signifies the Consonance one is leaving, and the second signifies the one to which one is moving. For example, the numeral 1 signifies the Unison, from which one first moves to the <term>minor Third</term>, represented by a 3' marked with an accent to distinguish it from the <term>Major Third</term>, which is marked with the same 3 without an accent. The same must be said of the two Sixths, which are marked 6' and 6. As for the Fourth, the Fifth, and the Octave, there is only one species of each, which is why we mark them as 4, 5, and 8.

It should also be observed that after one has moved from the Unison to the minor Third, one moves from the minor Third to the Unison, and likewise for the others, so that one may see both at once. Thus, when one sees two numbers with no others between them, they signify that all the examples they encompass, and which are between these two numbers, belong to the passages of the same consonance. Because there are only two examples for moving from the minor Third to the unison, 3' and 1 only govern two examples; this is easy to understand because the last example of each Consonance is marked by a <term>fermata</term><note>original: "point d'orgue"; a symbol indicating a pause or the end of a musical phrase.</note>. This being established, I place here the examples following the order and the numerical markings of which I have spoken. Anyone may place bars in their own copy to separate each passage from one consonance to the other, as I have done in mine (which I will freely lend for this purpose), and as has been done in the passages from the Unison and the minor Third to all the other Consonances.

### Examples of transitions from the Unison to all Consonances, and
### from these back to the Unison.

->From the Unison to the minor Third<-

<image-desc>A printed musical example containing two systems of notation, each with two staves (using four lines instead of the modern five). The notes are white mensural diamonds. Arabic numerals (3, 1, 5, 6, 8) and some prime marks (3') are printed above and below the staves to indicate the harmonic intervals or melodic movements between the voices. The music demonstrates transitions between unisons and thirds.</image-desc>

Now, one sees no transitions from the <term>Unison</term><note>Two voices singing or playing the exact same pitch.</note> to the major Sixth, because they are of no value <note>Meaning they are musically ineffective or prohibited in this style.</note>; as for the transition to the minor Sixth, the note that returns to the <term>Fifth</term><note>An interval spanning five notes of the scale, considered a "perfect" and very stable consonance.</note> resolves its harshness. This must be noted once and for all, so as to know why certain passages have three notes, whereas others have only two; this was done to show the <term>consonance</term><note>A harmonious-sounding interval between two notes.</note> that must precede or follow the transition in question. For example, the first transition from the <term>minor Third</term><note>A three-note interval that sounds "sad" or "soft" compared to the major third (e.g., D to F).</note> to the minor Third is followed by the Unison; the first from this Third to the Fourth is followed by the Fifth, and the following one from the Fourth to the Third is preceded by it, and so on for the others. Sometimes there are five notes, as in the second transition from a minor Third to the same minor Third, in order to show the proper sequence of Consonances; or four, as in the transition from the Fourth to the major Sixth, in the three following examples, and in several others.

Let us now see the examples of transitions from the minor Third to the other Consonances, and from them back to the said Third. They begin with two transitions from the minor Third to the same minor Third, for it is permitted to use two <term>imperfect consonances</term><note>Intervals like thirds and sixths; they are harmonious but considered less "stable" than the unison, fifth, or octave.</note> in a row, even if they are of the same kind; and then one moves to the major Third in three ways, and from the major to the minor in five ways, all of which are good and approved. For I include no bad or doubtful transitions, but only the good ones which can be used in <term>Duos</term><note>Musical pieces written for two voices or instruments.</note> of simple <term>Counterpoint</term><note>The art of combining different melodic lines so they sound harmonious together.</note>.

Afterward, one moves from the minor Third to the <term>Fourth</term><note>An interval spanning four notes of the scale.</note>, and vice-versa, in a single way; and then from the minor Third to the Fifth in four ways, and from the Fifth to the minor Third in six ways. The following examples move in three ways from the minor Third to the minor Sixth, and from this Sixth to the said Third in two ways; from which one moves to the major Sixth in three ways. Finally, one passes from this Third to the <term>Octave</term><note>The interval between a note and the next note of the same name higher or lower.</note> in three types, and in four ways for the reverse, as seen in the notes that follow.

### Examples of transitions from the minor Third to all other Consonances.

<image-desc>Six horizontal rows of musical notation. Each row contains two staves (upper and lower) with diamond-shaped (lozenge) notes and vertical bars separating short examples. Numerical annotations (e.g., 3', 4, 5, 6, 8) are placed above and between the staves to indicate musical intervals.</image-desc>

After having given the transitions from the <term>minor Third</term><note>An interval spanning three scale degrees, sounding "soft" or "sad."</note> to other chords, it is necessary to add those from the <term>major Third</term><note>A slightly wider three-note interval than the minor third, often described as sounding "bright."</note> to the same chords, without it being necessary to repeat those made to the minor Third, because they precede in the examples we have just given. It must only be noted that I did not wish to rank the quality of each example—namely as good, better, and very good—partly because Composers are not of the same opinion regarding this order and this preference for pleasantness and quality, and also to provide an opportunity for practice to those who wish to mark these degrees in their book, both by the judgment of the ear and by reason. And because one does not always have a <term>Singer</term><note>Original: *Chantre*. A professional singer available to demonstrate the music.</note> at one's command with whom one can test all these passages, the pipe organ or the <term>stringed organ</term><note>Original: *orgue à chordes*. This likely refers to keyboard instruments with strings, such as the harpsichord or clavichord, which the author previously discussed.</note> of which I have spoken will serve for this. One sees, then, in the Table which follows, four transitions from the major Third to the same major Third, then two to the <term>Fourth</term>, 3 to the <term>Fifth</term>, 3 to the <term>minor Sixth</term>, two to the <term>major Sixth</term>, and 5 to the <term>Octave</term>, and those which go backwards, or in the opposite direction, which may be called <note>original: "passages inuerses"</note> *inverse transitions*; both types are seen in the musical notes that follow.

### Examples of transitions from the major Third to other Consonances.

<image-desc>Musical notation printed across five systems of staves. The notation uses lozenge-shaped (diamond) notes. As for the examples of transitions from the <term>Fourth</term><note>An interval spanning four scale degrees.</note> to other <term>Consonances</term><note>Combinations of notes that sound stable and pleasant together.</note>, there are very few good ones; that is why I place them with those of the <term>Fifth</term> to other Consonances, to which I also add those of the two <term>Sixths</term><note>The intervals of the major and minor sixth.</note>, in order to complete this Proposition with the Table that follows. In this table, one sees first two transitions from the Fourth to the Fifth, and one from the Fifth to the Fourth. In the second place, one from the Fourth to the <term>minor Sixth</term>, and another inverted. In the third place, one from the Fourth to the <term>major Sixth</term>, and one inverted. In the fourth place, there is a transition from the Fifth to the <term>Semidiapente</term><note>A diminished fifth (an "imperfect" or dissonant fifth).</note>, which is <term>saved</term><note>Original: *sauué*. In music theory, this refers to "resolving" a dissonance into a more stable, consonant sound.</note> by the major Third that follows. In the fifth place, one sees a transition from the Fifth to the major Sixth, and one inverted; and three to the minor Sixth, and then two inversions. In the sixth place, one transitions in six ways from the Fifth to the <term>Octave</term>, and in five ways the other way around. In the seventh place, one sees two transitions from the Fifth to the minor Sixth. In the eighth place, from the minor Sixth one passes to the major in two ways, and vice-versa in three ways. In the ninth place, one transitions in three manners from the major Sixth to the major Sixth; and finally from the minor Sixth to the Octave in one way; from the major to the Octave in one way; and from the Octave to the major Sixth in one way.

I omit the transitions from the Fifth to the Fifth, and from the Octave to the Octave, both because they are of no value on the <term>Organ</term>, and because I have included them in the 21st Proposition of the 4th book on Composition, page 259, in the 3rd, 4th, and 5th examples. To which I add that those who wish to find which are the best transitions among several proposed ones may use the reasons we have provided from the eleventh Proposition of the same book through the 17th, and in the 8th and 9th Propositions. Additionally, the 10th contains all the other transitions from one consonance to another when they are made by <term>contrary motions</term><note>When two musical voices move in opposite directions to reach the next chord.</note>, for

Regarding transitions made through <term>similar motion</term><note>When two musical parts move in the same direction, both ascending or both descending.</note>, [the table] does not provide them, but it is easy to add them, as well as those made when only a single part moves. For example, the third transition from a minor Third to a major Third, which is made by similar motion, is marked by these numbers: 6, 5, 4. Here, the <term>Treble</term><note>Original: *Dessus*. The highest voice or part in a composition.</note> descends from 6 to 5, creating the minor Third, and the <term>Bass</term> descends from 5 to 4, creating the major Third. Thus, the Treble, having descended, finds itself at the same position from which the Bass began its descent; consequently, the similar motions of these two parts are very well explained by the preceding numbers. It is easy to reduce the similar motions of other transitions to numerical ratios.

As for transitions where one part <term>holds steady</term><note>Original: *tient ferme*. This refers to oblique motion, where one voice stays on the same note while the other moves.</note> while the other moves, they are just as easy to explain by numbers, like the ratios of simple <term>Consonances</term><note>Intervals that sound stable and harmonious.</note>. For example, when one wishes to express the first transition from a major Third to a Fifth, these three numbers—4, 5, 6—show that while the Bass holds steady on 4, the Treble moves from 5 to 6 to create a minor Third. When this is added to the major Third from 4 to 5, the Bass finds itself at the interval of a Fifth from the Treble. I wanted to point this out so that anyone can reduce all transitions of Consonances and <term>Dissonances</term> [to their mathematical ratios] without any difficulty.

The second transition of the second Table on page 234 of the fourth book on Consonances contains a transition from a major Third to a minor Third, in which only one part moves by a <term>minor semitone</term><note>The smaller of two types of semitones used in Renaissance and Baroque tuning, such as the move from C to C-sharp.</note>, as seen in the numbers 24, 25, and 30. Indeed, one only needs three numbers when one part holds steady. This is also shown in the third example of the fourth Table (12, 15, 16), in the third of the fourth, in the fifth and sixth of the sixth, and in the sixth of the seventh Table, to which one may add as many others as one desires. However, it suffices to add here the rest of the musical notation containing examples of the other approved transitions.

Now, it is not enough to read these examples unless one simultaneously considers the steps or intervals that each part makes from one <term>consonance</term><note>An interval that sounds stable and harmonious to the ear.</note> to the next, and the relationships the notes have with one another, along with the degrees of pleasingness found in each passage. This is done in order to derive the satisfaction and profit that can arise from <term>Harmony</term><note>The combination of different musical notes played or sung at the same time to produce a pleasing effect.</note>. This is so easy for those who have understood the numerical tables of passages which I explain in the fourth book on <term>Composition</term>, and the reasons for the pleasingness of chords in the book on Consonances, that there is no need to speak further of it. Furthermore, the practice of all these tables can be seen in the compositions for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 parts in the aforementioned fourth book. In these, one also sees passages of repeated Consonances, or of <term>replicas</term><note>Original: *repliques*. These are compound intervals, such as an octave plus a third, which function similarly to the simple interval.</note> of replicas, which follow the same laws as those of simple Consonances. As for the passages from simples to replicas, or the contrary, they cannot be made without intervals that are too large in one or both of the parts; that is why they are not in use. For the nature of Consonances is such that the pleasingness of their passages and their sequence depends on <term>conjunct degrees</term><note>Original: *degrez conjoints*. Movement by step (e.g., C to D) rather than by leap (e.g., C to G).</note>, which must be used as much as possible; or, if one uses larger intervals, one must only use those that are easy to sing.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*Explaining the <term>False Relations</term><note>Original: *faulſes Relations*. A perceived dissonance that occurs when a note in one part is followed by a chromatically altered version of that same note in another part.</note> for which some practitioners condemn the use.*<-

**P**roposition 8 and Proposition 21 on page 260 of the preceding book explain the forbidden false relations so clearly, and even other extraordinary relations, that I need only add a few remarks here. The first is that if one makes the <term>tones and semitones</term><note>The whole steps and half steps that make up a musical scale.</note> all equal—whether on instruments or with the voice—there is only a single false relation, that of the <term>Tritone</term><note>An interval consisting of three whole tones, often considered harsh or "restless."</note>, because it is then in no way distinct from the <term>False Fifth</term><note>Original: *faulſe Quinte*. Also known as a diminished fifth.</note>, as I have already remarked elsewhere. But if one observes the distinction between tones and semitones, it is certain that the two are different, and that the Triton exceeds the other by a <term>minor comma</term><note>Original: *comma mineur*. A very small musical interval resulting from the mathematical difference between two types of tuning.</note>, as I demonstrated in the 7th Proposition of the book on <term>Dissonances</term>. In that section, one must descend the notes of the Bass in the second example to <term>G-re</term> and <term>E-mi</term><note>Original: *Gre* and *Emi*. These are pitch names from the traditional solmization system; G-re refers to the note G, and E-mi refers to the note E.</note>, following the notice I give regarding printing errors at the end of the 7th book on Instruments, where page 217 was incorrectly placed for 127 at the beginning of page 75.

Now, the only reason they have for forbidding the false relation of the Tritone or the False Fifth consists solely in the fact that the ear feels struck and as if wounded by the relationship of the two notes, or sounds, that cause the Tritone.
