### Examples of False Relations of the Tritone.

<image-desc>A musical score printed on two staves (treble and bass clefs) showing eight short melodic progressions, labeled with Roman numerals I through VIII. Example I shows a cross-relation (tritone) between the re of the upper voice and the fa of the lower voice. Example III includes a decorative floral or star-shaped symbol between the voices.</image-desc>

Let us take the first example, which passes from the <term>Major Third</term><note>An interval spanning four semitones, considered a "sweet" but imperfect consonance.</note> to the <term>Fifth</term><note>A stable, perfect consonance spanning seven semitones.</note> by <term>contrary motion</term><note>When one musical part moves up while the other moves down.</note>. Let the two notes of the <term>Treble</term><note>The highest voice part; in the original French, "Dessus."</note> be *re, mi*, and the two of the Bass be *fa, mi*: I say that the *mi* of the Treble creates a <term>Tritone</term><note>An interval of three whole tones, famous for its harsh, dissonant sound; historically nicknamed "the devil in music."</note> with the *fa* of the Bass. The resonance of these two sounds remains in the imagination or in the ear when one plays the two *mi*s that form the Fifth; this Fifth does not have the power to erase the relationship of the Tritone, which is as harsh to the ear, in comparison to the Fifth, as pure black is to the eye when compared to the whiteness of snow. 

From this comes the reason why we do not follow the general rule here, which obliges one to pass from <term>imperfect consonances</term><note>Intervals like thirds and sixths that sound pleasant but require resolution.</note> to <term>perfect</term> ones by the closest steps—for example, from the Major Sixth to the Octave, and from the Minor Third to the Unison. One should not move from the Major Third to the Unison; rather, one would sooner pass to the Fifth from a Major Third than from a Minor Third, were it not for the encounter with this Tritone, which spoils everything. This is why, when the Tritone is not encountered—as seen in the three examples of the preceding Proposition that move from the Major Third to the Fifth—the passages are good.

Nevertheless, this relation is not so bad that it is not sometimes permitted, as I have shown in the same place in the fifth example moving from the Fifth to the Major Third, which is well-composed and allowed. Regarding this, one may remark that it is a rather marvelous accident to find the relation of a Tritone—which has already passed—more disagreeable than the Tritone itself, the use of which is permitted, as I have shown in the examples of <term>Dissonances</term>. 

This has led several to conjecture that one should not avoid this relation any more than those of the Second and the Seventh, which are very often encountered between the parts. They argue that this disagreement comes only from the preoccupied imagination of those who blame it, or from the fact that the Consonances one leaves, or those to which one passes, are not in their <term>harmonic justness</term><note>The mathematical purity of the musical tuning.</note> of numbers, because they are diminished or augmented by a <term>comma</term><note>A very small interval resulting from the difference between two slightly different ways of calculating a note's pitch.</note>. This is very easy to show, assuming one follows the system of the <term>Perfect Diatonic</term><note>A tuning system based on pure mathematical ratios (Just Intonation).</note>, which I explain in the *Book of Genres*; for when the intervals are perfect, one must conclude that the relation of the Tritone will not be bad, if this speculation is true. But it is very difficult to judge whether it will be disagreeable or not, because if the ears of all the great Masters do not agree, one cannot conclude which side should be followed. For even if there were a hundred who found this relation bad, and only two or three who judged it permissible and not bad, it may be that these few deserve to be followed in their opi-

### PROPOSITION VIII.

*To explain the Perfect, Imperfect, and Broken Cadences, which must be used in Musical Compositions, and what their types are.*

The Harmonic Cadence is the <term>modulation</term><note>The movement or progression of voices from one sound to another</note> of two or more parts by which the Song is finished. Because the end of a Composition must be perfect—in order to leave a particular contentment and an entire satisfaction to the ear and the mind—it must terminate with a <term>Unison</term><note>Two voices sounding the exact same pitch</note> or an <term>Octave</term> when it is a "perfect" cadence and does not proceed further, so that the listener can desire nothing sweeter, more agreeable, or more perfect. When the cadence is "imperfect," as happens in the middle or in other notable parts of the Song, it terminates with a <term>Fifth</term>, or with one of the <term>Thirds</term> or <term>Sixths</term>. 

Now, it is not necessary to explain the cadences of a part that sings all alone, because the <term>modal strings</term><note>The primary or "anchoring" notes that define the character of a specific musical mode</note>, or the principal notes of each mode which must serve for the Cadences of a simple Song, are so well marked in the 16th Proposition of the 3rd book of Genera <note>original: "3. liure des Genres"</note> that there is no need to speak of them further. 

The ordinary Cadence is made at the Unison or at the Octave between two parts of <term>simple counterpoint</term><note>A style where notes are set against notes of equal value, without complex rhythms or dissonances</note> when it is perfect. In such cases, the notes are of similar value and do not admit any dissonances; those are reserved for the Cadences of <term>figured counterpoint</term><note>A more elaborate style involving varied rhythms and decorative notes</note>, which uses <term>syncopations</term><note>Commonly known today as suspensions, where a note is held over from a previous beat to create a temporary clash (dissonance) before resolving to a pleasing sound</note>. By means of these, several dissonances are practiced which give a particular grace to the cadence. The cadence must be composed of at least three notes, although some believe that two are sufficient. But the examples that follow will make their use better understood than a longer discourse would. I say, therefore, that the following Cadences, which are made at the Unison and the Octave, are very agreeable and proper for ending Duos <note>Musical pieces for two voices or instruments</note> in simple counterpoint.

->Cadences at the Unison. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Cadences at the Octave.<-

<image-desc>A printed musical staff containing ten short examples of two-part cadences in white mensural notation. But when one finishes at the Unison, it is necessary that the second-to-last note of one of the parts forms a minor Third with the second-to-last note of the other, so that one rises or falls by a <term>semitone</term><note>The smallest interval in standard Western music</note> while the other moves by a whole tone to arrive at the Unison. The Imperfect Cadence is that which ends on the Fifth, and on the Thirds or Sixths, as I have already said; some call it *expectant* <note>original: "attendante"</note>, because one always waits for the perfect one to finish the Song. This is most often made in the Bass by the interval of a descending Fifth and an ascending Fourth, or vice versa, or by the interval of a Fourth and a Fifth which both descend; of which there is no need to give other examples than those in the pieces for 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 voices in the 4th book of Composition, and those for Instruments, in which one sees the proper Cadences for each part. ### PROPOSITION IX.

*Explaining Fugues and Counter-fugues, with their Leaders, the Consequences, Imitations, and Canons.*

Fugues can be created in so many ways that it would require an entire book to explain them all, particularly if one wished to include examples: but because I leave this long practice to good Composers, it suffices to explain in general what a *Fugue* is. It consists of two parts, the first of which is called the *Leader* <note>original: "Guide"</note>, because it precedes and shows the second part—which is named the *Follower* <note>original: "Consequence"</note>—by which steps and intervals it must sing. Because it mimics the first part, it is called *Imitation*, *Reply*, *Repetition*, *Echo*, etc. Now the follower usually begins to sing with a note that forms a Fifth <note>original: "Quinte"</note> or a Fourth <note>original: "Quarte"</note> with the first note of the Leader, in order to divide the Octave <note>original: "Diapason"</note> Harmonically or Arithmetically <note>A classic music theory distinction: a harmonic division of the octave places the fifth at the bottom, while an arithmetic division places the fourth at the bottom</note>, although the part that forms the Follower can begin at the Unison, or at the Third, etc., of the Leader, or at any other degree one wishes, whether consonant or dissonant. The Counter-fugue <note>original: "Contrefugue"; often referring to melodic inversion, where one voice goes up while the other goes down</note> occurs when one of the parts rises and the other descends by the same degrees. When the first note of the Follower is at the Fourth from the first note of the Leader, it is called a *Fugue at the Fourth* <note>original: "Fuga in Diatessaron"</note>, etc., which one sees clearly in the 3 examples that follow; of which the first distances the first note of the Reply by a Fourth; and the second distances it by a

->*Fugue at the Fourth. Fugue at the Fifth. Counter-fugue.*<-

Fifth; it is for this reason that it is named *Fugue at or toward the Fifth* <note>original: "Fuga in ou ad Diapente"</note>. Now these examples have a rest of a Minim <note>A half-note</note> in the Bass; and the Bass of the first, beginning on G <note>original: "Gut", referring to the note Gamma-Ut</note>, is distant by a Fourth from the C <note>original: "Cfa"</note> of the Treble: whereas the C <note>original: "C ut"</note> of the Bass of the second example is distant by a Fifth from the G <note>original: "Gsol"</note> of the Treble. As for the third example, it contains the Counter-fugue; and each of these examples contains a syncopation. There are still other Fugues that one calls *Double*, because when one part has imitated the Leader by starting at the Fifth, it then performs the Fugue at the Fourth, and the Bass and the Alto <note>original: "Haute-contre"</note> perform a thousand elegant figures, while the Tenor <note>original: "Taille"</note> and the Treble <note>original: "Dessus"</note> imitate each other; of which one can see examples in the 54th and 55th chapters of the 3rd book of Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most influential music theorist of the Renaissance</note>, and in the 14th book of Cerone <note>Pietro Cerone (1566–1625), an Italian theorist who wrote a massive treatise in Spanish</note>. # Book Five

begins to sing on the note where the Guide <note>The "Guide" or *dux* is the leading voice in a fugue or canon.</note> ends, and moves in the opposite direction, such as when it sings *la, sol, fa*, while the Guide sings *fa, sol, la.*

As for Canons, they can also be called Fugues; indeed, some practitioners do not wish to use the term *Canon*, which signifies nothing other than a *Rule* <note>original: "Regle"</note> among the Greeks. But because we do not concern ourselves with names, it suffices to say that this word is adopted to signify the arrangement of a number of notes serving 2, 3, or several voices, which sing the same notes in such a way that they create music with different parts, of which some begin earlier than others. This occurs when, after someone has sung *ut, re, mi, mi, re, mi, fa, fa, mi*; two others begin to sing the same notes in such a way that the first, who serves as the Guide to the other two, is singing the first *mi* when the second begins at the same time to sing *ut, re, mi, etc.* just like the first; nevertheless intoning the *ut* a fifth <term>Quinte: an interval of five scale degrees</term> higher than the first did. When the first is again on the first *fa*, the third begins to sing *ut, re, mi, etc.* intoning a fourth <term>Quarte: an interval of four scale degrees</term> higher than the first. This type of composition is called a *Canon* or *Fugue*; for the first part guides the others, as in Fugues, and the two others form the Consequences <note>The "Consequent" or *comes* is the following/imitating voice.</note> which imitate their *Guide*. Now, the following notes show more clearly what I have just said, and contain a Fugue composed by Mr. Coffin, one of the oldest and best disciples of du Caurroy <note>Eustache du Caurroy (1549–1609), a major French composer of the late Renaissance.</note>.

->Fugue in the Fifth and the Fourth.<-
<note>original Latin: "Fuga in Diapente & Diateffaron"</note>

->Three voices upon the six notes of Music. *For 3 voices.*<-

Where it must be noted that this character, *¶*, signifies the place where each part must begin the *ut, re, mi*, higher than the said *ut*, following the inscription <note>original: "superstition," here referring to the "riddle" or rule written above a canon</note> which serves as the key and understanding. Thus, if one wished to separate or set apart the three parts of this Fugue, it would be necessary to write the first as it is, and then one would have to place a whole-note rest <term>semibreue: a whole note</term> before the second, and three rests of three whole-notes before the 3rd part. And if there were a 4th, 5th, or 6th part, etc., one would have to place as many rests as the signs of repetition were distant from the first note of the first part.

I place here the example of a Fantasia <term>Fantaisie: a free-form musical composition</term> composed by Monsieur de la Charloniere, Counselor to the King and Honorary Provost Judge of Angoulême, so that those who love Harmony may consider the industry of his composition, and that they may find three parts upon the Tenor <term>Taille: the tenor voice or part</term> that he proposes, which sing in Canon or in Fugue, and which imitate even to their pause point <term>point d'Orgue: a fermata or sustained rest</term>, which the Spaniards call *Calderon* and the Italians *Corona*.

<term>Treble</term>, which was the last, enters first, and so with the others, following the

what shall be marked, and then one must re-enter according to the mark, or stop

parts have finished their Song: which is usually done at the finale. Now this
<term>Canon</term> is without two <term>Fourths</term> <note>A reference to avoiding certain dissonant intervals</note>, and without false relation: and to sing it
well one must have voices in good accord, who know how to give it the
grace and the air by advancing the measure a little, for if it were beaten heavily
and slowly, everything would be spoiled.

### PROPOSITION X.

->*To determine what must be observed to compose excellently for three and four parts.*<-

It seems that the perfection of <term>Harmony</term> consists in the number of four parts; for although there is always one that repeats one of the other three—that is, the <term>Octave</term> or the <term>Fifteenth</term>—nevertheless, this repetition gives a particular grace and charm to the composition. This must also be concluded for the fifth part and others that fill the music with chords. And because the <term>Bass</term> proceeds with slower movements, it is not ordinarily as <term>diminished</term> <note>Ornamented with fast, short notes</note> as the others, and often moves by intervals of <term>Thirds</term>, <term>Fourths</term>, <term>Fifths</term>, and <term>Octaves</term> to give room to the other parts, and particularly to the <term>Treble</term> <note>original: "Dessus"</note>, which should sing by <term>conjunct movements or steps</term> <note>Stepwise motion (e.g., C to D) rather than leaps</note> as much as possible. The <term>Tenor</term> <note>original: "Taille"</note> must particularly govern the <term>Mode</term> <note>The scale or tonal framework of the piece</note> and make the <term>cadences</term> in their proper places. The <term>Alto</term> <note>original: "Hautecontre"</note> should use very elegant passages to embellish the song or to delight the listeners. If the composition is for only three voices, one may leave out the Alto or the Treble; and if it is for eight, one must double each part, etc. Now, after having chosen the mode, one must begin with one of its regular <term>pitches</term> <note>original: "chordes"</note> as is customary...

to do in the <term>Tenor</term> <note>original: "Taille"; in this period, the Tenor was often the foundational melody or "cantus firmus" around which other voices were built</note>, to which one adds the <term>Treble</term> <note>original: "Dessus"; the highest vocal part, equivalent to the soprano</note>, and then the <term>Bass</term> <note>original: "Basse"</note>, and the <term>Alto</term> <note>original: "Hautecontre"; literally "high-against," the part written against the tenor, typically sung by high male voices</note>, although one can begin with whichever part one wishes, or compose them all together, according to each person's ability or will. <term>Zarlino</term> <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most influential music theorist of the Renaissance</note> has drawn up a universal Table for this subject in the 58th chapter, in which one sees first the <term>chords</term> <note>original: "accords"</note> that the Treble and the Tenor make together; and then by how much the Bass can descend below the said Tenor, in order to add the Alto which makes good harmonies upon the said Bass; but it should not meet at the <term>Unison</term> <note>When two parts sing the exact same pitch</note>, or at the <term>Octave</term> with the other parts, except in four places: namely, when the other parts make <term>Thirds</term>, <term>Sixths</term>, or the <term>Fifth</term>, and their <term>repetitions</term> <note>Intervals expanded by an octave, such as a Tenth (Third + Octave) or Twelfth (Fifth + Octave)</note>.

But all this can be better understood by the example of a <term>Trio</term> <note>A composition for three voices</note>: if the Treble is in Unison with the Tenor, it is necessary for the Bass to make a Third, Fifth, Sixth, Octave, or one of their <term>repliques</term> <note>repetitions/compound intervals</note> with the Tenor; and if the Treble makes a Third against the Tenor, the Bass will necessarily make a Third, Sixth, Octave, or Tenth below the said Tenor. The rest can be seen in the Table that follows.

## Table of chords that the four parts of Music can make.
### *Concerning the Unison.*

If the Treble is in Unison with the Tenor, the Bass will make a Third below the Tenor and the Alto a Fifth, or Sixth above the Bass.

But if the Bass is a Fifth below the Tenor, the Alto will be a Third, or a Tenth above the Bass.

Similarly, if the Bass makes a Sixth against the Tenor, the Alto could be a Third, or Tenth above the Bass.

If the Bass makes an Octave below the Tenor, the other parts could be a Third, 5th, 6th, 10th & 12th against the said Bass.

If it makes a 12th against the Tenor, the other parts could make the Third, 5th, 6th, 10th, 12th, or 13th against the said Bass.

In the same way, if the said Bass makes the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>original: "Quinziesme"; an interval of two octaves</note> against the Tenor, the other parts could make the Third, 5th, 6th, 10th, 12th & 13th against the Bass.

### *Concerning the Third.*

If the Treble makes the Third against the Tenor, the Bass will make the Third against the Tenor, and the Alto may make the Unison, or the Octave with the other parts.

If the Bass makes the Sixth against the Tenor, the Alto may make a Third or 10th against the Bass.

But if the Bass makes the Octave against the Tenor, the Alto will make the 5th or the 6th against the Bass.

Similarly, if the Bass makes the 10th against the Tenor, the other parts may make the Unison or the Octave.

### *Concerning the Fourth.*

When the Treble makes the Fourth against the Tenor, the Bass makes the Fifth against the said Tenor, and the Alto the 3rd or 10th against the Bass.

And when the Bass makes the 12th against the Tenor, the Alto makes the 10th against the Bass.

### *Concerning the Fifth.*

When the Treble makes the 5th against the Tenor, the Bass makes the Octave against it,

### *On the Sixth.*

If the <term>Treble</term> <note>original: "Dessus"</note> makes a Sixth against the Tenor, the Bass will make the <term>Fifth</term> against the Tenor, and the Alto will make the 1st [Unison] or the 8th [Octave] with the other parts.
If the Bass makes the Third against the Tenor, the Alto will make the 5th or the 12th <note>A 12th is a Fifth plus one Octave</note> against the Bass.
If the Bass makes the 10th against the Tenor, the Alto will also make the 5th or the 12th against the Bass.

### *On the Octave.*

If the Treble makes the Octave against the Tenor, and the Bass the 3rd, the other parts can make the 3rd, 5th, 6th, 10th, 12th, and 13th against the Bass.
Similarly, when it <note>The Treble</note> makes the Fifth against the Tenor, the other parts can make the Third.
And if the Bass makes the Octave against the Tenor, the other parts will make the 5th, 10th, and 13th against the Bass.
Finally, if the Bass makes the 12th against the Tenor, the parts will make the 10th or 17th against the Bass.

By this, it is easy to conclude what the Alto can do when the Treble makes one <term>Consonance</term> <note>A stable, pleasant-sounding interval</note> with the Tenor, and the Bass another. Now, although the Tenor immediately follows the Bass, and the Alto follows the Tenor, and the Treble is the highest, nevertheless the Composer can sometimes make the Bass rise above the Tenor, and likewise for the others, as we have seen in the examples of simple <term>Counterpoint</term> in the 4th book. But one of the most necessary things in every part of the Composition, and particularly in the <term>Cadences</term> <note>The concluding phrases or "musical punctuation" of a section</note>, consists in always making the Fifth and the <term>Major Third</term> heard, or their <term>repetitions</term> <note>Intervals expanded by an octave</note>: although one must never make the Fifth when one makes the Sixth, for fear of making a <term>Second</term> <note>A dissonant interval</note>, or its repetitions: nonetheless, one cannot always easily make these consonances heard in <term>Trios</term>, which is why one can sometimes dispense with them by making the Octave instead; although this is not permitted for four or more parts, except when the Sixth is put in place of the Fifth, for it is then necessary to make the Unison or the Octave and its repetitions. And if one wishes to have a <term>Harmony</term> where nothing is lacking, the lowest Octave must not be divided, nor the first Fifth grafted upon said Octave, for one must still add the <term>Fourth</term> to divide the 2nd Octave, before concluding by what we demonstrated in the first book of Consonances from the 35th to the 40th Proposition, and in the 5th book of Instruments when speaking of the tones of the <term>Trumpet</term> <note>Natural trumpets of this era could only play the notes of the harmonic series, which dictates these specific interval spacings</note>.

Beyond all the above, after having well considered the <term>text</term> <note>original: "la lettre"; the lyrics or words of the song</note> that one wishes to use, and chosen the <term>Mode</term> <note>The scale or "key" of the piece</note> proper to express it, the Tenor—or the part that particularly makes the Subject heard and which maintains the Mode—must make the cadences quite appropriately, following what the perfection of the discourse and the end of its sentences require; and it must proceed so regularly and so agreeably that it may be judged as the foundation or the soul of the entire harmony, so that if it touches the strings of an <term>Authentic Mode</term> <note>A mode where the melody ranges primarily between the keynote and its octave above</note>, the Bass...

Secondly, the **Tenor** <note>original: "Taille"</note> should not be further than a **Fourth** or a **Fifth**, or at most a **Sixth**, from the **Bass**; and the **Treble** <note>original: "Deſſus"</note> usually no more than an **Octave** from the Tenor. This is so that the **Alto** <note>original: "Hautecontre"</note> finds the space for its melody between these two parts in the plagal mode, like the Bass, while the Treble sings in the Authentic (or natural) mode, like the Tenor. Or, conversely, if the Bass and Treble touch the notes of the natural mode, the other two parts should touch those of its collateral [plagal] mode, so that the Treble has the same proportion to the Alto as the Tenor has to the Bass.

Thirdly, the Tenor or the Alto should not extend beyond their Octaves, or perhaps by only one or two notes when it facilitates the composition. This should be permitted even less for the Bass and the Treble, whose greatest range should only be a **Nineteenth** or at most a **Twentieth** <note>This describes a range of nearly three octaves, the limit of most human voices</note>, because voices do not have more reach than that. However, regarding instrumental music, one can give it as much range as the necks [of lutes] and keyboards allow. The practical use of this range, and everything we have said in this Proposition, can be found in the examples of Book 4, where one sees how different <term>Clefs</term> <note>The symbols at the start of a musical staff</note> are separated from one another by a Fourth or a Fifth to give range to each part. And when no Treble is used, and one places two or three Tenors with only a Bass, one should sing with equal voices.

Fourthly, the harmony and the movement must correspond so closely to the lyrics and the discourse that the listener judges them to be a single body, as if nature itself had created the composition. For this purpose, one must use the **Fourth**, and **Major Thirds and Sixths**, and many whole tones to express rigor, harshness, bitterness, and anger; and use semitones, and **Minor Thirds and Sixths** to signify laments, grief, and sighs. For this reason, one will use the Modes that have their semitones furthest from their beginning, such as the 7th mode (starting on <term>F-ut</term> <note>The note F</note>) or the 1st mode (starting on <term>C-ut</term> <note>The note C</note>), to express the first [harsh] passions. Use those that have their semitones at the beginning or in the second place of their Fifths and Fourths to explain the second [sad] passions. Accidental notes created by means of the <term>flat</term> <note>original: "bmol"</note> and the <term>sharp</term> <note>original: "dieſis"</note> also serve this purpose, for they are less vigorous and more languishing than the modal or natural notes of each mode.

As for the different movements, and the tempos and measures to be used for each subject, I speak of this very fully in the 6th book which follows.

Fifthly, one must not use <term>minim</term> or <term>crotchet</term> <note>original: "ſemi-minime"</note> rests except in places where the discourse has commas or colons; and at the end of sentences <note>original: "periodes"</note>, one can use rests of whatever duration one wishes. Otherwise, he who places rests inappropriately is like an Orator who would stop to rest in the middle of a word, or before the meaning of his speech was finished.

Sixthly, one must place each note under each syllable in such a way that no <term>barbarism</term> <note>In music, a barbarism is a mistake in prosody, such as putting a long note on a syllable that should be short and spoken quickly</note> is ever committed. This consists of lengthening a short syllable or making a long one short, which makes the Composer look ridiculous and makes him pass for an ignorant or ill-advised person—though one can sometimes put two or several notes under one syllable, when...

### PROPOSITION XI.

->*Explaining the manner of regulating, marking, holding, or beating the musical measure, which the Spanish call Compas.*<-

The beating of the measure, which Saint Augustine and the other ancient Latins call *Plausus* <note>original: "Plausus" – literally "clapping" or "beating time"</note>, is nothing other than the lowering and raising of the hand, which signify the time that must be given to each note: for example, the <term>semibreve</term> <note>the equivalent of a modern whole note</note> ordinarily lasts one raising and one lowering of the hand, which one can also do with the foot, or in any other manner one wishes; and the minim, which is ordinarily called the "white note," lasts one raising or one lowering, and the "black note" <note>the crotchet or quarter note</note> lasts half of a raising or a lowering, because one always makes four of them to the measure, which is composed of the raising and the lowering. These are equal in binary measure <note>two-beat time</note>; but the lowering or striking is double the raising in ternary measure <note>three-beat time</note>, in which one sings two white notes while striking [down] and only one while raising [up]: and for this reason, one places the number 3, either alone or with a 2 underneath it, at the beginning of the staves and lines when one sings in ternary measure, and the "C" with a stroke through it <note>the "cut-C" or 𝇼 symbol</note>, or without a stroke, when it is binary, or equal; or indeed, one places no sign there at all so that the measure may be free. It seems to me it would suffice to place the number 2 at the beginning, or in any other place one wishes, before notes that must be sung in binary measure, just as we are satisfied with the number 3 to mark ternary, so as to remove the multitude of signs and facilitate the practice of Music.

As for what concerns the different signs of the modes, and perfect and imperfect times, and of <term>Prolation</term> <note>the relationship between the values of semibreves and minims</note> both perfect and imperfect, I treat these very amply in the 30th Proposition of the following 6th book, which is particularly dedicated to musical time, and in which one finds everything one might desire here. Now, it must be noted that the measure is one of the principal parts, and one of the most necessary to Music, whether one sings in

### PROPOSITION XII.

->*Explaining everything pertaining to the Modes and the Tones of the Greeks and the Moderns.*<-

I have treated the Theory of Modes quite extensively from the 16th Proposition of the 3rd book until the end, and elsewhere; therefore, I add here only what concerns Practice, after noting that the number 6 in the 18th Proposition of the said book must be corrected, on page 188, line 5. It is stated there that the first mode has its second semitone at the 6th place, for it actually has it at the 7th or last interval of its octave. This was not marked in the list of errors for this book, which are at the end of the 7th book on *Instruments*, and which must be corrected before reading our books, as well as the other errors of the other Treatises found in the Prefaces or at the end of the books. 

Now, I have explained the <term>Cadences</term> <note>the concluding melodic or harmonic formulas that define a musical key or mode</note> and the manner of distinguishing the Modes from one another so clearly—as well as knowing which have more or less sympathy with one another—in the 3rd book, that I do not believe I should add more. This is true even if one follows the opinion of Mr. Doni <note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), an Italian music theorist known for his studies of ancient Greek music</note>, of whom I spoke in the 30th Proposition of the 7th book on *Instruments*. The Tones and Modes of the Greeks are very different from the modern ones, for he begins the Dorian tone—invented by Thamiris the Thracian—on <term>E-la-mi</term> <note>The note E in the medieval solmization system</note>. 

Consequently, if the Phrygian, invented by Marsyas the Phrygian, begins one tone higher, it will begin on the sharp accidental of <term>F-ut</term> <note>F-sharp</note>; and if the Lydian, invented by Amphion, by Olympus, or by Melanippides, begins yet another tone higher than the Phrygian, it will be on the sharp accidental of <term>G-re-sol</term> <note>G-sharp</note>, assuming one wishes to use our Harmonic Scale. Consequently, the Mixolydian, invented by Sappho the Lesbian, will begin a semitone higher, namely in <term>A-mi-la</term> <note>The note A</note>. 

And because the <term>plagal</term> <note>modes that sit a fourth lower than their "authentic" counterparts while sharing the same final note</note> tones descend a fourth below their Authentics, the Hypo-Dorian, invented by Philoxenus, will begin on <term>B-mi</term> <note>The note B-natural</note>, the Hypo-Phrygian on the sharp accidental of <term>C-ut</term> <note>C-sharp</note>, the Hypo-Lydian, invented by Polymnestus of Colophon, on that of <term>D-re</term> <note>D-sharp</note>, and the Hypo-Mixolydian on the <term>E-mi</term> of the Dorian. I do not wish to make a more curious inquiry into this, because one may await the treatises he has prepared on this subject, for which he gives the Titles in the 15th Chapter of his compendium on Tones and Modes. There, he promises to restore ancient Music and to show the use of Harmony, both vocal and instrumental, for the theaters; for the ancients used it in Tragedies, Satires, Comedies, and Dithyrambs; and by...

# Book Five

because they adapted gestures, dances, and all sorts of bodily movements to the different passions described in the verses, it is possible that their <term>tones</term><note>The author uses "tones" (French: *tons*) to refer to what we now call musical modes or scales, such as the Dorian or Phrygian.</note> had much more power over listeners than those of the moderns. We are weakened by the multitude of parts <note>The "multitude of parts" refers to polyphony, where many different melodies are sung at once.</note> used in compositions today, for one part hinders the effect of the other through its different movements and degrees of high and low pitch. From this, it happens that the <term>text</term><note>original: "la lettre"</note>—which the ancients considered the most important part—is almost never understood. Consequently, it has no power to impress its passions and affections during ordinary concerts, which have no greater effect than to tickle and please the ear. In contrast, the ancient tones served to excite or calm the passions, if the ancient Greek and Latin authors are to be believed.

Whatever the case may be, we can establish these tones just as well as they did, since we can begin them one higher than the other, following the "strings" of the system of each genre. We can even give the range of the entire system to each tone, since one can take fifteen notes ascending from any place in the system one wishes, whether using only the **Diatonic**, the **Chromatic**, or the **Enharmonic** genres in all the variety of their species. This is clearly seen in the arrangement of our ordinary <term>Modes</term><note>A "mode" is a specific type of scale, like a major or minor scale, but with more variety in the arrangement of steps.</note>. The first of these, or the **Dorian**, begins on <term>C-ut</term><note>The note C in the old system of solmization (C-D-E-F-G-A).</note>, as I said in the third book, and has its cadences on <term>E-mi, G-sol, and C-sol-ut-fa</term><note>The notes E, G, and C.</note>. The second begins one tone higher on <term>D-re</term><note>The note D.</note>, just as the **Phrygian** tone does in relation to the **Dorian** according to all opinions (though Glarean <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563) was a famous Swiss music theorist who redefined the system of musical modes.</note> begins the Dorian there). This mode has its principal notes on <term>F-fa, A-la, and D-sol</term><note>The notes F, A, and D.</note>.

Here it should be noted that **Mr. Doni** <note>Giambattista Doni (1594–1647) was an Italian scholar who tried to revive ancient Greek music and instruments.</note> maintains that the middle note of the **Dorian** tone (and the other <term>Authentic</term><note>Authentic modes are those where the melody typically stays between the lowest note of the scale and the note an octave above it.</note> modes) is not at the **Fifth** as is usually placed, but at the **Fourth**; we must await the proofs for this in his great treatises.

I say, however, that if the difference between tones depends solely on being high or low—that is, on their different place in the system—it would seem that one man could not use all the tones. For suppose the **Dorian** tone begins with a sound made of 40 beats of air <note>An early scientific attempt to describe frequency or vibrations.</note>, the **Phrygian** by 45, and the **Lydian** by 50; a man whose deepest voice only descends to 50 would be unable to use the first two tones. In reality, all sorts of voices, whether low or high, can use all the tones or ordinary modes of our practitioners, because they do not require one to start at a fixed degree of high or low pitch.

Furthermore, if the start of each tone depended on the reach, range, and convenience of the singing voices, I say that one person's **Dorian** would be another's **Phrygian** or **Lydian**. For example, someone who can sing a **Fourth** lower would begin their **Dorian** a **Fourth** lower than the other. Consequently, the tones would be confused, and nothing would be certain in this matter if we did not have recourse to the different placements of the <term>semitones</term><note>The smallest interval in standard Western music, like the distance between a white key and a black key on a piano.</note>. It is these semitones that constitute our various types of octaves and tones, and they are the only things that should be considered, without regard for how high or low the voice is. This is what would happen if three men sang the three principal tones, arranged as in the 7th chapter of Mr. Doni's book, following the **synton tetrachord of Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD) was a Greek mathematician and music theorist; a tetrachord is a four-note scale segment.</note>, to which he prefers that of **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Musician (1st century BC) was another influential Greek music theorist.</note>. I explain this in the following table, so that one may see the same arrangement of tones that he uses on page 41 of his book.

# Of Composition.

### Comparison of Musical Modes and Their Intervals

->**Lydian Mode** (Built on **C**)<note>The text uses "Cut," "Dre," "Emi," and "Ffa," which are the solmization syllables (C, D, E, F) used in the 17th century.</note><-
*Major Tone* to **D** | *Minor Tone* to **E** | *Major Semitone* to **F**

->**Phrygian Mode** (Built on **D**)<-
*Minor Tone* to **E** | *Major Semitone* to **F** | *Major Tone* to **G**

->**Dorian Mode** (Built on **E**)<-
*Major Semitone* to **F** | *Major Tone* to **G** | *Minor Tone* to **A** | *Major Tone* to **B**

For if the person singing in the **Dorian mode** has a pitch one tone higher than the person singing the **Phrygian**, and the third person singing the **Lydian** has their pitch in unison with the second—so that all three begin, one on their first string **E**, and the other two on their **D** and **C**—by singing in unison, these modes will not differ at all in their beginning or their end regarding high and low pitch. Instead, they will differ only in the order of their degrees—that is to say, their semitones and their major or minor tones. Now, it is so easy to see that by maintaining the difference in pitch within these modes, the **D** of the Phrygian corresponds to the chromatic **F-sharp** of the Dorian (which practitioners call the "accidental" <note>original: "feinte"</note> of **F**), that it is not necessary to speak of it further; for the mere sight of the simple keyboards of the **Spinet** <note>A spinet is a small, plucked keyboard instrument similar to a harpsichord.</note> shows all of this. 

And if one wishes to follow the precision of mathematical ratios, those of the aforementioned keyboards placed in the 5th Proposition of the 3rd book, and in the 22nd of the 6th book on Organs—or if those do not suffice, the two others from the same place, or the two from the 23rd Proposition—will satisfy the most demanding. Finally, if one divides the **Octave** into 24 equal quarter-tones <term>dieses</term><note>A "diesis" here refers to a quarter-tone interval used to divide the scale more finely than standard semitones.</note> by means of the 23 mean proportionals from the 7th Proposition of the 2nd book on Instruments, the Spinet or Organ divided in this fashion will provide the modes of every **Genre** in every way one might imagine them in practice; unless one prefers to be satisfied with the very exact division of the **Diapason** <note>In this context, "diapason" refers to the range of an octave.</note> from the 4th and 5th Propositions of the 3rd book on Genres.

Regarding vocal slides, runs, diminutions, trills, accents, and all that the Italians include under their *Trilli* (trills), *Gruppi* (turns or shakes), and *Strascini* (slurs), by which some believe the Genres or modes were distinguished from one another: these can be performed in all types of modes and tones. However, they say that runs <note>original: "passages"</note> are most suited for the **Diatonic**, trills for the **Enharmonic**, and accents for the **Chromatic**. To these one can add other vocal slides or runs, by which they would descend by three quarter-tones and ascend by five, whether in sequence or by interval—that is to say, the *eklysis* <note>original: "$\acute{\epsilon}\kappa\lambda\upsilon\sigma\iota\varsigma$", an ancient Greek term for lowering a pitch.</note> and the *ekbole* <note>original: "$\acute{\epsilon}\kappa\beta o\lambda\dot{\eta}$", an ancient Greek term for raising a pitch.</note> of the Greeks, along with their *agoge* (melodic motion), *ploke* (interweaving), *petteia* (compositional selection) <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\gamma\omega\gamma\dot{\eta}, \pi\lambda o\k\dot{\eta}, \pi\epsilon\tau\tau\epsilon\acute{\iota}\alpha$".</note>, and everything seen in the music attributed to **Euclid**, of which I have included the translation in the 17th Theorem of the first book of the *Universal Harmony*, along with that of **Bacchius**. But I do not know who will be able to—

# Book Five

...to show how the Greeks put all this into practice; for although we know the meaning of the vocal intervals called *straight* <note>original Greek: εὐθεῖα (eutheia); referring to a direct ascending or descending melodic line</note>, *inflection* <note>original Greek: ἀνάκαμψιν (anakampsin); referring to a melodic line that turns back on itself</note>, and *circular* <note>original Greek: περιφερὴς (peripheres); referring to a rounded or circumflex melodic shape</note>, and of other terms, it does not follow that we know the manner in which they carried their voices while singing what they meant by these words.

Those who wish to establish the difference between tones by semitones or other degrees will find satisfaction in the 8th Proposition of the 2nd book of *Instruments*, which contains all the divisions the Greeks made of the **Tetrachord** <note>The basic building block of Greek scales, consisting of four notes spanning a perfect fourth.</note>, and in the 2nd and 3rd Propositions of the 2nd book of *Dissonances*, where one sees eight kinds of semitones that can be practiced in our **Music**.

Now, whether we have neglected the true tones of the ancients and spoiled their melody and progression by taking too much care to find the way to assemble 2, 3, or several parts together—creating **Harmony** and **Concerts** which no longer have power over the passions, because what one part might do through its quick, light, and high-pitched movement, another undoes by its heavy, low, and slow movement—or whether we have made the said tones more perfect, and have laudably enriched and ennobled the ancient music (which was too poor) by the assembly of several voices that let the sweetness of consonances be felt through the mixture of dissonances; I leave that investigation to those who work on the restoration or restitution of Greek melody. 

I finish this book with the consideration of our **Modes**, of which each has the span of 2, 3, or four **Octaves**; it seems to me that they contain all the others. This does not prevent us from distinguishing them as first, second, etc., in the usual way: for example, the first, which is placed from **C** to **c**, represents the sound of the trumpet and is suitable for **Dances** and **Ballets**. However, there is no Mode that cannot be used for all sorts of subjects, since the different timings and movements contribute as much or more than the melody to joy, sadness, and other passions of the soul. Thus, the saddest tone can be made gayer than the most joyful Mode if one uses very light movements in the former and very heavy, mournful ones in the latter. From this, the Greeks called movement *male* and melody *female*. 

But I do not need to dwell on the other modes, lest I repeat the 29th Theorem of the first book of the treatise on *Universal Harmony* printed in the year 1627; the 13th and 14th articles of the 57th question on **Genesis** <note>Mersenne published a massive commentary on the Book of Genesis in 1623, which included extensive digressions on music.</note>; and everything I have said from the 15th Proposition to the end of the 3rd book of *Genres*. Furthermore, the 12 Duos of the first Proposition of this book show so clearly everything belonging to the 12 **Modes** and their cadences that it is impossible to consider them closely without becoming an expert in this matter. To this may be added all the examples from the preceding 4th book, those from all the books on *Instruments*, and those of the 13th article mentioned above, in which one sees the manner of singing all sorts of Latin and French metrical verses, for three, four, and five parts. Thus, the book that follows can be related to that article and to the 6th, 7th, and 8th, and particularly the 4th part of **Rhythmics**, which shows the properties of **metrical feet** and verses.

Now, before finishing this book, it must first be noted that we have in our music everything that belongs to the tones and modes of the Greeks, in whatever way one takes them, for they differ only...

# Of Composition.

As for the treble, and given that they all begin in the **Proslambanomene** <note>original: "Proslambanomene"; the lowest note of the ancient Greek musical system, equivalent to A</note>, or **A-re** <note>The lowest note in the medieval Guidonian scale.</note>, so that the **Hypodorian** <note>One of the ancient Greek modes or "keys" of music.</note>, which begins the lowest of all, has the fifteen strings of the entire system—as seen in the first Proposition of the 3rd book on Genera—and that the **Hypophrygian** begins only a semitone higher by ascending through the same system, and so on for the others, following the opinion of the **Aristoxenians** <note>Followers of the philosopher Aristoxenus, who believed musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than strict mathematical ratios.</note>, who established 13 different tones because they divided the **Diapason** <note>The interval of an octave.</note> into 13 semitones, as is still done now on the keyboards of the **Organ**, it is certain that we have the same privilege of beginning our **Ut** <note>The first note of the musical scale (modern "Do"). The text uses "Gut" or "Cut," likely variants of Gamma-Ut or Ut.</note>, or C, a semitone higher, and then another semitone, etc. And if one uses only the 7 tones of those who are satisfied with that number, such as **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician who wrote extensively on music theory.</note>, whose tones I explained in the 17th Proposition of the same book, and even if they are different not only in pitch but also in the order of their degrees or intervals—as are the 7 species of Octave explained in the 15th Proposition of the 3rd book—we have the perfect use of them in the **Diatonic Genus** <note>The standard musical scale consisting of whole tones and semitones.</note>, without it mattering much to know whether it is better to begin the **Dorian** in **Ut**, **Re**, and **Mi**, since the power of the tones depends not on their names, but on their effect.

In the second place, it must be noted that Ptolemy distinguishes the tones by the middle voice and by the last in the 15th chapter of his 2nd book, and that he takes each middle voice for the one that forms a **Fourth** with the first voice of the tone; because the highest voice being similar to the lowest of the Octave, one takes only 7 voices, so that the 4th is in the middle. I leave aside several other things, which will be seen in the 16th and 17th Propositions of the 3rd book.

In the third place, if the reader encounters anything pleasant and true in this book and in the others, I desire that he give thanks only to the Father and Author of all Truth, in which our happiness and the felicity of all the Saints consists, as Saint Augustine teaches in the 23rd chapter of the 10th book of his *Confessions*: **"Indeed, the blessed life is joy in the truth."** <note>original Latin: "Beata quippe vita est gaudium de veritate."</note> But because there is no truth that appears so evident to us in this world that one cannot encounter much difficulty and obscurity in it—as those know who have examined the principles, and who are forced to confess that all things are incomprehensible to them—one must have patience and voluntarily submit to divine providence, until it pleases Him to let us enjoy the clarity that the Angels possess in the vision of God, as the same Saint remarks in the 15th chapter of the 13th book: **"For they always see Your face, and there they read without the syllables of time what Your eternal will desires: they read, they choose, and they love; they read always, and what they read never passes away. For by choosing and loving, they read the very immutability of Your counsel. Their book is not closed, nor is their scroll folded, because You Yourself are this to them, and You are forever."** <note>original Latin: "Vident enim faciem tuam semper, & ibi legunt sine syllabis temporum, quid velit æterna voluntas tua: legunt, eligunt, & diligunt: semper legunt, & nunquam præterit quod legunt. Eligendo enim & diligendo legunt ipsam incommutabilitatem consilij tui. Non clauditur codex eorum, nec plicabitur liber illorum, quia tuipse illis hoc es, & es in æternum."</note>

->*Notice regarding violent movements.*<-

It must be noted, in favor of the eleventh Proposition of the 2nd book on Movements, that it is impossible for heavy bodies to descend toward the center of the earth according to a line divided in mean and extreme ratio <term>Mean and extreme ratio: Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio. Mersenne is critiquing the idea that falling objects accelerate according to a Fibonacci-like sequence (3, 5, 8, 13...).</term>, because it would follow that they would descend there within a half-minute of an hour, as you can conclude by assuming what is certain: namely, that their fall is three feet in the first half-second of time, and that three is the first term of the said line, just as five is the second, eight is the third, and so on, following the 5th column of the Table seen in the aforementioned Proposition. For if one continues the numbers of the proportionally divided line, the thirty-fourth [term], which shows the fall occurring in the 34th half-second, is 23,859,617, which represents the number of feet of that fall; this is greater than the number of feet in the semi-diameter of the earth, which is only about 17,175,000—that is, 1,145 leagues, each of which is 15,000 Royal feet <term>Royal feet: The *pied du roi*, a French unit of length equal to approximately 32.5 cm, slightly longer than the English foot.</term>. Thus, if the fall lasted one minute, and followed the proportion of the continuous sections of that line, heavy bodies would travel more than seventy thousand times the semi-diameter of the earth in the sixtieth or last half-second; that is to say, they would travel further than the distance from here to the stars, whatever distance Copernicus <note>Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543), whose heliocentric model greatly expanded the perceived size of the universe.</note> gives them. Furthermore, one cannot make this fall follow the segments of this line without falling into absurdities, because if one supposes the first space of the fall to be three feet and the second five, and these two numbers are joined to make the first, the weight will descend eight feet in this first interval; but the following spaces or numbers will no longer correspond to the phenomena of experience, and will always maintain a different proportion in their speeds, depending on the numbers that begin the progression. This is why one must rather follow the squared ratio of the times <note>Mersenne is correctly identifying the law of falling bodies (distance is proportional to the square of time), a principle also championed by Galileo.</note> to find this speed, when using bodies heavy enough and dropping them from our heights or—

# Book Five

<margin>193</margin>
...extraordinary, for light bodies, such as elderberry pith (which is 193 times lighter than lead) and other similar materials, seem to quickly find a certain place, or point, where they begin to descend at a steady rate. This is observed in their total fall, the beginning of which is almost equal to that of heavier bodies; however, the heavier bodies precede the light ones quite noticeably from the first or second toise <note>A toise is an old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or about 6.4 feet.</note> of their fall. From this, one can conclude with reasonable probability that in the fall of bodies made of lead, gold, etc., from here to the center of the earth, a point of equality <note>Mersenne is describing what we now call terminal velocity—the point where air resistance balances gravity and acceleration stops—though he considers it in the context of falling toward the Earth's center.</note> would be met, even though it may be impossible for us to determine it. This is the first thing of which I wanted to warn you, so that you may know that the progression of this proportionally cut line <note>original: "ligne coupée proportionnellement"; referring to a geometric model used to calculate acceleration.</note> goes too fast by the sixth half-second, in which the lead ball only travels 33 feet, and not 34 according to the sections of the said line. This line moves further and further away from the truth, which is also contrary to those who imagined that heavy bodies would take twelve minutes to fall from the surface to the center; an hour and a half to fall from the Moon; and 24 hours to fall from the Sun; for this is repugnant to experiments, and I do not know upon what foundations they can support such a proposition. I add only that there is no agreement on the cause that makes pieces [of metal], or other bodies that we call *heavy*, descend toward the center of the earth, even though the proportion of speed depends upon it. For some estimate that the desire to reunite with their whole <note>An Aristotelian view that elements (like earth) naturally seek to return to their place of origin.</note> makes them descend; others say that the spirits of the bodies push them down toward the center, and that the magnetic virtue <term>magnetic virtue: The 17th-century hypothesis that the Earth acts as a giant magnet, physically pulling objects toward itself.</term> of the earth attracts them. Be that as it may, experience has always shown me that the movement of bodies heavy enough to split the air without difficulty increases in a ratio of the square of the times of their falls <note>original: "raison doublée des temps"; Mersenne is confirming the Galilean law of falling bodies, where distance is proportional to the square of elapsed time ($d \propto t^2$).</note>.

The second thing consists of the violent movements <note>In early physics, "violent movement" refers to motion caused by an external force (like a shot or a throw), as opposed to "natural movement" caused by gravity.</note> of heavy bodies, of which I spoke on pages 222 and 225 of the 3rd book on Movements, and in Propositions 6 and 8 of *The Utility of Harmony*, and elsewhere. These movements are faster at the beginning of their violence than at the end of their natural fall, since experience shows that arrows travel so fast when leaving the bow that they can hardly be perceived, whereas they are seen very easily when they fall back to the ground. Furthermore, they have almost no effect when falling compared to the effect they have when shot with a bow. Likewise, an arquebus ball <note>A ball fired from an early type of portable long gun.</note> that takes twelve seconds to fall back down, when it has been fired perpendicularly upward, only travels 70 1/2 toises in the last 3 seconds of its fall, whereas it travels one hundred toises in the first three half-seconds of its violent movement. From this, it follows that violent movements do not decrease their speed in the same ratio as natural movements increase it; this is why it is necessary to correct what I said to the contrary in the places cited above or elsewhere. Let us now see what pertains to the Method and the Art of Singing well, to Accentual Music, and to Rhythmics, so as not to omit any part of Harmony.

# BOOK SIX
## ON THE ART OF SINGING
### WELL.

*It is not enough to have treated the movements, sounds, consonances, dissonances, systems, genres, modes, composition, the voice, and songs, if one does not know the manner and method of singing all kinds of Music well; this is why I am adding this book, which I divide into four parts. The first explains two very easy methods for teaching plainchant <note>original: "plain chant"; the monophonic, unison liturgical music of the Church.</note> and music to children and to all kinds of people, without using the ordinary nuances <note>original: "nuances ordinaires"; this refers to the complex system of "mutations" or hexachord changes used in traditional medieval and Renaissance music pedagogy, which Mersenne sought to simplify.</note>, which embarrass the mind more than they help it. The second teaches how one must perform all kinds of diminutions <term>diminutions: the technique of decorating a melody by breaking a long note into many shorter, faster notes.</term> to embellish the songs; the third shows what Accentual Music <term>Accentual Music: music that focuses on the rhetorical inflection and emotional "accents" of the text, much like the early Baroque recitative.</term> is; and the fourth explains what consists of Rhythmic Music <term>Rhythmic Music: the study of musical meter and time, which dictates the movement of Airs and dances.</term>, upon which all the movements of Airs and dances depend.*

*Now, this book is the most important and the most difficult of all, because its precepts cannot be put into practice without a good voice, which must be assumed to exist; but because a voice is not enough on its own if it does not learn to guide itself through all kinds of movements, steps, and intervals, I explain in this book how it must carry itself in laments, in diminutions, and in accents, and how it must execute everything that can fall under the imagination. I begin, therefore, with a very easy method, which Monsieur Desargues <note>Girard Desargues (1591–1661) was a brilliant French mathematician and architect, known as one of the founders of projective geometry. Mersenne frequently collaborated with the leading scientists of his day.</note>, an excellent Geometer, has arranged in terms that he recognized as suitable for instilling it into the minds of children, and for making them understand it in a short time with great ease. This is why I did not want to change them; his method serves as the subject for the first proposition, just as another very easy method for learning to sing and to compose will serve for the second.*

# FIRST PROPOSITION.

## *To explain an easy method for learning and teaching how to read and write Music.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' depicting a figure (possibly a scholar or teacher) seated at a desk or table, surrounded by a scroll-work frame.</image-desc>THIS method is divided into four parts: the first shows the order of sounds and the sequence they follow in ordinary songs; the second teaches how they are written; the third, how they must be read; and the fourth, how the Master should proceed with his Disciples to teach them with ease. Now, before beginning, it is appropriate to remark that the examples from the first proposition of the first book, those from the second and third of the third book on the Genres <note>The "Genres" refer to the three types of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>, and those from the nineteenth proposition of the fourth book on Composition, supplement the examples that one might require in the treatise that follows. I hold this treatise in high esteem because its author <note>Historians believe Mersenne is referring here to the mathematician Girard Desargues, who was developing new methods of perspective and geometry at the time.</note> is better suited to express the practice of the arts in a familiar way, using terms that demonstrate a powerful imagination and sound reasoning. He will reveal these qualities to us when he pleases in subjects much more useful and elevated than this one, when he shares with the public his thoughts on Perspective and on the different sections of Cones. Let us begin, then, with the order of letters and sounds used in the practice of Music.

->Order of Sounds.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' featuring a landscape scene with foliage and a figure in the distance, within an ornamental square frame.</image-desc>IN the practice of music today, seven different sounds are employed as the principal ones, which are heard or sounded by means of the voice and instruments suited for that purpose.

It is understood that these sounds are arranged and set out in sequence, one after the other, like rungs on a ladder or steps <term>steps: or "degrees" (degrez), the individual notes of a scale.</term>, and each is marked with one of the letters of the alphabet. For this purpose, the first seven—A, B, C, D, E, F, G—are used.

It is further understood that these sounds, rungs, or steps are different, being separated from one another by a certain difference or interval called a *tone*, or by a certain difference or interval called a *semitone*. I leave aside the alleged "species" <note>original: "pretenduës especes"; Mersenne is simplifying the theory by ignoring the complex mathematical divisions of different types of whole and half steps used in more advanced tuning systems.</note> of each of these *tones* and *semitones*.

The number of these seven sounds, rungs, or steps, and the seven letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, can be increased and multiplied at will. This is done by adding other similar ones on either side—either ascending or descending—always maintaining the same order of both the sounds and the letters. They are arranged and marked so that, starting from any note, the eighth will be of the same species as the first, or the eighth letter will return to being the same as the first in the count <note>This describes the principle of the "octave," where the eighth note (A to A, for example) sounds like a higher or lower version of the first.</note>.

Sometimes it is understood that from the sound or step marked A to the sound or step marked B, there is the interval or difference called a *tone*; then, following that, from the sound or step marked B to the sound or step marked C, there is only the interval or difference called a *semitone*. And until now, these have been named

# Orders of Sounds.

In that case, <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: "Bmol"; referring to the "soft B" or hexachord system using B-flat</note>, by which one means that this species of the order of sounds is named <term>B-flat</term>; that is to say, that which is sung according to this arrangement of sounds is called "singing by <term>B-flat</term>."

But in both cases, whether <term>B-flat</term> or <term>B-natural</term> <note>original: "Bquarre"; referring to the "square B" or "hard" hexachord system using B-natural</note>, one always understands, speaking generally, that from the sound or degree marked C to the sound or degree marked D, there is the interval named a *tone*; and that from the sound or degree marked D to the sound or degree marked E, there is also the interval named a *tone*; but that from the sound or degree marked E to the sound or degree marked F, there is only the interval named a *semitone*; then following that, from the sound marked F to the sound marked G, there is again the interval named a *tone*: and if one goes further, it is understood that from the sound marked G to the sound marked A, there is always the interval or difference named a *tone*; and if one continues, one must always proceed in the same manner and the same order as one began.

Likewise, in moving backward through these sounds or degrees—in reverse order of the letters of the alphabet—it is understood that from the sound marked G to the sound marked F, there is a *tone*, but from the sound marked F to the sound marked E, there is only a *semitone*; and following that, from the sound marked E to the sound marked D, there is again a *tone*, and from the sound marked D to the sound marked C, another *tone*; and in the case of <term>B-natural</term>, from the sound marked C to the sound marked B, there is only a *semitone*, then following that, from the sound marked B to the sound marked A, there is a *tone*. But in the case of <term>B-flat</term>, it is understood that from the sound marked C to the sound marked B, there is a *tone*, then following that, from the sound marked B to the sound marked A, there is only a *semitone*; and if one goes further, it is understood that from the sound marked A to the sound marked G, there is always the interval named a *tone*, and if one continues, one must always proceed in the same manner and the same order as one began.

When one has repeated this number of seven sounds several times on one side or the other—either ascending, descending, or both together—whether in the case of <term>B-flat</term> or <term>B-natural</term>, it happens that the intervals named *tones* and those named *semitones* are found intermingled in such a way that on one side of each of the *semitones* there are three *tones* in a row, and on the other side there are only two.

But one is free to change the order of these intervals afterward as needed, and to diversify at will the mixture or interlacing of these *tones* and *semitones*, by placing a suitable *semitone* in a place where there was a *tone*, or conversely, by placing a suitable *tone* in a place where there was only a *semitone*. This is what is called making <term>feints</term> <note>original: "feintes"; an early term for accidentals or musica ficta</note>, which are expressed by the words <term>diesis</term> <note>original: "diefis"; the sharp sign</note>, whose character is ♯, and <term>B-flat</term>, whose character is ♭. Now, the <term>diesis</term> signifies that one places a *tone* where there was only a *semitone*, and vice versa; and the <term>B-flat</term> signifies that one places a *semitone* instead of a *tone*, and vice versa.

# Orders of Sounds.

...number of four, five, or six, and more if one wishes, per staff <note>original: "bande"; here referring to the set of horizontal lines we now call a staff or stave</note>: but because one sees many of these staves in our preceding books—for example on page 253 of the *Book of Composition*, and everywhere else—there is no need to repeat them here.

Now, in each of these staves, each line and each interval or space between them, as well as those outside, represents one of these sounds; or rather, it is understood as the seat or the place of one of these sounds arranged as has been described.

And insofar as it is understood, as has also been stated, that each of the said sounds is marked <note>original: "cotté"</note> by one of the first seven letters according to their alphabetical order, it follows that on the same staves, each line and each space between them (and outside them) is likewise understood as the place or the seat of one of those letters that serve to mark these sounds.

In such a way that having assigned, chosen, or determined any one of these lines or spaces of the said staves to be the seat or the place of one of these sounds, it follows that the same spot—whether line or space—is also the seat or the place of that of the said letters which serves as the mark for that sound. Conversely, when one assigns some line or space on one of the said staves to be the seat or the place of one of those letters used to mark the said sounds, the same line or space of the same staff is also necessarily the place or the seat of that sound for which the letter serves as a mark.

And consequently, one has assigned upon each of the other lines and spaces of the same staff the seat or the place of each of the other sounds, and following that, of each of those letters which serve as their marks.

By this means, one has determined the places on the same staff where it is understood the sounds are placed, between which there is only the interval called a <term>semitone</term> <note>the smallest distance between two notes in Western music</note>, and likewise the sounds between which there is the interval called a <term>tone</term>. That is to say, one knows in which places on the staff the sounds are placed that form a <term>tone</term>, and those that form a <term>semitone</term>.

And although each line and each space between them (and outside) of each staff is understood as the place or the seat of one of the said sounds, and consequently of the letter by which it is marked—and it might seem that since one is excused from drawing a sound (insofar as that seems impossible), it would at least be necessary to draw each of these letters which serve as their marks at the place where they happen to be located—nevertheless, it is sufficient to mark a single one in its place at will, either on one of the said lines or in one of the said spaces of the same staff. This serves as a memorial, a guide, or a lead to recognize the place of each of the other said letters, and by this means to also know the place or the seat on a staff of each of the said sounds.

But the custom until now has been to draw this letter only on one of the lines of the staff, where one forms a character called a <term>Clef</term> <note>from the French word for "key," as it unlocks the meaning of the notes on the staff</note>. This character signifies that the place where it is drawn is the seat or the place of that letter which the character is understood to represent, and consequently of the sound for which that letter serves as a mark.

# Orders of sounds,

Up until now, we have mostly used only one or another of three out of these seven letters, which are used to mark the sounds: specifically F, C, and G, each of which serves as a clef, as has been mentioned.

<margin><image-desc>Symbol for a G-clef (treble clef)</image-desc></margin>
When one wishes to use the letter G, one draws or forms at the beginning of the staff <note>original: "bande"; here referring to the set of horizontal lines we now call a staff or stave</note> a symbol upon the line which is understood to be the place or the seat of the sound for which this letter G serves as a mark <note>original: "cotte"</note>.

<margin><image-desc>Symbol for a C-clef (alto/tenor clef)</image-desc></margin>
When one wishes to use the letter C, one draws at the beginning of the staff a character whose form is such [as the symbol shown] upon whichever of the lines one intends to be the place or seat of the sound for which the said letter C serves as a mark.

<margin><image-desc>Two symbols for F-clefs (bass clef)</image-desc></margin>
When one wishes to use the letter F, one uses one or the other of two different characters, whose forms are such [as the symbols shown], and one draws one of the said characters at the beginning of the staff upon the line which one intends to be the place or seat of the sound for which this letter F serves as a mark.

Thus, the letter G and the preceding characters make up what is called the *Clef* in the current practice of writing and singing music in Europe; which *Clef* signifies and serves to identify that the line on which one of these characters is drawn is the seat or the place of the sound for which the letter represented by that character serves as a mark.

When it is intended that the written song is of the species called *B-flat* <note>original: "Bmol"; referring to the "soft" hexachord where B is flattened</note>, one draws or places at the beginning of each staff, in addition to the clef, the letter b in the places where it happens that the sound marked by the letter b is located.

But when it is intended that the written song is of the species called *B-natural* <note>original: "Bquarre"; referring to the "hard" or square-shaped B, indicating a natural or sharp sound in this context</note>, the letter b is not drawn at the beginning of the staff.

Thus, when at the beginning of the staff there is this letter b drawn, it signifies that the written song is of the species called *B-flat*; and when this letter b is not drawn at the beginning of the staff, it signifies that the written song is of the species called *B-natural*.

I have not yet been able to recognize the reasoning upon which the third name of *Natural* <note>original: "Nature"</note> is based, which has been given to song, as every species of song seems natural to me.

And because sounds, from which music is fashioned, are currently intoned under the pronunciation of these six syllables *Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La* <note>These are the precursors to the modern Do-Re-Mi; the author also suggests adding a seventh, which would eventually become 'Si'</note>, to which a seventh can be added; and because—in order to always make the pronunciation of the syllables *Mi* and *Fa* fall directly on the lines or spaces which are the places or seats of sounds between which it is understood there is only a *semitone*—the sequence of these six syllables has been arranged in certain instances in a certain order. By this order, it happens that one intones the same sound, always marked by the same letter, sometimes under the pronunciation of one and sometimes another of the other said six syllables, namely *Ut, Re, Sol, La*.

Thus, one intones the sound marked C on various occasions, sometimes under the pronunciation of the syllable *Ut*, sometimes the syllable *Sol*, and sometimes the syllable *Fa*; and it is from this that it proceeds that one names the...

Similarly, because it happens that one intones the sound to which the letter E serves as a mark sometimes under the pronunciation of the syllable *La*, and sometimes of the syllable *Mi*, from this comes the saying *E, Mi, La*, or else *E, La, Mi*.

In the same way, because it happens that one intones the sound to which the letter D serves as a mark sometimes under the syllable *La*, sometimes under the syllable *Re*, and sometimes under the syllable *Sol*, from this comes the saying *D, La, Re, Sol*, or *D, La, Sol, Re*.

### *The easiest method, then, for learning to read and sing Music according to the practice currently accepted for writing and intoning it in Europe, would seem to be this one.*

That one becomes accustomed to carrying the voice high and low, or indeed to ascending and descending the voice according to the two different intervals named *tone or semitone*, or, as is commonly said, to intone the tone and semitone at will, whether ascending or descending, while pronouncing a single and same syllable, of which that of **La** seems today to be more suitable in France than any other. <note>The author is advocating for a simplified "fixed" system using only one syllable—"La"—rather than the complex shifting syllables (Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La) of the older Guidonian system.</note>

In this way, one becomes accustomed to ascending and descending with the voice at will, through as many conjunct degrees of sounds as one wishes, or intervals made all of whole tones, or all of semitones, in a continuous sequence, or indeed of whole tones and semitones mixed together and placed each as desired.

One also becomes accustomed in this way to carrying one's voice all at once, or in a leap at will, higher or lower than each of these conjunct degrees of tones and semitones; I mean, to ascend and descend with the voice at will through all species of intervals, large and small, or, as they are commonly called, concords and discords, whether perfect or imperfect, or even consonances and dissonances, perfect or imperfect.

And for this, the exercise of the voice and the training of the ear seem to be absolutely necessary for whoever is naturally disposed to sing, in order to make it familiar through habit.
