# Orders of sounds.

### *Reading written Music.*

THUS, reading written Music consists of knowing how much one must raise or lower the voice, and how long one must make it last at each occurrence and in each place, according to the intention signified by the note which is applied there; in this, memory assists, and judgment leads the way.

<margin><image-desc>A G-clef symbol positioned on the second line of a five-line musical staff segment.</image-desc>*</margin>
And one only needs to remember the letter that each of these characters represents—which we call a *Clef* <term>literally "key"; a symbol placed on a staff to fix the pitch of the notes</term>—namely, the one shown here <note>Referring to the G-clef in the margin</note>. One must also know that the presence of the *b* at the beginning of the staff <note>original: "bande"</note> signifies that the song is of the species named *B-flat* <term>Bmol: literally "soft B", indicating the use of flats</term>, whereas the absence of that same *b* at the beginning of the staff signifies that the song is of the species named *B-natural* <term>Bquarre: literally "square B", referring to the "hard" hexachord where B is natural</term>. Furthermore, one need only know by heart the name and the order, both forwards and backwards, of the seven letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, repeated several times and starting from whichever one is necessary. Finally, one must remember between which of these seven letters there is a whole tone, and between which there is only a semitone <note>A half-step</note>, whether in B-natural or B-flat.

Once this is simply known by memory, upon opening any Music book, in whatever part or clef it may be, seeing the start of the staff and the character of the *Clef*, one first recognizes if the song is by *B-natural* or by *B-flat*, depending on the absence or presence of the *b*. Furthermore, one knows the position of the letter that the *Clef* character represents, by means of which one easily comes to know the position of each of the other letters when they are named in sequence, forwards and backwards—or rather, ascending and descending. One begins naming them from the letter represented by the clef character, understanding that its position is the same as the clef, and each of the other subsequent letters follows a continuous sequence from line to space, and space to line, one after the other, whether ascending or descending.

Consequently, one easily discovers and notes the places on the staff where the semitones are located, as well as the places where the whole tones are located; and through practice, one becomes accustomed to discerning them, making this distinction familiar.

Those who are preoccupied with the use of an ancient method will have difficulty persuading themselves that there could ever be a method for learning to read and sing Music more easily than the one to which they are accustomed. I leave the judgment of this to those who are of a free disposition to make a pure trial of both ways.

# Orders of sounds.

...provided that this Student possesses the necessary qualities of voice, hearing, and judgment.

The Master should, at the beginning, intone <term>sound a note</term> into the ear of the Student with his own voice—which is best—or perhaps with some instrument. He should make the Student hear, imitate, or mimic that same sound with their own voice, then another, always pronouncing only a single and same syllable, which shall be **LA**, if one wishes. In this way, he should accustom the Student to mimic or imitate each of the sounds they hear while pronouncing that same single syllable. At the same time, he should make them observe and recognize the sensible difference the ear hears between mimicking and imitating a sound well, versus not mimicking or imitating it well; likewise, the sensible difference the ear hears between a very uniform, equal, or firm sound that maintains itself, and a variable, unequal sound, or one that slackens either upward or downward.

Furthermore, he should accustom the Student to recognize well by ear, and to intone with the voice while also pronouncing the same single syllable, two diverse sounds, separated or differing by the degree of a *tone* <note>a whole step</note> ascending and descending; then another two separated or differing by the degree of only a *semitone* <note>a half step</note>, also ascending and descending. He should accustom them in this manner to recognize well the sensible difference the ear hears between sounds separated or differing from one another by the interval of a tone, and those separated or differing from one another by the interval of only a semitone, ascending and descending.

He should further accustom the Student to intone, using that same pronunciation of a single syllable, several sounds separated or differing from each other by degrees consisting entirely of *conjunct* <term>stepwise or adjacent</term> tones, or a continuous sequence ascending and descending; then likewise all conjunct semitones, or a continuous sequence ascending and descending; and finally tones and semitones mixed together at will, whether ascending or descending.

And always with the help of his own singing, if possible, or else the sound of some instrument, the Master should finally accustom the Student to ascend and descend with the voice through all the intervals imaginable within this arrangement of according and non-according sounds: that is to say, through all types of *accords* and *discords*, or rather *consonances* and *dissonances* of all kinds, ascending and descending. He should make the Student accustom themselves to recognize well the sensible difference the ear hears between these various intervals, and how they touch the ear and make themselves felt to the hearing each in a diverse way, or some in a different manner than others.

This is where the skillful Master greatly assists the Student, and where practice brings familiarity over time. While the Master exercises the Student’s ear and voice in this manner—that is, through intervals taken in between—he shall propose to them, as the entire *gamut* <term>the full range or "scale" of notes</term> or rule for reading notes and recognizing or intoning the sounds of Music:

That they must know by memory, and must accustom themselves to pronounce familiarly, the names in a continuous sequence of the first seven letters of the alphabet **A, B, C, D, E, F, G**, repeated several times one after the other, forward

# Orders of sounds.

...and backwards, ascending and descending, or rather forward and backward, and starting from whichever it may be; I mean that once these seven letters are understood and repeated several times in sequence, one after the other—such as A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G—when it happens that they must be named starting with the letter C, while moving forward or ascending, one must say C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.

In descending or moving backward, one must say C, B, A, G, F, E, D, C, B, A.

When it happens that they are named starting with the letter G, moving forward or ascending, one must say G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, B. And in moving backward or descending, one must say G, F, E, D, C, B, A, G, F, and continue.

When it happens that they are named starting with the letter F, moving forward or ascending, one must say F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A; but in moving backward or descending, one must say F, E, D, C, B, A, G, F, E, D.

And likewise for starting from any of the other letters.

Furthermore, the Master will teach the disciple and let them know between which of these letters the *tone* <term>a whole step</term> is placed, and between which the *semitone* <term>a half step</term> is placed; and so that they remember it better and finally know it by heart, he will give it to them in writing, making them read and say it often, as follows:

That when the song is by *b quarre* <note>original: "b quarre"; this refers to "hard B" or B-natural</note>, from the letter A to the letter B, there is a *tone*; from B to C, a *semitone*; from C to D, a *tone*; from D to E, a *tone*; from E to F, a *semitone*; from F to G, a *tone*; from G to A, a *tone*. And in reverse, from A to G, there is likewise a *tone*; from G to F, a *tone*; from F to E, a *semitone*; from E to D, a *tone*; from D to C, a *tone*; from C to B, a *semitone*; and from B to A, a *tone*.

But when the song is by *b mol* <note>original: "b mol"; this refers to "soft B" or B-flat</note>, then from the letter A to the letter B, there is only a *semitone*; and from the letter B to the letter C, a *tone*; the rest remains everywhere the same as when the song is by *b quarre*. Thus he will easily make them understand that the difference between the order of sounds by *b quarre* and the order of sounds by *b mol* consists only in the transposition of a *semitone* between A and B, or between B and C.

Additionally, the Master will teach the disciple to recognize the clefs or characters that represent any of the said letters, and in what place each of these clefs is positioned according to how it is drawn. He will also teach how to discern that the song is by *b quarre* when there is no "B" drawn at the beginning of the <term>staff</term> <note>original: "bande"</note> in the place of the letter B; and that the song is by *b mol* when there is a "b" drawn at the beginning of the staff in the place of the letter B.

All of these observations and circumstances, once well understood, consist of so little and are so easy to conceive and retain in memory that a longer explanation would be tedious.

And when the disciple is well accustomed through frequent practice to ascending and descending with the voice through all types of intervals, conjunct degrees <note>notes moving step-by-step</note>, and others at will—which is commonly called "intoning" <term>singing the pitches</term> all types of consonances and dissonances, and of tones and semitones in ascending and descending...

## Orders of Sounds,

That he recognizes each of the characters, which are called the <term>Clef</term> <note>The key or clef symbol at the start of a staff</note>; the place where it is understood to be positioned; and knows which of the seven letters it represents, between which of said letters the *tone* and *semitone* are placed, that the absence of the *b* <note>The flat symbol</note> at the beginning of the staff signifies that the song is by *B-natural* <note>original: "Bequarre"; the "hard" hexachord or natural scale</note>, and that the presence of the same *b* signifies that the song is by *B-flat* <note>original: "Bmol"; the "soft" hexachord or flatted scale</note>.

At the opening of any book of <term>Music</term> in whatever part and <term>clef</term> it may be, this <term>Disciple</term> sees first by the absence or presence of the *b* at the beginning of the staff whether the song is by *B-natural* or indeed by *B-flat*; in what place the <term>Clef</term> is positioned, and knows which of the letters it represents, and has nothing more to do than name the said seven letters, repeated as much as necessary, ascending and descending through each of the lines and spaces of the staff in continuous succession, always beginning from the place where the <term>clef</term> is figured, and by the name of the letter that this <term>clef</term> represents. In doing so, he easily accustoms himself to noticing the place of each of said letters, high and low on the staff, and to discerning the places where the *semitones* are placed high and low on the staff, and between the *tones*.

So that having intoned—following the range of his voice and the extent of the song he undertakes—a sound for the first <term>note</term> he encounters; he only has to notice if the following <term>note</term> is on the same degree, or if it is higher or lower than the preceding one by a single or by several degrees, and by how many, and of what kind each is, whether of *tones* or *semitones*. If the following <term>note</term> is on the same degree, he will repeat for this following <term>note</term> the same sound he had intoned for the preceding one. But if the following <term>note</term> is higher or lower than the preceding one by a single degree worth a *tone* or else a *semitone*, then for this following <term>note</term> he will intone a sound higher or lower only by a *tone* or else a *semitone*. If the following <term>note</term> is higher or lower than the preceding one by several <term>intervals</term> and of different kinds, and he cannot at first intone that <term>interval</term>, then he will first ascend or descend there by the conjunct <term>degrees</term> <note>Stepwise motion</note> it contains; and then, resuming, he will intone in a single leap all the <term>degrees</term> as a single <term>interval</term>. And likewise in succession at every place.

The advantage received from this manner of learning to read and intone the words of <term>Music</term> is that the understanding finds itself greatly relieved; the memory and the sight do not have much to do, and it is almost only the hearing and the voice of the <term>Disciple</term> that work when he practices thus upon a music book. From this it follows that the spirit is not discouraged in the long exercise necessary for the apprenticeship of the <term>Arts</term>, as it is discouraged when it has several difficulties to combat and overcome at the same time, as in the ancient way of learning to sing because of the nuances and the various names that each <term>note</term> receives <note>A critique of the complex Guidonian solmization system (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la) which required "mutations" between hexachords</note>: which is not encountered in this method here.

### SECOND PROPOSITION.
*Explaining another method for learning to sing and to compose without ordinary notes, by means of letters alone.*

The preceding method showed the way to intone, and to learn to sing by means of the single note or syllable LA, or under whatever other syllable one wishes: unless one prefers to pronounce the first seven letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, instead of *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, etc.* which this method retains, so that it uses only the first letters U, R, M, F, S, L, to write Music. I gave examples of this a long time ago in the 16th article of the great Latin question on Music placed in our *Commentaries on Genesis* <note>original: "Commentaires sur la Genèse." Referring to Mersenne's "Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim" (1623).</note>: where I also advised that one can use ordinary numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. to write all kinds of Music. But before passing further, one must note what I have already said in the 19th proposition of the 3rd book of *Genres*, which is sufficient for those who understand it to sing, and what I have said in other places regarding the 7th syllable BI, NI, or ZA, which helps to avoid <term>mutations</term><note>The complex process in medieval/Renaissance music of shifting between hexachords.</note>.

I say then that if one follows the syllable ZA, invented by Master Le Maire, after the 6th syllable LA, the entire difficulty of the <term>B-flat</term><note>original: "Bmol"</note> and the <term>B-natural</term><note>original: "Bquarre"</note> will be reduced to the syllable ZA, which will be intoned a whole tone or only a semitone higher than LA; and for this reason one will always place a sharp below it when it is a whole tone higher: and if the sharp is not there, it will be only a semitone higher than the LA, as one sees here in ascending, where ZA is distant by a whole tone from LA, and consequently there is only a semitone from ZA to UT, both in ascending and descending:

On which it must be noted that it is easier to intone than the syllable SI, BI, or NI, because it is not necessary to change the opening of the mouth with which one pronounces the preceding *la*: which alone can be used instead of *ut, re, mi, etc.* as I said in the first proposition. # Orders of sounds.

Where it should be noted that I do not use two "z"s, one without a sharp and the other with a sharp—as Master le Maire <note>Jean Le Maire was a 17th-century French music theorist known for proposing the addition of a seventh syllable, "si" or "za," to the traditional six-note hexachord system.</note> does—so that there is never more than a semitone from **z** to the letter that immediately follows it in ascending, just as there is never more than a semitone from **M** to **F**. In this manner, there will always be only 7 different letters in each Octave; but because sharps are not used in standard printing houses, one can use some other character for this purpose. For example, a small acute accent can be placed over each letter that one wishes to raise by a semitone, as can be seen in the highest Octave written with Roman Italic in this fashion: *v, v', r, r', m, f, f', s, s', l, l', z*. This will prevent the need for a blank line, which one is forced to leave when adding sharps <note>original: "dieſes"</note> to the letters. As for the pronunciation of the sounds—whether under the single syllable, **LA**, of which I spoke in the preceding propositions, or under the syllables that I explain in the 19th proposition of the 3rd book of *Musical Genres*, or under such other syllables as one might wish, such as the syllables expressing the letters previously explained (A, B, C, D, etc.) or the names of numbers (*one, two, three*, etc.)—it matters very little, since in singing the letter or the subject, one has no need for any other pronunciation of syllables.

Let us now see the manner of composing for 2 or more parts by means of these letters; which we shall first do in simple Counterpoint <note>Simple or "plain" counterpoint involves note-against-note composition where all parts move in the same rhythm.</note>, because we have not yet explained the proper characters for marking the different measures for figured Counterpoint <note>Also known as florid counterpoint, involving varied rhythms and "diminutions" (shorter, faster notes).</note>, and for all sorts of diminutions, using the characters of standard printing houses.

Regarding the letters, it does not matter which ones are used, provided they have a range great enough to express the melody of all the parts: this is why we shall write the Duo that follows using the common letters of the Roman text, which serve for the printing of this work, and which are intended for the 2 highest Octaves.

This way of writing is very suitable for seeing all the chords without the need for any other score, provided that one simply knows the distance between the letters placed opposite one another, following the scale of sounds they represent—that is, following the order of *ut, re, mi, fa, sol*, etc. For example, the first letter of the Bass, *r*, is 5 sounds away from the first letter of the Treble, *l*, which means these two letters represent the two sounds of the *Diapente* <note>original: "Diapente"; a Greek-derived term used by music theorists to describe the interval of a perfect fifth.</note>, and they form the chord that practitioners call a **Fifth** <term>Quinte: an interval spanning five notes of the scale, considered one of the most stable harmonies.</term>.

If they are 3, 4, 6, or 8 sounds apart, they represent **Thirds**, **Fourths**, **Sixths**, or **Octaves**; and if they are ten sounds apart or more, they represent **Tenths** and other compound intervals <term>repliques: literally "replications," these are intervals larger than an octave that repeat the harmonic function of a smaller interval (e.g., a tenth is an octave plus a third).</term>, as happens with the 20th, 21st, 22nd, 27th, 28th, and 29th letters of the Bass and Treble, which form **Tenths**, both **major** and **minor**. Let us see another example for 3 parts, which is the second Duo on page 268, and then we will provide one for 4, so that those who wish to compose for their own pleasure—whether to recreate themselves by playing the Lute, the Spinet <note>a small, rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note>, or some other instrument capable of expressing several parts together, or to communicate their compositions—may have no difficulty with this way of writing music. Now, this manner of writing music, as well as the preceding one, teaches one to recognize all the Consonances and dissonances so easily—and even the art of part-writing and composing for as many parts as one wishes—that it does not take even an hour to understand its mechanism. For it is certain that all letters of the same name in each row make an Octave or its repetitions <note>The author means that two 'A's in different registers always form an octave, making harmony easier to spot than on a traditional staff.</note>. Just as those which are close to one another and follow immediately in the same row and have equal characters form Seconds, which are the primary or smallest Dissonances: for example, the **f**'s with the **g**'s, the **g**'s with the **a**'s, the **a**'s with the **b**'s, etc. And with letters from other rows, they form the repetitions of these dissonances, as happens from **G** to the three letters **A**, **a**, **a'**.

The fourth characters take the place of everything that practitioners can say or write about their binary and ternary measures, sesquialtera, or hemiola <term>hemiola: a rhythmic device where three beats are played in the time of two</term>, of their major and minor modes, both perfect and imperfect, and of the perfection or imperfection of both Prolation <term>Prolation: a system of rhythmic relationships in medieval and Renaissance music</term> and time, of which I shall speak more fully in the 4th part of this book: now no characters seem more suitable for this subject than the digits already used in practice; in which ternary measure is signified by 3, or by 3/2, although it is better expressed by 2, or 1/2, because the lowering of the hand is double its raising; for when the lowering lasts for 2, 4, 8, 12, or 24 notes, the raising lasts only for one, 2, 4, 6, or 12—that is to say, less than half. This is why the ratio of this measure is double, and not triple or sesquialtera; for to be triple, one must play 3 notes while beating [down] and one while raising; and to be sesquialtera, one must play 3 while lowering and two while raising, and so with the others to infinity. Even time will be marked by 1, or by 1/1, since it is in a ratio of equality, for the upbeat is equal to the downbeat <note>The author refers to the "tactus," the hand motion used to keep time; in even time, the upward and downward motions of the hand take the same amount of time</note>. I leave aside for now all these characters * and the other signs for augmentation, perfection, division, and alteration, with which Cerone <note>Pedro Cerone (1566–1625), an Italian priest and music theorist known for his massive 22-volume treatise "El Melopeo y Maestro"</note> fills his 17th, 18th, and 19th books, as they are useless or hardly necessary, since one can mark everything belonging to the diversity of notes and their values using numbers alone; I may speak of this more fully in the *Treatise on Rhythm*.

The fifth set of characters indicates the places where the parts must be silent, whether all together or while the others continue; these are nothing more than bars that cross 2 or 3 lines of the staves or bands, as seen on page 256, where one finds the 8 different note values and the signs or characters for rests, along with the dots that follow the figures. These dots are the fifth characters used in practice, where they always worth half the value of the note they follow, and are sung on the same pitch <note>original: "chorde"</note> as if one were continuing the said note. Because these dots are found in ordinary printing, we shall use them as well. As for rests <note>original: "silences"</note>, we have no need for them, because a part that must remain silent will have no letter above the words to be sung, and will necessarily be silent without needing to be warned by other signs; if all parts must be silent together, they will simply have no letters above the words.

All this being established, one can easily write, read, and sing every kind of music with the ordinary characters used in printing, without the need for traditional musical notes. In this way, all those who compose Airs and Motets <note>A motet is a short, sacred choral composition</note> can communicate their thoughts and designs to all sorts of people, and we can preserve many fine compositions that are currently lost or cannot be enjoyed for lack of musical type, which is very rare in France. I therefore include here two compositions for 7 and 8 parts to provide a trial of this method.

# Orders of sounds.

Now, if the order of these letters V, R, M, F, S, L, Z, v <note>original: "V, R, M, F, S, L, Z, v"; these likely represent the solmization syllables Ut (Do), Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Si, and the higher Ut</note> seems more difficult to remember than that of the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, it is easy to apply to them everything we have said about the others; thus, it does not matter which ones are used, as they all amount to the same thing.

It should be noted that regardless of which characters are used, the ease of composing music is so great that a person of wit and judgment can learn to compose without errors within one or two hours, which I demonstrate in the proposition that follows.

## IV. PROPOSITION.

->Learning to compose music correctly in a short time.<-

I first assume that one knows the order of sounds, and the degrees and intervals found between the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, A, of which we spoke in the first proposition. Secondly, that from A to a dotted B (B.), or an accented B (B'), there is always a tone <term>tone: a whole step, the standard interval between most notes in a scale</term>, and similarly from E to a dotted or accented F' there is a tone; and that there is only a semitone <term>semitone: a half-step, the smallest interval in traditional Western music</term> from A to B, and from E to F, when they are not accented. And from every other letter to its neighbor—namely from C to D, from D to E, from F to G, and from G to A—there is always a tone when they are not accented. If they are all dotted in this manner C’, D’, E’, and F’, G’, A’, there is also a tone between C’ and D’, F’ and G’, G’ and A; and consequently, there is a minor Third <term>minor Third: a musical interval spanning three semitones, often described as having a "sad" quality</term> from an undotted C to a dotted D, just as from D to E’, from F to G, and from G to A’. From this, it follows that a dotted A’ makes the same sound as an undotted B, and a dotted E’ the same as an undotted F. This being established, let us come to the composition of two parts, which people will sing everywhere in the same key <note>original: "ton"; here meaning the pitch level or key</note> and with the same meter, if they understand what I demonstrate on page 149 of the third book of *Instruments* <note>A reference to another of the author's works, likely *Harmonie Universelle*</note>. I repeat the subject here to serve as the Treble <note>original: "dessus"</note> for our *Duet*, which I begin an Octave above the sound I mentioned in the aforementioned place; for this subject, I mark it with the standard letters of the large Roman font; and because it begins on the MI of *E-la-mi* <note>A pitch in the medieval hexachord system corresponding to the note E</note>, the E will signify its first pitch.

---

|:---|:---|:---|

| Bass or Concordant. | a, a, c, | c̆ b̆' a, e, d, d, a, b', d, ē, c, d, e, |
| | O Lord | my God, how great Thou art in all Thy grandeur. |

# Orders of sounds.

Minor sixth, and the third letters *c* and *e* the major third. But the *a* of the upper part <note>original: "Dessus"; the soprano or highest voice</note> holds steady against the *c*, *b*, and *a* of the bass, such that three letters divide the *a* of the upper part into three parts. The first part is worth half a measure and creates a major sixth; the following two are each worth a quarter of a measure, the first of which creates a seventh, and the second an octave against the *a* of the upper part. For when one part performs a diminution <term>diminution: the breaking up of a long note into several shorter, faster notes</term> of three strings <note>original: "chordes"; likely referring to notes or musical lines</note> while the other part holds steady on a single note, the first and third must form consonant chords, while the second may form a discord <term>discord: a dissonance or clashing sound</term>, which makes the following chord sound more pleasant.

Now, there is no other diminution in this duo; so after this octave, the *e* of the bass makes a minor third with the *g* of the upper part, and the following letters together create the fifth, the major sixth, the minor tenth, the octave, the fifth, the minor third, the major sixth, the minor third, and finally the unison, which ends this duo. In this piece, the consonances follow one another in a very beautiful order, from which one can derive these rules: that the letters of different parts create pleasing conjunctions when they are separated from one another by 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, etc. That is to say, starting to count from one of them as one, two, three, four, five, six, etc., those found at the 3rd, 5th, 6th, 8th, and 10th positions form chords. Thus, after beginning a duo with a perfect chord—meaning a unison, an octave, or a fifth—one can join the letters that follow and which correspond to one another in intervals of 3rds, 5ths, 6ths, and 8ths. I omit the interval of a 4th, because one avoids this conjunction in duos of simple counterpoint <term>counterpoint: the art of combining different melodic lines</term>, though it is only forbidden by those who lack the authority to abolish its use entirely, which could be introduced. 

But to finish this proposition in few words, I say that one will compose correctly if one always uses thirds, or major and minor sixths, following one another alternately, occasionally mixing in the fifth and the octave; and if one uses contrary motion <term>contrary motion: when one voice moves up while the other moves down</term> as often as possible, and if one makes them move by conjunct degrees <term>conjunct degrees: moving step-by-step to the very next note in the scale</term>, or at least if one voice proceeds by a conjunct degree while the other moves by disjunct degrees, which practitioners call intervals; and finally, if one moves toward perfect chords through the imperfect ones that are closest to them—for example, from the minor third to the unison, and from the major sixth or minor tenth to the octave. Of this, I provide here another example in the 7th mode of F.

# SECOND PART
## ON THE ART OF EMBELLISHING THE VOICE, RECITATIVES, AIRS, OR SONGS.

**HAVING EXPLAINED THE MANNER** of arranging, writing, reading, teaching, learning, and composing *Music* in the first part of this book, I now add the manner in which one must ornament and enrich *Airs* and *Songs* to bring them to their perfection, so that nothing more might be desired but an excellent voice to perform them—the qualities of which I describe in the following proposition.

### PROPOSITION V.

->To explain the way to determine if a given voice is good, and what qualities it must possess.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial E featuring a small figure in a landscape within the letter's ornamentation.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH it is easy to conclude what the qualities of a good voice should be from what we have said in the book on the voice, it is nevertheless necessary to explain them more clearly here, so that those who teach singing do not waste their time on poor voices.

Now, there are 4 types of voices: namely the *Bass*, the *Tenor* <note>original: "Taille"; the standard middle-range male voice</note>, the *Alto* <note>original: "Hautecontre"; a high male voice common in French Baroque music</note>, and the *Soprano* <note>original: "Dessus"; literally "the one above," the highest vocal part</note>. As for their qualities, they must be accurate, steady, and flexible. Accuracy <note>original: "iustesse"</note> consists of hitting the intended pitch without being allowed to go higher or lower than the note <note>original: "chorde"; literally "string," referring to the specific pitch level</note> or the mark that must be struck and sung.

Steadiness <note>original: "L'égalité"</note> is the firm and stable holding of the voice on the same note, without being allowed to vary it by raising or lowering the pitch; however, one may soften or increase the volume while remaining on the same note. And the flexibility of the voice is nothing other than the ease and readiness it has to move through all kinds of steps and intervals, both ascending and descending, and in performing all kinds of *Passages* <term>Passages: rapid melodic ornaments or runs between main notes</term> and *diminutions* <term>diminutions: the division of a long note into many shorter, faster notes to decorate a melody</term>. This must be particularly observed in the *Soprano* voice, upon which the principal ornament of *Music* depends, as I have shown elsewhere, especially since it usually performs the diminutions and

# Embellishment

...that it reveals the beauty of the subject and of the text <note>original: "lettre"; refers to the lyrics or the literal message of the song</note> it recites: hence many prefer hearing the recital of a good Soprano <note>original: "Dessus"; the highest vocal part</note> to an entire concert, for reasons I have explained elsewhere.

Now, the Masters who teach singing can easily test whether a voice offered to them is true and steady, using the organ as well as the Viol, the Lute, and other instruments: for if it tunes easily and promptly to the unison of each pipe or string, it is certainly true. Furthermore, instruments that have more sustain <note>original: "tenuë"; the ability to hold a note steadily over time</note> are the most suitable for testing voices; although Masters who have a true voice and ear do not need an instrument to train the voices of children.

There are several other qualities one may desire in a voice, which are encountered quite rarely—for example, sweetness and a certain harmony, upon which depend the charms that ravish the listeners. For voices that are harsh do not please, even if they are true and possess the other qualities I have mentioned, because they have too much bitterness and brilliance <note>original: "aigreur, & d'eſclat"; suggesting a piercing or shrill quality that lacks warmth</note>, which wound delicate ears and prevent the sound from sliding pleasantly enough into the listener’s mind to master it and lead it wherever one wishes. Nevertheless, Masters can correct most defects of the voice through various industries <note>original: "industries"; here meaning skillful techniques or specialized training methods</note> which they should know or seek out, since nature produces very few good and perfect voices.

There is yet another quality of the voice that makes it full and solid, and which increases its harmony; this can be explained by the comparison of a channel that is always full of water as it flows, or by that of a body and a face that is fleshy and in good health. In contrast, voices lacking this quality are like a trickle of water flowing through a large channel, or a thin and gaunt face.

### VI. PROPOSITION.

->*To explain the manner used to form voices and to make them capable of singing all kinds of airs and songs, and particularly for performing Cadences.*<-

There is no difficulty in teaching those who have a good voice, because they naturally move to imitate and do everything one wants; this happens similarly with all other apprentices who have more need of the bridle than the spur—as was said of Aristotle when he was still a student. From this comes the Latin proverb "let the well-born rejoice" <note>original: "gaudeant bene nati"; a phrase suggesting that those naturally gifted with talent should find joy in their innate abilities</note>, by reason of the good qualities that nature and birth give to some and deny to others. This should be attributed to the order of Divine Providence, which uses all sorts of conditions, like so many voices, to compose the great concert of this universe, the beauties and charms of which we shall never fully understand until we are in Heaven.

# Of Songs.

Now, after one has taught how to form the tone and how to adjust the voice to all sorts of sounds, the student is accustomed to performing trills <note>original: "cadences"; in this period, a "cadence" refers specifically to a vocal trill or shake rather than a harmonic conclusion.</note>, which consist of rolls of the throat. These correspond to the shakes and hammerings <note>original: "tremblemens & martelemens"; rhythmic ornaments</note> performed on the keyboard of the Organ and the Spinet, and on the neck of the Lute and other stringed instruments. These trills are the most difficult to perform of everything found in songs, because one must only beat the air with the throat, which must produce a quantity of shakes without the help of the tongue. But they are as agreeable as they are difficult; for if other musical movements are the colors and shades, one might say that trills are the rays and the light. Those who do not have the natural disposition of the throat to make these trills and passages <note>original: "paſſages"; rapid melodic runs or divisions</note> make use of movements of the tongue, which are not as pleasant—particularly when they are made with the tip. As for those made with the middle of the tongue, they are necessary for certain passages that cannot be executed accurately enough without the help and shake of the middle of the tongue, due to the meeting of vowels that must be pronounced and made felt by the listeners.

Regarding tremors of the lips, they are neither pleasant nor permitted, any more than those that seem to be pulled from the stomach. It must also be noted that these shakes are not performed on a single string or note—like the vibrations produced by instrument strings—for they would be faulty, unless one wishes to counterfeit or imitate the Italian *Trillo* <note>original: "Trillo"; a 17th-century Italian ornament consisting of a rapid repetition of a single pitch, whereas the French "cadence" alternated between two pitches.</note>. Instead, they descend and ascend by a half-step or a whole step: for example, if the trill is composed of the three notes A, G, F <note>original: "la, ſol, fa"</note>, one must perform the shake on the G <note>original: "ſol"</note>, doing it 4, 8, 16, or as many times as one can or wishes: A, G, A, G, A, G, A, G, etc., as seen in the following example:

<image-desc>A single musical staff with five lines and a C-clef on the first line. It contains eight sixteenth notes (originally "doubles crochües") alternating between two pitches (the notes A and G), grouped in pairs with beams.</image-desc>

which has 8 sixteenth notes <note>original: "doubles crochües"</note> that must be performed in a time equal to the half-measure of the G. And if one wishes to perform this trill with total perfection, one must also redouble the trill on the note marked with a dot above it, with such delicacy that this redoubling is accompanied by an extraordinary softening <note>original: "adouciſſement"; a vocal ornament involving a slight swelling or sweetening of the tone</note>, which contains the greatest charms of the song at hand.

After one knows how to make these shakes, which also serve for all sorts of passages, one must learn to make the <term>vocal glides</term> <note>original: "ports de la voix"; literally "carriages of the voice," a technique of sliding smoothly between notes.</note>, which make Songs and Recitatives <note>original: "Recits"</note> very agreeable. These alone, when well executed, make a voice commendable even if it cannot perform trills (whether "hammered" or not). For the mind receives a singular contentment when it considers a voice that carries itself as it should through all sorts of degrees and intervals, and which, holding firm on the principal notes of the mode that animate the song, seems to charm and transport the ear and the mind of the listeners. However, these vocal glides are not marked in printed books; this can be done by placing a dot after the note on which one begins the glide, and then adding a quarter note, eighth note, or sixteenth note after the dot, which signifies that one must only lightly touch the preceding note to begin the note that follows. This will be better understood by the three preceding examples of the note, of which the first shows how one must carry the voice from C to D <note>original: "vt" to "ré"</note>; the second shows how it is carried from E to F <note>original: "mi" to "fa"</note>; and the third from

This, however, must only be done when appropriate, and in places where <term>ports de voix</term><note>literally "carriages of the voice," a vocal slide or portamento</note> have grace. The same must be concluded regarding <term>fredons</term><note>rapid divisions or warbles</note>, <term>roulemens</term><note>runs or melismas</note>, <term>martelemens</term><note>hammered repetitions of a note</note>, <term>tremblemens</term><note>trills or shakes</note>, and <term>adouciſſemens</term><note>sweetenings or softenings</note> of the throat and the voice. Here it must be noted that the Masters use different characters to signify the places and notes where the trills should be made: for example, Baillif, Boësset, and Moulinié <note>Jean de Cambefort dit Baillif, Antoine Boësset, and Étienne Moulinié were prominent composers of the French "air de cour"</note> place a cross or a double cross over the note upon which they wish one to perform a simple cadence, or two, three, or four trills; and another character in the form of the letter *m*, or a sharp sign, when it is necessary to double the cadence or multiply the trills.

One may use several other characters to signify other <term>accidents</term><note>expressive nuances or ornaments</note> of the recitatives, such as this small straight line, |, or this accent, ', to signify that one must perform the "plaintive accent" on the accented note, by raising the note slightly at the end of the pronunciation and giving it a little point, which passes so quickly that it is quite difficult to perceive; but it must only be raised by a semitone, which consists of a small effort of the voice. As for the Italians, they observe several things in their recitatives of which ours are deprived, because they represent as much as they can the passions and affections of the soul and the spirit; for example, anger, fury, spite, rage, faintness of heart, and several other passions, with a violence so strange that one would almost judge that they are touched by the same affections they represent in singing; whereas our Frenchmen content themselves with flattering the ear, and use a perpetual sweetness in their songs, which hinders their energy.

### ADVICE
For Masters who teach singing: wherein Italian Airs are discussed.

One of the great perfections of singing consists in pronouncing the words well, and in making them so distinct that the listeners do not lose a single syllable; this is noted in the recitatives of Baillif, who pronounces very distinctly and makes every syllable sound, whereas most others stifle them in the throat and press them so hard between the tongue, the teeth, and the lips that one hears almost nothing of what they recite, either for lack of opening the mouth enough or of moving the tongue as is necessary. This is what Masters must study, so that their students do them honor, and so that the Pages and other children who must sing before the King and in the Churches pronounce as well while singing as if they were simply speaking, and so that their recitatives have the same effect as a speech distinctly delivered. And for this reason, they must teach them the manner of pronouncing the five vowels *a, e, i, o, u* equally well while performing cadences and runs. Now, one of the things lacking in ordinary Masters comes from the fact that they do not themselves have good voices suitable for reciting and for executing the beauties that embellish the airs, and that they do not pronounce each syllable well enough to make—

### of Songs.

make their students perform the same things; so they are like those who would want to teach how to write well before knowing how to write well themselves. Furthermore, they should have traveled to foreign countries, and particularly to Italy, where they pride themselves on singing well and knowing Music much better than the French. For although everything they do is perhaps not to be approved of, it is nevertheless certain that they have something excellent in their recitatives <note>original: *recits* — a style of singing that mimics the rhythms of speech</note>, which they animate much more powerfully than our singers do, who surpass them in delicacy <note>original: *mignardise* — a term implying a dainty, refined, or even affected sweetness</note>, but not in vigor. Those who do not have the convenience of traveling can at least read Giulio Caccini, called "the Roman," who had a book printed on the *Art of Good Singing* in Florence in the year 1621. In this book, he distinguishes the passages proper to instruments from those that serve the voice, and divides the principal beauties of Songs into the **increasing and decreasing of the voice** <note>original: *augmentation & affoiblissement de la voix*, which he calls *Crescere, e scemare della voce*</note>, into **exclamations**, and into two sorts of passages which he names **trills** and **groups** <note>original: *Trillo* and *Gruppi*</note>, which correspond to our passages, rapid divisions, shakes, and throat-beats <note>original: *passages, fredons, tremblemens, & batemens de gorge*</note>. He adds that one must only perform the passages and the rolls of the voice on syllables that are long, and that the voice must be weakened or reinforced on certain syllables to express the passion of the subject; this is something one does naturally with very little judgment, even without having learned it. 

But our singers imagine that the exclamations and the accents that the Italians use in singing savor too much of Tragedy or Comedy; that is why they do not wish to perform them, even though they ought to imitate what they have that is good and excellent. For it is easy to temper the exclamations and to accommodate them to French sweetness, so as to add their most pathetic <note>In the 17th-century sense: "full of pathos" or emotionally moving</note> qualities to the beauty, clarity, and the softening of the cadences <note>or "falls" at the end of musical phrases</note> that our musicians perform with good grace when, having a good voice, they have learned the method of singing well from good Masters. The aforementioned Giulio joined his <term>chitarrone</term> <note>a large, long-necked lute used for accompaniment</note> to his voice in order to provide a <term>perpetual bass</term> <note>basso continuo</note>, as they still do now in Italy, where they almost always have a small organ or a <term>theorbo</term> <note>another type of large lute</note> in the recitatives they perform on stage when they represent <note>The nasal abbreviation mark over the 'e' indicates 'representent'.</note> some Comedy or some famous action. This can be seen in the *Flora* of Andrea Salvadori, which was performed in Florence <note>Nasal abbreviation for 'Florence'.</note> at the wedding of the Duke of Parma and Princess Marguerite, with such preparation that those who were spectators testify to having never heard nor seen anything like it—whether for the beauty of the recitatives that each character performed while speaking and singing on the stage, or for the majesty of the verses, or for the riches and the machines that represented lightning, thunder, and other storms with such perfection that the spectators remained astonished and ravished.

Giacomo Peri had begun in the year 1600 in Florence, during the wedding of the Queen Mother, to introduce the manner of reciting verses in Music upon the stage; this was followed by the *Flora* of which I just spoke in the year 1628; and the *Musical Drama of Saint Alexis*, performed in Rome in the year 1634, was the last piece of consequence seen with a very particular satisfaction. But our musicians are, as a whole, too timid to introduce this manner of recitative in France, even though they would be just as capable of it as the Italians, if someone were to push them and were willing to provide the expenditure required for such a subject.

# Embellishment

I return to the cadences and exclamations, which can be performed in an infinite number of ways, there being nothing so strictly regulated in matters that depend on the opinion and fancy of men that one cannot always add to them. Those who love a multitude of **passages** <note>original: *passages* — rapid melodic runs or "divisions" used to decorate a melody</note> and **diminutions** <note>original: *diminutions* — the technique of breaking a long note into many shorter, faster notes</note> may read those of Ignazio Donati; the 156 *passages* or **glosses** <note>original: *glosados* — a Spanish term for ornamented musical lines</note> of Pietro Cerone, in the 5th chapter of his 8th book; those of the *Fontegara* <note>OCR: *Fonregara*</note> by Silvestro di Ganassi, who fills 120 pages with these passages suited for flutes; and several others, particularly *The New Music* <note>original: *Le nuove Musiche*</note> by Giulio Caccini, of whom I spoke above. But it is enough to consider the examples that we will give at the end of this book, because they can serve as a model for posterity to show the manner of adorning and embellishing **Airs** <term>Air: a song or melody, specifically a refined vocal composition</term>, for it seems we have never proceeded with as much skill and refinement as we do now.

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*To explain the characters necessary to signify all the particularities of the Airs and Songs that one desires to perform with every kind of perfection; and the manner of properly performing cadences and shakes.*<-

I have already explained some signs or characters which are ordinarily used to signify and teach the manner in which they should be sung; but because they do not have much relationship with the movements of the voice they signify, we must see if better ones can be invented, particularly in the new way of writing Music with letters of which I spoke in the 2nd Proposition. I say first, then, that one can mark the **port de la voix** <term>port de la voix: literally "carrying of the voice," a technique similar to a portamento or a graceful slide between two notes</term>, which I explain in the preceding Proposition, with the line that follows the note, or the letter, upon which the said "port" begins, as is seen in this example, **DO-RE** <note>original: *VT-RE* — using the Guidonian hexachord system where "Ut" is the first note, now commonly called "Do"</note>. One can also mark this "port" by putting no distance or comma between the **V** and the **R** in this fashion, **VT RE**, or **VR**, or else by putting a line above or below the two letters, to signify that the voice must pass from **DO** to **RE**, lightly striking the **RE** on a [certain] place <note>Possibly an abbreviation for *lieu* (place) or *livre* (book).</note>, and rising softly, as if by a continuous movement, until the string [note] of **RE**.

In the second place, the **shakes** <note>original: *tremblemens* — rapid alternations between two adjacent notes, similar to a trill</note> which must be made on the note of the cadence where one must shake, will be very well expressed by a star, which has as many rays as there are shakes to be made; for example, if one must shake six times on the second letter or note **SOL** of this cadence **LA, SOL, FA**, it will be necessary to mark this shake by this star \*, putting it above or beside the letter, in this fashion: **LA, S\*OL, FA**. But because we do not have stars with 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, and 16 rays, one could supplement them with numbers; for an **8** placed over the letter or note where one must shake will show 8 shakes, and so on for the others. As for the **plaints** <note>original: *plaintes* — expressive, sigh-like ornaments</note> or **sighs**, the small point used by some Masters is quite suitable for that.

In the third place, there are many passions that one can make appear while singing, for which characters have not yet been invented, such as the great **exclamations** <note>original: *exclamations* — an Italian vocal technique, *esclamazione*, involving a forceful start on a note followed by a decrescendo and then a crescendo</note> of the Italian Airs, and the representations of the fainting of the heart; it seems that if the circumflex accent were not [already] em...

# Of Songs.

If the symbol used for **semiquavers** <term>semiquaver: a sixteenth note, known in the original as a *double crochuë*</term> in the second proposition were used, it would be fit to represent those great cries and vocal excesses, because it is composed of the acute and grave accents—just as the exclamation of despair and grief is composed of a sudden burst of voice and a small residue that descends to the **Third**, the **Fourth**, the **minor Sixth**, or other intervals, according to its magnitude and the power of the singing voice. However, I shall speak more fully of the characters suited for expressing anger, sadness, and other passions in the third part of this book.

In the fourth place, we lack characters to indicate notes or syllables that should be sung more loudly, just as one hears **bow strokes** <term>bow strokes: the movement of a bow across the strings of an instrument like a violin or viol</term> much stronger than others. And because the voice has as many degrees of force as there are intervals, we can divide this force into eight degrees, just as heat and other qualities are divided. Thus, the first degree would be fit for expressing very faint echoes, and the seven other degrees would signify the different levels of the most vehement passions, up to the eighth, which would represent the greatest exclamation possible—such as that of despair or some great mental or physical pain, like that which we imagine of Esau when he roared and cried out while asking for the blessing of his father Isaac. Now, these different degrees of force could be indicated by numbers, or by as many dots or accents; but because these have already served us for other purposes, it would be necessary to add new characters, although if we retain the ordinary use of notes, which carry the value of time with them, numbers could serve to mark the differences in the strength of the voice.

In the fifth place, if one wishes to regulate and write **Airs** <term>Air: a song or melody, specifically a refined vocal composition</term> so that everything required for their perfect execution is understood, the time of the meter must be marked; and if the composer intends for one or more notes and measures to be longer or shorter than usual, he must mark it with particular signs. Otherwise, one cannot perform the song according to his intention, as is experienced with Italian Airs, which are never sung according to the composer’s design unless they are first heard performed according to his method and spirit. This can be adapted in some way to **orations** <note>original: *Harangues* — formal public speeches or rhetorical addresses</note>, for certain characters could be used to signify the manner of reciting them to perfection.

It would, nevertheless, be more appropriate to always use each note in its own proper value to avoid so many different characters; for example, when one wants a **quarter note** <note>original: *noire* — literally a "black" note, known today as a crotchet</note> to last as long as a **whole note** <note>original: *semibreve*</note>, one should use that whole note instead of the quarter note, and likewise for the others. I leave aside several other things concerning the ornament and embellishment of Airs, because it is easy to imagine them by reading all that we have said about the **trills of the lute** <note>original: *tremblemens du Leut*</note> in the ninth Proposition of the book on instruments. I add only in favor of **cadences** <term>cadence: a musical sequence that concludes a phrase, often decorated with a trill</term> that one must stabilize the **trill** <note>original: *tremblement* — a rapid alternation between two notes, also called a "shake"</note> that must be made upon the note before starting it, and that one performs more of them as the note is longer. For example, one will make two on the **quaver** <note>original: *crochüe* — an eighth note</note>, four on the **quarter note** <note>original: *noire*</note>, eight on the **half note** <note>original: *blanche à queüe* — literally a "white note with a tail," known as a minim</note>, and sixteen on the **whole note** <note>original: *semibreve*</note>—though this number is not so strictly regulated that one cannot do more or less, according to the disposition of the voice. One does not stabilize, nonetheless...

# Embellishment

...less of a trill on an **eighth note** <term>eighth note: a note with a single hook, known in the original as a *crochüe*</term>, because it lasts for too little time. But cadences <note>In this period, *cadence* often referred to a trill or vocal ornament as well as a harmonic conclusion.</note> must be well-marked and sufficiently "hammered" <note>original: *martelées*; this implies a clear, rhythmic articulation of the trill’s oscillations</note>, lest they become too confused. However, those who perform them to perfection, by redoubling them on the **antepenultimate note** <term>antepenultimate: the third-to-last note in a musical phrase</term>, go so fast and so delicately that it is difficult to count the percussions of the air made by the throat, or to notice if the voice changes its pitch. When the cadence and the tremolos <note>original: *tremblemens*; a rapid alternation between two notes</note> are performed on a **sharpened note**, one must hold it as high as possible, as if one were descending by only a quarter-tone, and as if one were making only an **enharmonic diesis** <term>enharmonic diesis: the smallest interval in ancient Greek music theory, roughly a quarter of a whole tone</term> instead of a semitone.

### NOTICE.

It is not necessary to provide examples here for cadences, passages, and trills, because I have given enough of them in the **diminution** <term>diminution: the practice of breaking long notes into many fast, decorative notes</term> of the **Violin Treble**, which can be seen in the 4th Proposition of the 4th book on Instruments, and in the diminution of the *Air du Roy* <note>The "King's Air," likely a well-known courtly melody of the time</note>, placed in the 41st Proposition of the 6th book on Organs. Furthermore, one finds as many as one wishes in the Airs that **Mr. Ballard** <note>Robert Ballard (c. 1572–1650), the head of the sole music publishing house in Paris authorized by the King</note> prints every day; this is why I conclude the second part of this book with the Proposition that follows, for the sake of beautiful Songs.

## PROPOSITION VII.

->*To explain the Art and the method of creating good Songs, or Airs,*<-
->*on all sorts of subjects and lyrics.*<-

The Art of making good Songs on all sorts of subjects depends not only on the genius, the whim, and the inclination of those who compose them, but also on the judgment that must serve as a guide to Composers—as it does to other Artisans—in everything they undertake. This is so that they can provide the reasoning for the pitches, the steps, the intervals, the passages, and the trills that they employ in their compositions. Now, I assume here what I have already said regarding the rules necessary for making good Songs in the 5th and 6th Propositions of the Book on Songs, one of which pertains to **Melody**, and the other to **Measure**, which the Greeks call **Rhythmic**.

As for Melody, there is no need to explain its steps and intervals, since that has been done so exactly in the Book on Genres, in the one on **Consonances** and **Dissonances**, and in the 2nd book on Instruments; one can desire nothing more than the judgment to use them appropriately according to the different subjects that present themselves. For example, sad and amorous matters are very well explained by **major, mean, and minor semitones**, and even better by **Enharmonic Diesises**, if one were willing to accustom the voice to them. Similarly, the **minor Third**, which follows the nature of the semitone, and the **minor Sixth** are well-suited for expressing great laments and grief. Things that lean toward the grand and the harsh, or the rustic—such as martial and vigorous actions—are better represented by whole tones, and by **major Thirds and Sixths**, or by the **perfect or augmented Fourth**. I shall say no more about the embellishment of Melody, because it suffices to remark that if French Airs have some...

# On Songs

<center>### On Songs. ###</center>

...something commendable and particular over those of Italy, Germany, and Spain; this depends on the cadences and the trills <note>original: *tremblemens*; in this period, these are rapid oscillations between notes used for expression</note>, which those who sing well—such as the Bailiff <note>Henry Le Bailly (d. 1637), a celebrated singer and composer at the court of Louis XIII, known for his expressive style</note>—are accustomed to using when performing cadences and divisions <term>divisions: the practice of breaking long notes into many fast, decorative notes, also called "passages"</term>. At such moments, the voice possesses a great sweetness and redoubles all its charms. In my opinion, it is impossible to explain this clearly enough for those who have not heard such fine voices to understand. I also omit the various movements, an abridgment of which can be seen at the end of the final Proposition of the *Book of Songs*, because I treat them in the fourth part of this book. Furthermore, the examples I have given of all sorts of airs, dances, and ballets from the 23rd Proposition until the end of said book, and in all the books on Instruments, as well as those found from page 1632 to 1665 of the *Harmonic Question of Genesis* <note>original: *Queſtion Harmonique de la Geneſe*; a reference to Marin Mersenne’s own philosophical and scientific commentary on the Bible</note>, are sufficient to provide an understanding of the movements proper for Airs.

This being established, I say that one must consider the entire text <note>original: *la lettre*; referring to the lyrics or poetry of the song</note> and the design or intention of what it contains—and where it leads the mind—in order to accommodate it with a melody <note>original: *modulation*</note> and movements so fitting that, when sung, it has at least as much power over the listeners as if it were recited by an excellent Orator. This is so that the Composer, or rather the Singer, may bend and move their minds toward whatever he desires. For this reason, the said Composer must mark all the places in the song where the voice must be strengthened or softened, and where the accents of the passions <note>The "passions" refers to the theory of affects, where music was intended to evoke specific emotions like joy, sorrow, or anger</note> (which we shall treat later) must be made, so that the singer punctually follows the Composer’s design.

One must also notice the pitch at which the voice must begin, for experience shows that songs recited at certain pitches are much more agreeable and have more effect on the listeners than when they are sung at a pitch that is higher or lower. Now, it is easy to mark the proper pitch for each voice and each air, if one understands what I said in the 18th Proposition of the 3rd book on Instruments. To this I add only that there are certain pitches more natural, and consequently easier to sing, than others—such as that which the Greeks called the *Mese* <note>original: *Meſe*; the "middle" note in the Ancient Greek musical system, serving as a functional center</note>, which is to say the 8th string of their 15-string system. One may therefore call it the *Dominant* <term>Dominant: here meaning a reciting tone or a note that predominates in a melody, rather than the modern harmonic definition</term>, because the voice must touch this string more often than the others, which are touched almost only to make this one seem more excellent and to prevent it from becoming tedious. One can therefore consider this pitch as the fundamental of the Song, just as one considers the *mean* or *middle* <note>original: *medium* or *milieu*</note> in syllogisms <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note>, the Equator between the Tropics, and virtue between vices. It is this pitch that is often used in anger and other passions, and which Orators use most ordinarily in their Speeches.

But there is yet another thing in Airs that is more difficult to mark and to execute in singing than all that we have said until now: namely, a certain majesty that accompanies the pleasantness of the song and the harmony of the voice. This quality ensures that the same song possesses a "certain something" <note>original: *ie ne ſçay quoy*</note> that partakes of the grand and the beautiful, as happens with almost all other things that can be executed by human industry and which consist in action. This occurs in Dances, and in the manner of holding oneself on a horse, which gave rise to the term *Good and handsome horseman* in the Academy of Pluvinel <note>Antoine de Pluvinel (1552–1620), a famous French riding master who taught Louis XIII</note>. This is also observed in Perspectives, in paint—

# Embellishment

...paintings, in buildings, and everywhere else where there are things that possess grandeur and beauty. From this it follows that the simplest garment appears better on a well-formed body than the richest one in the world on a poorly-formed body. This can be understood, in a way, by the sound of a bell struck by a hammer; for it does not have the grace and harmony of the sound it makes when it is rung in full swing <note>original: *sonnée en branle*; this refers to the rich, complex resonance created when a bell is swung back and forth rather than simply being hit while stationary</note>. Almost the same thing occurs with all sorts of instruments, among which some are found to have a sound that is sweet, mellow, and harmonious. Thus, the sound of good bells—which have nothing sour or piercing about them, and which produce the Octave, the Major Tenth, and the Twelfth, as occurs particularly with the largest ones—powerfully strikes the spirit, which they charm and soften with their sweet murmur.

And if one is attentive to the sounds of every string on each instrument, one will find that there is always one that is the fullest, the most mellow, and the sweetest of all, and which possesses grandeur and beauty; this is why it is made to be heard very often. Now, it is particularly on this tone that Singers <term>Chantres: vocalists or cantors, particularly those trained in church or court music</term> must dwell, or which they must repeat most often, because the voice has more strength and vigor there, and even more sweetness. But it must be admitted that the accents of passion are most often lacking in French Airs <note>original: *Airs François*; the "Air de cour" was the predominant secular vocal genre in 17th-century France, known for its refinement</note>, because our Singers are content to tickle the ear and to please through their delicacies <term>mignardises: dainty, affected, or overly sweet vocal ornaments</term>, without caring to excite the passions of their listeners according to the subject and the intention of the lyrics <note>original: *la lettre*; refers to the poetic text being set to music</note>. Nor do they possess that majesty which arises from the beauty and grandeur of which I have spoken; and the Song does not always express the meaning of the words, for which one must take very particular care. I include many other things in the Proposition that follows to help in the creation of good Songs.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*To discover the techniques that serve to find and to compose good Songs and Airs of all sorts of styles.*<-

**One** of the great difficulties faced by Composers of Airs consists in avoiding repetitions and in finding Songs that have not yet been made. For if someone were to fall back into the same song as another, it would be judged that he was not its inventor, because Composers believe it is almost impossible for two or more people to create the same Song on a proposed subject, so great is the variety and difference in Music. This is similarly observed in Latin or French writing styles, in which one almost never encounters two identical works in all things; so that if one gives a theme to a thousand students in the same class, or if a thousand Orators describe some subject, all their themes and all their descriptions will be different and will not agree in every respect. This also happens with the versions of authors translated from one language to another, such as from Greek or Latin into French; in Paintings, Sculptures, Handwritings, and in everything consisting of action. However, the same person falls back more easily into the same Songs that they themselves have composed; thus, one of the greatest techniques <term>industries: creative skills or ingenious methods</term> of Composers depends on variety. I say, therefore, that there are several very useful things for always finding new Songs on the same subject, and...

# Of Melodies

...on the same note, as well as on different subjects: one of the principal methods is a **perfect knowledge of the fingerboard** of the Lute, the Viol, and the Violin, or the **Keyboard** of the Organ and the Spinet. This greatly aided Claudin <note>original: *Claudin*; likely referring to either Claudin de Sermisy (c. 1490–1562) or Claude Le Jeune (c. 1528–1600), both celebrated for their melodic grace</note> in creating the beautiful Melodies that one admires in his works. For it is easy to notice the beautiful strings <note>In this context, *chordes* refers to both the physical strings and the resulting harmonic intervals</note> that produce the best effects by testing and touching the aforementioned instruments.

The second method consists of **imitation**, and in the reading and consideration of the Airs and Melodies of those who have succeeded best in this matter. Among the French, these include Claudin, Guédron, Boësset, Chancy, Moulinié, etc. For just as those who wish to learn to compose in Latin read and imitate Cicero—turning his Latin into French, and then putting the French back into Latin until they can restore it in the same terms, thereby imprinting that style upon their minds and making the character of that Orator familiar to themselves—and just as those who wish to learn to compose in <term>Counterpoint: the art of combining different melodic lines</term>, both simple and figured, find nothing more advantageous than to read, score, and imitate the works of Eustache de Caurroy <note>A hugely influential composer of the French late Renaissance, known for his rigorous contrapuntal skill</note> until they have made familiar his excellent way of setting down and employing chords, and of mixing in **Dissonances** in such a way that they highlight the **Consonances** (just as shadows highlight colors); in the same way, those who wish to learn to make good Airs must so thoroughly imitate the best Masters—such as the Sieur Boësset, whom all of France considers a **Phoenix** in this matter—that they clothe themselves in their spirit until they possess a similar vein and genius.

The third thing is that one must well consider, understand, and **express the sense and intention of the words** and of the subject, in order to accentuate and animate it in such a way that each part produces the full effect of which it is capable. This happens particularly when the Composer is himself struck by the feeling he desires to imprint upon the minds of his listeners while creating and singing his Airs. Just as an orator has more power over his audience when he feels moved and entirely persuaded by his own reasons, this is also seen in those who have recourse to God for their illnesses and other necessities; for they feel themselves warmed and moved by certain extraordinary internal movements, which make them perceive and believe that their healing is near, and that divine goodness is beginning to help them.

The fourth thing that can help in making good Melodies, and particularly in varying them and avoiding repetition, depends on the consideration of **all possible Melodies** that can be made within the range of sounds, strings, or notes that one proposes. For example, when one chooses the range of a <term>Major or Minor Sixth: an interval encompassing six notes of the scale</term>, it is difficult not to find good Melodies there if one reads the 9th Proposition of the *Book of Songs* <note>Referring to another section of this same treatise</note>, since it contains all the possible modulations of that range; thus, one has only to choose the modulation judged most proper to express the proposed words.

And if one wishes to use the range of the **Octave**, all the possible Melodies found within the range of the eight strings of the <term>Diapason: here meaning the full span of an octave</term> (which I will communicate to those who desire them) can serve the same purpose; for besides each variety, they may repeat such notes as they please...

...or leave aside those they do not need. To which one may also relate the consideration of all possible **movements** <note>original: *mouuemens*; in this context, it refers to rhythmic patterns, tempos, and the "motion" of the melody</note>, joining them to the aforementioned modulations and varieties: of which I have provided an example in the 19th Proposition of the same book on Songs. Additionally, if someone is not satisfied with the ordinary degrees and intervals of the voice, or those of the standard keyboards of the **Organ**, they may practice all the others that I have explained in the 5th, 6th, and 8th Propositions of the 2nd book on Instruments, and in the 3rd book on Genres, where one may see everything that can be desired in this matter.

# NOTICE
## *Regarding Beautiful Melodies.*

Whatever rules and methods one may give for composing good and beautiful **Airs** <note>The *Air de cour* was the prestigious secular vocal genre in 17th-century France</note> upon all sorts of subjects and lyrics, it seems they cannot reach as far as the happy genius and natural inclination of those who create excellent ones without having learned or established any rules other than those provided by their imagination. This is easily concluded by the Songs of several **Organists** and players of the **Spinet** and **Lute**, who cannot create as good or as beautiful Airs as those of **Guédron** and **Boësset** <note>Pierre Guédron (c. 1570–1620) and Antoine Boësset (1587–1643) were the preeminent masters of the French courtly air</note>, even though they know the keyboard or the neck of the said instruments better than they do.

I know there are some who imagine that the Musicians of **Greece** <note>referring to Ancient Greek music theorists</note> so thoroughly understood the Genre and Species of Music, as well as the Tone, the Mode, and all the intervals or degrees that had to be used for every letter, and that they chose the species of meter, verse, and movements so perfectly, that one could not do better. But they will excuse me, if they please, from embracing this sentiment until they have at least shown me the possibility of this Art. 

In the meantime, I shall be of the opinion of those who say that the **Genius of Music** is similar to that of the Poet, the Painter, the Orator, and several other Artisans, to whom Nature—or rather the **Master of Nature** <note>A common theological reference to God as the ultimate creator</note>—has distributed certain gifts which Art <note>Here meaning "skill" or "learned technique"</note> cannot attain. It is not that I would not be of the contrary opinion if I believed one could establish a certain Art by which one could know which sounds, degrees, intervals, and movements must be used to produce a given effect in the mind or upon the body of the listeners; but I cannot persuade myself that the Greeks had this knowledge, since it is easy enough to judge that the most excellent men of Greece—namely **Hippocrates**, **Plato**, **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and the others—did not have it, and even that we know as much or more than they on this subject. 

Be that as it may, the keyboard of a small cabinet of wind or string organs can serve not only to create good Melodies, but also to examine all sorts of musical pieces in 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 parts, etc., whereas those who cannot play the keyboard need several people to test their compositions. I leave aside a thousand particulars that could be added to teach how to make good Melodies—whether regarding the melody itself, in order to touch the beautiful strings of the **Mode**, to mix them, and to return to the said Mode so appropriately after leaving it that the listener is ravished; or regarding the beautiful movements, which alone can make one notice in the Songs a certain majesty that partakes of the grand and the beautiful, as I have already remarked.

<summary>Mersenne argues that while technical rules and instruments like the keyboard are useful for testing music, true melodic beauty stems from "natural genius" rather than mere theory. He expresses skepticism that Ancient Greek musicians possessed a lost, perfect "art" of affecting the human soul that surpassed modern knowledge.</summary>
