# PART III.
## On Accentual Music.

---

This branch of Music will perhaps seem new to many, even though it is practiced by those who sing with perfection, and it fulfills the Art of the <term>Harmonic Orator</term><note>A speaker who applies musical principles of pitch, rhythm, and inflection to speech to better persuade or move an audience.</note>, who must know all the degrees, timings, movements, and proper accents to stir his listeners to whatever he wishes. This was done by Timotheus <note>Timotheus of Miletus (c. 446–357 BC), a celebrated Greek musician famous for his innovative and emotionally powerful style.</note> and the Danish Musician mentioned by Albert Krantz in the 5th book of his history of <note>original: "la Danie"</note> Denmark, chapter 3. There is no need to repeat that story here, as I have recounted it along with several others in the first Article of the 57th question on <note>original: "la Genese"</note> Genesis <note>This refers to Marin Mersenne’s own massive scholarly work, *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim* (1623), where he discusses the effects of music.</note>. Now, I follow the order and number of the preceding Propositions in order to continue this book by explaining everything concerning the Accents of the passions. This will greatly help in perfecting all kinds of Songs, which must in some way imitate <term>Harangues</term><note>Formal, persuasive speeches or orations.</note> so that they have members, parts, and periods, and use all sorts of figures and harmonic passages just like the Orator. In this way, the Art of composing <term>Airs</term><note>Melodies or songs, specifically the "Air de cour" popular in the French court.</note> and Counterpoint shall yield nothing to Rhetoric.

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*The Accents of which we speak here are in such great number that it is almost*<-
->*impossible to express them all.*<-

Experience teaches us that there are almost as many differences in Accents as there are men, although one does not notice it unless one reflects on the different ways of speaking. Now, this variety arises from the infinity of parts into which the interval—through which speech passes from low to high, or from high to low—can be divided. For although the Octave is divided only into 5 whole tones and two semitones when one sings diatonically, nevertheless each semitone is further subdivided by speech into an infinity of tiny intervals that are often imperceptible; and every such division can change the accent.

The force of the voice also creates many differences in the same accents, which receive more vigor from the vehemence of the speech than from being high or low pitched. High and low pitches have almost no power unless they are accompanied by the said vehemence, or by the dying weakness of the voice, which creates the accents of sadness, as we shall discuss in another place.

As for the ordinary accents mentioned by the Greeks, the Latins, and other nations, they identify only three: namely the grave, the acute, and the circumflex. Alternatively, there are the accents of Grammar, Rhetoric, and Music used by the Hebrews, for which they have as much esteem as the Alchemists have for their "spirit-body" and "body-spirit" <note>Early modern theorists often compared consonants to the "body" and vowels or accents to the "soul" or "spirit" of language; the author suggests the Hebrews saw accents as the vitalizing force of the text.</note>. This is because, they say, the consonants are

### PROPOSITION X.

->*Accents reveal what country one is from, and sometimes one's temperament and mood.*<-

Experience shows that the Gascon <note>A person from Gascony, a province in Southwest France.</note> has a different accent from that of the Provençal <note>A person from Provence, in Southeast France.</note>, and that the Provençal has one different from the Norman. If we knew the accents used by the Chinese, the Arabs, the Spaniards, and all other nations, we could recognize them by their accent alone, even if they all spoke the same language; but we content ourselves with discerning them by the diversity of their idioms <term>Idiomes: distinct languages or regional dialects</term>, which is why the specific observation of their accents has not been made.

And experience teaches that those who are quick and abrupt in their actions, and who are bilious <note>In the theory of the Four Humors, a "bilious" or choleric temperament was associated with being irritable or quick-tempered.</note>, have an abrupt and sharp accent; and those who are melancholic have one that is grave, slow, and heavy. And just as there are as many different temperaments and different moods as there are men, so too are there as many different accents and different manners of speaking. For although two or more people may have been raised together, devoted themselves to the same exercises, and be from the same country, one nevertheless recognizes a difference in their accents, and in the "air" they give to their speech and their discourse. This, it seems, can only come from the difference in their moods and the diversity of their organs <note>Referring to the physical vocal apparatus</note>, which comes from the difference in their temperaments.

### PROPOSITION XI.

->*The accent of which we speak here is an inflection or modification of the voice, or of speech, by which one expresses passions and affections naturally, or by artifice.*<-

This proposition contains the description of the accent, the type of which is explained by these terms, *inflection, or modification*, which applies to discourse, to song, and to the voice, insofar as we flex the voice while speaking and singing; but the accent is a more particular modification of speech than of song, to which it is difficult to give all kinds of accents, as I shall say in another place.

The distinction of this definition is explained in these words: "by which one expresses," etc., for nature itself teaches us which accents must be used to show and signify our passions and our affections, which are only expressed by artifice <note>In this context, "artifice" refers to "art" or "skillful construction" rather than deception.</note> with simple speech or with song; for song and discourse depend on Art and instruction. But we cry, we shout, and we give certain accents to the voice and to words without having learned how to do so. Now, these accents of passion are common to men...

## PROPOSITION XII.

->*Every passion and affection of the soul has its own proper accents, by which its different degrees are explained.*<-

We experience every day that anger is expressed by an accent different from that of admiration or sadness. And if we follow the division of the passions of the soul made by the Philosophers, we shall establish eleven kinds of accents. For they posit eleven passions: namely, six in the concupiscible appetite <term>Concupiscible appetite: the faculty of the soul that seeks simple pleasures and avoids simple pains</term>, which resides in the right side of the heart, or in the liver, as the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy.</note> would have it; and five in the irascible appetite <term>Irascible appetite: the faculty of the soul that deals with difficult obstacles, leading to emotions like anger or courage</term>, which is on the left side of the heart, or in the gallbladder; or in other places according to this Latin distich <note>A poem of two lines.</note>,

> The heart knows, and the lung speaks, the gall rouses anger,
> The spleen makes one laugh, the liver compels one to love.
> <note>original: "Cor sapit, & pulmo loquitur, fel commouet iras, / Splen ridere facit, cogit amare iecur."</note>

The first passion of the concupiscible appetite, or of concupiscence, is love, which is the root of all passions; for we hate nothing except when we believe it opposes and is contrary to what we love. Thus, all the disorder of the passions is born from love, which is divided into desire and joy, following the different movements it gives to the soul.

Hatred is opposed to love, and progresses into flight and sadness, so that the six passions can be reduced to these two primary ones, since they follow a progression of love and hate; for we desire nothing, nor do we rejoice in any thing, except those things which we love; just as we flee nothing, and are saddened by nothing, except those things which we hate.

Hope, audacity (or boldness), anger, fear, and despair belong to the irascible appetite; but Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher.</note> reduces these five passions to two—namely, hope and fear—just as the six passions of the concupiscible appetite are reduced to joy and pain, as he teaches in these verses,

> Drive away joys,
> <note>original: "Gaudia pelle," a snippet from Boethius's "Consolation of Philosophy," where he advises subduing the emotions to reach a state of reason.</note>

In the first place, the heart expands, blossoms, and opens in joy and in hope, like the sunflower <note>original: "heliotrope"</note>, the rose, and the lily in the presence of the Sun. From this comes the ruddy complexion of the face, because of the vital spirits <term>vital spirits: in 17th-century medicine, these were believed to be subtle, air-like substances in the blood that carried life and feeling throughout the body</term> that the heart sends upward. It so happens that if joy is so great that the heart is left without a large enough quantity of these spirits, one falls into a faint, and sometimes one dies from laughing.

On the contrary, when sadness is excessive, these same spirits retreat to the heart in too great a multitude and stifle it, because it can no longer move nor open itself. Thus, these two passions are similar to the flux and reflux <note>the high and low tides</note> of the sea; for joy is like the incoming tide <note>flux</note> that brings a great quantity of stones, shells, and fish to the seashore; and joy brings a quantity of blood and spirits to the face and to other parts of the body. But fear and sorrow are like the outgoing tide <note>reflux</note> that withdraws what it had brought: for fear and terror make the face pale and the countenance dreary and hideous by withdrawing the blood and spirits. This causes melancholy <term>melancholy: literally "black bile," one of the four humors, thought to cause gloom and sluggishness when it dominated the body</term> to corrupt the little blood remaining in the veins, filling the imagination with terrifying dreams. It is therefore necessary that the accents by which we express the different affections and passions of the soul be different: some must imitate and represent the flow of spirits and blood, and others the retreat. The former should be prompt, lively, and gay, similar to the flowers and scents of Spring, while the latter should be similar to rain, snow, Winter, and everything disagreeable. The former should be like harmonies and concerts, and the latter like dissonances and troublesome noises; in short, the former have as many perfections as the latter have imperfections.

Now we must see if it is possible to establish 4 principal accents according to these 4 different passions; for the accents of which we speak here can be called the speech or the discourse of the passions, just as ordinary words and speech are called the discourse of the mind. The latter depends more on artifice than on nature, whereas the discourse of the passions depends more on nature than on artifice, and consequently, it is less subject to dissimulation than the former. As for the accent of joy, it is certain that it is different from that of sadness; but the accent of joy includes those of desire and love, just as a triangle includes two right angles, and as the soul...

### PROPOSITION XIII.

->*One cannot express the accents of the passions unless one uses some new*<-
->*characters.*<-

We have had no signs until now by which we might mark and signify the accents of the passions, and the ancients have left us only the grave, the acute, and the circumflex <note>Standard grammatical accents used in Greek and Latin prosody.</note>, along with those of admiration <note>The exclamation point (!).</note> and interrogation; this is why it is necessary to find characters that are suited to signify and express love, hatred, sadness, anger, indignation, and the other affections of the soul.

I recall that Physicians have invented new names to signify the 6 muscles that move the eye, and that they have called *proud* the one that pulls it upward, and *humble* the one that pulls it downward. The two that carry it toward the nose are named *amorous*, and those that pull it to the left are called *muscles of indignation*. To which one may add the one or those that create the tonic movement, whether it be done by a seventh muscle or by the mutual cooperation of the six others.

Astronomers have also made use of new characters to explain the 12 signs of the Zodiac, the seven Planets and their aspects; and the Chemists <note>Likely referring to Alchemists.</note>, the Egyptians, the Chinese, and all sorts of artisans are not rebuked when they invent new characters to explain the particular observations and difficulties of their art.

And Musicians themselves have used at all times and in all places particular notes to signify the high and low of sounds, and the length of measures, as one sees in the books of the Greeks, the Latins, and other nations. One must therefore take this same liberty to mark the accents of the passions: and for this subject I divide each passion into 3 degrees, just as Physicians divide the degrees of the primary qualities into 4 degrees, and Philosophers into 8. And for the sake of brevity, I will relate all the passions to three principal ones, namely to anger, to joy, and to sadness: for envy, jealousy, and hatred are mixed and composed of sadness and anger; love is a joy begun, and if the absence of what we love afflicts us, it is a sad love, or an amorous sadness.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

*All the accents used to express the three passions to which we have*
*referred the others, require 9 different characters to be explained and*
*understood: namely, 3 for the 3 degrees of anger, and just as many*
*for the degrees of love and sadness.*

The first degree of anger is noticed in the voice when it rises
a little higher, and when one speaks with more vehemence: and if one
touches the pulse <note>original: "poux" (pouls). The author links emotional intensity directly to heart rate.</note>, one will easily judge that the heart beats faster, or
stronger: but it would be necessary to observe if this beat is sesquialter <note>term: sesquialter (a ratio of 3:2). In music and mathematics of this period, this represents a specific proportional increase.</note> to the
natural beat, or if it keeps some other proportion, in order to establish the first
degree of anger, and to have its internal character through the movement of the
pulse, or by that of respiration, and its external character by the sharpness,
or the strength, and the speed of the voice.

And because this accent comes from bile <note>note: Referring to the "four humors" theory where yellow bile was thought to cause irascibility or anger.</note>, one could represent this
first degree of anger by a point of flame, or fire, or by some
other character that signifies by how many degrees one must raise, or
strengthen, and quicken the speech at the first degree of anger. This
could perhaps be done with the eighth notes and sixteenth notes <note>original: "crochuës, & fredons." These are musical notations for fast-moving notes.</note> of Music.

The 2nd degree of anger gives a stronger blow to reason, which begins
to yield to passion; this can be explained by two points
of flame: and if the pulse of the first degree of anger is sesquialter to the
natural, the pulse of the 2nd degree will be double the speed of the natural, and consequently
sesquialter to the beat made by the 2nd degree <note>note: The author is calculating mathematical ratios between emotional states.</note>: for the double ratio is
composed of the sesquialter and the sesquialter <note>note: In Pythagorean music theory, two 3:2 ratios (fifths) do not perfectly equal a double (octave), but the author is using these as symbolic proportions.</note>. It must nevertheless be noted
that the natural beat does not pass all at once to the 2nd degree; nor
that of the 2nd degree to that of the 3rd: but it suffices to have established the final
period of these degrees, which one can reach either all at once, or by several
intervals, just as one can go from the lowest sound to the Fifth, without
using degrees or with the ordinary degrees.

The 3rd degree of anger, which rises as far as fury, can be represented
by a flame with 3 points: now the heartbeat will be triple the natural
rate, either in speed, or in strength, or in both. To which can be related
the range of the voice, which hardly rises more than a Twelfth <note>term: Twelfth (an interval of an octave plus a fifth).</note> from the
tone of ordinary speech, used without passion, up to the cry of fury
and despair: for if the voice rises higher, it becomes hoarse, and
disagreeable, and should rather be called a yapping than a human voice. From
this it follows that those who have come to this degree no longer say a word, or if they
speak, or cry out, they lower the tone. And then it is difficult, and perhaps
naturally impossible, for the pulse to beat more than three times faster in
anger than out of it. But because one must avoid as much as possible the
novelty of characters, a sharp accent can signify the 1st degree of anger,
two the second, and 3 the third: or if one wishes to use particular
letters, they could carry with them such a point, or sign as one wishes,
by which those who read the discourse will be warned that it is necessary to pronounce
the end, or some other part of the period with the first, 2nd, or 3rd accent
of anger.

# On Songs.

The same must be said of the accents of passion, of joy, and of
sadness, which have their beginnings, their progress, and their ends, just like
anger, diseases, and the other things of this world: although the pulse
and the voice of these two passions are not as easy to explain as
those of anger. One can nevertheless establish for them accents and
characters in proportion to those of anger.
Some have believed that the passions caused the weight of the
body to change, and that a man who is in anger is lighter by 8 pounds per hundred
than when he is sad; by a thirteenth part when he is at the highest degree
of anger, and by a twenty-fifth when he is extremely joyful. But
these remarks, or rather these imaginations, are entirely false, for inflamma-
tion and death bring a greater alteration to iron and to the
human body than do all the passions of the soul to the body; and nevertheless the
living body is no lighter than the dead one, nor hot and inflamed iron
than cold, as we have experimented very exactly.

## PROPOSITION XV.

*To know if one can express the aforementioned passions while singing Music,*
*and if one can make all kinds of accents.*

This proposition is very difficult to explain; both because it seems
that Music desires certain delicacies and charms which
cannot coexist with the vehemence and the harshness of the passions, and par-
ticularly with anger: for as for the accents of sadness and of
grief, it is easy to make them by means of the semitone that the voice makes while
languishing: and this is almost the only accent of French airs, in which one also
mixes, sometimes quite appropriately, the accent of joy, of love, and of hope.
But the Italians have more vehemence than we do for expressing the
strongest passions of anger through their accents, particularly when
they sing their verses on the stage to imitate the Scenic Music <note>Theatrical or dramatic music</note>
of the ancients. Now, the accent of anger is made by precipitating the last
syllables and by reinforcing the last sounds; and if one reflects on the ele-
vation of the voice, one will notice that it is often raised by a whole tone,
a Third, and a Fourth, while pronouncing the last syllable of the words
that serve anger, and at other times by the same intervals, or by the
<term>Diapente</term> <note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth</note>, by leaning the voice on the antepenultimate syllable. But the man-
ners in which anger is expressed are so diverse that there is almost no inter-
val that it does not practice, following its different degrees and the other passions
that accompany it: so that the Musician must consider the time, the
place, the persons, and the subject for which the accent must be made, so that he
marks the syllable upon which the voice must lean, and which it must
raise and reinforce.
I have noticed that the tone of anger often rises by an entire Octave
or more all at once; which is difficult to perceive if one
does not try to put these musical intervals into practice by making the same inter-
vals slowly and little by little, so that the imagination has leisure to compre-

I leave the research of the characters necessary to mark this passion, and the others, to the Composers who desire to create songs in which nothing is lacking, and particularly those who intend to accentuate them in all sorts of ways: this will give such grace and such an air to the songs and to the recitals <note>The author uses "recits" to refer to solo vocal performances or declamations</note> that all who hear them will admit they are animated, and full of vigor and spirit, of which they are destitute without these accents. Now, if the Composer of Airs judges that he cannot create the accents of the passions with the ordinary intervals of the Diatonic and the Chromatic <term>Diatonic and Chromatic: The standard scales and note relationships used in Western music</term>, that is to say with the Music commonly used, it is easy for him to practice the enharmonic diesis <note>A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone</note>, which I explained in the book on Genres, and in that of Lutes and the Organ. For example, if he finds that the Major Third is too small to express some passion and its accent, he can increase it by whatever diesis he wishes; that is to say, by that which makes only a quarter of a tone, or that which makes a third of it, or by such other interval as he shall judge proper for his purpose. I wanted to add this so that one does not imagine that the Greeks had, or could have had, other degrees and intervals than those which we can use just as well as they in all sorts of encounters, leaving us no reason to doubt that they could have made better songs than ours, particularly if one applies to them everything we have said, and what we shall add in the fourth part of this book, after having placed the following Proposition in favor of Preachers.

### PROPOSITION XVI.
*To show the utility that Preachers and other Orators can derive from the Accents of each passion.*

It is certain that there are no men who deserve more that one should labor for them than <term>Preachers</term> <note>religious orators or ministers</note>, since they are in some way the <term>Ambassadors of heaven</term> and the <term>Fathers of souls</term>, whom they beget and nourish by the force of the <term>word of God</term>; this is why this proposition will be very well employed, however little it may help them. But because there are many who possess almost all the qualities one could desire in an excellent <term>Orator</term>, upon whom others may model themselves, I shall only touch in passing upon the aids they can draw from this <term>Treatise</term>: which they may expand as much as they please. I say then, first, that the Preacher must know the range and the strength of his voice—for example, if it can reach all the degrees of the <term>Diapason</term> <note>the full range or octave of the voice</note> easily enough to be heard on every degree. In the second place, he must note the place in which his voice has the most strength and vigor, in order to use it when explaining the threats of God and other words that require the tone of anger. But because threats are sometimes greater and at other times lesser, it is necessary to divide this tone, or rather this sound of the voice, into as many degrees as there are different threats, and rebukes or reprimands, in order to bring as much judgment to the <term>pronunciation</term> as to the choice and the order or arrangement of the words.

In the third place, he must study how to properly produce the <term>accents</term> of <term>passion</term> <note>emotional intensity or suffering</note>, without however overstepping the bounds of the modesty of a <term>Christian Orator</term>, for fear of making himself ridiculous and hindering the fruit of the divine word, which alone can pierce and penetrate the hearts of those who consider it attentively. Now, it is difficult to believe the power of different accents if one does not experience them; this power is so great that those who use them appropriately can make their listeners tremble, even if they speak to them only in jest and for pleasure. And perhaps our Lord pronounced these words *I am he* <note>original: "Ego sum"; the words of Jesus in the Garden of Gethsemane</note> with such an accent and such a tone that they were capable of making the <term>Soldiers</term> who sought to arrest him tremble and fall. For the spirit and the ear of the listeners have a certain relationship to tones and accents which are capable of shaking them, and which strike them so powerfully when the words meet them, that the Orator leads them wherever he wishes.

It is not necessary to speak of every degree of the voice proper for each Passion, since preachers, being ordinarily <term>Philosophers</term> and <term>Theologians</term>, can conclude all that must be held regarding them if they read this book and what we have said of the degrees and intervals of <term>Music</term> and the <term>Voice</term>: moreover, I shall give an entire Treatise on the aids and utilities that <term>Orators</term> can draw from <term>Universal Harmony</term>, and the manner in which they must avoid or imitate songs in their <term>Speeches</term> and in their <term>Sermons</term>.

### PART IV.
On Rhythmics, *or measured movements*, on *Prosody, and on Metrics.*

<image-desc>Large ornate initial 'E' at the beginning of the paragraph</image-desc>
I had no intention of adding anything further to what I have said regarding Rhythmics from the 19th Proposition of the Book of Songs until the end, and particularly in the 24th where I explain the movements of each kind of dance, and in the 27th where one sees 23 types of movements and rhythmic or metric feet <note>The "foot" is the basic unit of poetic meter, such as an iamb or dactyl</note>: but since I have not yet treated the various signs that are customarily used in Music to signify the diversity of time, and the different value of notes and sounds, and since it is certain that our French language is capable of making all sorts of measured verses suitable for Music, as I have already shown in the great Harmonic Question on Genesis; I set down the following Propositions in favor of Rhythmics, and the Metric Art.

Now, I have placed a table of Rhythmic movements on page 179 of the Book of Songs, which can supply what one might desire here for French Prosody <note>The study of the rhythm and intonation of language</note>, which contains the Rhythmics necessary for all sorts of meters or measured verses suitable for making Airs <note>A type of song or light vocal piece</note>: I only add here that the Rhythmic Art has an extent as great as the numbers applied to the objects of sight, hearing, and touch; so that the understanding, which considers intellectual numbers in their purity, descends to the matter which accompanies them, and which makes them sensible, in order to raise it in some way to an intellectual and reasoning being, and to disengage it from alteration, mutability, and corruption.

### PROPOSITION XVII.
*Rhythmics is an Art which considers movements, and which regulates their sequence and their mixture to excite the passions, and to maintain them, or to increase, diminish, or appease them.*

<image-desc>Large ornate initial 'C' at the beginning of the paragraph</image-desc>
This description contains the principal effects and the highest design of Rhythmics, whether one considers it speculatively, or as a Practice; for those who use it on Drums and Trumpets, in dances and ballets, in Songs, and in verses, etc., have no other intention than to please the listeners and spectators, or to excite them to some passion or affection, whether of joy or sadness, and of love, or of hatred, etc. From this it comes that good Poets, like Virgil, use prompt movements represented by short syllables, by Dactyls, Anapests, and other similar feet to give a similar impulse, or a similar imagination to the reader or the listener. Now I hope that one

# On Songs.

One will easily understand the six books of the <term>Rhythm-Metrics</term> <note>original: "Rythmo-Metrique"</note> of Saint Augustine, and those of Terentianus, Hephaestion, Aristides Quintilianus, Martianus Capella, and others, by reading this fourth part, which contains all that is best and most significant from them on this subject. It is certain that these movements, when well-regulated and arranged, have a great power over the mind, or over the blood and the other humors, since many feel moved to sing and dance to the cadence when they see this exercise, even if they had no intention of doing so; and just as we often yawn upon seeing others yawn, one finds oneself also singing, leaping, or dancing without any preceding deliberation, as imitating nature precedes many of its movements. From this, it is easy to conclude that he who gives the most beautiful movements to his Airs, and who best impresses the passion of the lyrics upon the listeners, ought to be preferred above all others. 

But it seems as difficult to prescribe what the sequence of said movements should be to excite the listeners to a given passion, as it is to provide harmonic intervals and their sequence—that is to say, as it is to compose songs proper for the same end. And although one does not entirely change the species or the genre of the movement when one uses 2, 4, 8, or 16 <term>eighth notes</term> <note>original: "notes crochues"</note>, or sixteenth and thirty-second notes, instead of a half or quarter note, the effect is nevertheless different in proportion as this diminution distances the slower movements from their simplicity; it often causes one to no longer understand the species of the movement. This is similar to how it is much more difficult to understand a ratio explained in large numbers than when it is contained in its essential, primitive, and radical terms; for example, the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio of 9:8, which defines a whole tone in music theory.</note> ratio of the major tone is more difficult to understand as 36 to 32 than as 9 to 8, which differ only by a single unit. 

Now, if French Musicians and Poets do not wish to, or cannot, accustom themselves to the names that Greek and Latin Authors have given to movements or to feet and verses, they may change them; for example, they can name the <term>Pyrrhic-Anapest</term> the movement or cadence with which the French march is expressed on the Drum, because it is beaten in this fashion: u u u —. One can see the other feet and all kinds of verse explained by musical notes in the 5th, 6th, and 7th books of Salinas, and everything I have said regarding <term>Rhythmic and Metric feet</term> in the first <term>Theorem</term> of the 2nd book of the <term>Treatise on Universal Harmony</term> <note>Mersenne's own monumental work, "Harmonie Universelle" (1636).</note>, without there being a need to repeat it here, where I show the manner of reducing all kinds of metric feet or measured movements into verse, in order to join <term>Rhythmics</term> to <term>Harmony</term>. And for this purpose, I place here all the species of metric feet in musical notes, so that they may serve to understand what follows, for all kinds of verse are composed of them. The name of each is above the notes that represent it: it is only necessary to remark that each can be dissolved or diminished into a greater number of notes or beats, as one sees in the fourth <term>Epitrite</term> <note>A metrical foot consisting of three long syllables and one short one; here shown subdivided into smaller rhythmic units.</note>, which is dissolved and diminished by 16 eighth notes.

## PROPOSITION XVIII.
To reduce all kinds of feet, or Rhythmic movements into verse: & to explain the characters necessary for this effect: where one sees the number, the value, & the true pronunciation of the letters of the Alphabet.

I do not wish to dwell on proving that our French language has three kinds of time <note>Referring to syllable lengths: short, long, and perhaps intermediate.</note>, just as the Greeks & the Latins do, because I have done so at length in the 7th, 8th, 13th, & 16th articles of the 57th question on *Genesis* <note>The author refers to his own previous work, likely *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim* (1623).</note>, and because everyone can satisfy and convince themselves by reflecting on the different times they give to each syllable while pronouncing. Now, since the Airs & Songs in use today—or those which have been and always will be in use as long as one practices singing and verse—relate to the movements or feet from which Anacreon, Pindar, Horace, and the other Greek and Latin Poets composed their verses, it is not out of place to use their terms. I say then, first, that they distinguished their verses into *perfect*, *abundant*, and *diminished*. The *perfect* are those which lack no foot or syllable; they name them *acatalectic*; if they lack one syllable, *catalectic*; & if they lack two, *brachycatalectic*, which can be related to different cadences, and to dances, which lack some steps, or which have more than they need. But it is difficult to make our Musicians appreciate the names, the sequence, and the pleasure of these regulated feet or movements, and of the verses composed of them; that is why I do not include here the version of Hephaestion <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD who wrote a manual on meters.</note>, who explains very exactly all the types of verse used by the Greek Poets, for fear of taking great pains that would perhaps be of no use to them; for they do not wish to be constrained, and prefer to follow the movements that come into their imagination, rather than being forced by any rule, because they have more diversity, and they do not bore as quickly as hexameters, pentameters, sapphics, and the others, which go...

As for the second vowel *e*, there are similarly three types: namely the feminine, which is muffled and soft, like the *sheva* <note>original: "fœua"; the Hebrew grammatical point indicating a neutral or vocalic "e" sound</note> of the Hebrews, and which is not pronounced at the end of words followed by a word beginning with a vowel; this is why it would be appropriate to remove it, placing a comma to signify its absence, as one sees in these words, *il chemin' à pied* <note>he travels on foot</note>, for *il chemine à pied*: a practice used by many for a long time, particularly in rhymed verse.

The second *e* is written with an acute accent, *é*, and is pronounced like the Latin *e* in the word *domine* <note>Lord</note>. The third is pronounced with an open mouth, as in these words *testes, festes, etc.* <note>heads, feasts</note> instead of which one should write *tête*, so that no one pronounces the letter *s*: for it would be good to remove the superfluous letters from our writing—that is to say, those which should never be pronounced—in order to better establish the quantity, or the duration of French syllables, so that this *e* would be written with a circumflex accent to signify its length and its pronunciation between *a* and *é*. To this one can add the syllable *eu*, which is found in many words at the beginning, middle, and end; for it is more a vowel than a diphthong, and is indifferent, or doubtful, as in these words *Dieu* <note>God</note>, and *veu* <note>seen</note>.

The 3rd vowel is *i*, for which one must lengthen the tail when it is a consonant <note>referring to the letter "j"</note>, as in this word *j'ajoûte* <note>I add</note>: now the vowel *i* is common, that is to say, sometimes long and other times brief. The circumflex accent is proper for signifying its length, *î*.

The 4th vowel is *o*, which can be written with the same accent when it is long; it can also serve for all places where the syllable or diphthong *au* is pronounced like a long *o*; for example these words, *causes, faux, maux, pastureaux, & hauts* <note>causes, false, evils, shepherds, and high</note>: can be written thus *cofes, fôx, môs, pastureôs, & hôs*: although one could relate this *au* to the vowel *a*, since it is pronounced between *a* and *o*.

The last vowel is *u*, which is pronounced like the *upsilon* of the Greeks: and when it is a consonant it must be written thus, *v*; some reduce the syllable *ou* to this vowel, as *eu* to the *e*, and the *au* to the *ô*, for it seems that the syllable *ou* is not a diphthong, since it is almost always brief, as one experiences in the words *soudain, & mourir* <note>sudden, and to die</note>, unless the position makes it long, as in these words, *nourrir & rouller* <note>to nourish and to roll</note>: so that we have ten vowels in our language, as one sees in this table which contains an example for each vowel: now one could write the two vowels that correspond to these three syllables *au, eu, & ou*, in this manner *à, ê, ô*, or in such other way as one wishes.

And because one hears almost only the "e" in these words, some have believed it could be related to the acute "é," so as to write *humén* for *humain* <note>human</note>.

The 3rd <term>diphthong</term> <note>a sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable</note> is composed of "e" and "o," as in these words *beô*, *eô*, instead of *beau* <note>beautiful</note> and *eau* <note>water</note>. The 4th is composed of "i" and "é," as one sees in these words *ciel* <note>sky</note>, *bien* <note>well</note>, *fier* <note>proud</note>, etc.; and when one must not pronounce the <term>diphthong</term>, one puts two dots above it <note>a diaeresis</note>, as in this word *fïer* when it means "faithful" <note>original: "fidele"</note>, for the other means "ferocious" <note>original: "ferox"</note>. This must be noted for all kinds of verbs that are pronounced by <term>diaeresis</term> <note>dividing one vowel sound into two syllables</note>, such as these here: *marier* <note>to marry</note>, *enuier* <note>to annoy/bore</note>, etc., contrary to the nouns *meurier* <note>mulberry tree</note>, *halier* <note>thicket</note>, etc., which are pronounced by <term>synaeresis</term> <note>merging two vowels into one syllable</note>. As for words ending in *ien*, they make two syllables, such as *ancien* <note>ancient</note>, *terrien* <note>land-owner</note>, and *mien* <note>mine</note>, except for a few which make only one, such as *Chrestien* <note>Christian</note>, etc. Now, one can always distinguish the two syllables by two dots placed above.

The 5th <term>diphthong</term>, or rather <term>triphthong</term> <note>three vowel sounds in one syllable</note>, is composed of "i," "e," and "u," as in these words *Dieu* <note>God</note> and *lieu* <note>place</note>, which are difficult for Germans to pronounce; that is why we first have them pronounce *Diu*. The 6th is composed of "i" and "o," as in these terms *allions* <note>we went</note>, *venions* <note>we came</note>, etc., in which *io* makes only one syllable in the words *union*, *scorpion*, etc., and in the plural present tenses of verbs ending in *ier*; for *lier* <note>to bind</note> and *marier* pronounce *io* in two syllables in *lions* and *mariions*, even though one makes only one syllable in their imperfect tenses *lions*, *mariions*, etc. Now this <term>diphthong</term> can be preceded by the <term>diphthongs</term> *ai* and *ui*, which we will speak of later, as in *païions* and *apuiions*, that is to say, *we were paying* <note>original Latin: "soluebamus"</note> and *we were supporting* <note>original Latin: "fulciebamus"</note>.

The 7th is ordinarily written as *oy*, as in the <term>words</term> *Roy* <note>King</note>, *Loy* <note>Law</note>, etc., though it could be written with an *o* and an acute *é*, *Roé*, and *l'oés*; which causes wonder in children instead of *voé*. The 8th is *üi*, easy to pronounce in the word *aujourd'huy* <note>today</note>. The 9th is a <term>diphthong</term> that serves to pronounce verbs ending in *oyer*, and some terms that end with the feminine [e], like *coye* <note>quiet/still</note>; which one can approach by adding the 4th <term>diphthong</term> *ié* to the 7th *oé* in this manner, *ploiéïr*, or to the 4th *ié*, *metoïén*, etc. Some add a tenth for the last syllable of future tenses, which they compose of the acute *é* and the *i*, *éï*, instead of our *ai*, as in these verbs *direï*, *fereï* for *dirai* <note>I will say</note> and *ferai* <note>I will do</note>, but the acute *é* alone suffices for these terms: *diré*, *feré*, etc.

These ten <term>diphthongs</term> being well understood, one will not need all these others: *au*, *ay*, *ai*, *ei*, *eu*, *ie*, *io*, *oi*, *oy*, *ou*, *ui*, *uy*, which are in these words: *maux* <note>evils</note>, *bay* <note>bay</note>, *vain* <note>vain</note>, *plein* <note>full</note>, *peu* <note>little</note>, *pié* <note>foot</note>, *disions* <note>we said</note>, *tenois* <note>I held</note>, *roy* <note>king</note>, *doux* <note>sweet</note>, *bruit* <note>noise</note>, *luy* <note>him</note>, *diable* <note>devil</note>, *forgea* <note>forged</note>, *pigeon* <note>pigeon</note>, *boete* <note>box</note>, *beau* <note>beautiful</note>, *lieu* <note>place</note>, *vaillants* <note>valiant</note>, *vermeil* <note>vermilion</note>, *fouillé* <note>searched</note>, *dueil* <note>mourning</note>, *vieil* <note>old</note>, *œil* <note>eye</note>, and others: for they suffice to pronounce all our terms; that is why I put them all here together; and I come to the <term>Consonants</term>, which must be numbered up to 29 to facilitate French pronunciation for foreigners, and at the same time, the <term>Art of Meter</term> <note>the study of poetic rhythm and structure</note>.

### PROPOSITION XIX.
->*To determine all the French syllables that are long, short, or doubtful, and to give rules for this subject: and consequently to establish French Prosody.*<-

Since the quantity or the timing of our <term>syllabes</term> <note>the duration of a spoken sound</note> does not follow the measure of <term>Latine syllabes</term>, as one sees in *asspirons* and *respirons*, of which the 2nd syllable is short, even though the 2nd of *respiro* and *asspiro* <note>Latin: I breathe/I aspire</note> is long, we must measure our quantities by true pronunciation and by the French accent, without stopping at the fountain of <term>Hypocrene</term> <note>A spring on Mt. Helicon sacred to the Muses; here meaning Greek poetic rules</note>, or at the <term>Tibre</term> <note>The river in Rome; here meaning Latin poetic rules</note>, from which the <term>Seine</term> and the <term>Loire</term> <note>Rivers in France; representing the French language</note> do not take their waters.

Now the first rule serves for *e*, which is always short, even though it may be in the 2nd and 3rd person plural of Verbs, and whatever position may be encountered there, as one sees in these examples: *tu parles* <note>you speak</note>, *ils parlent trop* <note>they speak too much</note>, and in this measured <term>distique</term> <note>a couplet or pair of poetic lines</note>.
> Her chaste laughing eyes are arrows that force reason,
> and her golden sands are the binding chains of love.
This is why one could write the end of these words without the *s* or *i*; or the *f* and *t* by joining a small stroke after to signify that they are absent—for example, *for-ce-la raison* for *forcent*, etc.—but it suffices to know that these syllables are always short. Furthermore, this syllable must be pronounced, for one does not say "why *force*-they," but "why *forcent*-they reason" <note>The author is discussing the "silent" plural verb ending -ent and how it interacts with following vowels</note>. One would perhaps be better justified in writing these plurals without the *n*, because it is not heard, and *forcent* is pronounced like *forcet*; of which the last syllable *cet* is pronounced like when one imposes silence by a whistling *hush* <note>original: "cet"</note>.

The 2nd rule belongs to the syllable *au*, which is pronounced like a long *o*; which is always true, as one sees in *ôtel*, *ôtant*, *preuôt*, and *desôt*, for *autel*, *autant*, *preuost*, and *defaut*: unless a <term>voyelle</term> <note>vowel</note> or a <term>diftongue</term> <note>diphthong; two vowels joined in one sound</note> follows after, as in this example, *noyau ouuert* <note>open pit/kernel</note>, where *au* or *ô* is short.

The 3rd rule serves for the "open" sound found in *fête* for *feste* <note>feast</note>, etc., *bête*, *forêt*, etc. for *beste*, *forest*, etc., from which are excepted the common or indifferent <term>monosyllabes</term> <note>single-syllable words</note> *es*, *mer*, *ter*, *ses*, *les*, *tres*, *des*, etc., for one can make them short, as happens when one pronounces *mes amis* <note>my friends</note>, as if one were saying *mes amis* or *més amis*. Now this long *e* is encountered in several words, such as in *succés*, *orêzon*, *mêzon*, etc., and feminine adjectives ending in *esse*, like *Duchesse*, etc., but not in *tristesse* and *richesse*, which have their second syllable short.

The 4th rule belongs to all <term>voyelles</term>, which are short before a

The 5th rule is for diphthongs, which are always long, provided that they are not followed by other diphthongs or a vowel, for then they are always short: we are more consistent in this rule than the Greeks, who sometimes make it long before another diphthong or vowel: the hexameter verse <note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet.</note> which follows shows the truth of this rule.

->*Why, like leaping lambs, O mountains, did you skip so?*<-
->*Being supported by God, etc.*<-

The 6th rule is for the other vowels. Our *a, e, i, o, u, & ou*, which end a final word, are indifferent or doubtful <note>In prosody, "doubtful" or "common" syllables can be either long or short depending on the poet's needs.</note>. This is seen in the two measured Asclepiadean verses <note>A complex classical meter named after the poet Asclepiades.</note> that follow, for the first [syllable] of the first verse is long, *and the 2nd is short*; the *ra* of the first is long, *and that of the 2nd is short*; the first *qui* is short, *and the 2nd is long*; the first *peu* is long, *and the 2nd short, etc.*

->*Prized, prized shall he be, not he who is voluptuous,*<-
->*But he who lives on little, and shall be virtuous.*<-

The same must be said of the other vowels and syllables that fall within the rule.

The 7th rule is for final syllables that have any of the preceding vowels, and which are indifferent: Now, it serves only for the 7 vowels found in these words: *mal* <note>evil/bad</note>, *aler* <note>to go</note>, *honneur* <note>honor</note>, *vous* <note>you</note>, *on* <note>one</note>, *un* <note>one/a</note>, *amour* <note>love</note>; which are indifferent in their quantity, unless the consonant that follows makes them long by position <note>A term in prosody where a short vowel becomes long because it is followed by two or more consonants.</note>: the example of this indifference is seen in this distich <note>A pair of verse lines.</note>.

->*Upon the treacherous Basilisk, and the advancing Asp you shall go,*<-
->*And you shall trample the Dragon and Lion as you go.*<-

There are nevertheless some syllables that are always long, such as *â* in *degât* <note>damage</note>, *ien fit* <note>he made some</note>, etc., which must be reserved for the exceptions.

The 8th rule is for the position or meeting of 2 or more consonants which make the syllables long, unless one is a <term>liquid</term> <note>A consonant sound such as 'l' or 'r' that has a smooth, flowing quality.</note>, namely *l, r, m & n*, which sometimes make the syllable short, and other times long. These words *escler* <note>to brighten/sparkle</note>, *sangler* <note>to strap</note>, *regler* <note>to rule/regulate</note>, and *peupler* <note>to people/populate</note>, show *l* joined in a syllable with other consonants: and these others *libre* <note>free</note>, *sacré* <note>sacred</note>, *degré* <note>degree/step</note>, etc., show the same thing for *r*: but they are not liquids in *barrer* <note>to bar</note> and *branler* <note>to shake</note>, because they make their syllable without the other consonant: the distich which follows explains the rule.

->*Free, I wish to consecrate freely, and consecrate by offering*<-
->*For my offering the regulated body, regulating it from the heart.*<-

The *ô* and the *ê* prevent this indifference of the liquids, for *ôtre* and *être*, etc., are always long, and the feminine *e* <note>The "mute e" at the end of French words.</note> is always short, as in *repris* <note>retaken</note>, *retrait* <note>retreat</note>, etc. Nouns ending in *âtre* and *acle* are also always long: *idolâtre* <note>idolater</note>, *mirâcle* <note>miracle</note>, and *scable* <note>bench/stool</note>, etc. As for the doubling of consonants, it must not be used in short syllables; for example, one must write *homes* <note>men</note>, *toner* <note>to thunder</note>, *doner* <note>to give</note>, so-

The 9th and final rule contains everything that remains for composing measured verse <note>Vers mesurés: an attempt to adapt classical Greek and Latin quantitative meter (based on vowel length) to the French language.</note>, without needing the help of the Latins or the Greeks; for we make the 2nd syllable of *Arion* and *Lycaon*, and the first of *vanity* short, even though Athens and Rome <note>Referring to Greek and Latin poetic authorities.</note> lengthen them. One must therefore first make the vowel *a* short at the beginning and in the middle of a word of two or three syllables, so that the disyllable <note>A word of two syllables.</note> is an iambic foot <note>A metrical foot consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one.</note>, suitable for the end of a pentameter; and that the trisyllable <note>A word of three syllables.</note> is a bacchius <note>A metrical foot consisting of one short syllable followed by two long ones; the author calls it a "bacchean".</note> suitable for ending a hexameter verse, as one sees in the table that follows.

It is also short in the middle syllables, as in *to exhale, to swallow, to starve, felling, lover, consoler*, etc., although it is long in Latin. Otherwise, it is short both in the middle and at the beginning in these words: *odor, orange tree, adore*, etc. Pronunciation will teach the rest. *Booty* and *to wall* will show the same thing for the vowel *u*, which is long before in *to use*, and in the prescribed forms *we were, they were*, and in *to burn*, etc. The syllable or letter *eu* is also short in *to weep, to remain*, etc., and long before in *to hollow out*, and in derivatives of *fear*: *fear, luck, ripe, fearful, happy, to ripen*, etc. Now, this *eu* often changes into *u*, as we say *we read, we owed, they elected* <note>original: "lumes, dumes, elurent"</note> for *we read, we owed, they elected* <note>original: "leumes, deumes, eleurent"</note>. But it must be noted that the licenses of the Greeks and Latins should not be permitted in French poetry, for fear that they might breed all the difficulties of their <term>metaplasms</term> <note>alterations of a word's spelling or sound</note>, <term>ectases</term> <note>lengthening a short syllable</note>, <term>protheses</term> <note>adding a letter to the start of a word</note>, <term>epentheses</term> <note>adding a letter to the middle</note>, <term>paragoges</term> <note>adding a letter to the end</note>, <term>synalephes</term> <note>merging two syllables</note>, etc., which would take away the ease, beauty, constancy, and naturalness of our language. We can nevertheless lengthen the first syllable of polysyllabic words whose first three syllables are short, in order to make them fit into hexameter verses, as in these two words: *mercy* and *opinion*.

->*Mercy, Lord, by your great number of sweetnesses:*<-
->*The opinion of great thinkers is to be opinionated.*<-

This is also permitted in the words *sedition* and *laborious*, but one must not take such liberty in other words derived from them—for example, in *thinkers* and *labor*—nor in the repetition of consonants to lengthen short syllables, as the Latins did in *religion* <note>original: "relligio"</note> and *four* <note>original: "quaestuor"</note>, etc. This is both because we have more need of <term>parrelipse</term> <note>omission of letters</note> to cut back superfluous letters than of <term>prothesis</term> to add them where it is not necessary, and because it is not this addition, but reason alone, which must make us lengthen the syllables in certain words.

## PROPOSITION XX.

To explain everything belonging to <term>Metric</term> feet, and to measured verses, and particularly to the <term>Hexameter</term>, the <term>Pentameter</term>, and the <term>Sapphic</term>.

Although the syllables of rhymed verses are called "feet" by some, and consequently the <term>Alexandrine</term> or <term>Heroic</term> verse has twelve feet, nevertheless the measured foot, which serves to make verses similar to the Greeks and Latins, has at least two syllables, and often three or four. From this it follows that the <term>hexameter</term> verse has only six feet, even though it has at least 13 syllables and can have as many as 17, as one sees in these two verses:

->*Aeneas, his eyes fixed with a sorrowful countenance.* <note>Latin: "Aeneas maesto defixus lumina vultu."</note><-
->*And the hoof shakes the crumbling field with the sound of four-footed beasts.* <note>Latin: "Quadrupedumque putrem sonitu quatit ungula campum."</note><-

As for the value of all the feet used in measured verse, I have already explained them elsewhere; therefore, I only note here that all feet are composed of long or short syllables, and that what we say regarding the measure of verses can be applied to that of dances and all the melodies and branles, etc., played on instruments. Thus, the composers of Ballets and Steps can profit greatly from the reading of this book.

# On Songs.

Now, one of the most excellent verses is called the <term>Hexameter</term> <note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet</note>, for the reason that it has six feet, of which the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th are <term>dactyls</term> <note>A long syllable followed by two short ones</note> or <term>spondees</term> <note>Two long syllables</note>, as one wishes; there being only the 5th which always requires a <term>dactyl</term>, and the sixth a <term>spondee</term>. It must nevertheless be noted that it is permitted to place a <term>spondee</term> in the 5th place when the subject requires it, as Virgil did in his *The ox falls forward on the ground* <note>original Latin: "Procumbit humi bos"</note>, and in his *Increase* <note>original Latin: "Incrementum"</note>, and Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf, a poet who attempted to reform French poetry using classical meters</note> in the 38th verse of his translation of the Canticle, *Hear, O heavens, what I speak* <note>original Latin: "Audite cæli quæ loquor"</note>.

> *And by the bitter grief of the cruel plague infected.*

And in the 6th [verse] of the 103rd Psalm.

> *Of waters attached, restored as if by a suspended ceiling.*

Which I have given in their entirety at the end of the Commentary on Genesis, where one sees a great number of all sorts of measured French verses, without it being necessary to repeat them here. These verses serve for long-winded works <note>Major epic or narrative poems</note>, as one sees in Virgil's Aeneid, in Homer's Odyssey, etc.; but it suffices to give a single example of it.

> *World, recount the praise of the Most High, and sing his goodness.*

One often accompanies this verse with a <term>pentameter</term> <note>A line of five feet</note>, as one sees in Ovid, Catullus, Tibullus, and Propertius; and one calls the two together a <term>distich</term> <note>A pair of verse lines, often a couplet</note>: whereupon it must be noted that this verse of five feet can be measured and sung in three ways, as one sees by the characters of longs and shorts, which mark its quantity.

->Lutes and Psalteries joined to the Harp, sound forth.<-

| First manner. | Second manner. | Third manner. |
|-------------------|-------------------|--------------------|
| Lutes and --- | Lutes and --- | Lutes and --- |
| Psalteri --- | Psalteri --- | Psalteri --- |
| ons joined --- | ons | ons |
| to the Ha --- | joined to the --- | joined to the Ha --- |
| rp sound forth --- | Harp sound --- | rp sound forth --- |
| | forth | |

The last two feet are <term>anapests</term> <note>Two short syllables followed by one long</note> in the first manner: the second has a <term>caesura</term> or <term>cut</term> in the middle and at the end, and the third has a <term>choriamb</term> <note>A foot of four syllables: long, short, short, long</note>, and a <term>bacchius</term> <note>A foot of three syllables: short, long, long</note> in the 4th and 5th place: although these different manners always keep the same time: which also happens to the hexameter, which always has but one same time, whether it has only <term>dactyls</term> or <term>spondees</term>; this is why it is easy to sing all sorts of these verses to the same melody, by dividing one note into 2 to change the <term>spondees</term> into <term>dactyls</term>, or by making only one out of two to change the <term>dactyls</term> into <term>spondees</term>.

It must further be noted that this <term>hexameter</term> verse is all the more excellent when its words and its measures are more locked into one another, as happens when each word belongs to two feet, which is seen in these two verses.

> *Come, depart quickly from this place, for here is the Eternal,*
> *Glory, wealth, favor, will come to Phyllis in abundance.*

However, it suffices that the third foot is not made of a single word separated from the 2nd or 4th. As for the end, it is excellent when it is made by a word of 3 syllables, from which the <term>Bacchius</term> foot is formed: Which one must also

## Embellishment

conclude from the Adonic <note>A short meter consisting of a dactyl and a spondee</note> which finishes the Sapphic stanza: although a word of two long syllables finishes it well enough. As for monosyllables, they must be avoided as much as possible, and those of four and five syllables should be left to the Greeks. One must also not finish with a feminine syllable. For the *Pentameter*, it suffices to advise that the caesura <note>A rhythmic pause or break in a line of verse</note> of the third foot must be at the end of a completed word, or a monosyllable; and that it finishes excellently with a word of two syllables, as Ovid always did, who never finished with an anapest <note>A metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by one long one</note>, like this one:

->Because all my bones are with fear astonished,<-

Which finishes better thus:

->Because all my bones are astonished with fear.<-

Now, it must never be alone, but follow a preceding hexameter, of which here are some examples:

->Christ passed from heaven to the womb, from the maternal womb<-
->Into a stable, from there onto a very hard cross.<-
->Just as in the waters the parched Tantalus burns,<-
->The more gold the usurer has, the more the usurer seeks to have.<-

One can place Sapphic verses after hexameters, which are said to have been invented by Sappho, who is placed among the Lyric poets, and who is praised by this distich <note>A pair of verse lines</note> of Antipater of Sidon:

<gloss>Mnemosyne was struck with amazement when she heard the honey-voiced Sappho, fearing that mortals possessed a tenth Muse.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Μημοσύνην ἔλε θάμβος, ὅτ᾽ ἔκλυε τῆς μελιφώνου, / Σαπφοῦς, μὴ δεκάτην Μοῦσαν ἔχουσι βροτοί."</note>

Which Guillaume Naviere expresses by this French distich:

->Mnemosyne, marvelling to hear the sweet Sappho,<-
->Cried out: mortals have a Muse down there.<-

Now the Sapphic verse is of twelve syllables reduced to five feet, of which the 1st is a trochee, the 2nd a spondee, the 3rd a dactyl, and the 4th and 5th a trochee; there are three verses in each stanza, with an Adonic verse composed of a dactyl and a spondee, as one sees in this stanza by Horace.

<gloss>More often by the winds is shaken the huge pine, and lofty towers fall with a heavier crash, and the lightning strikes the tops of the mountains.</gloss> <note>original Latin: "Saepius ventis agitatur ingens / pinus et celfae graviore casu / decidunt turres feriuntque summos / fulgura montes."</note>

->Very often by the winds the pine is shaken.<-
->And with a greater fall a high tower falls,<-
->And the thundering shock of the lightning strikes<-
->The peaks of the mountains.<-

Now the third foot, which is a dactyl, must be linked to make the verse agreeable, so that the caesura is the last syllable of a word, as happens in Latin syllables; although monosyllables also have good grace in this cut, as one sees in *of* and *great* <note>original: "dez" and "grand"</note> in the first and second French verses, for the caesura of the third is *thun-* <note>original: "dreux" from "foudreux"</note>. Upon which it must be noted that rhymed verses have so accustomed our ears to the cadence of rhyme, that they receive no pleasure from measured verses <note>Verses based on classical meter rather than rhyme</note>, unless they are rhymed at the same time, like these:

->To render to you by these verses I wish, Redeemer,<-
->Thanks, and to sing of your celestial grandeur,<-
->Lift up, O good God, my devout prayer<-
->Toward its horizon.<-

### On Songs.

For although Leonine verse <note>original: "Leonifme"; a type of Latin verse based on internal rhyme</note> is not considered pleasing in the middle or at the end of Latin verses, nevertheless our French language receives grace from it. We experience that the peoples of the Levant use rhymes in their verses, as is seen among the Persians, the Hebrews, and the Turks. Therefore, it would be more appropriate to choose rhyme anew and add to it the measure of Greek and Latin verses; or if that is too difficult, it suffices to keep the quantity of the measures that are found within the rhymes. This will not prevent me from speaking of other types of measured verse, so that everyone may consider the effort that the great minds of this century have made on this subject, and so that their invention does not perish entirely.

## PROPOSITION XXI.

To explain Phalaecian, Iambic, Trochaic, Alcaic, and Asclepiadean verse.

The <term>Phalaecian</term> <note>A classical meter consisting of eleven syllables</note> has five feet like the Sapphic, of which the second is the first <note>The author likely means the first foot is a spondee</note>, the dactyl is the second, and the three others are trochees, as is seen in these four verses, the first of which has its feet marked by the signs of longs and shorts.

> *In God firm of heart place your hope,*
> *Who alone against evil can protect you:*
> *For at the time limited by his holy will*
> *Your troublesome sorrows will scatter far.*

It has its caesura <note>a rhythmic pause</note> at the sixth syllable at the beginning of the first trochee, as is seen in that of Horace:

> *The things that make life more blessed.* <note>original Latin: "Vitam quæ faciunt beatiorem."</note>

As for <term>Iambic</term> verse, there are several kinds, of which the <term>senarii</term> <note>verses consisting of six feet</note>, which have six feet, are suitable for tragic subjects. Their sixth foot must be a spondee. It receives in the 1st, 3rd, and 5th place the iamb, the tribrach, the spondee, the dactyl, and the anapest; and in the 2nd, 4th, and 6th place, an iamb, a tribrach, and an anapest—which is as frequent in the Comedies as it is rare in the Tragedies, as Hephaestion <note>original: "Epheſtion"; a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> remarks in his Manual. But I do not wish to stop at all the species of dimeters, trimeters, and tetrameters, whether Catalectic, Acatalectic, or Hypercatalectic <note>technical terms for verses that are shorter than, equal to, or longer than the standard meter</note>, since I do not expect them to be put into common use. Now, this great variety of feet, which is permitted in the iamb, makes it very easy to compose and brings a great diversity to vary the movements of Musical airs. But it is more difficult when it is composed solely of iambs, as is seen in this example, which is even more difficult because of the rhyme:

> *At the dawn of the rising Sun*
> *May it please our living God*
> *To preserve in your holy hand*
> *Mankind from all his enemies.*

And this one, which is dimeter like the other, is easier because it is not rhymed:

> *The Eternal is the most strong God,*
> *Who reigns all clothed in honor.*

Sedulius <note>original: "Sedule"; a 5th-century Christian poet</note> composed an Iambic Hymn, of which the stanzas follow the alphabetical order—

## Embellishment
<note>The author is discussing "measured verse," an attempt by Renaissance poets to apply Greek and Latin rules of syllable length to French poetry.</note>

Chaste, etc. in which he places indifferently the iamb or the spondee in the first and third foot, but the second and fourth are always iambic. Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a member of the Pléiade who championed "vers mesurés."</note> practiced this poetry extensively, as seen in several Dimeter, Catalectic, and Anacreontic verses, of which here is a fragment where he speaks of Cupid:
> If he weeps, take great care
> Not to be deceived by his tears;
> If he laughs, do not be softened, etc.
> And if he wishes to kiss you
> Refuse, flee: this kiss
> Is false, and treacherous, and mortal,
> His mouth is nothing but poison, etc.

The Trochaic verse becomes iambic if one adds a syllable or makes a pause before it, and the iambic becomes trochaic; this happens similarly between the dactylic and the anapestic. The Greeks call these changes Epilogues, <gloss>Epilogoi</gloss>, which are of three kinds, of which the first is called <gloss>Synadic Ending</gloss> <note>original: "Telosmos Synadikē"</note> because the feet that change into one another—namely the iambic and the trochaic—have three beats. The second species is named <gloss>Synadic Tetrameter</gloss> <note>original: "tetrametros Synadikē"</note> because of the four beats of the dactylic and anapestic feet. And the third is called <gloss>Tetradic Hexasemos</gloss> <note>original: "hexasēmos tetradikē"</note> by reason of the six beats of the Choriambic, the Antispastic, and the two Ionics.

It suffices to provide one example from Baïf for the Brachycatalectic Trochaic Dimeters:
> O what pleasure I have
> Gentle singer bird,
> When you come every year
> In the new season
> Promptly to rebuild
> Your retreat and your nest, etc.

The Alcmanian verse relates to our ten-syllable verse, which has its break or caesura at the end of the fourth foot. Horace <note>The Roman lyric poet.</note> gives it only four feet: namely two dactyls and two trochees, although the last trochee can be a spondee because of the indifference of the final syllable. It can be called Dactylic-Trochaic-Tetrameter; its caesura is at the beginning of the second dactyl. The following example is from Baïf:
> Turn that eye favorably beautiful
> And I shall live raised from the grave, etc.

The Asclepiadean verse is the French Heroic; it has 12 syllables and relates to our Alexandrine; it is with this that the Prince of Latin Lyricists <note>Horace.</note> began his first Ode, dedicated to Maecenas. It is composed of a spondee, a dactyl, a long caesura, and two dactyls; or of a spondee, two choriambs, and a pyrrhic or iamb. It is with this genre of verse that Rapin <note>Nicolas Rapin (1535–1608), a poet known for his experiments with measured verse.</note> began his first book of measured verse:
> Henry, branch of Mars, King generous and strong,
> Of virtues and honor the inviolable fort; etc.

In these, he keeps both the measure and the rhyme, to which many do not wish to restrict themselves, as much because of the difficulty as to imitate the Latin more closely.

Hephaestion <note>A 2nd-century Greek grammarian and authority on meter</note> explains other types of verse which are less in use; for example, the Aeolic, which can have six feet, of which the first is a spondee, an iamb, a trochee, or a pyrrhic; the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th are dactyls, and the 6th is a dactyl or an amphimacer, which is called a Cretic.
He also speaks of the Logaoedic, which ends with a double trochee; the other feet are dactyls: some call them Epodic and Alcaic. Now, these sorts of verse will be understood by the following Proposition.

## PROPOSITION XXII.

To explain Anapaestic, Paeonic, and major and minor Ionic verse, the Choriambic, the Antispastic, and all other types.

<insert>
The Anapaestic verse admits in every position the spondee and the anapaest, and sometimes the proceleusmatic; one also finds there the dactyl and the iamb in the Tragedians, though one prefers to call it Aeolic when an iamb occurs at the beginning, and Logaoedic when it ends with the Bacchius.
It is measured by dipody <note>pairs of feet</note>, like the Iambic and Trochaic, of which here is an example from Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf, a poet who attempted to introduce classical meters into French</note>, which has its third line in choriambic dimeter catalectic; and the 4th is dactylo-trochaic-tetrameter-brachycatalectic.
> The fountain springs, pure and clear always,
> And the void pierces it and uncovers the bottom,
> Nothing hidden will you see there;
> Living water, but I do not see the bottom of your heart.
As for Paeonic or Bacchiac verse, it is one of the most cheerful and excellent, by reason of its three short syllables, which seem to me more agreeable at the beginning than in any other place, as happens in the 4th Paeon.
I have given an example of this type of verse for four musical parts in the 57th question of Genesis, which begins thus:
> God shall arise suddenly, his enemies shall be broken, etc.
The rest of this 67th Psalm will be found in the said Question, with the new writing and orthography of Baïf <note>Baïf developed a phonetic spelling system for French</note>. Now there are three sorts of Paeonic verse; of which some are called Cretics, which can sometimes change and dissolve into Paeons of the 1st or 4th type; the 2nd is called Bacchiac, by reason of the Bacchius foot of which it is composed; and the 3rd is named Palimbacchius, because it is composed of the feet that bear that name.
Cratinus <note>An Athenian comic poet</note> gives examples of these verses in Hephaestion, after having invoked the Muses:
> "O Muse, celebrate a Cretic melody," <note>original Greek: Εὐφρα μῦσα χριτικὸν μελὸς</note> that is to say,
> Sweet Muse, sing an air in Cretic verse. To which he adds:

## Embellishment

<gloss>Hail, golden Muse, you have come sweetly somehow.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Χαῖρε δὴ μῦσα χρυσέα ἀδὴ ἥκεισ᾽ ὄπωσ."</note>
The example of Simmias <note>Simmias of Rhodes, a Greek poet known for his "pattern poems."</note> that follows contains only Cretics <note>A metrical foot consisting of a long, a short, and a long syllable (— ∪ —).</note> which do not create any dissonance.
<gloss>O lady mother, hear the songs of the nymphs.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Μάτερ ὦ πότνια κλύθι νυμφῶν ἀοιδᾶν."</note>
This is familiar to this Poet, although he sometimes dissolves the two long syllables of the Cretics, as one sees in this verse composed entirely of short syllables, except that he has placed the fourth species of Paeon <note>A foot of four syllables: three short and one long (∪ ∪ ∪ —).</note> in the fourth foot.
<gloss>To you once the final... of Zeus... newly created.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Σέ ποτε Διὸς ἀδὰ πύματα νεαρεχρε νεοχρήτων."</note>
Hephaestion <note>A Greek grammarian and writer on metrics.</note> remarks that this genre of verse does not exceed 30 "times" <note>Units of metrical duration.</note>, which he calls <gloss>Telachontesmon</gloss>; and that it can go as far as the hexameter. I leave aside the examples he reports for all these species of verse, in order to give some French ones taken from the aforementioned 67th Psalm, of which the 7th verse is Cretic, and the 52nd is Bacchean <note>A foot consisting of one short and two long syllables (∪ — —).</note>.

->Therefore sing to God, then sound to his name.<-
->Fill us with benefits, God our Savior.<-
The Palimbacchius <note>Also called an Antibacchius: two long syllables followed by a short (— — ∪).</note> is rarer than the others, of which here is the example:
->Great God who has made the beautiful star of the day.<-

I leave aside the example of dissolved Cretics, which are almost no different from Pyrrhics <note>A foot of two short syllables (∪ ∪).</note>, in order to speak of Ionics, which are "pure" when they have only major or minor Ionic feet. The example from Hephaestion has only the first foot as an Ionic, for the second foot contains the seven "times" that he calls <gloss>ephthimmeri</gloss> <note>original: "ἐφθιμμερη"</note>; the third foot is a choriamb, or a double trochee; and because it seems very excellent to him, he names it <gloss>Thrismiatsts Ioniko</gloss> <note>original: "Θρισμια τσ τσ ἰωνικῶ"</note>. Those that are Acatalectic Dimeters receive Molossi <note>A foot of three long syllables (— — —).</note> in the even places, as well as Choriambs.
The Brachycatalectic Trimeters, or Praxilleans <note>Named after the poetess Praxilla.</note>, have their first foot as an Ionic and the second as Trochaic: and the Acatalectic Trimeters have two Ionics and one Trochaic at the end, or one Ionic and two Trochaics. But the Brachycatalectic, which is called Sotadic <note>Named after Sotades, known for his "obscene" or satirical verses.</note>, is the most excellent among the Tetrameters, for it receives in three different places an Ionic, a Trochaic, or the foot composed of an Anapest and a Pyrrhic, or a tribrach and a trochee, or a foot composed of six short syllables. I leave aside the Acatalectics composed of three Ionics and one Trochaic, which Sappho used often.
Now it is appropriate to explain the terms used by the Greeks in their Prosody and Poetry, so that Musicians may understand everything that can serve their art. I say then that <term>Acatalectic</term> signifies the verse which has its last foot complete, which one can call in our French *Cadenced*: It is called <term>Catalectic</term> when it lacks one or two syllables in the last foot of the verse, or when the foot which should be three syllables is diminished by one or two of said syllables: our Poets call it *Short-cadenced*. When it has only one foot instead of its entire dipody <note>A unit of two feet.</note>, he calls it <term>Brachycatalectic</term>, and <term>Hypercatalectic</term>, or <term>Over-cadenced</term>, when it has one or two superfluous syllables. As for the <term>Dipody</term>, or conjunction of two similar feet, it is named *Tautopody*, by reason of the repetition of the same foot, for one puts two iambs together to make a Dipody. I leave aside some other terms whose explanation is easy.
As for the minor Ionic, it is nothing other than the major reversed, just as the Anapest is only an Anti-dactyl. One sees an example of this Ionic in the 12th Ode of the 3rd book of Horace, which begins, *It is for unhappy girls* <note>original Latin: "Miserarum est"</note>, etc., of which this French verse from the 46th Psalm follows the cadence.
