# Of Songs.
### Say, sing Odes, Songs to this great God.

Now it can receive a double <term>trochee</term> <note>a metrical foot consisting of a long syllable followed by a short one</note>, and the 3rd <term>paeon</term> <note>a foot of four syllables: two short, one long, one short</note>, which is sometimes changed into a <term>palimbacchius</term>: <term>molossi</term> <note>feet of three long syllables</note> also enter into it.

<term>Hephaestion</term> <note>a Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD</note> remarks that the <term>trochaic dipody</term> <note>a unit of two trochees</note> has seven beats when it precedes an <term>Ionic</term>, that it is the 2nd <term>epitrite</term>: and that the 3rd <term>paeon</term> always precedes the said <term>dipody</term>, which he names <gloss>five-beat</gloss> <note>original: "πεντάσημον"</note>, by reason of its 5 beats. I leave aside the great multitude of mixed verses found in <term>Anacreon</term> and <term>Aristophanes</term>, which are easy to judge by the feet that enter into this genre of verse, in order to finish this Proposition with the <term>choriambic</term> and the <term>antispastic</term>, of which the former takes its name from its principal foot; and when it ends with a <term>bacchius</term> or an <term>amphibrach</term>, it is <term>catalectic</term> <note>a verse missing a syllable in the final foot</note>. It also receives the <term>cretic</term> and the <term>dactyl</term>, which is an imperfect <term>choriamb</term>, and when it is <term>acatalectic</term> <note>a verse with a complete final foot</note>, its base is <term>iambic</term>, or the 3rd <term>epitrite</term>. If it is mixed, the <term>choriamb</term> dissolves into a <term>tribrach</term> and an <term>iamb</term>, that is to say, a <term>pyrrhic-anapaest</term>. Now there is no doubt that the mixture of these feet is very proper for making all sorts of excellent Airs, as one experiences when one puts the <term>iambic dipody</term> after the <term>choriamb</term>, added to which the beauty of all sorts of <term>Branles</term>, <term>Courantes</term>, and other dances and ballets, comes particularly from the movement and the sequence of these feet, as one can prove by the examination of all the movements that Monsieur <term>Belleville</term> <note>Jacques de Belleville, a prominent 17th-century French court dancing master</note>, the other Masters of dance, and the Composers of Ballets give to their <term>Branles</term>, and other pieces that serve for recreation: for they use the same feet as <term>Anacreon</term>, <term>Pindar</term>, <term>Theocritus</term>, and the other Poets, even though they follow nothing but their own genius, and have never heard mention of them: this is why one can call each species of verse, *Branle, Courante, etc.* following the movement of the verse: for example, the *Choriambic Branle, Anapaestic, etc.* for it is easy to find all the feet of which one composes the branles of <term>Poitou</term> and other regions, and to show that the most excellent Masters of France, Italy, and Spain have no movement which is not found in Greek verses.

I add that the <term>choriamb</term> can be named <term>penthemimer</term> when it is <term>monometer hypercatalectic</term>: and that it is nothing other than the <term>Adonic</term> verse: but one calls it <term>dimeter</term>, <term>trimeter</term>, etc. up to the <term>hexameter</term>, following the number of its feet, or its steps, as one does with other species of verse.

When it begins with the <term>trochaic dipody</term>, one names it <term>epichoriambic</term>, and relates it to the <term>Sapphic trimeter</term>. Where it must be remarked that besides the ordinary way of measuring or singing the <term>Sapphic</term>, one uses another, which consists of beginning with the <term>trochaic dipody</term>, either <term>heptaseme</term> <note>seven-beat</note> when its 4th syllable is long, or <term>hexaseme</term> <note>six-beat</note> when it is short: and then one makes the <term>choriamb</term>, and the <term>bacchius</term>, which they call <term>iambic cataclide</term>, because it is an <term>iambic dipody</term> diminished by one syllable: I put here the two ways of measuring this verse, so that the Composers of airs and ballets may see to which dances they can be related.

### PROPOSITION XXIII.

To explain the attempts made in this century to establish Prosody <note>The patterns of stress and intonation in a language.</note> and French Metrical Poetry for the benefit of Music.

Even though the Italians and several others have tried to establish a Metrical Art similar to that of the Greeks, in order to create measured verses of all kinds, I will nevertheless speak here only of the attempts of the French. Some of these have only desired a change in orthography <note>Spelling systems.</note>, so that there would be no letter in any word that was not pronounced, and so that foreigners might easily learn to pronounce our language; others have gone as far as the Metrical art of creating all sorts of verse, like the Greeks and the Latins. Now, although I have already spoken of both, I add this Proposition so that one may have a more distinct knowledge of them.

I say first that Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a member of the Pléiade who sought to revive ancient quantitative meter in French.</note> has worked the most on French measured verses; for besides several Greek and Latin poets of whom he made French versions in the same kind of verse, he set the 150 Psalms of David into measured verse of all kinds, both Latin and French, of which I have given several examples in the 17th Question on Genesis. But because he omitted rhyme from the verses—without which it seems the French and other nations can hardly tolerate them, either because of their harshness or because their ears are not accustomed to it—Rapin, Callier, and several others have added rhyme to the measures, in order to join regulated movements, or Rhythmics, to sweetness. 

There are others who have judged it appropriate to use these two kinds of verse: namely, measured verse without rhyme when they are only sung in Music (which makes their harshness vanish), and rhymed measured verse when they are read without music. Others have tried to add movements to the Songs similar to those they conjecture the ancient Greeks and Latins used; one can see several examples in the aforementioned question, where the French measured verses are by Baïf and the Music is by Jacques Mauduit <note>original: "Iacques Mdauuit"</note>. To which I shall add hereafter the 1st Song of the 3rd book of Horace's Odes, so that one may see the manner used by Monsieur du Chemin, Advocate in Parliament, to restore the melody and the rhythmic movements of the ancients. Perhaps this sample will excite those who love antiquity to urge him to share his thoughts on this subject with the public, so that we may experience the power of ancient music, or at least consider its art and beauty.

Finally, others prefer to use our rhymed verses without observing any measure other than what they judge fit to give beautiful movements to the melody. This is why they often lengthen short syllables or make long ones short when they judge that the Songs and Airs require it elsewhere—as is often experienced on these short syllables, *ce, de, le,* etc., upon which they sing 4 or 5 notes, for example, *ut, re, mi, fa, sol.* This is not as blameworthy as many imagine, unless one wishes to condemn the ancient Greeks, who used the same license, as I said in the 2nd Proposition of the book *On the Utility of Harmony*. Nevertheless, those who do not wish to take such liberties, and who prefer to observe longs and shorts in rhymed verse, will often find Iambic verses <note>A metrical foot consisting of one short syllable followed by one long one.</note> or other kinds that will be as or more agreeable than if they had been measured on purpose, because the measure occurs there without constraint, and the Composer of Airs has more opportunity to show his industry and art.

Where one can consider to which species of verse each belongs; for example, the 4th is <term>Iambic</term> <note>a metrical foot consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one</note>, <term>Dimeter</term> <note>a line consisting of two metrical units</note>, <term>Acatalectic</term> <note>a verse that has the complete number of syllables in its last foot</note>, or <term>Rhythmical</term>. And if one is content to know the feet without reducing them into verses, the first verse is composed of a <term>Cretic</term> foot <note>long-short-long</note> and a <term>Molossus</term> <note>three long syllables</note>; the second of an <term>Anapest</term> <note>short-short-long</note> and a <term>Molossus</term>; the third of a <term>Bacchius</term> <note>short-long-long</note> and the third <term>Paeon</term> <note>short-short-long-short</note>, though one could say it is a <term>Proceleusmatic</term> <note>four short syllables</note>, since the syllable *do* is short in *adorer* <note>to adore</note>. The 4th has two <term>Dipodies</term>, or <term>Iambic Tantopodies</term> <note>double feet</note>. The 5th has a double trochee, or a <term>Trochaic Dipody</term>, and then a <term>Spondee</term> <note>two long syllables</note>, and a <term>Palimbacchius</term> <note>long-long-short</note>; although one could reduce these movements to other species of feet.

Now, in whatever manner one takes the verses, Musicians can profit from all sorts of movements or rhythmic feet of which we have spoken until now: whereupon it is good to remark that the Composers of <term>Branles</term> <note>a type of French choral dance</note> and <term>Ballets</term>, and the Dance Masters, can call each rhythmic foot *a step*, and consequently verses that have 3, 4, 5, or 6 feet will be similar to Dances composed of 3, 4, 5, or 6 steps; so that each species of verse will represent each species of [step], etc. Thus, entire Ballets can be made by using the steps and movements of all the species of meters we have discussed; in favor of which I will later give examples of the principal types of meters or Rhythmic movements, so that Composers may use them to make their Songs pathetic <note>meaning "full of passion or emotion" in the 17th-century sense</note>, and so they may understand the manner in which the Greeks and Latins used movements, whether for singing or dancing, and that they may yield to them in nothing.

If one wished to have all the pleasure that can result from Music, it would be necessary to have all the manners of singing, and to have them appear one after the other, in order to judge in what way one surpasses the other: for example, one should have one or two <term>Madrigals</term>, or other <term>Italian Airs</term> sung by a dozen good Italian voices, as many <term>Sarabandes</term> by Spaniards, as many <term>Courantes</term> and <term>Airs</term> by the French, and then have them all sing the best pieces of Music that are made for Instruments, so that six <term>Lutes</term>, or whatever number one wished, would begin, and then a concert of <term>Viols</term> would follow, and finally a concert of <term>Violins</term> similar to the King's 24 <note>referring to "Les Vingt-quatre Violons du Roi," the famous orchestra of the French royal court</note>; for besides the pleasure of this variety, one would judge which concert gives more pleasure, and those who sing the best. But since no book can provide the practice of this Music, and it is not easy to encounter, it suffices to show what our France has invented, or what she has added to Music, or at least her attempts, which can only be praiseworthy, even if they had not reached perfection.

## Concerning Songs.

I am therefore providing a sample here, which may be imitated by those who are pleased to hear the verses of ancient Poets set to Music, unless they possess a genius fortunate enough to improve upon them: it will be easy for Composers of Airs <note>Airs: a term for melodic songs or tunes</note> to notice which of their measures this corresponds to.

### First Ode of the third book of Horace.

<note>original: "Odi profanum vulgus et arceo. Favete linguis: carmina non prius audita, Musarum sacerdos, virginibus puerisque canto. Regum timendorum in proprios greges, Reges in ipsos imperium est Jovis Clari, giganteo triumpho, Cuncta supercilio moventis." Translation: "I loathe the uninitiated crowd and keep them away. Observe a reverent silence: I, the priest of the Muses, sing songs never heard before for maidens and boys. The power of dreaded kings is over their own flocks, but the empire of Jove is over the kings themselves—Jove, renowned for his triumph over the Giants, who moves all things with his eyebrow."</note>

I hate the profane crowd and keep them away.
Keep silence: songs not previously
Heard,
Priest of the Muses, to Maidens and boys I sing.
Of kings to be feared over
their own flocks, over Kings themselves is the empire of Jove,
Renowned for his triumph over the giants,
Moving all things with his brow.
I hate the profane, etc.
Of Kings, etc.

There are no other differences in the stanzas that follow the first, except that in all the second lines the first syllable is long, and therefore must be half a measure: but because the syllable *fa* of *Favete* in the first stanza is short, there is a rest <note>original: "soupir," literally a sigh, the musical term for a quarter-rest</note> before it to make the said short syllable apparent, while nevertheless maintaining the same tempo.

If anyone desires several other Odes of Horace set to Music according to their proper movements <note>movement: here referring to the rhythmic meter or "feet" of the poetry</note>, I have no doubt that Monsieur du Chemin <note>Nicolas Du Chemin (c. 1515–1576), a famous Parisian music printer and composer</note> will show them and let them hear them quite freely, if they take the trouble to ask him: and I hope they will have the same feeling regarding these Odes, and those of Pindar, as I do; namely, that there is no Music more agreeable than that, provided that one brings to it everything required for a perfect concert, namely excellent voices and well-played Instruments.

But we must now see what concerns the movements that can be made in the binary and ternary measures of the Practitioners <note>Practitioners: professional musicians or composers as opposed to theorists</note>.

## PROPOSITION XXIV.
*To determine the vast multitude of movements that arise from changes*
*in time, or from the notes of a measure used in Songs*
*and Musical Airs.*

It is certain that the composers of Airs, <term>Branles</term> <note>A popular type of French Renaissance dance characterized by side-to-side movement</note>, and Ballets have no fewer varieties in the timing of their measures than in the <term>modulation</term> <note>In this context, "modulation" refers to the melodic progression or inflection of the voice, rather than a change of key</note> of which I spoke in the book on Songs. Consequently, they have not yet employed every species of movement, and there will always remain enough to occupy them for their entire lives. They may conclude this themselves by considering the changes of a <term>binary measure</term> <note>A measure in duple time, such as 2/4 or 4/4</note> in which one is permitted to place a <term>half note</term> <note>original: "blanche"</note>, a <term>eighth note</term> <note>original: "crochuë"</note> with a <term>dot</term> <note>original: "point"</note>, another eighth note, and three <term>sixteenth notes</term> <note>original: "doubles crochuës"</note>. This single measure can be changed in 120 ways, even while retaining the same notes and keeping them all on the same line. The second binary measure, composed of seven eighth notes and two sixteenth notes, can be varied in 336 ways. The third, composed of five eighth notes and six sixteenth notes, in 462 ways; and the fourth, composed of a <term>quarter note</term> <note>original: "noire"</note>, a dotted eighth note, two other eighth notes, and five sixteenth notes, in 1,512 ways.

### Four Binary Measures.

| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |

| 120 | 336 | 462 | 1,512 |

This suffices to demonstrate the great number of varieties in every other binary measure, which I shall freely provide to those who wish to use them to enrich their practice. I only add that this species of measure can be made in 36 ways even without using the dot, nor the diversity of order or positions that the notes can receive according to ordinary combination. If one uses this diversity, one will have 5,818 measures, all as different as the 462 measures that can be made from the third measure above. And when it is permitted to use all the dots that increase and follow the notes, one has 73 kinds of new measures without any regard to the diversity of positions or order; if that order is considered, one will have 18,622 kinds of binary measures where dots are included. If one adds this number to the previous one, the binary measure alone will yield 24,440 measures as different as the 1,512 of the fourth example above. I will also give these varieties with dots to those who desire them for their use, though they may find them themselves by the 10th Proposition of the book on Songs, which teaches how to find in how many ways any given measure can be changed, since it demonstrates the same varieties in Melodies. But so that every Musician may find all these varieties, I place the rule here using the example of the third measure, which, having 5 eighth notes and six sixteenth notes, one...

And if one uses four different <term>strings</term><note>Original: "chordes," referring to pitches or notes.</note>, for example E-mi, F-fa, G-re, and A-mi, the combination of 4 multiplied by the 4 aforementioned varieties will show that this paeonic foot can be varied in 96 ways.

But it must be noted that although it is not customary to have a note of the same value follow a similar note augmented by a dot—as I have done in the 1st and 4th preceding measures, in which the dots are after and before an <term>eighth note</term><note>Original: "crochuë."</note>, whereas a <term>sixteenth note</term><note>Original: "double crochuë."</note> usually follows the dot after the simple eighth note so that it equals it with the sixteenth note—one can nevertheless use them as I have done, there being nothing but to accustom the voice to it and accommodate the composition to it. For when it is a question of giving all the varieties, one does not only have regard for ordinary practice, but for everything that can be done, whether easy or difficult, and good or bad, as I did in giving all possible modulations in the 10th Proposition of the book of *Songs*, and in an entire volume where I placed the forty thousand three hundred and twenty types of modulations, or songs, of the 8 notes of each <term>Octave</term>.

If the dot could be placed after sixteenth notes, the variety would be much greater, but it is only placed after eighth notes and other notes of greater value, as one sees in the 24th Proposition of the 4th book of *Composition*. Now, Composers are free to use the types of measures that will be easiest and most agreeable to them, and to leave those that do not please them. To which they can add all the varieties of triple measure without dots, and with dots, without there being a need to put examples of them here, since they can be formed from the preceding ones; besides, they will have more pleasure in finding them themselves than if I gave them all ready-made. But the other feet contain several other kinds of measures which are easy to put into practice; for example, the Bacchius contains 5 beats, and is expressed with 5 quarter notes <note>original: "notes noires"</note> when it is divided, or with two half notes <note>original: "notes minimes"</note> and one quarter note. The Paeon similarly has 5 beats, for it is composed of an Iamb and a Trochee, like the Choriamb. As for the Epitrites, they are composed of 7 beats, so that they can be related to the terms of the sesquitertian ratio <note>A ratio of 4:3, where one value is 1 and 1/3 times the other.</note>, which creates the Fourth <note>original: "Diatessaron"</note>, because one must sing 4 notes on the downbeat <note>original: "en frappant" (striking)</note> and 3 on the upbeat <note>original: "en levant" (lifting)</note>, or conversely, 3 on the downbeat and 4 on the upbeat. In the same way, the Paeons resemble the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> in some fashion, because one must sing three notes on the downbeat and two on the upbeat, or vice versa; this is what should properly be called sesquialter <note>A ratio of 3:2</note> or hemiola movement and measure. For as for trochees and iambs, they form a double measure similar to the Octave rather than a ternary measure, since 2 beats against 1; just as the spondee forms an equal measure, rather than a binary one, so that it relates to the unison.

I leave the rest to the meditation of studious Musicians, who are not content with knowing how to practice ordinary things, and who desire to add to their art in order to surpass their predecessors and create new and extraordinary movements. This will be easy for them by considering the last two Propositions; for if they use each metric foot for a particular measure, and if they dissolve or diminish each beat or syllable into as many other smaller beats as they can, they will always encounter new varieties, without needing to use all the ancient or modern signs used to mark the major and minor modes, perfect and imperfect prolation, and perfect and imperfect time, which embarrass more than they help.

### PROPOSITION XXV.

*To explain the utility and use of the preceding variety of measures, or times and movements, and the syncopations <note>original: "contretemps"</note> formed from different movements. And to show that Practitioners abuse the terms binary, triple, or ternary, etc., when they speak of their measures.*

The utility of these varieties is so great in Music that no one can explain it unless they have used it, because of the great multitude of extraordinary movements found therein. It must therefore first be noted that every Composer can make such a piece of Music as he wishes, using a single kind of measure taken from the 73 binary measures that use the dot, or from the 36 of those that reject the dot. For example, if the King commanded the Masters of his Music to compose a fantasy or an Air of 336 measures, on the condition that they use only one of the said measures, and yet that all these measures were varied and different, they could not satisfy this command if they did not know this Proposition, which shows that the second measure preceding...

# On Songs.

The preceding measure can be changed or diversified in 366 ways; just as the fourth can be varied in 1,512 ways, so that one can sing for an entire hour by constantly varying a single measure, without ever repeating the same order of notes or movements.

In the second place, one can use the 36 measures without a dot, or the 73 with a dot within the same piece, without employing the changes of each of these measures; this will provide a particular satisfaction to the listeners.

In the third place, one must avoid identity, or the resemblance of movements—just as one avoids it with consonances—in composition, because one grows weary of hearing the repetition of the same movement. This is why some <term>Composers of Airs and Ballets</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Airs" referred to vocal songs and "Ballets" to courtly dance spectacles.</note> despise <term>Spondaic</term> <note>A metrical foot consisting of two long syllables.</note> and <term>Dactylic</term> <note>A metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones.</note> movements, and others of which types of verse are composed, by reason of the too frequent and continuous recurrence or repetition of the same feet and movements.

This is remedied by mixing all kinds of feet that can enter into the same type of verse, or by mixing verses of different types, as we have done in the <term>Dithyrambe</term> <note>A wild, choral hymn, originally Greek.</note> of the article of the 17th question on <term>Genesis</term> <note>Likely a reference to the author's own theological-musical commentary.</note>, which begins:
*The heart throbs, the trembling vitals leap within the fibers.* <note>original: "Cor micat, exultant trepida præcordia fibris."</note>

Or by diminishing the same foot and movement, and by using all the combinations and varieties that each measure can allow, as I said in the preceding Proposition. Now, it is certain that if one practices these varieties and mixtures, one will create more beautiful and different movements in one day than the most excellent makers of Ballets—who do not know this practice or who despise it—can make in a month, even though they say that this seems to shock common sense, and they consider themselves the most skillful men in the world. They would frankly admit this if they took the trouble, or rather the pleasure, of using all the varieties of which we have just spoken, by mixing feet and movements that are of the same nature, or indeed of different species, according to the passions of the listeners they wish to touch, or the things they wish to represent.

In the fourth place, when singing in several parts, one part can use one type of movement and another part another. For example, the <term>Bass</term> can use the <term>Spondee</term> or the Anapest, while the <term>Treble</term> <note>original: "Dessus," the highest vocal part.</note> performs the <term>Dactyl</term>, for they share the same time; and these counter-times will be agreeable if they are practiced appropriately, whether in an entire piece of music or only in a few measures. One part can also use the 1st and 2nd <term>Paeon</term> <note>A Greek metrical foot of four syllables, one long and three short.</note>, while the other performs the 3rd and 4th, and so on for the others. And even if one wishes, and if the subject requires it, one of the parts may perform feet of equal or double measure, while the other uses the ternary, sesquialtera, or sesquitertia measure or movement, etc. <note>These terms refer to rhythmic ratios: sesquialtera is 3:2, sesquitertia is 4:3.</note> And if there are 4, 5, or 6 parts, each can use different movements or feet; for example, the <term>Treble</term> will play 9 hooked notes <note>Quavers or eighth notes.</note> to the measure, to imitate the movement of the <term>Ditone</term> <note>A major third.</note>, while the <term>Counter-tenor</term> <note>original: "Hautecontre."</note> will perform the movement of the <term>Diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth.</note> with 7 notes, the <term>Tenor</term> <note>original: "Taille."</note> the movement of the <term>Diapente</term> <note>A perfect fifth.</note> by making 5 notes, the first <term>Bass</term> the movement of the <term>Twelfth</term> by making four notes in its measure, and the second <term>Bass</term> the movement of the <term>Octave</term> with three notes to the measure.

On this point, it must also be noted that <term>Practitioners</term> <note>Professional musicians or performers as opposed to theoretical scholars.</note> do not use the terms <term>binary</term>, <term>triple</term>, <term>ternary</term>, and <term>hemiola</term> <note>A rhythmic ratio of 3:2.</note>, etc., in their proper sense when speaking of their measures. For the <term>binary</term> or <term>double</term> measure should be composed of two notes against one—for example, three quarter notes, where two are played on the downbeat and one on the upbeat, or vice versa. Because this is in the same ratio as the movements that create the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"; the ratio of 2:1.</note>, one can call this measure the "Octave movement." As for what they call "Binary," it would be better named "equal measure," or "measure of equality," and "Unison movement," since it is composed of one note on the downbeat and one on the upbeat, which are of the same value and like <term>Unisons</term>. In contrast, in the double measure—which they call <term>ternary</term>—the note of the downbeat is double the value of the upbeat.

Now, ordinary <term>Composers</term> use almost exclusively these two types of movements because they find them the easiest and wish to avoid pain and labor. But if they wish to create something extraordinary, they can still use five types of excellent measures which will greatly enrich the variety of <term>harmonic movements</term>. I explain only three of them here; once they have put these into practice, I will give them the other two, and as many more as they could possibly employ or desire.

One of these three movements imitates the <term>Fifth</term> <note>original: "Diapente"; the ratio of 3:2.</note>, because it makes three notes or three beats on the strike <note>The downbeat.</note> and two on the lift <note>The upbeat.</note>, or vice versa, as seen in the 5th example of this table:

<image-desc>A musical staff showing seven examples of rhythmic patterns. Each example consists of a crotchet, two quavers, and another crotchet, all on the same pitch. The examples are numbered 1 through 7 above the staff.</image-desc>

So that its measure is composed of 5, 10, or 20 notes; just as the measure of the 2nd movement (or the 6th example) is composed of 7 beats, of which 4 are made on the strike and 3 on the lift, or vice versa. Finally, the third, which is seen in the 7th example, is composed of 9 beats—namely, 4 on the downbeat and 4 on the upbeat <note>The author likely means 5 and 4 to reach the total of 9, or is describing a specific subdivision.</note>. Now, the sixth measure is the movement of the <term>Fourth</term> <note>The ratio of 4:3.</note>, and the 7th is that of the <term>Major Third</term>. Thus, he who uses these movements will be as harmonic in his measures as in his melody. Furthermore, these will lead him to invent a great multitude of rules and observations for the use of <term>consonances</term> and <term>dissonances</term> which have not yet been considered.

In the fifth and last place, one must not imagine that one is always obliged to make the downbeat of a measure worth twice as much as its upbeat in double measure, or equally in simple (or unison) measure. On the contrary, it is often expedient to make the upbeat much shorter in order to reinforce the movement and give it more gaiety and energy. For example, instead of making the <term>Iambic foot</term> or the <term>Anapestic foot</term> <note>Rhythms borrowed from Greek poetic meters.</note> according to the ordinary value of these notes: <image-desc>A musical staff showing two short rhythmic patterns. The first pattern is a quaver followed by a crotchet. The second pattern is two quavers followed by a crotchet.</image-desc>, it is good to make them as they are in the first and second examples above, to make them more perceptible and vigorous. Likewise, the <term>Choriambic</term> movement can be made as it is in the third example; which must similarly be concluded for all other types...

## PROPOSITION XXVI.
->To explain Rhythmopoeia, or the Art of making beautiful movements upon all sorts of subjects.<-

Just as the Art of making Songs and Airs, and of composing every sort
of Music for as many parts as one wishes—which is named and defined
by the Greeks as <term>μέτροις, μέλοις, δίαυλαις, κρουστικοῖς μέλεσι</term> <note>original: "metres, melodies, flute-tunes, and instrumental songs"</note>—consists in knowing
the sequence and progress of the degrees and intervals of each system taken
within each genre, and in choosing the proper melody to express the passion
of the subject and of the text that one proposes, likewise the Art of arranging
movements, which the Greeks call <term>rhythmopoeia</term> <note>original: ῥυθμοποιΐα; the art of rhythmic composition</note>, consists in knowing and
choosing the feet or the meters, and the verses which are proper for expressing
passions, or the other things that one proposes, and which can be represented
by movement. Now we have explained all the species of
feet and verses, so that it is only necessary to add their properties, so
that Composers may use them, and that before beginning a fantasy,
or such other piece of Music as one can imagine, they may know
the movements which must be used, if they desire that their Music make
some impression upon the mind of the Listeners. I say then first that
perfect melody must be composed of harmony, movement, and
words, as Aristides <note>Aristides Quintilianus, a Greek music theorist</note> teaches in his first book, <term>perfect rhythm is that which is composed of harmony, rhythm, and diction</term> <note>original: μέτρος δ' ἔςι τῆλετον ῥυθμὸν ὁ ἔκτε ἀρμονίας καὶ ῥυθμοῦ καὶ λέξεως συνεστής.</note> and consequently that
the Composer must have a particular care for these three parts; for example,
he must choose the genre and the mode of Music, so that if it is more fitting
to use the degrees of the Diatonic, and of the Phrygian Mode, he avoids the
chromatic degrees, and the strings of the Lydian, and if the Song must be made
in the first or lowest strings of the System, which are named
by the Greeks <term>Hypatoides</term> <note>The lower range of the Greek scale system</note>, he does not touch those of the middle, nor of the—

After having chosen the melody, one must join to it the proper movement, which the Greeks call *Rhythm*, which is a system composed of different times, according to the subject being treated. If this movement is for dances, one must observe the downbeat and the upbeat, which they name *arsis* and *thesis* <note>original: "apsis & sisis"; the author likely inverted or misread the Greek terms for lifting and setting down the foot</note>, in order to raise the body in the former, and to lower it in the latter, which they did even while singing, and which is still done in village dances, where those who dance sing together.

In the second place, one must choose the species of movement, and the times necessary to execute the intended effect: and because equal movement is proper for spirits who love tranquility and peace, and who are friends of rest and solitude, if one wishes to induce this affection, one must use the Dorian mode of the ancients, and their *Hesychastic* style, with the spondaic movement, which admits all feet where the downbeat is equal to the upbeat, which are seen in the examples I have placed in the preceding Propositions. Now this equal movement is called <term>binary measure</term> <note>Time signatures with two beats, like 2/4 or 4/4</note> by ordinary Composers, as I have already remarked: but when one wishes to change this affection to enter into a more turbulent passion, one must use the Phrygian mode and a double movement, and feet where the downbeat or the *thesis* is double the upbeat, or the *arsis*, or vice versa, and particularly the iambic movement, which Poets use in their Tragedies, as is seen in Seneca; to which the *Diastaltic* relates. If one uses a pause equal to the first downbeat of the trochaic movement, it relates entirely to the iambic. The Choriambic movement partakes of these two feet, for it is composed of them; and the 3rd Paean partakes of the Pyrrhic and the Iamb which compose it. Certainly it is difficult to find the reason for these different effects of metrical feet, or of different movements, and to determine precisely for what each foot or verse is proper, especially considering that all Poets use all kinds of verse indifferently to represent or to excite all kinds of passions and affections, even though they try to put several short syllables in a row to express fast and light things, as I have said before: although those who are not constrained by words, and who content themselves with making <term>Branles</term> <note>A popular French Renaissance dance performed in a circle or line</note>, and other kinds of fantasies and dances for <term>Ballets</term>, can, it seems, use more kinds of movements, because they do not subject themselves to either prose or verse. Now if it is permitted to philosophize on this matter, one can say that the iamb is proper for expressing anger, because it imitates the promptness and lightness of fire in its beginning, and it redoubles its force in the second part of its movement, which is double the first that the Greeks make while lifting, like that of the *Pyrrhic*. Practitioners call this iambic and trochaic movement <term>ternary measure</term> <note>Triple time, such as 3/4</note>, although it is rather double. Those who desire to go further to find the reason for the effects of each movement, foot, or verse, must study to know the movements of the passions, of the blood, and of the other humors, which usually follow and accompany one another,

Scaliger is also useful for this subject in his book *On the Causes of the Latin Language* <note>original: "De causis linguae Latinae"</note>, and in that of the *Art of Poetry*. I add only that many are not of the opinion of Halicarnassus, who subjects Music <note>i.e., makes music subordinate to the rules of rhetoric</note>, for they judge it more appropriate that Music be subjected to the words, so that one makes syllables long and short in singing just as in speaking, and that songs be nothing other than a discourse embellished and elevated by an excellent Harmony. This must particularly be observed in measured verse, and even in rhymed verse as much as possible, so that the Listeners distinguish and understand all the words, and that Music does not make itself a slave to barbarism and ignorance. Now I return to Rhythmic movements, and to the Art of making them, of which it seems one cannot give a better instruction than by examples of all, or at least of the principal types of measured verse, which contain the movements and measures that the Greeks and Latins used in their Odes and their Songs. For although the table of Metric feet in the 17th Proposition suffices to make one understand everything belonging to movements, nevertheless the succession of several feet of the same kind will provide more clarity. But before putting down these examples, it is appropriate to remark that it is not necessary for Composers to observe the brevity of syllables so strictly that they are not sometimes permitted to lengthen them, as the Greek and Latin Poets have done, particularly when several short syllables meet in the same word, such as in *sedition*, *premeditate*, *pudicity* <note>modesty/chastity</note>, etc., which have all their syllables short; this is why one can lengthen their first syllable, as was done in the Latin word *Italy* <note>original: "Italiam"</note>, in order to make it a Dactyl. Be that as it may, and whatever liberty Composers wish to take regarding the movements, and for the timing of syllables and steps, or feet—which I do not intend to take away from them—I place here examples of each movement practiced by the ancients, both so that everyone may better understand all that we have said of feet, verses, movements, and their measure, and so that those who love antiquity may use them in their songs, and enjoy what they practiced that was most beautiful and best regulated; for as for the movements they join to the melody, they have no other rules than the steps under which they make them exercise, as can be seen in the examples of Dances that I have placed in Propositions 23, 24, 25, and 27 of the book on Songs, where I have tried to relate them to certain movements, leaving the liberty to each person to reduce them to such other feet or movements as they judge appropriate. I only add here another example of a *Branle à mener* <note>A "led" branle, a popular French Renaissance orchestral dance</note>, the song of which is judged very excellent, so that it may serve as an exercise for those who wish to determine to what genre of verse, or to what species of feet or movements it should be related.

<note>Musical notation for a Branle à mener, showing a melody line and a bass line in polyphonic style.</note>

For I do not doubt that one encounters all sorts of feet and verses in the fantasies and songs that serve now for singing, dancing, and drinking, since the imaginations of men are similar; there being, it seems, no other difference between the songs of modern Practitioners and those of Pindar and Horace <note>Famous Greek and Roman lyric poets</note>, except that the latter give the same time, the same measure, or the same quantity to their verses and to the words as to the melody and the movement of the body, and that they perhaps regulate the feet and steps better; whereas our Composers use only rhymed verses, which have no fixed measure. Now, it is enough to have begun the treatise on Rhythmics to introduce its use, and to excite those who have worked more on this subject to give it in its entirety. one should read Hephaestion <note>original: "Epheftion"; a 2nd-century Greek grammarian who wrote a definitive manual on meters</note> in his entirety, rather than just the fragments that are cited, if one wishes to know the full extent of the Metrics of the ancients and everything belonging to their verse. ### PROPOSITION XXVII.

*To give examples of all kinds of Rhythmic movements of the ancients, that is*
*to say, of their verses: to show the movements and the metrical feet of our*
*rhymed verses, and to explain the Art of finding them in all kinds*
*of words, both French and Latin.*

This Proposition, joined to the preceding ones, provides the *Rhythmopoeia* <term>Rhythmopoeia: the art of composing rhythmic patterns or the "making of rhythm"</term> or the Art of movements, without there being any need to seek it elsewhere; for all the kinds of rhythmic times or movements that I place at the end of this Proposition encompass the best of what the ancients had on this subject, particularly if one adds the freedom of diminishing long and short times.

As for the movements of rhymed verses, which are used only in France, among several verses that can serve as examples, I take those from the first Proposition of the 5th book of Composition, so that the reader does not depend on anything outside of our own books. Now, the first stanza that follows:

*   Since the Monarch of the Angels <note>French: "Puisque le Monarque des Anges"</note> short-short-long, short-long-short-long
*   Does not disdain our praises, <note>French: "Ne dedaigne point nos loüanges"</note> short-short-long, short-long, short-long-short-long
*   Sing the excess of his goodness, <note>French: "Chantez l'excez de fa bonté"</note> short-long-short-long, short-short-long
*   And living in innocence <note>French: "Et viuant dedans l'innocence"</note> short-short-long, short-long, short-long-short-long
*   Make known the power <note>French: "Faictes connoiftre la puiffance"</note> short-short-long, short-long, short-long-short-long
*   Of his divine Majesty. <note>French: "De fa diuine Maiefté"</note> short-long, short-short-short-short-long,

has the movements that I explain here in the same way that Demetrius and the other Greek or Latin Scholiasts <note>ancient commentators or grammarians</note> explain the feet of the verses used by the ancient Poets, with this sole difference: that the subject of our verses is more excellent and more elevated than that which served them. Thus, it only remains to give them a modulation <note>a musical setting or melodic inflection</note> that is appropriate to their divine subject, which can and should ravish both men and Angels. I say then, first, that the first verse is composed of a Dactyl, a Scolion, and a Palimbacchius, although one could make a Molossus of the last foot, because the last syllable of each verse can be long or short, according to the will of each person. One can also say that this verse is composed of a Trochee and an Anapest, which make an Iambic Dipody <note>a unit of two metrical feet</note>, and then an Iamb and a Spondee, which make the first Epitrite, if one makes the last syllable long, or the Antispastic, if one makes it short, as is seen in the longs and shorts marked across from the first verse. The second verse is composed of an Anapest, a Spondee, a Trochee, and a Spondee, which make the 2nd Epitrite if the last syllable is lengthened, or a Trochaic Dipody if it is made short. The 3rd verse is composed of the 2nd Epitrite and the minor Ionic, which makes a very beautiful movement. The 4th contains an Iambic Dipody composed of an Anapest and an Iamb, and a Trochaic Dipody...

-># On Songs<-

...so that this verse contains the two bases of the two principal species of verse. The [verse] is composed of a second <term>Epitrite</term><note>A metrical foot of four syllables: three long and one short.</note>, an <term>iambic dipody</term><note>A unit of two iambic feet.</note>, two iambs, and a syllable, so that one could name it <term>Hypercatalectic Dimeter</term><note>A line of two measures with an extra syllable at the end.</note>, or <term>Brachycatalectic Trimeter</term><note>A line of three measures lacking the final two syllables.</note>: like the first three catalectic dimeters. As for the third, it is composed of an iambic dipody made of an iamb and a <term>tribrach</term><note>A foot of three short syllables.</note>, and a <term>bacchius</term><note>A foot of one short followed by two long syllables.</note>, or of an iamb, a <term>proceleusmatic</term><note>A foot of four short syllables.</note>, and a spondee. From this it is easy to conclude that one can transport and find in our rhymed verses all the richness, variety, and beauty of the movements found in the verses of Pindar <note>Ancient Greek lyric poet famous for his complex odes.</note> and other poets, without it being necessary to practice <term>measured verse</term><note>Verses strictly following Greek and Latin quantitative rules rather than rhyme.</note>; although their practice further greatly increases the diversity of movements. As for the art of finding metrical feet in rhymed verses, and in Latin or French prose, nothing else is needed but the table of 27 feet on page 376 of this book; for if one places it before their eyes while reading all sorts of verse, or whatever words one wishes, one can mark all the long and short syllables of the verses, dividing them into feet, as I have done in the stanza of the six preceding verses. For example, one will find that the first verse of the second stanza, namely, ***His hand the source of all being*** <note>original: "Sa main la source de tout estre"</note>, is composed of an iambic dipody and the fourth <term>paeon</term><note>A foot of three short syllables and one long.</note>, with one remaining syllable, or of two iambs, a tribrach, and a trochee, so that it can be an <term>Acatalectic Iambic Dimeter</term>. I leave the other stanzas for the exercise of those who will apply themselves to this reduction of movements, which requires only common sense joined to the pronunciation of each word; for when one makes a syllable long that is short—for example, the first syllable of ***living*** <note>original: "vivant"</note>—and when one makes short that which is long—for example, the first syllable of ***being*** <note>original: "estre"</note>—the ear and the imagination are offended by it, so that one has difficulty enduring it, and everyone can mark the quantity, the time, and the movement of each word and syllable without any other master or teaching than the ear. This is not to say, however, that all syllables that sound [a certain way] to the ear when made long or short have this quantity by their nature (excepting a few whose pronunciation can only be long or short without great difficulty, as happens with our *feminine* [e], which is difficult to lengthen); for most pronunciations come only from usage and custom, which passes for law in matters of speech, just as words are regarding their meaning, which is no less voluntary nor better founded than their utterance or pronunciation, as I have shown in the *Book on the Voice*.

Now the twelve stanzas of the Psalm for which I have determined the feet in the first stanza show evidently, in the twelve <term>modes</term><note>Musical scales or systems used in composition.</note> to which they serve as lyrics, that our musical composers are very far from observing the movements and the timings that must be given to each syllable. From this it often happens that their songs lack grace, even though their composition in two or more parts may be good and follows the ordinary rules. But if they observe the quantity of which I have just spoken, they will easily succeed in making very natural and agreeable songs, so that no one will be able to find any fault in them, and those who do not know the secret of movements and metrical feet will admire them and will be unable to imitate them.

Let us now examine the examples of the principal types of verses used by Greek and Latin Musicians and Poets in their Songs, so that everyone may be able to imitate their movements. ### Embellishment
The Italians, Spaniards, Germans, and other nations can also mark the feet or rhythmic movements of their verses in the same manner, so that the Musicians of each Kingdom will have their metrical poetry without changing their rhymed cadences, or their cadenced rhymes. Now, I wish to add here the manner of singing used by the best Masters in France, which can be understood by the following example that I had promised in the second part of this book, so that nothing may be found wanting in our treatises, and so that everyone may imitate the method of those who teach singing in Paris, whose practice and Art consists of creating good Melodies <note>original: "Chants"</note>, and in diminishing and embellishing them.

#### PROPOSITION XXVIII.
To give examples of the diminution and embellishment of Melodies, and the method of creating good Melodies, and of embellishing them through diminution <term>Diminution: A technique where long notes are broken down into shorter, faster notes to decorate a melody.</term>.

The Example that follows serves not only to teach the Method of enriching Airs <note>Airs: Secular vocal songs, often for solo voice.</note> through all kinds of diminutions, and to provide an idea to follow and imitate, but also to show that the duration of syllables and the order of movements is not observed therein; which, without doubt, removes much of its charm, as is easy to judge for anyone who has the sense and understanding of long and short syllables: for all the syllables of the first verse are all made of an equal value, and the second syllable of the word *I adore* <note>original: "j'adore"</note> is lengthened there, even though it is short: but I have already given the measure and the quantity of this first stanza in the 23rd Proposition. And one cannot know what I have said in this fourth part on Rhythmics <note>original: "Rythmique"</note> without being able to mark the quantity of each syllable as well as I, which is why I add nothing to this discourse, except that our Composers of Airs can excuse their method of lengthening short syllables and shortening long ones by following the opinion of Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who wrote on the arrangement of words and musicality of speech.</note>.

Be that as it may, I place here an example to which everyone can add as much as they wish, for all the beautiful traits and all the kinds of diminutions and modulations cannot be found in a single Melody as short as this one.

And then, after having given this example, which shows the method of singing—or at least of composing—of the best and most experienced Masters, and of those who enjoy everyone's approval, I will explain all the ways in which Musicians mark their measures. This is so that everyone may recognize at first sight <note>original: "à livre ouvert"</note> everything that is customarily marked at the beginning and in other places of Composition for several parts, whether in old books printed and written two or three hundred years ago, or in new ones. For although I believe that numbers can replace all their Characters, it is appropriate to explain their artifice, as we do in the 30th Proposition of this book. As for the sequence that follows, it shows the Method of singing the Odes of Pindar and Homer, which can be compared with the Air that follows, in order to see if our Composers of France are more excellent than those of Greece, or of other nations.

### on Songs.

If the Musicians of Greece allowed themselves as much liberty as their Poets to shorten long syllables or to lengthen short ones, I do not doubt that they would approve of the preceding manner of singing. This manner should, in my opinion, be permitted to all kinds of Musicians who desire to excel in the Art of composing good Songs; for there is little reason to always restrict them to the strictness of shorts and longs, though they may sometimes use such constraint to show they are not ignorant of it. But they are not obliged to make all long syllables of the same length, for they can give the duration of a semibreve, a minim, a crotchet, or even a quaver <note>These are historical musical note values: whole, half, quarter, and eighth notes</note> to long syllables, provided that within the same measure or diction, they use notes of a lesser duration on the short syllables. This is seen in the *Ode of Horace* which begins *I hate the uninitiated* <note>original: "Odi profanum"</note>, which I have provided above; and in the Proposition that follows, by which I conclude what pertains to Metrical Poetry. I have already noted above the melodic variation <note>original: "diminution"</note> of the verse, *He preferred on earth* <note>original: "Maluit terris"</note>, from the *Hymn Born of the Noise of Saint Francis of Paola* <note>original: "Bruio natus"</note>, which is sung at the first Vespers of his Feast, so that one may see the manner of embellishing Latin Songs as well as French ones. Some imagine that in former times these variations, trills, glides <note>original: "ports de voix"</note>, and passages were used when singing <term>Neumes</term> <note>Early musical notation signs used in medieval church music</note> and the <term>Alleluia</term> in the Churches, instead of the quantity of notes now used on a single syllable; this displeases many, because of the faults and the coarseness and harshness of the voices, which has already led to the removal of many notes from several syllables. As for the conduct and modulation of Church Songs, it is certain that there are very good ones, as experienced in the <term>Hymns</term> *From the quarter where the sun rises* <note>original: "A solis ortus cardine"</note>, *Bounteous Creator of the stars* <note>original: "Conditor alme syderum"</note>, *At the sacred solemnities* <note>original: "Sacris solemniis"</note>, and *So that your servants may* <note>original: "Ut queant laxis"</note>; and in the <term>Proses</term> <note>A type of liturgical hymn, also called a Sequence</note>, *Praises to the Paschal Victim* <note>original: "Victimae paschali laudes"</note>, and *Sion, praise the Savior* <note>original: "Lauda Sion salvatorem"</note>. And perhaps the most skillful Musicians of this century could not succeed so well if they were given these words to set to Song. Be that as it may, the antiquity and beauty of these Songs, and of many others used in the Churches, deserve respect and render them worthy of consideration.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

*To explain the manner of singing the Odes of Pindar and Horace, and the means of making French verses as suitable for Music as those of Pindar and other Poets.*

Many are so charmed by the Odes of <term>Pindar</term> <note>A famous ancient Greek lyric poet</note> and the verses of other Poets that they despise our rhymed verses as unworthy of being compared to those of Greece, or even of being read. But we are not of this opinion, for there are those who maintain that we have several pieces of rhymed poetry that yield in no way to the best of the Greeks.

Be that as it may, it suffices to show how one can sing the Odes of Greek and Latin Poets, and how our rhymed verses can receive the same grace. For this purpose, I place here the first <term>Strophe</term> <note>The first section of an ancient Greek choral ode</note> of <term>Pindar</term> in such a way that one sees the song and the rhythm on each verse; for the let—

Best indeed is water; but gold, like a blazing fire <note>original: "ΑΡΙΣΤΟΝ μὲν ὕδωρ..." This is the famous opening of Pindar's First Olympian Ode.</note> shining through the night, stands out above lordly wealth. But if, my heart, you wish to sing of prizes, look no further than the sun for another star more warming in the day through the empty sky. Nor shall we celebrate a contest greater than Olympia, from whence the famous hymn enfolds the thoughts of the wise, to sing the son of Cronus when they come to the rich and blessed hearth of Hiero. <note>The transcription provided contains some Greek typographical errors or archaic ligatures; the translation reflects the standard reconstructed text of Pindar's First Olympian Ode.</note>

It is not necessary to give warning of the different notes of this song, which mark the long and short syllables, since they are so evident. It suffices to add that everyone should take the same liberty of marking the long syllables sometimes with a half note <term>minime: a half note in early music notation</term>, and at other times with a quarter note <term>noire: literally "black," referring to a quarter note</term>, or an eighth note <term>crochûe: a hooked note or eighth note</term>, either alone or with a dot, which often gives a graceful touch to the song and the syllable. However, the notes that follow immediately after to mark the short syllables of the same word must be of lesser duration; for example, if the long syllable has a half note, the short syllable must have a quarter note, etc. One can see the practice of this in the preceding song, and in the Ode by Horace which follows, without the need for a longer discourse. *Ode 4 of the 1st book of Horace.*

# On Songs.

As for the other stanzas of this Ode, they can be sung to this same melody, provided that one lengthens the syllables of one which happen to be short in the other; for example, the first syllable of the word *trahunt* <note>Latin: "they pull"</note> from the preceding stanza is short, whereas it is long in the word *iuncte* <note>Latin: "joined"</note> which corresponds to it in the second stanza: the same must be concluded for the other syllables.

Now, after having shown the manner of singing Greek and Latin Poetry, it is necessary to add the method for bringing French poetry to just as great a perfection. This is easy to do if one uses the same liberties as the Greeks, by employing verses measured by feet, or by long and short syllables, just as they did; since our rhymed verses are added to this, we shall be richer in our Poetry than they are in theirs. But because I have treated quite amply of the Metric Art, and of the manner of finding all sorts of feet and movements in rhymed verses, it suffices to add the following example to show the manner of singing the measured verses of Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a poet who attempted to introduce classical meters into French</note>, following the opinion of Jacques Mauduit <note>A French composer of the late Renaissance known for his experiments with "musique mesurée"</note>: the first is *Dactylic Hexameter*, and is measured by a simple monopody; as is the second, which is *Pentameter*; the third and fourth are *Anapestic Dimeter Acatalectic*; the fifth and sixth are *Dactylic Trochaic*.

Recant. <note>Likely a musical instruction or heading for the example</note>

Living Echo, seat of love, of my ardor, do not cool the violent heat; Nymph, burn with love. The fountain remains black and clear always: And there the person is seen and discovers the depths. You will see nothing hidden there, living Echo, but I do not see the depths of your heart. <note>This text uses Baïf's phonetic spelling system, which I have translated into standard English prose.</note>

I have only given one example here, because I have placed several others in the 57th question on Genesis, both in Latin and in French; but it is difficult to determine if these measured verses in our language are as good and can have as much efficacy in Music as the Greek ones, given that many despise them because they do not sound as well to the ear as rhymed ones, and because they believe that we are very far from the spirit, the industry, and the capacity of the Greek and Latin Poets. But they will perhaps change their minds if they consider the same measure, the same movement, and the same genres of verse, with subjects just as beautiful and material just as rich, which are treated no less well in our verses than in theirs, which in fact do not sound any better to the ear, there being only the single—

Before putting an end to this Proposition, it must be remarked that some imagine that the preceding Ode of Pindar was sung in the Dorian mode <note>original: "ton Dorien"</note>, because he places in the Antistrophe: *taking the lyre from the peg* <note>original Greek: διελὼν ἀπὸ φόρμιγγα πασσάλυ λάμβανε; Pindar, Olympian 1.17</note>; but this can be explained by the Dorian idiom, just as the "Music" of which the Poets speak is most often understood as the Encyclopedia of Sciences <note>The "circle of learning" or liberal arts</note>, or of good letters, to which honorable men apply themselves. This does not prevent their Odes from having been sung to the Harp, or to their other instruments according to the epithet *hymns that rule the lyre* <note>original Greek: ἀναξιφόρμιγγες ὕμνοι; Pindar, Olympian 2.1</note>, which he gives to the Hymns in his 2nd Ode. Nevertheless, if one wishes to understand the passages of Pindar, or of other Poets, as referring to certain instruments suited to expressing the Dorian mode rather than another—following the remark in the 30th Proposition of the 7th book on Percussion Instruments—I leave the free judgment of it to the readers. Let us now see all the kinds of measures used by our practitioners.

# PROPOSITION XXX.

## *To explain the Major Mode and the Minor, Perfect and Imperfect Time, and Perfect and Imperfect Prolation, with the Characters by which practitioners signify all these kinds of time.*

The understanding of all these terms and their practice depends on the four notes named the **Maxima**, **Long**, **Breve**, and **Semibreve**, <term>Maxima, Long, Breve, Semibreve: The primary note values in medieval and Renaissance music, descending in duration.</term> inasmuch as there are only these four notes whose value is increased or diminished by the characters placed at the beginning of the musical staves <note>original: "reglets de Musique"</note>. Now, musicians particularly use three or four kinds of characters for this subject: namely, the capital letters **O** and **C**, in which they sometimes place dots, or cross them with a line, as is seen in these first characters, and by one or three bars which cross two or three spaces, like those that follow. <image-desc>A row of musical mensuration signs including a circle with a dot, a circle, a broken circle with a dot, a broken circle, a slashed circle with a dot, a slashed circle, a slashed broken circle with a dot, and a slashed broken circle, followed by three vertical bars spanning multiple staff spaces.</image-desc>
Besides these characters, they also add the numbers 2 or 3, as is seen in the following Table, which explains this entire Proposition so clearly that one need not labor at all to understand it. For the first column shows first the **maxima** note, which alone belongs to the **Major Mode**, which is perfect or imperfect according to the characters placed at the beginning of the musical staves, which modify and determine the value of this maxima. For example, the **O 22** of the 5th column shows that the Major Mode is perfect, just as the **O** with a single **2** teaches that it is imperfect. And the **Minor Mode** of the 2nd column, which contains the **long** note (which alone is assigned to this minor mode, whether perfect or imperfect), is rendered perfect by this same character. From this it follows that the sign of perfection of the Major Mode makes the Maxima worth 3 longs; that is why I have put 12 in the 7th column, and 4 in the 8th opposite the Long and the Maxima, to signify that this Maxima comprises and is worth 3 longs, just as 12 comprises 3 times 4; and likewise for the others. The 3rd column belongs to the note that practitioners name...

<header>Embellishment</header>

<term>Breve</term><note>A note value in early music, originally meaning "short," though it is long by modern standards.</note>, and to <term>perfect</term> or <term>imperfect time</term><note>Perfect time refers to triple meter (3 beats), while imperfect refers to duple meter (2 beats).</note>, which belongs only to this note; now, it has its perfect time when one of the characters in the 5th or 6th column—opposite which one sees *perfect* in the cells of the 3rd column—is found on the staff lines. The 4th column contains the <term>Semibreve</term> note, and belongs to <term>Prolation</term><note>The relationship between the semibreve and the minim.</note>, both perfect and imperfect, which also has the characters of perfection or imperfection in the 5th or 6th column. Now, if one compares the squares or cells of each column with one another, one will know exactly the value of each of these 4 notes. For example, if one reads the 6th column descending to the margin, one will see *perfect* in the first 4 cells, and in the last 5 the numbers 27, 9, 3, 1, which signify that the <term>Maxima</term><note>The longest note value in mensural notation.</note> belongs to the <term>Major Mode</term>, the <term>Long</term> to the <term>Minor</term>, and the <term>Breve</term> to perfect time, and that the <term>Semibreve</term> has perfect prolation, and consequently that it is worth 3 <term>minims</term>, as one sees in the eleventh or last cell; just as the Breve is worth 3 Semibreves, the Long 3 Breves, and the Maxima 3 Longs, following the preceding numbers 27, 9, etc. On the contrary, the 5th column taken at the margin shows the imperfection and the lesser value of the said 4 notes, namely 8, 4, 2, 1, to show that the Maxima is worth only two Longs, the Long two Breves, etc.

Those who desire examples of all these times and these characters may see them in the 17th, 18th, 19th, and 20th books of <term>Pedro Cerone</term><note>An Italian theorist who wrote a massive treatise on music in Spanish (1613).</note>, unless they prefer to wait for them from Mr. de <term>Cousu</term>, <term>Canon of Saint-Quentin</term>, who promises an entire treatise on them with all the rules and examples of all kinds of <term>Composition</term>. As for examples, it is not necessary to give others than those which Mr. <term>Aux-Cousteaux</term>, an excellent musician, has recently had printed in three parts; for he has given 50 <term>Trios</term> which he set in the 12 <term>Modes</term>, both by <term>B-flat</term> and by <term>B-natural</term>, which can serve as a model for those who wish to learn to compose. And the Reverend Father <term>Charles d'Ambleville</term>, Jesuit, has also had printed the <term>Psalms</term> and <term>Hymns</term> of <term>Vespers</term> in both 4 and 6 parts, which abundantly supply all the examples one could desire here. This is why I put none here, and why I have given so few in the books on Composition; for there is neither pleasure nor profit in repeating what has already been done by so many people—especially since the shop of Mr. <term>Ballard</term><note>The prominent Ballard family held a royal monopoly on music printing in France for generations.</note> is so full and so well-supplied with all kinds of examples from the best <term>Masters</term> who have ever been (as I said in the 31st Proposition of the 7th book on Instruments), that one can wish for nothing more. The public, and particularly all those who make a profession of this Art or who receive pleasure from it, are greatly indebted to him, both because of the great time and care he has employed in inventing the beautiful characters <note>Referring to the elegant music typefaces used in printing.</note> which he uses—which so greatly surpass those of Italy and other places—and by reason of his proofreading, which is so exact that it is difficult to find a single error in an entire book.

Now it must be noted, for the understanding of the preceding <term>Table</term>, that in the 6th column in the middle, starting from top to bottom, all the <term>natural signs</term> (♮) and the <term>slashed natural signs</term> are put in place of the <term>C</term> and the <term>dotted circle</term> (☉) of Cerone's Table, because we do not have dotted ones in France, and the <term>C</term> of the 5th column (not dotted), opposite the slashed ones of the 6th, ought to be dotted. Everything else is correct; but our musicians are content to use the circle (O) and dotted circle (☉), and the <term>C</term> and natural sign (♮) for all kinds of signs.

<header>on Rhythmics.</header>

### PROPOSITION XXXI.
To explain the manner of singing all kinds of measures without the preceding characters, and to propose what seems most difficult in the Rhythmics of the Ancients.

ALthough I do not blame nor entirely reject the preceding signs of modes, time, and prolation <note>These refer to the complex system of "Mensural Notation" used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance to denote rhythmic relationships</note>; since it is necessary to know their value and accidents to understand the Music of the ancients marked in this manner, nevertheless I do not doubt that one can express their thoughts by numbers alone; for it is easy to designate each note of those subject to the preceding modes, to prolation, and of time; for example, the number one placed on the first line of the musical staff will signify that the <term>maxima</term> <note>The longest note value in medieval music</note> is worth three longs; being placed on the second line, it will serve to make it understood that the long is worth three breves; being placed on the third line, that the breve will be worth three semibreves; and being placed on the fourth line, that the semibreve is worth three minims; and when this unity is not there, one will know that they are worth only two of the preceding notes; or if one prefers to use one of the letters of the Alphabet, for example, P to signify the perfection of the major mode on the first line, of the minor on the second, of time on the third, and of prolation on the fourth; one will have all that can be desired on this subject, without any embarrassment and without using other characters than those of the Alphabet which are known to all those who know how to read. I leave aside the black notes, both square and lozenge-shaped; whether with a tail or without a tail, and with hooks or without hooks; and all the upright Cs and reversed Ɔs, barred, and divided by one, two, or three bars, of which <term>Cerone</term> <note>Domenico Pietro Cerone (1566–1625), an Italian music theorist</note> treats very amply in his *<term>Institution</term>*, and <term>Zarlino</term> <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), an influential Renaissance theorist</note> from the 67th to the 72nd chapter of the 3rd part of his *<term>Institution</term>*, in order to remark upon the greatest difficulties found in the <term>Rhythmics</term> <note>The study of rhythm and meter</note> of the ancients. I say then first that it seems their *<term>arsis</term>* and *<term>thesis</term>* <note>Greek terms for the "lifting" and "setting down" of the voice or foot in meter</note> is difficult to practice in songs, and even in the pronunciation of verse, because they want one to always raise the voice in the *<term>arsis</term>*, and lower it in the *<term>thesis</term>*, whereas our <term>Practitioners</term> are content to lower and raise the hand to make the sign of the measure, which the <term>Spaniards</term> call <term>Compas</term> <note>The beat or time-signature</note>. If one could take the elevation of the voice for its reinforcement; whether on the same tone or on different strings, and its lowering or its remission for its weakening, it would be easier to practice them while singing, just as one practices the <term>Echo</term> on <term>Instruments</term>, but the Greek Authors I have read, whether printed or manuscript, speak of the *<term>arsis</term>* as an elevation of the voice to a higher pitch, by which they want one to begin the first beat of the <term>Pyrrhic</term> <note>A metrical foot consisting of two short syllables</note>, which <term>Bacchius</term> and several others call <term>pyrrhichios</term> <note>original: "πυρριχιος"</note>, as the first of all the feet. They thus begin all the other feet that have short syllables at their beginning, for example, the <term>Anapest</term> by raising the voice, and those that begin with long syllables by lowering it; although Saint <term>Augustine</term> and several other <term>Latins</term> take the measure as our <term>Practitioners</term> do, namely for the raising and lowering of the hand.

<page-num>424</page-num>
<header>Book Five</header>

The second difficulty consists in knowing why they used only sixteen beats in *equal rhythm*, as Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author whose work "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury" was a standard textbook on the liberal arts, including music.</note> remarks following the Greeks in his 9th book, where he further determines the number of syllables for the *double*, *sesquialter* <note>A ratio of 3:2.</note>, and *sesquitertian* <note>A ratio of 4:3.</note> genres; but there is so much obscurity, and perhaps falsehood or contradiction, in what we read in the final chapters of that book, that I cannot imagine that several corruptions have not slipped into the text.

The 3rd difficulty seems even greater to me: namely, which rhythms one ought to use for all kinds of passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to emotions or "affections" that music was intended to provoke in the listener.</note>, and what order one should keep in all sorts of encounters to pass from one movement to another. Perhaps they knew this no better than we do, and just as the first person who happened by chance to compose hexameter verses made of *spondees* and *dactyls*, and *Pentameters* shorter by one syllable, was followed by all others, so the first person who introduced the number of beats or syllables for every other kind of verse or movement was similarly followed—even though he had no reason to establish this number of beats rather than any other he might have wished. Unless, that is, one says that he measured this number by the duration of the voice that a man can hold without taking his wind or breath. If anyone believes himself clear-sighted enough in antiquity to give peremptory reasons for these difficulties without resorting to chance and to what I have said here, he will greatly oblige the public if he shares them, and particularly all those who take pleasure in Poetry or Harmony. To which it seems Saint Augustine gives some entry and some sort of light in his 6 books of *Rhythmic Music*; this is why I provide them in the Proposition that follows, so that our Musicians may enjoy the beautiful thoughts of this excellent Father of the Church.

### PROPOSITION XXXIII.

*To explain the most particular points of Saint Augustine's 6 books on Rhythmic Music.*

I add this Proposition in favor of this great man, whose 6 books of *Music* <note>Augustine originally planned a vast work on the liberal arts; the books on "Music" specifically focused on rhythm and meter.</note> were lost even in his own time, as he himself remarks, in which I estimate he had treated the same things as Boethius. Be that as it may, the six books that remain to us should have as their title *On Rhythmics* or *On Metrics*, since he treats feet and verses (of which I have spoken in this 6th book) and not *On Music*, for which he contents himself with explaining the definition, which consists in knowing how to sing well or move the voice through all kinds of degrees and intervals. But I have explained so amply in the book on Songs and elsewhere what *Modulation* <note>The art of melodic movement and inflection.</note> and *Music* are, that it is not appropriate to speak of them further. Now, after having looked down upon the movements of the fingers and everything that instrumentalists have learned by imitation and custom—as opposed to the science that resides in the understanding—because parrots and several other animals are capable of this imitation by means of their external and internal senses and their memory, he concludes that Musicians who have only learned this art to draw profit, honor, and...
