## on Rhythmics.

Vanity; they do not know the science of Music, otherwise they would esteem it better than lucre and honor, which they prefer over it, for the sciences are placed among the honest goods, which are lovable in themselves. He <note>Referring to Saint Augustine in his treatise "De Musica"</note> employs the rest of the first book to speak of numbers, whose ratios—being the easiest to understand—please the most in all kinds of movements and time; but I have treated so amply of all their ratios, both in the book on Consonances and in that on the Utility of Harmony, and others, that I believe Saint Augustine himself would be satisfied with it. I only add that he calls multiple numbers *complicatos* <note>original: "multiples, complicatos"</note> and superparticulars *sesquatos* <note>original: "sesquatos"</note>, and that he names these two kinds of numbers *connumeratos* <note>original: "connumeratos"</note>, and the superpartients *dinumeratos* <note>original: "dinumeratos"</note>. And then he finishes with the ternary <note>The number three</note> as the first perfect number, which has a beginning, middle, and end; and by the quaternary <note>The number four</note>, which is even, and which he esteems greatly because 1, 2, 3, and 4 make the number ten, which is the last of the simple numbers. Now, I have treated very exactly of this quaternary and denary <note>The number ten</note> number in the 9th question of the *Preludes to Harmony*; this is why I come to the second book of St. Augustine, in which he tries to find why the arrangements of different times and movements—which are in the verses of which we have spoken in our Rhythmics—please the sounds and the spirit. The spirit considers the double ratio <note>2:1</note>, or the sesquialter <note>3:2</note>, etc., between two movements, of which one lasts an hour or a day, and the other 2 or 3 hours, or days, or centuries, just as between those which are the *iambic* foot or the *Paonic*; or those which are the sounds of the *Octave* or the *Fifth*, even though these two kinds of movements may be so slow or so fast that no sense is capable of perceiving them; from which it is easy to conclude that the understanding is far more excellent and more universal than the senses.

In all of the 2nd book, he joins the ratios of equality, the double, the sesquialter, and the sesquitertial <note>4:3</note> to the feet of verses, and shows in how many ways long times can be joined to brief ones in feet of 2, 3, 4, etc. syllables, which we have explained above both by discourse and by the example of feet, verses, and notes.

After having put the examples of all the feet, of which we have given the Table in the 17th Proposition, he agrees that verses composed of feet whose times are equal are the most excellent, as happens with <term>Hexameters</term> <note>A line of verse with six metrical feet</note> and <term>dactylic Pentameters</term> <note>A line of verse with five metrical feet</note>, because all their feet are composed of four times: from which he excepts the <term>Amphibrach</term> <note>A foot consisting of a long syllable between two short ones</note>, because it does not have its downbeat equal to its upbeat in the measure; for one must make a single time while lowering the hand in the *thesis* <note>original: "Noe" - likely a corruption of the Greek 'thesis' or 'downbeat'</note>, and 4 in the *arsis* <note>original: "apns" - likely a corruption of the Greek 'arsis' or 'upbeat'</note> while lowering it, or vice versa; whereas the <term>Spondee</term>, the <term>Dactyl</term>, the <term>Anapaest</term>, the <term>Proceleumatic</term>, etc., have their upbeat equal to their downbeat, which he names *plausus* <note>The beating of time</note>; so that all these verses are suited for binary measure, and those whose upbeat is to the downbeat as 3 to 2 for the ternary measure of the Practitioners. But the <term>Amphibrach</term>, which I have named <term>Scolian</term>, has its downbeat triple or sub-triple of its upbeat; that is why the Practitioners would name its measure quaternary, because it is divided into four parts, although it is rather ternary, as I have said elsewhere.

Having rejected this foot from among the others, he shows that all those of six times join very well together, namely the <term>Ionics</term> and the <term>Dipo-</term>

<header>Book Five</header>

...<term>Trochaic</term> <note>a foot with a long syllable followed by a short one</note> and <term>Iambic</term> <note>a short followed by a long</note> melodies with the <term>Molossus</term> <note>three long syllables</note> and the <term>Antispast</term> <note>short-long-long-short</note>, by reason of the <term>Senary</term> <note>the number six</note> number, of which the middle is equal to both of its sides; for it is composed of three pairs, and is the first circular and perfect number. The <term>Pyrrhic</term> <note>two short syllables</note> foot stands all alone; the <term>Trochee</term> does not join well with the Iamb, because of the different beat of their measure, as the downbeat of one is double the downbeat of the other. The <term>Spondee</term> <note>two long syllables</note>, the <term>Dactyl</term> <note>long-short-short</note>, the <term>Anapest</term> <note>short-short-long</note>, and the <term>Proceleumatic</term> <note>four short syllables</note> agree very well together, both in their timing and in their measure. The <term>Bacchean</term> <note>short-long-long</note> accepts the <term>Cretic</term> <note>long-short-long</note>, and the 1st and 4th <term>Paeon</term> <note>a foot of four syllables, one long and three short</note>; and the <term>Palimbacchean</term> <note>long-long-short</note> accepts the same feet, except for the 2nd Paeon, in place of which it has the 3rd; so that all feet of 5 beats can be joined to the Cretic and to the 1st and 4th Paeon. Among those that have 7 beats, the 1st and 2nd <term>Epitrite</term> <note>three long syllables and one short</note> agree; and then the 3rd and 4th, because the former begin their downbeat with three beats, and the latter with four.

In the 3rd book, he distinguishes *<term>Rhythm</term>* from *<term>Meter</term>* and *<term>Verse</term>*; in that the first signifies a movement regulated by the preceding feet without any determined end, as when one makes a hundred movements or any other number one wishes, all in a row without stopping—for example, one hundred or two hundred dactylic movements. The second has a certain number of feet, for example, 5 or 6, but it is not restricted to certain feet or certain caesuras <note>a rhythmic pause or break in a line of verse</note> in two determined places, unlike the third, which must always have a certain return and certain syllables and caesuras in determined spots, as happens in <term>Hexameter Verse</term>, which must have its caesura at the 5th beat, or after the first two feet, and which must be composed of two members that always correspond to one each other.

But there are particularly two things worthy of note in this book, one of which is that one cannot distinguish the Pyrrhic *Rhythm* from the *Proceleumatic* by the beat that marks the measure; this happens similarly to compound feet compared to the simple ones of which they are composed, which is why one must relate their movements to those of the simple ones as much as possible. The other consists in filling out imperfect verses by means of silences or pauses; for example, when the verse is *<term>Brachycatalectic</term>* <note>a line of verse lacking the last two syllables</note>, that is to say, when it lacks two syllables or two beats, one must make as many pauses as there are missing beats, so that the measure is found to be whole at the end of each verse, and so that each begins again by striking or lowering the hand. He further teaches that the smallest meter is composed of one foot and a half, and consequently of at least three beats, which correspond to a Pyrrhic and a half; and that the smallest verse is composed of eight beats, and the largest of 38. This also applies to the meter, which having only three beats, the silence of one beat must complete its two choreic feet, or its four beats; now, it is only the beating of the measure that allows one to discern the *rhythm* or continued movement of the *Pyrrhic* from the *Tribrach* <note>three short syllables</note> and other feet composed of short syllables. In the 4th book, he composes Meters of 7 Pyrrhics:
*Little white girl, fragile, good and slender,* <note>original: "Leucula, fragilia, gracilea bona"</note>
*The little soul who loves them will be like them:* <note>original: "Quæ adamat animula ſimilis erit eis"</note>
To which he adds these meters of eight Pyrrhics:
*A good man loves solid goods, and what he loves, he possesses:* <note>original: "Solida bona bonus amat, & ea quæ amat, habet"</note>
*Thus love lacks nothing, and those goods are God.* <note>original: "Itaque nec eget amor, & ea bona Deus eſt"</note>

### On Rhythmics.

He also gives examples of 14 kinds of Iambic meters <note>A metrical foot consisting of a short syllable followed by a long one</note>, and as many Trochaic <note>A long syllable followed by a short one</note>, and Spondaic <note>Two long syllables</note>, of which the 7th Trochaic is:
> All things were made by Truth, and the form of all is overturned; <note>original Latin: "Veritate facta cuncta sunt, omniumque forma euersitas"</note>
And the last two are Iambic:
> Blessed is he who sees God, he shall desire nothing more of good. <note>original Latin: "Beatus est videns Deum, nihil boni amplius voles"</note>
> The evil man seeks good things from without, hence the wretched man is in want. <note>original Latin: "Malus foris bonorum requirit, hinc eget miser homo"</note>
And the 4th Spondaic:
> He alone lives free who has already conquered error. <note>original Latin: "Solus liber viuit qui errorem iam vicit"</note>

But whereas there are only 14 species of meters in each of these three genres, he sets down 21 composed of Tribrachs <note>Three short syllables</note>, by reason of the different silences <note>rests</note> used to complete the imperfect ones. He shows which feet join well together, and sets down 568 kinds of meters, whether one uses silences or whether they are whole; he maintains that the last syllable of the last foot should not be made short or long indifferently when one continues with other similar verses, but that it must be given the quantity or time required by the nature of the verse. For example, it must always be long in every Spondee, and short in pure Trochees and Pyrrhics <note>Two short syllables</note>. But there is, it seems to me, nothing so remarkable in all this book as what he says of silences or pauses, which one can make not only at the end of an imperfect meter, but also in any other place one wishes, even at the beginning, in order to render the verse such as it shall please the Musician. For example, he makes a pause of one beat after the first three syllables *Now enough on the lands* <note>original Latin: "Iam satis terris"</note>, from the verse of Horace:

->Now enough of dire hail and snow upon the lands, etc.<-

He also makes two pauses after the first five syllables of this verse:
> He wanders among our native horses. <note>original Latin: "Gentiles nostros inter oberrat equos"</note>

And two others at the end, to reduce it to composite meters which have feet of six beats; for the first is a Spondee, which lacks two beats; the 2nd is a Molossus <note>Three long syllables</note>; the 3rd a Choriamb <note>Long-short-short-long</note>, and the 4th an Anapest <note>Short-short-long</note>, so that one would have to scan or measure this verse in this manner, to sing it according to the intention of Saint Augustine:

->- u - u - u -<-
->Gentiles nostros [pause pause], inter oberrat equos [pause pause].<-

And consequently, the locations and the number of pauses depend on the will of the Musician, who can give several kinds of movements and cadences to the same lyric, according to the feet to which he reduces it by means of pauses placed at the beginning, at the end, or in any other place he wishes. From this, Composers of Airs <note>Songs</note> can draw a thousand kinds of inventions, if they use the necessary silences, which serve to satisfy the meters and their imperfect feet, and the voluntary ones, which are used to lengthen each species of meter up to 32 beats. On this matter, I advise them to read all of this 4th book of Saint Augustine, which will teach them how to mix the feet and the number of pauses permitted in each place. Furthermore, in his 5th book, he treats very amply of verses, and particularly of senarii <note>Verses of six feet</note>, which he prefers above all others, the most excellent of which is the Heroic Hexameter; for example, the first of the *Aeneid*, *I sing of arms and the man* <note>original Latin: "Arma virumque"</note>, etc., which he measures and scans by setting the first syllable apart, in order to make two Anapests of what follows in the first member or the first part of the verse, in this fashion:

<header>Book Five</header>

*I sing of arms and the man,* <note>original: "Arma virúmque cano" — the famous opening of Virgil's Aeneid</note> so that the first part of the verse ends with a complete foot. Now, this first syllable can be compared to the beat one makes before starting the first step of the <term>Branles</term> <note>A popular type of French Renaissance dance characterized by side-to-side movement</note> or certain dance songs. He teaches several other things regarding the parts of verses, which he divides into 4 & 3, 3 & 5, 5 & 7, 6 & 7, 8 & 7, and 9, and reduces all <term>Senarii</term> <note>verses consisting of six metrical feet</note> to <term>Heroic</term>, <term>Trochaic</term>, or <term>Iambic</term> forms. But since he has written his five books to detach men of good spirit from sensible things by means of numbers and reason, and to transport them to God—and so that, as he says at the beginning of the 6th book, *they might cling to the one God and Lord of all, who presides over human minds with no intervening nature, through the love of unchangeable truth* <note>original Latin: "Vni Deo & domino-rum omnium..."</note>—it is reasonable that we enjoy the fruit he draws from it in this last book. This consists principally in showing that we have a certain kind of measure, time, and movement within the spirit, which alerts us to the numbers and rhythms of what resounds in our ears, or what gives pleasure to the other senses.

He establishes four degrees of numbers, the first of which is in sound; if he had taken our phenomenon of the number of vibrations made by strings, or the beats and movements of the air, he could have placed them in the hearing, where he places the second degree of numbers. For the little drum, or the membrane of the inner ear, endures as many small shocks as the strings make vibrations. The third degree consists in making the number of air movements go faster or slower, and this is what creates the low and high pitch in sounds. The fourth depends on the memory one has of these numbers, and the fifth consists in the natural approval we give to those that please us, or the disapproval of those that displease us.

Now, he holds that the first three degrees are more excellent than the fourth, because the soul becomes better by distancing itself from material numbers to unite with the spiritual and divine ones, by which it is reformed. Here it must be particularly noted that he holds that bodies and corporeal things do not act upon the spirit at all; rather, the spirit does everything it wishes with the body and in the body, except that it often opposes its own actions. From this, it happens that one is said to feel pain when the spirit is greatly attentive to the difficulty of its action, and pleasure when it attentively considers that the action of the body conforms to its own. Thus, all the passions that are transferred from the body to the spirit are nothing other than the different considerations of the spirit, which acts upon the body with such great rest in health that it hardly perceives its action, so easy is it; whereas it considers it very attentively in pain, because it then has much more trouble acting.

But the entire fifth chapter, and particularly the last third, deserves to be read for the beautiful thoughts of Saint Augustine, one of the principal ones showing what the soul acquires in converting itself to God: *For one turning toward the Lord, a greater care arises to turn away [from the world], until the unbridled impetus of carnal affairs rests—an impetus hardened by long habit and thrusting itself in through the tumultuous memories of his conversion. Thus, having quieted the movements by which he was drawn toward external things, he enjoys a free leisure within, which is signified by the Sabbath, if he recognizes that God alone is his Lord, whom alone one serves with the highest liberty.* <note>original Latin: "Conuertenti se ad Dominum..."</note>

After these elevations of the spirit, he returns to the <term>Sonorous Numbers</term>, which he names...

# On Rhythmics.

...them *Judicial* <note>original: "Iudiciales"</note>, when they serve the soul in judging their proportion, even when they have vanished; *progressive* <note>original: "progreßores"</note>, when the soul employs its own numbers to form itself toward its body and to move it; *reactive* <note>original: "occursores"</note>, when it uses them during the passions of the body; and *memorable* <note>original: "recordabiles"</note>, insofar as they remain in the memory. Thus, he establishes four types of numbers which depend upon the *Sounding* <note>original: "Sonores"</note> numbers. And because we are but a small part of the universe, we do not judge feet that are not proportioned to us—as happens with the Iamb <term>Iamb: a metrical foot consisting of one short syllable followed by one long syllable</term>, which is made of two movements, one of which lasts six months and the other a year. If the Sounding numbers were erased from the memory in the same proportion as they vanish from the ear, we could not judge any musical foot; for while the second part of the Iamb was being imprinted in the memory, the first would no longer be there, and consequently the soul would have no judicial numbers. This is similar to how the soul could not judge if a body is round or square if each part vanished from the memory as it did from the eye. But the past movement, remaining in some way in the memory, serves to make us remember when it is excited and, as it were, accompanied by a new external movement. After having considered the *Judicial* numbers, which serve only to judge movements subject to time, he attempts to rise to other numbers more sublime and excellent, which do not depend at all on the passing intervals of time, and which surpass all others. It is by their means that we judge that such or such a movement is not pleasing, and that we see the cause of the pleasure in the equality of the parts of all the Rhythmic feet we have passed through. On this subject, one must read his 11th chapter, where he compares the movements of the whole world to a verse, and shows the beauty of divine providence in all things.

<margin>Earthly things, being subject to celestial ones, join the cycle of their times in a rhythmic succession, like a song of the universe. In these things, nothing appears to us unordered or disturbed, because we are accustomed to their order according to our merits, unaware of what beauty divine providence works through us. <note>original Latin: "Celestibus terrena subjecta orbem temporum suorum numerosa successione quasi carmini uniuersitatis confociant..."</note></margin>

Now, his entire discourse tends toward making us understand the immutable and eternal numbers of the soul, through which it sees perfect equality and all other imaginable ratios and proportions in as great a perfection as the Angels see them. This belongs to pure Mathematics, which is in no way hindered by matter, nor by time and movements; from there he rises to God, who has imprinted this eternity in the mind. We see its beauty, but we do not possess it in its perfection, for we amuse ourselves by considering the beauty and equality of numbers and times in sounds (which are like its light) or in Architecture, which satisfies the eye through its equality and symmetry. Thus, unity compared to unity—that is to say, to itself—is the principle of pleasure in all the senses. And because this unity is found only in God in the full extent of His perfection, it distracts our mind when it is considered in others; though he provides an art by which one can reduce all these numbers to unity. This is done by relating their use to the benefit of one's neighbor, and by transporting the equality of numbers considered in the Pyrrhic <term>Pyrrhic: a metrical foot of two short syllables</term> and other Rhythms to the source of equality, which never changes—even though the equality of the times of the Pyrrhic, or Trochee <note>original: "Chorée"</note>, can be changed into that of the Spon...

# Book Five

<page-num>430</page-num>

idea, if one extends its duration. I leave aside what he says of the four **Cardinal Virtues** <note>The virtues of Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>, by which he intends for the soul to govern all these numbers, and which he places within **contemplation**, **sanctification**, **impassibility** <note>The state of being unmoved by suffering or emotion, often attributed to the divine or the perfected soul.</note>, and the admirable **order** that the **Saints** shall possess, so as to finish the summary of these books with an excellent comparison. He uses this to explain that the **world** was created from **nothing**, just as a **line** is produced by a **point**—which is nothing in regard to the said line—just as the line is nothing compared to width, nor width in comparison to depth. Now, I remark in these treatises, as well as in others, that this great **Doctor** <note>Referring to Saint Augustine, a Doctor of the Church.</note> imitates our Lord by relating everything sublime, excellent, and perfect that can be imagined in true **Religion**, in the **sciences**, and in the whole world, to these two precepts which contain the **Law and the Prophets**: *Love God with all your heart, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself.* This can be founded upon that **natural Commandment**, which may be called the principle of **Morality**: *Do, or do not do to others what you desire, or what you do not want done to yourself*; for this can be applied to God and to man. Because if a sensible man considers the manner in which he would want others to behave toward him, were he God, he would immediately see that he would desire all men to love him more than any other thing, and that they would rather endure all imaginable pains than to offend him in the slightest. Thus, man can do no better than to render to God what he would want rendered to himself if he were in His place; and the same light that leads us to our duty toward our neighbor teaches us at the same time what duties must be rendered to God.

### COROLLARY I.

Those who wish to know more particularly all the types of **verse** used by the ancients should read **Terentianus Maurus**, from whom **Saint Augustine** took a good portion of what he reports on **Rhythms**, **Meters**, and **verses** in his six books. For he contains many very specific things; for example, he discourses quite amply in his last chapter on the verses of **Horace**, *The sharp winter is loosening its grip* <note>original: "Soluitur acris hyems"</note>, for which I have given the **Music** in the 28th Proposition, as he does for several other verses of both Horace and other **Poets** in his other chapters, where he speaks of their quantity and their feet. It must only be noted that he holds that only **equal, double, and sesquialter** <note>A ratio of 3:2.</note> **measures** are proper for **Music**, and consequently that our **Composers** practice all that he says by using the measures they call **binary**, **ternary**, and **sesquialter**, or **hemiola** <note>Another term for the 3:2 ratio, often involving a rhythmic shift.</note>. One may also read what **Bede**, **Victorinus**, **Plotius**, **Fortunatianus**, **Rufinus**, **Servius**, and other ancient authors have said of Meters and verses, unless one prefers to dwell on what **Hephaestion** <note>original: "Ephestion"</note> has written of them.

### COROLLARY IV.

Some hold that Pasquier <note>Étienne Pasquier (1529–1615), a French lawyer and man of letters.</note> attempted to take away the glory from Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a member of the Pléiade who sought to adapt classical meters to French.</note> of having been the first to give a beginning to measured verse in our language, for the reason that, having wished to involve himself in making them, he had made the first syllable of *gracieux* [gracious] long, which is actually short; for which Baïf rebuked him with these somewhat mocking verses:

> You are an ungracious poet, Pasquier,
> When of the word *gracieux* you make the *gra* long:
> Go away, you pettifogger, to lengthen your "S,"
> Leaving poor French as it is.

This was because Pasquier was a Lawyer, for it is said that Lawyers stretch out the "S" to amplify the scrolls of their legal writings. Indeed, Jean-Antoine de Baïf testifies in the Preface of his Poems, which he addressed to the King in the year 1573, that no one had undertaken to make this sort of verse in French; where, having recognized that he had learned Greek and Latin Poetry from Dorat <note>Jean Dorat, a famous classical scholar and teacher of the Pléiade poets.</note>, he says:

> It is through him that, leaving the common track,
> In a new path I am the first to pass,
> Opening to your Frenchmen an unknown passage,
> Which none before me in France has held.
> No Poet has seen himself so bold as to undertake
> Even to enter there. Where should I begin?
> I see nothing trodden there; I see nothing open.
> I see everything covered with thickets and bushes.
> Shall I cease to go? Strength and courage
> Shall never fail me. I will clear the passage, etc.

Now, if this had not been true, there is no appearance that he would have dared to boast of it publicly without being rebuked by several Poets and other excellent minds who lived in his time; and Pasquier himself wrote nothing to the contrary while Baïf lived.

But since the greater part of this book has been employed in favor of verse, I wish to add to it the Meditation that an excellent Poet made on the 136th Psalm, *By the rivers of Babylon* <note>original: "Super flumina Babylonis"</note>, so that our Musicians may come to it to create sad and mournful Songs, and all Christians to console themselves in their sadness and grief, in imitation of the Israelites; when after, etc. Now if they wish to use Rhythms, it will be easy for them to give the measure of the time of each syllable and diction to their Music: for example...

# Book Five

Beneath the green foliage where we rested in the shade,
We suffered evils whose excess and number
Deprive us of the means to describe them;
But if ever anything tested our constancy,
It was the insolent pride, the unjust arrogance
With which our cruel guards pressured us to sing.

"Recite," they said, "those agreeable songs;
Cast into the winds all those admirable melodies
That crowned the end of your warlike deeds;
Celebrate on your lutes our righteous conquest,
And sing, while in the chains where fate holds you,
All that you used to sing amidst the laurels."

Thus spoke that inflexible troop,
When, demanding of us an impossible thing,
They envied us even this moment of rest;
But we held all these speeches in little esteem,
And each of us, reflecting on the misfortune of <term>Solyme</term><note>A poetic abbreviation for Hierosolyma (Jerusalem).</note>,
Seemed to say through tears these noble words:

"Could I truly sing while I am sighing?
Could I with my voice honor an Empire
That holds me in chains, both captive and confounded?
Do I feel the greatness of my losses so little?
Would I so easily forget so many suffered injuries,
That my tongue should be free where my body is no longer?

No, no; it must not be that for some threat
To which their ambition has carried their audacity,
I should consecrate the glory of my songs to their wishes;
Nor that the same melodies with which our animated voices
Celebrated the power of the great God of Hosts,
Should serve to tickle the ears of the wicked.

Is there any reason that could make me believe
That I ought to sing of my capture and their victory,
And join at the same time the <term>Cypresses</term><note>The cypress tree was a traditional symbol of mourning and death, contrasted here with the flowers of celebration.</note> and the flowers?
What means is there to accomplish all they command of me?
Their insolent voices demand songs from me,
And their bloody acts demand tears from me.

After they have destroyed our superb porticos,
After they have razed our magnificent temples,
They still hope to hear our concerts;
O unparalleled audacity! O ridiculous expectation!
To believe that my faith would allow me to sing for them
The <term>Hymns</term><note>Sacred songs of praise; the speaker argues that holy music cannot be performed for pagan entertainment.</note> reserved for the only God I serve."

When their rigor, to my fatal ruin,
Had torn me from the breast of my native land,
And constrained me to follow them into these sad deserts,
My eyes, in this misfortune which never had an equal,
Took leave of our temple with tears;
And my voice, with a sigh, took leave of all our melodies.

I cannot satisfy this homicidal band,
Even if I believed that their treacherous rage
Would allow itself to be softened by the sweetness of my Lute:
I cannot submit myself to the office of a traitor:
I cannot prefer my tyrant to my Master;
Nor the benefit of being free to my own salvation.

In short, let me succumb to the furies of war,
And let all the misfortunes of Heaven and earth,
Assembled in a jumble, be able to strike me down:
Let my soul be lulled into an eternal sleep,
If I make an impious man laugh at the Hymns of God;
And celebrate His name only to make it abhorred.

In these profane places where I am a tributary,
Lord, to praise You it is enough to be silent,
And to suppress Your name in order to bless it:
I must only invoke You with silence,
And I believe that among those where insolence reigns,
To not speak of You at all is to remember You.

Even though my soul, obliged to Your care,
Is so burdened with the fruits of Your goodness
That it can no longer sustain the weight:
I do not wish, however, to recount the wonders of it,
For fear of flattering their hearts and their ears,
And publishing Your glory where You never were.

If in this ungrateful field I sow Your praises,
And if I dare to sing in these foreign lands
The Hymns that in Zion <note>The biblical hill in Jerusalem, representing the holy city and the presence of God.</note> I sang in former times;
I wish to see my inhumane absence become permanent,
My fingers without movement, my lungs without breath,
My Lute without harmony, and my mouth without a voice.

Why did I not die then, when the barbaric flame,
Making but one brazier of so rare a city,
Confounded so many dead in the same tomb;
I would have acquired an immortal glory,
I would have made my zeal shine through my death,
And the fire of my heart through that of my body.

## Book Five

I would never have seen this fatal shore;
I would not have suffered this unworthy servitude
Whose extreme rigor overwhelms me with bonds;
Beneath the Altar of the Lord I would have my sepulcher,
And would not feel the eternal torture
That I feel in surviving the loss of my kin.

O glorious abode, O my dear fatherland,
Although throughout the universe your glory is withered,
It reigns forever within my memory:
In the midst of my heart its image is traced;
And I only make use of my thoughts
For the care they take in sustaining me with it.

I consent to languish in eternal torments,
To see the number of my chains multiplied,
And to find, if possible, a harsher conqueror;
I consent that Heaven itself oppose my vows,
If I can henceforth receive anything else
Than your thought in my soul, and your love in my heart.

Let me be the sole target of contempt and blame,
Let the Sun no longer give its flame to my eyes,
Let the lutes <note>original: "lutins" - likely a printer's error for "luths" (lutes), as the context refers to musical accompaniment</note> no longer tune their sounds to my voice,
If it happens that one day your misery forgets you,
Or if the restored pomp of your Palaces
Is not the unique subject of all my songs.

You cause my pleasures, you cause my tortures,
And as your ruin has bounded my delights,
Your restoration will bound my labors:
After your interests, there is nothing that touches me;
I love only your glory and prize my mouth
Only to sing of your blessings, and sigh for your woes.

But O just avenger, release your armed hand
Upon this jealous people, upon this treacherous Edomite <note>original: "Idumée" - referring to the Edomites, historical neighbors of Israel who were condemned by prophets for gloating over the fall of Jerusalem</note>
Who came to aggravate the burden of our displeasures;
Spare against him neither lightning nor tempest,
In his own nets envelop his head,
And turn against him the point of his own arrows.

He has despised the cause of the afflicted,
He has fanned the fury of the oppressors,
He has seen with a dry eye our profaned temples;
He makes his promenades of our deserted lands,
His songs of our tears, his treasures of our losses,
And seems to triumph to see us enchained.

The speaker vows never to forget their heritage, placing the restoration of their country above all personal joy.</summary>

## On Rhythm.

"Let them lose," he said, "this proud Empire,
Let a just fury lay lower than the grass
These polished Palaces, shining with wealth;
Let everything serve as fuel for the rage of the fire,
Let great Zion become a great Cemetery,
And let a sea be made of the inhabitants' blood.

Of all the rigors of a fatal carnage,
None is as harsh as the outrage
That this cruel neighbor has committed against us:
And certainly, I have suffered with more pain
The injurious arrows of his inhuman tongue,
Than all the mortal arrows from the hands of enemies.

And you, proud City, cruel Babylon,
Who make the purple of your throne from our blood,
You will see one day the end of your pride:
The height of your walls presages your fall to me;
You will serve as a target for all the blows of Heaven,
And under your own weight, you will be your own coffin.

The Lord, who from Heaven sees the evils I endure,
Tiring of permitting such a harsh punishment,
Will break all the chains that make us sigh;
He was rigorous toward us, He will be favorable to us:
His wrath threw us into the precipice,
And His compassion must withdraw us from it.

Come then, O my support, where pity calls You,
Reserve for Your fury this faithless race
Which swims in our blood, which bathes in our tears;
Oppose Your power to the progress of their glory,
And to leave nothing that marks their victory,
Tear from their brow the palms and the flowers.

If Your hand is fatal to the crimes of the guilty,
If Your favor is ready for the cries of the miserable,
I shall see them weep for the rest of their days,
I shall see their Palaces resolve into ash;
And under the same ruin, a single bolt of lightning
Will confound their pride and that of their towers.

Maintain that Your glory, and not my punishment,
Solicits my voice to pray to Your justice
To put these proud mortals under the yoke;
And that I never had such great sorrows
At seeing myself stripped of my own riches,
As at seeing the honor of Your altars profaned."

<note>The "altars" refer to the sacred spaces of the Temple in Jerusalem, emphasizing that the spiritual loss outweighs the material loss of wealth.</note>

## PROPOSITION XXXIV.

To determine if it is necessary or appropriate to use any of the species of the <term>Chromatic Genus</term>, or the <term>Enharmonic</term>, to sing verses—whether rhymed or measured—with as much perfection and energy as the Greeks.

Many have believed that Music would produce much greater effects if one used every species of the <term>Diatonic</term>, <term>Chromatic</term>, and <term>Enharmonic</term> <note>These refer to the three genera of ancient Greek music theory, distinguished by the tuning of the intervals within a four-note scale (tetrachord).</note>. They are able to experiment with this, since all their degrees and intervals are known; for I have explained them so clearly in the second book of Instruments, and in the version of the Music of <term>Euclid</term> <note>original: "Euclide"; referring to the ancient Greek mathematician to whom musical treatises were then attributed.</note>, article 3, which I placed in the 17th Theorem of the first book of the <term>Treatise on Universal Harmony</term> <note>original: "Traité de l'Harmonie Universelle"; the author's magnum opus.</note>, that there is no need to add anything to it. For example, the <term>Fourth</term> <note>original: "Quarte"</note>, or the <term>Tetrachord of the Soft Diatonic</term>, has for its three degrees the <term>semitone</term>, then an interval of three <term>dieses</term> <note>In this context, a "diesis" refers to a microtonal division of a whole tone.</note>, and another interval of five, which return almost to our <term>major semi-tone</term>, and to our <term>maximum tone</term>, of which I have spoken elsewhere. As for the <term>Soft Chromatic</term> <note>original: "Chrone mol"</note>, it proceeds by two <term>dieses</term>, each of a third of a tone; and then by its third interval composed of the tone, the semi-tone, and the third of a tone: just as the <term>Sesquialter Chromatic</term> <note>original: "Chrone sesquialtere"</note> first makes two <term>dieses</term>, each of which is <term>one and a half times the Enharmonic diesis</term>; and then it completes its <term>Fourth</term> by the interval of seven <term>enharmonic dieses</term>; which I explain in the said third article by the division of the tone into 12 equal parts. However that may be, I estimate that whoever wishes to put these divisions into use and practice, particularly in several parts <note>i.e., polyphonic music for multiple voices.</note>, will employ much time therein without being able to withdraw much contentment or satisfaction, and will frankly admit after having worked at it

# On Rhythmics.

<page-num>439</page-num>

throughout his life, that our Diatonic <note>The standard musical scale consisting of five whole tones and two semitones.</note>, as it is practiced now, with the sharps and flats <note>original: "diefes & bmols"</note> that are placed everywhere one wishes to change a whole tone into a semitone, and vice versa, is sufficient to execute everything that one can reasonably imagine of the ancients.

I wish nevertheless to repeat here the Octave <note>original: "Diapafon, ou l'O&aue"</note>, divided into 24 degrees, so that each whole tone has its 4 sharps, and so that if there are found any Poets so excellent in Music who wish to go further, without contenting themselves with ordinary modulation, they may use such intervals as they wish; for there is an enharmonic quarter-tone <note>original: "diefe enharmonique"</note> from the first to the second note, from the 2nd to the 3rd, from the 3rd to the 4th, from the 4th to the 5th, and so on for the others, so that each whole tone has 5 notes and 4 intervals, and that one can make three-quarters of a tone in a single interval, whether ascending or descending—for example, from the 1st to the 4th note, or the reverse. Similarly, one can make 5 quarter-tones from the 1st to the 6th note, or 7 from the first to the 8th, etc. so that one can increase or decrease each consonance or dissonance by an enharmonic quarter-tone, that is to say, by a quarter of a tone, or thereabouts. I leave aside several other particularities of this division.

->Octave divided into 24 Enharmonic quarter-tones.<-

<image-desc>A musical staff with 25 vertical lines above it, numbered 1 through 25. Each line corresponds to a note or division on the staff. The notes are represented by diamond-shaped heads, some with crosses, indicating sharps or other alterations. The staff appears to illustrate the 24 enharmonic divisions of the octave.</image-desc>

The Lord le Maire, of whom I have already spoken in this book, has placed this division upon the neck of the Lute by means of a new tuning, and several frets <note>original: "touches"</note>, some of which are made by small springs that the thumb touches beneath the neck. To which one can add small organ pipes which will produce the sounds of a recorder <note>original: "fleute douce"</note>, or such other stop as one wishes, so that the fingers of the left hand, touching certain keys placed between the ordinary ones, will make the said pipes speak, housed within the neck of the Lute or in a secondary body <note>original: "Contrecorps"</note>, without them interfering in any way with the Harmony and the resonance of the strings. One can also divide the tone into 3 equal parts, as Titelouze <note>Jean Titelouze (c. 1563–1633), a famous French organist and composer.</note> had done on a particular Spinet <note>original: "Epinette"</note> that he let me hear: but it requires entire centuries to bring these divisions and sections of the Monochord <note>A scientific instrument used to measure musical intervals on a single string.</note> to as great a perfection of practice as that of our Diatonic-Chromatic genre, which is used now in all Kingdoms: which suffices for the recreation of the ears and the imagination, and for singing the praises of God. This is why I have not included examples of pure Chromatic and Enharmonic music, having judged them useless until the practice of some good Composers has made them palatable. Those who desire to know more will find everything they could wish for in the third book of the *Genres*. I only pray all those who take the trouble to read our *Harmonic Treatises* in whole or in part, and who shall henceforth make use of Music, to employ principally their spirit, their voices, their fingers, and their instruments to praise God, for whom all things were made; for if one does not relate all that one can, all that one wishes, and all that one does to His honor and His glory, one must hope for no reward in the eternal...

# FIRST PROPOSITION.
### To determine how many species or kinds of sounds and musical instruments there are.

IT IS impossible to explain the diversity of all sounds if one does not speak at the same time <note>original: "quant & quant"</note> of the diversity of the instruments that produce them; this is why I join the two together. And because all kinds of sounds can be made by animals or by inanimate bodies, I treat them both in general and in particular.

Now, one can divide all instruments into the immobile and the mobile. The first belong to the waves <note>The author likely refers to the sound of wind or water against fixed objects.</note>, as they have no perceptible movement, such as rocks and mountains. For although many maintain that they tremble, and that sound cannot be made without the trembling of the bodies by means of which it is made, nevertheless one does not perceive this trembling. It is probable that the tremblings and the beatings of the air which strike the rocks and other similar bodies suffice to engender the sounds we hear, which one can call whistlings <note>original: "fifflemens"</note>, because they seem to imitate the whistlings one makes with the mouth when the air flows over the tongue while pronouncing the syllables CB, or ZB, or the letters S and Z. From this, one can conclude that man can imitate all kinds of noises, as I shall show in the book on the voice.

All bodies against which one pushes the breath or the wind to make every kind of sound imaginable—such as the edges of knives, combs, and all other bodies which seem to remain immobile—must be referred to this first genre of instruments.

But the mobile instruments include all those that use strings <note>original: "chordes"</note>, as well as pipes, bells, and generally everything that moves perceptibly, whether by the mere beatings of the air, or by the bow <note>original: "archet"</note>, by the fingers, by quills <note>original: "plumes," referring to the plectra used in instruments like the harpsichord</note>, or in any other manner one might wish. Thus, this subject could be extended unto infinity, although my design does not go so far; for I treat here only of the instruments which serve Music, and which are so much at the disposal of man that he can use them when he pleases. This does not happen with the noises of winds and thunders, which do not depend on our will, which has only those things which can fall—

# Book One

be placed under the governance of art; although the understanding, which is more universal than the art itself, can contemplate the noises of nature, and examine whether the different thunders, and the roarings and bellowings of the sea, are consonances and dissonances, of which I speak more fully in other places.

Now, one can divide all musical instruments into three types: namely, stringed instruments, those that use wind, and those that rely on percussion or striking. The first type includes the <term>Monochord</term><note>A single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals.</note>, the <term>Marine Trumpet</term><note>A long, triangular bowed instrument, not a brass trumpet.</note>, the <term>Colachon</term><note>A long-necked lute, also known as a Colascione.</note>, the Viols, the Violins, the Lyre, the Mandore, the Lute, the Harp, the Cittern, the Pandura, the Psaltery, the Spinet, the <term>Manichord</term><note>An early name for the clavichord.</note>, the <term>Hurdy-gurdy</term><note>original: "Vielle"</note>, and all others that are strung with chords, which we shall treat in this book.

The second type contains the Pan-pipes, flutes with one or two holes, Trumpets and Horns, the Trumpet, the <term>Sackbut</term><note>The Renaissance predecessor to the trombone.</note>, the Serpent, the <term>Zinks</term><note>original: "Cornets à Bouquin"; wooden instruments with a trumpet-like mouthpiece.</note>, the three-holed flute, the Flageolet, the transverse flute, the Fife, the German flute, the Bagpipe, the Musette, the Oboes, the <term>Curtals</term><note>original: "Fagors/Bassons"; early bassoon-family instruments.</note>, the Bombards, the Bassons, the <term>Kortholts</term><note>original: "Courtaux"; short-bored woodwinds.</note>, the <term>Rackketts</term><note>original: "Ceruelats"; compact, low-pitched woodwinds.</note>, the <term>Crumhorns</term><note>original: "Tornebouts"</note>, and the Organs, which I treat in the following books.

And the third type includes the <term>Jew's Harp</term><note>original: "Rebube, ou la Trompe d'acier"</note>, Castanets, Cymbals, <term>Bones</term><note>original: "Offelets"; rhythm instruments made of bone or wood.</note>, the <term>Xylophone</term><note>original: "Claquebois"</note>, and the Drums; for these three types contain all bodies that produce sounds by striking the air, or being struck by the air. Here it must be noted that it matters not at all whether the air strikes or is struck to produce the same sound, and that one would hear the same harmony if the air struck the strings in the same manner that it is struck by them—just as we would see all the same movements and phenomena in the heavens that we perceive now, even if the earth turned and the sun and stars were immobile: although one might imagine that the earth and the stars move together with different movements, like the strings and the air, and that God alone is immobile: but this consideration requires another place.

Now, I treat first of stringed instruments, insofar as they are simpler and easier to understand, for their strings represent lines and serve to explain and demonstrate everything that belongs to Music. But it must be noted that they can be further subdivided into instruments with necks, such as the Viols, and those that have no necks, such as Harpsichords; and those that have necks are divided into necks with frets <insert>touches</insert>, like the Lute, and necks without frets, like the Violin. Similarly, those that have no necks either use keyboards with jacks, like the Spinet, or have no keyboards at all, like the Harp. Finally, they are divided into instruments with gut strings and those that use metal strings. I leave aside several other divisions that one might imagine, because these suffice for Musicians, and several other divisions will be established after one has read the books on all the Instruments, which will provide new insights.

### II. PROPOSITION.
*...Explaining the material and the manner in which instrument strings are made.*

<image-desc>Ornate initial capital 'O' with floral and possibly animal motifs.</image-desc>
ONE can make the strings of musical instruments from all metals that can be drawn through a draw-plate <note>original: "filiere" — a tool used to thin metal into wire</note>, namely gold, silver, copper, brass, and steel; and from the guts or intestines of animals, which have several fibers that make them strong enough to endure the tension necessary for harmony. But one ordinarily uses sheep guts, whether because they have been found more suitable for this than others, or because they are more easily found due to the great multitude of sheep killed every day. Now, these guts are often 72 feet, and sometimes a hundred feet long, as I have experienced with a string of a hundred feet made from the gut of a Picardy sheep: which I note because the makers of racket strings <note>Tennis was a popular sport in 17th-century France; rackets used similar gut strings to musical instruments</note> had never made one so long from a single intestine. For if they want a certain length, or any other they desire, they join several guts together, which they twist so well that they appear as only one.

But they soak them for a day before twisting them on their pegs, in order to clean them and remove the grease and everything superfluous, leaving only the membrane woven of three kinds of fibers—namely straight, transverse, and oblique—from which it takes its strength. Then they must be stretched while quite soft and wet upon the said pegs, which are placed at the distance of the length one wishes to make the strings. This they do in the same manner as weavers who wind and twist thread upon their nails or pegs, going back and forth from one peg to the other until they have wound as many guts over them as are needed for the thickness of their strings. For example, the thinnest strings for rackets are composed of seven guts, and the thickest of twelve, which are called the "uprights" and the "cross-strings" by those who string rackets. From this, it is easy to conclude that the sixth strings of Bass Viols <note>The lowest string on a six-stringed viola da gamba</note> and the tenth strings of the great Theorbos <note>A large, long-necked lute used for bass accompaniment</note> are made of 48, or 50, and 60 guts, for they are at least 4 or 5 times as thick as the thickest racket string.

As soon as they have been stretched, they are twisted several times; and after they have been sufficiently twisted, they are wiped, rubbed, and polished, both with linens or hemp cords pressed along their length, and with a herb which is a species of horsetail <note>Equisetum, used historically as a fine abrasive like sandpaper</note> that they call *Pfeffe* <note>likely a regional term for Dutch rush or shave-grass</note>, and finally they are dried so that they may be fit for musical instruments or for other things to which one wishes to apply them.

Now, there is no doubt that the circumstances of time, place, and different waters make gut strings worse or better. From this it comes that the best strings come from Rome or other places in Italy, whether because the sheep of that country have guts that are more uniform and better disposed than those of France, by reason of the different herbs upon which they feed.

sent, or whether the waters in which they are soaked provide some particular disposition, or whether those who spin them add some technique to make them better that our craftsmen do not know. I leave aside the manner in which they must be oiled to preserve them, and several other circumstances that one can learn from the Rope-makers <note>original: "Cordiers"</note> and from those who sell these strings.

As for those made of brass <note>original: "leton"</note> and other metals, one uses steel draw-plates <note>term: "filieres" (plates with graduated holes used to taper wire)</note> of one square foot, or thereabouts, or of whatever length and width one desires, which are pierced with a great multitude of holes of different sizes in order to draw strings of all thicknesses.

But the industry used by the wire-drawers <note>original: "tireurs"</note> deserves to be considered, for they draw strings that are as slender as hair from all sorts of metals, as I shall say in the corollaries.

Now, whatever industry or diligence one may apply to drawing or spinning the strings, they always have some inequality, even if it is not perceptible, as much by reason of the different jolts and various movements given to them while drawing them, as by the different parts of which they are composed, which have different qualities according to the different locations they held in their mines, and the different parts of the earth and water from which they took their origin. To this one may add the different degrees of heat, and of rarefaction or condensation, that each part acquired in the melting and in the cooling, which create great differences in the pores of the metals; and then the different wear <note>original: "diminution"</note> of the different parts drawn at different times through the holes of the draw-plate. For even if a string of 20 or 30 feet is not perceptibly thicker in one place than another, nevertheless reason dictates that the end which passes through last must be thicker than that which passes first; for since the hole increases <note>i.e., wears down and widens from friction</note> after one has passed several fathoms of strings, there is no more reason to say that it increased by one part of the string than by the other, and consequently one must admit that a perceptible increase is made of an infinity, or of many imperceptible ones, just as it is said that from many of the imperceptible atoms of Democritus <note>Ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles</note> a perceptible body is made.

One could here treat several other difficulties belonging to strings, but I have spoken of them elsewhere. I add only that gut strings <note>original: "chordes de boyau"</note> are even more subject to deformity and inequality than those of metal, insofar as the guts from which they are made have their membranes and fibers more or less thick, and strong or weak, in one place than in another. This can easily be proved by the difference that Anatomists place between the intestines, to which they give different names as much by reason of their different lengths and thicknesses as for other reasons they provide. And then the Rope-makers sometimes twist the strings more in one place than in another, or do not apply equal diligence to all parts, whether in rubbing, scraping, polishing, or preserving them, or in other circumstances to which one can attribute the "falseness" <note>A musical term for a string that cannot be tuned perfectly or produces irregular harmonics due to physical defects</note> of strings, which most often comes from their inequality or some other similar quality.

# On Universal Harmony.

### COROLLARY I.
SINCE gold, silver, brass, and steel strings are used on the **Spinet** <note>A smaller, rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note> and on other instruments, one must note the methods used to draw them into wire. Now, after bars or ingots of these metals have been forged—being about 3 feet long and one inch in diameter—they are pulled through several holes in a **draw-plate** <note>original: "filiere"; a metal plate with graduated holes used to reduce the thickness of wire.</note> up to 28 or 30 times. This is done with the strength of four men, who use for this purpose a machine with four arms, or a lathe that is parallel to the horizon. For this task, they attach a cable to the shaft of the lathe, and to the other end of the cable they attach pincers which grip the end of the ingot, pulling it through the holes of the draw-plate until they have reduced the said ingot to the thickness of an **aglet-iron** <note>original: "fer d'éguillette"; the small metal tip at the end of a lace or drawstring.</note>.

And then they send the coil to other gold-wire drawers, who pass it through 30 different holes again, in order to spin the silver or other metals until their threads are as fine as hairs. I have tested that a thread from half an ounce of silver, made by what is called the *small-scale craft* <note>original: "au petit meſtier"</note> and which has passed through 60 or 64 different holes, is 574 feet long—that is, 97 **fathoms** <note>original: "toiſes"; a historical French unit of length approximately equal to 1.949 meters.</note>. But since it is certain that it can be stretched further by 3 fathoms, or 18 feet, I say that a silver thread weighing half an ounce, when thinned like a hair, is at least one hundred fathoms, or 600 feet long.

### COROLLARY II.
IF one wishes to know how much longer or shorter gold and other metals of the same volume as silver are when drawn through the same holes, one only needs to know the proportion of their weights. For example, since gold is almost twice as heavy as silver, gold can only be drawn to 50 fathoms. And because iron is almost a quarter lighter than silver, a half-ounce of iron drawn through the same hole will be 125 fathoms, or 750 feet long. It is easy to find the length of the wire of other metals, since it has the same ratio to that of silver wire as their weights have to that of the said silver. The wire I used for my experiment can carry a half-pound **standard weight** <note>original: "poids de marc"; the traditional French system of weights used before the metric system.</note> before breaking.

And being a foot and a half long, it makes one hundred vibrations <note>original: "retours"</note> in the space of one second of a minute when it is stretched with the said half-pound on a **monochord** <note>A scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundbox with movable bridges.</note> whose **bridges** <note>original: "cheualets"</note> are one foot and a half apart; and this string weighs about 3/4 of a **grain** <note>A very small unit of weight, roughly 0.06 grams.</note>.

### COROLLARY III.
SINCE I have explained the manner of drawing metals into wire, I wish also to add the manner of beating them and reducing them into small leaves, which are so thin and delicate that they float on water without being able to sink—though some maintain that they go to the bottom after having been on the water for 5 or 6 months. I have also experienced that they return to the water's surface when they have been pushed down.

They are extended into a very great volume by beating them first between...

After they have been beaten for the last time, it is found by experiment that one ounce of gold makes 1,600 leaves suitable for gilding whatever one wishes, of which each is more than 3 inches square, for it measures 37 lines <note>A "line" is a historical unit of measurement, usually 1/12th of an inch.</note>, and consequently it makes nearly 3 square fathoms <note>original: "toises." A toise is an old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.39 feet.</note>.

If silver and brass <note>original: "leton" (laiton)</note> can be beaten as thin as gold, they will occupy all the more space as they are lighter; because, being of the same weight as gold, they are much larger, as I have already said in the 2nd Corollary and elsewhere.

## COROLLARY IV.

Since a wire of half an ounce of silver can be drawn to 100 fathoms, a wire of one pound of silver can be 3,200 fathoms long, which is to say one great league; and consequently an ingot of 8 pounds, such as those that are drawn, can have the length of eight leagues, from which it is easy to conclude how much silver would be needed to circle the earth or the heavens.

The same can be applied to gold leaves; for since one ounce gives 1,600 leaves, a pound will give 256,000. Now, the 1,600 leaves reduced to square feet make a square surface of 105 feet, 91 inches, and 16 lines, of which the side is 10 feet, 3 inches, and 4 lines. And a pound of gold makes a square whose side is 41 feet, 1 inch, and 4 lines.

## COROLLARY V.

It is easy to know the diameter and the thickness of all kinds of metal strings <note>term: "chordes de metal" (metal strings). In this context, the author refers to wire used for musical instruments or scientific measurement.</note>, if one understands what I have said in the other corollaries; for since they follow the law of cylinders, it is a certain thing that their bases and their heights are reciprocal, and consequently that a string of one hundred fathoms at its base is one hundred times smaller than one which is only one fathom, when it is of an equal weight. Now, the bases are in a doubled ratio of their diameters, so that one must only take the sub-duplicate ratio <note>note: This is an archaic mathematical term for taking the square root.</note> of the bases to find that of their diameters, which is done by extracting the square root of the said bases.

And consequently, if the base of a cylinder 120,000 feet high is one, that of a cylinder 3 feet high is 120,000; their ratios are as 40,000 to one, which, when the square root is taken, gives the ratio of 200 to 1. By this, one sees that the diameter of a silver string of half an ounce, which is 100 fathoms long, is 1/300th of an inch—that is to say, the 16th and 3/4 part of a line—if the silver cylinder 3 feet high which has 120,000 for its base weighs 7 pounds, 12 ounces, and 3 <unclear>drachms</unclear>.

But it is easy to calculate exactly the size of the silver cylinder, whether it weighs as much as we have just said, or whether it weighs only half an ounce, or 8 pounds, or whatever other weight one wishes, either by means of water <note>A reference to Archimedes' principle of displacement to determine volume.</note> or in other ways that I explain in other places.

## III. PROPOSITION.

*To determine whether Musical Instruments were made in imitation of voices, or if the intervals of voices were regulated by those of Instruments; and consequently whether Art can perfect Nature, or if Nature perfects Art: and if one must judge artificial things by natural ones.*

<image-desc>An ornate initial capital 'E' with a face in profile and foliage.</image-desc> This proposition will serve to understand the judgment one can make regarding the dispute that Vincenzo Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), lutenist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note> had with Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), the most influential music theorist of the Renaissance.</note> in the year 1588, on the subject of the 4th Chapter of the first book of the *Supplement* which the latter wrote to respond to the *Dialogues* that the former had written concerning ancient and modern Music, in which he had criticized Zarlino’s *Institutions* in several places. Now, the principal subject of this dispute consists in knowing whether voices use Ptolemy’s Synton <note>original: "Synton de Ptolomée"; referring to the Syntonic Diatonic scale, a system of tuning that uses "just" or pure thirds.</note> while singing, and if one must adjust and correct the voice by instruments, or the contrary. As for Galilei's reasons, he bases them on the division of two kinds of Arts, some of which have no regard for their subjects except insofar as they use them to make the works they propose, as happens with Shoemakers and Carpenters, of whom the former cut leather and the latter wood in all sorts of slants, and consequently destroy their subject and the material of their Art.

But other Arts perfect their subjects, as is experienced in Agriculture, in Animal Husbandry, and in Medicine, both for men and for animals, which the Latins call *Veterinaria* <note>original: "Veterinaria"; Veterinary medicine.</note>, for Agriculture perfects plants, Husbandry perfects Animals, and Medicine the human body: from which he concludes that Zarlino titled his chapter poorly, since fruits and trees become domestic from the wild state they were in through the Art of Agriculture which grafts and cultivates them in different ways, and since Medicine corrects several defects of the body that children contracted in the mother's womb. And if one places the different ways of applying makeup among the Arts, one can say that Art, encountering the perfection of a beautiful face, can still enrich and enhance that beauty, and increase its grace, if women who are naturally beautiful are right to use makeup.

He further criticizes the other part of the same title, in which Zarlino says that one cannot draw conclusions about the things of nature from those of Art, inasmuch as the Physician forms an idea of health which he establishes as so perfect that there was never one like it in Nature; from which he then draws reasonings and conclusions for the natural health that is actually found in human bodies, for the health of a person is judged all the more perfect as it approaches more closely the universal idea of the Physician;

# Book One,

from which it follows that one can conclude and judge the things of Nature by those of Art.

<term>Zarlino</term> <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), an influential Italian music theorist</note> adds that <term>Musical Instruments</term> were made in imitation of natural ones, by which they must be corrected. But <term>Galilei</term> <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), lutenist and father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei</note> denies this proposition, because each instrument is made for the purpose intended by the <term>Artisan</term> in inventing and making it. For example, the saw is made for sawing, and the flute for sounding, and not for imitating nature: for even though nature can do many things that are not within the power of Art, she does not teach the manner of correcting; for she does not teach that one must pull the limbs to reset bones, nor any of the other operations of <term>Surgery</term>.

<term>Zarlino</term> further objects that a <term>painter</term> cannot reform and correct a defective human body, nor reduce it to a perfect symmetry and proportion by the model he sees in the painting of a natural body; but he ought to consider that the <term>Physician</term> can correct the said body by that which he has known as perfect in his mind, provided that the vice is not incorrigible and incurable: and that the Painter does not only imitate all the things of <term>nature</term> and of <term>Art</term>, but also everything that can be imagined by means of lines and colors, which often surpass those of Nature. From this it follows that he can make a body so beautiful that the eye will never have seen its like in Nature, as much regarding the features and proportions as regarding the shadows and colors: which he will similarly do with plants and animals when he wishes.

From which <term>Galilei</term> concludes that <term>voices</term> learn the true <term>intervals</term> of Music from Instruments, and not the contrary. Indeed, if one tunes Instruments according to the perfection of <term>Theory</term>, there is no doubt that they have no need of the voice, which can be corrected and adjusted by their means; for one cannot demonstrate whether voices sing accurately except by showing that they are in conformity with the perfect Instrument: which <term>Zarlino</term> would have admitted if he had considered it attentively.

Now there is no doubt that the <term>degrees</term> and the intervals of the voices belong to Art, although words belong to it even more; for if they did not depend on Art, those who teach children to sing would have no difficulty in making them intone and sing in tune: and all men would make the correct intervals without having learned them: which is against experience. This shows that apprentices have difficulty making <term>semitones</term> and the other intervals, both consonant and dissonant, until they have become accustomed to them through Art. And it is often believed that many sing accurately, even though they are further from accuracy than the organ, which uses temperament: which cannot be better demonstrated than by the perfect <term>system</term>. Of which it seems these two personages did not have enough knowledge; otherwise <term>Galilei</term> would not have denied that one can find three or four <term>Fourths</term>,

or consecutive fifths with a major or minor third in any genre other than the "incited" <note>original: "incité"; likely referring to the *enharmonic* or *diatonic* genus as described by Aristoxenus</note> of Aristoxenus, of which I shall speak in the discourse on the lute; and Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), a hugely influential Italian music theorist</note> would not have taken such pains to explain the *Syntonon* of Ptolemy <note>The "Syntonic Diatonic" scale, which uses pure major thirds (5:4 ratio)</note>, in which several degrees are missing, if he had possessed the knowledge of the keyboards that he proposes in the treatise on the spinet and the organs. Certainly, it seems to me that Art can be said to be superior to Nature, or to surpass Nature, in that it gives some degree of perfection to a subject to which Nature cannot give it; which does not prevent Nature from overcoming Art in several other things.

As for the voice, which served as the subject of their dispute, Zarlino believes that peasants naturally produce the true intervals of music when singing, and Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), father of Galileo and a theorist who argued for tempered tuning</note> maintains that there is as much difference between the true intervals and those of the voices of the ignorant as there is between the animals that Nature forms in marble, in the knots of Ash and Olive trees, and in many other things, and those designated by the learned hand of an excellent painter.

## PROPOSITION IV.

*To know which is the most pleasing sound of all musical*
*instruments, and which instrument must be*
*used to regulate the intervals and the*
*harmonic differences of tones.*

<image-desc>Ornate initial capital 'E' depicting a person's head in profile, possibly a classical figure, within a decorative frame.</image-desc>This question is difficult to resolve, for to judge soundly of things, one must call upon those who have more experience than others; otherwise, the arts would be miserable, as would those who make a profession of them, if they depended on the judgment of the first comer. Those who make a profession of music do not agree well on this difficulty, and one encounters a great diversity of opinions arising from the different affections that musicians bear toward the instruments to which they have devoted themselves and which they know best how to play. The same difficulty also arises because we have not yet heard all the instruments that can be made, or that are already in use in foreign provinces; and hardly a person is found who has heard all those we know at one and the same time, and in succession, so as to be able to give judgment on them. For to judge an absent instrument, heard three months ago, against one that is present and producing its effect now, there is, it seems, no likelihood of accuracy; for present things being accustomed to touch us more, the absent one might lose its cause through a failure of the imagination, which would not represent the sweetness of the absent sound as well. Or perhaps, as first impressions are the strongest and most violent, the absent one might win its cause by the report of the imagination, which would augment the thing beyond the truth; and that which would even prevent judgment when one had them all present—

instruments, is that they all possess some particular grace or beauty when they are well played.

The difference in temperaments <note>In 17th-century thought, "temperament" referred to the balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, choler, melancholy) which determined a person's personality and tastes.</note> found among men similarly causes the sound of some to seem more pleasing than that of others, so that these reasons, and several others that one might cite, can hinder the sincerity of <term>judgment</term> <note>The faculty of discerning truth or value.</note>. For the first reason causes <term>Organists</term> to judge that the sounds or voices of the Organ surpass the sound of other <term>Instruments</term>, while players of the <term>Lute</term>, <term>Viol</term>, <term>Harp</term>, etc., will say that the sound of these instruments touches the <term>affections</term> <note>The emotions or passions stirred by music.</note> better and is more pleasing. The second reason leads us to the suspension of judgment, which the <term>Pyrrhonists</term> <note>Followers of Pyrrho; ancient skeptics who believed that because human perception is subjective, one should withhold final judgment on the nature of things.</note> used to keep their minds in a state of indifference: inasmuch as one cannot judge which is the most pleasing of the sounds of all Instruments if one has not heard and compared them to one another—which has never happened, and which cannot be done, for we always leave more inventions to posterity than we ourselves have found.

The third reason often constrains us to admit that the sound of all kinds of Instruments is pleasing when they are good and well played, and that it is, it seems, impossible to judge which is the most pleasing; for if the Lute has some particular grace that is lacking in the Organ or the Viol, these two Instruments and their like have another privilege, namely that their sounds hold firm and remain as long as one wishes—even though the length or brevity of sounds should not be compared with their <term>sweetness</term> <note>In this context, "douceur" refers to the tonal quality or "softness" of the sound.</note>, since it is of a different genre.

The fourth reason is why soldiers, and those who have a temperament and blood that is boiling and warlike, find the sound of the <term>trumpet</term> more pleasing than that of the Lute or other Instruments; and why hunters set more store by the sound made by the <term>Horn</term> than by others, because they are accustomed to hearing it; for that which is familiar to us often pleases us more—unless <term>curiosity</term> and the desire for knowledge carry us toward seeing and hearing new things, and sometimes make us value less that which is common to us.

Now, all these difficulties are encountered in almost identical fashion in all things of the world that one might wish to judge; nevertheless, the reason of man, which wishes to resolve every kind of difficulty, does not fail to extricate itself from these <term>Labyrinths</term> and to find, albeit by groping, some general and universal judgments which are held as true by both experienced and learned men and by the ignorant. However, the former know what exceptions must be applied to general rules, while the latter do not, thinking that everything must be enclosed within said rules.

Certainly, men have almost judged, and have as if remained in agreement, that the sound of the Lute is the most charming, and the ignorant have stopped there; but those who know how to judge this with more restraint and reason have brought to it a great <term>distinction</term>.
