## Of Instruments.

Regarding those sounds which are made by stringed instruments, such as by <term>Lutes</term> <note>A plucked string instrument with a rounded back, popular in the Renaissance and Baroque</note>, <term>Mandoras</term> <note>A small lute-family instrument</note>, <term>Guitars</term>, <term>Viols</term> <note>A family of bowed string instruments held between the legs</note>, and the <term>Spinet</term> <note>A small, wing-shaped keyboard instrument where strings are plucked</note>, and those which are made by wind instruments, such as by the <term>Trumpet</term>, <term>Flutes</term>, and <term>Organs</term>; if we compare these together, it will be said that the German <term>Flutes</term> <note>The transverse flute, held sideways, as opposed to the recorder</note> have a more agreeable sound than other <term>Flutes</term> and <term>Organ</term> pipes, and that they yield only to the Human voice. But if we speak of the others, it seems that the sound of the <term>Violin</term> is the most ravishing, for those who play it perfectly, such as the Messrs. <term>Bocan</term> <note>Jacques Cordier, a famous French dancing master and violinist</note> and <term>Lezarin</term> <note>A celebrated violinist in the French royal court</note>, and many others, soften it as much as they wish and render it inimitable by certain tremblings <note>An early term for vibrato or trills</note> which ravish the spirit.

Those who play the <term>Lute</term> perfectly well will perhaps contradict what I have said of the <term>Violin</term>, because they find delicacies of which the <term>Violin</term> is not capable: to which they may add that they play 4 and 5 parts all together. However, we are not speaking here of the multitude of parts, or of the excellence of the instruments, nor of the mixing of harmonies, or of the different "stops" <note>Referring to the various tonal colors available on instruments like the organ</note> which are found and played upon the instruments; for the sweetness and excellence of the sound considered all alone is the sole subject of this discourse. Even though it is nearly impossible to judge this sound well without speaking of the quality of the instruments—the one being so joined to the other that they cannot be separated—we shall therefore be constrained to touch here upon something of what must be said in the chapter on the quality of instruments. Now, generally speaking, all sounds of instruments are produced either by wind, or by the movement of a string, or by percussion.

As for those made by wind, it can be said in general that all sounds made by the mere cutting of air are sweeter than the sound of other wind instruments, and any other that can be produced by a string; but they are not as agreeable as those made by the beating of a <term>Reed</term> <note>The vibrating strip of wood or cane in instruments like the oboe or bassoon</note>. For although they seem harsh, they have a natural gaiety that makes them preferred to that mournful and somber sweetness of the <term>Flute</term>; even though mournful sounds make a concert of several parts more agreeable than that which is made of gayer sounds.

This being presupposed, we must speak of the sounds made by strings, which are twofold: namely, the sound made at the same instant the string is struck, and that which remains after the percussion, which is produced by the movement of the string alone. The first approaches the gaiety of the reed sound, for it has something of harshness in proportion to how the string is touched.

But that which remains is similar to that of the German <term>Flute</term>, which it surpasses in sweetness. Consequently, the sweetest of all sounds is that which is made by the movement of the string after it has been touched or struck, as is seen in the <term>Lute</term>, the <term>Harp</term>, and the <term>Spinet</term>, and more than in any other, in the <term>Violin</term> and the <term>Viol</term>.

Now, there are only two means or two causes which can aid the sweetness of these two kinds of sounds: one of which is taken from the string, and the other from the manner in which it is touched.

<page-num>12</page-num>
<header>Book One</header>

## Book One

The <term>gut string</term> <note>original: "chorde de boyau"; strings made from sheep or animal intestines, providing a warm tone</note> yields a sweeter sound than one of <term>copper</term> <note>original: "cuiure"</note> or steel; and if strings of the same material differ in length, the one that is longer—when tuned to the same pitch as the shorter one—will yield a sweeter sound. Furthermore, a thicker string will yield a fuller and more massive sound than a thinner one, which yields a smaller and weaker sound.

The manner of touching the string also brings a great diversity to the sound, for it is different when touched by a human hand than when it is touched by a quill, an ivory plectrum, or a bow. For the sound is sweeter when the hand touches the string directly, as seen with the <term>Lute</term> and the <term>Harp</term>, whose sounds are much sweeter than those of the <term>Mandore</term> <note>a small, high-pitched lute</note>, or the <term>Spinet</term> <note>a small harpsichord where strings are plucked by quills</note>, or any other instrument whatsoever, inasmuch as the human finger tempers the sound with Art, and softens it as much as one desires.

The harp must also yield to the lute, because on the lute one touches the same string with two hands in different ways, whereas on the harp one touches it with only one; and because the lute creates diversity in the resonating sound by means of two or three types of "tremblements" <note>ornaments similar to vibrato or trills</note>, some of which lengthen and continue it, while others change it. But the resonating sound of the harp is sometimes harmful to other sounds.

As for the resonating sound of the <term>spinet</term>, it is the most excellent that can be imagined, but the <term>Musician</term> has no power over this sound, which is entirely uniform and cannot be varied or enriched with inventions like that of the lute—the poverty and riches of which I shall report in another place, and I shall say why it is admitted in some concerts and rejected from others.

Now, to speak of sounds more generally, we can say that the sweet ones are somber, muffled, and imprisoned, like those of <term>stopped flutes</term> <note>pipes closed at the top, sounding an octave lower than open pipes</note>, and that the gay ones are more open, like those of <term>Reeds</term> and <term>flutes</term> <note>original: "fustas"</note>, which <term>organ builders</term> call "in <term>resonance</term>." Sounds are almost all indifferent, provided they are not so weak that the hearing cannot perceive them, or so violent that it is offended by them. What makes them more pleasant is the variety with which one embellishes them, either in succession or joined together with other sounds.

Choose whatever sound you wish and hear it continually; it will put you to sleep or give you a headache. The sound of a flute placed on a windchest, being continuous, is marvelously troublesome and unpleasant; and that of a lute would be even more so, if it could continue as long as that of the flute. It is therefore variety that makes sound agreeable; and if it is not varied, it deserves rather to be called noise than harmonic sound. And because variety can only be made with time, all sounds need time to create some variety and some impression in the mind that makes us admire and desire them.

The sound made by the <term>percussion</term> <note>the initial strike or pluck</note> of the string lasts for almost only an instant and has almost no subsistence. That which is made by the vibration of the string—which can be called the second sound, or sound of <term>resonance</term>, or <term>reverberation</term>—goes on diminishing and dying, and is very little at the disposal of the Musician. He who could make a sound of percussion that was also a sound of resonance, and which participated in some way in the percussion, would create the sweetest and most agreeable sound of all those that can be encountered.

# On Instruments.

to enter into nature; for to imagine a sound of resonance <note>The author distinguishes between "resonance" (the sustaining tone) and "percussion" (the initial strike or pluck).</note> that lasted at the Musician's will, or a sound of percussion that was as sweet as that of resonance, that is reserved only for the blessed in heaven—even though the wind passing over the strings of a lute, making them ring out, gives us some idea of it.

Those who invented the sound made by a well-guided bow upon the string have found the sweetest sound of percussion, for it is less harsh than that of the finger, which makes the string bend more and lets it go with greater violence than the bow. The bow, through its percussion, does not stifle the sound of the resonance which mingles with the other; thus, a bow-stroke lasting an entire measure has, from the first instant, both full sounds mingling together, of which one is cheerful and pleasant, and the other sweet and harmonious.

One must therefore conclude that the sound of the Violin and the Viol is the sweetest and most pleasant of all Instruments, since it possesses at the same time the two sounds of which the lute's sound is composed at two different times. From this it follows that lutes appear so little in a concert of Viols, for only their percussion is heard—which is harsh and intrusive—while the sound of resonance is stifled because of its weakness.

The sound of spinets <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note> is also stifled, even though their strings have a resonance of longer duration because of the proportions they maintain, and because they all ring "open" <note>original: "à vuide" — referring to strings vibrating freely without being stopped by fingers.</note>, which binds them better with the resonant sounds of the viols, which have a continuous sound of percussion as well as resonance. Now, the sound of percussion in viols still has something harsh about it, participating somewhat in bitterness and hardness, and is not yet refined enough for the delicate ear—unless there is some distance between the place of percussion and the ear, which renders the sound sweeter and strips it of what is most harsh and earthy. And if one could imagine a music consisting only of the resonance of lutes or spinets—and particularly that of lutes, which carry such elegance in the left hand—and if one had removed all percussion (which would be similar to resonant viols without a bow), nothing could be added to such music; but it is reserved for the blessed in Heaven, where it will be divested of all the imperfection found in it now.

As for the comparison made between the sound of flutes or the trumpet and those made by stringed Instruments, it is easy to judge by what has been said, even though they are dissimilar. Those who measure the sweetness and excellence of sounds by their closest relationship to the voice—and for this reason judge in favor of flutes and flageolets <note>A small flute or recorder-like instrument.</note>, which they say imitate the human voice more closely than stringed Instruments do—are mistaken. They do not know what imitation is regarding sounds and Harmony. For even though the sound of the voice is made by wind like that of flutes, nevertheless one encounters many sounds and noises produced by wind that are very unlike the voice. And although the sound of Reeds <note>original: "Anches" — referring to reed instruments like the oboe or bassoon.</note> seems to imitate that of the voice, one must nevertheless consider flutes by including all their sounds with their pleasant trills and varieties, without leaving the key in which one is playing. I do not speak here of warbles <note>original: "fredons," referring to rapid vocal or instrumental trills</note>, because there is no instrument that does not perform them faster and with better definition than the voice.

Now, if the sound of Flutes—among which one may include the Trumpet—has more power over the mind, it is because of the stronger impression it makes in the air, or because of its particular quality. And indeed, beyond reason, experience shows that those who have a more delicate ear, and more refined and subtle spirits, take more pleasure in the sounds of stringed instruments; and those who have coarser and thicker spirits take a greater pleasure in the sound of the Trumpet and of Flutes, although this may perhaps not be so universal that the contrary might not happen due to specific reasons. But the sounds of instruments considered all alone, without regard to those which precede or follow them, give so little pleasure that we must not dwell on them any longer.

As for the sounds that make up melodies and chords, besides what I have said of them, I shall speak of them in the judgment that will be made regarding the excellence of instruments, where I shall say which is, or ought to be, the one that surpasses the others, whether used in a concert <note>an ensemble of instruments</note> or played all alone. Here one may remark that the sound of each instrument taken individually can be compared to a simple color, such as white and black; and a musical concert to paintings, some of which are made with such artistry that they must be seen from afar, and others from nearby. For paintings that have coarser colors which are sketched <note>original: "croquez"</note>—as painters say—and which possess much more artistry, require being seen from a distance, and are loved, cherished, and esteemed by the sons of Art. Others, on the contrary, which are very softened and finished, require being seen from closer up, and are more esteemed by those who are short-sighted and cannot consider wherein the artistry consists. In the same way, the music of Lutes is for those who do not wish to hear the music so much as the voice, and that of Viols is for those who, standing a little further away, prefer to hear it rather than see it. Now, this similitude will make us note in passing that a low sound <note>original: "son grave"</note> which approaches silence is similar to black, and the highest pitch <note>original: "aigu"</note> to white; for just as there are an infinite number of middle sounds between the low and the high, there is likewise an infinite number of colors between white and black.

I come now to the other part of this proposition: namely, which sound or instrument is most fit to regulate the intervals and the differences of sounds, and to serve as a canon or harmonic rule <note>original: "regle harmonique," referring to a standard for tuning</note>. If we follow the opinion of Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century Greek astronomer and music theorist</note>, who maintains in the 8th chapter of his 1st book that Flutes and weights hung at the end of strings are not accurate enough to establish the ratio of consonances, we shall find that the Monochord <note>a single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals</note> alone is fit for this. Now, Ptolemy's reasons are that it is difficult to make Flutes accurate enough, and to moderate and govern the breath as is necessary, which, being pushed more strongly or more weakly, makes different sounds; for the same pipe rises by a quarter or a half-tone when one pushes the breath a little harder, and if one increases it further, it rises to an octave or a twelfth, as I have said elsewhere. As for the weights that one suspends from strings, they cannot regulate the sounds because one does not

### On Instruments.

one never encounters strings that are perfectly equal, and since one cannot know precisely what their inequality is, consequently one would not know how to find the ratio of weights necessary to set the strings to all sorts of sounds: and furthermore, these same strings often raise or lower their pitch, even though they are stretched with the same weights; and even if they were perfectly equal, they would not maintain the ratio of sounds, because of the different elongations they would receive through the difference in weights, as I shall prove more fully elsewhere.

The same difficulty is encountered with sounds made by striking with different hammers on an anvil, or on vessels, whether full or empty, insofar as it is very difficult to maintain the same shape while making the said Vessels: to which one can relate Bells, Drums, and Cymbals, both ancient and modern.

# Book One

that which one sets as a foundation, does not lower or raise the sound that was heard before: this is why it is much more serene <note>In this context, "serene" implies a clear, stable, or reliable quality.</note> to make use of a single string, in which even then an inconvenience can occur; for if it is not equal and uniform in all its parts, it may happen that it will not produce a unison when divided in half, and consequently it will not show the correct ratios and intervals of sounds, as I shall prove in the treatise on the Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used since antiquity to measure musical intervals mathematically.</note>.

Nevertheless, if one asks which instrument is most fit to regulate a concert, and to keep the other instruments in tune and the voices in their proper pitch, so that they do not rise or fall over a long period, I believe one can answer that of all those known, it is the Spinet <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note>, or the Harp, but rather the Spinet than the Harp. Now, the reasons that experience has taught me seem infallible; for although some might say that the organ is more suitable, as being less subject to going out of tune than the strings of the Spinet, I respond that if one takes one of the reed stops of the organ, it is no less subject to loosening than strings; and if one takes a flute stop, it is too dull, and too far removed from the nature of the sound made by strings to be able to regulate other instruments; and furthermore, the bellows vary in a moment, being stronger at the beginning and in the middle than at the end of their movement, which provides little assurance.

But a Spinet well-tuned, whose strings have been well-stretched for a long time, and the pegs firmly set in their soundboard, resting on a steady base, whose quills <note>The plectra made of bird feathers used to pluck the strings in a spinet.</note> are not too strong, and covered with a small frame fitted with brass wire, will remain in tune for eight or fifteen entire days: and each instrument will easily judge by what tone it is discordant from the others, and will correct itself easily without touching the rest.

I have preferred the Spinet to the Harp, insofar as the Harp, being touched by the human finger, can be pulled with more or less violence from time to time, and thus the strings most violated will drop in pitch, and the least forced will remain in their tone, from which discord will follow: but the Spinet remains more equal, insofar as the Musician does not have the power to strike it harder at one time than another.

### PROPOSITION V.
*To demonstrate all the divisions of the Monochord, and consequently the entire science of Music.*

We have already proved that the Monochord is the most proper instrument for regulating sounds, insofar as it is the most accurate of all, and its construction is very easy. From this comes the fact that it is called the Harmonic or Canonical rule <note>original: "reigle Harmonique, ou Canonique"</note>, because it serves to measure the low and high of sounds, just as the ordinary rule of Geometers serves to measure straight lines, and the compass to describe Circles.

As for its construction, I have shown how it must be made in the preceding proposition: I add nevertheless that one can make it of all sorts

### of Instruments.

And if one wishes, there is no need for any other Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used since antiquity to measure musical intervals and the mathematical ratios of sound.</note> than the table of a Lute,
or another necked instrument to regulate all the sounds of Music,
whether one uses a single string, or several: But one must put all
the strings in unison, so that they represent only one and the same string;
this must be noted so that one does not believe that the multitude of
strings destroys the nature of the Monochord.

Now, although it is not necessary for the body of the Monochord to be
hollow, like the body of the Lute or the Viol, and a simple board may be suffi-
cient; it is nevertheless more convenient when it is hollow, because it re-
sonates longer, and the sound of its strings has more body. One can
make it in all sorts of lengths, according to the design one has, and because
if it is too long it cannot serve for strings that are short,
and if it is very short, it cannot serve for strings that are very long,
one must have several of them to test all sorts of strings—for example,
3 or 4: one of 3 feet, another of 6, and another of 12 or 24 feet: but the
tuning pegs must be so disposed that one can stretch all
sorts of strings to their best sound, or until they
break, in order to perform the experiments of which I speak elsewhere.

This cannot be executed if the pegs are not long and wide enough,
and far enough from their center, to break a string made of 144
sheep guts; that is to say, if they do not serve the Musician such that he
can lift a weight of six or seven hundred pounds by turning said pegs
with his hand.

Now all these Monochords are only necessary for performing all the
experiments on strings, from which one can draw some consequence in favor
of the nature of sounds and strings: for if one only wishes to observe the
low and high <note>original: "le grave & l'aigu"</note> of sounds, and all their differences, it is enough to have a Mono-
chord of one, two, or three feet. But so that the mind is in no way
restricted to certain lengths or widths, I show here how
all sorts of sounds can be found and marked on the Monochord
taken in general, after having noted that all parts of the string which
is stretched over said Monochord are equally tensioned; as I have
shown in a particular discourse.

One can use all sorts of strings, but those of brass <term>leton: an old term for brass or latten</term> or
steel are better than those of gut, because they are not subject
to so many alterations and changes, and they remain longer
in the tone in which they were set.

As for the division of the string by means of a bridge <term>cheualet: the bridge of a stringed instrument</term> of wood or
other material to find the intervals and the differences of sounds, it is done
firstly by the string divided into two parts, as one sees in the string
A B, which is divided at point C, for there is the same distance from A to C
as from C to B; this is why these two strings are in unison—that is to say, they have
the same sound as to the low and the high, of which we speak only here.

# Book First

And if one wishes to find the Octave, one must divide the string D F into three equal parts, and place the bridge at point E, so that the string E F makes the Octave below against the string D E.

This same Octave is found in the first line, for A B makes the Octave against A C; that is to say, if one stretches two strings of the same thickness equally, one of which is equal to A B and the other to C B, they will produce the Octave, for the reason that the string A B (or E F) will strike the air only once, and make only one sound, while the string A C (or C B) will make two. The other <term>consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound harmonious or "stable" to the ear.</note> will be found in the same manner on whatever string one wishes, or on two strings; for one must only add the two numbers, or terms of the ratio of each consonance, and divide the string into that many equal parts, so that the <term>bridge</term> <note>The "chevalet," a movable support used to change the vibrating length of the string.</note> being placed under the string at one of the numbers of the ratio, it allows the consonance one seeks to be heard, as I show in the <term>Fifth</term>, in the <term>Fourth</term>, and in the two <term>Thirds</term> and the two <term>Sixths</term>.

The two terms that make the ratio of the Fifth, namely 2 and 3, being added together make five; that is why one must divide the string into five equal parts, and place the bridge on the point that ends the second part, so that three parts remain on one side and two on the other: or if one wishes to use two strings, one must have three parts of length and the other two. One can further see what I have said of these divisions in the fourth Latin book of Consonances, Proposition 17 <note>original: "quatriefme liure Latin des Confonances, Propofition 17." Referring to the author's own *Harmonicorum Libri*.</note>, in which I place the lines that are not here: so that these two Books serve one another, insofar as what is missing in one is found in the other, as I have already remarked elsewhere.

Similarly, if one divides the string into seven parts, and the bridge stops the string at the end of the 3rd part, one will hear the Fourth: and the string divided into 9 parts and being stopped at the fourth will make the <term>Major Third</term>. But it must be divided into 11 parts to make the <term>Minor Third</term> with the bridge, which will stop it at the end of the fifth part: and into eight parts to make the <term>Major Sixth</term>, and into thirteen to make the minor.

One also finds the replicate <note>An interval doubled or extended by an octave.</note> of each consonance in the same way, for if one divides the string into 3 equal parts, one of the parts makes the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>An interval of two octaves.</note> above against the rest, that is to say against the other 4 parts. And if one divides it into 4 equal parts, one of the parts makes the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>An octave plus a fifth.</note> against the three others. One must still use the same industry to find all the dissonances, for the string being divided into 17 parts, if the bridge is at the end of the 8th part, it will make the <term>major tone</term>; and if the string is divided into 19 parts, it will make the <term>minor tone</term> with the bridge being at the end of the 9th part. Finally, if one divides the string into 31 parts, it will make the <term>major semitone</term> by placing the bridge at the end of the 15th part: if one places the bridge at the end of the 24th part of the string divided into 49 parts, it will make the <term>minor semitone</term>; and if one wants to find the <term>comma</term> <note>A very small interval resulting from the difference between two nearly identical notes in different tuning systems.</note>, it must be divided into 161 parts, and the bridge placed at the end of the 80th part.

And because it is the same thing to divide one line into 161 parts as it is to divide two, of which one has 80 parts and the other 81, it is just as easy to find the consonances on two separate strings as on a single one.

It must nevertheless be noted that two strings are more convenient than one, because one cannot hear the sounds of the two parts of the same string [at once]...

AE makes the unison with EI; secondly, that the Octave is from AI to EI; thirdly, that the Fifteenth is from AI to GI, and the Twenty-second from AI to HI. The Twelfth is from AG to EG, the Nineteenth from GA to FG; and the Fifth from A to G.

The Major Seventeenth is from AF to EF, the Major Tenth from AF to DE, and the Major Third from AF to BF.

The Fourth is from AI to AG, the Minor Third is from AG to BG or AF, the Minor Sixth is from AI to AD, the Minor Sixth <note>The author repeats "Minor Sixth" here, likely referring to different string segments.</note> is from AI to AF, and the Eleventh is from AI to AD. 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6

The Octave is from 1 to 2; the Twelfth from 1 to 3; the Fifteenth from 1 to 4; the Major Seventeenth from 1 to 5; the Nineteenth from 1 to 6; the Fifth from 2 to 3; the Fourth from 3 to 4; the Major Third from 4 to 5; and the Minor Third from 5 to 6. To which, if one adds the 7 and the 8 of the preceding Monochord, one will have as many dissonances as comparisons that can be made of each number with 7, which is so "unhappy" in harmony that it can produce nothing but dissonances with the other numbers from one up to thirteen.

But 8 makes the Minor Sixth with 3, and the Eleventh with 3; so that the number 8 produces two new consonances which are not found within the number 6. As for the repetitions of the Minor Third and the two Sixths, they cannot be found unless the number is increased, as we have shown in the book of consonances.

The major semitone <note>A small musical interval, roughly half a tone</note> creates a major twenty-eighth with the remainder, and a twenty-ninth with the total length, as seen in string A B, which is assumed to be divided into 20 parts; for A B creates the octave against B M, and B M creates the unison against the remainder, namely against M A.

The fifth A K (80) with the remainder K B (40) creates the octave, and with A B (120) the twelfth.

The fourth A C (90) creates the twelfth with the remainder C B (30), and creates the twelfth and the fifteenth against A B.

The major third A D (96) creates the fifteenth with 24, and the major seventeenth with A B.

The minor third A E creates the minor seventeenth with E B, and the nineteenth with A B.

The major sixth A F creates the fifth with F B, and the major tenth with A B; and the minor sixth A G creates the major thirteenth with G B, and the eleventh with A B.

It was necessary to use fractional numbers for the major tone and the major and minor semitones in order to maintain the division of the string into 120 parts; otherwise, a much larger number would have been required, which one could use instead of this one.

### PROPOSITION IX.
*To explain all the consonances and dissonances encountered in the Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note> and in the perfect System, whether one compares the whole string with the parts that are the ordinary degrees—diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic—or whether one compares each degree or sound with the whole string, or with its remainder: Consequently, the Monochord and the harmonic System will be considered here in every possible way.*

The Table that follows explains this entire proposition clearly enough, for it contains 6 columns, of which the 1st shows the letters of the "hand" <note>The Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic device for singers</note> or the musical scale; the 2nd divides the monochord into all the intervals of the octave that can serve harmony; the 3rd contains the numbers showing what remains of the string, such that the numbers of the 3rd and 5th columns which are opposite one another, when added, always equal the largest number, namely 3600, which represents the entire string or the lowest sound.

The 4th explains the ratios <note>original: "raisons"</note> formed from each number of the 3rd column to each opposite number of the 5th. Now, I have placed the names of the consonances in this 4th column when they are found to be perfect, and the other intervals or ratios with only the numbers that signify the terms of each ratio:

sound: For example, the 2nd number of the 3rd column, namely 1920 <note>original: "1910" - likely a typo in the source for 1920, a common value in these ratios</note>, is to the 2nd of the 5th column, 1680 <note>original: "1610"</note>, as 13 is to 12.

But it must be noted that the first number, which is always larger in this 4th column, corresponds to the number in the 3rd because it is the largest; and the lesser number always represents that of the 5th column, because it is always the smallest.

The 6th column represents the entire string <term>3600</term> <note>The number 3600 is used as a common denominator for easy division of the string length</note> and contains a perpetual comparison of this string with what remains of the column: for example, 3600 makes the octave with the first number of the 5th column, 1800; and of the same column, namely 1600, as 9 is to 4; and so on for the others. Now, the larger number of the ratios in the 6th column represents the entire string, and the smaller number represents what remains of the same string. Finally, the 1st column contains the ratios that the entire string makes with what remains of the 3rd column, and the larger number always represents the entire string.

Now, if one considers all these ratios, one will know almost all the relations, both good and bad, that can be encountered in musical compositions; and consequently, one will be able to find the reason why, among several passages made from one consonance to another, some are good and others are bad; and why, among several good or bad ones, some are worse or better.

But to find the ratios of the whole string with the remainder, and the other comparisons encountered with the numbers in this table, one must place 2 strings in unison on the <term>monochord</term> <note>A single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals</note>, or on some other instrument—for example, on the Lute, which can serve as a Monochord—and place the finger or the bridge at all the points on the string where the numbers of this table are, and one will have the satisfaction of knowing everything that can be considered regarding consonances and dissonances.

For if one always leaves one of the strings open—namely the entire string represented by the largest number 3600, which makes the <term>C sol, ut, fa</term> <note>A traditional way of naming the note C in the hexachord system</note>—and one places the finger on the other string at the place where the numbers should be, one will find that with the finger being on C (that is to say, at the middle of the string at the number 1800), one will produce the octave against the open string, and the unison against the remainder.

Now, that which is produced against the open string by the two parts of the divided string is always written in the first and sixth columns: so that the larger number of each ratio in the first and sixth columns always represents the open string, and the smaller numbers signify the two parts of the divided string.

This is why one reads "octave" at the top of both these columns, because 1800, which begins the 3rd and 5th columns, makes the octave with the open string represented by 3600.

As for what the two parts of the string produce when they are touched at the same time, it is written in the 4th column; for by placing the finger in the middle of the string, the two parts produce a unison, because they are equal.

Now it must be noted that this proposition is almost nothing other than a more ample explanation of the preceding one.

which one takes by chance, whether one takes it smaller or larger than the line that must be divided. Let there be, then, the line or the chord <note>original: "chorde" — in this context, a straight line segment</note> AB, which must be divided into 7 parts, and let the opening of the compass be taken at will as EF. I say that if one takes any line one wishes, for example CD, and marks 7 parts upon it equal to 7 openings of the said compass, the given line AB will also be divided into 7 parts by applying a ruler over each 7th part of the preceding line and over AB. This is practiced by means of an equilateral triangle <note>A triangle where all three sides are of equal length.</note>, in which all sides are proportional, as I show in the triangle that follows, which contains all the preceding lines. For one must subtract the part GC from the line DC, since the division into 7 parts goes only from D to G. One must therefore make the triangle so large that its base is equal to the line that was first divided at will, such as the base of the equilateral triangle HGD. I use this because it is easier to apply lines to it than in other triangles, because these 3 sides being equal, one has the said base by extending whichever side one wishes, for HD gives the base GD. 

Now, it must first be noted here that one can easily divide a given line into as many parts as one wishes, even if the opening of the compass is larger than the said line, or if it is equal to it. For if one wished to divide the line EF into 7 parts with a compass opening equal to GD—that is to say, which was 7 times larger than EF—it would be necessary to divide a line into 7 parts, each of which would be equal to GD, and consequently, it would be necessary to make the base of the triangle HGD 7 times larger than it is.

->[Image: A geometric diagram showing a large triangle HGD. Near the apex H, a horizontal line EF is drawn, divided into several equal segments. And if the opening of the compass is equal to the line that must be divided, as happens when one wants to divide EF into 7 parts by taking the same EF for the opening of the compass, the line DG will provide this division. Finally, if the opening of the compass is smaller than each part of those into which the proposed line must be divided, one must divide another line into 7 parts, each of which is equal to the said opening. For example, if the compass is only opened to the seventh part of the line EF, this line being divided into 7 and applied within the triangle will give the division of the other line GD. One must conclude the same thing for all other divisions into as many parts as one wishes, for each division is as easy as the other. In the second place, it is not necessary to see the line that must be divided, for it remains divided into as many parts as one wants after the one taken at will is divided. Now, one must hold one of the ends of the ruler on the top of the triangle at point H when one wants to mark the divisions of the preceding lines.

### COROLLARY.

One can conclude from this Proposition that the equilateral triangle is excellent and very useful, for it has great uses in Perspective and Geometry; and many find a greater pleasure in seeing this figure than any other, by reason of the perfect equality of its three sides and its three angles, each of which is sixty degrees—that is to say, a third of two right angles <note>Two right angles equal 180 degrees; therefore, one-third is 60 degrees, the standard angle of an equilateral triangle.</note>. To which one may add that it is difficult to find another thing by which one can better explain the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity than by this triangle. Now, I show the principal applications that can be made of the different encounters of the Stars <note>original: "Astres" — refers to celestial bodies, including planets.</note> with all the Consonances and Dissonances, and with all the divisions of the Monochord <term>Monochord: An ancient scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships of musical intervals.</term> in the Proposition that follows, so that the perfect Musician remains ignorant of nothing that can embellish and ennoble his Art.

## PROPOSITION XI.

->*To determine the number of aspects by which the Stars regard the earth, and the Consonances to which they correspond.*<-

Although one could posit an infinite number of aspects <note>In historical astrology and astronomy, an "aspect" is the angle between two celestial bodies as seen from Earth.</note> in the Heavens because the Stars make an infinite number of angles with the earth, nevertheless, Astrologers usually only notice five: namely Conjunction, Sextile, Square, Trine, and Opposition. They have called them by these names because the angles of these aspects are measured by the half, the third, the fourth, and the sixth part of the Heavens; for as for conjunction, it occurs at the same point of the circle, and consequently, it makes no angle because there is no distance between two planets that are joined.

*But Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), a key figure in the scientific revolution who sought to harmonize the laws of planetary motion with musical theory.</note> adds eight other aspects, namely the semi-Sextile, the Decile, the Octile, the Quintile, the Tredecile, the Sesquiquadrate, the Biquintile, and the Quincunx, the explanation of which is seen in the table that follows, and which serves to easily understand all that concerns the thirteen aspects, and the consonances and dissonances they make, or which they represent.*

For the first column shows the number and the natural order of the aspects; the second contains the names of the 13 aspects and the symbols of the ordinary ones, for the other aspects do not yet have any; although *Johannes Kepler* invented three or four, they are not in common use; and it is easy to assign them such symbols as one wishes. The third column contains the angles or the degrees of all the aspects; and the fourth explains the consonances that these degrees make with the entire circle, which is represented in the fifth column by 360, signifying the degrees of the circle or of the heavens in which the aspects are made. But the sixth column explains the consonances made by the same 360—that is to say, the whole circle—with what remains of the same circle after one has subtracted the degrees of each aspect. Now, this remainder is in the seventh column, whose numbers or remaining degrees make the consonances or dissonances with the whole circle in the fif-

One must similarly observe that the <term>aspects: The angular distances between planets in the sky, believed to influence earthly events.</term> which create the aforementioned harmonies produce no discord, whether one compares the side or the degrees of the aspect to the entire circle, or whether they are compared with the remainder. This occurs in the same way on the straight string of the <term>Monochord: A scientific instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships of musical intervals.</term> when one encounters these same harmonies there; so that what happens to one happens similarly to the other. But we must examine whether the power of the aspects follows the order of the <term>consonances: Intervals or chords that sound pleasant and stable to the ear.</term> they represent: that is to say, if the <term>conjunction: When two planets appear at the same point in the sky (0°).</term> is the most powerful of all aspects, just as the **unison** is the most powerful of all consonances; and if the <term>opposition: When two planets are on opposite sides of the sky (180°).</term>—which creates the **Octave**—is more powerful than the <term>trine: An aspect of 120°, or one-third of the circle.</term> which creates the **Fifth**, and so on for the other aspects compared to the other consonances.

### COROLLARY I.

One can exchange the names and the symbols of the aspects for those of the consonances: calling the conjunction the **unison**; the opposition the **Octave**; the trine the **Fifth**; the <term>square: An aspect of 90°, or one-quarter of the circle.</term> the **Fourth**; the <term>quintile: An aspect of 72°, or one-fifth of the circle.</term> the **major Third**; the <term>sextile: An aspect of 60°, or one-sixth of the circle.</term> the **minor Third**; the <term>sesquisquare: An aspect of 135°.</term> the **minor Sixth**; and the <term>biquintile: An aspect of 144°.</term> the **major Sixth**. One can, in the same way, give the names of the aspects to the musical consonances.

### COROLLARY II.

Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the astronomer who famously linked planetary motion to musical harmony in his work *Harmonices Mundi*.</note> holds that these aspects do not correspond to simple consonances, but to their <term>repliques: Compound intervals that span more than one octave (e.g., an octave plus a fifth).</term>, because the aspects are defined by the same segments of the circle that create repeated consonances. For example, he suggests that the trine does not correspond to the **Fifth**, but to the **Twelfth** <note>A Twelfth is an Octave plus a Fifth (ratio 1:3).</note>; the quintile to the **major Seventeenth**; the sextile to the **Nineteenth**; the biquintile to the **major Tenth**; and the sesquisquare to the **Eleventh**. I have explained this so clearly in the 4th column—which compares the segments (or the chords) and the angles of each aspect with the whole circle—that there is no need to speak of it further. Nevertheless, he denies that one should establish the number of aspects based on this consideration, lest he be forced to include an infinite number of them, due to the different "repliques" of each consonance that can arise from all the divisions of the Monochord. For one can divide the circle by means of aspects in such a way that one would find the hundred consonances for which I have provided the terms elsewhere.

### COROLLARY III.

This division of the circle corresponds perfectly to the division of the Monochord, as can be seen by comparing the universal table of said Monochord, in which I have explained all the consonances and dissonances of the <term>Perfect System: A theoretical framework in music theory intended to encompass all possible harmonic relationships.</term>. Here, he concludes that while circular geometry mirrors these ratios, the physics of sound and the reality of astronomical observations suggest that Kepler’s geometric models of the universe are more imaginary than physical.</meta>

-># Of Instruments<-

The circle and the straight line, being divided into similar parts, always represent the same <term>consonances: Intervals or chords that sound pleasant and stable to the ear.</term>, whether one compares the two remaining parts together, or each of them with the entire string; and consequently one can use a <term>Circular Monochord: A theoretical device where a string is stretched into a circle rather than a straight line to demonstrate that the same mathematical ratios apply to both shapes.</term>, provided that one can stretch a string in a circle in such a way that all its parts vibrate and sound freely, just as all the parts of a straight line do. This would occur if one could stretch it in the air so that it could vibrate freely, like the straight string of a Monochord or a Lute. The rim of a glass represents such a circular string, but if one places a finger on a part of the rim, it can no longer vibrate nor sound. From this it follows that it is necessary to use straight strings to regulate sounds, unless one wishes to use a wheel similar to that of the <term>Vielle: Also known as the hurdy-gurdy, an instrument where a rosined wheel (the "drum" mentioned here) rubs against strings to create a continuous drone.</term>, which I shall speak of in another place.

## COROLLARY IV.

One can conclude from this Proposition that the <term>aspects: The angular positions of planets relative to one another.</term> are not the cause of consonances, since they are found more easily and more naturally through the division of the straight string than by that of the circular one; and that one must not consider them according to the planes and surfaces of <term>effable or ineffable figures: Geometric shapes whose proportions can be expressed as rational numbers (effable) or only as irrational roots (ineffable).</term>, but according to the simple rational sides of the said figures. To this I add that there is no need to consider these figures at all, since the nature of consonances is nothing other than the ratio of several movements of air, which are pleasing to the ear or to the mind, as I have demonstrated in the book on Consonances. Consequently, the consideration of <note>Kepler’s figures: Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) proposed in his 'Mysterium Cosmographicum' that the distances between planets were determined by the five Platonic solids (cube, tetrahedron, etc.) nested within each other.</note> Kepler’s figures is in no way necessary for the understanding of Music.

## COROLLARY V.

There is no need to explain the Consonances that occur in the movement or in the distance of the Stars, both because I have spoken of them quite fully in the second book of the treatise on <term>Universal Harmony: Marin Mersenne’s encyclopedic work, 'Harmonie Universelle' (1636), which sought to link the laws of music to the laws of the universe.</term> (from the 4th Theorem to the 9th), and because the movements of the stars are not known well enough to know if they make perfect Consonances. As for their distances from the earth, they are known even less than their movements, so that nothing can be demonstrated in this matter. Experience teaches that the diameter of the Planets is much smaller than one imagines, because their rays <note>original: "leurs rayons nous trompent" — referring to the optical glare or "irradiation" that makes bright stars look larger to the naked eye than they truly are.</note> deceive us, and because telescopes <note>original: "lunettes d'approche"</note> prevent these rays. For the diameter of Jupiter [♃] is only one minute of a degree, though it seems to be three when one does not use these telescopes. Thus Kepler had reason to reform the measurements and distances he gives to the Planets, and consequently their Consonances or Dissonances. From this one can conclude that the cube he places between Saturn [♄] and Jupiter [♃], the tetrahedron between Jupiter [♃] and Mars [♂], the dodecahedron between Mars [♂] and the earth, the icosahedron between the earth and Venus [♀], and the octahedron between Venus [♀] and Mercury [☿] are not established well enough to serve for any consonances other than imaginary ones.

## PROPOSITION XII.

### *To explain the diagram of the Monochord and all its divisions.*

If one understands the preceding Propositions, there is no need to explain the <term>Monochord: A scientific instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundbox, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between musical intervals.</term> here, seeing as I have discussed it so extensively and precisely that one could (it seems to me) desire nothing more, unless practitioners find the discussions too theoretical. One can also see the method of constructing it at the end of the fourth Proposition, where I explained <term>Ptolemy’s harmonic rule: A method established by the ancient scientist Claudius Ptolemy for dividing a string to produce the notes of a musical scale.</term>; nevertheless, I am providing a specific diagram here, so as to accommodate practice and usage so well that there is no instrument maker or musician who does not understand it as well as I do, and who could not restore Music by its means, even if it were entirely lost and erased from human memory.

Let there be, then, the Monochord I G L, of whatever length and width one wishes, upon which the string A B is attached at the top to an iron pin, and at the bottom to the tuning peg G, so that it may show all the intervals of Music by means of 24 bridges; in place of these, one can use a single one by moving it all along the string between its two stationary bridges A C and B D, which determine the length of this string. I have given this string only 7 and 1/2 inches of length, which one can double and multiply as many times as one likes: for example, if one wants the string to be 16 times longer, one must take 16 times the length of this one, and consequently make each division 16 times larger than those on this Monochord. Its use consists in finding the places where one must place and fix the <term>bridge: A small, movable support placed under the string to change its pitch by shortening the vibrating length.</term> under string A B or C D, to hear whatever consonance, dissonance, or interval one wishes, in order to then transfer them onto all sorts of instruments, both stringed and wind, and to consider the numbers, lines, and <term>ratios: The mathematical relationships (like 2:1 or 3:2) that define musical intervals.</term> which explain or constitute all the harmonic degrees, and which serve as signs or causes of the pleasure one receives. Now, it must first be noted that the three strings stretched upon it are of the same length, and that the same degrees found on string A B are also on string C D, but with this difference: the degrees that are at the bottom on C D are found at the top of B A, on which they go in reverse to those of C D. This was not done without reason.

Secondly, it should be noted that the second string F, which is in the middle, has no divisions, so that it always represents the entire sound, and sounds <term>open: Playing the full length of a string without stopping it with a bridge or finger.</term> against all the divisions of the other two strings; and at the same time, one can more easily imagine that the 48 stationary bridges of these two strings can be replaced by a single movable bridge, which one moves under string F: whereby we see that movement is the great spring of nature, and that it can do as much as an infinity of bodies.

Thirdly, the tuning pegs G serve to tighten and loosen these three strings, in order to bring them into <term>unison: Two or more notes sounding at exactly the same pitch.</term>, whether they are made of sheep gut or of brass; for it matters not at all, though it is quite appropriate to use one from a Lute and the other from a Spinet, in order to notice the diversity

# Book One

Although this <term>Monochord: An ancient scientific and musical instrument used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</term> marks only the degrees of the <term>Diatonic genre: The most common musical scale consisting of whole and half steps.</term>, it is easy to mark those of the <term>Chromatic: A scale moving by half-steps.</term> and <term>Enharmonic: A complex scale using "quarter-tones" or very small intervals.</term> genres as well. I have done this on a four-foot Monochord, which contains these three genres in perfection; from those, I have taken only the Diatonic to transpose into a smaller volume on this figure, whose thickness is marked by AH and BI. However, the length of its three strings must be measured from the top of the two nuts or <term>bridges: Small pieces of wood that support the strings and define the vibrating length that creates the sound.</term> that bound the sound of said strings—that is to say, from A to B. And if one wishes to strengthen the sound of the strings, one can make an opening on the soundboard or at the sides of the Monochord, similar to the <term>rose: An ornamental carved sound-hole found on instruments like lutes.</term> of Lutes, or the <term>sound-holes: Openings in the body of a stringed instrument that allow the sound to resonate.</term> <note>original: "ouye"</note> of Harps or Viols; likewise, one may use iron tuning pins similar to those of <term>Spinets: A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</term>, in order to tighten them with a hammer.

Whatever the case may be, it is enough that one finds all kinds of intervals and degrees in their proper tuning upon the Monochord, regardless of its material, shape, or the number of strings it may have. Indeed, the number of strings does not prevent it from being called a Monochord, because they are all tuned in unison—though it matters very little what name it is given, provided that one understands its use and practice.

Some people put 8 strings on it, and others 15, or as many as on a Spinet, so as to be able to hear all the intervals of Music at the same time, but it all comes to the same thing. As for the larger numbers positioned opposite the bridges of string CD, they continue the ratios of all its divisions: so that the numbers following from bottom to top—that is, from A to B—signify the length of the strings resting on each bridge. Now, I shall remark upon several other things in the Corollaries that follow, so that one may more perfectly understand all the divisions of this Monochord, after noting that this figure serves as many individual Monochords as it has bridges, each of which always supposes a new division of the string. But all these divisions relate to the largest number of each string, which shows into how many parts it must be divided to have and to make heard the 25 degrees marked by the bridges or by the divisions of this Monochord.

### COROLLARY I.

The <term>comma: A very small musical interval, specifically the difference between a major tone and a minor tone, with a ratio of 81:80.</term>, which is the difference between the major and minor tone and whose ratio is 81 to 80, is only marked on the first Octave of strings AB and CD, as one sees between their first two bridges. This is why only this first Octave has 9 sounds or 8 intervals, because the interval of the comma would have been too small in the other Octaves. As for the two following Octaves, they have only 8 sounds and 7 intervals due to the absence of the comma. From this, it follows that the first degree of each of these two Octaves makes the minor tone, just as the second makes the major, so that the <term>Major Third: A musical interval encompassing two whole steps.</term> may be perfectly in tune from <note>original: "C sol vt"</note> C to <note>original: "E mi la"</note> E. As for the other places where the comma must be found to have the three genres in their perfection, I have spoken of them in the books on Theory; and later I shall discourse upon them again in the treatise on the Lute, the Spinet, and the Organ. Now, although I have not included any <term>sharps: Symbols (or here, divisions) indicating a note raised by a half-step.</term> <note>original: "dieses"</note> or minor semitones,

### COROLLARY II.

If one wishes to omit the degrees of the Octaves and only mark their extreme sounds, the five numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 show the five Octaves marked on the 1st and 3rd strings. And if one wishes only to hear a <term>consonance: A combination of notes that sound pleasant and stable together, such as an Octave or a Fifth.</term>, for example the Fifth, the fifth <term>bridge: A movable block (labeled G in the author's diagram) used to change the vibrating length of the string.</term> G will sound it against the whole string, which will be found divided into three parts, making the Fifth against two of its parts <note>The ratio of a Fifth is 3:2; the whole string is 3 parts, and the bridge stops it at 2 parts.</note>. ## PROPOSITION XIII.

*Explaining the difference and the distance between one consonance or dissonance and another by means of the Monochord; and the manner in which one must divide the same string into two parts to produce all kinds of consonances and dissonances.*

This Proposition is not difficult, though it is worthy of consideration, for when one wishes to find some consonance or <term>dissonance: A combination of notes that sounds tense or "harsh," requiring resolution.</term> on the same string, it must be divided into as many equal parts as there are units in the two terms that constitute the dissonance or consonance. For example, if one wishes to find the Octave on a string, it must be divided into three parts, so that when the finger is placed at the end of the two parts, it produces the Octave, and the larger part, which is double the smaller, produces the lower sound of the said Octave <note>The ratio 2:1 represents an Octave; 2 + 1 = 3 total parts.</note>. It must be divided into five parts to produce the Fifth, since its terms 2 and 3 make 5. The same must be said of the Fourth, which is found on a string divided into 7 parts <note>Ratio 4:3; 4 + 3 = 7.</note>; of the major Third, which is marked with the string divided into 9 <note>Ratio 5:4; 5 + 4 = 9.</note>; and of the minor Third, which divides the same string into eleven parts <note>Ratio 6:5; 6 + 5 = 11.</note>, etc.

But when one wishes to find two or more consonances on the same string—for example, the Octave and the Fifth—one must multiply the sum of the terms of one by the sum of the terms of the other. Consequently, one must multiply 5 by 3 to get 15, which signifies that the string must be divided into 15 parts to find the Octave and the Fifth there. For if one places the finger upon 10, one will produce the Octave, insofar as 5 and 10 of the string will sound the Octave <note>10 divided by 5 is a 2:1 ratio.</note>; and if one places it on 9, one will produce the Fifth <note>If the finger is at 9, 6 parts remain (15-9=6). The ratio of 9 to 6 is 3:2, which is a Fifth.</note>. From this, one can conclude that the Fifth differs from the Octave only by a single unit [on this scale]. This also happens every time one compares any other dissonance with that which follows it or precedes it immediately. For if one skips one, two, or three, the difference between the two compared will be the <term>binary: The number two.</term>, and for three it will be the <term>ternary: The number three.</term>, etc. For example, to find the Octave and the Fourth on the same string, one must multiply 7 by 3 to get 21, which shows that the...

A <term>string: In this context, the specific vibrating length of wire or gut on a monochord instrument.</term> divided into 21 parts gives the Octave by placing the finger on 14, and the Fourth by placing it on 12—which is two units less than 14. <note>The author uses a specific mathematical method: for the Octave (ratio 2:1), the sum of the terms is 3. 21 divided by 3 is 7; 7 times 2 is 14. This is because the finger placed on 21 creates the Fifth, just as it creates the Fourth when placed on 20. It must nevertheless be noted that the portion by which the Fifth is larger than the Octave is not the same as that by which the Fourth exceeds the Major Third; for the first is 1/2, and the second is 1/15. The same must be said of other <term>dissonances: Intervals that sound clashing or unstable, requiring resolution.</term> or <term>consonances: Intervals that sound stable and harmonious, like the Fifth or Octave.</term>, whose differences are explained by parts that are smaller as their terms are expressed by larger numbers.

Now, there are several things to note here, of which I will explain only a few that will serve for understanding and finding the others. I say first, then, that the Octave is no different from the Major Sixth than by a single unit, no more so than the Fifth, when one follows this method; for 3 multiplied by 8 (which is the sum of the terms of the said Sixth) gives 24. Now, the finger being placed on 16, it creates the Octave, and if one places it on 15, it gives the Major Sixth. But when one compares the Octave with the Minor Sixth, the string must be divided into 39 parts, so that the finger being placed on 26 makes the Octave, and being placed on 24 it makes the Minor Sixth—which is distant from the Octave by 2 parts, just like the Fourth. By this, one sees that <term>superpartient ratios: Ratios where the numerator is larger than the denominator by more than one (e.g., 5:3 or 8:5).</term> follow the same laws here as <term>superparticular ratios: Ratios where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator (e.g., 3:2 or 4:3).</term>, when they are compared or joined with multiple ratios.

I say in the second place, that if one wishes to find three or more consonances on the same string, one must multiply the parts of the string (already divided for two consonances) by the sum of the terms of the third consonance, and so on for the others. For example, if one wishes to find the Octave, the Fifth, the Fourth, and the Major Third, one must multiply 5 by 3 to get 15, and 15 by 7 to get 105, and finally 105 by 9 to get 945. This signifies that the string must be divided into 945 equal parts to serve as a <term>Monochord: A scientific instrument with a single string used to demonstrate the mathematical properties of musical intervals.</term> for the four aforementioned consonances. The Octave will be found at 630, which is 2/3 of 945. The finger being placed on 567 will give the Fifth; if one places it on 540, one will have the Fourth; and finally, if it is placed on 525, one will produce the Major Third. From this, it is easy to conclude into how many parts one must divide a string to make it serve all the consonances and all the dissonances; for if one multiplies the number that gives the 4 aforementioned consonances by 11 (that is, by the sum of the terms of the Major Third), and then by 8 and by 13 (which are the sums of the terms of the Major and Minor Sixths), one will have 1,081,080 for the number of equal parts of a string, which will give the 7 simple consonances of Music.

It is not necessary to add the manner of finding dissonances on the same string, since it is in no way different from the preceding method. For since the sum of the terms of the Major Tone is 17, and that of the Minor is 19, it is evident that one must multiply 19 by 17 to have the string divided into 323 equal parts. This string, being touched at its 171st part, will make the Major Tone, and the Minor on its 170th; by which one sees that these two tones differ only by a single unit, just as two consonances do when they follow each other immediately. ## COROLLARY.

If one understands this Proposition, one will be able to divide all types of strings or lines into as many equal parts as one wishes without a <term>compass: A tool for drawing circles and measuring distances, commonly used by builders and mathematicians.</term>. # PROPOSITION XV.

->*Determining how much the intervals of the Monochord of Equality are smaller or larger than those of the Harmonic Monochord, and if the ear can perceive the differences.*<-

It is certain that it is not enough to have proposed a very easy Monochord to equalize all intervals, if at the same time it is not accurate enough to satisfy the ear, and to satisfy the Practitioners <note>Professional musicians and performers.</note> and those who maintain that the comma <term>comma: A very small musical interval (specifically the Syntonic Comma, roughly 1/9th of a whole tone). Now, it is evident that this smaller number is larger than it should be by about 146 parts, for the number $133,333\frac{1}{3}$ makes the perfect Fifth of 2 to 3 with [200,000].

But those who do not like large numbers can use the smaller ones found in the first column of the preceding figure—namely those that follow—which are precise enough to mark the frets <note>original: "touches"</note> without offending the ear. Therefore, I return to the remaining considerations regarding the Harmonic Monochord, whose terms are set in their great accuracy, so that there may be nothing significant in the intervals—whether consonant or dissonant—that is not perfectly understood by those who take the trouble to read the preceding books and those that follow.

### COROLLARY I.

This division of the neck of musical instruments is not new, since all the Makers <note>original: "Facteurs," referring to instrument builders</note> and those who play them usually employ it without knowing the reason for it. Thus, one can say that the preceding numbers, which correspond to the 11 mean proportionals <term>mean proportionals: mathematical values used to divide an interval (like an octave) into equal parts</term>, are nothing other than what is practiced on the neck of the Lute and the Viol. Nevertheless, they are useful for dividing necks more surely, more exactly, and more quickly than is currently done, without the need to "feel it out" little by little. For if one marks these numbers on a sector <note>original: "compas de proportion," a calculating tool used by engineers and musicians</note> made of brass or wood, where each leg is one foot long, one will have placed the frets in their greatest accuracy on a hundred necks sooner than the Makers can place them on a single instrument. 

And if one takes the liberty of composing music according to this division, one will find that there is no "false" Fourth, no Fifth, and no Octave that is superfluous <note>augmented</note> or diminished. This is because the "false" Fourth of instruments creates the major Third; the "false" Fifth creates the Tritone; the superfluous Fifth creates the minor Sixth; the "false" Octave is nothing other than the major Seventh; and the superfluous Octave creates the minor Ninth. Consequently, composition will be much easier and more pleasant, and a thousand things will be permitted that many believe to be forbidden. This in no way prevents speculation following the ratios of consonances of which I spoke previously, since the object of the understanding <note>the mind/reason</note> is quite different from that of the senses.

### COROLLARY II.

I shall treat further the equality of whole tones and semitones in the 5th, 6th, and 7th Propositions of the second book on instruments. There, it will be seen that Aristoxenus <note>a Greek philosopher and music theorist who argued that the human ear, rather than math, should be the judge of music</note> followed this division, and I will explain several ways to divide the Octave, the minor Sixth, or other consonant or dissonant intervals into twelve equal semitones. This can easily be applied to quarter-tones; for if one finds a mean proportional number between the 13 preceding numbers to fill their 12 intervals, there is no doubt that one will have 25 proportional numbers. These will divide the Octave into 24 equal quarter-tones, which will be easy to use for the Enharmonic genus <term>Enharmonic genus: A style of ancient Greek music using very small intervals, roughly equivalent to quarter-tones</term>, whether on the necks of fretted instruments or others. # PROPOSITION XVI.

->*Determine what is the strength of all types of strings, whatever length or thickness*<-
->*they may have; and find what is the range of their sounds from the first*<-
->*or the lowest to the highest; consequently, give the weight necessary*<-
->*to break each given string: furthermore, find the weight that gives*<-
->*an equal tension to all types of strings, or different*<-
->*tensions according to a given ratio.*<-

**This** Proposition can be divided into three parts, of which the first shows the strength of strings considered by their length alone, and what the range of their sounds is from the lowest to the highest. The second shows the strength of strings considered by their thickness, and what weight is necessary to break all types of given strings, whatever thickness or strength they may have. The third teaches whether one can know when two strings differing in length or thickness are equally stretched, and what weight or what force is necessary to stretch them equally, or to give them tensions that have whatever ratio one desires.

The first part must be determined by experience, which shows the weight that can break each given string, and the string that can carry the given weight. Here are the experiments I have made, observing all the circumstances necessary for this subject; from which one may conclude what the strength of each string is. First, a string of pure gold, whose diameter is 1/6 of a line <term>line: a historical unit of measurement, approximately 2.25 millimeters or 1/12 of a French inch</term>, as is that of the other strings, has a range of an eleventh <note>This refers to the musical interval—an octave plus a fourth—representing the pitch range from a slack string to its breaking point.</note>, and carries 23 pounds before breaking: alloyed gold has the same range of sound, and carries the same weight: for if there is a difference, it is imperceptible. The silver string carries as much weight as the gold one, and yet it has only a range of a tenth <note>An octave plus a third.</note>. The iron string has a range of a nineteenth <note>Two octaves plus a fifth.</note>, and carries only 19 pounds before it breaks. Finally, the strings of copper and brass carry 18 and a half pounds. But brass—that is to say, yellow copper or latten <term>latten: a historical term for a brass-like alloy</term>—has the range of an eighteenth, and red copper of a seventeenth only. From this, it is easy to conclude that gold and silver strings are softer than the others, and consequently that they stretch more; from this comes the fact that they have a smaller extension of sound than the others; this similarly happens to the red copper string, but not so imperceptibly as to the others: this is why the experiments made on sounds are found to be more accurate on iron strings than on the others, because iron yields less and holds firmer, and after it, latten, or yellow copper.

## On Instruments.

For example, what strength do double, triple, or quadruple strings have? Suppose what I have said and tested regarding strings of all types of metals is true: can we say how much double or quadruple strings will carry compared to the previous ones? For although it seems that a string of double thickness should be double in strength, and consequently should only be able to carry twice as much weight as the double force, nevertheless, when two simple forces are joined and united, it seems they ought to be stronger than when they are separate. Indeed, many say they have noticed that if one takes two men, each of whom can only lift a weight of one hundred pounds, they will be able to lift a weight of three hundred pounds if they join their forces together.

From this it follows, it seems, that when a string is double the size of another, it should support a weight triple that which is supported by the half-size string. For example, if the half-size carries eight pounds, the double will carry twenty-four. This same conclusion would have to be drawn for beams and other pieces of wood, stone, and so on. Now, one can consider this force in two ways: first, when the strings or other bodies are stretched perpendicularly from top to bottom, with the weight suspended at the bottom end and the other end attached at the top, or held by hand, or by some other instrument. Second, when the strings or other bodies are stretched horizontally, as are the beams and joists of a floor, or the strings of a Monochord <note>A monochord is a scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundbox, used to demonstrate mathematical relationships between intervals.</note> laid parallel to the horizon.

I shall speak here only of strings and other bodies in the first manner, after having assumed that the diameter of my metal strings is only the sixth part of a line <term>A "line" (*ligne*) is a traditional French unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch, or approximately 2.25 millimeters.</term>. Thus, a string the thickness of one line—that is, one having one line in its diameter—is thirty-six times as thick as the aforementioned strings, which are small cylinders. This is why strings of the same length have the same ratio as their bases; now, the base of the string that has a diameter of one line contains 36 times as much as the base of the string that has only a sixth part of a line for its diameter.

Following this, it must be said that if the iron string I used carries 19 pounds <note>The "livre" or French pound was slightly heavier than the modern English pound, roughly 489 grams.</note> before it breaks, then the one with a diameter of one line will carry 19 times 36 pounds, which is to say 684 pounds—assuming that the forces of several strings being reunited and joined together are not greater than when they are separate. This would be true if all experiments matched those I conducted with silk; for two silk threads twisted and joined together do not carry twice as much weight as when one takes just one of these threads. On the contrary, I find that they carry less, and that the same thread, when doubled into four, carries much less than four simple threads. This defect may arise because the silk weakens as it is twisted, or because the silk I used was not uniform, or because the two or four threads do not assist equally and at the same time in carrying the weight and resisting the force.

It would be necessary to take simple, double, and quadruple iron strings to make the experiments more accurate; for two twisted threads are merely touching, but the double and quadruple strings of iron, or some other metal, have the forces of two or four simple strings so perfectly joined...
