# Book One

<meta>catchword: thickness</meta>

...and united, they form but one and the same force. Now, when this experiment has been verified, it will be easy to determine what weight will break a given string, or what string will be needed to carry a given weight: I say only that all the experiments I have made on this show that several separate strings sustain a greater weight than when they are united. The third part considers the **equal tension** of strings, which consists in knowing how much greater the force or weight must be to stretch a string that is double, triple, or quadruple in length or thickness to an equal tension as a string that is subdouble, subtriple, or subquadruple <note>In this context, "subdouble" means half the size, "subtriple" means one-third, and so on.</note>, or taken in whatever ratio one wishes. This is difficult to determine, for on one hand it seems that a double weight ought to equally stretch a string of double length or thickness; and on the other hand, the finger does not find an equal tension in the strings, for one appears softer and the other harder, which seems to show that the tension is unequal. To this I respond that the longer the string is, the softer it must be, and the more it must approach the earth toward its middle when it is stretched horizontally, even though it is stretched as strongly as a shorter string. This is seen in the experience of ropes attached to boats pulled by men or by horses; for whatever force is employed to tighten these ropes, they always form a "belly" or a circle in the middle and cannot be made parallel to the horizon. Experience shows that they break before they become parallel; and even supposing they could endure the violence necessary for this parallel tension, it is nevertheless not necessary to make them equal in tension to those that are so short that they seem to be parallel to the horizon when stretched with an equal weight. Thus, the difficulty consists solely in knowing what weight is necessary to make the double string have an equal tension with the subdouble.

For one will know at the same time how much the double, quadruple, or thousandfold string, etc., falls short of being parallel to the horizon when it is of equal tension with the subdouble or sub-thousandfold string, etc., and according to what ratios or proportions the middle of these stretched strings approaches the earth and leaves the parallel line. Furthermore, one will know how much one must multiply the force or the weight that stretches the longest strings equally, so that they may be as parallel to the horizon as the shortest ones. If anyone desires to know if the ropes of boats are tightened in proportion to some small part of those same ropes that are made parallel to the horizon with a weight—supposing that one must double the weight to equally stretch a string of double length—one need only measure the length of the longest. For if it is thousandfold, a thousandfold weight or force will be needed to tighten it equally; but if the weights must follow a squared ratio <note>Original: "raison double." In 17th-century mathematics, this often referred to the duplicate ratio or the square of the proportion.</note>, and a string one foot or one toise <note>A "toise" was a traditional French unit of length, approximately 1.9 meters or 6.4 feet.</note> long is stretched with one pound, it will require 1,000,000 pounds—that is to say, a million pounds—to equally stretch a string a thousand times as long.

Perhaps Music will give us the resolution to this doubt, assuming that unison or other consonances <note>A "consonance" is a combination of notes that sound pleasant or settled together, such as an octave or a fifth.</note> can serve us here to judge equal tension; for we have determined elsewhere what weight is necessary to set two strings that are double or quadruple in length and in...

# On Instruments.
D

...thickness at unison, at the octave, or at whatever other interval one might wish: which must be assumed here for the understanding of this difficulty.

First, when strings are double in length, the force or the weight that stretches the double string must be four times <note>quadruple</note> the weight that stretches the half-length <note>sub-double</note> string, when one wants to set them at unison; and if the string were four times as long <note>quadruple</note>, a sixteen-fold <note>sexdecuple</note> weight would be needed; that is to say, one weighing sixteen times as much as that which stretches the quarter-length <note>sub-quadruple</note> string: in such a way that the length of the strings follows the simple ratio of lines and roots, and the magnitude of the weights follows the double ratio of planes or squares.

But when strings are double, quadruple, or a thousandfold in thickness, and equal in length, the weights follow the same ratios as the strings, for the double weight puts the double string, and the quadruple the quadruple string, at unison: consequently, if unison signifies an equal tension, we will have satisfied the greatest difficulties of this Proposition: for the strings will be as far from an equal tension as they are far from unison, so that it will be necessary to add or subtract as much from the weights to stretch the strings equally as it is necessary to add or subtract to set them at unison.

Now, a great difficulty arises in this experiment of strings set at unison: namely, why a quadruple weight is needed to set a string of double length at unison, given that only a double weight is needed to put a string of double thickness there, since if this thickness were stretched out lengthwise, it would be double the length of the half-length string stretched by a given weight. But I will give the reason for this in another place, for it is enough to respond to the difficulty of the third part of this Proposition, in favor of which I say first that an equal weight, or an equal force, gives an equal tension to all sorts of strings equal in thickness, even though they are different in length, particularly when they are stretched perpendicularly—that is to say, when the string is attached at the top and hangs down; for the weight or force acts more uniformly on all parts of the string than when it is stretched horizontally and it rests on one or two <term>bridges: the wooden supports on an instrument, like a violin or lute, that hold the strings up and transmit vibrations to the body</term>, or on some other support which prevents the force from being distributed equally. To which one may add the heaviness of the horizontal string, which pulls it down toward the middle: which does not happen when the string is stretched from top to bottom; and perhaps these two different arrangements of the string cause musical instruments to have a different effect when they are held perpendicularly while playing than when they are parallel to the horizon, even though their strings are so short and so taut that the "belly" or the circle they form in the middle when they are horizontal is not noticeable.

Secondly, I say that the thicker strings of equal length require a greater weight to be equally stretched, which must, it seems, be increased in the same proportion as they are thicker. And thirdly, that no length—of strings equal or unequal in thickness—prevents the said strings from being equally stretched by the same force, since the same weight or the same force breaks them at least as easily when they are long as when they are short, for which I provide the reason when I examine all the difficulties...

...that is brought against the equal tension of all parts of a string stretched by a given force; for I now wish to explain what concerns the movement of strings, since it is by this means that the harmony of the instruments we are treating is formed, and it is not possible to hear them without this movement, which occurs by a very rapid vibration <note>original: *tremblement*</note>, of which I will explain several very remarkable particulars in the third Book, from the 6th to the 20th Proposition, which can be joined to that which follows.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

### *To determine in what proportion the returns and vibrations of strings decrease.*

This difficulty is, it seems to me, one of the greatest in Music, especially since the experiment <note>meaning scientific observation</note> of it is no less difficult than the reasoning; nevertheless, I do not find it difficult if I follow my experiments. I say then first that there is every appearance that the decreases in the vibrations of a string attached by its two ends occur in geometric proportion—that is to say, if the second return <note>the back-and-forth movement of the vibration</note> is smaller than the first by a 20th part, the 3rd is smaller than the 2nd by a 20th part, and so on until the last: or, if one wishes a more familiar and easier example, if the diameter <note>the width of the arc of vibration</note> of the first return is 16 parts, and the 2nd is 8, the 3rd will be 4, the 4th will be 2, the 5th one, the 6th a half, the 7th a quarter, and so on until the last which completes the cycle <note>period</note> of all the others.

As for the truth of the experiment, I find that when a string is pulled 12 inches, or 12 other units away from its straight line, it only returns to the eleventh unit at the 2nd return: so that we can say that the ratio of the decreases of these returns is *sesquionziesme* <term>sesquionziesme: a ratio of 12:11</term>, that is to say from twelve to eleven, for there is no more reason for the second return to be less than the first by an eleventh part than for the third in comparison to the 2nd, or the 4th in comparison to the 3rd, since the force <note>original: *violence*</note> that the string endures at the first return is no greater in regard to the force it endures at the second than the force of the 2nd in comparison to the 3rd; which can also be said of the resistance of the air, although there is some difficulty in the different tensions of the string, which perhaps resists more the tension it receives from the second return until the first, than the tension of the 2nd return resists that of the 3rd return: but I will speak elsewhere of these different resistances of strings.

Now, before finishing this Proposition, I wish to provide a table by means of which one can know the diameter of each return; for example, if Musicians wish to know the diameter of the 132nd return of a Lute or Viol string, they will find in the table that if the diameter or the path of the first return is 10,000,000,000 units, the diameter of the 132nd return will be only one unit: where it must be noted that *the diameter of the returns* is the line described by the point of the string furthest from its rest, as seen in this figure, in which the string A B attached at A and B, being pulled to point C, and returning to point D, makes the movement A C B D A, of which C D is the diameter, upon which all the returns are made and

the vibrations: in such a way, however, that point C of the <term>string|chorde</term> always remains on the line CD, as if on its Equator, or on its <term>Epicycle|a term from ancient astronomy describing a small circle that moves along a larger one, here used to describe the path of a point</term>, and that the movement of each point of the string is parallel to the diameter CD, as is easy to judge. It must also be noted that each point of the string moves more slowly in proportion to its distance from point C, and its proximity to point A or B; that is to say, if it is in the middle of C and D, its movement is twice as slow, because its diameter is twice as small; and if it is a hundred times smaller, its movement will be a hundred times slower. For the ratio of the movement of each point of the string to the movement of another point is the same as the ratio of their diameters, and consequently, if there is an infinity of points in the string, there is an infinity of movements, even though they compose a single movement of the entire string.

Having established this, I propose that if one imagines that the diameter CD—that is to say, the first <term>return|retour, meaning one back-and-forth swing of the vibration</term>—is divided into 10,000,000,000 parts, and I assume that the diameter of the second return is smaller by one-eleventh part than the diameter of the first pull <note>original: *traction*</note> ACB, then the diameter of the second return, which goes from D to F, is smaller by one-eleventh part than that of the first return. Consequently, if the first return or its diameter CD is 10,000,000,000 parts, the diameter of the second return will be 9,166,700,000 parts, the third 8,402,800,000, and so on until the 1,584th return. The size of these can be seen in the following table, in which the first number has 56 digits—namely, a one followed by 55 zeros—so that it contains ten septillions <note>original: *dixfeptilions*. In the 17th century, Mersenne used a specific system for naming massive numbers; 55 zeros would today be called ten septendecillion in the short scale</note>, following the very easy method of counting to infinity which is explained in the third book of *The Truth of the Sciences* <note>original: *la Verité des Sciences*, a 1625 work by Mersenne</note>, where one will find several things regarding Music that I shall not repeat here.

The numbers on the right hand, which go from top to bottom—namely 0, 1, 2, etc.—show which return one is looking for; that is, whether it is the 3rd, the 4th, the 100th, etc., of the entire period of the string's returns. The number that begins opposite it, from right to left, shows the magnitude of the diameter of that return. I have placed on the table that as 12 is to 11, so 100,000 is to 91,666 2/3, though one sees only 91,667 in the second line of numbers, in order to avoid that small fraction, which is of no consequence. Now, the unit of each row that one sees repeated in the last twelve lines shows that the numbers of returns opposite said units are only one part of those of the return contained by the number of the first line which ends opposite said unit. For example, the unit of the 7th line shows that the size of the 1,056th return, opposite which said unit sits, is only one part when the first return contains all the parts signified by the numbers of the first line, which descend as low as that unit and which have 40 zeros after the one. ## PROPOSITION XVIII

### *To determine the duration of the returns or vibrations of each string, and the ratio of the duration of one to that of another.*

This Proposition is much more difficult than the preceding one; especially since one cannot observe the final vibration or return <term>return: a single back-and-forth oscillation of a string</term> of the strings, whether they have only one of their ends fixed, or they are attached by both ends, for the final returns are so small that they cannot be perceived; this happens almost always at the end of all kinds of natural or artificial movements, when they end by diminishing little by little. This is why I will only note here what can be tested by experience, namely that strings three or four feet long on all sorts of instruments vibrate perceptibly for the space of a sixth part of a minute of an hour—that is to say, ten seconds—or while a steady pulse beats about 10 times; for the string that has been plucked appears wider and thicker than it is during this time <note>This refers to the "motion blur" or visual persistence of a vibrating string</note>, during which one also hears the sound it makes, so that one cannot doubt it is still vibrating quite strongly. I said "at least," for I have no doubt that it vibrates for the space of a third of a minute, which lasts twenty seconds <note>The original French text here says "deux secondes" (two seconds), but this is almost certainly a printer's error for "vingt secondes" (twenty seconds), as the author immediately equates it to 20 pulse beats and uses the figure to calculate a ratio of 90 later on the page.</note>, or 20 pulse beats. But be that as it may, it is easy to know the number of its returns, provided that one assumes the duration of the entire period of said returns; for if it vibrates a hundred times every second, as happens with many strings, it will vibrate two thousand times before finishing its returns.

As for the duration of the returns of a string that is suspended in the air and moves in its semicircle <note>The author is now describing a pendulum—a string fixed only at the top with a weight at the bottom</note>, it is much longer; for when one moves it away from its vertical line, it moves for more than half an hour before coming to rest, as one experiences with a string three and a half feet long from which a musket ball is hung. For if one moves it one foot away from its vertical line, its back-and-forth swings last at least half an hour, and consequently it makes at least 1,800 returns before coming to rest. From this, it follows that the number of returns it would make if fixed at both ends is perhaps equal to those it makes when free at one end, although the latter last at least ninety times as long as the former, the duration of which is only a third of a minute, as I am now assuming.

From this, one can conjecture that there is the same ratio between the speed of the returns of the string fixed at both ends and those of the other <note>i.e., the pendulum</note>, as there is between the duration of the returns of the latter and the duration of the returns of the former; this will occur if, being fixed at both ends, it makes 90 returns in the space of one second, and if, being fixed at only one end, its returns last 90 times as long as those of the other. The same must be said of each return of one compared to each return of the other, and consequently the table from the preceding Proposition can serve equally for both types of string. Now, it is not necessary to explain the durations of these returns, since anyone can observe them accurately enough—that is to say, until they are no longer perceptible. For our experiments cannot go further,

...and what remains of the duration of the returns <term>returns: oscillations or vibrations</term> is subject only to reason, from which one cannot expect the resolution of this difficulty, since it has no previous experience from which it can draw this truth.

But if one compares two or more strings fixed by both ends, one can say that the longer one vibrates longer than the shorter one, and that the length of time follows that of the strings; and because the longer ones make fewer returns than the shorter ones in the same amount of time, it appears that all strings that differ only in length make as many returns as one another <note>Mersenne suggests that while the frequency differs, the total number of vibrations before coming to rest might be the same for different lengths</note>. Consequently, the duration of the returns of the longer string compensates for the speed of those of the shorter, which gathers into a short time what the longer one does in a long time: so that one can compare the extent of the greater time to rarefaction, and the abbreviation of the lesser time to condensation. One can also make the same comparison between the duration of the return of two or more strings that are fixed only by one end <note>A "string fixed by one end" refers to a pendulum</note>, but it suffices to have remarked all that I have said here to give the learned the curiosity to go further.

### PROPOSITION XIX.

->*What are the uses derived from the preceding movements for Medicine, Mathematics, and several other things.*<-

It is easy to note the uses that can be derived from the movements and returns of the strings of which we have spoken in the preceding Propositions. For if Physicians wish to observe whether the pulse of their patients goes faster or slower on the second, 3rd, 4th, or 5th day, etc., than on the first, and by how much faster it goes, the string fixed by one end <note>the pendulum</note> will show it to them. For if the pulse beats more slowly on the first day or the first hour than on the 2nd or 3rd day, or the 2nd or 3rd hour, etc., it will be necessary to shorten the string to show its greater speed; and following the shortening that is made, one will know by how much the pulse goes faster. For example, if each return of a string of three feet is equal to each beat of the pulse, and the next day it is necessary to shorten the same string to 2 feet 7 inches <gloss>3/4</gloss> <note>The text here is likely describing the total length of the pendulum or a specific reduction; mathematically, for a pulse twice as fast, the length must be one-quarter of the original</note>, so that each of its returns is equal to each pulse of the patient, it is a certain thing that his pulse will go twice as fast, because the length of two strings, of which one is three feet and the other is <gloss>3/4</gloss> of a foot <note>9 inches</note>, is in the duplicate ratio of 2 to 1, or in the sub-duplicate ratio of 1 to 2 <note>This refers to the law of the pendulum: the period is proportional to the square root of the length. To halve the time (double the speed), the length must be reduced to one-quarter (9 inches is 1/4 of 36 inches/3 feet)</note>.

Astronomers can also use this string to justify the operations they perform during Eclipses of the Sun and Moon, for it will show exactly how many minutes or seconds have passed from one observation to the other. And Musicians will be able to make known throughout the world what time should be employed for each measure when singing all sorts of pieces of Music, just as they can signify at what pitch they must be sung by means of the returns of the string that is attached by both ends <note>using frequency to standardize pitch</note>: but I will treat this more fully in the eighteenth Proposition of the third book.

Finally, both types of string can serve for all the uses derived from ordinary clocks, whose certainty they surpass. Added to which...

**Of Instruments.**

one can make three or four clocks for two liards <note>original: "deux liards" — a French coin of very small value, suggesting these "clocks" are nearly free to make.</note>, which will mark the seconds <term>seconds: the text uses "secondes minutes," an archaic term for the second division of the hour</term>, as experience teaches, when one attaches a cord three and a half feet long to a nail; for if one attaches some weight to the other end, which hangs freely toward the center of the earth, each of its returns <term>returns: oscillations or swings of the pendulum</term> will last exactly one second, that is to say that it will make 60 returns in one minute of an hour, and consequently 3600 returns in one hour.

It must, however, be noted that the first returns last a little more time than the others that follow, although the difference is very small; for if the first return of a cord is two feet wide, and one takes another equal cord whose first return is only one inch, by the time the first has made 30 or 40 returns, the second will have made 31 or 41—that is to say, it will have surpassed it by one return. This is almost imperceptible on each individual return of one compared to each return of the other; but what is imperceptible in a small space is perceptible in a large one. From this it follows that atoms, which are not perceptible individually and in detail, become palpable and visible when they compose the bodies that we see; and that the returns of Lute strings, and of other instruments, which cannot be numbered because of their too-short duration, are easily numbered by means of a longer cord <note>a pendulum</note>, which gives the leisure to count its goings and comings. These are perhaps a little faster at the end than at the beginning, as we have said of the returns of the cord that is fixed by only one of its ends, in favor of which I add the following Proposition.

### PROPOSITION XX.

->*Determine the number of swings and returns of each string suspended by one end, and free at the other, to which a weight is attached; and how much longer it must be to make its returns slower according to the given ratio.*<-

The string which is attached only by one end has its goings and comings much slower and more delayed than that which is attached by both ends; for experience shows that a string or a thread, or any other cord one might wish, makes only one return in a second, or while the pulse <note>original: "le poux" — an archaic spelling of "le pouls"</note> beats once, when it is three and a half feet long. Here it must be noted that it does not matter at all what weight one attaches to this cord, for a weight of half a pound and a weight of 8 pounds bring almost no variation to its returns. For if weight B of half a pound, which hangs from cord AB attached to a nail at point A, is moved to point K, it does not return more quickly from K to B when it weighs eight pounds than when it weighs only half a pound. The reason for this can be taken from the fact that both weights only descend from K to B over the interval B, which is traversed as quickly by a small weight as by a large one, or if there is some difference, it is not perceptible. For experience shows that a stone, or a ball of lead or iron of eight pounds, does not descend more quickly from fifty feet high than a stone or a ball of one ounce. To which one cannot respond that this is because heavier bodies are more hindered by the air than lighter ones on the grounds that they have a larger surface area which touches and...

# Book One

...that cuts the air; for even though the surface areas of the heaviest and the lightest objects are equal, one nonetheless sees that they move as fast as one another. This is experienced with two balls of equal size, one made of iron and the other of boxwood <note>a dense, heavy wood often used for fine carving</note>, which is six or seven times lighter than the iron one; yet the speed of their movement is equal.

Furthermore, even if the heavier object had more surface area than the lighter one, it does not follow that the difference in these surfaces would make their movement equal, unless said difference was as great as that of their weights. Now, experience teaches that a cube of lead or stone, octuple [eight times the volume] of another cube of the same material, does not descend any faster, even though it weighs eight times as much and its surface area is only quadruple [four times] that of the smaller one; thus the ratio of their weights is double that of their surfaces. However, I shall speak more amply of these descents in another place, where I will demonstrate that heavier bodies descend faster, and provide the means to experiment with it.

As for the length that the string A B must have to make its returns <term>returns: oscillations or swings of the pendulum</term> faster or slower according to whatever ratio one wishes, it must be in a squared ratio <note>original: "raison doublée" — a 17th-century mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares (e.g., to double the time, you quadruple the length)</note> of the slowness desired. For example, if the string A B, which is one foot long, makes each return during half of a pulse-beat <term>pulse-beat: "battement de poux," the resting heart rate used as a makeshift timer</term>, it must be four feet long to make each return during one full beat of the same pulse; and if it makes each return in one second <term>second: "seconde minute"</term> when it is 4 feet long, it must be 16 feet long to make each return in 2 seconds, and so on following this pattern to infinity.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram showing the mechanics of a pendulum or vibrating string. A horizontal line at the top serves as a base with points labeled K, α, A, β, P, N, L, and S. From point A, a vertical line descends through point M to point B. Multiple overlapping circular arcs are drawn swinging from various points on the top line, with labels including C, D, E on the arcs and G, F, H, I, B, X, R along the bottom. A small hand icon points toward the vertical line at level M.</image-desc>

Now, one can consider the movement of these strings attached by one end, or by both, in a vacuum <note>original: "le vuide"</note> just as well as in the air; but because we do not know if a vacuum is possible, nor if it is something real—and consequently we can have no experience of it—it is difficult to know whether these strings, being pulled out of their straight line, would return to it, or at what speed they would move. Furthermore, I have treated all these particulars, and several others, in my second Latin book, *On the Causes of Sound* <note>original: "liure 2. latin des causes du son," referring to Mersenne's *Harmonicorum Libri*</note>, from Proposition 27 to 31; so that it only remains to treat instruments in particular, after having considered what suits them in general. This we shall do by beginning with the Lute, which many consider the most excellent of all instruments.

# BOOK TWO
## OF STRINGED
### INSTRUMENTS

#### PROPOSITION I.

->*Explaining the shape, the parts, the pitch or tuning, and the temperaments of the Lute and the Theorbo.*<-

The two figures that follow show so clearly everything belonging to the Lute and the Theorbo that it is almost unnecessary to explain them, except for the benefit of those who have never seen one. As for the different names that one might give to this instrument—such as the phorminx <note>original Greek: φόρμιγξ</note>, the chelys <note>original Greek: χέλυς, meaning "tortoise shell"</note>, the *tortoise* <note>original Latin: Testudo</note>, the *cithara* <note>original Latin: Cithara</note>, etc.—I leave that dispute to the Grammarians; one may consult Athenaeus, Pollux, Aristides, and the other Greeks. Since we possess the objects themselves and can explain the reality of the instruments, the names serve very little purpose, being used indifferently to mean whatever one wishes, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

The first figure on the right is nothing other than the Lute augmented with a new neck α, β, δ, which serves to give a greater range to the last four strings—that is, to the 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th. These have a sound that is lower <term>grave: low-pitched</term> as they are longer, and stronger as they are thicker. This Lute with two necks is called a *Theorbo* <note>a large lute with an extended neck for long bass strings</note>; it often has only a single string for each course <term>course: a pair of strings tuned together</term>, even though this one here has all its courses doubled, except for the chanterelle <note>the highest-pitched single melody string</note>. One could further increase the number of these necks, although these two are sufficient. However, it must be noted that the Italians begin counting their strings from the thickest, so that they end with the chanterelle, whereas we begin with it; otherwise, one would not understand their Tablatures <note>a form of musical notation showing finger positions rather than pitches</note>, of which Vincenzo Galilei <note>original: Vincent Galilee; father of the famous astronomer Galileo and an influential music theorist</note> wrote a book, and which I will speak of later.

The Lute formerly had only six courses of strings, but four or five others are now added lower down—that is, the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, and 11th courses—in order to play the basses, even though Tablature is only marked with six lines or parallel rules, as I shall describe later. Some have wished to put 15 or 20 courses of strings on the Lute, but the soundboard <term>table: the top wooden face of the instrument</term> is so burdened that it is often forced to burst and break; therefore, it is not advisable to use more than 10, 11, or 12 courses.

The nut <term>Sillet: the bridge at the top of the neck that holds the strings in place</term> of Lutes is ordinarily made of ivory, though it can be made of other very hard materials so that it resists the strings that rest upon it and press it continually. This can be seen at the nut of the second neck βγ, which limits the length of the last four courses of strings; for the rest of the neck...

<header># On Instruments</header>

[...the body is] typically composed of 9 or several ribs <term>ribs: 'éclisses', the curved wooden slats forming the vaulted back of the instrument</term> similar to the three seen at ξ, ο, ω. The thickness of these ribs is about one line <note>original: 'une ligne', a historical unit of measurement roughly 2.25mm</note>, or thereabouts, like that of the soundboard <note>original: 'table'</note>, which is glued to the edge of the said ribs. The round in the center of the soundboard is called the **Rose**, and provides the entrance and exit for the sounds. Regarding the third part of the Lute, it consists of its neck, which has nine frets <term>frets: 'touches', here referring to gut strings tied around the neck to mark pitch</term> made of gut strings. The letters on the neck of the Theorbo <note>a large, long-necked member of the lute family</note> show the place where the fingers are placed to press the strings, and those of the Lute show the frets themselves, or the strings that cross and determine the nine different lengths of the strings, such that the neck of fretted instruments can serve as a **Monochord** <note>a single-stringed device used since antiquity to measure musical intervals</note>. Fingers of the left hand are not usually placed directly on the frets, but a little above them, so that their sound is clearer: for example, one does not place the finger on the *b* or the *c* of the Lute, but across from the *b* and the *c* of the Theorbo, which has 21 strings, whereas the Lute has only 19. But I will later explain fully everything pertaining to the frets of the Lute, and the manner in which each finger must be moved to draw perfect harmony from it.

It should also be noted that a small pulley is used at the peg of the **chanterelle** <term>chanterelle: the highest-pitched string of a lute, which carries the melody</term>, so that it does not break so often; this is done because one is forced to stretch it much tighter than the others in proportion to its thickness, because it must produce very high sounds. And because it is difficult to make it rise as high as the Nineteenth <note>an interval of two octaves and a fifth above the bass</note>, as I will say when speaking of the tuning of the Lute, it is often lowered a Fifth lower than the 2nd string.

Regarding the tuning of the Lute, I have set it out in three ways: namely by letters, by numbers, and by notes, so that those who know the Theory of Music only through numbers may see the intervals of the sounds of each string by the numbers on the strings of the Theorbo; that those who know it only by the letters of the **Gamut** <term>gamut: 'gamme', the traditional system of naming notes using C-D-E-F-G-A-B</term> may understand the same tuning by the letters C, D, etc., which are across from each number on the same Theorbo; and that those who only understand the science of sounds through notes may understand the same tuning expressed by the notes beside the Lute, across from its neck. Now, the notes represent all the strings explained here by the terms of the Gamut and by the numbers, whose intervals are written between them.

By which we see that the first 6 strings of the Theorbo follow each other by conjunct degrees <note>stepwise movement</note> from the **C** of *C sol* to the **A** of *Amila*, which form the span of a **major Sixth**. But it must be noted that this tuning is called the **old tuning** <note>original: 'le vieil ton'</note>, which is still used now in concerts, and which serves as the foundation for all other tunings that have been practiced or invented since this ancient tuning used in Italy and elsewhere, and which is also marked by the aforementioned notes. Now, although it begins here with the **C** of *C sol*, so that it represents the tuning of our Theorbo, it is easy to leave this **C** to take the **D** <note>original: 'RE'</note> that follows, which represents the 10th or last string of the Lute, to which one can just as well add an eleventh course, as with the Theorbo.

### Second Book

I have included the three types of clefs used in music in this notation chart so that one may know how they must be sung. The bottom clef and the top one signify the same thing and differ only in their shape, for they both mark the same **B-flat** <note>original: 'b mol'</note> or the **F** <note>original: 'F ut fa'</note>. The second character, which goes upward, signifies the **natural clef**, and the third represents the **B-natural** <note>original: 'b quarre'</note> clef. Now, the range of this tuning is a **Twentieth**, and if one removes the first **C** <note>original: 'VT'</note>, it would be a **Nineteenth**; however, it cannot be marked by smaller numbers than those found on the **Theorbo**. Here it must be noted that I have not placed the **G** <note>original: 'G re sol'</note> on the 6th string, as many do, because I would not have been able to mark the **whole tone** made between the 7th and 8th strings using the letters of the **Harmonic Hand** <term>Harmonic Hand: also known as the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic system where different parts of the hand represent specific notes in the musical scale</term>. For if one puts the **G** on the 6th, the **F** is found on the 7th, and consequently the **E** <note>original: 'E mi la'</note> on the 8th, which makes only a major semitone with the said **F**. Thus, one would have to create a new letter to mark a "ficta" <note>an accidental or note outside the standard scale</note> lower by a semitone than the said **E** to create a whole tone from the 7th to the 8th string; however, this difficulty is not encountered with numbers and is of no importance.

I will explain the fourth way of marking the tuning of the **Lute** using its **Tablature** characters when I demonstrate how to translate ordinary music into Tablature for the Lute; for we must now see what its **Temperament** <term>Temperament: the system of tuning where intervals are slightly adjusted from their pure mathematical ratios to allow for playing in different keys</term> consists of, along with that of other necked instruments.

Now, we call **Temperament** the alteration made to intervals, both consonant and dissonant, for which I explained the true reasons and exact proportions in the books on Theory—and even in this proposition, when I explained the tuning of the **Theorbo** as if it were just and perfect. This Temperament is marked alongside the Theorbo and consists of 12 equal semitones into which the **Octave** is divided. This is found by dividing the open strings (or the Lute itself from the nut to the bridge) into 100,000 parts, of which the **b**—that is to say, the first fret—contains 94,444; the second 89,298, and so on for the others until the 9th or 10th fret, following the numbers of this Temperament. The 13th number, namely 50,363, represents the half-point of the string, even though this number is too large by 363, since 50,000 is exactly half of 100,000. This is why I have provided the other row of numbers, which gives the semitones much more accurately than the first, as one can see by comparing them. But the two other rows of numbers on the left side of the Lute show the distance of the frets in their greatest perfection: the first has only 13 numbers to mark the 12 semitones that make up the Octave of the Lute, and the second row shows that 19 frets are needed, following the 19 numbers that can serve all three **Genders** <term>Genders: refers to the three ancient Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</term>, as I have stated in the books on Theory, from which other ways to divide the neck of the Lute can be derived.

Many **Instrument Makers** <term>Instrument Makers: 'Facteurs d'instruments', specifically luthiers in this context</term> divide the length of the Lute, or the open string, into 18 parts, where the 17th part marks the first fret; then they divide the remainder of the string into 18 parts, of which they again take 17 to make the second semitone, and so on until they have 8 or 9 semitones. From this, one must conclude that these semitones are smaller than the major semitones (which are in a ratio of 16 to 15) and larger than the minor semitones (which are 25 to 24), and that they approach the former more than the latter. One could similarly divide the string into 17 parts to take 16, or into...

# Of Instruments.

...several other much more accurate and better ways, which I will speak of after having shown the best of what the Greeks had in their music, and particularly everything that Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century scholar whose work *Harmonics* was a foundation for Renaissance music theory</note> taught. This is so that all those who play the Lute may know if they use the temperament of Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus was an ancient Greek philosopher who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than by strict mathematical ratios</note>, or some other genre, species, or system, and so they remain ignorant of nothing that can bring them pleasure or profit, or anything that can bring them prestige in the excellent company in which they find themselves. But before entering into this discourse, it is necessary to explain the manner of constructing the Lute, and to provide the figure of the Pandora <note>A stringed instrument of the lute family with a scalloped body, often with metal strings</note>, whose tuning and number of strings is similar to that of the Lute.

### PROPOSITION II.

*To explain the manner in which the Lute and the Pandora must be constructed, and all other instruments similar to them; how they must be strung to perfection, and how one can know if the strings are of good quality.*

This treatise on the Lute would not (it seems) be perfect if I did not explain its construction, which will serve for understanding that of the Mandore <term>Mandore: a small, high-pitched member of the lute family, a precursor to the mandolin</term> and of all other instruments that imitate the Lute, which some write as *Leut*, and which foreigners call *Laud*, *Lauto*, etc. Now, one must first have a form, or a mold, of the same shape and size as the body of the instrument one wishes to make. One begins with the rib <term>Rib: one of the thin, curved strips of wood (staves) that form the rounded back of a lute</term> in the middle of the bottom, or back: for it must be bent into a curve and attached to the thick end of the said mold with a peg, after it has been glued at the smaller top end onto the piece of wood ordinarily called the block <note>original: "le tasseau"</note>, or the "heart" of the Lute, which forms the point of the mold.

In the second place, one must arrange the other ribs on the two sides of the previous one, the number of which can be 6, 12, etc., according to the will of the makers <note>original: "Facteurs"</note>; and in arranging them, one must glue them lightly against one another, applying them to the back of the form just like the first. In the third place, they must be reinforced <note>original: "consoler"</note> on the outside at the thick end; that is to say, they must be surrounded by another rib that is the length of the soundboard, in order to bind them and hold them firmly in the position they have taken on the mold. The mold is then removed from inside the body after having cut the pegs by which the ribs were attached to it. In the fourth place, one must again bind and embrace the same ends of the ribs from the inside with another rib placed opposite the outer one, which the makers call the lining <note>original: "la fausse, ou la contrebragne"</note>. One must also glue small strips of vellum or paper over the joints on the inside. Fifthly, a "false soundboard" is placed in the body of the Lute to keep it in shape, and to apply it onto a very straight board to set it so that it does not warp; and when it is perfectly set, it is applied to the plank from which the soundboard <note>original: "la table"</note> is to be made, which is cut exactly to the width and length of the body it is to cover. Sixthly, one bars the soundboard <term>Barring: the process of gluing wooden struts (braces) to the underside of the soundboard to provide structural strength and affect the tone</term> by dividing it into eight equal parts, in order to glue its six bars on the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th parts; for the neck begins at the eighth part where the soundboard ends.

As for the Rose <note>The decorative, carved soundhole of the lute</note>, it must be situated so that its center meets...

# Second Book

on the 5th part, upon which the 4th bar is glued. However, one also uses two or three other small bars placed to the side when the soundboard is weak: indeed, all the bars cross the soundboard and end at the ribs <note>The thin strips of wood that form the sides of the lute's body</note> on both sides. They are made of the same material as the soundboard, though they can be made of other wood, and are one or two lines <note>A "line" is a historical unit of measurement, roughly 2.25 millimeters</note> in thickness, and can be up to half an inch. When they are glued under the soundboard, it is applied to the edges of the ribs, onto which it is glued. But it should be noted that the instrument makers <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> add still other small bars lower than the first of the large ones, or in other places depending on the weakness of different soundboards, or following the experiments they have conducted to give a better harmony to the Lutes.

As for the bridge <term>Bridge: the wooden piece glued to the soundboard that holds the strings in place</term>, to which all the strings are attached, it is placed between the first and the second part of the soundboard; for after having divided these two parts into three other equal parts, the said bridge is glued on the second part encountered as one moves upward. Now, it must be noted that the quality of the Lute depends particularly on the bracing <note>original: *barrure*; the internal support system of the instrument</note>, which must be neither too strong nor too weak: for when it is too firm, the sound is not pleasing, and the chanterelles <term>Chanterelles: the highest-pitched strings of a lute</term> cannot vibrate as well on such a soundboard as they do on weaker ones, which tremble and vibrate more easily, even if the spaces between the bridge and the nut are equal. It is not easy to find the reason for this, since the makers maintain that this phenomenon cannot be attributed to the different arrangements of the bridges, the nuts, or the pegs. However, it is difficult to achieve perfection in the bracing without long experience and a great multitude of observations, due to the difference in soundboards—some of which require firmer bracing and others weaker, depending on their material, their thickness, and several other factors that makers may observe.

Once all this is done, the neck is added, which is glued to the block <note>The internal wooden support at the top of the body</note> after it has been cut obliquely, or at a bevel. This neck is nothing other than a piece of wood which must support the fingerboard <note>original: *touche*</note> that is glued upon it, and which is of the same length; finally, the head is glued to the end of the neck, which serves as the pegbox for the Lute, for it holds all the pegs used to string it and to put it in tune. But it must be noted that the neck or the fingerboard must be of the same length as the interval from the beginning of the soundboard to the middle of the rosette <note>The decorative carved soundhole of the lute</note>: that is to say, the neck must have five parts and the soundboard eight, so that it creates the proportion of the Minor Sixth <note>The mathematical ratio 5:8 corresponds to the musical interval of a minor sixth</note> with the said neck, ensuring that nothing is found in the Lute that is not harmonic. It is now necessary to explain the manner in which Lutes are strung—that is, how to attach, arrange, and tension the strings, and to accommodate and adjust the frets to make them ready to be played and sounded.

Regarding the strings with which one mounts the Lute, they must be proportioned to its size: that is, they must be thicker or thinner as the Lute is longer or shorter. Now, I will provide tables in the *Treatise on the Spinet* <note>Referring to another section of Mersenne's work on keyboard instruments</note> which show the exact proportion that the strings of each instrument must maintain; therefore, it suffices here to provide a few examples, though they are not necessary for those who understand the proportion of notes that mark the tuning of the Lute.

I come now to the choice of strings, which depends on the eye, the hand, and the ear; for one knows if the strings are good or bad according to whether they split the air evenly after they have been plucked with one of the fingers while both hands hold them taut. ### *On the different types of knots.*

It must be noted that Makers and
those who play the Lute must learn 
to tie the knots that are necessary 
to attach the frets onto the
neck, and the strings to the bridge, so 
that they hold firm without coming 
loose: and consequently, one must learn

double, which is often joined with 
the simple or double slipknot, either horizontally or 
perpendicularly. There are several other knots which can also serve 
different occasions: for example, the weaver’s knot, which is one of the strongest;
the Gordian knot, which is considered the most beautiful of all; the brush knot 
<note>original: *nœud de pinseau*; likely referring to the knot used to secure bundles of horsehair</note>,

Sailor’s knot, with which he ties his cables; the knot composed of two square knots pulled 
against one another; the brush and crossbow knots, and several others which 
are all different, and which serve many uses that one can apply 
to new instruments.

<header>Second Book</header>

of the Monochord <note>The monochord was an ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between musical intervals.</note>, of which instrument necks are a shortened version. But since not all Makers <term>Makers: original: *Facteurs*; refers to luthiers or instrument builders</term> wish to take the trouble to instruct themselves on the said Monochord, I wish to assist them by teaching them a very easy method to accurately divide all sorts of necks, whether for Lutes or other instruments, so that they may place all the frets <term>frets: original: *touches*; the gut or metal markers on the neck that determine the pitch of the notes</term> in their proper places.

For this purpose, one must imagine that the two full lines AC and BD represent the open strings, and consequently the space between the bridge and the nut of the Lute: let CD be the bridge, and AB the nut <note>original: *fillet*; the slotted strip at the top of the neck that holds the strings in place</note>. I say first that we will find the fret <note>Mersenne is listing the frets in the order of their mathematical discovery, not their physical order on the neck.</note> for the octave, which is *n*, if we divide the parallelogram AD into two equal parts at point *n*, which will be the Octave above the open strings.

Secondly, we will have the 7th fret *h*, which makes the Fifth against the open string, and the Fourth against the fret *n*, if we divide the parallelogram AD into three equal parts, of which one part taken descending from the nut toward the bridge gives *h*.

In the third place, we divide the line AC or BD into four equal parts, of which one part being removed while descending from the nut gives the fret *f*, which makes the Fourth against the open string; but because the string had already been divided at point *n* into two parts, one must only divide *n*A into two other parts in order to place the said *f* in the middle.

In the 4th place, if we divide the line AC into five parts, of which one part being removed while descending from the nut gives the fret *e*, which makes the Major Third against the open string; and if one removes three parts, we will have the 9th fret *k*, which makes the Major Sixth against the open string, and which is the last [fret] on Lutes.

In the fifth place, we will have the 3rd fret *d*, if we divide the line AD into six equal parts, for the sixth part being removed starting from the nut while descending, we have *d*, which makes the Minor Third against BD; and if we divide AD into eight parts, the three parts being removed from the nut downwards give the 8th fret *i*, which makes the Minor Sixth against AC, so that we have found the seven frets which make the seven consonances of the Octave, namely N, H, F, E, K, D, I.

We must now find the five other frets which make the dissonant intervals, the principal of which is the tone, or the major second, which we will have by dividing AD into 9 or 10 parts; for the 10th part removed will give the 2nd fret *c*, which will be the minor tone against AD, and the 9th part removed will give the *c* that makes the major tone <note>The "minor tone" and "major tone" are two slightly different sizes of a whole step used in older tuning systems like Just Intonation.</note>. And because we have already divided AD into five parts, we need only divide the last part in two to have the entire string divided into 10.

As for the 1st fret *b*, although we can find it by dividing AD into sixteen parts—or rather the last eighth part of the division that has already been made, in two parts, so that the 16th part being removed gives *b*, which makes the major semitone against AD—nonetheless, one can find it in several other ways by means of the frets that make the Consonances. However, it is quite useful and easy to find it as I have described, especially since one finds the 6th fret by its means; for if D*b* is divided into four, and the 4th part is removed, it gives the sixth fret *g*; and if one divides the same D*b* into three parts, the last...

So that there are only the tenth and eleventh frets left to mark, that is to say *l* and *m*, of which the first is found by dividing *dD* into three parts, for the 3rd part removed gives *l*, which makes the Fifth against *D*; and if one divides *eD* into three equal parts, the 3rd being taken away gives the eleventh fret *m*, against which it also makes the Fifth. I leave aside several other ways which can be used to place the frets in their proper places, because it is not possible to understand what I have said of the Monochord <note>A scientific tool with one string used to measure musical intervals.</note> in the fifth Proposition, and elsewhere, unless one knows at the same time all the ways that can be used to set and arrange the frets of the Lute, and of all other instruments, whether one wishes to include the Chromatic <note>A scale using half-steps.</note>, as is usually done, or the Enharmonic <note>A scale using intervals smaller than a half-step, like quarter-tones.</note>.

I will only remark for the sake of those who make Lutes and who play them, that the fret *c* makes the minor tone against the open string, and that if they wish to make the major tone, the fret must be raised as far as the dotted line which is on line *c*, for *Bc* is the 9th part of the string *BD*: but from *A* to the said dotted line, there is only the 10th part of the string *AC*, so that the major and minor tone do not differ more than a ninth and a tenth part. Now these two parts differ by a ninetieth part, that is to say that if the string *AC* is divided into nine and into ten parts, each ninth is larger than each tenth by one ninetieth part of the line *BD* divided into 90 parts; for the ninth part of *BD* contains 10/90 of the said line, and the tenth part of the same line contains only 9/90. So it can be said that the major tone exceeds the minor tone by only a ninetieth part, which one sees from fret *c* to the dotted line: and consequently that the ear recognizes a ninetieth part of the line *AC*, or *BD*, or of the string of each instrument, when it can discern the major tone from the minor. But the tone of the instruments being neither major nor minor, it is between fret *c* and the dotted line, for temperament <note>The system of tuning that slightly adjusts intervals to allow playing in different keys.</note> makes the minor tone increase by half a comma <note>A very small musical interval, the difference between two slightly different tuning ratios.</note>, by which it diminishes the major, in order to make only one of the two, as I have already shown elsewhere.

It is easy to find how much each other interval is larger or smaller than the others, and which semitones are marked by these frets: for example, that the major [semitone] is from *A* to *b*, and the minor from *b* to the dotted line, and that the middle one is from *b* to *c*, since the major tone contains these two semitones. Finally, regarding the strings of the Lute, it must be noted that besides what I have said of them until now both in general and in particular, they make other sounds than those one usually hears, which are called natural [sounds], for the finger that touches them performs the function of a bridge; so that one hears a false sound <note>Mersenne is describing the vibration of the segment of the string between the nut and the finger, which produces an unintended, often dissonant, pitch.</note> which follows the length of the string taken from the bridge or the nut to the finger that touches it: for example, if one touches the string one foot from the bridge, and it is four feet long, the part from the bridge to the finger will make the Fifteenth <note>A double octave (ratio 4:1).</note>, and the part from the finger to the nut will make the Fourth <note>A ratio of 4:3.</note> against the whole string.

Now although these sounds are not usually noticed, because the

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*Explaining the Genres and the Species of Music that the Greeks proposed, and all that was best in their Practice and their Theory.*<-

---

Although these discourses apply just as well to the Viol and the Mandora <note>A small, lute-like instrument, often considered a precursor to the mandolin.</note> as to the Lute, I nevertheless place them here because the Lute has taken such an ascendant over other stringed instruments—whether because refined people have given it this advantage, or because it has acquired it through its own excellence and perfection—that almost no account is made of the others, unless the extraordinary excellence of those who play them raises them up and makes them recommendable. Be that as it may, the Lute deserves these discourses, and those who play it are skilled enough to understand them, provided they are studious enough to read them; and because Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), an ancient scholar whose work "Harmonics" is a primary source for Greek music theory.</note> is the most learned of all those who have taught us the music of the Greeks, it seems to me that I can do no better than to explain what he says in his first two books.

He admits, then, in the second chapter of the first book, that the action and the goal of the musician consists in keeping the laws of the <term>canon</term> <note>Literally "rule," referring here to the "Harmonic Rule" or the mathematical division of a string to find correct pitches.</note>, or the Harmonic Rule, which do not contradict the senses and which are accepted by most men. To which he adds that reason is more just and more exact than the senses, and that it belongs to the learned and to those who know Theory to show that all things in nature are made with a beautiful order, and that she does nothing by chance. This is particularly observed in the objects of the two senses that he calls "rational," namely, sight and hearing.

And because it seems that the disciples of Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that the human ear, rather than mathematical ratios, should be the judge of musical intervals.</note> have given too much weight to the ear, and that those of Pythagoras <note>The famous philosopher who believed music was governed strictly by mathematical ratios and numerical proportions.</note> have refused the experience of feeling in order to follow only the reason of numbers, he blames both sides; for true reasons must agree with the operation and perception of the senses. This is true, and it shows evidently that he [Ptolemy] had not devoted himself to Practice, or that he did not have an ear as good and as delicate as our Organists, our instrument makers <note>original: "Facteurs d'instrumens"</note>, and other practitioners, who easily recognize and feel the interval of the <term>comma</term> <note>An extremely small interval, the difference between two slightly different versions of the same note in different tuning systems.</note>, even though Ptolemy believed it was not perceptible to the ear.

In the fifth chapter, he says that the Pythagoreans rejected the—

# of Instruments. 57

eleventh among the <term>Consonances</term> <note>Consonances are intervals that sound stable and harmonious to the ear.</note>, because its ratio of 8 to 3 is superpartient <note>A superpartient ratio is one where the larger number contains the smaller number plus more than one part of it; in this case, 8 contains 3 twice, with 2 parts left over.</note>, for it is a double superpartient of 3; and because only multiple ratios <note>Ratios like 2:1, 3:1, where one number is a clean multiple of the other.</note> and the two greatest superparticular ratios <note>Ratios where the numerator is exactly one greater than the denominator, such as 3:2 or 4:3.</note>—namely the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>The ratio of 3:2, which produces a Perfect Fifth.</note> and the <term>sesquitierce</term> <note>The ratio of 4:3, which produces a Perfect Fourth.</note>, of which the double ratio is composed—are fit for <term>consonances</term>. This he refutes in the 6th Chapter, insofar as all simple intervals that are dissonant do not change their species nor their quality when one adds an <term>Octave</term> below or above them: because the two sounds of the <term>Octave</term> have the same power, and are so similar that they appear only as a single sound. From this he concludes that the <term>Twelfth</term> has the same ratio to the <term>Eleventh</term> as the <term>Fifth</term> has to the <term>Fourth</term>, and that the <term>Fifteenth</term> has the same relationship to the <term>Twelfth</term> as the <term>Octave</term> has to the <term>Fifth</term>, especially since 4, which is the largest term of the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>Representing the ratio 4:1.</note>, is the <term>sesquitierce</term> of 3, which is the largest term of the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>Representing the ratio 3:1.</note>; and that 3, which is the largest term of the <term>Fifth</term>, is the <term>sesquialter</term> of 2, which is the largest term of the <term>Octave</term>. From this he further concludes that the <term>Fifteenth</term> is just as much sweeter and more harmonious than the <term>Twelfth</term> as the <term>Octave</term> is sweeter than the <term>Fifth</term>. Upon which I do not dwell, because it is easy to know what is true or false in these positions if one understands what I have said when speaking of the quality, the sweetness, and the preeminence of <term>Consonances</term>.

In the 7th Chapter, he divides harmonic intervals into three species: namely, those whose extreme terms are heard in the same way as if there were only one (that is to say, the <term>Octave</term>, <term>Fifteenth</term>, Twenty-second, etc.); those that form an agreement (that is to say, the <term>Fifth</term> and <term>Fourth</term>, whether simple, or repeated and composed with the <term>Octave</term>); and those that are fit for singing (that is to say, those whose superparticular ratios are smaller than the <term>sesquitierce</term>, such as the <term>Major Tone</term> and the minor tone, etc.).

In the 8th Chapter, he maintains that there is no better way to examine harmonic intervals than with the <term>Monochord</term> <note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge used to measure musical ratios.</note>. As for the four chapters that follow, he employs them to explain the manner in which the disciples of <term>Aristoxenus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that music should be judged by the ear rather than by mathematical ratios.</note> use to establish the ratios of <term>consonances</term> and other intervals. He blames them in the 9th chapter for measuring <term>consonances</term> by their intervals <note>In this context, meaning the physical distance or "space" between notes.</note> instead of explaining them by their sounds. For example, they say that the tone is composed of two parts, or two equal intervals similar to the five intervals from which they compose the <term>Fourth</term>, which they say are similar to the 12 intervals or parts of the <term>Octave</term>. But he wants the tone and other intervals to be expressed differently, and that one should say it is the ratio of two sounds, which is called the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio 9:8.</note>, and likewise for the others; so that it is not enough to say that the tone is the excess or the distance from the <term>Fifth</term> to the <term>Fourth</term>, otherwise one could not make it heard, nor place it upon the <term>Monochord</term>, unless one simultaneously placed the two intervals of which it is the difference.

In the 10th Chapter, he touches upon several difficulties that are explained in the Proposition that follows, so that this one may not be too long; otherwise, one can join them together and make only one of the two.

<summary>This page discusses the mathematical classification of musical intervals, defending the eleventh as a consonance and critiquing the followers of Aristoxenus for defining music by physical distance rather than precise mathematical ratios.</summary>

Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), a Greco-Roman mathematician and music theorist.</note> assumes the ratios of the consonances that the Pythagoreans provided to refute the positions of Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek philosopher who argued that the ear, rather than math, should judge musical intervals; he believed a tone could be divided into two equal halves.</note>, and consequently, he composes the <term>Diton</term> <note>original: "Diton"; an interval consisting of two major tones, slightly wider than a modern major third.</note>, or the Major Third, from two major tones, and the Minor [Third] from a major tone and the Pythagorean half-tone, which is called the <term>Limma</term> <note>original: "Limma"; from the Greek for "remainder," it is the small semitone left over when two major tones are subtracted from a perfect fourth.</note>, meaning the residue or the interval that remains to complete the Fourth. Since this is less than half of a major tone, it follows that the Fourth does not contain two and a half tones, nor the Fifth three and a half tones, as they [the Aristoxenians] claim. This he demonstrates by the smallest [numbers] that one can choose for this purpose, of which the first is 1536, of which 1728 is the <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>The ratio 9:8, representing a standard major tone.</note>, just as 1944 is the <term>sesquioctave</term> of 1728; from which it is easy to conclude that he makes the Pythagorean Major Third with 1536, of which 2048 is the <term>sesquitierce</term> <note>The ratio 4:3, representing a Perfect Fourth.</note>, and that the <term>limma</term> is the ratio from 2048 to 1944. Now, the ratio of these last two numbers is greater than that of the two preceding ones, for the excess of 2187 over 2048 is greater than their fifteenth part and less than their fourteenth; but the excess by which 2048 surpasses 1944 is only greater than their nineteenth part and less than their eighteenth, as one clearly sees in the following table.

Salinas <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a blind Spanish music theorist who wrote extensively on the mathematics of tuning.</note> demonstrates in another manner in the 24th Chapter of his 4th Book that the Fourth is larger than two and a half tones when, of two tones, one is major and the other minor, and consequently that the Fourth surpasses the true Major Third by more than half of a major tone. For if the sound A, or the number 1920, and the sound B, or the number 1440, make a Fourth; and if sound D, or the number 1800, makes the Major Third downwards with 1440, and C or 1536 makes the same Third upwards with 1920, and E or 2048 makes a Fourth downwards with C, as one sees in the following table—in which there are four equal major semitones, namely EB, BC, DA, and AF—it will follow that since there is a Fourth from B to A, and since EB and AF are the two excesses by which it surpasses the Major Third, these two excesses are larger than the major tone. That is to say, two <term>sesquiquindecimal</term> <note>The ratio 16:15, a major semitone.</note> ratios surpass the <term>sesquioctave</term> [9:8] by the same interval as the <term>Diesis</term> <note>A tiny musical interval resulting from the difference between certain semitones.</note> surpasses the <term>Comma</term>, which is to say the minor <term>Comma</term>, as one sees in the following numbers: for the major tone is less than two major semitones by the ratio of 2048 to 2025, which is the same ratio by which the Fifth from 2025 to 1350 is less than the interval from E to F.

To which Ptolemy adds that one cannot divide the <term>sesquioctave</term> ratio into two equal ratios, insofar as of the two ratios that most closely approach this half, the <term>sesquiseptdecimal</term> <note>The ratio 18:17.</note> is too small, and the <term>sesquisedecimal</term> <note>The ratio 17:16.</note> is too large; so that the half-tone is so hidden between these two ratios that it is impossible to express it by numbers, whether whole or fractional. And because the 15th part is less than the 16th, by 243, and that it is more...

This is why the **limma** <note>original: "limma"; the Pythagorean minor semitone.</note> of Pythagoras is smaller than this half-tone, in the ratio of 258 to 256, or 129 to 128, which he considers so small that it is not perceptible to the ear. He also criticizes them for setting the **Major Third** at a ratio of 81 to 64, because comparing these terms is too difficult to understand; in fact, the true ratio of the **Major Third**, which is 5 to 4, is much easier to grasp, and at the same time sweeter, as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

He shows in the 12th Chapter that the **Octave** does not contain 6 major tones; and that they are almost too large by a <term>sesquisextaquatrial</term> <note>original: "sesquisoixante-quatriéme"; the ratio 65:64.</note> ratio. There, he also remarks that the sounds made by two strings of equal tension but different thickness have the same ratio as the circumference or the circuit of said strings; consequently, one must tighten the thicker string much more strongly than the smaller one to bring them into **unison**, in proportion to how much thinner the latter is than the former. I have spoken of this so fully in the book on strings that there is no need to say anything more about it here.

Finally, he explains in the 12th Chapter the three genres of Music according to the division of Aristoxenus, after having noted that the smallest of the **Consonances**, that is to say the **Fourth**, is composed of three intervals suitable for singing. These two extremes are called **stable** <note>These are the "fixed" notes of a tetrachord that do not change regardless of the tuning style.</note>, because they are always in a <term>sesquitertial</term> <note>original: "sesquitierce"; the ratio 4:3, which defines a perfect fourth.</note> ratio, whatever variety is found between the two other middle terms. Now, the diversity of the Genres comes from this variety of intervals which fill the **Fourth** and which create the difference between the species of each Genre; for if the first 2 intervals at the bottom are smaller than the 3rd, which completes the **Fourth**, one has the **Chromatic** genre and the **Enharmonic**; and one has the **Diatonic** when no interval of the **Fourth** is larger than the other two combined. But to perfectly understand the division of Aristoxenus, one must note that he divided each tone into 2, 3, 4, or 8 parts, and that he called the fourth part the **Enharmonic diesis**; the 3rd, the **Chromatic diesis**; and the fourth joined to the eighth (that is to say, 3/8 of a tone), the **Sesquialter Chromatic diesis**. This will be easily understood if one divides the tone into 24 equal parts, so that each half-tone has 12 parts, each **Enharmonic diesis** has 6, and each **Chromatic diesis** has 8; to which he adds another diesis of 9 parts, which he makes the <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2.</note> of the preceding one.

He composes 6 types of **Fourths** from the preceding intervals—namely 2 Diatonic, 3 Chromatic, and one Enharmonic—as can be seen in the following table, where each number signifies the parts of the tone contained in each interval. For example, the first number at the top of the **Enharmonic Fourth**, which is 48, signifies that the last interval of this **Fourth** contains two tones, each of which has 24 parts; and 6, which is the 2nd number, signifies that the 2nd interval of the same **Fourth** (that is, the **Enharmonic diesis**) is composed of 6 parts of the tone, and likewise for the others.

<meta>catchword: Chromatic</meta>

From which it is easy to conclude that he divides all the intervals of the **Fourth** into 60 parts, since the numbers of each of these 6 genres, when assembled, always make 60. Upon this, Salinas <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a Spanish music theorist and organist.</note> remarks that the **Hexameter** verse is divided into 2 unequal parts, of which one contains two and a half feet, as one sees in this half-line: *Arms and the man I sing* <note>original: "Arma virumque cano"; the famous opening of Virgil's Aeneid.</note>, and the other contains three and a half: *Who first from the shores of Troy* <note>original: "Troiæ qui primus ab oris"; the continuation of the line from the Aeneid.</note>, just as the **Fourth** contains two and a half tones, and the **Fifth** 3 and a half tones; and that the tone is divided into 2 or 4 equal parts, like the spondee into 2 long syllables, or into 4 short ones. But I have explained in the first Theorem of the 2nd book of *Universal Harmony* <note>original: "l’Harmonie Vniuerselle"; Mersenne’s own encyclopedic work on music theory published in 1636.</note>, all the relationships of Metrics with **Consonances**.

Now the **Lute**, the **Viol**, and other similar instruments maintain this division in their <term>temperament</term> <note>The adjustment of intervals from their pure mathematical ratios to make them playable in all keys.</note>, so that one can say that all the makers of these instruments are disciples of **Aristoxenus**, who by this means reduced all Music to equality of parts, to avoid the great diversity of intervals that are encountered in the ratios that I have deduced elsewhere when speaking of the perfection of the **Diatonic** genre. There are still several who believe that this division of Aristoxenus should be preferred to all others, which **Vincenzo Galilei** <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), father of the scientist Galileo and a prominent music theorist who favored Aristoxenian practical tuning over Pythagorean math.</note> endeavored to prove in favor of his Aristoxenian friends, because this System is the easiest of all, and because the judgment of sounds depends entirely on hearing—without which reason cannot even know if sounds exist, and to which reason always has recourse when it wishes to judge their differences and their properties.

Furthermore, the **Octave** being always composed of 5 tones and 2 semi-tones in each **Diatonic** species, if each tone were divided into 2 unequal semi-tones, many of these semi-tones would be useless in Music, whether they are considered alone or joined to other intervals. For example, 2 parts never make the <term>minor semi-tone</term> in singing, and yet it occurs between the sharp of D <note>original: "diese de D la re sol"; the note D-sharp or E-flat in the old system of naming notes.</note> and the flat of E <note>original: "B d’E mi la"; 'B' refers to the 'soft b' or flat symbol applied to E.</note>, and between the sharp of G <note>original: "diese de G re sol"</note> and the flat of A <note>original: "B d’A mi la re"</note>. Now he maintains that this semi-tone is never practiced, whether alone or with other intervals.

He says the same thing of the interval by which the **False Fifth** surpasses the **Tritone**; of that by which the **Major Seventh** surpasses the **False Octave**, which is called diminished; of that by which the **Major Semi-tone** surpasses the minor; of that by which the **Minor Ninth** surpasses the **Augmented Octave**; of those where the intervals between the sharp of D and of F surpass the tone; of that by which the **False Fourth** surpasses the **Major Third**; and of that by which the **Minor Sixth** surpasses the **Augmented Fifth**. From this happens a great number of **Thirds** and **Sixths**, augmented and diminished, and consequently a great disorder and a strange confusion in Music; and this disorder would increase further if one used different tones between the fixed strings, even though they exist potentially between the movable ones.

This is why he concludes that Aristoxenus chose the <term>Intense Diatonic</term> <note>original: "Diatonic incité"; a specific tuning where the whole tones are equal and the semi-tones are equal, facilitating practical performance.</note>, which has all its tones and semi-tones equal, after having considered that the other Systems cannot subsist, inasmuch as **Pythagoras** put the major semi-tone on top and the minor below, and **Didymus** did the opposite by putting the major below and the minor on top: that the Tritone of the former surpassed the False Fifth, and that the Tritone of the latter was smaller, etc. From which he took the opportunity to compose all the intervals of the Diatonic genre, and of the
