**Chromatic** scale of equal semitones. For example, the **Fifth** of 7 semitones, and the **Tritone**, and the **diminished Fifth** of 6, of which the former is found between 4 strings, and the latter between 5: now **Galileo** <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642). His father, Vincenzo Galilei, was a famous music theorist who championed Aristoxenus.</note> says that this interval is in the same ratio as the side of a square to its diameter <note>This refers to the square root of 2, a mathematical ratio essential for dividing the octave into equal parts.</note>.

The **minor Sixth** is composed of 8 semitones, the **major** of 9, the **minor Seventh** of 10, the **major** of 11, and the **Octave** of 12; from which it is easy to conclude that the division of **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek philosopher who argued that the ear, rather than mathematical ratios, should be the judge of musical intervals.</note> is the easiest, and that it contains no interval that cannot be put into practice. To this he adds that sound is a **continuous quantity**, and not discrete, and consequently that one must follow lines rather than numbers, since no interval can be divided into two equal parts by means of numbers—except for the **Fifteenth** and its repetitions—but only by means of lines. And then he says that the **unison** represents the center of the circle, and the **Octave** the circumference; there are only these two inalterable **consonances**, for they cannot be increased or decreased in the slightest without offending the ear, whereas the others, such as the **Fifth** and the **Fourth**, allow for different types of alterations that are easily tolerated. Now this Author is not to be blamed for having defended his friends; for after having done them this good service—which led him to say that the **Fifth** of the **Lute**, being between the just **Fifth** (whose ratio is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>The ratio of 3:2, which produces a mathematically perfect Fifth.</note>) and that of keyboard instruments (which is too diminished), is the most pleasing—he confesses in favor of the truth that the **Pythagorean Fifth** is more pleasing than the **Aristoxenian** one, and that nature does not have regard for our conveniences; so that it does not follow that the system of **Aristoxenus**, in which the fifth contains 7 twelfths of the **Octave**, is more perfect than that in which it is just.

Now if one understands what I have said about **Consonances** and **Dissonances**, one will not need another light to recognize that it is not true that the division of **Aristoxenus** is easier than that which follows the accuracy of the intervals I have explained in several places: and likewise to demonstrate that of all possible systems, that which follows the **Harmonic numbers** is the easiest to sing and the most natural, as one experiences when good voices sing several parts together. These voices cannot perform everything marked in compositions of simple or diminished <term>counterpoint</term> <note>The technique of polyphonic writing where multiple independent melodies are combined.</note> as they are ordinarily used, unless they observe the distinction of the **major** and **minor tone**, and that of the **major**, **mean**, and **minor semitone**, and many others that I have explained.

This in no way prevents the use of equal tones and semitones on the **Lute**; this is done for the sake of convenience and to avoid the confusion and the multitude of frets that would be necessary to find and create all the just intervals on the neck. For if it were as easy to mark the just **consonances** there as the imperfect ones, there is no doubt that practitioners would do so, since they approach them as much as they can by raising or lowering the frets, more or less according to the goodness and accuracy of their ears. Now it is necessary to explain by how much the **Consonances** and **Dissonances** are altered on the neck of the **Lute**, and consequently what its <term>temperament</term> is; this I shall do in the Proposition that follows, although it could have been joined to the preceding one, as the preceding one was to the second-to-last: but I distinguish them so that the Reader may catch his breath.

But because there are three major tones in the Diatonic, it is necessary that a comma remains after their division into major and minor semitones; this is why there are three commas in the Chromatic genus, of which the one between the two D notes belongs to the Diatonic. Now the letters and the radical numbers that follow will allow for a better understanding of what concerns the Chromatic than would a more tedious discourse.

From this it is evident that there are only seven Chromatic strings <note>In this context, "strings" refers to the specific notes or pitches themselves.</note>, which divide the 5 tones of the Diatonic into semitones, namely the 3rd, 4th, 6th, 8th, 9th, 12th, and 15th, for which one could find 7 new names to enrich the scale, or the Harmonic Hand <note>A mnemonic device used by medieval singers to find notes, attributed to the monk Guido of Arezzo.</note> of Guido of Arezzo <note>original: "Guy Aretin"</note>, and to teach children what Salinas <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a Spanish music theorist known for his work on just intonation.</note> seems to have proposed only for the learned.

Now, just as the Diatonic was invented for the division of Consonances into major and minor tones and major semitones, and the Chromatic to divide the said tones into major and minor semitones, likewise the Enharmonic has been added to divide the major semitones into a minor semitone and a diesis <note>The smallest interval in ancient Greek music, often a quarter-tone.</note>; so that it is necessary to divide all the minor tones into 2 minor semitones...

with its 8 intervals, the 16 sounds of the Chromatic [genus] will form the major semitone with its 15 intervals, and the 25 sounds of the Enharmonic [genus] will form the minor semitone with its 24 intervals: so that the proper interval of each Genus is found within that same Genus. One can say that the whole tone is proper to the Diatonic, since it takes its name from the tone and contains 5 tones; and among these tones, the major is more natural to it, since it has 3 of them and only 2 minor tones. Similarly, the major semitone is proper to the Chromatic, since it has 7 of them and only 5 minor ones; and finally, the minor semitone is proper to the Enharmonic, since it has 12, even though it has only 7 dieses <note>A diesis is a very small musical interval, often the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note>.

This being established, one must explain the temperament <note>Temperament refers to the system of adjusting the "pure" mathematical intervals of a scale so they fit into an octave, allowing instruments to play in different keys.</note> of the Lute, which consists of dividing the Octave into two equal parts, each of which makes the Tritone <note>A tritone is an interval of three whole tones.</note> composed of 3 equal tones. Each of these tones is larger than the tone used for the Organ and the Spinet <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument related to the harpsichord.</note> by a sixth part of a diesis—which one must imagine to be divided into 12 equal parts—in order to understand the alteration of each interval and each fret of the Lute. Now, since each tone is increased by one-sixth part, the major Third is increased by a third of a diesis, and each semitone is too large by the 1/12th part of the same diesis. But since this temperament depends on the division of the Octave into 12 equal parts, one must explain the method that can be used to divide the double ratio <note>The "double ratio" (2:1) is the mathematical definition of an octave.</note> into 12 equal ratios; from this, one will easily conclude by how much each consonance on the Lute is smaller or larger than it ought to be when it is in its perfection.

### PROPOSITION VII.

> *To demonstrate that the major and minor tone, the Octave, and all other intervals can be divided into two or several equal parts; from which it follows that one can divide the Octave into 12 equal semitones: where one will see the method for finding one and two mean proportionals <note>A geometric method used here to find the exact points for placing frets to achieve equal temperament.</note> between two given lines, for doubling the cube, and for placing the frets on the neck of the Lute and other instruments.*

Those who do not know Geometry, and who use only common Arithmetic, believe and conclude that the tone cannot be divided into two equal parts. From this comes the fact that they divide the major tone into two parts, one of which is called the *Apotome* and the other the *Limma* <note>These are Greek terms for the two slightly different semitones that make up a Pythagorean whole tone.</note> by musicians who follow the tradition of Pythagoras and Plato, as can be seen in Ptolemy and in the other Greek authors I have mentioned, and in Boethius, Faber, and Glarean <note>These are major historical figures in music theory, spanning from Ancient Greece to the Renaissance.</note>. Others divide it into two unequal semitones, one called *major* and the other *middle*, when the tone is *major*; and when the tone is *minor*, the second semitone is likewise *minor*. But it is just as easy to divide both types of tones, and all sorts of musical intervals, into two equal parts as into two unequal parts. For if one stretches a string that is the mean proportional between the two strings that form the tone, the Octave, or any other interval, the said tone or other proposed interval will be divided into 2 equal parts: so that the first semitone of the major tone will be exactly equal to the second semitone.

...only two <term>mean proportionals</term> <note>A mean proportional is a geometric method to find a middle value between two lengths that maintains a consistent ratio. It is essential for dividing musical intervals equally.</note> between one and the other extreme, and the mean, to divide the given interval into 6 equal parts by the discovery of 5 mean proportionals: which will similarly occur if one first finds two mean proportionals, and then another proportional between them, one will have eleven mean proportionals, which will divide the given interval into 12 equal parts. Consequently, one can use this invention on the neck of the **Lute**, and of other instruments, on which one wants the **Octave** to be divided into 12 equal semitones, as I will say later. And because one can describe a mean proportional between all the said lines, one can find 23, 47, 95, etc., mean proportionals; and consequently, one can divide each interval into 12, 24, 48, and 96 equal parts.

The third manner of dividing each interval into several equal parts still makes use of only the discovery of 2 mean proportionals, for one finds 8 of them if one finds 2 means between the first 2 means and the extremes. And if one does the same thing between all the preceding ones, one will have 18, then 38, 78, and so on to infinity. From this, it appears that one can divide each given interval into 3, 9, 19, etc., equal parts. And if one adds the discovery of a mean proportional between each pair of the said 2 mean proportionals, one will have 13, 27, 55, etc., mean proportionals. If one takes a mean proportional between the 8 means, one will have 17, 35, etc., and finally, if between the 17 one takes 2 means, one will have 53, and so on for the others.

As for the other divisions which suppose 6, 10, or 12 mean proportionals repeated one or several times and mixed together, **Geometers** have not yet found the way to do it, and consequently one cannot divide the tone, nor any other interval, into 7 or 13 equal parts, etc. From this, it is easy to conclude into how many equal parts one can divide each interval both geometrically and mechanically; this is why it is not at all necessary to give examples of the tone, or of other intervals, since that depends on **Geometry**, and this division is not in use in true **Harmony**. <note>The author refers to "true Harmony" as the system of "Just Intonation" based on pure mathematical ratios, which he contrasts with the "tempered" or equal divisions used for practical instrument making.</note>

Let the 2 strings A and C be in a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "sesquioctaue," the 9:8 ratio that defines a major whole tone.</note> ratio to make the major tone; I say that the line or string B will divide it into 2 equal parts, which are the 2 semitones of **Aristoxenus**, insofar as it is the mean proportional between A and C. And if one finds another mean between A and B, and then between B and C, one will have 3 mean proportionals which will divide the tone into 4 equal **dieses**.

From this, it is easy to conclude that it is the same thing to divide ratios by 2, 3, 4, etc., as it is to find the simple ratio through the repetition of which the said ratios are composed.

Some have demonstrated the manner of finding two mean proportionals by means of a single <term>parabola</term> <note>A symmetric open curve; here used in the context of conic sections to solve classical geometric problems.</note>, which they will perhaps share with the public one day, if it pleases them; this is why I do not speak of it here.

### COROLLARY I. ###

One can also find the 2 mean proportionals by means of numbers, when one knows the magnitude of the 2 given lines; for example, one will have the number of the means between the 2 preceding lines G A and B H, if one multiplies G A (which I suppose to be 100 feet, and B H to be 200) by itself, and if one then multiplies the product, namely 10,000, by B H, that is to say by 200, one will have 2,000,000 <note>The original text mistakenly says 100,000 then doubles it to 200,000; the calculation for a cube root usually involves the product $a^2b$.</note>, of which the <term>cube root</term> 125 <sup>9921</sup>/<sub>10000</sub>, or 126, gives the length of the smaller of the mean proportionals.

And one will have the larger [mean proportional] if one first multiplies B H by itself, and then the product by G A: or if one finds a number that is to 126 as 100 is to 125, or a line that is to D B as G A is to D B, which is easy to find by the 11th [proposition] of the 6th [book] of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements*, the foundational textbook of geometry.</note>.

This is because the 9 lines—of which the smallest is 5 parts and the largest 8, forming the minor sixth—are in continuous proportion. And because one does not need two mean proportionals between two given lines in this division, which is entirely geometric, it is much better and more convenient; although the 8 equal semi-tones of this sixth are different from the equal semi-tones of the <term>Octave</term> <note>original: "Diapason"</note>, which we have divided into 12 equal intervals by means of eleven proportionals. Those who desire other ways to divide the Octave, and the neck of the Lute and the Viols into 12 equal semi-tones, can see Zarlino in the 4th book of his *Supplement*, chapter 30, where he applies this division to the neck of the Lute; and Salinas, his contemporary, in his 3rd book, chapter 31. Thus, it has been nearly 60 years since the invention of the equal semi-tones of Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek philosopher who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than solely by mathematical ratios, making him a precursor to equal temperament.</note> was renewed by these two musicians. Now, I shall give still other means for dividing the Octave and the entire keyboard in the *Treatise on Organs* and elsewhere.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*To determine whether the Diatonic, or the Type of Music used now, is the Syntonon of Ptolemy, or the Diatonic of Pythagoras, Archytas, or Aristoxenus, or some new type: wherein are seen all the different species of the Diatonic, and those of the Chromatic and the Enharmonic, which the Greeks proposed.*<-

The Italians have practiced much on this question, and particularly Zarlino and Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591), an Italian lutenist and father of the astronomer Galileo, who wrote extensively on music theory and tuning.</note>: but if one considers the poverty of that Type [of music], following the description made of it by Ptolemy, it is evident that our music—which has all its thirds and sixths consonant, and which uses the mean semi-tone, the minor [semi-tone], and several others—is not the <term>Syntonon</term> <note>Also known as the "intense diatonic," a tuning system proposed by Ptolemy that uses ratios closer to modern "just intonation."</note> of Ptolemy, nor any other of all those the Greeks proposed. This I show by the enumeration of all their distributions, which there is no need to speak of if one wishes to be content with the systems I have already proposed, each of which is more perfect than all those of the Greeks. But because many believe that the distributions of Ptolemy and others he reports are not understood perfectly enough, and they imagine there are great secrets in the depths of their doctrine—the deprivation of which robs us of the hope of reaching the marvelous effects of their Harmony—it is necessary to go deeper into this matter. This is so that the excessive respect some bear for the ashes of the Greeks does not throw us into a perpetual distrust of our own strengths, and into despair of arriving at so great a perfection of Harmony as that which they practiced, according to what can be conjectured from the books they have left us.

Now, the three most famous species of the Diatonic were those of Pythagoras, Didymus, and Aristoxenus, as Galilei remarked in his response...

# Of Instruments

...in the Supplement of <term>Zarlino</term> <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590) was an influential Italian music theorist who championed the use of "just intonation."</note>; the system that was practiced in the time of Pythagoras, and which lasted until <term>Glarean</term> <note>Heinrich Glarean (1488–1563) was a Swiss theorist who expanded the system of musical modes from eight to twelve.</note>, following the opinion of all those who wrote up to his time, is called <term>Diatonée</term> <note>The Pythagorean Diatonic scale, characterized by its use of strictly mathematical whole tones.</note>, because all the tones are major, even though this term could apply to the Diatonic that <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century mathematician who wrote an influential treatise on harmonics.</note> calls *Synton* <note>original: "Synton", referring to the "Syntonic Diatonic," which uses both major and minor whole tones.</note> in the first chapter of his second book on Music, and which is attributed to <term>Didymus</term> <note>An ancient Greek theorist known for the "Comma of Didymus," the difference between a major and minor whole tone.</note>, since it has as many tones as the other, although it has two species—namely the major, like that of Pythagoras, and the minor, of which the ancients did not speak, as seen in Plato, Aristotle, and the others, who only remembered the major tone, which they called <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>original: "sesquioctaue", meaning the ratio of 9 to 8 (1 1/8).</note>, because of the ratio of 9 to 8 that exists between its two extremes.

**Universal Harmony**, that to add more would be like lighting the Sun; and the systems I have explained in the Theory encompass the three <term>genres of Music</term> <note>The Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales used in ancient Greek theory.</note> so perfectly that nothing more could be desired, for composers can use whatever Chromatic or Enharmonic degrees they wish within these systems. But one must not imagine that it is necessary to proceed solely by the degrees of these Genres when one takes the liberty of using some of their intervals; for the melodies would lack grace and would be too constrained. This is why the musician must reserve full liberty to employ sometimes the Enharmonic <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small interval, roughly a quarter-tone, used in the Enharmonic genre.</note>, sometimes the Chromatic semitone, and then the Diatonic degrees within the same melody, following the design they have and the effect they wish to produce. And there is no doubt that the Greeks, who put this into practice, did the same thing, provided they were judicious and skilled.

As for the Diatonic of **Aristoxenus** <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist (4th century BC) who emphasized the ear's perception over mathematical ratios.</note>, I have already spoken of it when discussing temperament. I will only say here that the <term>Octave</term> of Aristoxenus does not have all its tones equal, if it follows the numbers proposed by **Ptolemy** in the second book of his *Harmonics*, chapter 14, as can be seen in this Table.

Now, one may observe from all these Tables that they did not assign the same degrees <note>The specific mathematical intervals or "steps" between notes.</note> to the lower <term>Tetrachord</term> <note>A grouping of four notes; the building block of ancient Greek musical systems.</note> as they did to the upper one, even though everywhere else they use only a single type of Tetrachord or Fourth for each Genus, or each species of Genus. From this, it seems to me one can conjecture that all these tables are full of errors. But be that as it may, they can serve neither true Theory nor Practice; otherwise, I would have taken the trouble to reduce all these species into a single System composed of whole numbers, as I did for the System of <term>Fabius Columna</term> <note>Fabio Colonna (1567–1640), an Italian polymath who designed the "Sambuca Lincea," a harpsichord capable of playing ancient Greek intervals.</note>. Nevertheless, this discussion is not useless; for it serves at least as a faithful history, which shows the industry of the Ancients, and makes it clear that we have no reason to believe the [legendary] effects of their harmony—which were not particularly distinguished—if they had no other brilliance than that derived from their science and their writings. We must place more faith in these [mathematical records] than in some light and perhaps thoughtless report made by Historians, and those who have not forgotten to praise their own Nation. Since that nation was accused of lying by Saint Paul <note>A reference to Titus 1:12, where Paul quotes a Cretan philosopher saying, "Cretans are always liars." The author is using this to cast doubt on the accuracy of ancient Greek historical claims regarding the power of their music.</note>, I have nothing more to say on this subject.

Now, I have placed the 8 standard letters of musical Practice <note>The letter names A through G used in Western music.</note> opposite each number of the Diatonic species, starting with <term>E mi la</term> <note>The note E. In the old system of "solmization," notes had multiple names based on their position in different overlapping scales.</note>, because they start all their Fourths with the semitone at the bottom. This is so that if one wishes to sing all these species, or experiment with them on instruments, one begins each Octave with E; however, one will find only the Fourth and the Fifth to be in tune—which, in all the species of this Genus as well as the <term>Chromatic</term> and the <term>Enharmonic</term>, range from 120 to 90 and 80. For Ptolemy used this number 120 for all the species of every Genus, as seen in the preceding tables. This may have been caused by his use of secondary numbers for some reason he did not express, or perhaps he did not wish to render the intervals of each species in their exactness, so as not to be forced to find numbers too large, which he would have had to use to explain the true proportions without fractions.

<header>Second Book</header>

### PROPOSITION IX.

*Explaining the manner of playing the Lute in perfection, and how to position or move each hand and each finger as is required to play it well.*

The art, science, and skill of the hand is so great that many have called it one of the principal instruments of wisdom and reason. It is through the hand that reason sends its thoughts and decisions throughout the world by means of writing, and through which it explains its concepts as clearly as the tongue does. We see this experienced by the deaf and the mute, who "write" in the air with only the movement of their hands and fingers; with these movements, they can deliver great discourses and entire orations as quickly as, or even faster than, one can with the tongue <note>The author is referring to early forms of sign language or manual communication used by the deaf in the 17th century.</note>.

But without lingering on all the masterpieces the hand creates, it suffices here to consider its movements on the Lute and on all other instruments. These movements are so marvelous that reason is often forced to admit it is not capable of understanding their lightness and speed, which surpasses the readiness of the most vivid imagination one can encounter. This is experienced when one tries to count the sounds the hand makes, the strings it touches, or its <term>tremblemens</term> <note>original: "tremblemens." In this period, this term referred to musical ornaments such as trills, shakes, or vibrato.</note> within the time of a single measure. But since the practice of this cannot be better understood or explained than by those who teach how to play the Lute, I wish to provide the treatise that <term>Monsieur Basset</term> <note>Jean Basset (c. 1600–1636), a celebrated French lutenist and composer in Paris.</note> wrote at my request. I would describe his praises and virtues here, if his modesty did not prevent me, and if they were not already well known in Paris, where he teaches according to the method contained in this Proposition and in the two that follow.

->*The Art of Playing the Lute.*<-

In which one will see the manner of correctly placing both hands, and of making <term>tablature</term> <note>A system of musical notation using letters or numbers to indicate finger positions on the frets rather than pitches on a staff.</note> so intelligible that it will be understood without difficulty; the variety of ornaments and their use will also be explained with useful and curious examples.

### Article I. *Of the conditions required for one who wishes to learn to play the Lute.*

Most of those who have written on the arts and sciences require three conditions to acquire perfection: namely *Nature*, *Discipline*, and *Exercise*, without which one cannot arrive at the goal one has set. Now, one must understand by the word *Nature* the inclination and natural disposition we have toward certain sciences and particular Arts, just as it happens that some are inclined toward Painting or Sculpture, and others toward Architecture, Geometry, etc. *Discipline* signifies the Method and the instruction of good Masters, and *Exercise* is nothing other than the Practice of their precepts. Now, these last two parts can compensate for a lack of the first; for just as the most sterile land is made fertile by the care and diligence of the laborer, so those who might believe themselves incapable of learning this art should rest assured that they can overcome the defects of nature and inclination by putting into practice the teachings we are about to give. And if it were necessary to provide examples of this,

I could provide a great number of these examples, but this truth is recognized without contradiction by the experiences we see every day; this is why I come to the things that are most useful, and say first that it is necessary that he who wishes to devote himself to this noble exercise to receive perfect contentment, know a little Music, so that he understands the value of the measures contained in his <term>tablature</term> <note>Unlike modern staff notation, tablature for the lute uses letters or numbers to indicate which frets the fingers should press.</note>, even though there are men who have an ear so delicate that they can (being taught) tune and play the Lute with as much precision as the best Musicians in the world: but those who are provided with these rare natural qualities must not despise this art, without which nature is imperfect and blind.

I add nonetheless that the delicacy of the ear alone is not enough, because it is also necessary that the equality of the two hands be conformed to precision; so that they both set off at the same time, otherwise one notices great imperfections in the touch; this happens from the bad precepts of the one who plays the Lute. But those who have both hands equal, and so nimble that they are capable of executing everything that one can imagine, ravish the listeners, and remind me of the opinion of <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who famously argued that humans are the most intelligent of animals because they possess hands, which allow them to interact with and shape the world.</note> Anaxagoras, who situated human wisdom in the hands—even though men are not wise simply because they have hands, since they have them rather because they ought to be wise, in order to execute what art and reason dictate to them.

## *II. On the positioning of the right hand, and how one must use it.*

After having spoken of the excellence and the equality of the hands, one must show the place where they should be placed on the Lute, for this positioning serves as our first foundation, for the reason that one cannot play it without great constraints and without bad posture if the hands are not well placed. I begin then with the right hand, in order to imitate the most skillful of this time, and say in the first place, that the Lute, resting against a table or another object, must be supported by the weight of the right arm: although one can hold it without this support by means of two small buttons of ebony or ivory. In the second place, the top of the hand must be seen as much from the side of the little finger as from the side of the thumb, which must be extended toward the <term>rose</term> <note>The "rose" is the intricately carved decorative soundhole in the center of the lute's soundboard.</note>. 
3. The first finger that follows, which is called the Index, must be very far from the thumb; and the 2nd and the 3rd, which are named <term>Medius</term> and <term>Medicus</term> <note>Latin terms for the middle finger and the ring finger. "Medicus" (the doctor's finger) was so named due to an ancient belief that a vein ran directly from this finger to the heart.</note>, must be very close to the first, and incline as close as possible to the little finger. 
In the 4th place, the little finger must be rested upon the soundboard of the Lute near the <term>bridge</term> and the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The "chanterelle" is the highest-pitched string on the lute, used for playing the melody.</note>, for those who put it behind the said bridge contract a bad habit, which afterwards turns into second nature: so much so that it is difficult for children, who are accustomed to this bad practice, to change it when they are older. This is why it is necessary to have small Lutes built for them, so that the spacing of the strings is conformed to the size of their hand, and so they may position it correctly all at once, just like adults.

Now, I have remarked that one should see as much of the top of the hand from the side of the little finger as from the side of the thumb when it is situated as we have just described, because the fingers must be as close to the strings as one another.

This is why I come to the use of the fingers, and first to that of the
thumb, the joint of which near its tip must not be bent, because
it must be fully extended as if it were without a joint. The reason for this is
that one could not easily strike the tenth string at the same time
as the fourth, because of the great distance that would be found
between the thumb and the tenth string if it were bent while striking the
fourth. The first finger <note>The index finger.</note> next to the thumb—which must nevertheless be
placed far from it when in use—must strike the strings with the corner of the
tip that is toward the thumb, rather than from its center; this must be
carefully observed so that its action is free to perform upstrokes or
downstrokes <note>original: "releuer, ou pour rabattre"</note> on the strings. Now, when one strikes only a single string with the first
finger, it must be lifted from underneath while keeping the tip of the finger very firm;
but when one strikes three or four strings, as often happens, one must
keep the said tip looser, so that the finger can glide more easily
over the strings that one wishes to lift or strike down.

As for the second and third fingers, the strings must also be lifted
from underneath; and when they are not being used, they must be kept resting
loosely near the little finger. The hand being thus disposed, one must take
care that while the fingers are acting, the back of the hand does not jerk
outward, so that it cannot be perceived that the hand is labored by the
movement of the fingers.

### III. *On the position of the left hand.*

There is no one who does not desire and seek to have good grace in everything
they do, as is experienced in all honorable actions that
one is obliged to display before the eyes of others. From this comes the fact that
one does not hold in high esteem an equerry <note>A specialist in horse training and riding.</note> who can make a horse go well to the right and
left, at a walk and a gallop, if he is not skillful and if he does it with constraint; for
liberty of action is what gives good grace to the deed. Now, so that one
may entirely enjoy this liberty, which consists in the placement of the left hand
and in practice, one must place the thumb above the first <term>fret</term> <note>original: "touche"</note> near the edge of the neck on the side of the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The highest-pitched string of the lute.</note>, in such a way that its
tip is placed upon the said fret and turned toward the head of the Lute. And the
wrist must be moderately raised, so that the tips of the fingers are very
close to the strings.

As for the first finger, it should be placed a little sideways toward the head of the
Lute; but when it is placed at the same fret as the second—for example,
if one must play two 'e's <note>In lute tablature, letters designate frets; 'e' usually refers to the fourth fret.</note>, one with the first and the other with the second finger—one must
then straighten the first finger. One should also always keep the first
finger away from the second when they are not on the same fret; but if one must
perform an open <term>vibrato</term> <note>original: "tremblement à l'ouuert"; likely a trill involving an open string.</note>, all the fingers must be joined together
against one another, in order to increase its strength.

The second finger, being placed on the fret of the Lute, must be situated almost
straight; that is to say, it must lean almost as much toward the bridge as
toward the head of the Lute. The third and fourth fingers must be curved
in a circle, and have their tips near the strings when they are not in use,
so that they are more ready to be placed. And if the hand moves down by one or
two frets, the thumb must follow it equally: for example, if one has played the...

### IV. On Shakes.

**A**LTHOUGH past centuries have produced men of great excellence
in all manner of arts and sciences, and particularly in the one of which
we treat, one may nevertheless say that they become more perfected the
further they progress: as is easy to prove by the use of
shakes <note>original: "tremblemens"; these are trills or similar ornaments</note>, which had never been as frequent as they are now. From this
it follows that the playing of our predecessors lacked the delicacies <note>original: "mignardiſes"</note> and the refinements
that embellish our own with such diversity. But since shakes
differ as much in their effects as in their names, I shall attempt to
make them known, and to distinguish them by characters that I have expressly
invented for this purpose, for everyone names and depicts them as they please.

<margin>First shake.</margin>

### V. On the Ornament Called the Plaintive Accent.

<margin>
2. Shake.

**A**LTHOUGH the action of the left hand does not cause any shaking of the string to execute this delicacy <note>original: "mignardiſe"; a term for musical ornaments or graces</note>, I have nonetheless not wished to change the name that is ordinarily given to it, and I do not represent it differently than the preceding one, except that I add a small dot before it, so as to discern it from the first, as one sees here <image-desc>musical notation: letter e with a dot to its left and a horizontal bar above it</image-desc>. Now, this shake is never performed on an *a* <note>In lute tablature, 'a' represents an open string.</note>; this is why, if it must be performed on a *b* <note>'b' represents the first fret.</note>, one must strike the string open, as if it were an *a*, and after the sound of the string is half-faded, one must let the finger fall from above onto the fret of the *b* without making any shake.

But if it must be performed on a *c* <note>'c' represents the second fret.</note>, and there is a small stroke above the character, as one sees here <image-desc>musical notation: letter c with a dot to its left and a horizontal bar above it</image-desc>, one must place the first finger on the fret of the *b*, and after having struck the string with the right hand, one must let the second finger of the left hand fall from above onto the fret of the *c*, as was done for the preceding *b*: but if there is no stroke above it, as one sees <image-desc>musical notation: letter c with a dot to its left</image-desc>, one must do as above for the *b*. And if it must be performed on a *d* <note>'d' represents the third fret.</note> without being accompanied by the small stroke above, one should place the first finger on the fret of the *b*, and let the fourth finger fall on the fret of the *d*, as we have said above. But if it is accompanied by the stroke, one must place the second finger on the fret of the *c*, and let the fourth finger fall on the fret of the *d*, as was done with the other fingers.

Now, in whatever place this shake is made, if it is not on a *b*, there must always be a finger placed above <note>Meaning at a lower fret, closer to the nut of the lute.</note> the one which is to mark the letter. And then one must observe a similar distance between the two fingers of the left hand (whether it is accompanied by this stroke or without it) as that which is kept in the observation of the first shake, of which we have spoken above.

### VI. On Two Kinds of Hammerings, and the Ornament that Some Call "Broken Glass" or "Sigh."

<margin>

And when one strikes the second string with the right hand, one must perform the shake with the left hand, and in finishing the shake, one must rest the finger very firmly in the same place it was before, so that the string, after the shake is finished, has the sound of a *b*. As for the *broken glass* <note>original: "verre cassé"; a term for a close vibrato produced by rocking the hand.</note>, I add it here, even though it is not now as commonly used as in the past, because it has a very good grace when performed appropriately: and one of the reasons why modern players have rejected it is because the ancients used it almost everywhere. But since it is just as flawed to make none at all as it is to make them too often, one must use moderation; its figure is <image-desc>comma followed by a dot</image-desc>, the preceding comma followed by a dot.

And to do it well, one must place the finger of the left hand at the place where it is marked; and when the string is struck with the right hand, one must shake the left hand with great violence, raising it toward the head of the Lute and lowering it toward the bridge without lifting the tip of the finger from the string in any way. But the thumb of the left hand must not touch the neck of the Lute when making the said shake, so that the action of the hand may be more free.

### VIII. On the left-hand strokes.

WE also perform other <term>delicate graces <note>original: "mignardises"; small, decorative musical ornaments.</note></term> that are called *left-hand strokes*, which are very agreeable when they are well executed: in effect, it is almost only the left hand that contributes to them, for after the right hand has struck the string, the left hand produces two or three letters in succession from that single strike of the right: for example, if one wants to play these 7 letters, one must first strike the <gloss>a</gloss> <note>The letter 'a' represents an open string.</note> with the thumb, which is why I put the <gloss>p</gloss> <note>original: "p" for "pouce" (thumb).</note> to signify it, beneath the said <gloss>a</gloss>. As for the <gloss>e</gloss> and the <gloss>a</gloss> which follow, one must only let the first and second fingers fall from above, one after the other, without striking with the right hand, as demonstrated by the characters that are above the said letters.

<image-desc>A snippet of lute tablature on a five-line staff, showing the letters 'a', 'e', and 'a' with arched ornaments connecting them and a 'p' beneath the first 'a'.</image-desc>

The <gloss>a</gloss> of the fifth string must be struck with the thumb, and the three other letters with the left hand alone, like the two preceding ones on the sixth string. I will provide yet another example, in which the first two letters must be struck with the right hand, and the third, which is the <gloss>a</gloss>, upon which there is a shake, must be struck with the left hand alone; that is to say, when the finger of the left hand is lifted from above the <gloss>b</gloss> <note>The letter 'b' represents the first fret.</note>, the string must be plucked by that motion a single time, and at the same instant the fingers of the left hand must be placed on the <gloss>b</gloss> and the <gloss>a</gloss> without striking with the right; and while placing the little finger, the shake must be made like that of the broken glass.

ALTHOUGH many skillful men have cultivated this art with such skill and dexterity, in which there are those who succeed today

# On Instruments.

...so successfully in our France, there is nonetheless only <term>Adrian le Roy <note>Adrian le Roy (c. 1520–1598) was a famous French lutenist, composer, and music publisher who wrote several instructional books.</note></term> who has given in writing some precepts of his instruction; they have perhaps believed it more glorious to keep this Art hidden than to divulge it. From this it comes that the pieces which leave their hands are never played according to their intention if they have not first been heard or learned from the masters themselves. Now, since this art has never been taught except in private, one should not find it strange if I use specific signs or particular precepts, although I retain the general ones as much as possible, since they are used by those most knowledgeable in this profession.

And for this subject, one must first consider the letters of the <term>Tablature <note>A system of musical notation for the lute that uses letters to represent finger positions on the frets rather than musical pitches.</note></term> and the place where they are positioned. In the second place, that the numbers which precede them represent the fingers of the left hand, which must be placed on the neck of the Lute: one ordinarily places the first finger on the *b* <note>In French tablature, 'a' represents an open string and 'b' represents the first fret.</note>, which is why I do not put a number there unless it is necessary to use another finger. Now, after having placed the fingers of the left hand, one must note the <term>shake <note>original: "tremblement"; a general term for musical ornaments like trills or vibrato.</note></term> and its type when it is required. In the third place, one must consider which fingers of the right hand should be used to pluck, and if there are <term>sustained notes <note>original: "tenuës"; indicated by lines to show how long a finger should hold a string down.</note></term> represented by certain straight or curved lines, which teach one to hold the left-hand fingers from the beginning of the letters where the said lines start until they finish: this serves to make the sound of the string last longer, examples of which will be seen at the end of this discourse, divided into several precepts that follow.

I. Precept. The *a* is always played <term>open <note>original: "à l'ouvert", "à vuide", or "à corde avalée"; all terms indicating the string is plucked without any finger pressing a fret.</note></term>; this is done with the right hand alone, without the help of the left, unless one must perform a shake, or when letters placed opposite each other must be plucked together, just as it also happens that those following one after another are plucked according to the rank they hold.

II. When there is a dot under a single letter, it must be plucked with the first finger of the right hand, and if there is no dot, it must be plucked with the second; this should only be observed from the <term>chanterelle <note>The highest-pitched, thinnest string of the lute.</note></term> to the fourth string, for the other strings must be plucked with the thumb: as seen in the first example.

III. The neck of the Lute is ordinarily divided into nine <term>frets <note>original: "touches"; gut strings tied around the neck to mark the notes.</note></term>, the first of which is called *b*; that is to say, if there is a *b* marked on the chanterelle or on the second string in the Tablature, the first finger of the left hand must be placed there above the fret *b*. And if there are several *b*s forming a chord, the first finger must be laid across the strings from the first letter to the last <note>This describes the "barre" or "bar" technique used by string players to press multiple strings with one finger.</note>: although sometimes the second finger is used with the first, as seen in the second example. But it must be noted that after having placed the fingers of the left hand, one must pluck as many strings with the right hand as are marked in the Tablature. Now, the second fret represents the *c*, the third the *d*, and so on for the others, up to the ninth fret marked by the letter *k*, beyond which one can still place the fingers; this is done only rarely, as the strings do not speak as clearly there.

IV. The *p* found under a single letter signifies that it must be plucked with the thumb, even if it is not ordinarily plucked so, as—

...as the third example teaches me.

V. The **p** that follows the chord, and whose leg crosses the strings, indicates that one must strike with the thumb all the strings that are crossed by the said leg, as is seen in the fourth example.

VI. When the leg of the **p** has a dot at the top, one must strike several strings together with the thumb and the first finger; however, when striking a chord in this fashion, the thumb must strike a single string, and the first finger all the others: as the fifth example teaches.

VII. The thumb and the first finger are also used together for striking after which there is only a stroke and a dot above: this occurs when one leaves a string to be struck between the first finger and the thumb. For example, if one must strike the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 7th together, one must strike the 7th with the thumb—which must be left resting on the 6th—and with the first finger, one must pluck them upwards from the 2nd to the 4th, as is seen in the 6th example.

VIII. There is no sign to signify the style of striking that is ordinarily called <term>pincer <note>literally "to pinch"; here it refers to plucking the strings with individual fingers simultaneously rather than a brush or strum.</note></term>: which is done when one strikes a chord with three or four fingers, as happens when one plucks the 4th, 3rd, and 2nd, of which the 4th is struck by the thumb, and the other 2 by the 2 following fingers consecutively: and if there are 4 letters in the chord, one employs the 3rd finger, as is seen in the 7th example. But if it is necessary to pluck five letters that have no sign after them, the thumb strikes 2, and the other fingers 3; and if there are 6 letters, the thumb strikes 3, as the 8th example teaches.

IX. The stroke that follows the chord, and which has a dot above it on the side of the <term>chanterelle <note>The highest-pitched string on the lute, usually the first string.</note></term>, signifies that one must strike 2 or 3 strings with the first finger alone in an upward motion: but when the dot is below on the side of the 6th string, one must strike down across the strings with the same finger, as is seen in the 9th example.

X. When it is necessary to strike two strings together, whether distant or close, they must always be struck with the thumb and the second finger, unless there is a stroke after the chord, which signifies that they must be plucked upwards with the first finger, or that there is a dot at one of the two letters, to show that they must be struck with the first and the second finger, as is seen in the 10th example.

XI. When it is necessary to strike three strings with three fingers without the help of the thumb, there is a dot at the letter which is toward the sixth string, which shows that one must strike the letter where it is placed with the first finger, and the two others with the following fingers, as is seen in the eleventh example.

XII. Although I said in the second Precept that the strings which are below the 4th must always be struck with the thumb, nevertheless if there is a dot under any string whatsoever, it must be struck with the first finger; if there are two, with the 2nd; and if there are three, with the 3rd; as is seen in the twelfth example.

XIII. The <term>Tenuës <note>literally "holds"; refers to the practice of keeping fingers pressed on the strings to allow notes to sustain or ring out.</note></term>, of which I spoke at the beginning of these Articles, and for which I promised the example at the end, are so necessary that without them the harmony is entirely imperfect: besides which, it is poor form to lift the fingers so often when there is no need; one must therefore mark and practice them exactly, and even when there are none marked, one must not fail to keep the fingers on the strings for as long as one can. Many mark them only in the Basses, but it is also necessary to use them in the other parts, and especially where one desires that they

be observed. Now, it should be noted that these sustained notes <note>French: *tenuës*</note> are performed on all kinds of instruments, and everything we say about the Lute can and should be applied to the Mandore, the Cittern, etc.

XIV. The bars that cross the six lines <note>The horizontal lines of the lute tablature staff.</note> create the division and the separation of the measures; the notes or other signs that are ordinarily placed above the first line, which represents the **chanterelle** <note>The highest-pitched string of the lute.</note>, serve the same purpose. For the white notes with tails <note>Equivalent to modern half notes or minims.</note> show that the sound of the letter must be made to last the duration of a half-measure. This usually lasts for the <gloss>7200th</gloss> part of an hour, or <gloss>1/120th</gloss> of a minute—that is to say, during the **diastole of the heart** <note>The phase of the heartbeat when the heart muscle relaxes; Mersenne often used the human pulse as a natural metronome.</note>. This rule will be easily understood by the fourteenth example, which shows that when there is only one note for seven or eight letters, they must all be made of the same value; that is, they must be struck as quickly or as slowly as one another, from that note until another is encountered.

XV. When there is an eighth note <note>French: *crochuë*</note> over a single letter, and a chord follows afterward, one must prepare the right and left hands to play that chord before touching the letter where the eighth note is. For example, if one must strike an *a* on the 3rd string which has an eighth note, and then a chord that has a quarter note <note>French: *noire*</note> above it, one must rest the thumb on the 9th string before touching the *a* of the 3rd on which the eighth note sits; this serves to allow for greater speed.

XVI. Finally, when it is necessary to perform a passage with the thumb and the first finger, I place a <term>pé</term> <note>A 'p' mark indicating the *pouce* (thumb).</note> beneath the first letter of the passage, and a <term>point</term> <note>A dot indicating the index finger.</note> beneath the one that follows, in order to signify that all the letters of the passage—from the first eighth note until a quarter note is met—must be struck by the thumb and then the first finger reciprocally. In this way, the first finger strikes immediately after the thumb, and the thumb after the first finger, until the end of the passage, as can be seen in the sixteenth or last example. Let us now see the different ways of tuning the Lute, so that one may play and set upon it all sorts of musical pieces.

### PROPOSITION XI.

->*To teach the manner of tuning the Lute in all sorts of ways.*<-

This Proposition contains two parts, the first of which comprises everything concerning the tuning of the Lute, whether it be common and ordinary, or new. Now, it is certain that one must have a naturally excellent ear to learn to tune the Lute without knowing music; for since those who know it perfectly encounter great difficulties therein, those who are ignorant of it find even more. This is why I teach the order that I have always seen kept, and which is still practiced now by the most skillful, in order to assist them. For this subject, I first suppose that the Lute is well-strung, and that the frets <note>French: *touches*</note> are well-positioned, according to the proportions of which we spoke previously, and of which I shall speak again later. Secondly, one must know what the **unison** and the **octave** are, because it is by their means that I provide understanding. This being established, one must begin with the **small sixth string** <note>Original: "petite sixiesme chorde." While "sixiesme" usually refers to the lowest string, in some historical French contexts or specific tunings, the numbering or string size might vary; here it likely refers to starting the tuning process from a specific reference string.</note> by setting it to whatever pitch one wishes, provided it is neither too high nor too low, and then one must...

put the thick string, that is to say its companion, an Octave lower; for one must always begin the tuning with the thinnest strings of each course, although one can begin with the thickest. Afterward, one must tighten the fifth course so that it makes a unison when open with the *e* <note>In lute tablature, 'a' represents an open string, 'b' the first fret, 'c' the second, 'd' the third, 'e' the fourth, etc.</note> of the thick sixth course, and one will be certain they are in tune; and then one must tune the thin string to the unison of the thin sixth.

One tunes the 5th with the 4th, just as the 6th with the 5th, and so on from string to string up to the **chanterelle** <note>The highest-pitched single string of the lute.</note> according to the tablature that follows, in which all the open strings marked with the letter **a** make a unison with the letters placed below the **a**s, which are located on the other strings. But before passing to the tuning of the other strings, one must go over the previous ones again in order to tune them as accurately as possible. And then one must tune the thin seventh to the unison of the 4th string open, and its companion an Octave lower. The thin 8th is sometimes tuned to the unison of the *d* <note>The third fret.</note>, and at other times with the *e* <note>The fourth fret.</note> of the 5th, in order to play in B-flat <note>French: *b mol*</note>, or in B-natural <note>French: *b quarre* (square b), used for natural or sharp notes.</note> according to how the pieces are composed. The thin 9th is tuned to the unison of the *c* of the 5th for a flat, or the *b* of the same 5th for a flat, and its companion an Octave lower. The thin 10th is tuned to the unison of the 5th string open, and the thick string to the Octave, like the others: which is seen in this tuning which is for flats and sharps.

->Ordinary Tuning. &nbsp;&nbsp; ♭ ♯ ♭ &nbsp;&nbsp; New, or Extraordinary Tuning.<-
->6 5 4 3 2 1 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 7 8 8 9 9 10<-

<note>The diagram above illustrates the fret positions on various strings required to match the pitches of the lower diapason strings (7–10). The "Ordinary Tuning" refers to the *vieil ton* (old tuning) standard in the Renaissance, while "Extraordinary" refers to the transitional tunings emerging in the early 17th century.</note>

Now it must be noted that this tuning is divided into three parts: the first belongs to the tuning of the first six ranks <term>courses</term> of strings; the second puts the last four ranks in tune both by B-flat and by B-natural; and the third shows how the new tuning, which is called "extraordinary," is different from the common one that precedes it. For it is certain that they are similar from the 3rd string down to the 10th, and that they are only dissimilar in the 1st and 2nd strings, which create a minor Third, or a major Third against the others; for the second string sometimes makes a minor third with the third, and at other times with the first, following the different tones and tunings one wishes to use. But it is so easy to tune the Lute in a thousand different ways, as one can conclude from the treatise on **Combinations**, that it is not at all necessary to speak further of it. The preceding tuning of the 10 strings of the Lute is similar to that of the figure I placed on page 46 of this book, but it shows how one must tune the 8th and 9th strings, both for B-flat and for B-natural; as for the notes that follow, they show how the Italians mark their tuning.

But if one does not wish to take the trouble of pressing the neck and using the left hand, one can tune the Lute note by note, like the Harp or the Spinet; this could be done by fitting it with 15 strings, of which the twelve thickest would only be played open <note>Played "open" means striking the string without pressing it down against a fret on the neck.</note>, and the 3 thinnest—namely the **chanterelle**, the 2nd, and the 3rd—would be played both open and on the neck. This would bring new graces to the Lute, because the harmony of open strings is greater and lasts longer.

To this, one can relate the **Guiterrons** or **Cifterons** <note>Large, hybrid stringed instruments of the 17th century.</note> which have fourteen single courses of strings, and which differ from **Theorbos** <note>A large lute with an extended neck for long bass strings.</note> in that their soundboards are longer and wider, and their backs are flat like that of Guitars; this gives them a different sound and a different harmony than Lutes. But it is enough to provide here the tuning of the Theorbo as practiced in Rome in this fashion.

## PROPOSITION XII.

*To explain the universal Tablature of the Lute, and all its tunings with a new figure, and with Examples.*

Although the tablature that follows serves only to demonstrate the art and manner of translating Music from notes into Lute tablature <note>Tablature is a system of notation using letters or numbers to show finger placement rather than pitches.</note>, and though it lacks the grace and arrangement of pieces usually composed for playing on this instrument, I nevertheless provide all the characters that must be used to play this four-part piece. This follows the precepts given previously, so that it may serve the understanding of everything I said in the 9th and 10th Propositions of this book. As for the tuning of this tablature, it is "extraordinary" or "new" in B-natural <note>original: "b quarre". In the 17th century, this refers to a tuning using natural or sharp notes rather than flats.</note>, in which the D-re-sol <note>A solmization pitch roughly corresponding to D.</note> is at the same pitch as the F-fa-ut <note>A pitch roughly corresponding to F.</note> of the four parts of the song that follows.

The other tablature, which has only the Soprano in notes, serves for the Lute's Bass, which provides the chords seen while the voice recites the lyrics and sings the Soprano. But I wish here to add a rule so general and so easy for transcribing anything one wishes onto the Lute that one will find no difficulty, regardless of whatever different tone or tuning one might imagine. I suppose, then, first a Lute fitted with ten courses of strings, like the one of which I gave a figure, or rather a Lute with six courses, like the one that follows, which represents the simplicity of ancient Lutes—especially since the four other courses added since then are not played on the neck, but only open. Secondly, I suppose that one transcribes whatever piece one wishes according to the common tuning, or the extraordinary one, which practitioners call the "old" and "new" tuning. And because the open strings create the tuning marked on the left side of the copperplate figure of the Lute that I gave in the first Proposition, it is evident that the range of this common tuning is a Twentieth—that is to say, a...

A hexachord <note>A series of six notes.</note> above the double octave <note>original: "Disdiapason".</note>, or a twenty-first if one adds an eleventh course <note>A "course" refers to a pair of strings tuned together.</note>, following the eleven notes of this tuning: but it has a range of only a fifteenth <note>Two octaves.</note> when one considers only the first six courses where I stop for now, in order to provide here a table where the first column signifies the six strings by the six Roman numerals: the second contains all the steps of the range of the Lute, the third shows the letters which serve for the **tablature**, and which correspond exactly to the letters, or characters of Music.

Where it must be noted that the letters only go up to the letter *e*, until they begin again at the letter *a*, because if one went up to *f*, it would be in **unison** <note>The same pitch.</note> with the said *a*: for example, the first *f* at the bottom of the fourth column, which is across from the *a* of the 3rd, shows that *f* of the 6th course of strings is in unison with the 5th course when played open. Now, the 4th column continues its letters until *u*, in order to show that if one continues to touch the 6th string toward the **bridge** <note>original: "cheualet"; the wooden piece on the body of the instrument that holds the strings.</note>, one will make all the sounds of the 6th, 5th, 4th, & 3rd string until that of the 2nd played open: but it is not customary to touch the strings higher than *e* or *f*, because the sounds of the open strings are more pleasant: from which one must only except the **chanterelle** <note>The highest-pitched string.</note>, which is played up to the letter *K*, that is to say up to the 9th fret which makes a **major Sixth** with the sound it has when open.

<header>### Of Instruments</header>

Italians, instead of using our letters, use the zero (0) for 'a', and then 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. for b, c, d, e, etc. Consequently, all the zeros placed beside the numbers signify the same open strings <note>original: "chordes à vuide"</note> as the 'a's in the 3rd column—that is to say, the six courses marked by the six Roman numerals. Now, since one can produce every semi-tone from the first to the last 'E' just as on the Organ and the Spinet <term>Epinette: a small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</term>, and since these semi-tones are equal, or can be made equal, it is certain that one can begin on any key or musical note on whatever string or fret one wishes. Consequently, there is no piece of music that cannot be set for the Luth <term>Lute: a plucked string instrument with a deep round back</term>, whether in its natural key or transposed a Third, Fourth, or Fifth higher or lower. For example, if one follows the old tuning <note>original: "accord ancien"</note>, one will tune the six courses of strings as they appear in the first column; if one uses the new tuning by the "natural" <note>original: "# quarre" (B-natural). This refers to the transition toward "D-minor" tunings or other "Accords Nouveaux" popular in 17th-century France.</note>, the Lute will have a range smaller by a minor Third than the common tuning, as seen in the 6th column, in which the two letters C and E signify the chanterelle <term>the highest-pitched string on a lute</term> and the second string. Their rank is marked by the number I in the 7th column and by II in the 8th, for the course is at the same pitch in the new tuning by the "natural" and by the "flat" <note>original: "b mol"</note>, which is marked in the 7th column, showing its two strings differ from the two of the "natural"—namely the chanterelle and the 3rd string.

Now, the entire secret of these tunings consists solely in this: the common tuning causes the strings to ascend from the 4th course, first by a Ditone <term>a major third</term>, and then by two Fourths, just as one does on the Viole <term>Viol: a bowed, fretted string instrument</term>. The new tuning by the "natural" makes them ascend by a Ditone, by a Sesquitone <term>a minor third</term>, and by a Ditone; and by the "flat" it makes them ascend by a minor Third (or Sesquitone), by a major Third (or Ditone), and by a minor Third. This is contained so clearly in the table that there is no need to speak further of it. This is why I come to the other instruments that imitate the Lute and are played like it, after having given the preceding example of its Tablature <term>a system of notation using letters or numbers to indicate fret positions rather than pitches</term>, which clarifies everything we have said until now; for the notes beneath the tablature show the order the letters must follow to express the same thing, so that the letters provide the true score <note>original: "partition"</note> of the preceding air which is in four parts. One finds excellent musical composers who compose all sorts of pieces using letters instead of notes.

If one considers this reduction of notes into letters attentively, one will admit it is not without artistry, owing to the extraordinary way the letters are arranged, because they correspond to the dots following the notes, or for other reasons that one will easily find by comparing each letter to each note, and the rhythmic value of one to the other.

As for the song <note>original: "air"</note> in four parts, it may serve as an example to those who study how to create good melodies, and how to compose parts that sing well against the Treble <note>original: "Deſſus"</note>. For its author <note>Referring to Antoine Boëffet, mentioned on the previous page.</note> is, without contradiction, the most skillful in all of France in this matter, in which one must employ a great multitude of nuances that are difficult to acquire without long practice and a natural inclination. Such inclination is usually the origin and the root of everything that appears excellent and extraordinary in the arts and sciences.

The other piece of tablature that follows has only the Treble of the four preceding parts, but it teaches how to join the Lute to the voice, which is not done without a particular skill, for it must be played specifically at the right moment...

In this period, a "recit" was a solo vocal piece or a specific section of a larger work</note>, and to make the harmony of the voice appear as if it were joined with two or three others. This custom of marrying the voice to the instrument is very common in France, in Italy, and in other provinces: from which one can infer that it is good, and that the most refined minds have perceived that the voice alone is not mellow, succulent, and nourished enough to provide the perfection desired for these solos—a perfection which one would find in a voice that could perform all the musical parts together, and which would never need to catch its wind or stop.

Large Theorboes <term>Theorbo: a large, bass lute with an extended neck and additional unstopped bass strings, used primarily for accompaniment</term> are now used, which are tuned to chapel pitch <term>ton de chapelle: the standard pitch used in French sacred music, which was generally lower than the pitch used for chamber music</term> to accompany the voice; but I leave this consideration to examine the pieces that follow, which show the practice of different tunings, or "Chords" of the Lute, from which one can learn much; then I will speak of the Mandore <term>Mandore: a small, high-pitched member of the lute family, often considered a precursor to the mandolin</term>, which is nothing other than a diminished and shortened Lute.

<header>concerning Instruments.</header>

### *Examples of Lute Tablature with their explanation.*

Many might imagine that I have taught the instructions for playing and tuning the Lute in vain if I did not provide several pieces to put them into practice, whose authors are sufficiently recommended to be esteemed by everyone. But I ask the reader to excuse me if I do not express their specific manner of playing them exactly; this is because each player has a unique and greatly different style. Furthermore, I do not intend in this small treatise to explain the inventions of others, but only my own. The signs and characters I have invented for this purpose can serve the same end for those who wish to use them; this will be a means by which authors make themselves intelligible, both to those present and those absent. And if I have omitted to explain many difficulties that might be encountered, I can say of this work what Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was an ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> said of Medicine in his first Aphorism: "Life is short, and art is long" <note>original: "Que la vie eſt briefue, & l'art eſt long." This is a translation of the famous Latin aphorism "Ars longa, vita brevis."</note>. Truly, there is no art in the world more full of difficulties than this one; nevertheless, I will try to provide an explanation where they occur. I will begin then with the common tuning <term>ton Commun: the standard tuning for the Renaissance lute, typically G-C-F-A-D-G</term>, since it was the origin of all the new tunings.

The bar preceding the first letter of the Courante <term>Courante: a lively French dance in triple meter, a staple of the lute repertoire</term> that follows shows that the first finger of the left hand must be laid across as many strings as the length of the bar indicates; this serves so that the first finger is fully positioned <note>a "barre chord" technique</note> for the chord that follows. It should be noted that the bars used to divide the measures are different from those representing the first finger of the left hand; the former cross all six lines entirely, whereas the others do not cross them unless the finger must be laid higher than the sixth string.

The holds <note>original: "tenuës." In lute tablature, these lines indicate that a note should be sustained or "held" while other notes are played.</note> which go beyond the end of the lines show that all the fingers must be used for what follows. I do not place the Common tuning before the Courante because I have already explained it with the illustration of the Lute found in the first and eleventh Propositions; as for the others, I place them only before the first two Allemandes <term>Allemande: a stately German dance in duple meter, usually the opening movement of a suite</term>, because the third is in the same tuning as the second. I leave out several types of tunings <note>original: "accords." In this period, "accord" referred to the specific interval relationship between the strings (the tuning), not just a harmony.</note> that can be applied to the Lute, because it would require a volume of more than a hundred pages to include them all, as can be seen in my full large volume, in which I have included all those that can be made from the eight notes of the Octave, in place of which one can use any other set of eight notes one wishes. Those who desire a greater multitude of tablature pieces for the Lute can see those printed every year by Monsieur Ballard <note>Pierre Ballard (c. 1581–1639) was the leading music printer in 17th-century France and held the royal monopoly on music printing.</note>; and future centuries will perhaps see even more excellent ones than those used now.

### Allemande by Monsieur Mezangeau

<note>original: "Allemande de Monfieur Mezangeau." René Mezangeau (c. 1568–1638) was a pivotal figure in the French lute school. He was highly regarded at the court of Louis XIII and is often credited with innovating the new tunings that transformed lute music in the 17th century.</note>

This piece is an <term>Allemande: a stately, moderate dance in quadruple meter that usually serves as the foundational movement of a Baroque suite</term>. While the *Courante* on the previous page was energetic and triple-metered, this Allemande offers a more somber and flowing melody.

The music is presented in five systems of **lute tablature**, a specialized notation system:

*   **The Staff:** The six horizontal lines represent the six main "courses" (pairs of strings) of the lute.
*   **The Letters:** Instead of notes on a scale, letters indicate where the fingers should be placed on the frets.
    *   The letter **a** indicates an open string.
    *   The letters **b, c, d, e,** and **f** indicate the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth frets, respectively.
*   **The Bass:** Beneath the six lines, the Greek letter **α** (alpha) is used to mark the <term>diapasons: the extra bass strings that run alongside the fretboard and are always played open</term>.
*   **Rhythm:** Above the staff, vertical lines with flags (resembling modern stems) dictate the duration of the notes, from longer minims to faster quavers and semiquavers.

The layout is precisely organized with vertical bar lines to separate the measures. Decorative flourishes at the start of the piece and double bar lines at the end of sections provide visual cues for the performer to navigate the structure of the dance.

# Book Second

I would have included a greater number of pieces in this treatise, but having only intended to give a few examples to help readers grasp the principal points of the preceding instruction, I believed that these four suffice, provided they are studied attentively. And if it is objected that all the ornaments and <term>mignardises: delicate ornaments or "graces" played on the lute to add expression</term> that can be performed on the Lute could not be contained in so little material, I frankly admit it; nevertheless, those who practice these well can be assured of having acquired a great readiness to execute other works of greater difficulty. Furthermore, it seems to me that in these first attempts where everyone is a novice, one should easily excuse those who begin a work without perfecting it; I hope, however, that if what I have said here meets with public satisfaction, I shall one day make it more perfect and complete by the grace of God, without whom we can do or think nothing as we ought.

Now, after having given all these pieces of <term>tablature: a system of musical notation using letters to indicate which frets to press rather than specific pitches</term> for the Lute, it must first be noted that they lack several symbols necessary to play them according to the intention and method of Master Basset, which is explained in the 10th Proposition. But those who wish to mark them will find them in my own copy, where they are added by hand—since printing houses do not have these specific characters—and they may transcribe them just as easily, as I will freely lend my copy to them, unless they prefer to consult the aforementioned Basset, who will accommodate them. However, it is necessary to have their paper washed in alum water so that it does not bleed <note>original: "boive point" — literally "does not drink," referring to the ink spreading on porous paper</note>, so they may write whatever they wish upon it.

In the second place, anyone may invent new characters to express their own method, as there is no obligation to use one set over another, though it is appropriate to retain those already in use and only add those that are missing, as we have done in this tablature.

In the third place, the tuning <note>original: "l'accord"</note> is not marked on the first piece of music because it uses the ordinary tuning, which is expressed in the eleventh Proposition. The tuning for the "new tone" is placed before the second piece and not after, as some do, so that everyone can begin the piece without having to turn the leaf. As for the fourth piece, it does not have its tuning marked because it is in the same tone as the third.

In the fourth place, there is a way to make the Lute easier than it is, either by adding the eleventh and twelfth courses of strings, and some frets under the basses, or pedals, as does Master le Maire. He has assured me that his method makes the Lute easier than the Guitar, and that he is the inventor of the seventh syllable **SI**, which is added to the six notes of <note>original: "Guy Aretin"</note> Guido of Arezzo, **ut, re, mi**, etc. <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033) was the monk who created the hexachord system (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la). Jean Le Maire (c. 1581–1650) is credited with introducing "si" to complete the major scale.</note> In place of "SI," he uses **ZA**, which I speak of more fully in the book *The Method of Singing Well*, and for which he promises to give a treatise to the public along with a way of singing and composing without the ordinary notes.

In the fifth place, one can tune the Lute by means of the Organ, the Voice, or some other Lute that is already in tune, without needing to test the chords upon it; this is because the Organ pipes that produce the same tones required for the Lute will make its strings vibrate when they are at the Unison or the Octave. The Octave can be distinguished from the Unison by a lesser vibration <note>This refers to the phenomenon of sympathetic resonance, where a string vibrates automatically when its pitch is sounded nearby</note>, as I have said in the *Book of Consonances*.
