# on Instruments.

this manner of tuning is more subtle and curious than it is useful, for the reason that it takes too much time to adjust the <term>pegs: the wooden pins at the head of the lute used to tighten or loosen strings</term> to give such a tension to the strings that they vibrate more or less strongly to the sounds of pipes, the voice, or another Lute; thus, a good ear is better, and is more prompt and useful than anything one can imagine on this subject. Regarding this, one may see what I say concerning the Tablature for the deaf in the seventh Proposition of the third book which follows, where I examine the number of <term>beats: the acoustic phenomenon (pulsations) heard when two notes are slightly out of tune with each other</term> made by the strings of the Lute, upon which one plays the Air by Master Boësset that I have included in that Proposition, and which begins *Divine Amaryllis*; the tablature shows that it can be played in four parts on the Lute, as I have already remarked, and if fine minds take the trouble to perfect this instrument and make it easier to play, they could make it capable of the aforementioned four continuous parts, either by increasing its strings or its frets.

In the sixth place, if the sounds of the strings have the same effect on <term>Organ pipes</term> as voices do, the Lute can put an Organ out of tune; this will happen if one lowers or raises their sound by a semitone, or a quarter of a tone lower or higher than that of the pipes, which will "beat" as if they were not in tune, even though it seems that the sound of the strings is too soft and too weak for this effect: but I shall speak further of this discord in the book on Organs.

In the seventh place, the neck of the Lute can serve as a <term>Monochord: a single-stringed ancient instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically</term> as much for the just intervals of <note>Ptolemy and Pythagoras were ancient Greek theorists whose tuning systems were based on mathematical ratios</note> Ptolemy or Pythagoras, as for the equal ones of Aristoxenus; so that there is no need for another instrument to regulate all sounds.

In the eighth place, one can make its body so large that a child might be housed within it to sing the <term>Dessus: the highest or soprano vocal part</term>, while the Lute player touches the Bass, as I also remark in the treatise on the Viol; for one can make the <term>ribs: the curved strips of wood that form the sides of the lute's body</term> in such a way that the back of the Lute will open and close like the door of a room, to enclose a child therein, whose singing, being well-concerted with the strings, will give great contentment to the listeners.

In the ninth place, one can make springs which will supply a good portion of the <term>tremblements: trills or shakes</term>, the beats, and the <term>mignardises: delicate ornaments or "graces" played on the lute to add expression</term> which are made on the neck, and one can put several Organ pipes inside the body, or under the neck, which will make harmonies with the strings that are touched: this has already been practiced by some. Indeed, there is a way to put twelve or thirteen pipes into the body of the Lute, the mouths of which would be positioned toward the neck, which will perhaps give more harmony to the Lute through their different cavities than they will harm it; and their small keys being found under the ordinary frets of the neck, one will make each pipe speak with the same fingers used to press the frets to shorten the strings: so that one will have an <term>organized Lute: a hybrid instrument combining the lute with a small pipe organ</term>. But because one must use bellows to make the pipes speak, it will be easy to make their wind-trunk from a leather channel, which will be joined under the neck, and to hold them under one of the arms like that of the <term>Musette: a small, bellows-blown bagpipe popular in the French court</term>, in order to dispense the wind as evenly as possible. And if these bellows are too inconvenient, they can be made in such a way that they will be raised by the movement of the foot which marks the time: which will in no way prevent one from playing the Lute alone, because

# Second Book

everything belonging to the Organ can be separated from it whenever one wishes; for it is not necessary to fix the <term>windchest: the wooden box in an organ that holds pressurized air</term> and the <term>valves: mechanisms that allow air into the pipes</term> so tightly into the neck that they cannot be removed by means of certain movable boards, which nonetheless join so precisely that no air can be lost. And if one were willing to go to the necessary expense, one could enclose <term>bellows</term> within the Lute, which would rise on their own by means of one or two endless screws <note>original: "vis sans fin," referring to worm gears</note> and other springs that would make no noise; for we possess mechanical devices much more difficult than these.

One could also join the Harp and several other instruments to the Lute, although it seems the clutter would be too great, and the combination of several instruments joined together detracts much from the ornament and the quality of each. There is almost only the Organ upon which the mixture of different kinds of wind instruments succeeds, although it is not impossible to mix those that use strings, and to compose them of as many different instruments as there are <term>stops: sets of pipes in an organ producing a specific sound</term> in the Organ, which could similarly be joined with the aforementioned instrument.

In the tenth place, the Lute is very well-suited for expressing the <term>Chromatic genus: a musical style using semitones to create more intense or varied emotion</term>, which also applies to other instruments whose frets produce semitones. It is esteemed in France as the noblest of all, whether because of the sweetness of its melodies, the number and harmony of its strings, its range, its tuning, or the difficulty of playing it as perfectly as Messieurs <note>Messieurs l'Enclos, Gautier, etc., were the premier French lutenists of the 17th century</note> l'Enclos, Gautier, **Blanc-rocher**, Merville, le Vignon, and several others who are living now. Finally, it should be noted that the **Theorbo** <note>a large, bass lute with an extended neck for long bass strings</note> should have only one string for each <term>course: a pair or single string played together as one note</term>, to which must be compared the **Cisteron** or **Guiterron**, whose back is flat like its soundboard and which has fifteen courses of strings. Thus, the Theorbo, of which I provided an illustration in the first Proposition, is more like a double-necked Lute than a true Theorbo, which does not usually have such a short and round body. However, it is so easy to understand its shape by looking at the preceding ones that there is no need to speak further of it; therefore, I come to the **Mandore**, which can be called a small Lute, since it is an abbreviated version and serves as the <term>Treble: the highest part in a musical arrangement</term> in its ensembles.

It only remains to add that everything I say about strings and their properties in the third book and elsewhere can be applied to the Lute and other instruments. If one understands the tables I have provided in the books on the Voice and Songs, one can use Lute <term>Tablature: a system of musical notation using letters or numbers to show finger placement rather than pitches</term> for writing, for explaining all sorts of sciences, and for sending secret letters that cannot be deciphered. In this way, a lute player will be able to perform anything he wishes by means of his instrument: for example, he could represent the two mean proportionals, the duplication of the cube, the squaring of the circle, the proportion of the movements of all the heavens and their stars, the velocity of falling weights, and a thousand other things through the tones and melodies of his instrument, if he understands the full content of this work. This is similarly to be understood for Organists and those who play other instruments capable of all sorts of proportions.

## PROPOSITION XIII.

->*Explain the form, the tuning, the tablature, and the playing of the Mandore.*<-

**A**fter having spoken of the Lute, it is necessary to explain the instruments which depend on it and which are also played with the fingers, or with the tip of a quill held between the thumb and index finger, or tied to one of the other fingers. Now, the Mandore is one of the most common and simplest, for it usually has only four strings, although some are made with six or a greater number in order to make them approach the excellence of the Lute, of which it is the shorthand and the diminutive; this is why it is called *Lutelike* <note>original: "Luthée"</note>.

The second part consists of the <term>soundboard</term> <note>original: "table"</note> ABDE. The third part is called the <term>shell</term> <note>original: "donte," likely a regional term for the vaulted back</note>, the *body*, or the *belly*, which is made of <term>ribs</term> <note>original: "eclisses"</note> of fir, or other wood, which are cut and bent into melon-like ribs, two of which appear in this figure. This figure is taken from a Mandore one and a half feet long, which is its ordinary length. The head of the neck P H has four pegs, with which one tunes the strings, although many put six pegs for ornament. But it must be noted that the string E B serves as the <term>chanterelle: the highest-pitched string on a plucked instrument</term>, and consequently it is the thinnest, and the three others always increase in their thickness, so that the fourth P D is the thickest.

As for the tuning, to which one must primarily pay attention, I have marked it with musical notes and ordinary tablature, through which one sees that the 4th string is at a <term>Fifth: a musical interval spanning five notes of a scale</term> <note>original: "Quinte"</note> from the 3rd, this 3rd at a <term>Fourth: a musical interval spanning four notes</term> <note>original: "Quarte"</note> from the 2nd, and the 2nd at a Fifth from the chanterelle, which rises the highest. This is why this tuning is called "from Fifth to Fourth," insofar as the four strings...

this is why it is called **tuning in Thirds**.

These three sorts of tunings are also marked with the ordinary letters;
the highest of which shows the most common one; and one uses the **unison** to
tune the **Mandore**, because it is easier to understand than the other
**Consonances**, and because the ear immediately notices its smallest
defects; it is called **tuning by unison**. Now, this very easy discernment of the
imperfections of the unison deserves some reflection on all perfect things,
whose smallest faults are perceived at first sight, just as one
experiences with learned and virtuous men, who recognize
many imperfections in their knowledge and in their actions, of which
the ignorant and the vicious are unaware, or from which they believe themselves exempt:
but this is not the place to examine the reasons for that.

As for the letters of the three tunings, one must suppose that they signify the

**minor Third**, to *e* to make the **major Third**, to *f* to make the
**Fourth**, to *g* to make the **fifth**, to *h* to make the **minor Sixth**, 
and to *i* to make the **major Sixth**, which contains the range of the
necks of most instruments.

when they are played open, and each fret shortens each
string by a semitone, it follows that *h* shortens it and makes it rise by seven
semitones, of which the **fifth** is composed on necked instruments: from which

makes it rise by a **Fifth**, and consequently to the **unison** of the **chanterelle**.

As for the **black note** <note>The "note noire" corresponds to a quarter note in modern notation.</note> placed above this row of letters, it shows the duration these three sounds must last: the same must be said of all the other letters that have notes expressed or implied, as is seen in the sequence of **quarter notes** and **eighth notes** <note>original: "crochuës" – literally "hooked notes."</note>, which have the same value in **Tablature** as they do in vocal music. Now, when composers place one or several letters that have no notes above them, they maintain the same rhythmic value as those that precede them which do have notes. For example, the *e* on the **chanterelle**, which follows the *d* on the second string (which has an **eighth note**), has no note above it; therefore, it must be made to last the time of an **eighth note**, which is to say the eighth part of a measure. This being established, it is easy to note the number of measures in each tablature by the number of notes, as can be tested in this one, which is divided into three parts. The first part has two **quarter notes** and one **eighth note** expressed, and one **eighth note** and one **quarter note** implied, all of which make a full measure. The second part has two **eighth notes**, one **quarter note**, and one **sixteenth note** <note>original: "double crochuë."</note> expressed, and one **eighth note**, one **quarter note**, and one **sixteenth note** implied, which also make one measure. -># Of Instruments<-

Now, even though the **Mandore** <term>Mandore: a small, high-pitched member of the lute family, often played with a plectrum</term> has only four strings, one can nevertheless perform nearly everything on it that is done on **Lutes**. It complements Lute ensembles because of the vibrancy and sharpness of its sounds, which so thoroughly penetrate and occupy the ear that Lutes struggle to make themselves heard. I leave aside a thousand delicacies that depend on a beautiful touch and the imagination of the player, for it is as difficult to express this through speech as it is pleasant to hear it; the rarities and charms of Music have no written characters capable of representing them to someone who has never heard them. Those who possess perfect mastery of the Mandore pass the quill <note>original: "plume" — here referring to a plectrum made from a quill, used to strike the strings</note> so quickly over the strings that they seem to produce the same chords they would if they were plucked simultaneously. But it is not necessary to extend the discussion of this instrument any further, since it is nothing other than a shortened Lute.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

### *To explain the figures, the tuning, the tablature, and the strumming patterns of the Guitar.*

The first **Guitars**, the invention of which seems to have come from Spain, had only four courses of strings. The first is a single string, called the **chanterelle** <term>chanterelle: the highest-pitched string of a stringed instrument, used for the melody</term> as on other instruments, because it serves the treble part and often carries the main melody. Now, this first figure represents these Guitars very well, the neck of which is

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a stringed instrument identified as a guitar. The neck features eight frets labeled with lowercase letters b, c, d, e, f, g, h, and i. The headstock shows four tuning pegs numbered 1, 2, 3, and 4. The body is decorated with elaborate scrollwork and floral patterns, featuring a central circular ornamental soundhole or rosette.</image-desc>

divided into 8 frets <note>original: "touches"</note>, so that each string can rise as high as a minor sixth <note>original: "Hexachorde mineur" — referring to the interval reached at the 8th fret</note>. The left side shows its depth, as well as the ornaments and figures that the **Makers** <note>original: "Facteurs" — craftsmen who build musical instruments</note> add to embellish and enrich it; but they take particular care that the **rosette** <note>original: "rose" — the decorative carved soundhole</note> is well-crafted.

As for the other figure that follows, it shows everything belonging to the five-course Guitar, which is in use today. These five courses have ten strings, although many people only put a single string for the *chanterelle*. The neck A B has ten pegs, and the fretboard has 8 frets like the previous one. But there are several things in this figure that the other lacks: first, the tuning by musical notes, where the first note corresponds to the 5th or last string, the second to the 4th, the third to the 3rd, the fourth to the 2nd, and the fifth to the *chanterelle*. This is indicated by the numbers above them. These notes are pronounced as follows: **D, G, C, E, A** <note>original solmization: "RE, SOL, VT, MI, LA"</note>. Now, besides this tuning <note>original: "accord"</note> by notes, it is also marked with the ordinary letters of the **tablature** <term>tablature: a form of musical notation indicating instrument fingering rather than musical pitches</term>, of which the first descending one—which is opposite the soundhole <note>original: "rose"</note>—begins by giving whatever pitch one desires to the 3rd string <note>original: "chorde"</note>, whose open sound is marked by the first two *aa*. Now, the *c* <note>the third letter of the alphabet, representing the second fret</note> of this same string must be tuned to the **unison** <term>unison: two or more musical parts sounding the same pitch</term> of the *a* of the 5th string; then one must tune the *c* of the 5th to the unison of the *a* of the 2nd; the *d* of this 2nd to the unison of the *a* of the 4th, and the *c* of this 4th to the unison of the *a* of the **chanterelle** <term>chanterelle: the highest-pitched string of a stringed instrument, usually used for the melody</term>. It is easy to judge the others by their letters; for example, <gloss>Made by Henri le Roy</gloss> <note>original Latin: "Henri le Roy fecit"</note> the last also gives the same tuning by unisons; the same happens to the middle one if one considers the first six rows of letters, for the last two make the Octave.

As for the tablature, it is presented here in two ways: namely, in the Italian style using numbers, and in the Spanish style using the characters found on the letters, which serve for French Tablature. Now, it is very easy to understand these two types of tablature by comparing them to one another, since each row of the Spanish is placed beneath each row of the Italian, and they both go as far as the letter *P*. If anyone wishes to use harmonic numbers to express the tuning of the Guitar, they can take no smaller ones than these: 27, 36, 24, 30, 40, of which the first creates a **major hexachord** <term>major hexachord: a six-note musical scale common in medieval and Renaissance theory</term> with the last. # Of Instruments.

The length of its neck, which ends at C, is such that the neck is as long as the distance from the middle of the **rose** <note>The decorative soundhole cover</note> to the bottom of the body, marked E. F and G show the location and the shape of the **bridge** <term>bridge: the wooden piece on the body of the guitar that holds the strings in place</term>, and D marks its thickness. The back, which cannot be seen here, is sometimes flat like the soundboard, and at other times slightly convex; this does not matter much, for whatever shape is given to it, its sounds carry something of the cauldron and always seem to groan <note>The author likely prefers the refined tone of the lute over the guitar’s "metallic" or folk-like qualities</note>. Now, I will shortly provide its tablature more accurately than it appears on the copperplate, so that no one may be mistaken.

Regarding the other **tablature** <term>tablature: a system of notation using letters or numbers to show finger placement on frets</term> on the left, whose five lines are marked by numbers, it signifies the same thing as the one below, where the five lines are covered with the letters *b*, *c*, *d*, etc., which represent the **frets** <note>original: "touches"</note> of the Guitar’s neck. Now, each capital letter following the ✠ <note>A cross symbol often representing a specific chord in the Alfabeto system</note> shows each chord, so that those who know how to play this instrument need no other tablature than these letters, to which correspond the characters placed on the first five lines of the **Spanish Tablature**, which is marked by letters like ours. It should be noted that the ✠ of the **Italian Tablature** means that one must place the first finger on the second fret *c* of the last string—that is, the **chanterelle** <term>chanterelle: the highest-pitched string of the instrument</term>—which the Italians count as the last, whereas we count it as the first. The number 2 signifies that one must place the 2nd finger on the *c* of the 4th string, so that this chord requires only two fingers. When there are 3, 4, or 5 characters, one must use all the fingers, or lay one finger across two or three frets of different strings <note>A technique known today as a "barre"</note>, as seen in chord H, which is played on all five strings and corresponds exactly to the chord marked by 3 in the tablature. This is so easy to understand that it is not necessary to speak of it at length.

This is why I come to the various **strumming techniques** <note>original: "bateries"</note> used in playing this instrument, which are practiced in common or triple time. The simple strum of common time <note>original: "mesure binaire"</note> consists of two beats: the first moves upward and the other downward, or vice versa, according to the will of the player.

When one wishes to double or triple this strum, one strikes all the strings 4 or 8 times with one, 2, 3, or 4 fingers, as desired. As for the thumb, it only strikes the chanterelle when moving upward, and all the strings when moving downward. The simple triple strum <note>original: "batterie ternaire"</note> consists of three beats, which always begin with a downward motion according to the movement of the piece, as is customarily marked in the tablature. When this strum is redoubled, it has five beats, where the fifth strike is downward, either with the finger alone or with both thumb and finger; however, the strike of the finger must be heard as distinct and separate from the strike of the thumb. Now, it is customary to strike on the **rib** <note>original: "eclisse" - the side of the guitar</note> where the soundboard ends when one wants a softer strum, and near the bridge when one wants it louder, although one may strike anywhere from the bridge to the frets. But the thumb, which strikes after the fingers, must follow them immediately. It should also be noted that one does not ordinarily double or triple the strums on difficult pieces, but only on the easiest ones, such as on **Passacaglias** <note>original: "Passe-cailles" - a popular repeating bass-line dance</note>; for other pieces, one is content with the simple strum, or the doubling of syncopations <note>original: "contre-temps"</note>, which make up two-thirds of the measure and begin or end with said syncopation composed of three equal beats.

As for the distance of the frets, the Makers <note>original: "Facteurs"</note> determine it by ear, as they do for other fretted instruments, for they raise and lower them until the chords satisfy them, although one can seat and place them easily without using ear or experience, if one understands the treatise on the Lute. Now each string has the range of a Twelfth, or a Thirteenth by means of its frets, of which *m* makes the Octave with the string played open.

Regarding the manner of playing the Cittern with both the right and left hands, one must do with the right hand using the quill <term>plume</term> <note>a plectrum made from a bird's feather, used to pluck wire strings</note> what was said when explaining its function in the treatise on the Lute; for one must strike as many strings as there are letters with dots underneath, and down-stroke <note>or 'lower'</note> all those whose letters are found without dots. Regarding the left hand, the example of the sixteen chords that follows will teach which fingers one must use to touch each letter, or fret. But it should be noted that the sixteen musical notes which are below signify the letters of the first and second lines <term>regle</term> above: for example *ut, re, mi, fa* <note>original solfège: equivalent to C, D, E, F</note> signify the *a* of the first line, and the *a, c,* and *d* of the second, and then one goes back up to the *d, f, h*, etc. of the first line to sing *sol, la*, etc.

### Difficult Chords of the Cittern.

<image-desc>A detailed musical diagram. The top part shows a four-line cittern tablature with sixteen numbered chords (1 to 16) using letters such as a, c, d, e, f, h, and i. Below the tablature is a corresponding five-line musical staff showing the same chords in standard musical notation.</image-desc>

Now, one must touch the *d* of the first fret with the second finger, and the *c* with the first: for as for the *a*'s, they are played open <note>played without pressing any fret</note>, as I have already said. The *c* of the second fret is touched with the first finger. The *d* and the *c* of the third fret with the same fingers as the first. The first *d* of the fourth fret with the second finger, the *c* with the first, and the other *d* with the third. The fifth and sixth frets are like the fourth. The *f* of the seventh with the first finger, and the *h* with the third. The *h* of the eighth with the second finger. The two *f*'s with the first finger by laying it across all the strings <note>a "barre" technique</note>, and the *i* with the pinky finger. The ninth fret is like the sixth. The *h* of the tenth with the pinky finger: the *f* with the second, and the other *f* with the first. The eleventh like the fourth: the twelfth like the tenth. The *b* of the thirteenth with the first finger, and the *c* with the second. The first *c* of the fourteenth with the second finger, and the other with the first: the fifteenth like the second, and the sixteenth like the fifth. This is sufficient to understand everything belonging to the Cittern.

## PROPOSITION XVI.

### *Explaining the figure and the tuning of the Colascione.*

**A**ll instruments that have only one, two, or three strings can be related either to this one or to the Monochord <term>Monochorde</term> <note>a single-stringed instrument used since antiquity to measure musical intervals</note>: for example, the various sticks used by the poor and the blind, upon which they stretch one, two, or three strings over a pig's bladder or some other hollow body to create the Drone <term>Bourdon</term>, which some call the *Flemish Bass* <note>original: "Basse de Flandre"; a folk instrument also known as a bladder fiddle or bumbass</note>, and which they join with the Violin, Cymbals, and Drums to increase the Harmony.

<image-desc>A full-page illustration of a Colachon, a stringed instrument with a small pear-shaped body and an exceptionally long neck. The neck features sixteen frets, labeled on the left with numbers 1-16 and on the right with letters b-r. Parts of the instrument are marked with capital letters: 'A' at the pegbox, 'B' at the neck heel, 'C' at the bridge, 'D' at the rosette, and 'E' at the bottom of the body. To the right of the instrument's neck, there is musical notation on a staff showing three notes—representing an open tuning of an octave and a fifth—along with technical symbols including numbered lozenges and a bracketed musical staff.</image-desc>

The Colascione <term>Colachon</term> <note>a long-necked lute popular in Italy</note> similarly has only two or three strings, and is an instrument four or five feet long used in Italy; its open tuning <term>accord à vuide</term> consists of an Octave and a Fifth, as seen in the notes provided to the side, although it can be tuned in several other ways. It has the shape of a Lute but has only one neck <term>manche</term> which is very long to give range to its three strings: those who only put two strings on it tune it to a Fifth; but I have combined the Octave with the Fifth in this one.

The Rebec <term>Rebec</term> <note>a bowed, pear-shaped instrument of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> similarly has three strings which are tuned in Fifths <term>de quinte en Quinte</term> like those of the Violin; this is why I do not speak of it more amply here, for besides the fact that it is no longer in use, the Violin (which we will treat later) contains its range and is more excellent. Now, it must be noted 
<margin>♢3</margin> that one may give whatever shape one wishes to the soundboard <term>table</term>, 
<margin>♢2</margin> and to the body of all other instruments without 
<margin>⊐3</margin> changing or altering their species, their natures, and their properties; this is why one should not believe that I have omitted any instrument when I do not include all the different figures of Lutes, Viols, Lyres, and other instruments. These different forms bring no more variety than the different shapes of circles, squares, ellipses, hexagons, etc., that one gives to the same sundial <term>horologe Solaire</term>; otherwise, one could say there are five hundred different species of Viols and Lutes, etc., which is contrary to truth and experience.

Some make the soundboard of the Colascione half of wood and half of parchment; one could...

<header>on Instruments.</header>

[one can] also make it of glass, and of several other materials: but it is better that it be made entirely of Fir <term>Sapin</term> <note>In the context of 17th-century luthiery, "sapin" often refers to spruce or silver fir, which remains the standard wood for instrument soundboards due to its resonance.</note>, like that of other instruments. Now, it is enough to have treated the instruments that are in use in France and among our neighbors, without it being necessary to invent or propose new ones, such as the new Lyre of Monsieur Doni <note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), an Italian theorist who invented the "Lyra Barberina," an attempt to recreate ancient Greek music.</note>, of which he sent me the design; for it belongs to the inventors to explain what they have found, so that they may receive the full honor for it. I will only say that no Engineer has yet been found who has replaced, by artifice and by machines, the movement of the fingers of the right and left hands on instruments with necks—whether fretted or unfretted—nor who has demonstrated the proportion that the hollow of the instrument must have with the neck and the soundboard to produce a perfect harmony; of which we may speak further in other Books. For I wish to finish this one with a consideration of the machines that served the ancients for throwing stones and arrows, in order to remark that Music and the sound of strings are not useless in war.

Indeed, they used Unison <term>Vnisson</term> to know if the strings of their bows and their crossbows <term>arbalestes</term> were well-tensioned, as Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance; he applied musical theory to the tensioning of catapults.</note> remarked in the 18th chapter of his 10th Book. This was done by turning the handles of the winch or the tensioning device until the two strings of the two parts of the catapult produced a Unison with one another. However, I do not believe he understood Music well, since he says that each string was stretched until its resonance was equal throughout; for a single string always makes an equal sound in all its parts, whether one tensions it little or much, if one judges the equality of the sound by its pitch <term>aigu</term>. And if one judges by the force and the volume, the sound is only equal on the parts of the string that are equally distant from its middle, as one experiences on the Lute <term>Luth</term> and on all other instruments whose strings sound louder when they are touched near the bridge <term>cheualet</term> than when they are touched in the middle, which is the softest of all the parts.

But since muskets and other firearms have caused the loss of the use and knowledge of Catapults, Scorpions, and the Crossbows of the ancients—who made their strings from women's hair or from twisted sinews, as Vitruvius says in the same place—I will not dwell any longer on this antiquity. It suffices to conclude that one can use strings made of the same hair to string the Lute and the Viol <term>Viole</term>, as well as the other instruments of which we have spoken; for since these strings were strong enough to shoot and send the bolts of Crossbows very far, and they supported the tension and the strain of winches, hoists <term>singes</term> <note>Literally "monkeys," a period term for a type of mechanical windlass or crane.</note>, and compound pulleys <term>polyspastes</term> <note>A system of multiple pulleys used to gain mechanical advantage in tensioning heavy siege engines.</note> without breaking, there is no doubt that they will not break by the force of the pegs used to string the Lute and the Viol. Now, I wish to finish this Book with the Canticle *Te Deum laudamus* <note>original: "Te Deum laudamus"; Latin: "We praise Thee, O God," a traditional Christian hymn of praise.</note>, paraphrased by an excellent Poet, so that those who join their voices with their Lutes may use it to create very beautiful airs, and that they may henceforth make themselves pleasing to God...

# BOOK THREE
## ON STRINGED INSTRUMENTS.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

### TO DETERMINE THE MATERIAL,
->*the shape, the tuning, and the use of the Spinet.*<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial "L" containing two small figures (putti or cherubs) intertwined with floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

THE <term>SPINET</term> <note>original: "Epinette"; a small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note> holds the first or second place among the instruments that are harmonious—that is to say, those that express several sounds together, and which "sing" multiple parts and create various consonances. I say the first *or the second place* because if one considers it well, and if one judges the dignity of musical instruments by the same criteria used to judge the quality of voices, one would undoubtedly prefer it to the <term>Lute</term>, which is its competitor; but the convenience of the Lute, its grace, and its sweetness have given it the advantage.

Now, to speak properly of the Spinet, we must consider its material, its shape, its parts, its strings, its sounds, its harmony, and its use, both in ensembles and when it is considered on its own; this we shall do succinctly and as clearly as possible.

As for the Material, three things must be considered in stringed instruments. Just as <term>anatomists</term> <note>Early modern scientists often used the human body as a model for understanding mechanical or musical structures.</note> divide the human body into the head, the thorax, and the limbs—where the head is the seat of reason and the home of the senses, and the thorax is the place of the vital organs—so too can one divide every kind of musical instrument into the body, the soundboard, and the neck, as the craftsmen do.

The *body of the Lute is what one calls the <term>ribs</term> <note>original: "éclisses"; the thin wooden strips forming the sides</note>, the back, or the <term>vaulted shell</term>* <note>original: "donte"; an archaic term for the curved back of a lute</note>; but in the Spinet, it is the case, which can be made of any kind of wood. However, experience and reason have taught craftsmen that a great distinction must be made between woods, because they require different handling and application. Those that are more porous and resinous, and which consequently contain more air, have different uses in the making of instruments than those that are denser, more material, and more "earthy."

The craftsman must therefore pay regard to two things when he makes instruments: namely, the harmony or resonance of the instrument, and its strength and solidity. These two things require wood of opposite qualities; for harmony requires the wood to be thin <note>original: "delié"</note> and, consequently, fragile and subject to warping, while solidity requires it to be thick and coarse. Yet, that which is coarse is dull in sound.

Craftsmen who give a great deal of sound to Spinets make them of short duration, and thus they require constant repair; and those who make them too massive make them dull and inconvenient. Consequently, if one wishes to make the body of the Spinet, one must imitate nature in the structure of an animal, which makes the bones hard and coarse for the support of the body, and the muscles soft and delicate for the use of movement.

# Book Three

The *two crossbars*, and all the <term>wrestplanks</term> <note>original: "sommiers"; the heavy blocks of wood into which the tuning pins are driven</note> serve the role of the bones, and the four thin panels that must be flexible serve the role of the muscles.

As for the *wrestplanks*, they are ordinarily made of beech wood, because this wood is very hard and very resilient, qualities which boxwood, ebony, ivory, or other hard woods do not possess.

The side panels are made of linden <note>original: "tillot"; also known as lime or basswood</note>, or some other white wood, so that the <term>Spinet</term> <note>original: "Epinette"</note> may be lighter; otherwise they can be made of any other wood one wishes, provided that the thickness is proportioned to the hardness of the wood: for the harder and more solid the wood, the thinner it must be, and the softer the wood, the thicker it must be, so that they provide as much substance as one another.

The bottom can also be of whatever wood one chooses, but craftsmen make it of fir for large Spinets, and make it one finger thick, so that they are lighter and more portable.

As for the soundboard, it must be of resinous wood, such as cypress or cedar, and principally of fir <note>original: "sapin"; in modern instrument making, this usually refers to spruce</note>, which is the most esteemed of all woods for this use. Its thickness is about one <term>line</term> <note>A historical unit of measurement roughly equal to 1/12th of an inch or 2.25mm.</note>, and when it is well glued and supported upon the slats or wrestplanks, it is this part properly which composes the instrument; for if one stretches strings over a fir soundboard of this thickness, it yields a sound even if there is no box, chest, or instrument body behind or beneath it. The rest of the structure serves almost entirely to keep it in place so that it can support the tension of the strings.

Nevertheless, the surrounding walls increase the sound and give it a certain quality, making it sweeter, sharper, more piercing, more hollow, or drier, and more articulate than it would be otherwise.

To seek the reason why this must be so would be to repeat what has been said elsewhere.

But if someone asks whether the instrument would have any sound if the soundboard were made of oak, one must reply that it would indeed have some, provided that the walls and the bottom of the instrument were thicker and stronger than usual, and that the strings were much thicker, longer, and stronger. Nonetheless, the sound would be barely intelligible and below the range of the human voice.

For the strings must have the strength to vibrate the soundboard of the instrument and the air behind it to produce sound; consequently, if the soundboard is very solid, the string must be very strong; and if the soundboard is immobile, it will produce no sound at all.

One can say the same thing of every other kind of material, such as metal, stone, or glass, which would have the same disadvantage as oak, in that it would be difficult to assemble them because these materials do not join well together. At most, one might make a poor Spinet with much time, industry, labor, and money: as happened to someone in our time who made a very beautiful <term>Golden Lute</term> <note>original: "Luth d'or"; likely a reference to a decorative or experimental instrument made of precious metal rather than wood.</note> that was of little quality.

The soundboard of Spinets must be pierced with several openings arranged diagonally or at an angle across it to allow for the passage of the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "sautereaux"; the wooden uprights that hold the plectra to pluck the strings</note> which touch the strings to make them tremble and sound.

The projection that extends beyond the body of the instrument, and which seems to continue the said body in a straight line, is called the <term>neck</term> <note>original: "manche"; here referring to the keyboard shelf or the part of the case extending around the keys</note> by craftsmen and players of instruments, and serves to stretch the strings upon it, so that they...

### Of Stringed Instruments.

...have sufficient length, and so that the Musician may place his fingers upon them to produce a variety of tones from the same string; now, there are as many pegs at the end of the necks as there are strings on the instrument, so that they can be raised or lowered at will, as is seen on the lute, the viols, the mandoras, the guitars, and the violins. And although the Spinet seems to lack a neck—its shape being entirely of one piece and uniform, and having no protrusion—nevertheless, if we consider the use of the neck, we will find that the <term>wrestplank</term> <note>original: "sommier"; the heavy block of wood that holds the tuning pins</note> which receives the tuning pins performs the same office as the tail of the neck does for the lute; and Harpsichords have a "tail" almost entirely similar. Finally, the said wrestplank had to be a neck continuous and uniform with the soundboard, by reason of the multitude of strings.

We would speak here of the strings of the Spinet, of the material from which they must be made, and of their thicknesses, lengths, and tensions: but it is first necessary to explain how it must be played, for although one makes the bow used to play the Viol or the Violin after they are mounted with their strings, it is not the same with the Spinet, for which one must make the keyboard and the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "sautereaux"; the vertical wood pieces that pluck the strings</note> which serve it as a bow, before placing and gluing the soundboard in its place.

Now, what is called the *Keyboard* in the Spinet is composed of several pieces of wood, long and flat at the end, which are arranged according to the order of the musical tones and semitones, and move from top to bottom as they enter the body of the Spinet; and upon the extremity of the end which is hidden inside, there is another small piece of wood which serves to touch the strings, and which is named a *jack* <note>original: "sautereau," literally "little leaper"</note>, because of its use, for it jumps when one plays the Spinet.

As for the keyboard, it was so named because it contains all the <term>keys</term> <note>original: "clefs"; in 17th-century French, "clef" referred to both the musical clef and the physical key of the instrument</note> of Music: but it is difficult to explain, and hard to understand for those who have not seen one, which is why I will give a figure of it in the propositions that follow.

Now, one may give whatever shape one wishes to the Spinet, for it is the same as with <term>scioteric clocks</term> <note>original: "horloges scioteriques"; a type of sundial that tells time by the shadow of the sun</note>, or the Sun itself, which one can trace and describe in whatever shape one wishes without prejudice to the hours marked thereon. Provided that the shape of the Spinet does not hinder the arrangement of the necessary strings, it matters very little whether it be round, square, oval, or a *parallelogram*—which is its ordinary form. And the width of this *elongated square*, or *parallelogram*, is one and a half feet or thereabouts, and its length is according to how much one wishes to lengthen the string and lower the pitch to which one wants to set it. Certainly, it would not be useless to research the most suitable shape of all to aid the sounds, and to experiment whether the round shape—which has so many privileges in other things—would be the best for this purpose: which could also be researched for the shape of other instruments, but I leave this curious inquiry to the craftsmen.

The strings of the Spinet are ordinarily of brass and steel; for of the 49 strings that are stretched on the common Spinet, the first 30 (or the thickest) are of brass, and the others, which are more delicate, are of steel or iron, because they rise higher in pitch than those of brass, even though they may be equal to them in length and thickness, as we remarked in the discourse on the difference of sounds made by strings of all sorts of metals.

### Third Book

One can also put strings of gut, silk, gold, and silver on the **Spinet**, but experience shows that those of gut are not so suitable as those of **brass**, because they change their pitch too easily in dry and humid weather, and are not so uniform and equal in all their parts as those of metal; and those of silk are even more unequal than those of gut. As for those of gold and silver, it is not necessary to use them for these instruments, especially since those of brass are in no way inferior to them, and they can be tuned higher.

The number of strings is equal to the number of keys, so that if one increases one, one must also increase the other; for example, if one makes a "just" Spinet, which has all the consonances and dissonances in their perfection, one needs 73 strings, so that each octave has 19, as we will show when explaining the keyboards of the Spinet, and in the treatise on the perfect organ, where we will show that one needs 97 strings on the Spinet, and as many pipes on the organ to play in all sorts of keys, all sorts of musical pieces, and to use the <term>chromatic</term> <note>a style of music using sharps and flats to create half-steps</note> and <term>enharmonic</term> <note>a style of music using very small intervals, smaller than a half-step, often associated with ancient Greek music theory</note> genera.

As for the tension of the strings, they must be stretched over the two <term>bridges</term> <note>original: "cheualets"; the wooden strips on the soundboard that support the strings and transmit their vibration</note> which are glued onto the soundboard.

Now, craftsmen have only 7 or 8 thicknesses of strings, and consequently make the same thickness serve for 6 or 7 different sounds. But if one wished to string a Spinet with total perfection according to the rules of harmony, one would need as many different thicknesses of strings as the Spinet has notes, namely 49; for the proportion of these thicknesses and lengths must follow the ratio of the intervals that exist between the sounds: so that if the thickest has 16 parts in its circumference, the smallest should have only one part, because 16 is to 1 as the lowest sound of the Spinet is to the highest.

The same must be said of the length of the strings, the proportion of which is a little better kept by the craftsmen than that of the thickness, but not perfectly. Now, there is no need to explain these proportions more particularly, because they depend on the knowledge of the <term>monochord</term> <note>a scientific instrument with a single string used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</note>, of which we have already spoken elsewhere. And whoever knows the ratio of the steps of the octave, namely <term>do</term> <note>original: "vt"</note>, <term>re</term>, <term>mi</term>, <term>fa</term>, <term>sol</term>, etc., knows the ratio of the thicknesses and lengths that must be given to the strings; for example, if the longest is four feet, the shortest should be half a foot.

The same must be said of the <term>Harp</term>, whose strings are similarly arranged, so that one can say that the Spinet is a harp laid down and overturned, or on the contrary, that the harp is an inverted Spinet as far as the strings are concerned, for they are different in other things: but I shall make a specific discourse on the length and thickness that the strings of the Spinet and other instruments must have to render a perfect harmony, and I will give two tables for this subject later in this Book.

I come now to the <term>temperament</term> <note>the system of slightly adjusting the tuning of intervals so that an instrument sounds acceptable in multiple keys</note> of the Spinet, which is similar to that of the organ; it also has as many keys in each octave as the organ. This is why I will say only here that one must approach as <unclear>closely</unclear> as one can the truth of each consonance, which is the goal of every <unclear>sort</unclear> of temperament, for I reserve the rest for the treatise on Organs.

As for the tuning, which depends on the said temperament, it is not easy to <unclear>receive</unclear>...

### Of Stringed Instruments.

...presenting this is difficult, both because the Masters use different methods to tune the **Spinet**, and because this tuning presupposes a just and delicate ear, there being no science that teaches one to tune this instrument without the judgment of the ear—unless weights attached to the end of each string were to give us all the correct sounds. However, the strings always stretch and cannot last for long without breaking; and furthermore, they would need to have a perfect proportion in length and thickness, and a perfect equality; and finally, the weights would bring too much trouble and too much inconvenience. Nevertheless, I will explain later what pertains to these weights and to the tension they give to the strings.

Someone might say that knowing the thickness of the <term>tuning pins</term> <note>original: "cheuilles"; the pegs around which the strings are wound to adjust tension</note> and the length of the strings, the eye without the ear could testify to the tension of each string by seeing how many turns the string makes around each pin, and consequently how much tension each string would have, which seems to be as great as the volume of the string has diminished. For it must be noted that the string one stretches becomes thinner in proportion as one stretches it more: so that if, for example, it becomes half as short <note>The author likely refers to the string's thickness or diameter decreasing by half as it is stretched</note> through tension, it will also be half as thin as before.

But I respond that the eye is not subtle enough, even aided by <term>compasses</term> <note>original: "compas"; a tool for measuring distances or proportions</note> or other instruments, to discern how much the tension of each string makes it thinner than before, nor what length of string surrounds the pins. And then, even when one knew these details, they would not suffice to achieve the tuning of the **Spinet**, since there are strings that make more turns of the pin than others, and consequently become thinner, even though they do not rise <note>in pitch</note> as much; as experience demonstrates with thinner strings, which rise much higher in proportion than the thicker ones do, even though one does not give them as many turns of the pin: but I will speak again of this manner of tuning.

Now it is a certain thing that there is no other better way to tune the **Spinet** than by assuming a good ear, which hears the accuracy of the <term>intervals</term> <note>original: "accords"; here referring to the harmonic relationship between notes rather than modern chords</note>: which is done in this manner. First, one must begin at the first key or string of the second <term>octave</term>, and tune the 10 or 12 strings that follow by moving from <term>Fifth</term> to <term>Fifth</term> <note>an interval of five notes, such as C to G</note>: so that one approaches as close to the <term>just Fifth</term> <note>a "perfect" fifth, based on pure mathematical ratios</note> as will be possible to find the other intervals. Then one must so divide the Fifths into <term>Major</term> and <term>Minor Thirds</term>, that the major ones are a bit weakened <note>narrowed</note>, and the minor ones a bit stronger <note>widened</note> than their perfect accuracy requires: and these 10 or 12 keys being in tune, one should set the others to their Octaves. But it is necessary to explain more particularly what method one must use to tune this instrument very quickly and accurately, which players consider a great secret of the art: for since we treat the sciences liberally, we must forget nothing that can serve the perfection of **Music**. This is why we will provide the most accurate and prompt way of all those that have been tested until now, while explaining the figure of the **Spinet**.

# ### Book Three

...nuing, or keeping true, will be marked by one of these three terms: **strong**, **just**, or **weak**. We must now see if one can include the various <term>stops</term> <note>original: "jeux"; the different sets of strings or sound qualities controlled by registers</note> that several have tried to introduce into the **Spinet**, as has been done in the organ, so that it might encompass all kinds of stringed instruments just as the organ contains all kinds of wind instruments; however, the one has not succeeded as well as the other, despite the various Panodions <note>The "Panodion" was an experimental multi-voiced instrument of the era</note> and other instruments invented for this purpose.

Now, the <term>viol stop</term> <note>original: "ieu des Violes"</note> is the most excellent of all those that one can add, for as for that of **Lutes** and **Harps**, the **Spinet** imitates them well enough when it is strung with **gut strings**. But before deciding if one can join the viol stop to it, one must consider all the stops that are practiced now. And first, the common stop, which is the foundation of the others, can be called the **fundamental stop**, to which is sometimes added a similar stop at the <term>unison</term>, or another at the <term>octave</term>, in order to make it more full of harmony, and so that it has a greater effect in concerts and upon the listeners. One can still add another stop of a **Third** or a **Fifth**, of which some might have lute strings, and others **brass** or **steel**. These are all the stops that have been used until now, which one can call a **double** or **triple Spinet**. And these stops are all played together, or separately as one wishes, by opening or closing them with certain springs and <term>registers</term> <note>original: "regiſtres"; the sliders used to engage or disengage different sets of strings</note> that one pulls or pushes according to the will of the maker and the musician.

As for the **viol stop**, one can use **gut strings** or **brass**; but the difficulty consists in finding the means to make a bow that touches the strings as loudly or as softly as one desires. Now, the hand of the musician can supply this, for in proportion as one lowers or raises the strings to meet the bow, they will be touched more harshly or more delicately. And one can imagine a movement by springs, or with the foot, which will keep the bow always moving, so that it touches each string as long as one wishes. But I do not believe that one can replicate the graces of the left hand, nor the <term>trills</term> <note>original: "fredons"; rapid ornamental notes or shakes</note>, and the sweetness and raptures of the bow strokes, with which the excellent players of **Viols** and **Violins**, such as Messers **Maugars**, **Lazarin**, **Bocan**, **Constantin**, **Leger** <note>These were famous virtuosos of the French court; André Maugars was a renowned violist, while Bocan and Constantin were celebrated violinists</note> and some others, ravish the spirits of the listeners.

The Germans are usually more inventive and ingenious in **Mechanics** than other nations, and particularly they succeed better in the invention of musical instruments: which I can confirm by the method they have found recently to make entire sets of **Viols** heard on **Harpsichords**, even though a single man touches the keyboard, just like that of another **Spinet**.

But they have no need of a bow, because they place four or five wheels parallel to the keys, though higher than the keys: now, one presses the strings as little as one wants upon the said wheels, which make the sound last as long as the finger remains on the key, and which strengthen or weaken it according as one presses the key more or less hard. The circumference of the wheels is covered with well-glued leather to serve as a bow, and they are made to turn with the foot by means of other wheels and other springs, which are hidden under the wheels. This is difficult to understand without seeing the figure, of which I will speak later.

### On Stringed Instruments

Regarding the use of the **Spinet**, it has this excellent quality: a single person can play all the parts of a concert, which it has in common with the organ and the **lute**. However, its chords and tones approach the true proportions of harmony more closely than they do on the lute; and it is easier to play several parts on the **Spinet** than on the said lute.

As for the **Harp**, it seems to surpass the Spinet in that it retains the resonating sounds longer; for the Spinet's sounds are muffled by the cloth near the <term>quill</term> <note>original: "plume"; the plectrum, often made of a bird's quill, that plucks the string</note>, although one might say that this resonance of the Harp harms rather than serves the harmony unless the player dampens it with their fingers—a function performed by the small pieces of cloth on the **Spinet**. The Spinet has this advantage over the organ: it does not depend on wind or bellows, which force organists to have an assistant to play. The **Spinet** has no need of this, for it represents, without much noise, everything that is done on the organ; furthermore, it is easier to touch and to tune, and it costs much less.

It can likewise be blended with all sorts of instruments, as experience teaches, and even with voices, which it guides and maintains in pitch; but it blends particularly well with **Viols**, which have a sound of percussion and resonance like the Spinet.

The same can be said of **Harpsichords** and <term>Manichords</term> <note>original: "Manichordions"; an early keyboard instrument where the strings are struck by tangents</note>, of which the latter is weaker in sound than the Spinet, and the former is usually louder. To this, one can add regarding the style and shape: the keyboard is at one of the ends of the **harpsichord**, whereas in the **Spinet** and the **Manichord**, it is in the middle. Now, as for the quality of a Spinet, it depends on several conditions and details, but particularly on the <term>bracing</term> <note>original: "barres"</note> placed beneath the <term>soundboard</term> <note>original: "table"</note>, since it is difficult to brace Spinets perfectly. This is one of the greatest secrets of the craft, the research of which I leave to the **Makers** <note>original: "Facteurs"</note>.

### Of Stringed Instruments.

C. The strings H N M are attached at one end to the small iron pins that are seen along the back on the soundboard <note>original: "table"; the resonant wooden surface of the instrument</note> E G M C, and at the other end they are wound around the iron tuning pins E F. However, their length, which serves the resonance, is bordered and determined by the <term>bridge</term> <note>original: "cheualet"</note> E N, whose two arms form an obtuse angle; and L M shows the other bridge, which is set with small pins that limit the length and the harmony of the strings. G H shows the mortises <note>slots or openings</note> through which the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "sautereaux"; the plucking mechanism of the spinet</note> pass. P and O serve as lids for the two small boxes in which one places the spare strings, the spinet's tuning hammer, or whatever else one wishes. As for the *Keyboard* <note>original: "Clauier"</note>, (which contains all the <term>keys</term> <note>original: "marches"; literally "steps"</note>, the primary or diatonic ones of which are marked with their own letters), I have removed the top board that sits on line V X, so that one may see the ends of the small iron pins that attach the keys, of which the Chromatic keys or <term>accidentals</term> <note>original: "feintes"; the raised keys, usually black on modern pianos</note> are much narrower.

Now, each octave of the Spinet has 13 notes, as one sees by the 13 that are engraved on the board Q R, which is raised to close the keyboard, and which belong to the first octave marked by *C-sol-vt-fa* <note>original: "C sol vt fa"; a reference to the note C in the hexachord system</note>. This is so easy to understand that there is no need to dwell on it, for it is enough to have eyes to see the 12 semi-tones into which this octave is divided by means of the sharps, which are between the diatonic notes and which represent the accidentals of the keyboard. But one must not forget the tuning <note>original: "accord"</note> of this instrument, which also serves for the *Harpsichord* <note>original: "Clauecin"</note> and for the *Clavichord* <note>original: "Manichordion"</note>, and which shows the method and practice used by the greatest masters of this art.

I say first, then, that one can take the tone or sound of *F-vt* <note>the note F</note> as the foundation of the tuning. Secondly, one must make the fifth narrowed <note>original: "quinte foible"; a "weak" or slightly flat fifth used in temperament</note> going upward—that is to say, the second note, which is at *C-sol* <note>the note C</note>, should not rise all the way to the perfect fifth of the <term>monochord</term> <note>a single-stringed device used to measure pure mathematical intervals</note>. This reduction is signified by the letter *d* <note>diminuée</note>, which indicates that all the notes where it is encountered must be weakened and diminished. As for the octaves that appear between the fifths, they are always tuned pure <note>original: "iustes"</note>. Now, the five rules above contain the tuning of the diatonic keys, just as those below contain the tuning of the accidentals—that is to say, the Chromatic keys. After one has tuned the first fifth from F to C, one tunes the C below to the octave; and from this C, one rises to the fifth at G, from which one passes to the G above; and then one tunes the D above to the fifth with the same G. In the seventh step, one descends from this D to the octave below; and from this lower D, one rises to the A above, with which it makes the fifth; and from this A, one rises to the higher A to make the octave. In the eighth step, one rises from the lower D to the fifth at E, from which one descends to the octave, that is to say, to the lower E; and finally, one rises from this E to the fifth at *B-natural* <note>original: "# mi"; in the naming system of the time, "Mi" on the "hard" hexachord was B natural</note>, which makes the twelfth row of these five lines.

One then comes to the tuning of the accidentals, beginning at the upper F, with which one must tune the *B-flat* <note>original: "b fa"</note> to the fifth. But this fifth must be widened <note>original: "augmentee"</note> whereas the previous ones were diminished; this is why I have placed the letter *f* <note>forte</note> beneath it to signify that it must be strong, as well as the one that follows. As for the three others, they are marked by *d* because they must be diminished. The 11th or last row of notes signifies the "defect" of the tuning or of the keyboard <note>the "wolf interval" that occurs when tuning in a circle of tempered fifths</note>. Now, one can make Spinets as large as one wishes—for example, 4 or 5 feet long—but what one might desire in this one will be explained so clearly in the treatise on the Harpsichord that follows that it is not necessary to lengthen this discourse.

### PROPOSITION III.

->*To explain the figure, the parts, the keyboard, and the range of the harpsichord.*<-

This figure represents the double harpsichord, as one can see by the two ranks of strings it contains, of which the first is wound around the first tuning pins Z Z, and the other around the second pins L L. From this, it follows that there are four <term>bridges</term> <note>original: "cheualets"; the wooden strips that support the strings and transmit vibration to the soundboard</note>: namely, two straight ones, N M and P O; and the other two, namely T and V X, which determine the harmonic length of the two ranks of strings. These are called *hooked bridges* <note>original: "cheualets à croffe"; referring to the curved or "crosier" shape of the bridge on the treble side</note> because of their shape.

The smallest strings are secured by the pins T T, and the largest by those following the line G B, of which those underneath at B H etc. do not appear, due to the side of the harpsichord covering them. G F E signifies the continuous side, which could not be seen without placing the harpsichord at an angle and crosswise, as *it is here in Perspective*.

As for the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "fautereaux"; the vertical wooden components that pluck the strings</note> R Q, which are almost parallel to the second straight bridge and very close to it, they enter through 49 small holes pierced through a wooden rail called a <term>mortise</term> <note>the guide rail for the jacks</note>. Now, each jack has two pieces of scarlet or other cloth to stifle and dampen the sound of the two ranks of strings. And because the perspective did not allow for them to be represented in such a way that those who have never seen one might understand their shape, I have placed a complete one on the left side, namely K O, which rests perpendicularly on the end *k* of the <term>key</term> <note>original: "marche"; the physical wooden lever the player presses</note> *g h k*, of which *g h* is the end where the finger strikes to lower it and make the jack K O jump. However, the end of the key K is doubled with a piece of cloth so that the jack does not make a noise when falling back down; *i* shows the location of the pin that stops the key.

As for the jack, it is difficult to understand all its parts unless one considers it very closely, for it is composed of seven pieces: namely, the arm K O; the <term>tongue</term> <note>original: "languette"</note> *l m*, which has a small spring made of hog's bristle or some other sufficiently strong hair, which meets the point *l* after passing through two small holes made in the jack very near the small wood *l m*. The fourth part is an iron pin that passes through the jack and the small wood, for which it serves as an axle; the <term>quill</term> <note>original: "plume"; the actual plucking element</note> *m* is the fifth part, which touches the strings and makes them sound. The sixth consists of a small piece of leather glued over the engraving at the bottom of the hollow, in order to prevent noise from the point *l* as it falls back after striking the string; and the seventh is the piece of cloth *n*, which sits in a saw-cut made at the top of one of the jack's teeth.

The case, or the assembly of the harpsichord, is E F G H B D K, and C A I is the place where the keys are located. The arms of these keys, equal to the arm *h k*, are hidden by the front piece, upon which I have placed the range of the keyboard using the ordinary letters of the <term>harmonic hand</term> <note>original: "main harmonique"; the Guidonian system of naming notes</note> C D E F, etc., which signify C-fa-ut, D-sol-re, etc. <note>These are solmization syllables used in the 17th century to identify the position of a note within overlapping hexachords</note> and which belong to the 29 primary or <term>Diatonic</term> keys, which are marked with numbers 1, 2, 3, etc. As for the <term>accidentals</term> <note>original: "feintes"; the raised keys, like the black keys on a modern piano</note> which are between the large keys and which serve to produce the semitones or chromatic steps, there are twenty of them, the first of which is the accidental of the

<margin>Summit or Finish <note>original: Greek "ΚΟΛΟΦΩΝ" (Kolophon); likely used here to indicate the top-most part or the "finishing" bridge of the apparatus</note></margin>

This figure represents the double harpsichord, as one can see by the two ranks of strings it contains, of which the first is wound around the first tuning pins Z Z, and the other around the second pins L L. From this, it follows that there are four <term>bridges</term> <note>original: "cheualets"; the wooden strips that support the strings and transmit vibration to the soundboard</note>: namely, two straight ones, N M and P O; and the other two, namely T and V X, which determine the harmonic length of the two ranks of strings. These are called <term>curved bridges</term> <note>original: "cheualets à croffe"; referring to the curved or "crosier" shape of the bridge on the treble side, resembling a shepherd's or bishop's crook</note> because of their shape.

The smallest strings are secured by the pins T T, and the largest by those following the line G B, of which those underneath at B H etc. do not appear, due to the side of the harpsichord covering them. G F E signifies the continuous side, which could not be seen without placing the harpsichord at an angle and crosswise, as *it is here in Perspective*.

As for the <term>jacks</term> <note>original: "fautereaux"; the vertical wooden components that pluck the strings</note> R Q, which are almost parallel to the second straight bridge and very close to it, they enter through 49 small holes pierced through a wooden rail called a <term>register</term> <note>original: "mortise"; the guide rail that holds the jacks in place and allows them to slide up and down</note>. Now, each jack has two pieces of scarlet or other cloth to stifle and dampen the sound of the two ranks of strings. And because the perspective did not allow for them to be represented in such a way that those who have never seen one might <unclear>understand the mechanism</unclear> <note>The OCR ends abruptly here</note>...

Now, after having explained the principal parts of the Harpsichord <note>term: "Clauecin" — the primary keyboard instrument of the Baroque era, where strings are plucked rather than struck</note>, which ordinarily has fifty keys <note>original: "marches," literally steps</note>, we must not forget the hammer *fcd*, since it serves to tune and to string it; for one makes the loops of the string with its small hook, as seen at string *b*. Its head *e* serves to strike the tuning pins <note>original: "cheuilles"</note> LL and ZZ to drive them into the wrest-plank <note>term: "sommier" — the thick block of wood that holds the tuning pins</note>: *a* marks the peen <note>the thin end of the hammer head</note>, and *e* the handle, which is bored with a square hole at the end *f*, so that it may turn the pins—which are round—without slipping.

But the one which has its strings arranged in triangles, beginning at *n*, is extraordinary. Now, it is not necessary to remark that they now make Harpsichords which have seven or eight kinds of stops <note>original: "ieux," literally "games" or "plays," referring to different sets of strings</note> and two or three keyboards, and that these stops are varied, and pulled, joined, or mixed together like those of the Organ, by means of several small registers <note>sliders that move the jacks</note>, pins, and springs; these ensure that the jacks <note>term: "sautereaux" — the upright wooden pieces that hold the plectrum to pluck the string</note> touch only a single row of strings, or that they touch two or more, because sight and experience will reveal more of this than discourse. Therefore, I come to the explanation of another sort of Spinet, which is not used in France but is in use in Italy, after having noted that many prefer to use a single keyboard that is pushed or pulled to change the stops, rather than the aforementioned springs, which are not ordinarily so reliable; that others use 2 or 3 keyboards to vary the stops; and that there are still many inventions that can be added to this instrument, in which more than fifteen hundred entirely different pieces have been counted. But I shall explain several other things belonging to the Spinet in the discourse on Practice, in which I shall show everything that can be done upon it, and particularly the greatest diminutions <note>term: "diminutions" — fast, decorative melodic passages or "divisions" of longer notes</note> of which the fingers are capable for the chords, which can be played with both hands, and all the graces <note>ornaments</note> that it is customary to practice.

### PROPOSITION IV.

->*To explain the form, material, and parts of the Manichordion.*<-

The Manichordion <term>Manichordion — an early name for the clavichord, derived from the Latin for 'single string,' though it has many</term> has its keyboard of forty-nine or fifty keys <note>original: "touches ou marches"</note>, like the Harpsichord, although it is different in many things, as one sees in this figure **A B C D**, of which the two sides are **A C E** and **C H T B**, and the two others, which go from **B** to **D**, and from **D** to **E**, do not appear. The soundboard **R D M** supports the five bridges, marked by **1, 2, 3, 4,** and **5**, of which the first is the highest, and the others decrease in size. The 70 strings are wound around the 79 pins **R S**, and all the strings pass over and are supported by the bridges. The seven small mortises <note>slots or openings</note> **M K** serve to let the sounds out, and the strings end at **P Q O**.

But one must notice what is most particular to this instrument, namely the pieces of scarlet or other cloth which cover all the strings in the space between **O N P M**, and which dampen their sound so much that it cannot be heard from afar, and it is very soft: this is why it is very suitable for those who wish to learn to play the Spinet without the neighbors being able to perceive it; from this comes the fact that one can call it the *muted or mute spinet.*

Now, even though there are 70 strings, nevertheless each key does not have its own particular string, because there are several rows of two strings in unison, and the 37th and 38th keys share the same row of strings: which happens similarly to the 39th, 40th, 42nd, 43rd, 44th, 45th, 47th, 48th, and 49th. All the other keys have a particular row of strings. As for the bridges, the first carries six rows of strings, that is to say 12. The second has 9 rows, or 18, of which the first 8 are doubled and twisted, so that there are 20 strings in double. The 3rd bridge supports 8 rows of strings, that is to say 16. The 4th contains three rows, or 6 strings, and the fifth has 9 rows: now, one could make a single bridge instead of these five.

It must also be noted that the perspective hides the first five keys, for the keyboard is equal to that of the Harpsichord. But the keys, which are attached with the iron pins **I L**, do not have jacks like the Harpsichord, but they have tangents <term>crampons — small brass blades that strike and stay in contact with the string</term> like the brass one **Y V**, which touch and lift the strings. One sees the 49 tangents in the line **M N**. **X** shows the tip of key **Z**, which is placed in the guide-rack <term>diapaſon — here referring to the slotted wooden rack at the back of the keys</term>, which appears a little beyond the tangents; **R L** show the pins that attach the keys to a bar underneath: and the curved lines that go from these pins to the tangents represent the bodies <note>arms</note> of the keys. **A B I** and **H** can serve as small boxes to put strings, pins, a hammer, and several other things.

As for the strings, their sound is determined by the part which is from the—
