...staples <note>original: "crampons"; metal pins or studs used to divide the string's length</note> up to the bridges <note>original: "cheualets"</note>, for the part that remains between the staples and the scarlet <note>likely referring to scarlet-colored wool cloth used for damping</note> does not sound: from this it follows that one and the same string can serve several staples, each of which produces a different sound according to the distance from the point where it touches the string to the bridge of said string.

It is not necessary to explain the range of this instrument at the bottom, because it differs only in the arrangement of the keys from that of the <term>Harpsichord|Clauecin; a plucked keyboard instrument</term>. That is why I come to its range at the top, which I have set out in full without omitting any note: that is to say, I have filled the four octaves below by placing eleven notes between the two notes of each octave. The 29 numbers, each of which is opposite each note, show the order of said notes, which are all separated from one another by a half-step <note>original: "demy ton"</note>: so that I do not think anything else is necessary to understand everything belonging to this instrument.

One must also notice the small straight bridge O P, which is covered with iron pins that determine the harmonic length of the strings, which pass as far as Q O, where their loops are attached to other iron pins. As for the pieces of cloth signified by all the dots included between P O N, they are twisted around the strings in order to dampen <note>original: "aſſourdir"</note> them and prevent them from sounding from the cloth to the staples marked in line N M, each of which is made of brass similar to staple Y V. It is customary to lift the small lid D S to place strings in its small chest; but these minor practices depend on the will of the <term>Maker|Facteur; an instrument builder</term>.

I come to the lid E G F D, upon which one sees a low octave, which is filled with all the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic degrees <note>referring to the three genera of ancient Greek music theory revived in the Renaissance</note> that one can imagine, or which can serve to perfect and increase the harmony and the refinements of instruments: for each whole tone is divided into four <term>dieses|dieſes; a microtonal interval smaller than a semitone</term>, and each half-step into two. For example, the first UT RE <note>the notes C to D</note>, which is from C-sol to D-sol, comprises five notes, the first of which is separated from the second by a single diesis; that is why I have marked this diesis with a single cross <note>referring to a sharp-like symbol</note>, as I have the 3rd note with a double cross, for the reason that it is separated from the first note by two dieses. Similarly, a triple cross precedes the 4th note, because it is three dieses away; so that only one diesis remains from the 4th to the 5th note to complete the whole tone. 

But it must be noted that I have used three types of notes so that they show the distinction of each degree, and that one may see in a moment to which genre each note belongs: for all those that are worth a full measure, and which are called <term>semibreves|ſemibreues; a whole note</term>, or white notes without stems, belong to the Diatonic genre, of which they constitute the 8 sounds. The <term>Minims|Minimes; half notes</term> or white notes with stems signify the five sounds of the Chromatic genre, and the twelve black notes belong to the twelve Enharmonic sounds: so that this octave has 25 sounds, and consequently 24 intervals: which is so easy to understand that there is no need for a longer discourse.

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*To determine what length and thickness the strings of a spinet must have to produce a perfect harmony.*<-

There are usually four full octaves on the Spinet, and twenty-nine keys on its keyboard, not counting the <term>accidentals</term> <note>Original: "Feintes," referring to the raised keys (sharps and flats).</note>, which are either single or double. When they are single, there are five in each octave, so that the octave of the Spinet is divided into thirteen sounds, strings, or steps. Consequently, these thirteen strings must all be different in length and thickness if one wishes to have a perfect harmony; and because there are forty-nine steps in four octaves, forty-nine types of strings are needed, whose lengths and thicknesses constantly decrease from the thickest to the slenderest. For although tension can compensate for length or thickness—as is experienced on Spinets, Harps, and other stringed instruments in use today—nevertheless, the harmony will be more perfect if one observes the harmonic ratios in the length and thickness of the strings. As for the length, it comes closer to this proportion, although the difference in these lengths is not harmonic; for the string that produces <term>C</term> <note>Original: "C fa vt"</note> is not an <term>eleven-to-ten ratio</term> <note>Original: "sesquidixiesme"</note> of that which produces <term>D</term> <note>Original: "D sol re"</note>, and this one is not a <term>ten-to-nine ratio</term> <note>Original: "sesquinuefiesme"</note> of that which produces <term>E</term> <note>Original: "E lami"</note>, etc. As for the thickness, the harmonic proportion is observed even less in the difference of thicknesses than in that of lengths; for strings of the same thickness often serve seven or eight keys, whereas they ought to maintain the same ratio as the lengths to produce a perfect harmony.

The table that follows contains the thicknesses and lengths that the strings should have; but one must assume the length and thickness of the first—that is, the thickest—in order to regulate all the others by it. One could also take the last—that is, the slenderest and shortest—as the foundation of the harmony, for one may begin with whichever string one wishes. Now, the following table—which assumes that the thickest string is 1/5 of a <term>line</term> <note>A traditional French unit of measure, about 2.25 millimeters.</note> and 5 feet in length, as the thickest string of Spinets and Harpsichords usually is—shows the thickness and length of each string. The first column contains the number of strings; the second, the proportion that the strings have to one another (that is, the proportion of the sounds); the third, the length of the strings; the fourth, the thickness of said strings divided into thousandths (that is, into a thousand parts); the fifth reduces the large numbers of the preceding column into smaller terms; the sixth contains the diameters of said strings, which are divided into thousandths; and the seventh reduces them into smaller numbers.

Now, since the diameter of the 1st or thickest string is 1/5 of a line, let the line be divided into 1,000 parts; the diameter of said string will be 200, and its circumference or its thickness will be 629, and likewise for the other strings up to the 4th octave above, according to the proportion that follows, with the reduction into smaller parts step by step.

## PROPOSITION VII.

->*A deaf man can tune the Lute, the Viol, the Spinet, and other stringed instruments, and find such sounds as he wishes, if he knows the length and the thickness of the strings: from this comes the Tablature of the deaf.*<-

ONE can have several kinds of strings, which may be equal in length and thickness, such as those of the <term>Monochords</term> <note>An ancient scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals.</note>; or unequal in length and equal in thickness; or unequal in length and thickness, like those of Harps and the Spinet; or equal in length, and unequal in thickness, like those of Viols and the Lute. Now, in whatever manner they are different, a deaf man can set them to whatever tuning he wishes, provided that he knows their differences in material, as well as in length and thickness. This I shall demonstrate first with strings that are equal in all things, in order to begin with the simplest, because when they are stretched by equal forces, they produce a <term>unison</term> <note>Two notes sounding at the exact same pitch.</note>, since equal things added to equal things leave them equal.
Now, here are the general rules which must be used to create all sorts of tunings, which will serve here as proof and demonstration, insofar as we have shown elsewhere that they are true and infallible.

->*First Rule.*<-

If the strings are equal in length and thickness, and one produces the low sound which is in <term>C</term> <note>original: "C fa vt"; a specific note in the traditional hexachord system of music.</note> when it is stretched with the weight of one pound, one must stretch the other with four pounds to make it rise to the <term>octave</term> <note>The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency.</note>, for the reason that weights are in the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>In modern terms, the square of the ratio; to double the frequency (2:1), one must quadruple the weight (2²:1).</note> of the harmonic intervals to which one makes the strings rise; now the interval of the octave is 2 to 1, of which the ratio of 4 to 1 is the square.

->*Second Rule.*<-

One must also add to the aforementioned weight the sixteenth part of the greatest weight, or the smallest, so that the tuning is just: for example, one must add four ounces to the four preceding pounds to make the octave just: consequently, 4 1/4 pounds against 1, being suspended from two equal strings, produce a perfect Octave.

->*Third Rule.*<-

When the strings are equal in thickness, and unequal in length, and one wants to set them to unison, the forces that stretch the strings must be in the square of the ratio of the length of the strings: for example, if one is two feet long and the other one foot, and the latter is stretched by one force <note>i.e., one unit of weight</note>, one must stretch the former with 4 pounds, and add 1/4 of a pound, as I said in the other rule, to make it rise from the Octave it was producing below, un-

### Fourth Rule.

When strings are equal <note>The original French text here says "equal" (*esgales*), but the context and the examples provided (ratios of 2 to 3) suggest the author intended to say "unequal" (*inesgales*).</note> in thickness, and equal in length, the forces that have the same ratio as the thicknesses will bring them into <term>unison</term> <note>Two notes sounding at the exact same pitch.</note>; for example, if one has a thickness of 2, and the other 3, and the first is tensioned with 2 forces, the second being tensioned with 3 forces will be at unison: and if the string were a hundred times thicker, a hundredfold force would bring it to unison.

### Fifth Rule.

If the strings are equal <note>As in the previous rule, the examples (2 to 1) indicate "unequal" strings.</note> in thickness and in length, one must offset the length and the thickness to bring them to unison, following the simple ratio of the intervals for the thickness, and the <term>duplicate ratio</term> <note>In the mathematics of this period, a "duplicate ratio" refers to squaring the ratio (e.g., if the ratio is 2:1, the duplicate ratio is 4:1).</note> of the same intervals for the length; that is to say, that the ratio of the forces must be composed of the simple ratio and the duplicate ratio of the intervals. For example, if one string is thick and long as 2, and the other as 1, and one wishes to bring them to unison: if the one that is as 1 is tensioned by one pound, the one that is as 2 must be tensioned by 6 1/4 pounds, because the ratio of 1 to 6 1/4 is composed of the ratio of one to two (which offsets the double thickness of the string) and that of one to 3 1/8 (which offsets the double length).

### Sixth Rule.

If the strings are equal in length, and unequal in thickness: for example, if one is three parts thick and the other one part, and one wishes to make the one of three parts descend or ascend by some interval, such as an Octave, one must first bring them to unison by the 4th rule, by tensioning the one of 3 parts with 3 1/8 pounds, and the one of 1 part with one pound; and to make the string of three parts rise to the pitch of the one of one part, the ratio of the force must be the duplicate of the ratio of the Octave <note>The ratio of an Octave is 2:1; the duplicate (squared) ratio is 4:1.</note>, and consequently it must be tensioned with the force or weight of twelve pounds and twelve ounces, or the sixteenth part of twelve pounds, as I said in the second Rule. And if one wishes to make it descend to the Octave below, the force must be subquadruple of three—namely 11 1/4 ounces—for one must decrease twelve ounces by a sixteenth part, just as one must increase twelve pounds by a sixteenth part. Finally, if one wishes to make string 1 rise to the Octave above string 3, when they are at unison, it must be tensioned with 4 1/4 forces if the other is tensioned with three.

### Seventh Rule.

If the strings are unequal in thickness and length, they must first be brought to unison by the fifth Rule; then one must take the two strings of that 5th Rule, which are at unison when one is tensioned by one pound and the other by 6 1/4. In the third place, the forces must be in the duplicate ratio of the intervals to which one wishes to raise one of the strings: for example, if one wishes to raise the string tensioned with 6 1/4 pounds up to the Octave, it must be tensioned with 26 9/16 pounds and 9 ounces, for 26 9/16 pounds contain 4 times 6 1/4 pounds, and the sixteenth part of 25 pounds.

### Eighth Rule.

One must observe the same Method in the decrease of forces, weights, or tensions when loosening the strings to make them descend, which is kept during the increase of weights that make the same strings ascend; but the ratios must be the <term>sub-duplicate</term> <note>The square root of the ratio.</note> of the intervals to offset the different lengths, and not duplicate as before: that is to say, one must decrease the forces in the same ratio as one increased them,

If they are equal in length and tension, their length <note>The original French reads "longueur" (length), though context suggests the author likely meant "grosseur" (thickness or gauge), as length is already stated as being equal.</note> must be proportioned according to the 2nd table. 3. Now, even though the ratio of the tension of strings unequal in length and thickness must be composed of simple ratios, and doubled by the intervals to be put in <term>unison</term> <note>When two strings vibrate at the exact same pitch.</note>, nevertheless the simple ratio suffices to put them at the intervals of the Octave following the 4th Table, without the practice of the 5th and 6th rule being necessary: for if strings A and B, equal in thickness, are tensioned with the same force, and if B is double the length of A, string B makes the Octave below A; and if string C, equal to B in length but double in thickness, is put in unison with B by a double force, C will be an Octave with A if it is tensioned by a force that is double the force tensioning A.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*That one can know the thickness and length of strings without measuring them,*<-
->*and without seeing them, by means of sounds.*<-

ONE can imagine several ways to find the length and the thickness of strings: first by the <term>compass</term> <note>In this context, a "compas" refers to calipers used for measuring diameter.</note>, which is used to measure the thickness and length of all sorts of bodies, but the strings of instruments are so delicate that the compass cannot serve to find their diameter. 2. One judges their thickness by touch, for by handling them one judges roughly how much some are thicker than others; but this examination is too coarse and too uncertain. 3. One measures them by the holes of <term>draw-plates</term> <note>Original: "filieres". Metal plates with holes used to pull and size wire.</note>, for the wires or strings that pass through and are drawn by the same hole are of equal thickness; but because one does not know the proportion of the holes of the draw-plate, and even if one did know it, one does not ordinarily have a draw-plate, nor holes to measure the thickness of strings, and as this instrument only serves for metal strings, this manner cannot be useful to Musicians. 4. One can measure them by water or other liquids, for that which makes twice as much water flow out of a full vessel will be twice as thick, if they are of the same length: but strings of <term>gut</term> <note>Original: "boyau". Most instrument strings at this time were made from sheep or goat intestines.</note> are spoiled in water, and this way of measuring bodies is too difficult and too uncertain for several reasons that I deduce elsewhere. 5. By scales, for that which weighs twice as much will be twice as thick, if it is of the same material and the same length: but the weight of an instrument string, for example, the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The highest-pitched, thinnest string on a lute or violin.</note> of a Lute, is so small that one has difficulty...

This is why it is necessary to use another way to measure the thickness <note>The French "grosseur" refers to the gauge or diameter of the string.</note> of the said strings; for as for lengths, it is very easy to know them by the compass alone, or by the comparison of one to another. Now, this way can be called *harmonic*, since it is practiced through sounds in this manner.

If one wants to know how much thicker one of two strings of the same length and same material is than the other, one must tension the thinner one with a force, and the ratio of its thickness to that of the other will be the same as the ratio of the previous force to the force that brings the thicker one to <term>unison</term> <note>When two strings vibrate at the exact same pitch.</note>; for example, if the thinner one is tensioned by one pound, and the other by 12, the latter will be 12 times thicker. One will find the same thing if one begins with the thick one; and if one does not want to take the trouble of tensioning them and putting them in unison, it is enough to note the interval of their sounds and their weights. For if the one tensioned by a lesser weight has the higher sound, it is thinner; now, one will find the proportion of their thicknesses by considering the ratio of the 2 weights and the 2 sounds. For example, when they are tensioned by the same weight, if the sound of the thinner one makes a <term>Fifth</term> <note>A musical interval where the higher note vibrates 1.5 times faster than the lower note; the ratio of their string lengths is 2:3.</note> above, its thickness will be to that of the thicker one as 4 is to 9. But because we suppose that their tensions are unequal, one must find the ratio of their tensions; I suppose then that the small one has 3 units of tension, and the thicker one 4; their tensions will be as 3 to 4, and consequently their thicknesses will be as 1 to 3, insofar as the triple ratio is composed of the squared ratio <note>original: "raison doublée." In 17th-century mathematics, the "doubled ratio" refers to squaring the ratio. For a Fifth (3:2), the square is 9:4.</note> of the interval of their sounds and the sesquialter <note>A ratio of 3:2. Here, the author uses it to describe the relationship between the tensions (3 and 4) and the resulting thickness.</note> of their tensions.

These proportions are based on the rules of the preceding Proposition; this is why it is not necessary to explain them more fully, for one can use the said rules to find all kinds of thicknesses of strings, without using any other measure than that of sounds, which is the most accurate of all, provided that one uses it correctly. As for lengths, they are no more difficult to find than thicknesses, for assuming that one knows the proportion of the thicknesses, one will find the lengths by the sounds; for example, if strings of the same thickness make an <term>Octave</term> <note>An interval where the higher note vibrates exactly twice as fast as the lower one.</note> with one another with the same weight, the one making the Octave above is shorter by half. But if the weights are different, one must know the difference, since all kinds of strings differing in both thickness and length can be put in unison, or at whatever interval one wishes, by means of different tensions. Now, the mere application of the rules of the other proposition removes all the difficulties that may be encountered on this subject, and everyone can draw up tables similar to the preceding ones to find all kinds of lengths and thicknesses of strings by their sounds.

For example, assuming it takes 3 strings to cover a <term>line</term> <note>A *ligne* is a traditional French unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch.</note>—which is the 1/12 part of an inch—the proposed string will have a diameter of 1/36 of a line. In this way, that which was not perceptible enough to be measured will be made very perceptible and easy to measure. This happens similarly with many other things; for example, one has difficulty seeing and measuring a very tiny grain of sand, but when one takes it with many others, it is easy to measure. But if one wishes to prevent the string from being spoiled, one must have a cylinder upon which the King’s foot is marked and divided into lines, in order to wrap several turns of the string around said cylinder to cover the entire King’s foot, or a notable part, such as an inch, a line, etc.

If one wishes to use water to find the thickness of a string that is, for example, made of copper, one must fill the vessel into which one wants to submerge the string, or mark the place inside the vessel where the water touches, in order to see how much water it will displace or make rise. For having found the base, or the diameter of the cylinder of water equal in height to the string, one will have the thickness of the string. One can also measure the thickness of metal strings by first reducing them to a cube or a globe by means of melting; but since the first method preserves the metal and gut strings in their entirety, it is the most useful and the easiest, even though it is not strictly "geometric" <note>By "geometric," the author means mathematically perfect or theoretical.</note>. This is because in turning the strings around the cylinder of wood or metal, one can press their coils more or less tightly, making more or fewer of them fit onto the King's foot depending on the force with which they are pressed. Nonetheless, one will come closer to their true thickness by this means than by any other, which suffices in this matter where things cannot be found more exactly through <term>mechanics</term> <note>Here referring to the practical application of physics and manual measurement.</note>. But I shall speak more fully of the different ways of weighing all sorts of bodies and knowing their size by means of water in the *Book of Bells*; and one can see what I have said about it in the *Books of Theory*.

certain places on the instrument, which will show when the strings are in tune; however, a single mark printed on the string is enough to know by how many tones it rises or falls, provided that one can measure its shortening or its lengthening by means of this mark, or by the turns of the tuning peg. This can be done easily if one compares the mark on the string with some other mark on the <term>Table</term> <note>The "Table" refers to the soundboard or the flat face of the instrument.</note> of the instrument, which will reveal how much the string lengthens, or must be lengthened, for each tone or semi-tone.

Nevertheless, because a string that has already been used—and which has expanded and lengthened—has suffered some alteration, it stretches more easily the second time than the first, and the third time more easily than the second, and so on. This is observed in all sorts of strings, which lengthen more and more over time, even if one does not give them any new tension. It is not possible to tune an instrument by knowing only the first tensions that one experienced with the strings, unless one also knows by how much the extension of each string must be greater the 2nd, 3rd, or 5th time than it was the first. This is why it is enough to note here how much each string stretches from its lowest tone to its highest before it breaks, so that one may conclude, by dividing the extension into equal parts, how much each tone or semi-tone makes the string extend more or less. However, the extensions are not always equal, even if one adds equal force, for the final stretches are almost always greater than the first ones. Experience shows that Lute strings stretch by at least a twentieth part before they break; for the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The *chanterelle* is the highest-pitched string on a lute or violin, typically made of the finest gut.</note> which is five feet long, and which one tensions with half a pound, stretches by three inches or thereabouts from the extension it receives from that half-pound until it breaks under the force of three and a half pounds. And after it is tensioned by a half-pound, the second half-pound that one adds to it makes it lengthen by half an inch, and the third makes it lengthen by another half an inch, and so on until it breaks—there being no other difference except that the final lengthenings are a bit larger than the first.

As for strings made of <term>brass</term> <note>original: "leton"</note> and other metals, they lengthen much less than those made of gut, because their fibers are not capable of such great lengthenings as the filaments of gut strings. Gut strings lengthen in almost the same fashion as glue or spiderwebs, because they are composed of a great multitude of <term>spermatic parts</term> <note>In 17th-century biology, "spermatic parts" referred to the solid, fibrous parts of an animal body—like nerves, membranes, and tendons—which were thought to be formed from primary reproductive matter.</note>. Now, since the shortening and lengthening of strings can serve to know how dry or humid the air is whenever one wishes to test it, one must follow the method explained in the proposition that follows; though I do not doubt that one could prescribe some other method to recognize these two qualities. I shall speak more amply of this in another place, and many observations can be made there for the clarification of difficulties in Physics, and particularly to remedy the accidents that prevent the movement and play of machines from succeeding according to the undertaking and the will of the Engineers.

## PROPOSITION XI.

->*How to determine how much the air is drier or more humid each day by means of sounds and strings.*<-

EXPERIENCE shows that the strings of the Viol rise higher in pitch in humid weather than when the weather is dry; indeed, they rise by a tone, a Third, or even a Fourth when the weather is damp and rainy. This being established, we must see if it can be said that the air, or the weather, is exactly as much more humid as the strings rise higher. That is to say, if a string rises higher by a Major Third <note>In music theory, a Major Third is an interval where the frequencies of the two notes are in a ratio of 5 to 4.</note> (the ratio of which is 4 to 5), is the air more humid by a fourth part than it was before? Since the greater term of the Major Third is one-fourth larger than its lesser term, the string that produced the lower note of this Third in dry weather now produces its higher note in humid weather; consequently, it strikes the air five times in humid weather for every four times it struck in dry weather.

This occurs because humid weather swells and shortens the string, or stretches it more than it was stretched in dry weather. Thus, one might say that the humidity shortens it by a fourth part, since a string must be one-fourth longer to produce the Major Third <note>Mersenne is explaining that if a string's pitch rises, it behaves as if its physical length has been reduced.</note>, although this shortening does not appear in the physical length because a greater tension compensates for this shortening. I am speaking here of strings that are fixed between two bridges and cannot actually lengthen. There is no need to consider whether the string becomes thicker in humid weather, for that is not perceptible, and such a small increase in thickness brings almost no difference to the sound. Therefore, one must only consider the greater tension of the string, which humid weather increases just as if one were increasing its weight-load. For when a string is stretched by a weight of one pound, it must be stretched by one pound and 9 ounces to make it rise to a Major Third, because one must square the ratio of that Third, as I have said elsewhere <note>Mersenne refers to the law of strings: to raise the pitch, the tension must increase by the square of the frequency ratio. For a Major Third (5/4), the tension must increase by (5/4)² or 25/16. Since 16 ounces = 1 pound, 25/16 is 1 pound and 9 ounces.</note>. And if it rises by a Major Tone, it behaves as if one added 17/64 of a pound to the weight of the pound that stretched it in dry weather.

It is very easy to find all the other tensions caused by different degrees of humidity by squaring the ratios as I have described. However, it is very difficult to know if the degrees of this humidity follow the ratios of the sounds or of the weights: that is to say, if the humidity is as 9 to 8 when it produces the two sounds of a <term>Major Tone</term> <note>A Major Tone is the interval of a whole step, defined by the ratio 9:8.</note>, or if it follows the squared ratio of the tone, or the tripled ratio of the solids. Thus, could one say that the weather is more humid by an eighth part when the string rises by a tone? Or more humid by 17 parts over 64, because the <term>sesquioctave ratio</term> <note>original: "raiſon ſeſquioctaue" — the 9:8 ratio of a whole tone.</note> when squared creates the ratio of 17 over 64? Or more humid by 217 parts over 512, because the sesquioctave ratio when tripled gives the ratio of 217 over 512?

Those who follow the simple ratio of lines will hold the first opinion; those who choose the squared ratio of squares will follow the second; and those who take the tripled ratio of solids will follow the third. One might also see if it is better to combine all these ratios with one another...

But one must consider other factors regarding the different materials of strings; for gut strings <note>made from sheep intestines, the standard for most instruments of the era</note>, or those made of hemp thread, change and swell more easily and more noticeably than strings of steel, brass, or silver. This is because metals are not as porous or as soft as gut strings; for this reason, the latter should be used to judge whether the air is more humid or drier, because brass strings do not change their sound as easily on the Spinet <note>a small, rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note> as gut strings do on the Viol. Furthermore, a gut string may absorb so much humidity that it slackens rather than tightens, which shows that it is difficult to establish something certain regarding this occurrence and this experiment. Now, one may consider two or three effects on the strings: they either become shorter, or thicker, or they produce a sharper sound. Regarding their shortening, it is noted that the ropes used to ring bells are shorter in winter than in summer; the same happens to those suspended from church vaults to lower the lamps, as is observed in Cathedrals with very high vaults, where said ropes shorten in winter by a toise <note>A French unit of length, approximately 6.4 feet or 1.95 meters</note> or thereabouts. Busbecq <note>Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq (1522–1592), a Flemish diplomat and herbalist who served as ambassador to the Ottoman Empire</note>, Ambassador to Constantinople for Ferdinand, King of the Romans, recounts a very remarkable thing on this subject in his first Epistle: namely, that an engineer who had undertaken to raise an obelisk onto a pedestal, having recognized that the ropes of his machines were too long by an inch, sprayed them with water. This caused them to shorten exactly as much as was necessary for his enterprise to succeed happily, which earned him great credit among the people who were beginning to mock him; and this shows the difference between an ordinary engineer and one who understands the nature of things.

As for thickness, one can find how much it increases once the shortening is known: for suppose, for example, that a string shortens by a 20th part, it will also thicken by a 20th part; and if it shortens by half, it thickens by half; unless it only receives different levels of condensation within the same volume, so that it remains always of the same thickness, and that this thickness is merely rarer in dry weather and more dense and solid in humid weather.

As for tension, it can be judged in two ways: first by the sound, for if the string of a musical instrument rises in pitch by a Fourth <note>An interval where the frequency ratio is 4:3</note>, it will show by how much its tension has increased. That is to say, the tension of the string in humid weather will be to the tension of the same string in dry weather as 16 is to 9; for the tensions, and the forces that cause the tensions, must be the squares of the simple ratios maintained by the harmonic intervals, as I have demonstrated elsewhere <note>Mersenne’s Law: To raise the pitch by a certain ratio, the tension must be increased by the square of that ratio. Since a Fourth is 4/3, the tension must be (4/3)² or 16/9</note>.

But if one supposes that the string becomes thicker in humid weather in the same proportion as it shortens, its tension must be increased as much as its thickness has increased: that is to say, if its thickness has increased by a twentieth part, its tension must be increased by a twentieth part to explain the intervals to which the string has risen. For example, instead of applying the tensions of 16 to 9 to the aforementioned string, if the string has thickened by a 20th part, one must add the ratio of 21 to 20 to the ratio of 16 to 9 to determine the tension of the string in humid weather; for the...

<header>### Third Book</header>

Simple ratios of tensions compensate for the different thicknesses of the strings. If the pitches rise in the same proportion as the ropes of bells, and if all others shorten in humid weather or in winter, it is easy to know how much the strings of instruments will rise; for if they shorten by an 8th part, the instruments will have risen by a major tone <note>A major tone is a musical interval with a frequency ratio of 9:8</note>, given that the string has 9 parts in dry weather and has only 8 in humid weather: it is easy to add several other examples.

One can therefore conclude how much the strings of instruments would shorten if they were not held by the tuning pegs; for example, they would shorten by a fifteenth part when they rise by a major semitone. Similarly, one can say by how much the strings, which shorten because they are free, would receive a greater tension if they were fixed, for the squared ratio of the lengths of the string in dry and humid weather will give the tension: for example, if the string shortens by a fifteenth part, the ratio of its length in dry and humid weather will be from 16 to 15, which when squared gives the ratio of 256 to 225, which is to say almost from 17 to 15; consequently the string of the *Viol* <note>The viola da gamba, a bowed string instrument common in the Renaissance and Baroque</note> which rises by a half-tone, is tighter by two parts out of 15 than it was before, assuming that it does not thicken at all through the tension; otherwise, one must add as many degrees to the aforementioned tension as the humidity has added new parts to its thickness.

Now one can arrange strings in two ways to find the proportions and differences of weather humidity; first, by suspending them, as are the ropes of bells and lamps, for if one graduates the wall or the wood to which they correspond—that is to say, if one divides the surface against which they are suspended into several equal parts, of which the lowest is level with the end of the string when it is at its greatest length, and the highest is level with the place where the string is at its shortest—the middle degrees will mark the different shortenings of the string, and consequently the different degrees of humidity or dryness, just as the degrees of the weather glass <note>original: "Verre Calendaire"</note>, which is called a *Thermoscope* <note>An early scientific instrument, a precursor to the thermometer, used to show changes in temperature or atmospheric pressure</note>, show the degrees of cold and heat; which I explain by the string *A B C*, of which the

<margin>A</margin>greatest length is *A C*, and the shortest *A B*, so that it has the space *B C* for its shortening, which one can divide into as many parts as one wishes, in order to know if the weather is more humid
<margin>B</margin>by 2, 3, or 4 degrees, when the string shortens by that many parts.
Secondly, one can make use of strings that are fixed at both ends, such as those of the *Viol*, the *Lute*, and other stringed instruments, for if one suspends a weight in the middle of the
<margin>C</margin>string, and one divides the surface against which the string (which holds the suspended weight) descends, so that the lowest division is level with the weight, one will see the different degrees of humidity by the different elevations of the weight, just as one recognizes the different degrees of light and heat by the different elevations of the Sun. But because we do not know if, among all degrees of humidity, each one makes the strings shorten equally—that is to say, if the 2nd degree makes them shorten as much as the 1st, the 3rd as much as the 2nd, etc.—one cannot determine this difficulty except in general for the different degrees of humidity.

### COROLLARY I.

Some consider it a great secret—something that seemingly can be deduced from this proposition—that all sorts of heavy loads can be lifted by means of the Sun. For if one attaches a cable to a load during dry weather and in the Sun, the rope will shorten when the weather becomes more humid and when the light is no longer present. One could, in the meantime, secure the load at the same height it has reached, in order to attach it anew to the rope when the Sun illuminates it. This process can be continued until it is raised to the place where it is to remain. For example, if it must be raised by 100 *toises* <note>An old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet</note>, and the rope always shortens by one *toise*, the Sun will lift the load in the space of 100 days. However, if the load is too great, it is very likely that it will prevent the shortening of the cable, and consequently, this "secret" is useless.

### COROLLARY II.

When strings shorten due to humidity, it seems that all their parts shorten equally, assuming that the air surrounding them is equally humid everywhere; for there is no reason to prevent this equality when the string hangs freely downward, or when it carries a very light load. But when it is fixed and stretched upon the Monochord <note>A scientific and musical instrument with a single string used to measure intervals and string properties</note>, or upon other instruments, it may swell more toward the middle, where it seems to endure less stress <note>original: "violence"; in this context, it refers to mechanical strain or tension</note>, because it is softer in that place than near the bridges; consequently, it is more susceptible to the humidity of the air. One might object that the string is more open and porous in the places where it is hardest and where it seems most tightly stretched, but all these difficulties are treated elsewhere.

### COROLLARY III.

It seems that the swelling of strings is caused by water or vapors that seep into the pores of the strings when they do not shorten. This causes every part of the string to endure greater strain, because each particle of humidity forces each part of the string to make room for it and to expand more strongly than before, or into places other than those it occupied, which were proper and natural to it. But when they shorten, they seem to do the same thing as a man who draws himself in and pulls the parts of his body together as best he can when he is very cold, or when he prepares for combat. This is similarly observed in insects and worms that crawl upon the earth, for they gather themselves and shorten to make themselves stronger, to avoid blows, and to preserve themselves.

Now, after having considered all these particularities of strings, we must see what length they must be on the Spinet <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note> and on other instruments to produce sounds that the ear can judge, and how one can determine their pitch when the ear cannot perceive it.

### PROPOSITION XII.

->To determine what thickness and length the strings of instruments must have to produce agreeable sounds that can be judged by the ear; and how one can know the tone or sound of all sorts of strings when they are too long, too loose, or too short to produce sounds that can be heard.<-

EXPERIENCE shows that strings that are too long or too short do not produce a perceptible tone, or at least not an agreeable one if they do; for example, if one stretches a Lute string 12 feet long, it cannot produce a sound that the ear can judge. This is why those who make musical instruments proportion them to the length and thickness of the strings. Now, a string whose diameter is 1/2 or 1/3 of a *ligne* <note>A "line," a historical French unit of length equal to 1/12 of an inch (approx. 2.25 mm)</note>—such as the thickest string of an ordinary Spinet <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument similar to a harpsichord</note>—is 4 or 5 feet long, and the others are long and thick in proportion to that one, which serves as their rule. Thus, the length of the string must be to its thickness as 3456 is to 1, since there are 3456 parts of 1/6 of a *ligne* in 4 feet. And if one measures the thickest strings of the largest Theorboes <note>A large lute with an extended neck and extra bass strings</note> and Lutes, one will find that they are no more than 4 feet long from the nut to the bridge, and one will know the ratio of their length to their thickness once their diameter has been taken. But to know the true ratio that the length of the string should have to its thickness to produce the best sounds possible, one must rely on experience. And because Spinet-makers say that strings of the same thickness as the thickest ones of the Spinet or the ordinary Harpsichord sound perfectly when they are given 4, 4 and a half, or 5 feet in length, one may retain one of these proportions; and because a string 5 feet long can be 1/2 or 1/3 of a *ligne* in diameter, the best proportion of length to thickness will be 2440 or 2160 to 1.

As for the second part of the Proposition, it is very easy to resolve, since we have explained the manner of knowing how many times each given string vibrates <note>original: "tremble," referring to the oscillation or cycle of the string</note> in a given time—that is to say, how many cycles and return-trips it makes. For since the depth or height of the sound is measured and determined by the number of vibrations of each string, one cannot know said number without knowing simultaneously the quality of the sound—that is to say, what place it holds in the Harmonic System. This will be more easily understood by examples than by longer discourse. I suppose, then, that a Lute or Spinet string is 15 feet long, and that it is too long for the ear to judge the sound it makes. Now, if it is stretched with a force of 6 pounds, it will make 10 cycles in one second; and because the sound that corresponds to Chapel Pitch <note>A reference pitch used in 17th-century French music, which varied by region but served as a local standard for tuning</note> is made by 60 cycles in the space of said second, one will know that the sound of 10 cycles is a Nineteenth <note>An interval of two octaves and a fifth</note> lower than said Chapel Pitch, since sounds are to sounds as cycles are to cycles, and there is the same ratio of 60 to 10 as from 6 to 1, which contains the ratio of the Nineteenth.

Similarly, if the string is too short, and it is only one inch—that is to say, the twelfth part of a King’s foot <note>The *pied de Roy*, a standard unit of length in pre-revolutionary France, roughly 32.5 cm</note>—it is a certain thing that the ear will not be able to judge the sound it makes, but if one gives it the span...

Furthermore, because a string has no sound that can enter into harmony as agreeable or even passable unless it is at least half a foot long, it follows that it must be 288 times longer than it is wide to begin rendering a harmony that is bearable. And because this number approaches 300, one can say that the length of strings must be three hundred times their diameter to produce their first <note>Meaning the highest usable musical note in this context</note> sound. Finally, because these same strings can produce sounds that the ear can judge even when they are 12 feet long, one can say that strings produce sounds that do not exceed the capacity of the ear when their length is to their diameter as 6,912 is to 1. THERE are two principal reasons why some strings sound better than others. But the eye is not often subtle enough to notice the flaws in a string, and the hand which finds it equal in all its parts is often mistaken; for if it is softer or harder, rarer or denser, and drier or more humid in one place than in another, it will not yield an equal and uniform sound, because the gut <note>original: "boyau"</note> from which the string is made is not equal in all its parts, whether there be a greater multitude of fibers in one than in the other, or the fault comes from the workman.

As for strings that are all good, and of which some sound better on certain instruments than on others, this can happen because they are better proportioned to some than to others. From this comes the fact that thicker strings yield more harmony on large Lutes than on small ones; and that one ordinarily encounters a string on each instrument which sounds better than all the others, and which has a tone—among all those it can have through its different tensions or its different shortenings <note>Referring to the act of pressing the string against frets to change its pitch.</note>—which surpasses all the others. This happens perhaps when the string is at unison with the soundboard <term>table</term> <note>The "table" refers to the top plate or soundboard of the instrument, usually made of spruce, which vibrates to amplify the sound.</note> of the Lute, and consequently the best tones among those it makes afterward must be at the Octave and at the Twelfth of the said soundboard. This must be understood when the string is long enough, for if it were too short in proportion to its thickness, or too long in proportion to how thin and delicate it is, it would not make the best of its tones heard, even though it were at unison with the soundboard of the Lute or other instruments.

Now, I have shown in the twelfth Proposition the proportion that must be kept between the length of strings and their thicknesses to produce a good sound, and I shall say elsewhere how to find the pitch of the soundboard of all sorts of instruments. That is why it suffices here to conclude that one will know which string sounds best of all others on a proposed instrument when one knows the pitch of the instrument's soundboard; for that string which, having the length and the required tension, is at unison with the said soundboard will yield the best sound. And if several are found of the same thickness, length, and tension that are at unison, the one whose parts are more uniform will sound better; and if all the parts of some are as equal as those of the others, they will sound equally.

If those who place as much value on a good string as on the entire instrument take the trouble to find the pitch of the soundboard, I believe they will find contentment in comparing these two unisons, and they will admit which unison is the most powerful and most excellent of all <term>consonances</term> <note>Musical intervals that are perceived as stable and harmonious.</note>, as I have proved in the books on Theory. For the union that occurs between the pitch of the soundboard and that of the string yields a ravishing harmony, for it makes almost but one same sound of the two; although I do not wish to reject other reasons that can be brought for the quality of strings—for example, that the air enclosed in the body of the instrument must be very well proportioned to the length of the string, which must not find too great a quantity of air to vibrate, etc.

Now, it is easy to prove that the instrument helps the quality of the string, inasmuch as it is no longer so good when it is put on another instrument of equal size, although one encounters other strings that do...

## COROLLARY.

If one wishes to know what the harmonies of the soundboard contribute to the strings, one must observe how one or several strings sound at the unison, the Octave, and the Fifth of the soundboard, etc.; and whether the quality of the string tuned to the unison surpasses the quality of that at the Fifth as much as the quality, or sweetness, of the unison surpasses the sweetness of the Fifth.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

*To determine how many strings, or keys of the keyboard, one can play in the space of one measure—that is to say, how many notes per measure can be made on the Spinet; and whether the bow goes as fast on the Viol and the Violin; or if the tongue and other organs that create passages and trills <term>fredons</term> <note>Rapid, bird-like vocal or instrumental ornaments.</note> can make as many notes per measure as the Spinet.*

ONE can play the strings of the Lute and the Spinet in two ways: namely, all or several at the same time, as happens when one presses down several keys of the keyboard at once to make various consonances or dissonances; or one after the other, as is done in melodic runs <term>passages</term> and trills, and it is of this latter manner that I speak here. Now, it must be noted that Musicians have invented notes to signify all their measures—that is to say, all the timings or species of duration that they give to sounds and voices, from which they compose all sorts of songs and motets. The note that signifies one measure is white <note>The "semibreve" or whole note.</note>, and serves as the foot, the standard <term>diapason</term>, and the rule for all the others, which ordinarily increase or decrease their values by halves. Thus, the second note is worth half a measure, the third a quarter, the 4th an 8th part, the 5th a 16th part, the 6th a 32nd part, and the 7th a 64th part, which is the smallest of all those they have invented, because they have judged that one could not sing a note in less time than the 64th part of a measure.

From this it follows that no one can strike one or several strings more than 960 times in the space of one minute of an hour, or 57,600 times in an hour. As for the comparison of speed used on the Viol, the Spinet, or other instruments, it is very difficult to judge anything other than that those who play them to perfection can strike them with equal speed. To this I add that the voice and the throat cannot move as fast as instruments: which one will be forced to admit after comparing an excellent Spinet or Viol player with an excellent singer <term>Chantre</term>.

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*To determine if one can strike the strings of instruments, or their keys, so fast that the ear cannot discern if the sound is composed of other different sounds, or if it is unique and continuous.*<-

THIS difficulty seems very great to me, for one can acquire a very great speed of hand through long practice, and perhaps we have not yet experienced the full power of art in this matter. Now, we can judge the speed necessary to strike strings to create a sound composed of several sounds from different strings by the speed of the "returns" <term>retours</term> <note>The back-and-forth movement of a vibrating string; what we now call cycles or frequency.</note>, which represent the sound to the ear in such a way that it cannot discern if it is made of a single trembling and if it is continuous, or if it is made by several interrupted tremblings. Experience teaches that the thickest strings of the largest instruments—for example, those of the Spinet and the Theorbos <term>Tuorbes</term> <note>A large, long-necked lute with extra bass strings.</note>—descend as low as the unison of an organ pipe 8 feet long, and consequently their sound is made by 30 vibrations <note>original: "retours"</note> or thereabouts. Now, the ear cannot perceive if this sound is made of different vibrations—that is to say, by an interrupted movement or by a continuous movement. From this I conclude that if one strikes the same string 30 times while these 30 vibrations are occurring, the ear will be unable to distinguish if it is struck several times, and will perceive this sound as if it were unique and continuous. For since one cannot discern the beats, or the turns and returns of the string that is in unison with an 8-foot pipe, one will similarly be unable to discern the...

# On Stringed Instruments

movements of the bow, which will touch the same string as often and as quickly as the said vibrations <note>The original uses "retours" (returns), referring to the back-and-forth oscillation of a vibrating string.</note> occur. For if the bow, or the finger moving 30 times in one second, produced a sound that could be heard, it is certain that it would be in unison with the said string, since their vibrations would be equal; consequently, one would have two sounds in unison—namely, that of the string and that of the bow. The bow's sound would be much weaker than that of the string because it would move less air, although one might say that only a single composite sound would be made from the movement of the string and that of the bow, insofar as its back-and-forth motions would correspond exactly to the cycles and vibrations of the string.

If the string were so long that it was in unison with a 4-foot organ pipe, and it struck the air only ten times in the space of a second, the ear could perceive that the sound was not continuous. This is because the eye can discern these 10 vibrations well enough to count them—assuming, nevertheless, that the sound of each vibration is distinct and discontinuous, and that there are as many different sounds as there are vibrations. For if the sound of the first vibration is continuous with the sound of the second, and all the sounds of the cycles and vibrations form only one same continuous sound, the ear cannot count or recognize each part of the sound made by each cycle, unless it judges each part of the sound by its different strength or magnitude.

For example, since the sound of the string that makes 10 vibrations in a second weakens in the same proportion as the string's vibrations diminish, if the second vibration is less than the first by at least one-nineteenth part, and the other vibrations always diminish in the same proportion (as I now suppose), it follows that if the first part of the sound has 20 degrees of strength, the second part will have only 19, the third will have only 18 1/20, and so on for the others. Consequently, the ear will distinguish these parts as if they were different sounds, provided it is delicate enough to perceive these small differences.

But I do not believe that one encounters ears so precise that they can notice the diminution of each part of a string's sound. Therefore, I come to the other consideration of several strings differing in length, thickness, or tension, which produce different sounds regarding low <term>graue</term> and high <term>aigu</term> <note>In 17th-century music theory, "grave" and "aigu" are the standard terms for low and high pitch.</note> pitches. I say that it is easier to notice the speed of the bow or the finger on these different strings than on a single string, because they have greater differences, and the low and high of their sounds cannot join together so closely that the ear does not perceive the difference—particularly when the strings create dissonances. From this it follows that one cannot touch the strings of an instrument so quickly that the ear does not judge that several are being touched, even if the speed is equal to the touching of several strings at the same time. However, the speed can be so great that the ear will be unable to judge whether they are touched one after another or all together, though it is difficult to determine what this speed must be to deceive the ear and make it believe it receives several sounds at the same time which are actually made at different times.

### PROPOSITION XVI.

->*To determine at what speed the strings of instruments must move in order to produce a sound.*<-

THIS proposition is one of the most difficult in Music, especially since the ear cannot perceive sounds that are too weak. This is experienced by many who have hearing that is more or less sensitive, although one might say that every kind of movement produces a sound, particularly when the air is even slightly agitated. But because it is difficult, and perhaps impossible, to prove that movement produces a sound when no ear can hear it, it is sufficient to show what the movement of strings must be to produce sounds that the ear *can* perceive. This is very easy if one understands what I have said elsewhere. Experience shows that the cycles <note>Original: "retours." This refers to the back-and-forth oscillation of a vibrating string.</note> of the strings diminish according to the proportion of 12 to 11. I have shown that the 132nd cycle is only the one-hundred-thousandth part of the first displacement <note>Original: "traction." The initial distance the string is pulled or plucked from its resting position.</note>, and that one hears the sound of a string clearly enough for the space of 2 or 3 seconds <note>Original: "secondes minutes." In the 17th century, minutes were "prime minutes" and seconds were "second minutes."</note>, even if it is touched very weakly and the first displacement or impulse is only a quarter of a <term>ligne [a unit of measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch, about 2.25mm]</term>. It follows that strings produce very perceptible sounds even though their movement is quite slow. For, assuming that one hears the said sounds while the string vibrates 132 times, it will not travel the distance of an <term>inch [original: "pouce," a French inch, roughly 2.7 cm]</term> in the time of a second, and consequently it will not travel the distance of five feet in the time of a minute—which lasts long enough to take a walk of sixty paces, even if one walks quite slowly, as anyone can test.

One must therefore conclude that it is enough for the strings to move as fast as a **Tortoise**, which travels the distance of an inch while the pulse <note>Original: "le poux." Before the common use of chronometers, the human heartbeat or pulse was used as a standard measure of time.</note> beats once; seeing even that one can still diminish this distance by half and more. So, if one takes the trouble to calculate the path made by the vibrations of thick strings when lightly touched, one will find that it is enough for them to travel the distance of one *ligne* in a second to produce a perceptible sound.

### PROPOSITION XVII.

->*One can know how many times the strings of the Lute, the Spinet, the Viols, and other instruments strike the air: that is to say, how many times they vibrate, or how many cycles and returns they make during a concert, or in any other time that one might wish to determine.*<-

IT is very easy to know the number of beats, or cycles, of all the strings of whatever instrument one wishes, if one has understood what I have said of these vibrations elsewhere—provided that one knows the number of instruments being used and the length of time the concert lasts. Nevertheless, I wish to repeat here what is necessary for the understanding of this proposition: first, that the string which is in unison with an open 4-foot <term>Organ pipe</term> makes 48 vibrations in the space of a three-thous... <note>The text cuts off mid-word ("troiſmilli"), likely meaning "three-thousandth of an hour."</note>

one thirty-six-hundredth part of an hour, which is to say in the space of one second <note>Original: "seconde minute." In the 17th century, minutes were "prime minutes" and seconds were "second minutes."</note>, which is the duration of a heartbeat, or of a very slow and sluggish pulse. Secondly, that the cycles <note>Original: "retours." This refers to the full back-and-forth oscillation of a vibrating string.</note> of the strings multiply in the same proportion as the sounds become higher in pitch; and consequently, when one knows the number of cycles of a string for a known sound, one simultaneously knows the number of cycles for all kinds of strings whose sounds are known.

Now, this being presupposed, I wish to draw up a table by means of which one will know immediately how many cycles the strings of all the instruments in an ensemble make, or how many times they strike the air; and because each period <note>Original: "periode." A complete vibration cycle.</note> of the string includes its outward movement and its return, the number of air strikes is twice as great as that of its cycles; that is why the following table will show only the cycles, the numbers of which, when doubled, will give the number of strikes.

And because ensembles in multiple parts usually span a range of 2, 3, or 4 octaves, and all instruments taken together can extend up to 8 octaves, as I have shown in a specific discourse, the following table contains 8 columns, each of which has an entire octave. But it must be noted that the first column, which is in the margin, serves as a guide for the 8 following it, whose numbers representing the cycles or the strikes of the strings are in the same ratio as those of the said column; as for the first column of cycles, it includes the lowest octave, and the eighth contains the highest.

Now, each octave has 19 strings, notes, or characters, since one cannot notate multi-part music without using this number in each octave, as I have proven elsewhere <note>Mersenne is likely referring to a 19-tone division of the octave, a common theoretical pursuit in the Renaissance and Baroque to allow for more pure intervals in various keys.</note>. As for the use of this table, it is so easy that there is almost no need to explain it, for the first number of the first column, namely 6, signifies that the lowest sound of all instruments—namely the sound of a 32-foot organ pipe—is produced by 6 cycles of the string, which strikes the air 12 times within the space of a heartbeat; and the other numbers that follow, both in this octave and in the 7 others, always represent the number of cycles of each string that corresponds to each note or letter of the octave marked in the margin. For example, the first or smallest number of the 8th octave signifies that the lowest string of the 8th octave makes 768 cycles in the space of one pulse-beat, that is, in the time of one second; and the second number of the same column, namely 800, signifies that the string which has this sound makes 800 cycles in the same time.

From this it follows that one will know how many times the air is struck by each string by looking at this table; for if one wishes to know the number of strikes of each string of one of the octaves—for example, the fifth, which shows the number of cycles—one must take the numbers from the 6th octave, which are double those of the 5th, since I have already said that each period of the string is composed of the turn and the return, and consequently contains two strikes of the air. But if one takes one of the columns for the strikes and not for the cycles, the preceding column will give the number of cycles: for example, if the 6th column is taken for the number of strikes, the 5th will give the number of cycles, which are all—

But so that the use of this table may be better understood through examples rather than discourse, I shall take one of the airs by Monsieur Boësset, printed in the year 1630, which begins with the words *Divine Amaryllis*. It is set for 4 parts, each of which sings 22 measures without any pauses.

The voice, or the lowest note of the Bass, is on **F-ut-fa** <note>original: "F ut fa"; this is a traditional name for the note F in the Guidonian hexachord system.</note>. Because those who perform the Bass in a chamber setting do not ordinarily go lower than a 4-foot open Organ pipe—which is in unison with the thickest string of the Spinet, measuring 3 feet in length—it follows that the lowest note of the aforementioned air corresponds to the first, or smallest, number of the 4th Octave in the preceding table; that is to say, to the number 48.

Now, if one adds the beats, or vibrations <note>original: "retours"; literally the "returns" or back-and-forth cycles of a vibrating string or air column.</note>, of these 4 parts, one will find 12,560 1/2, and one will have the total vibrations of this song: which is so easy to do for those who understand Arithmetic that there is no need for us to dwell on it.

### COROLLARY I.

It must be assumed here that the vibration of the strings ceases after the measure—that is to say, as soon as one has lifted the fingers or the bow from the strings. For if they still vibrate afterward, as usually happens with the strings of Lutes and Viols, and if one wishes to know the number of all these vibrations, one must first know how long they vibrate after their sounds. Once the duration of these vibrations is assumed, it will be just as easy to find the total number of vibrations as it is to find those that occur while the sounds follow the measure. And if one sings this air with 24 Lutes, Viols, or Violins, such that each part has six instruments, one must multiply the preceding number of vibrations by 6, and one will have 75,362 vibrations that the strings of said instruments will make in the span of 22 measures. Now, it must be noted that the time of one measure should only last one second of a minute—that is, the 1/3600th part of an hour—and that if it lasts longer (for example 2 or 3 seconds, as often happens), one must double or triple the preceding number of vibrations, as is very easy to conclude from these discussions.

### COROLLARY II.

One can derive the utility of these vibrations, particularly in the comparison of the movements of the heart and the pulse <note>original: "poux"; an archaic spelling of "pouls," referring to the heartbeat or arterial pulse.</note>, and of several other natural things, with the said vibrations. Now, one can consider how much more or fewer vibrations each musical part must make relative to the other to make a concert perfect; though this difficulty is no different from the one proposed when asking how far apart the parts should be from one another—that is, how low <term>grave</term> or high <term>aiguë</term> they must be to make excellent Music. For higher sounds are made by the multiplication or addition of vibrations, just as lower sounds are made by the division or subtraction of those same vibrations; indeed, all Music is nothing other than the addition or subtraction of said vibrations, or of the beats of the air, as I have already remarked in another discourse.

### COROLLARY III.

It is likely that those who take pleasure in lifting their spirit to God, and who desire to offer Him as many movements of their love and acts of adoration as the strings of the instruments they hear make vibrations, will not say that knowledge of the number of air beats is useless. And those who have enough judgment to consider that Music is nothing other than the number of different beats of the air—and that sound, properly speaking, is nothing if the ear does not give it the nature of sound, and that it would be truer to say that we feel movements of air than to say we hear sounds—will frankly admit that it...

### COROLLARY IV.

Now, it must be concluded from this proposition that if some were able to play 64 sixty-fourth notes <note>original: "crochuës"; while literally "hooked notes" (usually eighth notes), the context of 64 notes per second implies extremely rapid divisions or sixty-fourth notes.</note> within the space of one measure—which lasts 1/60th of a minute <note>one second</note>—they would be moving their fingers, hand, or bow as many times as the string for B-flat <note>original: "B fa"; the note B-flat in the hexachord system of solmization.</note>, which is found in the 3rd Octave of the preceding table, completes its vibrations in one second; and consequently, it would not be possible to distinguish or count the movements of the bow, or the fingers, or the trills <note>original: "fredons"; rapid vocal ornaments.</note> of the throat that would produce the said 64 notes. This is because the imagination cannot distinctly count more than 10 beats of a string in one second, although one may judge a greater number in a confused manner. However, it is difficult to explain how the sound of a string is produced when the bow touches it 64 times in a measure; for if this string does not vibrate more times than it is touched, it seems that the movement of the bow, or the finger touching the string, is the same thing as the said vibrations. Following this, it must be said that the string would have the same sound even if it did not vibrate at all, insofar as the one who touches it supplies the vibration that comes from the tension of the string, since he makes it complete 64 cycles and as many returns in the space of one measure; but I will treat this difficulty in the discourse on the Lyre.

### COROLLARY V.

If one understands the table <note>original: "tablature"; here used to mean a systematic chart or record of frequencies.</note> of the vibrations or beats of strings, one can name the sound each string can make even if one does not hear its sound at all, provided that one sees its vibrations. For if, for example, it makes only 6 vibrations in the span of the measure of the said table, one is certain that it produces the Twenty-second <note>an interval of three octaves.</note> against the lowest note of the preceding air; and if one stretched a cable <note>original: "chable"; a thick, heavy rope.</note> that made only three vibrations in the same time, it would produce a sound 4 Octaves lower than the lowest note of the said air; but I have already treated this difficulty in the 12th Proposition.

### COROLLARY VI.

What has been said until now can also serve for the table of the trembling or shimmering of bells, and the movement of all other bodies—for example, the movement of tree leaves, birds in flight, and other bodies that beat the air. This is because when a body beats the air as many times as the strings of instruments, one can say that it is in unison with the said strings. From this, it follows that one can provide no other formal and immediate reason why one bell has a lower or higher sound than another, except that the parts of one shimmer faster, and consequently beat the air more often. It must nevertheless be noted that we do not hear the air-beats of all kinds of bodies, even though they are

...as frequent as those of the string of the **Lute**, the **Viol**, and **Bells**; as happens when the struck air is not enclosed, and its movements are not reflected, as they are by the soundboard <note>original: "table"; the resonant top surface of a stringed instrument.</note> and by the body of the instruments. From this it follows that one has difficulty hearing Lute strings that move in open air while they are held at both ends with the fingers, because the sound, not being reflected, is not strong enough to be heard, as I have already remarked in another place.

### COROLLARY VII.

It is easy to conclude from this entire discourse that one can determine the sounds, the consonances, and the dissonances made by the movements of the wind, thunder, hail, cannonballs, and arrows, provided that one knows how many times the air is struck by these bodies. For one knows the number of these beats when one hears the sound or noise of said bodies, if one has an ear good enough to judge the low pitch <note>original: "gravité"; meaning depth or gravity of sound.</note> or the high pitch <note>original: "l’aigu"; the sharpness or treble of a sound.</note> of the sound. The same must be concluded regarding the noise made by a candle flame, and the different noises one observes in art or in nature; this can further serve to judge the lightness and the weight of moving bodies, or the force with which they are pushed, as I show in another discourse.

### COROLLARY VIII.

But so that one does not leave this discourse without gaining some profit from it, it seems to me that **Musicians** ought to consider that since the strings they touch never refuse them their movements, and obey their will so promptly as to even break when it pleases them, they should imitate this so punctual obedience by following the will of God and the good movements He gives them to do good and to avoid evil. For since there is no movement that does not lead back to the **First Mover** <note>A philosophical and theological term for God as the original source of all motion in the universe.</note>, it is very reasonable that the movements from which one receives such great contentment, and from which one draws such great harmony, should lead us to Him whose **Providence** incessantly beats the measure of the harmony of the **Universe**, and governs the great concert of the whole world. This is for fear that it be said in Eternity that Musicians were more stupid and more irrational than inanimate creatures, and that they be so wretched that the strings from which they drew such harmony serve on the great day of Judgment to bind and afflict them—if they have so little wit and judgment that they do not relate the harmony of their strings and their voices to the glory of Him who alone deserves the praises of all **Creatures**, whom the **Royal Prophet** <note>Refers to King David, the traditional author of the Psalms.</note> exhorts to their duty by his final words: *let everything that has breath praise the Lord* <note>original: "omnis spiritus laudet Dominum"; the final verse of Psalm 150.</note>.

## PROPOSITION XVIII.

> *All the Musicians of the world will be able to perform the same piece of Music according to the Composer’s intention—that is to say, at the pitch he intends it to be sung—provided that they understand the nature of sound. A new way of marking and beating Time is explained here.*

This proposition is one of the most beautiful in **Practical Music** <note>Practical Music (musique pratique) refers to the study of performance and composition, as opposed to "speculative music" or mathematical theory.</note>, for if one were to send a piece of music from Paris to Constantinople, Persia, China, or elsewhere, even though those who understand the notes and are familiar with ordinary composition could sing it while keeping the tempo, they nevertheless cannot know at what pitch each part should begin. That is to say, they cannot know how low or high the first or the other notes of the bass should be; for if the Chinese, for example, have voices that are lower and deeper than the French, they will start each part lower than we do, and if they have higher voices, they will start higher. I know that one can give a warning at the beginning of the piece of music that it should be sung at **Chapel Pitch** <term>ton de Chapelle; a standard of pitch used in 17th-century French sacred music, though it varied significantly by location</term>, or higher or lower by a semi-tone, etc. But many do not know what **Chapel Pitch** is, and it is too difficult to transport an Organ pipe or some other instrument. Even if it were sent in such a way that it lost none of its shape, it would speak higher or lower according to the wind <note>In this context, "wind" refers to the air pressure provided by the bellows.</note> that one wishes to give it, and consequently, one would not have complete certainty regarding the low or high pitch of the sound.

Now, the Composer will give a certain and universal sign of the pitch at which he desires his music (or any other he wishes) to be sung, if he places next to one of the notes of the Bass, or of the other parts, the number of vibrations <note>original: "battemens de l'air"; literally "beats of the air," referring to what we now call frequency or Hertz.</note> of the air that makes the sound. For example, if he puts "96" next to the first note of the air by **Master Boësset** <note>Antoine Boësset (1587–1643), a famous superintendent of music at the French court</note> of whom I spoke in the preceding Proposition, everyone who knows the nature of sound, or the manner in which it is made, will sing the proposed Music according to his intention, or that of any other Composer, and each part will take the pitch according to their desire.

Indeed, one cannot better represent sound than by the number of said vibrations, since they are in no way different from the sound, which is called the "sounding" or "sonorous number." And if one wished to compose with notes of the same value—for example, with those called **semibreves** <term>semibreues; in modern notation, a whole note</term>, which are ordinarily worth a full measure—one could use all sorts of tempos by making the value of the notes follow the low or high pitch of the sounds (that is, the frequency of the vibrations of the air). This can happen in two ways: for one can decrease the value of the notes in the same ratio as the number of vibrations increases. From this, it follows that the **Treble** <note>original: "Dessus"; the highest vocal or instrumental part.</note> will go faster than the **Bass**; for when the Treble sings an **Octave** higher, the semibreve note will only be worth a **minim** <term>minime; half the value of a semibreve, or a modern half-note</term>, which is to say half a measure. And if it sings a **Fifteenth** <note>An interval of two octaves.</note>, it will be worth only 1/4 of a measure, insofar as the number of vibrations that make the Treble is 2 or 4 times greater than that of the vibrations that make the Bass.

But it is not necessary to know the number of vibrations to make the same notes serve different times, for it is enough to know how much...
