As for the manner used to find the sound once one has the number of air vibrations in a given time, I have explained it elsewhere; therefore, I will only say here that a string 48 or 24 feet long, being stretched by a given force or by a known weight of any kind, shows the number of air vibrations that make each sound, for the vibrations multiply in proportion as the string is shortened. Thus, if it beats the air three times in a moment when it is 24 feet long, it beats it 72 times when it is only one foot long.

### COROLLARY I.

Since Musicians know how many air vibrations are needed to make all sorts of sounds through the preceding propositions, it is reasonable that they offer as many movements of their hearts, and as many acts of reverence and adoration to God, who is the prime mover, and whose order and guidance are necessary for every trembling of a string and every movement of the air. May the movement of the strings, which is so prompt and so fast that it cannot be perceived or measured, make us hasten our step to approach Him to whom all our movements and all our thoughts belong.

### COROLLARY II.

If one wishes to determine the pitch of the voice at which one wants the proposed note or part to be sung, there is no means more general and more certain than to give a proper name to each pitch, taken from the number of air vibrations that make all sorts of tones or sounds. For example, if one wants to sing the preceding air by Master <term>Boësset</term> <note>Antoine Boësset (1587–1643), a famous composer of *airs de cour* at the French royal court.</note>, and one wishes to begin with the first note of the <term>Bass</term>, one must say that it is at the pitch of 48, insofar as the string that makes this sound vibrates 48 times in the time of one measure, which lasts 1/60 of a minute—that is to say, in one second.

### COROLLARY III.

Since I have shown the way to sing every kind of music in the same pitch as the Composer desires it to be sung in all places of the world, it is still necessary to explain how one can keep the same tempo <term>mesure; here referring to the time or speed of the music</term> according to the intention of the same Composer, even if he be dead or absent. This is very easy by means of a suspended string <note>This is an early description of a pendulum used as a metronome</note>, the uses of which I have given elsewhere; for it is enough for the Composer or the Music Master to mark the length of the string in the margin of the composition, where each swing <note>original: "retour"</note> shows the time of the measure. For example, if he wishes each measure to last only one second, he will mark 3 1/2 <note>This refers to 3.5 feet, a length that approximates a one-second pendulum swing in 17th-century units</note> which signifies that the string hanging from a nail, and which holds a weight attached to the other end, makes each of its swings, or each return, in one second of a minute. If one wishes to hasten the tempo, and that it lasts only half a second, the string must be shortened in a sub-doubled ratio <note>The square root of the ratio; the author is describing the physics of a pendulum where frequency is related to the square root of its length</note> of the times or measures, that is to say it must be made 4 times shorter; and if one wishes it to last 2 seconds, it must be made fourteen feet; if it should last 3 seconds, it will be 28 1/2 feet, and for 4 seconds, it will have 52 feet, etc. for the lengths of the strings are in a doubled ratio <note>A squared ratio</note> to the times.

Now, if all the Musicians in the world communicated to each other the different times of their measures and the pitches of their compositions in this manner, they would know which movements are suited to give pleasure to all sorts of men, whose inclinations they might know: for 50, which is in the margin of the Song of the 2nd Corollary, signifies the pitch, and 14 signifies the tempo of the measure.

### COROLLARY VI.

### COROLLARY VII.

There is no difficulty in finding the number of vibrations of any proposed string, for if one extends it 10 or 12 **toises** <term>toise: a historical French unit of length, roughly 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet</term> long on a **Monochord** <term>Monochord: an ancient scientific and musical instrument with a single string used to measure mathematical intervals</term>, or on some other plane, or if one suspends it from top to bottom so that it is attached and fixed at both ends—either on both sides with two bridges, or on one side with a nail and on the other with a weight—one will easily count its vibrations, especially since it will make a very small number, for example 2 or 3 in each second. 

But it requires 2 or 3 people to observe the number of these vibrations exactly, one of whom counts the vibrations while the other counts the seconds; for if one divides the number of seconds by the number of vibrations, one will know how many it makes in each second. And if one extends a string of a **Spinet** <term>Spinet: a smaller, rectangular version of a harpsichord</term> or **Lute** to 100 or 120 feet, as I have done, one will find that each vibration of this string occurs in one second, and that half of the same string makes two vibrations in a second, the quarter makes 4, the eighth part 8, the sixteenth 16, the thirty-second 32, and so on for the others. This is because the number of these vibrations increases in the same ratio as the length of the string decreases: so that when the string of 100 feet long makes one vibration in a second, or in one beat of the heart and the pulse, it makes 100 when it is only one foot long, and 200 when it is only half a foot. But I have explained these vibrations so fully in another place that it is not necessary to speak of them here.

9 and 4; and say: if 4 gives 9, how much will 3 (which is the weight suspended from the gold and iron strings) give me? In this way, one can lengthen or shorten the said strings so that they are all in unison; for since the gold string, for example, has a sound lower by a Fifth than the iron string, if one divides the gold string into three parts and shortens it by one third (so that it has only two parts of length), it will be in unison with the iron. Conversely, if one divides the iron string into two equal parts and lengthens it by one of those parts (so that it has 3), it will be in unison with the gold string.

The same must be said of other strings according to the relationship they have with one another, from which it is easy to conclude several things in favor of the <term>Spinet: a smaller, rectangular or wing-shaped member of the harpsichord family</term>. Secondly, one will know the weight of all the strings with which the Spinet will be strung; and experience will teach how long each metal remains without changing its tune, and how much the sound of one is more pleasing, and louder or softer, than the other. 

I leave aside other considerations to remark upon the different sounds of metals that cannot be drawn through the holes of a <term>draw-plate: a tool used to thin metal into wire by pulling it through increasingly small holes</term>, because they heat up and melt; and even though they could be drawn, such as the fine tin called English or Cornish tin, nonetheless, once drawn, it is not possible to stretch them tightly enough over the bridges to produce any sound, for they break after being stretched. We must now explain the second part of this Proposition, which teaches that the sounds of metals containing more Mercury are deeper (more grave); that those containing more fixed Sulphur yield higher (more acute) sounds; and that a body is heavier when it has more mercury, and lighter when it has more sulphur; consequently, high sounds follow the lightness of bodies, and deep sounds follow their weight.

I explain this by first assuming that there are metals and other bodies that partake more of mercury or sulphur than others, as we see by experience when performing a <note>original: "viue anatomie"—a "living anatomy" or chemical analysis through heat</note> "live anatomy" and the separation of principles. However, it is very difficult to know exactly what quantity of sulphur or mercury is in each body, and particularly in gold, which is so perfectly mixed that it is impossible, or very difficult, to separate its mercury from its sulphur—even though it can be rarefied into a very beautiful <gloss>tincture</gloss> separated from any other solvent or mixture, which cannot return to a solid body once it has been passed through the <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term>.

I assume, in the second place, that a metal is less subject to corruption when it contains more mercury and less sulphur, and that one containing more sulphur and less mercury is more imperfect and more corruptible. For the qualities of mercury—namely, cold and moist—are directly opposed to those of fire. Furthermore, nature always separates the impure and sulphurous parts as much as she can, leaving only the weight of sulphur sufficient to congeal the mercury and reduce it into a paste capable of receiving metallic hardness and compaction. She similarly rejects the excess of mercury's natural qualities to arrive at such a perfect temperament of these two substances and their qualities that she can preserve the body against the test and violence of fire, and other things that share the nature of fire—such as <term>antimony: a brittle, silvery-white metalloid</term> and <term>aqua regia: literally "royal water," a highly corrosive acid mixture</term>—and this is what we call <gloss>fixation</gloss>. But when metallic matter is congealed by the accidents of the mine before it is well purified, the metal is too full of superfluous and combustible sulphur, which causes the parts of the metal not to bind well together, and consequently they are easier to separate b... <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>

fire or by other agents, more or less according to the degree of their imperfection. This being established, one can conclude that gold, being the most perfect of metals, has more <term>Mercury: in alchemy, the principle of fluidity, density, and "metallicity"</term> than <term>Sulphur: the alchemical principle of combustibility, heat, and "dryness"</term>; and that other metals decrease in perfection according to their greater quantity of sulphur. Now, experience teaches us that the most perfect metals are the heaviest and yield deeper (graver) sounds; and that those containing more sulphur yield higher (more acute) sounds, because sulphur is dry and hot, participating more in the nature of air than mercury, which is aqueous, moist, and cold. From this, it follows that these bodies are more "rare" <note>meaning less dense or having more internal space</note>, having their parts further apart and more mixed with impurities and air, which makes them suitable for sound. Mercury, on the contrary, makes the parts of a body more compact and tightly packed, so they are not mixed with as many parts of air—which is the primary medium of sound.

One might nevertheless raise an objection in favor of lead, which is heavier and yields a duller sound than other metals, even though it is more imperfect than them regarding metallic solidity. However, it does not have this imperfection because of an abundance of combustible sulphur, but because of the "rawness" of its mercury, which is greater than in other imperfect metals. This is why its sound is as deep as or deeper than gold; for just as an excess of heat and dryness makes a body's sound high, likewise the excess of moisture, cold, and wateriness found in lead makes its sound deeper and duller.

As for pure copper <note>original: "cuiure franc"</note>, it is more perfect and less sulphurous than yellow copper <note>original: "cuiure iaune," referring to brass</note>, which has more airy, impure, and combustible sulphur. Consequently, it seems it should have a duller sound, even though one does not notice a difference between the sounds of a copper string and a <term>brass: an alloy of copper and zinc</term> string—perhaps because the difference is not perceptible, any more than the difference in their weights, as can be seen in the preceding tables.

One might also object that purified mercury is heavier than gold, and yet it is not as "perfect." But it suffices to say that natural mercury does not weigh as much as gold, which surpasses it by a sixth part; for mercury contains some sulphurous and inflammable parts, and others that are excessively aqueous and moist, which dissipate easily in fire. It is held, nonetheless, that mercury from Spain is the most perfect.

Now, these impurities cause the parts of mercury to be further from one another and less compressed, making its body less heavy within the same volume than if it were purified. But art <note>referring to the "art" of chemistry or alchemy</note> can purify it so much that it approaches the purity of the mercury found in gold. Fire can consume the rawness and all the filth found in mercury, even if it is not "fixed" <note>meaning made solid or non-volatile</note>, since the metallic sulphur would need to stop it, as it does in other metals. This common mercury can be so purified that it will weigh more than gold by a twentieth part, because gold has sulphur which makes it less heavy than if it had only its mercury. This is why gold is less heavy than perfectly purified common mercury, which is as heavy and as perfect as the mercury of gold purified by nature.

If anyone wishes to test this, they must fill two equal tubes, one with gold and the other with mercury <term>sublimated: a process of purification where a substance is heated into vapor and then condensed back into a solid or liquid</term> seven times, and weigh the gold and the mercury each separately; but one must discard the volatile parts of mercury at each—

## COROLLARY.

If the Alchemists could provide us with a certain knowledge of the temperament of every body through their three principles: for example, which principle predominates in a person who has 4 degrees of <term>cholere: choler or yellow bile, one of the four humors thought to cause a hot, dry, and irritable temperament</term>, of joy, or of sadness; and assuming a man weighs a hundred pounds, how many pounds he has of each type of <term>salt: the principle of fixity and earthiness</term>, how much <term>sulfur: the principle of inflammability and heat</term>, and <term>mercury: the principle of fluidity and volatility</term>, both in weight and in size; which principle decreases, alters, or increases in all sorts of diseases and passions of the soul; how much each meal increases the three principles, and how much is dissipated every day; in what weight and quantity the three principles must meet in someone who has the qualities of a Musician, and in what quantity and weight they are in each metal—they would help us greatly. They would oblige us to follow their manner of reasoning, both regarding sounds and weights as well as other qualities of bodies, which I have already treated in the books of Theory according to their principles.

But if one wishes to explain the reason for the diversity of sounds without departing from ordinary Philosophy or Medicine, one must say that the lowest sound comes from the metal or body that is most earthy and heavy, having more water mixed with its earth; and that the high sound comes from the fire and heat within each body. For we experience that the more a man has bile and choler, the louder and higher he speaks; this is represented by the strings of instruments, which are the thinnest and shortest, and by all sorts of movements that are sudden and light.

## PROPOSITION XX.

-> *To explain the proportions of all the parts of the Spinet and the Harpsichord, and their construction.* <-

Spinets are made in various sizes, but they differ little in their design; therefore, it suffices to explain how to make one two-and-a-half feet long and 16 inches wide on the inside, and to note what is unique to larger ones. I say first, then, that the one I describe here has a frame four-and-a-half inches high, and that the boards forming the bottom and the sides of the case are joined with <term>dovetails: a strong carpentry joint where interlocking "tails" and "pins" resemble a bird's tail</term>. Then, one glues the two bars B N and A E across the bottom opposite the ends of the two small boxes O and N, so that they are slightly further apart than the length of the keyboard. They are one inch thick and 17 <term>lignes: an old French unit of measurement, roughly 1/12th of an inch</term> high. After this, the <term>wrest-plank: the heavy block of wood (sommier) that holds the tuning pins</term> is placed and glued against the right side of the assembly at the height of the bridge-work, which serves to support the <term>pins: the metal pegs used to tune the strings</term>, and which is glued within 14 lines of the edges of the case. The wrest-plank and the bridges are also fastened with small pins that are riveted.

...so that everything holds more firmly, and shims are placed under the <term>sommier: the wrest-plank or pinblock where the tuning pins are set</term> to support it. One also glues the balance rail, which serves to carry the <term>clauier: keyboard</term>; it is made 2 and a half <term>lines: a historical unit of measurement, about 2.25 millimeters</term> thick and 16 lines wide. After having pierced it with as many holes as needed using a punch—corresponding to the number of <term>marches: the lower keys or "naturals"</term> and <term>feintes: the upper keys or "sharps and flats"</term> that must rest upon it—one places the pins through a small piece of cloth. Simultaneously, one pierces all the keys to allow these pins to enter easily, so that they may pivot freely like a <term>bacule: a seesaw or rocker motion</term> when they are touched to play the <term>Epinette: a Spinet, a small harpsichord-like instrument</term>, as seen at the points between E and F. A strip of cloth is added under the back end of the keys to level the keyboard. At the very end of these same keys, one places small pins G and H, which enter the saw-cuts of the <term>Diapason: here referring to the guide rack at the back of the keys</term> I and K; this rack keeps the keyboard straight and in place, and it is made to the height of the bars and 8 or 10 lines thick.

The holes for the keyboard pins E and F are drilled at one-third of the length of the keys to provide the pivoting action at the back. Then, the keyboard is divided into 49 or 50 keys, narrowing the back of each by half a key-width on each side. It is from the middle of these keys that one marks the guide rack for the alignment of the keyboard; however, the saw-cuts must end by widening into a <term>queuë d'aronde: a dovetail shape</term>, so that the 50 pins at the ends of the keys have enough clearance and do not touch the sides.

Now, while the keyboard is still just a single piece of wood, it must be placed on the balance rail and secured at both ends with two pins placed at the first and last keys. This allows one to drill the holes in the middle of the keys, though the holes for the sharps must be four lines higher than those of the naturals. One must also mark the mortise piece above the ends of the keys and trace the <term>mortaises: the rectangular slots or mortises</term> on the top and bottom. Then, it must be sawn in two, so that one half can be glued to the soundboard and the other onto a small board of <term>sapin: fir wood</term>, which is then glued very straight, opposite the first, onto the two bottom bars. For this purpose, one makes this piece—which is of very soft <term>hestre: beechwood</term>—eleven lines wide, planing it until it is very thin and slender.

This fir board must be pierced, and the mortises widened slightly from the inside. Then, a piece of sheepskin is glued on top, which is cut cleanly to the size of the mortises with a small <term>fermoir: a type of carpenter's chisel</term>. Because there are only 25 of them, small spacers made of thick Spinet strings are inserted through holes made with a needle-point punch, and then they are riveted under the board. Afterward, the straight <term>cheualet: bridge</term> F-G is placed along the mortise piece, where the first lower pin F is three inches away from the <term>plume: the quill or plectrum</term> of the first <term>sautereau: the jack, the vertical mechanism that plucks the string</term>, or from the first string K. The other bridge is broken into two parts, as seen at B-H-I, where the small end I is approximately 3 inches away from the end of the straight bridge G. The section H-I is four inches long.

After the guide rack has been sawn, it must be glued into the place where it was marked by the ends of the keys. Then, the lower mortise piece must be fixed and glued perfectly upright, partly on the guide rack and partly on the bars, so that the jacks do not interfere with one another. These jacks must be made of <term>cormier: service tree wood</term> or <term>poirier: pearwood</term>; then they must be marked with numbers to recognize them if they become mixed together. It is easy to set them...

These tongues should be made of hornbeam, and their spring—made from a hog’s hair—must not be too strong, so that it returns them gently. Afterward, a saw-cut is made at the top of the <term>sautereau: the jack, the vertical wooden piece that plucks the string</term> in order to insert a piece of cloth to dampen and silence the sound of the string. The quills must be trimmed so that they do not extend past the strings by more than their own thickness; and to ensure they are all the same length, the strings must be spaced upon the <term>cheualets: bridges</term> to set the pins as evenly as possible.

When all this is done, the <term>table: soundboard</term> is braced with three bars on the underside; one is placed at the bottom along the mortise-piece between the bridge and said piece; it is one foot long and 1.5 units high. The two other smaller bars are angled behind the bridge, one on one side and the other on the opposite side. Another large bar of the same length is glued, starting opposite the middle of the keyboard and extending to within ten jacks of the top end; however, three small notches are cut underneath it, and two in the smaller bars, so that they provide more harmony to the instrument.

The bottom support piece is also installed to carry the soundboard at the front, opposite the keyboard at the height of the <term>tringlage: the guide-rail system</term>; this is why it is glued against the small cases, the triangles, and the <term>sommier: wrest-plank or pinblock</term>, and it is further secured with pins so that it holds better. After the <term>feintes: the "accidental" or sharp/flat keys</term> have been placed and everything is quite dry, the keyboard is lifted out to clean the bars and the <term>marches: the "natural" or lower keys</term>, and to polish them with <term>preſle: horsetail or scouring rush, a plant used as a natural fine abrasive</term>, and to glue the soundboard in place permanently. For this purpose, one uses awls and <term>eſtraignoirs: clamps or presses</term> all around the edges to make it join perfectly; its thickness is only one <term>line: approximately 2.25 millimeters</term>. When it is dry, moldings are added at the top and bottom; then the pins are spaced to hold the strings by their loops, along with the tuning pins in the wrest-plank to tension them. It is also customary to scrape the soundboard and polish it with horsetail, which is likewise done to the keyboard.

One must also not forget to place pieces of cloth on the parts of the keys where the jacks rest and strike, so that they make no noise; however, they should only be glued at the two ends so that they remain softer and gentler in the middle where they touch the jacks. This being done, the keyboard is returned to its place, the tongues are quilled, and the jacks are trimmed as they are made to "speak" <note>This refers to "voicing" the instrument—trimming the quills until each note produces the correct volume and tone.</note>; so that nothing remains but to string the Spinet with good yellow and white strings. The yellow <note>original: "iaunes" — brass strings</note> are for the first octave, of which the first four must be of the third thickness (which the makers call *number three*), the following of the second, and the last of the first; and those of the other higher octaves must be of the three other thicknesses of the white <note>original: "blanches" — iron or steel strings</note> ones. Now, this Spinet of two and a half feet is at the octave of <term>ton de Chapelle: Chapel pitch, the standard reference pitch for church music</term>; and the one made three and a half feet long, 17 inches wide, and 5 inches high in construction, is at the fourth of said Chapel pitch, to which the five-foot long Spinet descends. But the wrest-plank of these larger Spinets is not straight; for after following the side board halfway, it angles and meets the piece behind the guide-rails 16 lines lower than the top edge. ### PROPOSITION XXI.

->*Explaining the new inventions that our century seems to have added to the Spinet and Harpsichords.*<-

IT seems that those of the previous century did not have Harpsichords, nor Spinets with two or more stops, such as we have now, which have four stops and four rows of strings, and which are named <term>Eudisharmoste: from the Greek for "well-proportioned harmony"</term>, of which the largest corresponds to the 12-foot stop of the Organ, the second is at the Octave, the third at the Twelfth, and the fourth at the Fifteenth above, whether they have only one keyboard, or whether they have two or three. One can also add a new stop at the major Third, or rather at the Tenth or seventeenth major, which are the repetitions of the said Third: which could serve for the investigation of nature, by considering why two strings that are at a Fifth produce a nasal sound <note>original: "nasardent," referring to the specific overtone quality of the 'nasard' organ stop</note>, and what effect those that are at the Third, whether major or minor, have, etc. Now, although there are only four stops in the Eudisharmoste, one nevertheless varies them in several ways according to the number of combinations, sets of three, and sets of four that can be made from four different things, of which I have spoken very extensively in the book on Airs and Songs.

One can also attribute to our time the invention of drums or barrels <note>original: "barillets," referring to the pinned cylinders used in mechanical clocks and instruments</note>, which are used to play several pieces of Music on Spinets without the labor of the hand; for the Germans are so ingenious that they play more than 50 different pieces by means of several springs, which even make ballets dance with several figures that jump and move to the rhythm of the songs, without it being necessary to touch the instrument after having wound its springs. And I do not doubt that one could fill an entire city with Music, so that there will be no house that does not have its harmony when some spring is released, of which I will perhaps speak in the book on Organs. Similarly, harmonic spinning wheels have been invented for spinning and winding thread, which sing or remain silent when one wishes; and every artisan can mix Music into his works by means of wheels, cranks, pinions, lanterns, and several kinds of springs, which compose the <term>Automata: self-operating machines</term>, which each names as he pleases—for example, Mador and Angelique. Some make two rows of strings speak with a single quill of a <term>sautereau: jack, the vertical wooden piece that plucks the string</term>, and others quill the jacks so delicately that the harmony of the strings is much more ravishing; and I have no doubt that one can still add several refinements and several stops to Harpsichords, the research of which belongs to the <term>Facteurs: instrument makers</term>.

### PROPOSITION XXII.

->*Explaining the diagrams of the parts of the Spinet, and the manner of playing the Harpsichord, and all that can be played upon it.*<-

Before explaining the manner of playing the Harpsichord, it is necessary to provide here the diagrams that serve to understand the construction of the Spinet, especially since they were not included in the 20th Proposition, which cannot be understood without them. The natural keys <term>natural keys: original "marches," the lower, main keys of the keyboard</term>, of which only half are visible, are made of a single piece of wood, which is divided nearly along the lines marked here. D-B shows the locations of the tuning pins, and finally E-K D is the hitch-pin rail, equal to the one inside which is also seen in the previous figure.

[...the accidentals] are almost as different in their touch as in their uses. But be that as it may, it is enough to note what is necessary for the beautiful touch of the Harpsichord <note>original: "Clauecin"</note>; which consists first in carrying both hands together over the keyboard in such a way that they are in no way forced or distorted, and that their regulated movement gives no less satisfaction than the sound of the strings. In the second place, that the left hand should play two or three good chords while the right makes diminutions <term>diminutions: the practice of breaking long notes into rapid, decorative melodic figures</term> and passages, and vice versa. In the third place, one must perform the cadences—whether simple, double, or triple—so clearly that confusion does not obscure their beauty and charms. In the fourth place, one must keep the measure as accurately as can be done, and consequently one should play 16 semiquavers <note>original: "doubles [crochuës]"</note> or 32 demisemiquavers <note>original: "triples crochuës"</note> in the same time as 4 quarter notes <note>original: "noires"</note> in binary measure, and 12 semiquavers or 24 demisemiquavers in ternary measure in the same time as one plays three quarter notes. As for the trills <note>original: "tremblemens"</note>, beats <note>original: "battemens," likely mordents</note>, hammerings <note>original: "martelemens"</note>, mewings <term>mewings: original "myolemens," a delicate, sliding ornament or vibrato-like effect</term>, plaintive accents, etc., one can perform them on the keyboard almost as one does on the neck of the Lute, for which there is no need to repeat the discourse found in the preceding book.

Now it must also be noted that the lightness of the hand is very different from its speed, for many have a very fast hand, yet it is quite heavy, as shown by the hardness and harshness of their playing. Now those who have this lightness of hand can be called absolute masters of their hands and fingers, with which they press as little as they wish upon the natural keys <term>natural keys: original "marches," the lower, main keys of the keyboard</term>, in order to soften the sound of the Spinet as one does that of the Lute; so that they make very soft echoes heard, and at other times sounds so strong that they are compared to lightning and thunder, as happens when they triple or quadruple the cadence by making 32 demisemiquavers or 64 semidemisemiquavers <note>original: "quadruples crochuës"</note> in the passages, or in the triple and quadruple cadences, of which several examples are seen in the piece that follows, in which the trills that are made while descending are marked by this comma **,** and those that are made while ascending by this other mark **,** which resembles the letter **c**, although they may be marked with such other characters as one wishes. I leave aside several refinements that the great masters perform on the keyboard—for example, certain passages in which two conjoined sounds are heard at the same time while one of the fingers holds one of the keys depressed, so that the string which has been struck preserves its resonance. And this industry can serve to make heard several very sweet chords on the Spinet which will be composed of resonances alone, and consequently will nearly equal the sweetness of the Lute.

### On Stringed Instruments

...that there are 50 keys <note>original: "marches"</note> in the Harpsichord, each number will signify each key; for example, 40 will represent the sound of the 40th, and so on for the others. Now, the piece of music that follows was composed by the King, and set in Spinet tablature <note>original: "Epinette"</note> by *Monsieur de la Barre*, Organist and *Spinet* player to the King and Queen. His beautiful touch can serve as an example and a rule for those who desire to acquire perfection on this instrument. One may conclude its excellence by this composition, in which there are several measures of 32 and 64 notes: this is why I use demisemiquavers and hemidemisemiquavers <note>original: "triples & quadruples crochuës"</note> to mark the great speed of the hand, which often touches 32 or 64 notes or keys of the keyboard in the time of one measure, as I have often experienced. This is why I give here the time of this measure, which lasts a little less than one second—that is to say, the 1/3600th part of an hour—so that the author of this tablature often touches 32 notes, and sometimes 64, in the time of a heartbeat or a pulse; which is very remarkable.

There are still several other things in this tablature that must be considered; and particularly a quantity of trills <note>original: "tremblemens"</note>, which enrich the manner of playing and bring charms to it that are difficult to imagine if one has not heard them; nevertheless, one can envision a good part of them from the discourse I have made regarding the trills of the *Lute*.

I omit several things belonging to the Spinet—for example, that one can place two or three on the same table; that they can be made to descend as low as the largest pedals of the Organ; that the division of the whole tone or the Octave into twelve equal semitones cannot serve this instrument, because its tuning depends solely on the tension of the strings and is judged by the ear, without sight or touch being able to remedy it—unless one assumes very equal and unalterable strings, and uses weights to stretch them according to the harmonic proportions of which I spoke in the "tablature of the deaf" <note>This likely refers to a visual diagram of musical ratios that does not require hearing to understand</note>, which shows the possibility of this effect rather than its reality and existence. There are similarly several things to consider regarding the alteration caused by different impressions of the air upon the strings, and in the diversity of sounds which depends on the diversity of the mines from which the copper and other metals are drawn to make the strings.

Regarding the manner of learning to touch the *Spinet*, one must first understand the range of the keyboard, and accustom both hands to touch all sorts of keys to make all sorts of sounds as quickly as the imagination can conceive. And then one must learn to play chords with both hands, and to do so promptly both on the *Diatonic* and natural keys, which are normally white, and on the accidentals <note>original: "feintes"</note> or *Chromatic* keys, which are black. In the third place, one must accustom oneself to trills <note>original: "tremblemens"</note>, and all sorts of hammerings <term>hammerings: "martelemens," likely referring to mordents or repeated-note ornaments</term>, slides <term>slides: "coulemens," where one note flows into the next</term>, and softenings <term>softenings: "adoucissemens," a term for appoggiaturas or delicate graces</term>, and to diminish <note>See "diminutions" on the previous page</note> all sorts of subjects and parts, sometimes into 8 quavers, and 16, 32, and 64 for binary measure; and then into 12, 24, and 48 for ternary measure.

One can also use other sorts of measures, for example, the *sesquialtera* <term>sesquialtera: a musical ratio of 3:2, usually indicating three notes played in the time of two</term> and the *sesquitierce* <term>sesquitierce: a musical ratio of 4:3</term>, as the ancients did; upon which it must be noted that people are mistaken when they believe that binary measure is in a double ratio and ternary in a triple or sesquialtera ratio, for binary is in...

### Book Three

->Third Book<-

...ratio of equality like the unison, and the sesquialtera <note>A musical ratio of 3:2, where three notes are played in the time of two</note> of practical musicians <note>original: "Practiciens"</note> in a double ratio like the Octave, so that we now only use these two types of measure. For to use the sesquialtera, the downbeat <note>original: "frapper"</note> would have to last one and a half times as long as the upbeat <note>original: "leuer"</note>: or on the contrary, that is to say, it would be necessary to play two notes against three, and consequently the measure would be composed of five notes, to correspond to the ratio of the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"</note> which is called ***Hemiolia*** <note>Greek for "one and a half"</note>: and to make the triple measure which corresponds to the Twelfth, the beat would have to last three times as long as the lift, and one would play three notes against one: and finally to beat the sesquitertia <note>A ratio of 4:3</note> measure, one would have to play 4 notes while lowering, against 3 notes while lifting, in order to compose a measure of 7 notes, and to imitate the ratio of the Fourth <note>original: "Diateſſaron"</note> in time.

And if one wished to go further to find the two Thirds and the two Sixths in the order of measures and diminutions <note>The practice of breaking long notes into many fast, decorative ones</note>, it would be necessary to play five or six notes while lowering against 3, 4, or 8 notes while lifting: which is not so difficult that one cannot accustom the imagination and the fingers to it; and one already finds some who play whatever number of notes they wish while lowering against any other number proposed while lifting. But the principal ornament depends on a beautiful touch, and on the maintenance of beautiful songs which must perpetually serve as the subject, while the different parts and counter-striking patterns <note>original: "contre-batteries," likely referring to complex rhythmic or chordal textures</note> are heard; otherwise, all that one does resembles a body without a soul, and a racket <note>original: "tintamare"</note> that makes more noise than it gives pleasure to those who seek proportion in harmony, and who prefer order to confusion.

Now, perfection consists particularly in touching certain tones and certain strings <note>original: "chordes"</note> so appropriately that the spirit of the listener is charmed and ravished by them, and that he desires nothing more than to go to Heaven to enjoy the inexplicable pleasures of seeing God most clearly, and to join the harmony of his songs to those of the blessed. This must also be understood of all the other instruments of which we have spoken, and of which we shall make other discourses, for each has such particular graces that it is difficult to know which one ought to be preferred over the others. Be that as it may, I give here the piece of Music for 4 voices of which I have already spoken, so that one may see a part of what the Spinet <note>original: "Epinette," a small harpsichord-like instrument</note> can do when touched by the most excellent Masters; it can similarly be played on the Harp, since the Harp is nothing but an inverted Spinet, which is why I shall give no example for that instrument; and because the keyboard of the Organ is not different from that of the Harpsichord <note>original: "Clauecin"</note>, there is no doubt that Organists can play it, although there are certain particularities to the touch of the Organ which are not found in that of the Spinet, as I shall say in a specific book, in which I will give another example to show what the Organ can do, and what is proper to it. But one cannot bring a greater perfection to the Spinet than by making its sounds last as long as those of the Viol <note>original: "Viole"</note> or the Organ, and by making the division of its keyboard and its semitones so accurate that it responds to Theory. As for the duration of its sounds, I have already spoken of it, and the Germans show by experience that Harpsichords are capable of making excellent Viol concerts heard by means of wheels which substitute for the strokes of the bow <note>Mersenne is referring to experimental "bowed keyboards" like the Geigenwerk, which used rotating wheels to create sustained sounds</note>: which can be done in several ways; but the accuracy of the intervals and the steps of the keyboard depends on a good ear, and on several things which

### PROPOSITION XXIV.

->*Explaining the form, the tuning, the range, and the use of the Harp.*<-

One can raise several difficulties regarding this instrument, for example, namely whether the Harp of David, which the Hebrews call the *Kinnor* <note>original: "כנור Cinor"; a lyre-like instrument mentioned in the Bible</note>, was similar to ours, and to the cithara of the Greeks; but since no vestige of antiquity appears to us from which we might conclude the truth of the matter, it suffices to describe ours here. It is represented by this figure composed of three parts, one of which is called the neck <note>original: "clauier"; while usually meaning "keyboard," here it refers to the harmonic curve or arm of the harp where the tuning pins are located</note>, which is marked by **A**, **B**, and **D**. **L**, **E**, and **I** represent half of the soundboard, on which one sees the two rows of pins **D** and **H**, each of which is similar to **S** and **V**: one can call them buttons, and they serve to hold the strings firm in their holes, which are plugged with these buttons after having made a knot at the end of each string so they cannot escape. But it must be noted that the strings do not touch their pins upon exiting their holes, as they do when one uses bray pins <note>original: "harpions, ou cheuilles crochuës"; L-shaped pins that touched the string to create a buzzing sound</note> or hooked pins, which make them buzz <note>original: "nazarder"; to produce a nasal, buzzing tone</note>, the use of which has been abandoned to avoid this imperfection.

One also adds a brass wire joining each button, near which it is attached to the soundboard at the exit of each hole, so that the strings bear upon it, and so the wood of the soundboard does not wear out. Now, the length of the strings is taken from these brass wires—acting as so many bridges—up to the iron tuning pins seen in the neck **A B**, which has three rows, the first of which shows how the strings are wound. Their shape is similar to the pin **α β**, of which the first part **α** is square and is placed on the side of the neck that is not visible, by which one turns the said pins with the key **ABC**: this is done by taking the two branches **C B** with the right hand to put the square end of the pin **α β** into the hole **A** of the third branch. As for the strings, those of the first row of buttons are attached to the first row of pins on the neck, those of the second row to the second, and those of the third row to the third: but the third row of buttons does not appear because half of the soundboard is hidden.

The other two rows of strings also do not appear wound to the 2nd and 3rd row of pins on the neck, in order to avoid the clutter and confusion of the strings, of which there are only two rows here—namely the ordinary ones of simple Harps, where each tone is not divided into two semi-tones, which are wound to the first row of pins by the end **β**, which is round, and

### THE ANATOMY OF THE HARP.

The figure above depicts the instrument in its entirety, showing the arrangement of its various parts which allow it to produce such a harmonious range of sounds. To understand its construction, one must observe the following labels:

The separate diagram at the top center illustrates a tuning tool <term>tuning tool<note>original: "clef"; a wrench-like tool used to turn the pins and tighten the strings</note></term> or perhaps a structural joint, marked with the letters **A** and **B**. Beside it, a small mechanical component, likely a bridge pin or a specific part of the internal mechanism, is indicated by the Greek letter **beta** (**β**).

On the instrument itself:

*   **M** marks the head of the carved pillar, the vertical support that resists the tension of the strings.
*   The neck—the curved top arm of the harp—contains the tuning pins. These are organized in repeating sequences of the musical scale, labeled **A, B, C, D, E, F,** and **G**, which guide the musician in setting the correct pitch for each string.
*   The joint where the neck meets the soundbox is identified by the letters **B**, **C**, and **D**.
*   **H** and **G** represent the two large, ornate rosettes <note>These are decorative soundholes carved into the soundboard to allow the air inside the body to vibrate more freely, enhancing the volume.</note> located on the soundboard.
*   The lower section of the soundboard and the sturdy base of the instrument, which rests against the player, are marked with the letters **F**, **E**, **K**, **I**, and **L**.

The harp is a <term>chordophone<note>from the Greek 'khorde' (string) and 'phone' (sound); a general category for all instruments that produce sound via vibrating strings</note></term> of great complexity. Because each note requires its own string, the tension exerted on the frame—particularly at the neck (**A-D**) and the soundboard—is immense, requiring the finest craftsmanship in wood selection and joinery.

## Of Stringed Instruments.

...which is pierced by a small hole, through which the string is passed so that it does not slip, just as is done with the pegs of the Lute and other instruments.

The four wooden panels shown between E and H show half of the external body upon which the soundboard is placed; consequently, they indicate that it is composed of eight panels, although one could make it round or in any other shape one desires. F and G show the soundholes <note>original: "ouyes", the openings in the body that allow the sound to project</note>, which are made in the shape of a trefoil. Now, there are 29 strings in this first row, which make up four full octaves, like those of the Spinet <term>Spinet: a small, rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</term>; so much so that one can say the Harp is an inverted Spinet, to which one could fit a keyboard similar to that of the Harpsichord in order to use it as a Spinet. This is done by some Italians, who call it the **Grave-cymbale** <note>original: "Graue-cymbale", from the Italian "gravecembalo", an early name for the harpsichord</note>, imitating the ancient Epigonius of Ambracia or the Simicon, the figures of which Vincenzo Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591) was an influential Italian music theorist and the father of Galileo Galilei</note> provides on pages 40 and 41 of his *Dialogues on Music*.

The second row of strings, which provide the semitones <term>semitones: the half-steps between notes, like the black keys on a modern piano</term>, appears here and is attached to the second row of pins, so that there are 57 strings in this Harp. However, the 29 strings of the third row, which are in unison with the 27 of the first, are not marked, as they are on the side of the soundboard that is hidden. Thus, this Harp, which is called "triple," would have 86 strings, were it not for the semitones encountered in the Diatonic scale <term>Diatonic: the standard seven-note scale (like do-re-mi)</term> which reduce the number of strings in the second row; for since each octave has two semitones, and there are four octaves on the Harp, it follows that eight strings must be removed from the second row, and consequently only 78 strings are needed to string the triple Harp to perfection.

One could also add a fourth row of strings in unison with the second, or at the octave of the first, to increase the harmony; however, the clutter of strings would be so great that the fingers could not manage such a multitude, unless one used one or two keyboards, as is done on Harpsichords, which have three or four different rows of strings that can be varied in six or seven ways to have several different stops, as I mentioned above. Those who have heard Flesle <note>likely a reference to a celebrated harpist of the era, possibly "La Flelle"</note>, who plays the Harp to perfection, do not know whether they should prefer it to the Lute. The Harp has this advantage over the Lute: all its strings are played "open" <note>played without pressing them down against a fretboard</note>, and its tuning can more closely approach perfect accuracy than that of the Lute. As for the imperfection experienced in the sound of its strings—which, by not being dampened quickly enough, often cause dissonance with the other strings being played—this is easily stopped, just like the strings of the Spinet, by using the fingers with which one touches the strings.

I leave aside all the refinements and delicacies that can be used when playing the Harp, since one can apply many of those practiced on other instruments to it, even though the manner of touching and plucking its strings is very different from that used on others, for both hands play it in the same fashion. Certainly, if one considers the "shaking of the neck" <note>likely referring to vibrato or specific left-hand ornaments</note> on the Lute, which the Harp lacks, I believe one will admit that the Lute is more charming and deserves to be called the King of Instruments, though everyone is free to believe what they wish.

Regarding the tuning of the Harp, it is similar to that of the Spinet, for all its strings proceed from semitone to semitone, such that it contains 28 semitones, the exact sizes of which are not easy to determine, as they can...

### On Stringed Instruments

...be equal or different according to the temperament they are given, which there is no need to speak of here, since I have treated it amply in the discourses on the Lute, the Spinet, and the Organ: from which one will conclude whether the <term>Enharmonic genus<note>One of the three types of scales in ancient Greek music, characterized by using very small intervals called quarter-tones.</note></term> can be applied to the Harp. Its ordinary tablature is no different from musical notes, although one can use the number of its strings for this purpose: for example, one can mark the Octave by 1 and 13, the Fifth by 1 and 6, etc. because the first string makes an Octave with the 13th, and a Fifth with the 6th; and because there are 49 strings—namely those of the first two rows, which all have different sounds—one must use 49 numbers, each of which will always signify its own string. Now, one can begin with the shortest, which is called the <term>chanterelle<note>The highest-pitched string on an instrument.</note></term>, and finish at the longest A K, which serves as the <term>bourdon<note>The lowest-pitched string, often providing a deep drone.</note></term> and the <term>Proslambanomene<note>original: "Proslambanomene"; a Greek term meaning "the note taken in addition," referring to the lowest note of their musical system.</note></term>, as the Greeks say, in order to follow the order kept for other instruments; although one can similarly begin counting 1, 2, 3, etc. by the thickest string, as the Italians do, since it serves as the base and foundation for the other strings, like unity to numbers.

As for the pieces played on the Harp, they are not different from those played on the Lute and the Spinet, which is why one can repeat here those I have placed above. But I provide yet another figure of a simple Harp, so that one may consider the manner of the ancient <term>harpions<note>Also known as "bray pins," these were wooden pegs that touched the strings to create a buzzing or trembling sound, a common feature of Renaissance harps.</note></term> which give a certain unpleasant trembling to the strings, and the reasons for the 23 intervals of the 24 strings that make the Twenty-fourth; for the numbers on the right of the body explain them. One also sees the names that the Greeks gave to each string in the writing between the said strings: the characters at the top of the lines were taken from Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on music theory.</note> and other ancient Greek authors. However, I have placed the letters of our ordinary scale on the tuning pins, so that one may understand by this single figure how <term>Guido of Arezzo<note>original: "Guy Aretin"; the 11th-century monk regarded as the inventor of modern staff notation.</note></term> adapted the characters of the Latin alphabet to the strings of the Greeks, of which some were mobile—namely all those across from which I have not placed the Greek word <term>immobile<note>original: "ἑστὼς" (hestōs), meaning standing or fixed.</note></term>, because the strings with this word always remained at the same pitch on the instruments, whereas all the others could be raised or lowered according to the difference of the genres and their species.

As for the musicians of our century, they alter all the strings by placing <term>flats<note>original: "b mols"; the term refers to the "soft B," which is the origin of the modern flat symbol.</note></term> in all sorts of keys, although they almost always retain some invariable tones—for example, the principal strings of the mode they are treating, which they call <term>Modals<note>The fundamental notes that define a specific musical mode or scale.</note></term>, as I have said elsewhere. From this, one can conclude that this Harp can serve to learn a good portion of the music of the Greeks and that of the moderns. I leave the antique Harp engraved at the bottom of this one, as I provide several other much better-made figures in the Proposition that follows: but one can consider here the notes or characters of the <insert>modern</insert> Greeks, with their interpretation seen opposite them, even though we do not know their use or true explanation. I add further that harps are made of whatever size one wishes—for example, four or five feet—and that the Lute has the advantage over it of being more portable, but in return, a greater number of parts can be played on the Harp than on the Lute.

->Book Three<-

## PROPOSITION XXIV.

### *Explaining the ancient depictions of the Harp, and other instruments of the Greeks and Romans.*

Since many desire to know the customs of antiquity, I do not wish to omit the instruments used by the *Greeks*, the *Romans*, and the *Egyptians*, provided that the ancient marbles of *Italy* and the medals do not deceive us. The following figures were taken from these sources and were sent to me by Messrs. *Gaffarel* and *Naudé* <note>Jacques Gaffarel and Gabriel Naudé were renowned 17th-century scholars and librarians interested in "curiosities" and ancient history.</note>, both excellent men. Now, the first three figures at the bottom—namely **f d g**, **h i**, and **m n l o**—and the two at the top, **I K L** and **M N O**, show the different shapes of their *Citharas*, or *Harps*, or the instruments they called <term>Testudo<note>Latin for "tortoise"; refers to a lyre made from a shell.</note></term>, <term>Chelys<note>Greek for "tortoise"; another term for the lyre.</note></term>, <term>Phormynx<note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument often associated with Homeric bards.</note></term>, etc. The letters **e** and **m** show the belly and the back of the *Tortoise*, or the top and bottom of its shell. This is because the first invention of this instrument is attributed to *Mercury*, who, having emptied the *Tortoise*, pierced its shell, strung it with gut strings, and added the two branches seen in our figures to attach the strings. He tuned his voice to their sound, as *Homer* remarks in his hymn. *Horace* gives it the name *Lyre* in the 10th Ode of his first book; but it is very difficult, and perhaps impossible, to know if their *Cithara*—which some believe to be the *Guitar*—was different from their *Lyre* of seven or nine strings. Therefore, it suffices to read what *Vigenère* <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and scholar.</note> reports in his notes on the *Amphion* of *Philostratus*, where he includes two ancient figures and gives a *Moral* and *Physical* meaning to all the parts of this ancient instrument. It must only be noted that the "tone" is not a <term>consonance<note>A stable, pleasant-sounding musical interval.</note></term>, as he supposes in order to find his <term>septenary<note>A group of seven, often associated with the seven planets or celestial harmony.</note></term> within the consonances, for it is one of the dissonances of Music. He should have used the <term>unison<note>Two notes of the same pitch.</note></term> instead of the tone. This does not prevent us from being greatly indebted to this excellent man, who enriched our language with a great number of works drawn from antiquity and several experiments he provided. Those who desire to know the notes of several instruments and their inventors may read the treatise *Plutarch* wrote on *Music*, as well as *Athenaeus*, *Pollux*, and all the ancient authors, and await the particular treatise written on them by Lord *Saumaise* <note>Claude Saumaise (Salmasius), a preeminent classical scholar of the time.</note>.

As for the parts of these ancient instruments, **d**, **h**, **l**, and **I** represent the crossbar, which is tied to the branches or horns **f**, **g**, **n**, **o**, and which holds the pegs **h l**, used to tighten the strings. The shell serves as the soundboard, which is straight in figure **h i**, near which one sees the <term>Plectrum<note>A small tool or "pick" used to pluck or strike strings.</note></term> of the ancients. This is nothing other than a stick with which they struck the strings, as is done now with the *Psaltery*, of which I shall give the figure and usage.

The three instruments in the middle sound when the hand that grips them by their handles **R**, **V**, and **a** shakes and rattles them. **R Q** and **Z a** show the form of ancient <term>Sistrums<note>original: "Cistres"; ancient Egyptian percussion instruments consisting of a metal frame with sliding crossbars.</note></term> used in *Egypt*. But it must be noted that the bars of iron, or brass, or some other material **S T** and **b c** move horizontally from **S** to **T** and from **T** to **S**, in order to strike the body of the *Sistrum* **Q** and **Z**, and to produce sounds in unison, just as the rings of the *Cymbals* or steel triangles do which are used today. The instrument **V X** moves...

...as for what the Egyptians represented upon it to honor their Isis, I leave that research to the critics, for it is enough that I faithfully provide all that I have been able to find in ancient marbles and medals.

The flutes **A C** and **B D** are equal, and both can be played through the mouthpiece at **A B**. Their finger holes <note>original: "lumieres"; literally "lights," referring here to the openings or tone holes of the flute.</note> are represented by **E F**; they each have only five holes, and are attached and held together by the bars **G** and **H**. One can see other ancient instruments in the *Dialogues* of Vincenzo Galilei <note>Vincenzo Galilei (c. 1520–1591) was an Italian lutenist, composer, and music theorist, and the father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei.</note>, pages 40 and 41, where he includes a form of Harp with 35 strings, which he calls the <term>Simmicum<note>original: "Simique"; an ancient Greek stringed instrument.</note></term>, and another of 40 strings that he names the <term>Epigonion<note>An ancient Greek stringed instrument named after Epigonus of Ambracia.</note></term>. One will also find other remarks that I have made in the first Latin book on instruments. As for the number of strings on the ancient Lyre, for which we have provided the figures here (which are also reported on page 129 of that Author), there are only seven. Because they could only be played as "open" strings <note>Meaning the strings were not pressed down against a neck to change their pitch; each string produced only one note.</note>, they could not produce any variations other than those depending on their seven sounds, or their six intervals, the different places where they were struck, and the stronger or lighter touches, just as happens now with our **Psaltery**, the figure of which I am about to explain, since it seems to be one of the most ancient of all instruments.

### PROPOSITION XXV.

->*To explain the construction, the tuning, the range, the Tablature, and the use of the Psaltery.*<-

This instrument is often mentioned in Holy Scripture, which the Hebrews call <term>נבל</term> <gloss>nebel</gloss> <note>A Hebrew term for a stringed instrument, often translated as a harp or lute, though its exact ancient form is debated.</note>, but we do not know the shape they gave to it, nor the number of its strings. For although the <term>Decachord<note>A ten-stringed instrument mentioned in the Bible, particularly in the Psalms.</note></term> precedes the Psaltery [in texts], and it seems that the word serves as its description, many nevertheless believe they are two different instruments. Be that as it may, this figure represents the one used today, upon which are placed thirteen courses <note>original: "rangs"; sets of strings tuned to the same note or octaves.</note> of strings, each of which has two strings tuned in unison or at the Octave, to which others could be added at the Fifth and the Fifteenth to increase the harmony. Its triangular shape **G H K C** shows a truncated triangle, which one can make equilateral, or isosceles, or in any other manner one wishes. The numbers that go upward signify the 13 courses of strings, which contain 26 in total. Their tuning is marked by the letters of the Gamut <note>The "Gamme" or the traditional scale of musical pitches used in the 17th century.</note> on the left hand, of which the first signifies **G-re-sol** <note>A pitch in the hexachord system equivalent to a G.</note>, which is a Fourth lower than the second letter **C**, so that the second **G-re-sol** has its Octave below it. But the other letters follow by adjacent degrees and show the sounds and intervals of each string, as can be seen in the following table, which shows the accuracy of all the steps and intervals, both consonant and dissonant.

The two sides of the Psaltery **E G** and **K D** show the wooden triangles that serve as bridges for the strings, except for the last one **C G**, which has a separate bridge marked with the letter **B**. Now, this string serves as a <term>drone<note>original: "bourdon"; a string that provides a continuous low-pitched bass note.</note></term> and is attached to one of the iron pins that run all along the side **K C**, like the other strings, and on the other side to the tuning pegs, which are similar to those of <term>Spinets<note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note></term>, and which serve to tighten the strings with the hammer **a b δ**; this is done by turning **e δ** once the peg has been inserted into the...

### Book Three

...psaltery among the percussion instruments <note>Instruments played by striking, like a modern dulcimer</note>, even though one can touch its strings with a quill or the fingers, like the Harp, the Mandore <note>A small, lute-like instrument</note>, and the Cittern. The letter P signifies the depth, or the thickness of the Psaltery, which one can make in all sorts of sizes; for one can give five or six feet of extension to the largest string, as is done for those of the largest Harpsichords <note>original: "Clauecins"</note>, although one only gives them one foot of length on each side or thereabouts, so that they may be portable.

The small iron pieces N O, which have three holes and are shaped like lilies, attach the lid that closes the Psaltery. This instrument has the privilege over others that one can learn to play it in the space of one or two hours, which makes it valued by those who do not have more time to devote to this exercise. Now, these first strings are made of brass <note>original: "leton", likely latten, a brass-like alloy</note>, and the others of steel, which have a certain sharpness and cheerfulness not found in other instruments, as much due to the small leaps and rebounds of the stick as to the brevity and tension of the strings. These are capable of all sorts of songs, provided that one installs all the necessary strings; for although this one is tuned in B-flat <note>original: "b mol"</note>, it is very easy to tune it in B-natural <note>original: "b quarre"</note>. If one wishes to play two or more parts together on this instrument, one can use two sticks, or play one, two, or several parts with the left hand while the right hand strikes the strings with the stick.

As for its construction and its material, it is no different from that of the Spinet <note>original: "Epinette", a small harpsichord</note>, of which I will speak later. But one can make the Psaltery double or triple by means of three or more traversing bridges <note>Small wooden supports that divide the strings</note>, in order to play the three genres of Music <note>Referring to the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales</note> on the same instrument; it can also serve for learning to sing and to pitch one's voice accurately. Indeed, it can be played with such industry and skill that it will give no less pleasure than other instruments. As for its Tablature <term>Tablature: A simplified musical notation that shows string placement rather than musical pitches</term>, it can be marked by musical notes, or by the letters of the Harmonic Hand <note>The Guidonian Hand, a medieval mnemonic tool used to teach singers to find pitches</note>, A, B, C, etc., or by the numbers which some use while singing *one, two, three, four, five*, etc., instead of *ut, re, mi, fa, sol*, etc. <note>These are the syllables of the hexachord system, the ancestor of modern "do, re, mi"</note>. Thus, the first thirteen numbers can serve for all the songs of which this instrument is capable: for provided that one knows the sound of each string, the "one" will serve for the lowest pitch, the "two" for the second, the "three" for the third, and so on up to the thirteenth, which signifies the highest sound.

Certainly, the harmony of this Psaltery is very pleasant because of the clear and silvery sounds rendered by its steel strings; and I have no doubt that one would receive as much or more contentment from it as from the Spinet or the Harp, if someone were found who played it with as much skill as one plays the Harpsichord. Be that as it may, one can receive pleasure from this instrument cheaply and quite conveniently, since one can have it with all its science for one crown <note>original: "escu", a gold or silver coin</note>, and one can carry it in a pocket. Now, some place a division from top to bottom through the middle, or at any other place on the strings they wish, in order to have two Psalteries in one and to play Duos <note>Duets</note> upon it. One can also string it with strings of all the metals of which I spoke in the 19th Proposition of this book, in order to experiment with how much more harmonious the sound of some is than others. One can also string it with strings of gut, or of silk,

Now, after having spoken of the instruments that are played with the fingers and which have keyboards, it is necessary to explain everything belonging to those played with a bow, which we shall do in the following book. For as for the Harp, and the <term>Psaltery</term> <note>An ancient stringed instrument played by plucking or striking</note> of the Royal Prophet <note>King David, traditionally associated with the psaltery and harp</note>, and of all the other instruments mentioned in Holy Scripture, the most learned Rabbis confess that they cannot know their true forms, nor the manner in which they were played; and I have not undertaken this treatise to fill it with conjectures, or to guess, but to demonstrate that which exists, and which cannot be denied by those who do not renounce their senses, experience, and reason.

This instrument is composed of twelve sticks which continually diminish from the twelfth, **D E**, to the first, **A B**. The largest stick is ordinarily 10 inches in length, and consequently the last must be three and 1/3 inches, in order to create the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning an octave and a fifth</note> whose ratio is 3 to 1, although the makers diminish them so little that the first is only double the last, because they compensate for the length with the thickness; but I shall show more exactly in the books on Theory what proportion exists between solid bodies and their sounds.

As for the base of these cylindrical sticks, it is customarily **elliptical**, although it may have any other shape one desires: for example, round or square, for they can be made as <term>parallelepipeds</term> <note>A six-faced solid figure where every face is a parallelogram</note>, in the form of prisms, etc. One can know the volume of each stick by finding the area of the ellipse at their ends, of which the greater diameter is 1/2 or 1/10 part of the length, and the lesser is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>original: "sesquialtere"; a ratio of 3:2</note> to the greater; for the height or length of the cylinder multiplied by its base will give the solidity, and consequently the quantity of the stick.

It must also be noted that one bores a hole through each stick near its two ends, in order to attach them together such that they are separated by means of a small <term>bead</term> <note>original: "patenostre"; literally a rosary bead, used here as a spacer</note> or ball, for fear that they might touch; otherwise, one could not strike them as distinctly one after the other as is required to distinguish their sounds, which give as much pleasure as those of other instruments when one performs the <term>diminutions</term> <note>The breaking of long notes into many short, rapid notes</note> and <term>trills</term> <note>original: "fredons"; rapid musical ornaments</note> of which this scale is capable. Now I come to the instruments that are played with the bow, so that nothing is missing from this work.

# BOOK FOUR
## OF STRING INSTRUMENTS.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

**TO EXPLAIN THE SHAPE, THE MATERIAL,**
*the parts, the tuning, the range, and the use of Violins.*

<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop cap 'L' showing a man standing in a rural landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>
The Violin is one of the simplest instruments that can be imagined, especially since it has only four strings and no frets on its neck; this is why one can play all the just <term>consonances</term> <note>intervals that sound harmonious and stable to the ear</note> on it, just as with the voice, because one can touch the string wherever one wishes. This makes it more perfect than fretted instruments, in which one is forced to use <term>temperament</term> <note>a tuning system that slightly compromises the purity of intervals to allow playing in different keys</note> and to weaken or increase the greater part of the consonances, and to alter all the musical intervals, as I shall show later.

To this one may add that its sounds have more effect on the minds of listeners than those of the <term>Lute</term> or other stringed instruments, because they are more vigorous and pierce more deeply, due to the great tension of their strings and their high-pitched sounds. And those who have heard the **24 Violons du Roy** <note>The "Twenty-Four Violins of the King," the first permanent orchestra in Europe, famous for its discipline and brilliance at the French court</note> admit they have never heard anything more ravishing or powerful; hence this instrument is the most suitable of all for dancing, as is experienced in ballets and everywhere else. Now, the beauties and graces practiced upon it are so numerous that it can be preferred to all other instruments, for the strokes of its bow are sometimes so ravishing that one has no greater displeasure than to hear the end of them, particularly when they are mixed with the <term>tremblements</term> <note>trills or ornaments</note> and the <term>flatterments</term> <note>a type of vibrato or gentle wavering of the pitch</note> of the left hand, which constrain the listeners to confess that the Violin is the **King of instruments**.

For although one plays several parts together on the Lute and on the <term>Spinet</term> <note>a small, wing-shaped keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family</note>, and consequently these instruments are more harmonious, nonetheless those who judge the excellence of music and its instruments by the beauty and excellence of melodies and songs have powerful enough reasons to maintain that it is the most excellent; the best of these is taken from the great effects it has on the passions and on the affections of the body and mind. But before moving further, we must explain the shape of Violins, the smallest of which is called the **Poche** <note>literally "pocket"; known in English as a kit violin, used by dance masters because it could be tucked into a coat pocket</note>, because it is so small that the violinists who teach dancing carry it in their pockets.

This instrument is composed of three parts, like other instruments: namely, the soundboard **L E**, the neck **D B**, and the body, of which only the side **M D** is seen. It often has three openings, which are marked here as **G**, **F**, and **E**, which has the shape of a heart, and the two openings **G** and **F** are called the **sound-holes** <note>original: "ouyes," literally "hearings"</note>. The top of the neck **D B**, upon which the strings are stretched, is

Where it must be noted that I have put <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: *B fa*</note> opposite 32, because if <image-desc>sharp symbol</image-desc> <term>B-natural</term> <note>original: *mi*</note> were there, the Fifth would be false, for it would be less than it should be by a semi-tone. Furthermore, we have no syllable in the harmonic hand, which is usually called the <term>Gamut</term> <note>The full range of pitches in the musical system</note>, which makes the Fifth below <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: *B fa*</note>; from which one can conclude that the invention of the six notes and the names of the gamut is imperfect, since it cannot represent all the intervals of the voice. But it is easy to supply what is missing by adding a *fa* in **E-mi-la**, and by saying **E-fa-mi**, as I have shown at greater length in the *Practice of Composition*. Now these seven Fifths make the Twenty-ninth, that is to say, four Octaves, so that Violins have as much range as the keyboard of <term>Spinets</term> and Organs.

As for the range of each part, it is four fifths which make the major Seventeenth, for besides the three Fifths it makes on the open strings, it rises another fifth by means of the neck which is touched. And excellent Violinists who master this instrument can make each string rise up to the Octave by means of the neck, upon which they find 144 semi-tones to transpose the 12 <term>modes</term> to such a place and at such a pitch as they wish. Now the 2 preceding figures suffice to make one understand those of the other parts, which differ only in size, as happens with other instruments, of which the largest shake a greater quantity of air, and make sounds that are lower and deeper.
