Nevertheless, if they wish to take the trouble, it is not so difficult that it cannot be practiced. For if the thickest string of the <term>Alto</term> <note>original: *Haute-contre*</note> is lower by a Fifth than that of the <term>Treble</term> <note>original: *Dessus*</note>, these four strings must be <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 3:2, representing a perfect fifth in musical intervals</note> to those of the Treble in both length and thickness—that is to say, they should be three feet long if those of the Treble are two feet. And if the thickest string of the <term>Tenor</term> <note>original: *Taille*</note> descends more than an Octave below that of the Treble, they must have all their dimensions double those of the Treble. Finally, if the thickest string of the Bass is at the Twelfth or the Fifteenth of the Treble, it must have its strings three or four times thicker and longer. But I have given a particular discourse on the ratio of all kinds of strings in the treatise on the <term>Spinet</term> <note>A smaller, rectangular cousin of the harpsichord</note>, where one sees the exact proportion of their sizes.

Now it must be noted that the middle parts—that is to say, the Tenor, the <term>Fifth part</term> <note>original: *Cinquiesme partie*; a standard middle voice in five-part Renaissance/Baroque compositions</note>, and the Alto—are of different sizes, even though they are all in unison. Consequently, when the surface area of the Alto is to that of the Treble as nine is to four (that is, <term>double sesquiquarte</term> <note>The ratio 9:4</note>), and their bodies have the same ratio as 27 to 8 (that is, <term>triple surtripartissante 8</term> <note>The ratio 27:8, which is the cube of 3:2</note>), the surface of the Tenor should be to that of the Treble as 4 to 1, so that their solid volumes would be as 8 to 1 (that is, octuple). And finally, the surface of the Bass should be to that of the Treble as 16 to 1, and the body of the former to the body of the latter as 64 to 1. This must similarly be observed in Viols, Lutes, and all other instruments used in ensembles, especially since I shall not speak further of these proportions in the other discourses.

As for the <term>Tablature</term> <note>A form of musical notation indicating instrument fingering rather than musical pitches</note> of Violins and Viols, it is no different from ordinary musical notes; although those who do not know their value may use numbers or such characters as please them to mark their lessons and their conceptions, and to write particular tablatures, such as those for the Lute and the Guitar. However, notes are better than letters, inasmuch as they mark the sounds, the value of the measures, and all kinds of time, and they are more universal throughout Europe. Now, if one wishes to abandon the names by which the ancients expressed their modes—namely *Dorian*, *Phrygian*, *Lydian*, *Ionian*, and the others—and wishes to impose upon them names more intelligible than those of the Greeks, one could call the Tone or mode of the Violin the *gay and joyful mode*; that of the Viol and the Lyre, the *sad and languishing mode*; that of the Lute, the *prudent and modest mode*; that of the Trumpet, the *hardy and warrior tone*; and so with the others, following the property of each instrument.

It must further be noted that the Violin is capable of all genres and all species of Music, and that one can play the <term>Enharmonic</term>, and every species of <term>Diatonic</term> and <term>Chromatic</term> upon it, because it is not limited by any frets <note>original: *touches*</note>, and it contains every imaginable interval which exists potentially upon its neck. This neck is similar to <term>prime matter</term> <note>A philosophical concept from Aristotle referring to a pure potentiality that can take on any form</note>, being capable of all kinds of forms and figures, there being no point upon the tou-

# of the Instruments.

[The fingerboard] of the Violin that does not produce a particular sound: from which one must conclude that it contains an infinity of different sounds, just as the string, or a line, contains an infinity of points; and consequently, that it can be called *Universal Harmony*. Now, I wish here to explain the manner of playing it with perfection, in order to join Practice to Theory, so that those who desire to play this instrument without the help of any Master may do all that they please upon its four strings.

### PROPOSITION II.

->*To explain the manner of playing the Violin, and of placing each finger upon the spots of the fingerboard to play all sorts of musical pieces, both with <term>flats</term> <note>original: *B mol*</note> and with <term>naturals</term> <note>original: *# quarre*, literally "square B," used to indicate natural or sharp notes</note>.*<-

Since the Violin has only four strings, of which the open tuning is ordinarily in Fifths, as I have shown in the preceding discourse, if one produces all the sounds that can be drawn from these strings, one will play it perfectly. But in order to proceed in an orderly fashion, and to avoid obscurity and confusion, I first show how one must place the first finger, which is called the index—that is to say, the one closest to the thumb—upon the 4th string, and then how to place the 2nd and the 3rd, and what each finger does.
   Now, I begin with the fourth string, because it is the lowest, in order to follow the method used in France, although it would be just as easy to begin with the first, which is called the <term>highest string</term> <note>original: *la chanterelle*</note>.
   I say then, first, that the 4th string produces <term>G</term> <note>original: *G re sol vt*; names based on the Guidonian system of solmization</note> when open, that is to say, without the help of the left hand, which serves only to hold the neck and to shorten the strings, just as the right hand serves to hold the bow and to strike the strings in a thousand different ways, as I shall say later. But one makes this 4th string rise to <term>A</term> <note>original: *A mi la re*</note>, which is to say one tone higher, by placing the first finger upon it, following the intervals of the Monochord that I explained in the fifth Proposition. And if one withdraws this same finger slightly toward the <term>nut</term> <note>original: *fillet*; the ridge at the top of the fingerboard</note>, it rises only by a half-tone to produce the <term>ficta fa</term> <note>original: *fa feint*; a term for accidentals or notes outside the standard scale</note> which is between A and G: this must be noted once and for all, because each finger can produce the half-tone and make each string rise or fall by that interval in all the places one wishes, according as it is necessary to produce the <term>accidentals</term> <note>original: *accidents*; sharps or flats</note> encountered in different compositions.
   The second finger, which is the middle one, produces <term>B-natural</term> <note>original: *♯ mi*</note> on the same string by moving it forward toward the bridge; and <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: *B fa*</note> by withdrawing it toward the nut. And the third finger, moved toward the bridge, produces <term>C</term> <note>original: *C sol vt fa*</note>, and if one moves it forward a little more, it makes the same string rise by a half-tone and produces the sharp of C, in place of the fourth finger.
   The 3rd string, which follows the 4th, produces <term>D</term> <note>original: *D la re sol*</note> when open; but if one finds an F by transposition in this D, one must place the 4th finger on the 4th string very near the place where the 3rd produces C, instead of playing the said F on the open 3rd string. Now, the first finger placed on the 3rd string produces <term>E</term> <note>original: *E mi la*</note>, and by withdrawing it toward the nut, it produces the flat <note>original: *fa*</note> on E by accidental between D and E. The second finger makes it rise to <term>F</term> <note>original: *F vt fa*</note>, that is to say, by a half-tone; and if one moves it toward the bridge, it produces the sharp of F. The third finger produces the said <term>G</term> <note>original: *G re sol*</note>, which one...

is called the Clef, so that we have already made the Violin ascend a full Octave by playing all the tones of the **Diatonic** scale, and all the semi-tones of the **Chromatic** scale, so that one can play all sorts of Music, whether through the natural hexachord, by <term>flats</term> <note>original: *b mol*</note>, or by <term>naturals</term> <note>original: *♯ quarre*</note>. Now, if one moves this same finger toward the bridge, one will produce the <term>sharp</term> <note>original: *Dieſe*</note> of **G** <note>original: *G re sol*</note>, which is to say that it will be raised by a semi-tone higher than **G**. For example, if there is an **F** <note>original: *fa*</note> in **A** <note>original: *A mi la re*</note>, which is found as an open note on the second string, one must place the 4th finger on the 3rd string, or advance the sharp of the **G** instead of the **F** of the **A**.

The second string played open makes **A** <note>original: *A mi la re*</note>, and when the first finger is placed upon it, it makes **B-natural** <note>original: *♮ mi*</note>, and by pulling it back a little, it makes **B-flat** <note>original: *B fa*</note>. The second finger makes **C** <note>original: *C sol vt fa*</note>, and by moving it forward it makes the **C-sharp**, which is a semi-tone higher than the said **C**. The third finger makes **D** <note>original: *D la re sol*</note>; and the 4th finger, which is located on the 2nd string, makes the **F** in **E** <note>original: *E mi la re*</note> by accident, without it being necessary to sound the <term>highest string</term> <note>original: *chanterelle*</note>, which makes the **E** <note>original: *mi*</note> of the said **E** <note>original: *E mi la*</note> when open. But the first finger placed on the said highest string makes **F** <note>original: *F vt fa*</note>, and by moving it toward the bridge it makes the **F-sharp**. The second finger makes **G** <note>original: *G re sol*</note>, which is at the Fifteenth <note>Two octaves</note> from that of the 4th string open, and by moving it forward it makes the sharp that is between G and A. The third makes **A** <note>original: *A mi la re*</note>, the fourth finger makes **B-natural** <note>original: *♮ mi*</note> when moved forward and away from the third finger, and by bringing it closer it makes **B-flat** <note>original: *B fa*</note>. If one moves it closer to the bridge than the position of **B-natural**, it makes **C** <note>original: *C sol vt fa*</note>, and then **D** <note>original: *D la re sol*</note>; so that the Violin has a range of a Nineteenth.

One can also note several things for the understanding of the Violin: for example, that the same finger touching the two adjacent strings—namely the fourth and the third, the 3rd and the 2nd, or the 2nd and the highest string—always makes a Fifth across all parts of the fingerboard. And if the Violin were tuned differently, for example by a Fifth and a Fourth, the same finger could make perpetual chords by always touching two or three strings; but the bridge would have to be lower than it is, and it would need to imitate that of the **Lyre** <note>Referring here to the *Lira da braccio*, a multi-stringed bowed instrument with a flatter bridge for chordal playing</note>, of which I shall speak in another place.

As for the different <term>trills</term> <note>original: *tremblemens*</note> that one can make with the left hand, I explain them in the treatise on the Lute: it must only be noted that one must use as many bow strokes as there are beats of the finger that <term>hammers</term> <note>original: *martele*, referring to a percussive finger articulation or vibrato</note>, if one wants the hammering to be pleasing; but one must only let it flow for the trills that are made without hammering.

### PROPOSITION III.

*To determine if one should add a fifth string to Violins to draw from them a perfect Harmony, and in what the perfection of a beautiful touch consists.*

One could string Violins with five strings, which would perhaps cause the ordinary four-stringed ones to be abandoned, just as the **Rebec** was abandoned—which had only three strings with a range of a Twelfth—as soon as the Violin was invented, with which one goes up to a Sixteenth. Now, since the Violin seems to be the most perfect and the most excellent of all other instruments, as much for the variety of its <term>diminutions</term> <note>fast melodic passages or divisions</note>, its syncopations, its ties, its <term>feints</term> <note>ficta or chromatic alterations</note>, and its beautiful melodies, as for its admirable sweetness...

### of Instruments.

Regarding different movements that have not yet been discovered, it would not be out of place to add a fifth string, so that the instrument might have a large enough range for all the <term>modes</term> <note>The sets of scales used in Renaissance and Baroque music, preceding the modern major and minor system.</note>; for one can only play three or four modes on the four strings of the Violin—namely, the seventh, which begins on **F** <note>original: *F ut fa*</note>, and the ninth, which begins on **G** <note>original: *G re sol ut*</note>, where the final cadence falls on the fifth below.

As for the other modes, they are defective, because their final cadence is at the Fourth, which creates the <term>plagal</term> <note>A version of a mode where the range of the melody is shifted, often making it difficult to reach the lowest notes on a standard four-string violin.</note> mode, which does not produce good effects. For example, the first mode, which is in **C** <note>original: *C sol ut fa*</note>, is imperfect on the Violin because its cadence falls at the Fourth, which is to say upon its plagal **D** <note>original: *D la re sol*</note>. The same thing happens in **E** <note>original: *E mi la*</note>, or in the 5th mode, which is very suited for sadness and for spiritual elevations; thus, one cannot do without the fifth string if one wishes to practice the twelve modes on Violins, unless one makes use of <term>transposition</term> <note>Shifting the music to a different key or pitch level.</note>, which is very natural to them. But since each instrument is prized all the more for making greater variety with fewer strings, and because one touches almost exclusively the <term>highest string</term> <note>original: *chanterelle*</note> and the second string on the Treble Violins, this fifth string is not necessary, and one can even play well enough with three.

As for the perfection of Practice, it consists in the "beautiful touch," which is the base and the foundation of the pleasure that must satisfy the ear. Because this instrument has no <term>frets</term> <note>original: *touches*; horizontal strips on the neck of instruments like the lute or viol that mark where to place fingers.</note>, one must adjust the fingers so precisely on each spot of the neck that the sounds convey a proportion as well-regulated as if there were frets as on the **Viol**. Secondly, one must sweeten the strings with <term>trills</term> <note>original: *tremblemens*; in this context, it could refer to a vibrato-like shaking or a rapid alternation of notes to sustain the sound.</note>, which must be made by the finger closest to the one held firmly on the string, so that the note is "nourished." But one must press the fingertips as hard as possible on the neck so that the strings produce more harmony, and lift them very little off the neck so as to have enough time to carry them from one string to another. Thirdly, if one wishes to succeed perfectly, the hand that holds the **bow** must be at least equal in speed to the left hand, since it brings out all the different movements that enrich the melodies and give beauty to the songs. Fourthly, one must draw the bow across the strings and repeat the strike of the finger several times on the same tone, and then on another, continuing thus from top to bottom to create <term>graces</term> <note>original: *mignardises*; delicate ornaments or "sweetenings" of the melody.</note> which are very agreeable due to the beautiful modulation that gives great pleasure to the hearing, though one must proceed with judgment.

Now, the Violin has this advantage over other instruments: that besides the various songs of animals, both of the air and the earth, it imitates and counterfeits all sorts of instruments, such as voices, **Organs**, the **Hurdy-gurdy**, the **Bagpipe**, the **Fife**, etc. Thus, it can bring sadness, as does the **Lute**, and animate like the **Trumpet**; those who know how to play it in perfection can represent everything that falls into their imagination. I leave aside an infinity of other remarks belonging to this instrument—for example, that one can play a **Courante** <note>A lively French dance.</note> and several other pieces of Music with a single stroke of the bow; that one can "flutter" the strings with 8, 16, or 32 finger-strikes in the space of one measure; and that one must place the three fingers of the left hand—that is, the index, the middle, and the ring—

## PROPOSITION IV.

*To explain the shape and the dimensions of all the parts of the Violins, the manner of forming ensembles with them, and the musical pieces appropriate for this subject.*

As for the **Bass** **A E**, whose four pegs are marked by four numbers, it is so well made that there is no need to stop for its description: its **fingerboard** <note>original: *touche*</note> from **D** to **B** is one-third the length of the soundboard **D E**, and is equal to the width it has across the middle of the **soundholes** <note>original: *ouyes*; the f-shaped openings on the instrument’s face.</note> **H I**, or the **bridge** **G**: its bow is **K L**: I leave all its other parts, of which I have spoken in the explanation of the preceding figures. I have made its bow **S T V** very large, in order to show that bows are all the better the larger they are, provided they are not inconvenient, because the strokes and the hits last longer.

The tuning of the open strings of all the parts of the **Consort** <note>original: *Concert*; an ensemble of instruments of the same family playing together.</note> is seen beside the Bass, and begins three fifths—that is to say, a thirteenth—lower than the fourth open string of the Treble. I have put the last upper fifth to show that one can still add a Treble higher up: for as for the penultimate fifth, it belongs to the fingerboard of the Treble; that is why I have only put the numbers beside the first seven notes, which signify the six fifths of the open strings of the Violins. Now, a single clef suffices for all these lines, but I have put them in six different places, so that everyone may see their proper positions. There remain only the two figures of the ancient Lyres, namely **X Y** and **Z**, which were taken from the medals of **Nerva**, **Domitian**, and **Hadrian** <note>Roman Emperors whose coinage often depicted musical instruments.</note>, which are in the cabinet of the most illustrious **Rosinus the Venetian**.

I come now to the Consorts that one can make with 500 different Violins, though 24 are sufficient, of which there are six Trebles, six Basses, four **Altos** <note>original: *Haute-contres*</note>, four Tenors, and four **Fifths** <note>original: *quintes*; the third middle part in a five-part string ensemble.</note>. But before setting down the piece of music, one must consider that one must always **pull the bow down** <note>A down-bow stroke.</note> on the first note of the measure, and that one must **push it up** <note>An up-bow stroke.</note> on the note that follows; for example, if the measure consists of 8 **eighth notes** <note>original: *crochuës*</note>, one pulls the bow down on the 1st and on the 3rd, 5th, and 7th; which one pushes up on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, and 8th: so that it is always pulled on the first note of each measure composed of an even number of notes. But if it is composed of an odd number, as happens when there is a dot after one of the notes, one pushes the bow up on the first note of the following measure, so as to pull it again on the first note of the 3rd measure, which must similarly be said of all the other notes and measures.

...will not be in tune when both are touched with the finger or the bow, because the bow can apply greater tension to the string by making it sound away from its straight line; and Violin players maintain that the sound of the strings is sharper when the bow touches harder. It may also happen that the Violin, which was tuned in a dry place, will go out of tune in a humid place, and vice versa; I omit a thousand accidents of the Violin, for example, that it loses a great part of its harmony when a key or something similar is placed on its bridge; that Rosin <note>original: *Colophone*; a refined resin</note> is more suitable for rubbing the hair <note>original: *soye*, literally "silk," but referring to horsehair</note> of its bow than pitch-resin, to soften the harmony; that the treble string <note>original: *chanterelle*</note> of the Sopranos is as thick as the fourth string of Lutes; and that the strength of this instrument's sound comes from the shortness of its strings.

Now, several peculiarities may be noted in the preceding Fantasia; first, that it contains the range of all the Violins, and reveals their nature and character. And then, that each sharp <note>original: *diese*</note> only serves for the note to which it is applied, whether it is seen before, above, or below it, except at the end of the first part of the Soprano, where the sharp also applies to the notes that follow. In the third place, that the King's Twenty-Four Violins <note>The *Vingt-quatre Violons du Roi*, the elite royal string orchestra</note> call "Quinte" or the "Fifth part" that which ordinary Musicians call "Alto" <note>original: *Haute-contre*</note>, and they call "Tenor" <note>original: *Taille*</note> what we call "Alto"; so that our Alto is their Tenor, which is why I follow their order in the example from the Latin book. The fifth part of the preceding notes is the closest to the Soprano in terms of high pitch; this is why it should be between the Soprano and the Alto, and consequently, it should be played by the smallest of the three Violins that are tuned in unison. From this comes the fact that Violin players call this part "Alto," the [actual] Alto "Tenor," and the Tenor "Fifth part." In the fourth place, I have included the ornamentation <note>original: *diminution*; the technique of breaking long notes into many fast, melodic notes</note> of the first thirty measures of the Soprano, so that one may see the manner in which Violinists are accustomed to ornament all sorts of songs. To this I add that one easily transposes each tone in twelve ways, by means of sharps and feigned accidentals <note>original: *fa feints*</note>, or flats <note>original: *b mols*</note> which they call accidentals, as seen in the example of the first mode which begins in C <note>original: *C sol vt fa*</note>.

The length of the <term>Viol</term> <note>The viol (or viola da gamba) family differs from the violin family by its fretted neck, six strings, and C-shaped soundholes.</note> is measured from the endpin **I**, up to the letter **A**, which shows the location of the <term>pegs</term> <note>original: *cheuilles*; the wooden pins used to tune the strings.</note>, although if one only wishes to measure its length by its strings, it is from the <term>bridge</term> **G** to the <term>nut</term> **B** <note>original: *fillet*; the small ridge at the top of the neck where the strings rest.</note>, because they only vibrate and sound between these two points: this occurs similarly in other instruments, where the length of the strings is bounded by the nut and the bridge. **M**, **L**, and **K** show the thickness of the body, or the height of the <term>ribs</term> <note>original: *éclisses*; the curved wooden sides of the instrument's body.</note>, which is greater or lesser according to the will of the <term>Makers</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*; refers here to luthiers.</note> and the harmony one wishes to draw from it. The end or part **M C** of the <term>fingerboard</term> **B M C** does not touch the <term>belly</term> <note>original: *table*; the front soundboard of the instrument.</note> of the Viol marked **C D E G**, but rather sits in the air, so that one may easily pass the fingers between it and the belly. The bridge **G** is two, three, or four fingers high, of which the left foot **G** is supported by a small post that one can see, and which is reset through the <term>soundhole</term> **E** <note>original: *ouye*; the resonance holes in the belly, often shaped like a C.</note> if it has fallen. **H** shows the place on the <term>tailpiece</term> **H I** where the six strings are attached; and **I** shows the strings of brass or iron wire that attach the tailpiece to the endpin **I**.

Regarding the <term>bow</term> <note>original: *archet*.</note>, I have already explained it in the treatise on the Violin, but this one is too long, for its length should be no greater than the distance from the bridge to the head of the neck, though it matters very little whether it be longer or shorter; provided that it is fit to touch the strings as is necessary to draw out the harmony and the charms of which the Viol is capable when it is touched by a masterly hand.

As for the notes that are to the side, they show the tuning of the Viol played on <term>open strings</term> <note>original: *à vuide*; strings played without pressing them against the frets.</note>, which first has two <term>Fourths</term>, then a <term>major Third</term>, and finally two more Fourths; so that the Third is enclosed by four Fourths, which demonstrates the value placed on this <term>Consonance</term> <note>An interval that sounds stable and pleasing.</note> and the necessity of its use; for even though one can tune the Viol in several other ways, nevertheless, use and practice show that this tuning is the best, or the most convenient and easiest of all. The numbers next to the pegs, which I repeat here, show the <term>fundamental ratios</term> <note>original: *termes radicaux*.</note> of this tuning—that is to say, the smallest numbers by which it can be expressed without using fractions. I also add the names and letters of the <term>standard scale</term> <note>original: *Gamme ordinaire*; the hexachord system of naming notes.</note>, so that everyone can understand this tuning, which has a range of a <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>A range of two full octaves.</note>, as seen from **D** to **D**, or from 320 to 80.

### Of Instruments

One can also mark this <term>tablature</term> <note>A system of notation using letters or numbers to show finger placement rather than pitches on a staff.</note> without lines and without notes, by using numbers and placing them opposite the letters representing each string; for example, the preceding tablature will be marked thus, so that:

<insert>
Songs and musical pieces can be expressed in very little space, although it is necessary to mark the duration <note>original: *le temps*</note> of each number or letter, whether by musical notes or otherwise.
</insert>

Certainly, if instruments are valued in proportion to how well they imitate the voice, and if of all artifices one esteems most that which best represents nature, it seems that one must not deny the prize to the Viol, which mimics the voice in all its modulations, and even in its most expressive accents of sadness and joy. For the <term>bow</term> <note>original: *l'archet*</note> which produces the effect we have mentioned has a stroke nearly as long as the ordinary breath of a voice, with which it can imitate joy, sadness, agility, sweetness, and strength through its liveliness, its languor, its speed, its relief, and its pressure. Likewise, the <term>vibratos</term> <note>original: *tremblemens*</note> and <term>grace notes</term> <note>original: *flatteries* (literally "flatteries" or "endearments");</note> of the left hand, which is called the hand of the neck, naturally represent its carriage and charms.

And if it is said that the Organ, the <term>Musette</term> <note>A small, courtly bagpipe.</note>, the Flute, etc., can provide a sustain and continuity much longer than the Viol, one can respond that—except for that and a few dainty cadences—they lack all the rest, and that it is not possible to manage their wind in such a way that they can produce the effect we just described. And if one alleges the Luth, the Harp, the <term>Spinet</term> <note>original: *Epinette*; a small harpsichord.</note>, etc., I admit that they have something of the dainty effect of the Viol, but it is aborted, for they lack the means to maintain sustained notes. As for the Violin and the modern Lyre, one can call them imitators of the Viol, just as they are of the voice; but they do not equal it, for the Violin has too much harshness, inasmuch as one is forced to string it with strings that are too thick to ring out in the subjects for which it is naturally suited; and if one strings it like the Viol, it will differ only in that it has no <term>frets</term> <note>original: *touches*.</note>.

As for the Lyre, it approaches more closely, but it is not capable of the passages executed on the Viol—which are the true image of the voice's agility—because its <term>bridge</term> <note>original: *cheualet*</note> is too flat; this is done so that several strings can be played together in chords. Those who have heard excellent players and good <term>consorts</term> <note>original: *concerts*; ensembles of instruments of the same family.</note> of Viols know that there is nothing more ravishing, after good voices, than the "dying" strokes of the bow, which accompany the vibratos made on the neck. But because it is no less difficult to describe their grace than that of a perfect Orator, one must hear them to understand them.

Now, before finishing this discourse, one must note two things that happen as much to the strings of the Viol as to those of the Lute and other instru-

...ments, the first of which is particularly noticeable in the thickest strings, which produce four or five different sounds at the same time: for when one plays the thickest string of the Viol with a stroke of the bow, one hears the natural sound of the string, and then another sound at the Octave above; in the third place the Major Tenth, and finally the fourth sound which rises to the Twelfth of the first sound: so that the same string, touched by the finger or the bow, produces the four sounds that correspond to the four numbers 1, 4, 5, and 6. This happens just as well with brass strings as with those of gut; which is why one cannot take the reason for this from the number of intestines that compose a gut string. <note>Mersenne is refuting a folk belief that the multiple pitches heard in a string were caused by the multiple strands of animal gut used to manufacture it.</note>

Now, one usually only hears these four sounds when playing the thickest strings, for the <term>chanterelle</term> <note>The highest-pitched, thinnest string on an instrument, used for the melody.</note> and the two or three others that follow on the Lute do not produce these intervals as noticeably; they are better understood on the Viol than on the Lute, for the reason that the stroke of the bow lasts longer, and gives more time to the ear and the imagination to notice them, than does the sound of the Lute, which ceases much sooner. But I shall speak more fully of this marvelous phenomenon in the treatise on the Lyre.

The other thing that happens to strings consists in the tension, which makes them rise higher on certain Viols than on others, even though they are all of the same length, and there is an equal distance from their <term>bridges</term> <note>The wooden support that holds the strings up from the body.</note> to their <term>nuts</term> <note>original: *fillets*; the ridge at the top of the neck where the strings pass into the pegbox.</note>: for there are Viols upon which one breaks twenty or thirty chanterelles before being able to find one that rises high enough, and others upon which all sorts of chanterelles rise easily; for which the instrument makers give no other reason than the hardness and strength of the <term>soundboard</term> <note>original: *table*; the top resonant surface of the instrument.</note> which breaks the strings, whereas it preserves them when it is less strong, and when it trembles and vibrates more easily.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

*To determine whether a string that is touched and pressed by the bow makes as many cycles and returns in the same time as one that is plucked by the finger, when they are in unison.*

If the <term>unison</term> <note>Two notes sounding at the exact same pitch.</note> of all sorts of strings is enough to demonstrate that the number of their cycles and their returns is equal in an equal time, there is no doubt that they vibrate as many times as one another, and consequently that the one touched with the bow makes as many returns against the movement of the bow as if it were touched by a quill or the finger. But since the bow always pushes the string from the same side, while its stroke is made from right to left, or from left to right, it seems that it cannot return in the opposite direction, and contrary to the bow which holds it in the same state, and which preserves it in the position it has given it, when it has pushed it as far as it could go. To which one may add that the vibrations <note>original: *tremblemens*</note> of the string are not entirely necessary to produce the sound, for one often experiences that several bodies being pressed, rubbed, and moved against stones, tiles, wood, or hard earth make sounds similar to those of Viols, even though one perceives no vibrations or returns in the friction of the said bodies.

Nevertheless, it must be concluded that the string makes as many vibrations of-

<page-num>197</page-num>
<header>of Instruments. 197</header>

under the bow than under the finger, and that the sound of Viols is no different in this regard from that of Lutes; consequently, the strings would produce no sound, or would not produce the same sound, if the bow or some other force pushed them so steadily from right to left, or left to right, that they could not have their free returns—unless that which pushes them made as many returns as the strings must make, as happens with the winds that strike rocks, trees, and houses, creating various noises.

   Now, there are several things to consider regarding the sounds made by the bow when touching and pressing the string, for the turns and returns <note>Mersenne is describing the back-and-forth cycles of a vibrating string.</note> of the string can occur just as well from top to bottom and bottom to top as from right to left, as happens when one weighs down on the string, or strikes it, or pulls it from top to bottom, and vice versa. This is why we must see how the bow causes it to make its returns; whether it makes them larger or smaller than when the string is touched by a finger, and whether it decreases or increases their number. Then, we must seek the reason why the sound the string makes by means of the bow is different from that which it makes when touched by the finger or a quill <note>Referring to the plectrum used on instruments like the harpsichord or mandore.</note>; for since the string always makes an equal number of turns and returns in an equal time, it seems the sound should be the same. This does not happen, and consequently, the bow contributes something particular. It does this by rubbing the string and by enclosing air between itself and the string; this air is forced to undergo as many "comings and goings" as the string does, whereas the string only strikes the free air when touched without a bow. This is why one can say that the sound of the <term>Viol</term> <note>The Viola da Gamba, a bowed string instrument held between the legs.</note> and other bowed instruments is composed of three or four kinds of movements: namely, that of the string and the free air, that of the constrained or enclosed air, and that of the bow, which governs the movement of the string as one wishes. For the bow prevents the string from making its cycles as large as it would if it were plucked as strongly as it is bowed; and because it holds the string at whatever distance from its center line one desires, it strengthens or softens the sound according to the pleasure of the one holding and moving it.

   Now, one can explain what the bow does to the <term>vibrations</term> <note>original: "tremblemens"</note> of the string by comparing it to what a finger does when passed very quickly over the holes of a <term>Flageolet</term> <note>A small, high-pitched flute popular in the 17th century.</note> while it is being played. This does not change the number of vibrations or beats of the wind, nor consequently the pitch of the sound, but it gives it a new movement which is almost similar to the <term>trills</term> <note>original: "fredons"; vocal ornaments or rapid divisions made in the throat.</note> made by the throat, which do not change the tones or the pitch of the voice, but serve only as a new ornament.

   And because the strands of horsehair that make up the hair of the bow are not continuous, the air moved by the string easily insinuates itself among the said hairs, whose movement and pressure alter the qualities of the sound. If we examine this more particularly, and consider how the atoms of air or of the string being moved mix with the movement of those of the horsehair, one will find it not at all strange that the sound produced by these two movements is different from that produced by the vibrations of the string alone. One can further remark on many things that are particular to the bow; for example, that it holds the same sound as long, and as weak or as strong, as one wishes—which the Organ cannot do, for it cannot af-

weaken or strengthen its sounds according to the desire of the organists <note>While "organist" usually refers to a keyboard player, Mersenne often uses it here to mean any musician skilled in the "organon" or instrument.</note>. But so that one does not doubt in any way that the string makes as many returns <note>vibrations or back-and-forth cycles</note> when it is touched by the bow as when it is touched by the finger, I wish to explain the manner of experimenting with it and seeing it very clearly. This will occur if one stretches a string a hundred feet long, which makes each of its returns in one second of time, whether one touches it with the bow or the finger. There is no other difference except that the bow can so constrain the string that the first vibration will be no larger than the thousandth or the last, whereas they are always decreasing after one has touched it with the finger. From this, it happens that the bow makes sounds much more equal than the finger, and that one can imitate the song of all sorts of birds, and an infinity of other sounds and noises by different pressures and different strokes of the bow, which is not possible to imitate on the Lute, on the Spinet <note>A small, rectangular keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note>, or on the Organ.

Now, one can experience the said tremblings of the strings touched by the bow on Viols and on Violins by putting a finger against the said strings; one feels the tremblings so strongly that, unless one is deprived of the sense of touch, it is not possible not to notice them in all parts of the string that is touched. And even if one did not have the experience, reason is sufficient to conclude that the movement of the bow—being sometimes very fast and at other times very slow—cannot produce the same pitch, and that it is necessary that the identity or equality of the treble <note>the highness or pitch of the note</note> proceeds from an equal movement. In this subject, that movement can be nothing other than the vibrations of the string, the number of which cannot be unequal in an equal time without changing the pitch—that is to say, the highness of the sound—as I have demonstrated elsewhere.

# PROPOSITION IX.

->*To explain the capability of Viols in Ensembles, the division and science of their necks, and the pieces of Music that can be played upon them, and the manner of tuning them to play in Ensembles.*<-

ALTHOUGH Viols are capable of all sorts of Music, and the examples I have given for the ensemble of Violins can serve them, they nevertheless require pieces that are sadder and more grave, and whose measure is longer and slower; hence it is that they are more suited for accompanying voices. Now, one can play all sorts of pieces not only in five parts, as is ordinarily done on Violins, but in six, seven, twelve, and as many parts as one wishes; which can similarly be executed by all other instruments that have enough range. But it is enough to put here the beginning of a Composition in six parts, which has two Trebles, two Basses, a Tenor, and a Counter-tenor.

Now it must be noted that the English ordinarily play their pieces a tone lower than the French, in order to render the harmony sweeter and more charming, and consequently their sixth string, when open, produces *C-faut* <note>C3 in the Guidonian hexachord system.</note> whereas ours produces *D-re-sol* <note>D2 or D3 in the hexachord system, the standard bottom string for a French bass viol.</note>, as seen in the notes beside the Viol; from which it follows that they mark several flats and sharps, of which

...which we do not ordinarily use. As for the division of the neck of the **Viol**, it is no different from that of the neck of the **Lute**; for this reason, I am merely adding here a new way to divide it. This method depends on the **eleven mean proportionals** <note>These are mathematical values used to divide an octave into twelve equal semitones, the basis for "equal temperament."</note>, the invention of which I provided in the fourteenth and fifteenth Proposition of the first book, and in the seventh of the second book. But one must first suppose that the entire string—that is, the length of the Viol from the **nut** <note>The small ridge at the top of the neck.</note> to the **bridge**—is divided into 200,000 equal parts. Having removed 11,230 parts, one will have the number 188,770 for the location of the first fret at the top, and so on for the other numbers which are across from the letters of each fret until the last, 100,000, which gives the last fret **n**, which makes the **Octave** above the entire string expressed by **a**.

And if one takes the difference between these thirteen numbers, one will have the twelve other numbers which are on the right hand, in order to engrave them upon the **proportional compasses** <note>Also known as a "sector," this was a calculating instrument used by engineers and musicians to find proportions without long division.</note>, and to mark the frets upon the neck of the Viol and other instruments with a single opening of the compass. For since the thirteen numbers on the left hand are in continuous proportion, it is certain that the twelve on the right are also in continuous proportion, and consequently that all the openings of the compass will keep the same proportion. For example, if the first opening taken on the first difference, 11,230, is a quarter of a foot—that is to say, three inches—there will be the same ratio from three inches to the second fret as there is from 11,230 to 10,599, and so on for the others. In this way, these 12 differences or numbers will show the twelve openings, or the twelve points of the compass, that must be transferred onto the neck one wishes to divide; and because one ordinarily puts only nine frets, of which **k** is the last, 7,072 will mark that fret. This is easy to understand if one simply looks at the numbers that follow.

Now, this table has five columns. Thus, if one divides the neck into 200,000 parts, the 12 descending numbers will mark the 12 frets of the neck. The fourth column contains the differences of the numbers in the third and shows the places where the frets must be placed. so that the entire line AV is related to its parts VB, VC, VD, etc., in the same ratio as the number 200,000 is to the numbers 188,770; 178,171; 168,178, etc. But because this method is somewhat long, Monsieur de Beaugrand <note>Jean de Beaugrand (c. 1584–1640) was a French mathematician and official in the court of Louis XIII; he was a contemporary of Descartes and Mersenne.</note>, Counselor and Secretary to the King, the Royal Household, and the Crown of France, and a most excellent geometer, has invented and had engraved a line on the **proportional compass**, which he calls "Harmonic." By means of this line, one can find all at once where to place all the **frets** <gloss>touches</gloss>, provided that the position of the first one is known.

Its construction is not difficult, as I clearly demonstrate: for the line AB being drawn from the center of the proportional compass—like the line of the circle, which has equal parts—it must be divided to make it Harmonic so that it is in the same ratio to lines AC, AD, AE, etc., as the number 11,230 is to the numbers 10,599; 9,993; etc. Then, one must engrave next to it the same alphabetical letters found in the table. But to use it with a common compass, one must take the interval between the **nut** <term>fillet: the ridge at the top of the neck that holds the strings in place</term> and the first fret of the **Lute**, the **Viol**, or any other instrument as desired, and apply it to points BB on each leg of the proportional compass as follows: having done this, the opening CC will give the distance from the second fret to the third, the opening DD the distance from the third to the fourth, the opening EE the distance from the fourth to the fifth, and so on for the others. As for the interval from the first fret to the nut, it will be found by dividing the distance between the **bridge** <term>cheualet: the wooden support for the strings on the instrument's body</term> and the nut into two parts such that the part on the bridge side is to the part toward the nut as 47 is to 3. That is to say, if the length from the bridge to the nut is divided into 50 parts, three must be removed to find the first fret, which must be taken at the same opening of the proportional compass at CC, for BB represents the nut.

<image-desc>A diagram of a "proportional compass" or sector. It consists of two legs radiating from a central pivot point labeled 'A'. Each leg is marked with a scale of letters ranging from B at the top down to N near the pivot. A vertical scale in the center shows the proportional distances between these letters (B through N), illustrating how to find the decreasing distances between musical frets using geometric ratios.</image-desc>

I do not wish to omit the method used to teach children how to play the **Viol** and to understand its neck, after noting that it has six strings and seven frets, and that the Treble, the Tenor, and the Bass are all tuned in the same manner relative to each other. This is done with open strings in this way: the **chanterelle** <term>the highest-pitched string</term> is tuned a **Fourth** from the second string, the second a Fourth from the third, and the fourth a Fourth from the fifth, and the fifth a Fourth from the sixth, which serves as the **Bourdon** <gloss>the lowest, heaviest string</gloss>; but the third string is tuned a **Major Third** from the fourth. And if one presses the *c* <note>In French lute and viol tablature, 'c' represents the second fret.</note> on the neck, it is found to be a Fourth, like the others are at the Fifth. As for the **Alto** <note>Original: *Haute-contre*.</note>, its tuning is only different from the other parts in that the 3rd and 4th strings make a Fourth when open, and the 4th and 5th make a Major Third when open, or a Fifth when one presses the *d* <note>The third fret in tablature notation.</note> of the 4th string. Now, it is customary to tune the four parts of the Viol, considered together, to the note **A** <note>Original: *A mi la re*, a term from the hexachord system of solmization used to identify the pitch A.</note>, which is taken on the second string of both the Treble and the Bass, by which all Viols are ordinarily regulated because it serves as the foundation for all Music: but the note **A** <note>Original: *l'a la mi re*.</note>...

The Treble <note>The "Dessus" or Treble Viol, the highest member of the viol family.</note> is tuned an Octave above the Bass. Having established this, I will explain the neck of the Viol, whose six strings are represented by the six lines running from right to left. Each of these corresponds to the notes or syllables of the six names placed at the beginning, opposite each string, when it is played "open" <note>An "open" string is played without pressing down any fingers on the frets.</note>. This is signified by the letter **A**, because in the letter-based system of musical notation <gloss>tablature</gloss>, the sound of each open string is marked by the letter *a*. We mentioned this in the second Book when discussing the Lute, and what we say here regarding the neck of the Viol can be applied to the Lute as well, since its neck and standard tuning are entirely similar to the Viol, as I have already stated elsewhere.

Now, this neck is so easy to understand that one only needs to place the fingers once or twice on the seven frets <gloss>touches</gloss> of each string, while using the ear and, if possible, the voice to match the sounds they produce so as not to forget them. For example, the highest string <gloss>chanterelle</gloss> will produce eight sounds: the first is open, played only with the bow; the second sound is made by placing the first finger of the left hand on the second fret marked by **B**. The seven transverse frets marked below by the numbers 1, 2, 3, etc., limit the length of the strings, which they shorten little by little, semitone by semitone <gloss>demy-ton</gloss>, as seen in the preceding figures and in these lines representing the neck.

One must follow the same pattern for frets **C**, **D**, **E**, **F**, **G**, and **H**. The fret **H** creates a Fifth with the open highest string; because of this, it creates an Octave with the next string when that string is played open. Thus, one can tune all the strings of the Viol by Octaves, since the **H** fret of the thinner string makes an Octave with the string following it when played open—except for the third string, because its interval with the fourth string (both played open) is only a major third <note>Mersenne notes the exception of the 3rd string, which is tuned a third below the 2nd, rather than a fourth.</note>. But if one wishes to tune the Viol by Unisons, one must touch fret **F** of the thicker strings and compare them to the next higher string played open. As for the sharps <note>original: "dieses"</note> found on some frets, they signify the semitones and represent the "accidentals" <gloss>feintes</gloss> of the Harpsichord <note>original: "Epinette"</note> and the Organ. I have added this for the benefit of those who love the consort of Viols.

Furthermore, if one wishes to teach children to sing all the semitones of the Viol, one can use the scale I explained in the *Practice of Music*. I demonstrate this here by adapting it to the range of the Treble and Bass Viols, using the preceding neck diagram where the Octave is divided into thirteen sounds; for this reason, one must use thirteen syllables.

The same must be said of the other Octaves of the Viol, whose range reaches as high as the Fifteenth <note>A double octave.</note> if one only touches the open treble string <gloss>chanterelle</gloss>, or up to the Nineteenth <note>Two octaves and a fifth.</note> when one uses its seven frets <gloss>touches</gloss>, which have the range of a Fifth.

I also wish to add what pertains to the bowing strokes <gloss>traits d'archet</gloss>, which are done in a manner entirely opposite to those of Violins; for on the Viol, one pushes the bow upward on the first note, and pulls it on the second, and so on consecutively. Now, one can similarly lower the pitch of Viols to make their sounds sweeter and to join them with the voice; some do this quite successfully by tuning them in Fourths like other Viols, in order to join them with the Organ or the voice. As for the general tuning of a consort of Viols, Fontanego <note>Sylvestro di Ganassi dal Fontego (1492–1550), an influential Italian musician and author.</note> remarks in his *Rubertine Rule* <note>original: "regle Rubertine," referring to the treatise *Regola Rubertina* (1542).</note> that it is done in three ways. The first is when the Tenor <gloss>Taille</gloss> and the Counter-tenor <gloss>Haute-contre</gloss> begin a Fourth higher than the Bass, and the Treble <gloss>Dessus</gloss> an Octave higher than the said Bass. The second puts the Tenor and Counter-tenor at a Fifth from the Bass, against which the Treble makes the Octave. The third has the Tenor play a Fourth against the Bass, and the Treble a Fourth with the Tenor, so that the Treble creates a minor Seventh against the Bass.

### PROPOSITION X.

->*To explain the shape, tuning, and use of the Lyre.*<-

The shape of the Lyre <note>Here referring to the *Lira da gamba*, a large bowed instrument used for chordal accompaniment.</note> is very little different from that of the Viol; nevertheless, its neck and the fingerboard of the neck are much wider, especially since it is covered with fifteen strings. The first six of these form only three ranks <note>Pairs of strings tuned in unison or octaves, similar to a 12-string guitar.</note>, and if one wishes to double each rank, as is done on the Luth, one would have twenty-two strings. The two thickest strings are placed off the neck, as can be seen from **H** to **K**; and the small nut **H I** is added to tension them. It is not necessary to advise that one can add a second neck similar to the second neck of Theorbos <gloss>Tuorbes</gloss> <note>Lutes with extended necks for long bass strings.</note> to place as many Basses as one desires, since this is already practiced on Viols. It must also be noted that the bridge <gloss>cheualet</gloss> **K** is longer, lower, and flatter than that of Viols, because it supports a greater multitude of strings, of which three or four must be touched at the same time with a single stroke of the bow in order to play chords. Now, the sound of the Lyre is very languishing and suited to exciting devotion and making the spirit turn inward upon itself; it is used to accompany the voice and recitatives.

## PROPOSITION XI.

***Determining why a string struck open produces several sounds at the same time.***

It seems that Aristotle was aware of this phenomenon when he posed the question of why the low sound contains the high one in the 8th Problem of the 19th Section, and why it becomes higher at its conclusion in the eleventh <note>original: "8. Probleme de la 19. Section... onziesme"</note>; to which one can relate the 12th and 13th Problems, and from which several other Problems of the same Section can be understood, such that this Proposition is very useful for Aristotelian Philosophy. But it must be noted that he did not know that a string, when struck and played open <gloss>meaning not pressed down against a fret</gloss>, produces at least five different sounds at the same time. The first of these is the natural sound of the string, which serves as the foundation for the others, and which is the only one considered for singing and for the parts of Music, because the others are so weak that only the best ears hear them easily. Now, one must choose a profound silence to perceive them, though this is no longer necessary once the ear is accustomed to them. If Musicians cannot hear them as soon as they touch a string of a Lute, a Viol, or another instrument—as happens to many Lute players who are so biased and preoccupied by the natural sounds of the string that there is (it seems) no more room in their common sense or their imagination to receive the idea or the nature of these delicate little sounds—they must have patience. Or, they should take a Bass Viol, touch the 6th, 5th, or 4th string at night, and remain very attentive; for it is difficult to touch it delicately with the bow without hearing several sounds at the same time.

As for me, I have no difficulty in this, and I have met several Musicians who hear them as well as I do. I have no doubt that everyone would hear them if they applied the necessary attention. This is why I set down here the observations that I have verified very exactly more than a hundred times, as much on a Viol and on a Theorbo <term>Theorbo: a large, long-necked lute with additional bass strings</term> as on two Monochords <term>Monochord: a scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals</term>, one of which has strings of brass and the other of gut and brass, one being three feet long and the other four feet. Thus, it is very certain that these different sounds do not come from the other strings on the instruments—which vibrate without being touched, as I have mentioned elsewhere—since a single string on the Monochords produces the same sounds.

Now, these sounds follow the ratio of these numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. One hears four sounds different from the natural one: the first is at the Octave above, the second at the Twelfth, the third at the Fifteenth, and the fourth at the Major Seventeenth, as is seen by the aforementioned numbers which contain the ratios of these consonances in their lowest terms <note>These numbers represent the harmonic series: 1 (fundamental), 2 (octave), 3 (twelfth/fifth), 4 (fifteenth/double octave), and 5 (major seventeenth/major third)</note>. Here, two things must be noted: first, that no sound is ever heard lower or deeper than the natural sound of the string, for they are all higher; and second, that these sounds follow the same progression as the "jumps" of the trumpet, which I shall discuss in the book on wind instruments. That section serves to understand this difficulty, which is why one may read and join the treatise on the trumpet with this Proposition.

Besides these four extraordinary sounds, I still hear a fifth, higher-pitched one, which I hear particularly toward the end of the natural sound, and at other times a little after the beginning; it creates a **Major Twentieth** with the natural sound, to which it relates in a ratio of **three to twenty**. <note>The author is describing the harmonic series. A Major Twentieth is an interval of two octaves and a major sixth; in terms of frequency ratios, this is 20:3.</note> But I experience almost always that the **Twelfth** and the **Major Seventeenth** are heard more distinctly than the others; from this, it often seems that one hears only one of the two, which is easily mistaken for the **Fifth** and for the **Tenth**, if one does not pay very exact attention. And when one hears the **Octave** and the **Fifteenth**, the latter is heard more distinctly than the former; so that several difficulties must be examined here, and particularly why some are heard better than others, why not everyone hears them, how it is possible that a single string makes several sounds at the same time, why it produces those I have mentioned rather than others that do not rise so high, why it produces none deeper than the natural sound of the string, and why one hears only the **Twelfth** in **Organ pipes**.

I say first, then, that the sounds which make the **Twelfth** and the **Major Seventeenth** are usually heard more distinctly because they are further removed from the natural sound of the string, with which the sound that makes the **Octave** has such a great resemblance that the ear takes them for one and the same sound, as I have said in the treatise on the Octave, from which one can take everything useful to this subject; this is why I only add that the sound at the **Fifteenth** is heard a little more distinctly, because it is more different from the natural sound, and it <term>beats the air</term> <note>original: "bat l'air"; a 17th-century term for frequency or vibrations.</note> four times while the natural sound beats it only once. Secondly, not everyone hears the same sounds because they do not have a good enough ear, or a judgment subtle enough to discern and notice them, or because they do not bring enough attention to it, or are not sufficiently detached from preoccupation. Now, the same thing is found in the other senses, for many perceive odors that others cannot smell because they do not have a sufficiently exquisite sense of smell.

As for the third difficulty and the two others following it, it is more difficult to answer them; for although it is true that the string making the natural sound contains those making the other sounds—as **Aristotle** notes in the *Problems* <note>Referring to the "Problemata," a work attributed to Aristotle containing early observations on music theory.</note> that I have cited, and from which he draws the reason why the low sound makes the high one heard, inasmuch as sound is to sound as string is to string—nevertheless, he only concludes this of the **Octave**, whose high sound is half the low one, which he compares to an **obtuse angle** that contains the **acute** one. Thus, one can understand his 11th Problem regarding the higher-pitched sound, and not only the weaker one; a conclusion **Septalius** <note>Ludovico Settala (1552–1633), an Italian physician and commentator on Aristotle.</note> could easily have drawn from the preceding Problems.

Furthermore, Aristotle’s reasoning is not universal; for even if a string is twice as thick or as long, it can produce sounds higher than one that is thinner and shorter, which happens through different tensions or different materials, as I clearly demonstrated in the third book. And then, the immediate cause of sounds is taken from the **number of beats of the air**, as I demonstrated in the same place, and not from the length of the strings. This is why it must be examined how it can be done—

He discusses the physics of vibration, citing Aristotle's theories while arguing that frequency (air beats) rather than just string length determines pitch.</summary>

...that the same string <note>original: "chorde"</note> strikes the air differently at the same time; for since it produces the five or six sounds of which I have spoken, it seems entirely necessary that it must strike the air 5, 4, 3, and 2 times in the same duration that it strikes it only once. This is impossible to imagine, unless one says that half of the string strikes it twice while the whole string strikes it once, and that at the same time the 3rd, 4th, and 5th parts strike it 3, 4, and 5 times. However, this is contrary to experience, which clearly shows that all parts of the string make an equal number of returns <note>vibrations or oscillations</note> in the same amount of time; for the entire string, being continuous, has only a single movement, even though its parts move more slowly the closer they are to the bridges <note>original: "cheualets"</note>.

From this, it is easy to conclude what I have already demonstrated in the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th books: namely, that a low sound <note>original: "son graue"</note> does not come absolutely from the slowness or tardiness of movement. This is because the parts of the string that move more slowly than those in the middle do not produce sounds lower than the natural sound <note>original: "son naturel"; the fundamental frequency or the primary pitch of the string</note>, which proceeds particularly from the aforementioned middle parts. Since the natural sound is the strongest, it must come from the greatest movement; for one always hears the higher-pitched sounds above the natural sound, and never below it, as I have stated above.

Now, since every sound is determined as being low or high by the number of beats <note>vibrations</note> against the air, and since the string can only strike it a certain number of times in the same duration, it is necessary that the air, having been struck, reflects back upon the string, and that as the string makes its return, it gives the air a new movement. This can be conceived in two ways: for one could say that the air has a greater tension—that is to say, it is so disposed that when it is struck, it moves faster and has more frequent returns than the string or other bodies by which it is struck. This is similar to a string stretched on an instrument, which moves much faster than the finger, the quill, or the bow by which it is touched, due to the disposition it has acquired through its tension. 

Or, one could say that the air, having been struck and sent, for example, to the right side of the string, returns after the string moves to the left side, so that the string meets it on the way and pushes it a second time, adding a new movement to it. This causes the air to henceforth create the Octave above <note>a 2:1 ratio</note> along with the movement or natural sound of the string, which always keeps the same time for the same number of returns, while the air makes two returns for every one of the string. But when the string meets it a third time, it imprints yet a third movement upon it, so that it has three returns against one to create the Twelfth <note>a 3:1 ratio</note>, and then the Fifteenth <note>4:1</note>, and the Seventeenth <note>5:1</note>.

To this, one may add that the air, having been struck by the string, divides itself first into two parts, then into 3, 4, 5, etc., which produce the preceding sounds, because this division is the easiest of all. And if one admits the atoms of Democritus <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the world is made of indivisible units called atoms</note>, one could say that the different parts of the string which strike the air differently divide and break the Sphere of the air into 2, 3, 4, and 5 parts; or that the same part of the string breaks it differently according to its different dispositions, so that one of the parts of the air breaks into two, another into three, four, or five parts, etc.

Now, if we suppose that the entire string contains all the sounds that can be made by its division, it must be said that it only makes those appear which come from the first, second, or third bisection <note>original: "bisection"; the act of cutting into two equal parts</note>, of which

I have spoken of this in the book on Consonances and in the one on Dissonances.

Certain people have recourse to the different surfaces of the string <note>original: "chorde"</note> to explain all these sounds, and say that the middle produces a sound different from that made by the exterior surface; but there is no reason to believe that the string is divided into several concave cylinders which cover the convex cylinder of the middle, like the layers of an onion <note>original: "peaux d'oignon"</note> cover one another. And even if the string were woven from these different cylinders, it could not make different sounds if it did not strike the air 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 times at the same moment. This is no easier to explain by a multitude of cylinders than by other means, whether one attributes the high pitch <note>original: "l'aigu"</note> of the sound to the returns of the internal air or the external air.

### COROLLARY I.

If the sound of each string is more harmonious and agreeable the greater the number of different sounds it makes heard at the same time, and if it is permitted to compare moral actions to natural ones, and to transport Physics to human actions, one can say that each action is all the more harmonious and agreeable to God when it is accompanied by a greater number of motives, provided they are all good. For example, when one fasts to macerate the body and to make it more obedient to the spirit; and then to satisfy the commandment of the Church; in the third place to reserve something for the poor; and finally to imitate the fasts of our Savior and to practice the love we bear for Him. For one can compare all these motives to all the sounds that accompany the movement of the string, and say at the same time that the intention which is the strongest—and which has the principal and most excellent end—is similar to the dominant and natural sound of the string, since it is the most perceptible and the cause of all the other sounds which are made by more hurried movements or more frequent returns <note>vibrations</note>.

### COROLLARY II.

It is more probable that these different sounds come from the different movements of the external air than from those of the internal air, and that the former, being struck by the string, makes many small movements similar to those of the water in glasses that one makes ring by pressing a finger on the rim, or to those of the water into which one plunges the end of a Monochord, of which the brass <note>original: "leton"</note> string is partly in the water and partly in the air. For when it is touched, the water makes several shudders <note>vibrations</note> which would perhaps make the preceding sounds heard if the hearing were delicate enough. Indeed, I have often experienced that the sliding of the finger on the rim of the glass makes two or three sounds at the same time, as I shall say in the book on Bells, which similarly produce several sounds.

### PROPOSITION XII.

->*To explain the shape, the tuning, and the range of the Symphony, or the Hurdy-Gurdy, which some call the Lyre; and the Spinets which imitate the playing of Viols.*<-

If men of high social standing <note>original: "hommes de condition"</note> commonly played the <term>Symphony</term> <note>At this time, "Symphony" or *Sinfonye* referred to the hurdy-gurdy, a stringed instrument played with a crank-turned wheel.</note>, which is called the Hurdy-Gurdy <note>original: "Vielle"</note>, it would not be as despised as it is; but because

Because it is only played by the poor, and particularly by the blind <note>original: "aueugles"</note> who earn their living with this instrument, it is held in less esteem than others, though they do not provide as much pleasure. This does not prevent me from explaining it here, since science belongs no more to the rich than to the poor, and there is nothing so low or so vile in nature or in the arts that is not worthy of consideration.

It must first be noted that the Hurdy-gurdy <term>Vielle; a stringed instrument where a crank-turned wheel rubs the strings like a bow</term> is composed of two main parts, like other instruments: namely its soundboard <note>original: "table"</note> A B C

<image-desc>A detailed vertical woodcut diagram of a hurdy-gurdy (vielle). The instrument has a pear-shaped body (A, B, C) and a long neck (E, F, G, H) containing a keybox. D, and its neck E F G H, which continues to M L to hold the four pegs <note>original: "cheuilles"</note>, which tension its four strings. Of these, the two on the sides—namely δ D H K and Y N C I—serve as two Drones <term>Bourdons; strings that produce a constant humming pitch</term>, which can be tuned to unison or to the octave of one another.

The two other strings ε and ζ are stretched along the length of the neck and serve as a perpetual Monochord <note>original: "Monochorde"</note>, for they produce all sorts of tones like the Spinet <note>original: "Epinette"; a small harpsichord</note>, by means of the keys <note>original: "marches"</note> marked by the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, etc., up to 10. This is because this figure was taken from a small Hurdy-gurdy which has only ten keys; however, one can make them with 49 keys, or as many as one wishes.

One can increase the number of strings, which are usually tuned to unison or the octave, like those of double or triple Harpsichords <note>original: "Clauecins"</note>. But if one installs six drones tuned to the Octave, the Twelfth, the Fifteenth, the Seventeenth, and the Nineteenth <note>These intervals correspond to the natural overtone series described on the previous page</note>, following the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, one will have a perfect Har-

mony, which can be varied in different ways by adding or removing whichever strings one wishes, and by moving them away from the wheel N O P. For these drone strings and the others cannot sound if they do not touch the wheel, which serves as their bow. This is why the wheel must be well-polished, so that the strings do not suffer from jumps while rubbing against it. It is also necessary to rub it with Rosin <term>Colophone; a resin used to create friction between bow and string</term>, just like the horsehair or silk of ordinary Violin bows; otherwise, the strings would not sound. However, this wheel lacks the charms of the bow, although one might remedy this imperfection.

Now, each key of the Hurdy-gurdy's keyboard has two small perpendicular pieces of wood, which may be called the tangents <note>original: "touches"</note>, since they serve to touch the two strings that are in unison when one pushes the

This occurs with all the other keys when they are allowed to return to their ordinary position, which they take when their ends do not appear on the side F H, as is seen at the end of the fifth key.

It must also be noted that the keyboard <term>clauier; the box housing the keys and tangents</term> marked E F G H is similar to a small raised box on the soundboard δ O Q C D, so that the branches of the keys with their tangents <term>touches; the wooden pieces that press against the string to change its pitch</term> may be housed inside; and that this box is joined and glued to the said soundboard, beneath which is the body and the concave, or the hollow of the Hurdy-gurdy. However, it is hidden by means of a cover, which is attached to the side F H. The wheel is similarly covered by a piece of fir, curved in a circle like the handle of a wooden bucket, which is held by the small pieces of wood α β: though I have left both uncovered so that all the parts of this instrument may be seen.

As for the bridges <term>cheualets; the supports that hold the strings above the body</term>, the highest one marked R, which is near the wheel, has its notches or slots a little lower than the upper surface of the wheel, so that the strings rest upon it and the wheel touches them when one turns the handle, or the crank <term>manivelle</term> Y, which is joined to the end of the tailpiece V at point Z. At the other end, the two middle strings are attached at the points ζ. If one wishes to use three, four, or several other strings on this bridge, one must make as many teeth and add as many tangents to the keys. The two other bridges S and T serve to determine the length of the Drone <term>Bourdon; the low-pitched accompaniment strings</term> strings, which are attached at points δ γ and extend to the last pegs 13 and 14; the other two are tied and wound to the first and second, which are marked 11 and 12. Now, these pegs <note>original: "cheuilles"</note>, which are horizontal here, are usually perpendicular to the end of the neck, which is so covered that one only sees the heads of the pegs. But I have uncovered this entire instrument to facilitate understanding; if one adds 2, 3, or 4 drones, one must make several teeth of different heights on bridges S and T, so that the strings touch other parts of the wheel from the place where string O touches to P: which is very easy to understand.

The letter X shows the soundhole <note>original: "ouye"</note> of the Hurdy-gurdy, and one can add other soundholes as on the Viol, and several details and circumstances, both for ornament and for convenience—for example, a small box to hold strings and rosin <term>colophone; a resin used to create friction between the wheel and strings</term>; this depends on the industry and the will of the makers <note>original: "Facteurs"</note>. And because they can make Hurdy-gurdies five or six feet long, and of all other manner of sizes, there is no doubt that one could create ensembles of them, which would perhaps move the spirit more than those of other instruments.

Regarding the layout of this figure, if one looks at it from the side D T, seeing the letters according to their ordinary arrangement, one will see it in the same way as those who play it hold and view it; for they place the left arm underneath, in order to push the keys with the left hand and create whatever intervals they wish by the movement of the fingers, while the right hand turns the crank, and consequently the wheel, which makes the strings sound, to which small pieces or tufts of cotton are attached.
