But because the left hand cannot perform the <term>gentillesses; ornaments or graceful techniques</term> of the viol neck upon the keyboard of the **Hurdy-gurdy**, it is deprived of several beauties of which it would be capable, if one could supply all the trills and the ravishing strokes of the bow by some industry. Many have sought this by gluing a skein of horsehair, or raw or spun silk, upon the wheel, and by making mobile or immobile bows in several fashions; but no one has been able to replicate the movements of the skillful hand of those who charm the ears with instruments with fretted and unfretted necks <note>original: "manches touches, & non touches"</note>, of which I have spoken in the preceding discourses.

The **tablature** <term>tablature; a system of musical notation indicating finger positions rather than pitches</term> of the Hurdy-gurdy is no different from that of Music, although one could invent another specifically for the blind, since they can be taught to read and write, as I have said elsewhere, where I demonstrated the manner of teaching the deaf to read and write, for whom I prepared tablature in the 17th Proposition of the third book.

As for the invention of **Spinets** <term>Epinettes; here referring to keyboard instruments designed to sound like bowed strings, such as the Geigenwerk</term> which serve to play viol parts, they have until now used a single large wheel, upon which all the strings of the Spinet rest, just as the four strings of the Hurdy-gurdy do; or five different parallel wheels, as they do in Germany. However, a bow of horsehair stretched above or below the strings would better imitate the **Viol**, if one could remedy all the accidents that hinder its movement.

Now I have no doubt that the industry of the **Makers** <term>Facteurs; craftsmen who build musical instruments</term> can avoid them, especially since there is a way to make the hairs of the silk blend into one another, or to make one part pass over while the other passes under, so that no knots are encountered. Furthermore, the bow can be kept equally taut by means of pulleys over which it passes, because they can be moved closer or further away with screws, in order to tighten the silk when it becomes loose. Regarding this, it must be noted that the strings must be very close to the wheels, or to the silk of the bow, so that they speak as soon as one touches the keyboard, whose keys can be lowered more or less to make the strings speak louder or softer.

Small springs can be added to create trills upon the strings, in order to imitate the <term>tremblemens; trills</term> and <term>flatemens; a gentle vibrato or ornament specific to the viol</term> of the left hand; and if one adapts mechanisms to turn the wheels or the bow, there will be no need for a man or a foot to play this instrument, but only the hand to touch the keyboard—like that of ordinary **Harpsichords**—which will make a concert of five or six Viols heard when one plays five or six parts upon it.

It is not necessary to provide tablature here for this sort of Spinet, nor for the Hurdy-gurdy augmented by as many strings as one wishes, because those I have given for the Spinet and for the Viols can serve. As for the **Drums** or **Barrels** <term>Tambours ou Barillets; pinned cylinders used in mechanical instruments</term> used to make Spinets play by themselves, I shall speak of them in the book on Organs.

I am adding a figure of the **Hurdy-gurdy** covered by its lid, so that nothing is missing from this treatise, and so that it may be understood in every possible way.

### PROPOSITION XIII.

*To explain new stringed instruments, and the tuning of the Lyre used in Italy.*

It is certain that one can always add new inventions to instruments, and that future ages may possess some that have not yet occurred to the imagination of the <term>Builders; instrument makers or "facteurs"</term>. For example, one could make **Harpsichords** that have every tone divided into four parts, to produce <term>enharmonic quarter-tones; microtonal intervals smaller than a semitone</term> everywhere, following the System that I explain in the *Book on Genres*. In this way, the same keyboard would serve for as many Organ pipes, which would sound like a recorder and accompany each string. And I have received word from Rome that Master Giovanni Battista de Bonis of Cortona, a city in Tuscany, makes excellent ones which have all the keys "broken" or <note>meaning split keys to allow for different sharps and flats</note>...

cut, and which are tuned with an admirable ease in all sorts of ways that one can imagine. I have also been informed that the triple-row harp <term>triple-row harp; original: *Harpe à trois rangs*; a Baroque harp with three parallel rows of strings to allow for chromatic playing without pedals</term> was invented thirty or forty years ago by Lord Luca Antonio Eustache, a Neapolitan gentleman and Chamberlain to Pope Paul V: and that Lord Orazio Michi has brought this instrument to its perfection, which he plays most excellently: this is why I add here the discourse made by Lord Stefano Landi <note>Stefano Landi (1587–1639) was a famous Roman composer of the early Baroque</note>, which was sent to me by Monsieur Bouchard.

He says, then, that the two outer rows correspond to the white or principal keys of the harpsichord <term>harpsichord; original: *Cymbale*</term>, and that the inner row performs the role of the accidentals <term>accidentals; original: *feintes*; literally "feints," referring to the black keys</term> or the black keys, to which are added the *A-mi-la-re* and the *D-la-re-sol* <note>solmization syllables used to identify specific pitches in the hexachord system</note> from the outside, in order to equal the inner black keys to the outer white ones. By this I imagine he wishes to describe that species of double harp which has recently been brought to France, and which may be called the Harmonic Pyramid <term>Harmonic Pyramid; original: *Pyramide Harmonique*</term> by reason of its shape, for it has strings on both sides, of which the largest are on the left hand, and the smallest on the right. But it has much more range <term>range; original: *estenduë*</term> than the ordinary triple-row harp, whose harmony it far surpasses, for it rises a fifth above four octaves—which is to say it has a range of a thirty-third.

He adds that when the outer strings are tuned by B-natural <note>original: *♯ quarre* or "square B," the ancestor of the natural and sharp signs</note>, those of the inside are tuned by B-flat <note>original: *♭ mol* or "soft B," the ancestor of the flat sign</note>, and when the latter are tuned by a sharp, the former are tuned by a natural: and that it is the most difficult instrument of all, because of the difficulty of making it, tuning it, and finding the string with which one must begin the air or the song; for whereas the hand and eye easily distinguish the white keys from the black on the keyboard of the spinet, there is difficulty in discerning the strings of the three rows of the harp. This is because they are all similar to one another, and although some have wished to mark them with different colors, one still finds great difficulty in moving the hand with great speed and lightness.

Finally, he finds so many difficulties in it that he hopes to write an entire book about it, in order to teach everything concerning it, so that one might play the four parts <note>referring to four-part polyphonic music</note> upon it with much more grace and charm than on the organ. I leave aside the Barberini Lyre <term>Barberini Lyre; original: *Lyre Barberine*; a complex stringed instrument designed to play ancient Greek modes</term>, of which Monsieur Doni—most learned in antiquity—will soon give us a book: and the Theorboes <term>Theorboes; original: *Tuorbes*</term> upon which one can play all sorts of songs with open strings, in order to finish this Proposition, which I wish to conclude with the tuning <term>tuning; original: *accord*</term> of the Lyre used in Italy. This was sent to me by the same route from Lord Girolamo Landi, Superintendent of Music for the Most Illustrious Cardinal Barberini; for since it had been a long time since my discourse on the Lyre was printed when I received the remarks of this excellent Master of Music regarding the Lyre, the Harpsichord, and several other instruments, I wished to place this tuning here, so that it may be compared with that of Monsieur le Baillif (which I placed in the 10th Proposition, page 207) and with that at the bottom of the Lyre on page 205.

He notes that the first two strings, which are off the neck, are octaves, like the thick strings of our Lyre <term>Lyre; here referring to the Hurdy-Gurdy or the Lyra da Braccio</term>, and that one can play all sorts of musical pieces upon them: that this instrument is the most suitable of all for singing stories and sonnets, and particularly sublime and elevated things both in the common tongue and in Latin <note>original: "tant en langue vulgaire qu’en Latin"</note>, because it accompanies the voice as easily as the Organ, and with more variety, because one can soften the sounds as much as one wishes. Now the Bass voice is more suitable than others to be joined to this instrument, in order to supply the roughness of the Fourth <note>the musical interval of a perfect fourth</note>, which is sometimes found there without the Fifth below it: but it produces a very good effect when the voice performs the Fifth. I leave aside what he says of the Arm Viol <term>Arm Viol; original: *Viole à bras*; the violin family</term>, which has only four strings similar to those of the Violin, of which I have treated so amply in this book that it is not necessary to speak of it: one must only note that the Lyre of which I have just discoursed is played on the arm, like Violins, whereas ours is called a Leg Viol <term>Leg Viol; original: *à iambe*; referring to the Viola da Gamba</term>, because it is placed between the legs to be played.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

->*To explain the construction, the parts, and the shape of the Marine Trumpet,*<-
->*and the manner of playing it.*<-

Even though one could give the name Monochord <term>Monochord; an instrument with a single string used for scientific and musical measurements</term> to this instrument, it is nevertheless called the *Marine Trumpet*, either because sailors invented it, or because it imitates the sounds and melodies of the ordinary trumpet so perfectly that there is almost no way to distinguish them from one another. It has several other very remarkable features which I shall explain after giving its construction. Now I place here two different figures, of which the one on the right hand, A C E D, represents its ancient form, and the one on the left shows the new form which has been found to be more convenient and better for resonating. I come then to the first, <unclear>of</unclear> which the neck A B has two tuning pegs P O to tighten the two strings Q and N, the latter being held by the piece of wood F, which is laid and glued <unclear>quite</unclear> flat against the soundboard C D N, which can be made of fir, or such other <unclear>wood</unclear> as one wishes, as one makes those of other instruments. But this <unclear>piece</unclear> of wood serves only to hold the string, which is passed through a small hole into the body of the instrument, and then a knot is tied at the end to make it hold.

As for the bridge G H, it is easily removed from under the string when one wishes, and only its leg G rests firmly on the soundboard, for the other leg H lightly touches the small square piece of glass, ivory, or metal that is glued to the soundboard, so that this leg makes small vibrations <note>original: "fremiſſemens"; this "trembling" bridge is what creates the trumpet-like buzzing sound</note> upon it when the string is touched with a bow, of which I do not provide the figure here because it is no different from that of the Viols. I show the figure of the rosette <term>rosette; original: *rose*; the decorative carved soundhole</term>, although it is not necessary (which is why I did not put one on the second figure), or one may put two or three others there. A small bit of ivory or horn is also placed at the end of the leg H, so that it strikes the glass more strongly.

The second string Q does not need glass, and succeeds better than the other—

# Book Fourth

...[the cen]ter, as I will say in explaining the second figure. **K** signifies the bridge, over which it passes to find the hole that follows after: although it is more appropriate to say that the small curved piece of wood **L** is the true bridge, since the sound of the string begins at **L**.

Now, I have set this second string at the <term>Fifth; a musical interval of five scale degrees</term> of the first string **G N**, because it brings great variety to the tones of this Trumpet: the numbers that go from one to eleven show its most remarkable sounds, of which the first is made by touching the open string, and the 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. are heard when one touches it with the thumb or index finger at the places marked by these numbers.

But before explaining all its tones, and the manner of playing and fingering it, I come to the second figure **P S**, whose neck shows its three sides, in order to make it known that one can make this Trumpet with three sides or three soundboards; each of which will have a string similar to string **Z**, which could be shorter in whatever ratio one wishes, so that it makes the sound of <term>Clarions; high-pitched, clear trumpets used in military signals</term>, and of all sorts of Trumpets: and in that case, the neck must be made <note>original: "au tour"</note> on a lathe, so that one finds space for the three <term>tuning pegs; the wooden pins used to tighten or loosen the strings</term>. The bridge **Y** is seen in its correct size in figure **αβδ**, where the notch or groove **α** shows the place where the string rests: and the end **δ** is the one that bears lightly upon the soundboard, so that it rises and beats very quickly against the soundboard when one presses the string with the <term>bow; the tool, usually made of horsehair, used to vibrate the string</term>.

Where it must first be noted that it is very difficult to adjust this bridge so that it trembles as it should, for if it is off by even a little, its vibration becomes too loud and disagreeable, or too weak: so that one is often several hours finding the point of perfection it requires. Secondly, one uses a small piece of wood that is fitted into a groove made on the other bridge **X**, which is glued to the soundboard,

### Of Instruments

...so that the aforementioned piece serves as a movable bridge <term>Movable bridge; a bridge that can be shifted to change the string's length or tension</term> to be moved to the right or left until the bridge **Y** meets exactly the spot where it vibrates moderately to contribute, along with the vibration of the string, to making the sound of the Trumpet.

In the third place, I have marked all the letters of the Scale, or the Harmonic Scale of Guido of Arezzo <note>original: "Guy Aretin"; an 11th-century monk who developed the system of solmization</note> on one of the sides of this instrument, so that it may be used as a Monochord: for the **Γ** <note>the Greek letter Gamma, used to denote the lowest note of the medieval scale</note> signifies the lowest sound, which descends a tone lower than the *Proslambanomenos* <note>original: "Proslambanomene"; a Greek term for the "added note" at the bottom of the two-octave system</note> of the Greeks, which corresponds to our **A re**, so that after having touched the open string, it rises by one tone as it is shortened from **Γ** to **A**; and if one shortens it to **♮** <note>the "square B" or B-natural</note>, it rises by a Major Third, which is produced by the whole string **Γ** against **♮**, and so on for the others until the twentieth row of letters, that is to say, up to the two **ee**, which make the Major Twentieth, or the Major Hexachord <term>Hexachord; a musical scale of six notes</term> on the Disdiapason <term>Disdiapason; a musical interval spanning two octaves</term> against the open string.

In the fourth place, I have also put seven numbers higher than these two **ee**, because this instrument rises an Octave higher, as I will say later. This being established, one must also know that this instrument is played with the bow from **P** to number seven, or on the other instrument on **N**, and for this purpose one must turn the head of the instrument **A**, and place it against the chest, while simultaneously leaning the bottom end **C D E** against some wall, or against the ground.

Now the side **P T** is a very accurate Monochord, which begins with **G ut**, **A re**, **♮ mi**, etc., up to the twentieth syllable of the Harmonic hand <note>The "Guidonian Hand," a mnemonic tool used to teach singing</note> **E la**: where it should be noted that it contains the first mode, insofar as after having ascended a Fifth from **G ut** up to **D sol re**—that is to say, after having made the first species of the Diapente <note>original: "Diapente"; the Greek term for the interval of a Fifth</note>—it ascends from **D re sol** to **G re sol** by the first species of Fourth; the minor tone is found from **F** to **A**, and the major from **A** to **♮**; the major from **C** to **D**, the minor from **D** to **E**, and the major from **E** to **F**, and so on for the others while ascending; as for the major semitones, they are from **♮** to **C**, and from **F** to **G**, etc., for there is no middle semitone in B-natural <note>original: "♮ quarre"; literally "square B," referring to the natural note rather than the "soft" B-flat</note>.

The first point where this instrument begins to make the sound of the Trumpet after that of the open string is marked by the first dotted line opposite ***d***, which is to say that it makes the Twelfth with the open string, since **P d** is a sub-triple <note>A 1:3 ratio, corresponding to the interval of a twelfth</note> of **P Γ**: the second sound is made at the second dotted line ***g***; the 3rd at the 3rd **♮ ♮**, the 4th at the 4th ***dd***, and the 4th at the 4th marked with the number **2**: so that these four sounds correspond to these four numbers **3, 4, 5, 6, 8**. As for the other sounds that follow by degrees, they are marked by the five numbers that follow **2**, namely by **3, 4, 5, 6,** & **7**, which make all the degrees of the Major Hexachord, including the sound of point **2**.

As for the manner of playing this instrument, it is so difficult that one meets few men who play it well, because one must slide the thumb, or another finger, with a certain measure and speed, from number seven to the ***d***, which makes the first sound; this is not easy to imitate. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that it can be played perfectly once as much time has been spent on it as is spent on playing the Viol or the Lute. If one began to play at the vibrating bridge **Y**, one would find the same points and the same divisions that are found at the top, as experience teaches; but it is more convenient to have the bow touch in...

# Fourth Book

Here it must be noted that the string mimics the sound of the military Trumpet <note>The military trumpet was a natural brass instrument without valves, producing sounds based on the harmonic series</note> more perfectly the tighter it is tensioned, and it should be neither too thick nor too thin: the thickest racket strings, that is to say those made of twelve sheep guts, are of a good thickness.

-> PROPOSITION XV. <-

-> *Explaining the main phenomena of the Marine Trumpet and its properties.* <-

The first Phenomenon of the string of this instrument consists of the vibration, which composes a sound different from that of all other strings, for example those of Violins and Viols, insofar as it is composed of the ordinary vibration common to all types of strings, the friction or touch of the bow, like that of the Viols, and the trembling of the bridge <term>Trembling; here referring to the "tromba marina" bridge where one foot is loose and drums against the soundboard</term> which is unique to it. As for the light beatings of the fingers, which are called *flutterings* <note>original: "flatemens"; a period term for a type of vibrato or soft trill</note>, every instrument is capable of them. Now, it is the trembling of the bridge that makes it imitate the sound of the Trumpet, which is very remarkable for finding the reason for the trembling sounds of the military Trumpet, which is not observed in other wind instruments, for example Oboes, Cornets, and Hunting Horns.

The second Phenomenon is common to all strings that produce five or six different sounds at the same time, as I noted in the treatise on the Lyre. But the third is very particular, and consists in the fact that the sound of the Trumpet cannot be produced at any point on the string of this instrument except at the specific points and divisions of which I have spoken, namely at the open string P Γ, at d, g, ♮ <note>The "square B" or B-natural</note>, dd, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, & 7: which similarly happens below at points A, ♮, & D which correspond to the upper points 4, ♮, & d; but the fingers cannot reach as far as these points; which could nevertheless be supplemented by some ingenuity. It must also be noted that the second and third sounds of the military Trumpet, which are not ordinarily produced on this instrument, will be found there, provided that after its first open sound one touches the string in the middle at point G, where it will make the first leap to the Octave <term>Octave; the interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency</term> of its first sound, because P G is half of P Γ. And the second leap will be made by a Fifth <term>Fifth; an interval spanning five notes of a western scale, such as C to G</term> from G to d, which one begins only to touch with the thumb of the left hand.

Now, it is difficult to give a reason for this Phenomenon that satisfies everyone, for why can this string not imitate the sounds of the Trumpet at points a, ♮, c, e, f, aa, cc, ee, & i? It is certain that the points where it imitates them arise from the first, second, and third bisection <term>Bisection; the mathematical act of dividing a string exactly in half</term>, etc., as I proved in the treatise on the Monochord, and that nature always, or often, shows that she loves these divisions into two equal parts, as the easiest of all possible ones, and that all kinds of strings being touched produce all the sounds together, and at the same time, which are produced by the military Trumpet, and by this one at different times and by leaps. But since the bow touching the Viol always produces good sounds wherever its strings are touched by the left hand, and that the string of this...

Trumpet has all the other effects of those of the Viol, it seems that it should always produce good sounds in whatever place one might touch it from *d* until the number two <note>In period monochord diagrams, "number two" often refers to the midpoint of the string, which produces the octave</note>, which does not happen; for besides the fact that it can hardly ascend from *d* until the finger touches it at *g*, nor from *d* to *g*, the sounds it produces between these points are very disagreeable, and do not well imitate those of the military Trumpet <note>The military trumpet, being a natural brass instrument, only produces notes from the harmonic series; the Marine Trumpet mimics this limitation</note>, from which they are so different that there is no one who is not astonished by it, when one comes to encounter the quality and the beauty of the sounds of *d*, of *g*, of *♯♯*, etc.

As for the other sounds, one can hardly judge their tone, which is difficult to suffer and to support without displeasure: this must be understood regarding these two figures <note>Referring to the technical diagrams provided in the original printed text</note>, for what occurs at string *Z Y* happens similarly at string *N G*. The difficulty seems even greater when one considers that the bridges should tremble just as well when one touches points *a*, *c*, *e*, *f*, etc. as when one touches *d*, *g*, etc. Be that as it may, it trembles so poorly at these points that their sounds are worthless, and they are very disagreeable: and it suffices that I have explained the true Phenomena of this instrument to give occasion to great minds to seek out the true reasons for them. I add nonetheless that these leaps and these points, which imitate the sounds of the military Trumpet, are nothing other than a demonstration on a large scale of what the string does when played open <note>original: "à vuide"; meaning the string is played without being pressed down to the fingerboard</note>, namely the Octave, the Twelfth, the Fifteenth, the Seventeenth, the Nineteenth, etc., one after the other, at points *G*, *d*, *g*, *♯♯* and *dd*, etc. which it produces all together at the same time, of which a longer discourse will be found in the treatise on Lyres: and what I shall say in the discourse on the military Trumpet will also serve for this one. Now, if one could find the reason in the trembling bridge <term>Trembling bridge; a "bray" bridge where one foot is not fixed, allowing it to rattle against the soundboard to create a brassy sound</term>, one could say that the sections of the string imitate the sound of the Trumpet when the number of beats <note>vibrations</note> of said bridge agrees with the number of beats of the string: but constant experience shows that the same thing happens even if one removes the trembling bridge and leaves a fixed one there, there being no other difference except that the sounds of the string resting on the trembling bridge vibrate more strongly and are more brilliant. And when one presses the string so firmly with the fingers of the left hand that it touches the wood, it sounds equally well in all places, as if it were strung on a Viol.

### COROLLARY.

One will always find new properties of strings if one takes the pains to examine them in every possible way: now, it is certain that they produce several different sounds, or a single sound composed of several at the same time, and that one hears only those which harmonize together, namely the repetitions of the Octave, the Fifths, and the repeated Thirds, and sometimes some others, for example the Twentieth: but it is not certain that every string produces every possible sound at once; and if it does produce them, we do not know why we hear almost only the aforementioned Consonances. Experience also teaches that of two strings of the same thickness and material, whether of brass <note>original: "leton"</note> or gut <note>original: "boyau"</note>, etc. which are in unison, one being touched sometimes causes the other to tremble more strongly than it trembles at the sound of

### PROPOSITION XVI.

*To determine to which principle, and to which mechanical power, the force of the pegs and hammers used to mount and tension the strings belongs.*

IT is certain that the force of the pegs relates to the **Wheel and Axle** <note>original Latin: *axis in peritrochio*</note>, and that the Wheel depends on the **lever**, the power of which one cannot understand unless one comprehends the force of the pegs; this is why it suffices to explain here the force of the lever, by repeating the figure from the second Addition I made to **Galileo's** treatise on **Mechanics**. Now this principle would be recognized more perceptibly in pegs if one made larger instruments: for example, if one made **Bass Viols**, **Theorbos** <note>A large, long-necked lute used for basso continuo</note>, **Guitarrons** <note>A large-bodied Spanish guitar</note>, **Harps**, etc., two or three **fathoms** <note>original: *toises*; a unit of length approximately 6 feet</note> long, and if it were necessary to use strings as thick as the little finger of the hand, or those made of one hundred and forty-four gut strands, whose diameter is nearly three **lines** <note>A "line" is an old measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch</note>, it is certain that one would need pegs whose heads were two or four feet wide, and that each peg would be similar

### PROPOSITION XVII.

*Explain the manner of dividing a string all at once, or a line into as many equal parts as one wishes, with any compass opening, or with any other measure that shall be given, without changing it.*

ALTHOUGH I have demonstrated the manner of dividing any string or line one wishes by means of the equilateral triangle in the 10th Proposition of the book on the **Monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used to identify musical intervals through mathematical ratios</note>, which is the first of the stringed instruments, I nevertheless add here another method, which has no need for a triangle, so that **Instrument makers** and other craftsmen may make such divisions as they wish, whether with all sorts of compass openings smaller or larger than the string, or the line that must be divided, or with a ruler, or other sort of instrument they may encounter: which can serve them to transfer the divisions of the **Lute** neck <note>the fretting positions</note>, and of other instruments engraved in small scale on a **brass** plate <note>original: *lame d'airain*</note>, or other material, to whatever other measure they wish.

Now, I wish to add here an examination of the line that **Salinas** <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a blind Spanish music theorist and organist</note> proposes in his third book, chapter 31, to divide the neck of instruments into twelve equal semitones.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

->*Determine if one can mark the twelve frets of the Lute by the segments of a line cut in mean and extreme ratio.*<- <note>The "mean and extreme ratio" is today commonly known as the Golden Ratio</note>

SALINAS has conceived of a new way to divide the neck of stringed instruments by means of a proportionally cut line: but I find that he has failed in several things, and that this Section cannot serve his purpose. Now, the first error into which he has fallen consists in his belief that the **Mesolabe** <note>A geometric instrument described by ancient authors for finding mean proportionals, used to solve problems like doubling the cube</note>, of which **Vitruvius** <note>A Roman architect and engineer whose works were foundational to Renaissance technology</note> speaks in his 9th book, was suitable for finding as many mean proportionals as one wishes; and nonetheless it can only serve to find two between two given values: although after finding two between the double and the half, one can find nine others by taking a mean proportional twice between the four given values, as I have shown in the seventh Proposition of the second book: and if he understood it in this manner, he is excusable. The second error appears in that he should have shown that one can find as many continually proportional lines as one wishes, not only according to the ratio of the line cut in mean and extreme ratio, but also between two given lines which are in a double ratio, which is the question at hand: for even though by removing the smallest segment from the largest by a continual subtraction one finds continually proportional lines, in the same ratio as the segments of the proportionally cut line, yet it is far from the case that the thirteenth largest is only double the first, or the smallest, since the first is more than double the fourth, as **Monsieur Hardy** <note>Claude Hardy (1604–1678), a French mathematician and close associate of Descartes</note>, a most excellent Geometer, has demonstrated.

But one will understand this more clearly by the figure of Salinas A B, by means of which he cuts the line A B in mean and extreme ratio, by adding perpendicularly at point B half of A B, which is B C, and then by joining these two lines by the diagonal A C; from which, B C being removed, the line D A which remains, being transferred onto A B, gives the larger segment A E, and B E which remains is the smaller segment of the line A B cut in mean and extreme ratio, the properties of which I explain in the second book of movements.

Now √5+1 is in a larger ratio to 3 - √5 than 2 is to 1 <note>The author is demonstrating that these geometric proportions do not align with the simple 2:1 ratio of the musical octave</note>, since the term that is in a subdouble ratio <note>A ratio of 1:2</note> to √5 + 1 is √1 1/4 + 1/2, whose square root—being less than what is required—is 1 1/2, because the square root—less than what is required—is one, which is the square root—greater than what is required—of 3 - √5, assuming that the square root of five is two, which must be larger, since it only gives four. Therefore √5+1 has a larger ratio to 3 - √5 than 2 to 1, and consequently, given four lines in continuous proportion following the ratio of the proportionally cut line, the first is in a larger ratio to the fourth than 2 to 1.

This does not prevent us from admiring the excellence and the liveliness of the spirit of Salinas, considering that it is difficult for a man deprived of sight from his cradle to have been able to have the figures of his book engraved, and particularly the one that I have placed in the ninth Proposition of the third book of *Genres and Modes*, since the most clear-sighted would have difficulty making one like it. But Divine goodness is accustomed to compensating on one side for what is lost on the other.

### PROPOSITION XIX.

->*To examine the ways that Zarlino has given to divide the neck of instruments into twelve equal semitones by the invention of two, or several mean proportionals, or otherwise.*<-

AMONG the means that Zarlino <note>Gioseffo Zarlino (1517–1590), an influential Italian music theorist.</note> explains for dividing the Octave, or the Diapason <note>original: "Diapason"; the Greek term for the interval of an octave.</note> into twelve equal intervals, he places one in the thirtieth Chapter of the fourth book of his *Supplement* <note>Referring to Zarlino's *Sopplementi Musicali* (1588).</note>, which consists of numbers: and for this subject he takes 60 and 30, which are in a double ratio <note>2:1, the ratio of an octave.</note>, which he multiplies by one another to have the product 1800, whose root serves him for the sixth interval of the twelve that must be found, because it is the mean proportional between 30 and 60. And then he multiplies the same number 1800 by 30 and by 60, and says that one must take the fourth root <note>original: "$\checkmark$ QQ", meaning *quadrato-quadratica* or the root of a root.</note> of 54,000, but he does not say what sort the root of 108,000 should be.

In the third place, he wants one to find two continued mean proportionals between 30 and the fourth root of 54,000; between the fourth root of 54,000 and 1,800; between the square root of 1,800 and the anonymous root of 108,000; and between 108,000 and 60. Now if this were true, the fourth root of 54,000 would be the mean proportional between 30 and the square root of 1,800, whereas this root is the fourth root of 1,620,000; for the mean proportional number between 30 and the square root of 1,800 is the square root of the product coming from the multiplication of the square root of 1,800 by 30, which is to say of 1,620,000, whose fourth root is the mean proportional between 30 and the fourth root of 1,800, and not that of the number 54,000, as it seems he wishes to say. Be that as it may, I have given another way of finding eleven mean proportional numbers between two other numbers taken in a double ratio to divide the necks, the Monochords, or the Diapason into twelve intervals, or equal semitones. Let us now see his two other ways which are very good, but they depend on the Mesolabe <note>An ancient mechanical instrument used to find mean proportionals, essentially solving the problem of doubling the cube.</note>, which is attributed to Archytas or to Eratosthenes, which he explains in the 25th Chapter of the second book of his *Institutions* <note>*Le Istitutioni Harmoniche* (1558).</note>, and in the eleventh Proposition of the third book of his *Demonstrations*, in which he shows against Vincenzo Galilei <note>A theorist and father of Galileo Galilei; he championed the 18:17 ratio for lute fretting.</note> that the semitones of the Lute are not 17 to 18, because twelve sesquiseptimal <note>original: "seſquidixſeptieſmes"; the ratio 18:17.</note> ratios are not the double ratio, as one sees between these two numbers 1,156,831,381,425,976 and 582,822,237,229,761, which contain these twelve ratios; for this last number is too large, and should be 578,415,690,712,988 to make the just Octave. He similarly shows that thirteen sesquiseptimals are larger than the Octave, because they are the ratio of 2,082,296,486,567,568 to 9,907,978,032,905,937, in place of which one would have to put 10,411,482,433,337,84 to make the Diapason just; so that a number is needed between the one that makes twelve sesquiseptimal ratios and the one that makes thirteen: and if the makers increased each sesquiseptimal interval ever so little, they would arrive at the accuracy of the Octave.

As for the first way that he gives in the 30th Chapter, it is good, and he explains it so amply that nothing needs to be added to it. The other way consists in diminishing each major tone by the sixth part of a comma <note>A small interval resulting from the difference between musical ratios, such as the Syntonic comma (81:80).</note>, of which he speaks in the 32nd Chapter, for since six major tones exceed...

### PROPOSITION XX.

->To explain several instruments from India and Turkey.<-

The majority of the instruments used by the Indians are made of canes, as one can see by these figures: the first of which, being the most extraordinary, was taken from an instrument from China that arrived in England through the mediation of Monsieur Hardy, Counselor <note>Claude Hardy (1604–1678), a French mathematician and friend of Descartes and Mersenne.</note>, to whom I am entirely indebted. Now, the cane A B is hollow; it begins at A and ends at B. C and D are two large gourds <note>original: "Courgues"; archaic French for gourds or pumpkins.</note> which are hollow and open at the bottom. The five letters E, F, G, H, and I show the locations of the five pegs—similar to peg G—which serve to tighten the strings. Part K is the bridge where the strings are attached. L and M are the places where the gourds are grafted to the cane, which is dotted with black spots. The exterior surface of the gourds is enriched with gold and various figures on all sides. The Indians are accustomed to carrying this instrument on the right shoulder and playing it with combs or iron thimbles <note>original: "doitiers"; finger-picks or plectrums worn on the fingertips.</note> that they tie to the ends of their fingers.

The second Indian instrument is composed of half of an Indian fruit Q P, which they cover with the skin of a snake, and the neck O N is made of an Indian cane. Monsieur Giovanni Battista Doni <note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647) was an Italian music theorist who sought to reconstruct ancient Greek music.</note>, Gentleman and Secretary to Cardinal Barberini—to whom ancient Music will owe its restoration when he has published his excellent works on this subject—sent me this portrait, along with several others from the cabinet of Claude Menestrier <note>Claude Menestrier (1584–1639) was a noted collector and scholar of antiquities.</note>. The first of these is a Turkish instrument, which has its body R S made of half an Indian nut <note>original: "noix d'Inde"; likely a coconut.</note>, and its neck T V made of inlaid pieces of ivory and ebony, profiled with silver. It has only a single string, like the Monochord, and is similar to the Colascione <note>original: "Colachon"; a long-necked lute from Southern Italy.</note>, of which I included a figure in the second book. The string is attached at end X, and then passed through hole V. He also sent me drawings of an antique Carnelian <note>A semi-precious gemstone often used for seals.</note>, in which there are four birds, of which the two on the left hand hold a Flute and a Hunting Horn, whether they serve as symbols to signify something, or because some ballet was danced in the form of birds, as our composers of Dances and Ballets do now, dressing the dancers as all sorts of quadrupeds and birds. I omit the figure of a "Tire-lyre" <note>A traditional ceramic money box or piggy bank.</note>, or antique earthenware coin-cache, where one sees a figure between two pillars playing a Bassoon, and an antique square bell, and another in an oval shape, because those which they...

# FIFTH BOOK
## ON WIND INSTRUMENTS.

ALTHOUGH all musical instruments might be called "wind" instruments, since it is impossible to produce sounds without the movement of air—which is a kind of wind—nonetheless, it is customary to give this name to those that are blown into by the mouth, or that are made to sound with bellows, in order to distinguish them from those that use strings, or those that are beaten like the Drum. Now, I have wished to create a specific book for these instruments because of their great multitude, and the particular difficulties encountered in their proportions, and in the manner in which one must use them to produce all kinds of sounds, so that those who prefer them to stringed instruments might find enough to satisfy them, and so that confusion does not enter into our treatises. But before explaining wind instruments, one must state what the wind is that one uses to play them, which I shall do in the first Proposition.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*To explain the nature of the wind used to make wind instruments sound, and whether water can be used instead of wind for this purpose.*<-

IT is certain that the instruments (of which we speak) can sound with every kind of wind, whether it comes from nothing other than the simple movement of air, like that of the bellows used for Organs and Musettes <note>A small, bellows-blown bagpipe popular in 17th-century French courts.</note>, or whether it is mixed with vapors and water, like that of the mouth, which is so full of water that the reeds and the channels of the instruments become entirely damp and wet. Now, even though winds come from above, or from below, or from whatever other side one might wish, and whether they are excited by Aeolipiles <note>original: "Aeolopiles"; an ancient scientific device consisting of a hollow sphere with a spout that, when filled with water and heated, produces a powerful jet of steam or "wind."</note>, by gunpowder, saltpeter, or in whatever other manner one might wish, they are not different from the movement of air. This air can be considered in two ways: namely, in its purity, and with the mixture of vapors and exhalations that it ordinarily contains in the atmosphere—or the expanse that receives vapors, whether it reaches as high as the greatest mountains (such as Tenerife <note>Mount Teide on the island of Tenerife was frequently cited by 17th-century natural philosophers as a benchmark for measuring the height of the atmosphere.</note>, whose foot begins at the town of Garachico, from where one must travel two and a half days to reach the top) or whether it be larger or smaller.
As for the purity of the air, one can say that it begins where the expanse of the said vapors ends, and that it ends at the atmosphere of the Planets, although we do not know if the said air is too thin and too refined to produce sounds, unless one judges it in proportion to that which is heated by fire, and which is thinned by the rays of the Sun, which gather in the focus of the

parabolic and spherical mirrors: for if the <term>rarefactions</term><note>Rarefaction is the thinning or reduction in density of a medium, like air, which the author suggests behaves similarly to the way mirrors reflect light.</note> are similar, there is no doubt that one can sound instruments in every part of the air where they can exist without being consumed by the heat of the flame. But we do not yet know if the nature of air is different from that of water, and if it is nothing other than rarefied water, or if it is composed of all the tiny bodies that exhale and rise from all the great bodies of the world, and particularly from water and the earth. In the same way, one could say that the body of every animal exhales a certain quantity of vapors all around itself, which make up its atmosphere—similar to that of a magnet, which fills its sphere of activity with a quantity of magnetic rays. From this, one can derive the reason for several particular virtues of plants and animals that serve or harm health, just as it happens that a rotten grape spoils the others, according to this verse:
> ->*A grape takes its blue color from seeing another grape.*<- <note>original: "Uuâ conſpectâ liuorem ducit ab uuâ." This quote from the Roman poet Juvenal traditionally refers to how one person is corrupted by the company of another, but here the author uses it to describe the physical transmission of "vapors" between objects.</note>

Those who believe that air is composed of <term>atoms</term><note>The author is referencing the "atomist" theory, which suggests the universe is made of tiny, indivisible particles.</note> can say that wind instruments sound when they are struck by a large enough multitude of these small bodies, which move all the way to the ear of the listeners; and that if the earth does not push them further than each animal pushes its own, then the sphere of air is very small, followed by the void or the <term>ether</term>, in which instruments cannot sound. But it is more likely that the air is continuous from the earth to the <term>firmament</term><note>The heavens or the sky.</note>, and perhaps beyond to infinity, or as far as it has pleased God to extend it; and that the air we breathe is only different from the other in that it is mixed with several heterogeneous bodies, which are called vapors and exhalations. These are perhaps around the Moon, the Sun, and the Stars, just as they are around our earth—which we would place among the Planets if we were on the Sun or on Mars.

It remains now to consider whether water can be used to make these instruments sound; this is very easy to resolve by experience, which shows that it is not possible to make them speak, in whatever manner one blows into them between two waters <note>Meaning while submerged.</note>. For they make no sound when their <term>lumiere</term><note>In this context, the "light" or "aperture" refers to the mouth-hole or labium of the instrument where the air is split to create sound.</note> or their mouthpiece is submerged in water. Water can only serve to make them warble and trill when the aperture is out of the water, as happens with the small instruments used to imitate the song of the **Nightingale** or other birds; because the wind that is pushed in insinuates itself into the water and causes it to rise in many small particles, which are the cause of the lessening, the trembling, and the hammering of the sound.

Now, I will first explain those that have only one hole, and then those that have two, three, or several; and because among those that have two, three, or several holes, some have <term>bocals</term><note>A bocal is a curved metal tube that connects the mouthpiece to the body of instruments like the bassoon.</note> or mouthpieces—which one might call embouchures—and others have <term>plugs</term><note>The "tampon" or block found in recorders and duct flutes.</note>, <term>mouths</term><note>original: "lumieres." As for the simplest instrument, it is difficult to determine, for it seems on one hand that the <term>Eunuch flute</term><note>Also known as a mirliton or kazoo-style instrument; it does not produce its own pitch but vibrates along with the player's voice.</note> and others that only return the voice they have received—for example, cracked pots, shells, and other concave bodies into which one speaks to reinforce the voice—are the simplest of all. To these, one may add that straw pipes are very simple, and there is no instrument more rural or rustic, nor easier to make, unless one prefers the horns of oxen, rams, or other animals, which I shall discuss in the discourse on hunting horns.

I set aside various sounds produced by winds when they meet rocks and other bodies, because they are not at our disposal and cannot serve music, even though it may happen that they perform all the parts of a concert by means of several holes that are sometimes found in rocks and mountains. Thus, one may be mistaken in imagining that the sweet confusion of sounds heard near woods, forests, rocks, caverns, etc., comes from some distant music.

This must be noted so as not to pass off as a miracle or a prodigy what is merely natural, and so that our religion—whose essence is so holy and so true that it is worthy of God—is not held in contempt when people try to support or confirm it with actions that the ignorant sometimes proclaim as extraordinary and miraculous, even though they have nothing supernatural about them. As I show in several places in this work, this can serve to destroy superstition and to strengthen true devotion, which consists particularly in loving God with all our affection and our neighbor (that is, all other men) as ourselves, and in practicing all the actions prescribed by true religion, whether of the body or the spirit, with the sincerity and purity that God desires from a rational creature.

# PROPOSITION IV.

*To explain the rustic pipes [Chalumeaux] with one or several holes, and their use.*

The five pipes or flutes that follow are the simplest of all, since they have only one, two, or three holes. The first on the left is made of willow bark (or some other tree), which is peeled away when the sap is rising; thus, one makes a pipe [chalumeau] that is open at both the top and bottom, as seen in A-B. The second flute has no other holes than the one at the top where it is blown (marked A), the one at the bottom (marked B), and the window <term>lumiere</term><note>original: "lumiere." Literally the "light," this is the fipple or mouth-cut of a flute where the air is split to create sound.</note> marked C. Now, these two flutes cannot make different sounds except by the different force of the breath given to them.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of five primitive wind instruments. 1. A bark pipe (A-B). 2. A simple pipe with a mouth-hole (A, C, B). 3. A straw pipe with a vibrating tongue (B) and two finger holes (A, 1). 4. A thin straight pipe. 5. A rustic shawm-like instrument with a flared bell (C) and three finger holes (1, 2, 3).</image-desc>

Regarding the 3rd and 5th pipes, which are made of wheat-stalk <note>original: "bled." Here referring to the straw or stalk of grain used to make primitive "oaten" pipes.</note>, it is easy to understand how they are played. A and 1 on the 3rd show the two holes made at the two ends, and B shows the way the pipe must be cut so that the part which is raised serves as an mouthpiece for pushing the wind, or as a <term>languette</term><note>A vibrating reed or tongue cut directly into the stalk of the straw.</note> to vibrate it, while one holds two fingers over the two holes A and 1, trilling by closing them, and by...

...opening them as quickly as possible. The fifth <term>pipe</term><note>original: "chalumeau"; here referring to a simple reed pipe.</note> has its <term>reed</term><note>original: "languette"; the vibrating tongue that produces sound.</note> at the top, as shown at A; but it should be noted that the top of this pipe ends in a knot that serves as a <term>plug</term><note>original: "tampon"; a stopper used to close the end of a pipe.</note>, so that the wind does not escape, but rather descends to the three holes at the bottom, which serve to make three different tones. However, one can produce ten or twelve different tones by means of these three holes, as I will show when speaking of the three-holed flute, which is played alongside the drum.

The fourth pipe is called the <term>Eunuch flute</term><note>A "mirliton" or kazoo-like instrument that colors the sound of the human voice rather than producing its own pitch.</note> by some, but the difference in its sounds does not come from its holes, nor from its length, as happens with the others. For it produces no sound other than that of the mouth or the tongue that speaks, whose force and resonance it increases by means of its length and capacity, and by a small skin of thin leather, as delicate as an <term>onion skin</term>, which covers the top where one sees A. This is so that the wind and the voice pushed through hole B, which forms the <term>mouthpiece</term><note>original: "emboucheure".</note>, strikes this skin like a little drum, giving a new pleasantness to the voice through its small vibrations which reflect it. The box or the <term>bell</term><note>original: "pauillon".</note> A B serves to cover the said skin, and its holes provide an exit for the voice, though they are not strictly necessary. Now, four or five different parts of these flutes are made for a full concert, which has this advantage over all other flutes: it imitates a concert of voices more closely, for it lacks only actual pronunciation, which one can approach very nearly with these flutes.

This is something that <term>organists</term> and <term>instrument makers</term><note>original: "Organistes & Facteurs".</note> should carefully note, in order to invent new stops that imitate human voices much better than their <term>Regals</term><note>A small, portable pipe organ that uses reed pipes to produce a buzzing, nasal sound.</note>, and to so deceive their listeners that they believe they are hearing a better concert than one of voices—which are often deprived of the sweetness of harmony and the charms that come from the little skins one can add in various places on the pipes and flutes.

### PROPOSITION V.

->*To explain the form, range, tablature, and use of the three-holed flute.*<-

ALTHOUGH one could group this instrument with the preceding ones because it has only three holes—namely two in front marked 2 and 3, and the other behind marked 1 (unless one wishes to count the first hole of the plug A where one blows, the second B which serves as the <term>window</term><note>original: "lumiere"; the opening in a flute where the air hits the sharp edge to create sound.</note>, and the last at the foot C, to find six holes)—I have nonetheless wished to separate it, as much because of its great range as for its <term>tablature</term><note>A form of musical notation indicating finger positions rather than just pitches.</note>, which I provide here in two ways: namely, by standard musical notes, and by the marks used by those who do not know the value and use of ordinary notes.

Now, it is so easy to understand this tablature that there is no need to explain it, except for the instruction of those who have never seen it, or who do not know how to play flutes or the <term>flageolet</term>. It is therefore for their benefit that I say, first, that the notes contain a range of a <term>seventeenth</term><note>An interval spanning two octaves and a third.</note>, and that I have changed the clef because one can only ascend a <term>tenth</term><note>An interval of an octave plus a third.</note> with the first clef of <term>F-flat</term><note>original: "F vt fa"; the F clef in the Guidonian hexachord system.</note>, using only five...

...rules, where it must be noted that many do not include the first four notes within the range of this tablature, because they do not follow sequentially through every step of the **Octave**. For after the **Fourth**, or the four sounds *ut, re, mi, fa* <note>The notes C, D, E, and F.</note> produced by the four lowest notes of this instrument, one cannot produce the next four notes to reach the **Fifth** above, which completes the Octave. This is why one may begin this tablature with the fifth note, which is an Octave above the first, and which is found at **G** <note>original: "G re sol"; a specific pitch in the Guidonian hexachord system, here referring to the G above middle C.</note>, so that it encompasses only the range of an **eleventh**, which contains everything that can ordinarily be performed with this Flute.

### Tablature for the Three-Holed Flute.

<image-desc>A musical score and tablature for a three-holed flute (galoubet). Two horizontal staves show notes in standard notation, while a three-line tablature system above each staff indicates fingerings with vertical strokes (closed holes) and circles (open holes). To the right of the musical score, a vertical illustration of the flute itself is shown. It is labeled with letters 'A' at the mouthpiece, 'B' on the body, and 'C' at the foot. The three finger holes are numbered 1, 2, and 3 from top to bottom.</image-desc>

The notes preceded by **flats** <note>original: "b mols".</note> signify the <term>accidentals</term><note>original: "feintes"; notes outside the standard scale, such as sharps or flats.</note>, or semitones, which are made by moderating the breath, or through the skill of the fingers by closing the holes more or less, in order to play songs that use flats. Now, the note on the **C** clef <note>original: "C sol vt fa"; Middle C.</note>, which begins again at the bottom on the first line, continues the tones we started on the other clef, and serves as a root to complete the rest of the range, as shown by the notes that follow. As for the other symbols, they must be explained so clearly that there will be no further need to speak of them in the discussions of other Flutes that use them.

I say, then, in the second place, that the black lines which fall perpendicularly across the three lines of the tablature signify the number of holes that must be closed to produce the sounds marked by the notes below. For example, the first three lines on the three rules signify that one produces the first note by closing the three holes and pushing the breath as weakly as possible. The next two lines show that one must close the two holes marked one and two, and uncover the last hole marked three, to produce *re*, or the second note. The small line that follows again signifies that one must only close the first hole to produce *mi*, or the third note. And the three zeros, or the three circles, teach that one must uncover all the holes to produce the fourth note, or *fa*. 

But one cannot continue to *sol* <note>The note G.</note> until the Octave, and one is forced to jump all at once to the **Fifth** above, in order to reach the Octave of the first note. This Octave is reached at the top when one begins again to close the holes and increases the force of the breath. This must be noted all the more carefully because the same thing happens with several other wind instruments, such as the **Flageolet** and other Flutes, which rise to the **Octave**, and sometimes to the **Fifteenth** <note>A range of two octaves.</note>, and the **Twenty-second** <note>A range of three octaves.</note>, depending on how much one increases the wind. Indeed, there are men who can produce a range of a Twenty-second on the—

V iiij <note>A printer's signature mark for gathering the pages.</note>

### PROPOSITION VI.

->*To explain the form, construction, tuning, range, and tablature of the Flageolet and the six-holed flute.*<-

This instrument is one of the most pleasant <note>original: "gentils"</note> and easiest of all those in use; for although the <term>chalumeaux</term><note>simple rustic reed pipes made from stalks of wheat or feathers</note>, or the horns of oxen or rams that shepherds place at the end of a hollowed elderwood stick, are also easy to prepare, they are nevertheless far removed from its perfection. Now this instrument has six holes, as one sees in this figure, of which the sixth is closest to the foot <note>original: "pate"</note> **C**; the fifth and the first are on the back, and the fourth, third, and second are on the front, as is the sixth. Here it must be noted that the first may be taken for the last, as happens when one descends from high to low, and the last may be taken for the first when one ascends from low to high.

<image-desc>A vertical woodcut diagram of a flageolet. The top mouthpiece is labeled 'A', the 'lumiere' (window) is labeled 'B', and the foot is labeled 'C'. Along the side, the six finger holes are numbered 1 through 6, with dotted lines indicating their positions. Numbers 1 and 5 appear to be slightly offset or have specific notes in the text regarding their placement on the back of the instrument.</image-desc>

Regarding the arrangement of the hands and fingers with which one stops these six holes, it must be noted that the left hand stops the first, second, and third holes; for its thumb stops the first, which is behind, the index finger stops the second, which is in front, and the middle finger stops the third hole. In this way, each hand governs three holes, since the left stops the three holes closest to the window <note>original: "lumiere"; the opening where the air hits the sharp edge to produce sound</note>, and the right hand governs the other three, of which the thumb stops the fifth, the index finger the fourth, and the middle finger the sixth, or the one closest to the foot **C**.

There are others who use four fingers of the left hand for the Flageolet—namely the thumb, the index, the middle, and the ring finger <note>original: "medicus"</note>—and two of the right hand—namely the thumb and the index—but the middle finger is used to stop the foot. The window of the Flageolet is marked by **B**, and its mouthpiece by **A**. It can be made of all sorts of materials, but particularly of boxwood <note>original: "buis"</note>, ivory, plum wood, ebony, and all sorts of hard woods. But it is not necessary to specify the proportions that its holes must have, because the figure shows their distances and their sizes. It is only necessary to note that the <term>Diapason</term><note>In this context, the physical scale or tuning system</note> of Flageolets does not follow that of strings, nor that of Organ pipes, as I shall show later, for it suffices to explain here its range and its tablature, which **Le Vacher**, who is the most excellent maker <note>original: "Facteur"</note> of Flageolets that we have, marks in this manner.

By this, one sees that one can use musical notes to mark the tones, the range, and the songs of the Flageolet, insofar as they serve as a universal tablature for all sorts of instruments, as I showed in the preceding book.

# of Wind Instruments.

### Tablature and Range of the Flageolet.

<image-desc>
A diagram of a musical instrument and its corresponding tablature and notation. On the left is a vertical illustration of a flageolet, labeled with letters and numbers: 'A' at the top mouthpiece, 'C' at the first hole, followed by holes numbered 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, and 1, and 'B' at the bottom. 

To the right of the instrument are four systems of notation. The first and third systems are 6-line tablatures for the flageolet, using dots (representing closed holes) and circles/zeros (representing open holes) arranged vertically. The second and fourth systems are standard 5-line musical staves showing the corresponding pitches in white mensural-style notation. The final note in the fourth system shows a zero with a slash through it in the tablature above it, indicating a half-closed hole.
</image-desc>

Now, the first two lines contain the tablature of the Flageolet in the natural key <note>original: "# quarré," referring to the "square B" or hard hexachord which uses no flats</note>, and the last two in the flat key <note>original: "b mol," referring to the "soft B" or hexachord using flats</note>. However, the last fifteen notes, and the fifteen rows of other characters that correspond to them, are sufficient to explain the said tablature and the range <note>original: "estenduë"</note> of this instrument, which consists of a <term>Fifteenth</term><note>An interval of two octaves (8+7 notes)</note>. This is contained within those fifteen notes, even though I have included the ten preceding ones to follow the practice of those who teach the Flageolet. These teachers begin with the note G <note>original: "G re sol"</note> by fingering only the last three holes (six, five, and four) and leaving the other three open (three, two, and one). They also include the two sharps <note>original: "dieses"</note> that one sees on the first line of notes to signify that they are played in the natural key <note>original: "# quarré"</note>, even though these are superfluous for those who understand the practice of notation, in which the mere absence of a flat signifies the natural.

But this tablature is so easy—given that all the lines with zeros, or those without small vertical lines, indicate that one must open the holes corresponding to those lines—that there is no need to explain it further. I will only provide one example to demonstrate its use. If one wishes to play the lowest or deepest tone of the Flageolet, which is marked by the last note and the last row of small lines, this row teaches that one must close all six holes (represented by the six lines) and that one must close the hole of the foot <note>original: "pate"</note> halfway. This is indicated by the line crossing the last zero. This will be understood even better by the discussion that follows, as it teaches the actual manner of sounding the Flageolet.

# PROPOSITION VII.

*To explain the measurements of the Flageolet, and the manner of playing it perfectly in one or more parts, with an example of music.*

IT IS a certainty that the <term>tuning system</term> <note>original: "Diapaſon," referring here to the physical measurements and scale of the instrument</note> of this instrument does not follow the proportions of consonant intervals and other tuning systems, as can be seen in the preceding figure, in which the distances of the holes do not have the same ratios between them as the tones they produce. This is easy to prove by experience; for if the <term>makers</term> <note>original: "Facteurs"</note> followed these proportions, the Flageolet would rise at least an <term>Octave</term> <note>An interval of eight notes</note> from the sound it makes when its six holes are closed, when one leaves only the fifth and sixth holes closed. This is because the body of the Flageolet—taken from the top of the <term>window</term> <note>original: "lumiere," the opening where the air hits the sharp edge to create sound</note> **C** to the <term>foot</term> <note>original: "pate," the bottom end of the instrument</note> **B**—is double the length of **C** to hole **4**; and yet, this part of the body only rises by a <term>Fifth</term> <note>An interval of five notes</note>. From this, it is evident that the rest of the body contributes to the gravity of the tone, and consequently that the wind which exits through the fourth hole (when only the 5th and 6th are closed) does not all exit through said hole, and that some parts of it pass through the other following holes—namely the 3rd, 2nd, etc.—and through the opening of the foot, as one experiences by placing a hand opposite said holes.

And one might say that the air exiting through these holes, and what remains of the body of the Flageolet from the fourth hole to **B**, causes the pitch to drop by a <term>Fourth</term> <note>An interval of four notes</note>. Furthermore, if the distance of the holes followed the proportion of their tones, the fourth hole would need to be only an eighth part further from the window than the 5th; and yet it is a fourth part further away, even though it only makes the Flageolet descend by one whole tone. The same must be said of the third hole in regard to the fourth. As for the 3rd, 2nd, and 1st, they are a little better regulated. Now, it must be admitted that experience alone can provide the <term>measurements</term> <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> of Flageolets, since one sees no reason why the fifth hole should be further from the 4th, and the 4th from the 5th to produce their two tones, than the 3rd hole from the 2nd, and the second from the first. However, I have no doubt that there is some reason for this differing distance of holes, whether it be taken from the nature of the wind, which is breathed in differently, or from the manufacture of the Flageolet and other instruments, in which the same thing happens. But I leave this research to those who wish and are able to go further, especially since it suffices to have noted the correct distance and the true arrangement of the holes in the two preceding figures to serve as a model for those who wish to make Flageolets of all sizes, in which the same proportions must be roughly observed. This is why I come to the manner of playing it, which consists particularly in blowing the wind as is required, and in closing and opening the holes following the tablature. I say then, first, that one must close the holes in such a way that the wind cannot escape, so as to make the pitches true, and that they must only be half-closed when one wishes to make the <term>accidentals</term> <note>original: "feintes," referring to sharps and flats</note> or the <term>half-tones</term> <note>semitones</note> belonging to the <term>Chromatic</term> <note>A scale moving by half-steps</note> style; for one can play twenty-eight half-tones in succession on the Flageolet to play all sorts of chromatic pieces; and if there are men...

It also introduces the technique of "half-holing" to achieve a full chromatic range of twenty-eight semitones.</summary>

->### On Wind Instruments.<-

...who can cover the holes in such a way as to create quarter tones for <term>enharmonic sharps</term> <note>original: "dieſes Enharmoniques," referring to the smallest intervals in ancient Greek music theory, rarely used in 17th-century practice</note>, they will be able to use that style on this instrument. But after one knows how to play all the notes, it is necessary to become accustomed to speed and rhythm, in order to perform all kinds of <term>passages</term> <note>Rapid melodic runs</note> and <term>diminutions</term> <note>original: "diminutions," the practice of breaking long notes into many shorter, faster notes to decorate a melody</note>, and to employ all the sweetness and <term>delicacies</term> <note>original: "mignardiſes," refined ornaments</note> of which the Flageolet is capable. This cannot be done without finger speed, as they must cover and uncover the same holes six or eight times within the time of one measure to imitate the ornaments of the <term>throat</term> <note>original: "gorge," referring to vocal trills and coloratura</note>, the Viol, Lutes, and other instruments.

**Secondly**, it must be noted that there are two ways of playing this instrument and others that have <term>windows</term> <note>original: "lumieres," the mouthpieces where air is directed against a sharp edge to produce sound, like a recorder</note>: one comes from the breath alone, or the wind that one pushes, and the other from <term>articulation</term> <note>original: "l'articulation," the use of the tongue to define and separate notes</note> and the movement of the tongue. The former imitates the **Organ**, and the latter represents the **voice**. The former is practiced by villagers and apprentices, and the latter by the Masters. Finally, the former resembles dead or mute things, and the latter resembles living things, because it implies the movement of organs—particularly that of the tip of the tongue—whereas the other can be practiced with a bellows instead of the mouth.

Now, although each hole produces only one note, and the Flageolet also has but one note when all its holes are closed—rising to the **Octave** when one pushes the wind harder, without passing through the intermediate intervals—I can nevertheless produce all the sounds of the <term>Hexachord</term> <note>A six-note scale: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note>, namely *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>Equivalent to the first six notes of a major scale: C, D, E, F, G, A</note>, without uncovering any hole, whether the <term>foot</term> <note>original: "pate," the bottom opening of the flageolet</note> is open or closed. One can experience this provided that the wind is first pushed very weakly, and that it is always increased little by little until the Flageolet produces its natural and ordinary tone—that is to say, the aforementioned *la*. However, these sounds cannot serve for Music because of their weakness and instability, for they resemble the noises one hears inside the ear.

I also produce the range of a **Major Third** by gradually closing the foot, though this is only used to descend lower by a semitone or a whole tone. I wished to note this so that one might consider that what excellent Masters—who play an instrument to perfection—say is not far from reason: namely, that the use and perfection of each instrument extends to infinity, insofar as one always notices something new according to the different ways in which it is used. But I have tried to produce the same Hexachord with other Flageolets without using the holes, and I did not succeed. This is why one should not make a general rule of it; I only add that the one with which I performed this experiment is made of **boxwood**, and is four inches and five <term>lines</term> <note>A "line" (ligne) was a historical unit of length, roughly 1/12th of an inch</note> in length, as seen in the two preceding figures that were based on the said Flageolet.

**In the third place**, experience shows that it is difficult to prevent the flageolet from leaving its natural tone to rise to the **Octave**, for one often cannot make it take its ordinary tone even if the wind given to it is very weak—particularly when it is only three or four inches long, like the one I have illustrated.

And when it <term>octaves</term> <note>Jumps up an interval of eight notes due to overblowing</note> while the holes are closed, it often returns to its natural tone upon opening the holes, instead of continuing its tones in the upper Octave,

### Book Five

...so that it <term>octaves</term> <note>overblows to produce a note an octave higher</note> much more easily when the holes are closed than when they are open, because the breath must be stronger. From this comes the fact that it is easier to make the instrument take its natural tone by opening the last hole than by closing it, the reason for which is not easy to find.

It must however be noted that the hole closed with the thumb of the left hand—that is, the sixth hole—must be half-open, and not entirely uncovered as shown in the tablature, to produce the notes that pass the Octave, because the tones are better and more natural that way. As for the tone that octaves instead of remaining in its natural place, this happens only through the fault of the one playing the Flageolet, who distributes more wind than is necessary; for the tone will be very natural if the holes are well closed and the wind is given with discretion. Those who are left-handed put the thumb of the right hand on the sixth hole, a practice which should be noted for all wind instruments. I add here the tablature for the **six-holed Flute**, even though I do not provide an illustration of it, since the illustration of the Flageolet makes it sufficiently understood; it differs only in that all six of its holes are on the front, whereas the Flageolet has two in the back, as I have said.

->Tablature for the Six-Holed Flute.<-

<image-desc>A musical notation diagram for the six-holed flute. It features a musical staff with thirteen notes forming an ascending scale. Directly below the staff is a tablature grid consisting of six horizontal lines representing the finger holes. Each note on the staff is aligned vertically with a specific fingering pattern indicated by circles (open, closed, or crossed) on the grid lines.</image-desc>

Now, it is so easy to compare the preceding tablature with this one that there is no need to speak of it further. Therefore, I will proceed to the explanation of other Flutes, and first those of England, which are ordinarily called <term>douces</term> <note>original: "douces," meaning "sweet" or "soft," referring to the Recorder</note>, because of the sweetness of their tones and their harmonies. This follows an example in four parts, which shows the manner of performing Concerts <note>Ensemble pieces</note> with as many parts as one wishes, using four or five kinds of Flageolets.

The example that follows is a <term>Vaudeville</term> <note>A popular, light urban song of the period</note> in the third mode transposed by a Fourth: the Treble <note>original: "Deſſus," the highest part</note> is played with <term>D la re sol</term> <note>The note D in the hexachord system</note> all closed, and all open at the Octave. For the other parts, one closes and opens <term>C sol ut</term> <note>The note C</note> and <term>G re sol</term> <note>The note G</note>. This is so easy to understand that it is not necessary to speak of it at greater length. This example and the others used for the instruments that follow were composed by Sieur **Henry le Jeune**, who understands their range and extent very well. Those who desire other examples may consult the Masters of the art, for it is enough that this one demonstrates the properties of the Flageolet and the range of all its parts, so that it may be used in all kinds of concerts. This should likewise be noted for the other wind instruments, which each have a particular example used to understand their nature.
