## PROPOSITION VIII.

### *To explain the shape, range, tablature, and use of English Flutes, which are called recorders [douces], and having nine holes, with an example for four parts.*

<margin>a</margin>These Flutes are called <term>douces</term> <note>literally "sweet," the period French term for the recorder</note> because of the sweetness of their sounds, which represent the charm and softness of voices. They are called "eight-holed" because the eighth hole, which is near the <term>foot</term> <note>original: "pate"; the bottom end of the instrument</note>, is doubled, so that this instrument can serve both left-handed and right-handed players. Now, one places this Flute in the mouth just like the preceding ones, and the first hole is marked with a "white zero" <note>a symbol in the fingering chart</note> to signify that it is at the back, and that it must be closed with the <margin>b</margin>thumb of the left hand. The three following fingers of that hand serve to close the second, third, and fourth holes, just as the three fingers of the right hand close the fifth, sixth, and seventh. The eighth hole is intended for the little finger, which is called the <term>auricular</term> finger. This is represented so clearly by <margin>c</margin>this figure <note>referring to an illustration likely appearing on the next page</note> that there is no need for a longer discourse, for the eight numbers show the order of the eight holes. "A" signifies the mouthpiece [embouchure], of which the <margin>d</margin>slit is represented by the end "D." "B C" signifies the length of its body, and the end "E F" shows yet another sort of mouthpiece, which serves for the Tenors [Tailles] and the Basses, which are two and a half feet in length. The Tenor is one foot five inches long, and the Treble [Dessus] is only eleven <term>lines</term> <note>An old unit of measurement; a "ligne" was 1/12th of an inch. Eleven lines would be just under an inch, which may be a printer's error for eleven inches, or refers to a specific part of the headjoint.</note>. But to understand the harmony of <margin>e</margin>all the parts, it must be noted that when their eighth hole is open, the Treble is at the Ninth, and the Tenor along with the <term>Haute-contre</term> <note>the high-tenor or alto part</note> is at the Fifth.

...of the Bass: for the Alto [Haute-contre] is no different from the Tenor [Taille], since the range of the one is sufficient to play both parts, as is the case with several other wind and string instruments.

Now, these Flutes make up the <term>small consort</term> <note>original: "petit ieu"; a set of instruments of smaller sizes/higher pitches</note>, just as those that follow after make up the <term>large consort</term> <note>original: "grand ieu"; a set of larger, deeper instruments</note>, but they can all be tuned together, just as the large and small stops of an Organ are.

As for their range and their <term>tablature</term> <note>a diagram showing where to place fingers rather than just musical notes</note> which follows, both for <term>B-flat</term> <note>original: "b mol"</note> and <term>B-natural</term> <note>original: "# quarre"</note>, it is no more difficult than that of the <term>Flageolet</term> <note>a small, high-pitched flute discussed earlier in the book</note>. Each small perpendicular line that falls upon the musical staff shows the holes that must be closed to produce the sounds represented by the notes directly above. The zeros (or the letters "o") signify the holes left open, and when they are filled in or black, they must be closed. I will give only one or two examples to explain this practice: the first serves for **C** [UT], or for the **D** [RE] of the **G** scale <note>original: "G re sol vt," a traditional name for the note G and its associated hexachord</note>, which is produced by closing the first four holes and the seventh, and opening the others. And to produce **F** [FA], which is a <term>fourth</term> higher, one closes only the first, the third, and the seventh holes; likewise, to produce the **G** [SOL] that follows, one closes only the third and the seventh holes.

### ->of Wind Instruments.<-

The <term>tablature</term> <note>a diagram showing which finger-holes to cover</note> clearly demonstrates how many holes must be stopped or unstopped to produce all the other tones, as well as the range of this instrument. Its range spans a <term>fifteenth</term> <note>two full octaves</note>, much like that of the <term>Flageolet</term> <note>a smaller, simpler high-pitched flute</note>, although some musicians only attribute a range of a <term>thirteenth</term> <note>an octave plus a sixth</note> to it. However, it should be noted that one can play a melody or a song on the <term>recorder</term> <note>original: "Fluste douce"</note> and, at the same time, sing the bass part—though without articulating the words—because the wind coming from the mouth while singing is sufficient to make the flute sound. In this way, a single person can perform a <term>duet</term> <note>original: "Duo"</note>.

The large flutes shown here were sent from England to one of our Kings. I have had two different <term>consorts</term> <note>original: "jeux"; sets of instruments designed to be played together</note> engraved on this plate: specifically, the small consort composed of the three flutes **A B** and **C D**. The <term>stoppers</term> <note>original: "tampons"; the blocks inside the mouthpiece</note> and the place where the wind enters can be seen in figures **K** and **G**, which have all the <term>fontanelles</term> <note>original: "boëttes"; the perforated wooden boxes that protect the metal keys</note> **A** and **C** hidden. The bass of this small consort, **A B**, serves as the <term>treble</term> <note>original: "Dessus"</note> for the large consort, which begins where the other ends. It is not necessary to label or explain the holes, as they are represented here as they appear in nature; the white ones are located on the back.

Now, the largest instruments have fontanelles to enclose the keys, without which one could not close the holes, because the fingers of the hand cannot reach such a great distance. This is why the Bass **B** has the key **f**, which one presses with the little finger to open the hole located under the box opposite **g**. But the Bass of the large consort, **L N**, has three fontanelles: the largest, **Y Z**, and the two others, **b** and **c**. As for the large one, I have removed it and moved it to **O Q**, so that all the <term>springs</term> <note>original: "ressorts"</note> can be seen uncovered, allowing our craftsmen to make similar ones.

**Q** shows the arrangement of the two keys appearing at the top of the box **Z**; depending on whether the little finger presses the first or the second, hole **S** or **T** opens to produce their sounds. **V** and **X**... <note>The text ends mid-sentence, likely referring to further mechanical details of the springs or levers.</note>

### Book Five

...show the <term>springs</term> <note>the metal mechanisms for the keys</note> hidden under the small <term>fontanelles</term> <note>original: "boëttes"; perforated wooden boxes used to protect the delicate brass keys on large instruments</note> *b* and *c*. These are touched with the foot <note>referring to the bottom of the hand or perhaps a foot-pedal mechanism on exceptionally large pipes, though usually meaning the lowest finger keys</note>, which presses the small brass squares visible on these boxes opposite *b* and *c* to raise the springs. This is demonstrated at the tail of spring *h*, which is pushed perpendicularly against the blade *K* to raise it and open the hole, which is as large as a window; this can be judged by the openings which are proportioned to its shape. The same must be said of the <term>Tenor</term> <note>original: "Taille"</note> marked *a*, which has as many holes and keys, and which also serves as the <term>Alto</term> <note>original: "Haute-contre"</note>.

As for the <term>bocal</term> <note>original: "canal" or "emboucheure" *e d*</note>, which enters the recorder through hole *I* (hidden and covered by box *L M*), it is used to blow wind into the instrument through opening *d*. This is necessary because these recorders are so tall that the mouth cannot reach the <term>labium</term> <note>original: "lumiere" M; the edge where the sound is produced</note>, nor the mouthpieces *L* or *I* of the Bass, nor that of the Tenor marked *K*. The Bass stands 7 to 8 feet high from the top of box *L* down to the <term>foot</term> <note>original: "pate"</note> *N*. From this, one can judge the size and distance of its eleven holes, and those of the Tenor, which here maintains its proper proportions in a smaller volume. The pipe *e d* hooks onto an iron loop opposite the second hole from the top, as seen opposite *d* and *l*.

It is not necessary to speak of their <term>tablature</term> <note>fingering charts</note>, because it follows the same rules as the previous one. Therefore, I only remark that the sound of these recorders is judged so sweet by some that it deserves the name "charming" and "ravishing"—though I do not believe this manner of speaking belongs to any pleasures other than those of Heaven, which reveal the ravishing object of the blessed, which never tires and never ceases. In contrast, all other pleasures immediately become tedious and turn into unbearable displeasure and pain, as the most steadfast minds well know.

This plate also contains the figure of the <term>Fife</term> <note>original: "Fifre"</note> **E F**, of which I speak in the following Proposition; but before leaving this one, I provide an example in four parts for the recorders.

Of Wind Instruments.

## PROPOSITION IX.

### *Explaining the shape, range, and fingering chart of the German Flute and the Fife.*

<image-desc>A vertical woodcut illustration of a transverse flute (German Flute). The instrument is labeled with letters and numbers: 'A' and 'B' at the ornamental cap; 'C' marking the position of the internal stopper (tampon); '1' for the embouchure hole; '2' through '7' for the finger holes; and 'E' and 'D' at the foot. The flute is depicted with a slight curve, which the text notes was characteristic of the specific high-quality model used for the drawing.</image-desc>

Although I should have (it seems) joined this type of flute with the flageolet, because it has six holes to be stopped like it, I nonetheless wanted to set it apart because it is not blown from the top **A B**, like the others, but through hole **1**: so that the part **A B C** serves only as an ornament. **C** represents the place where the <term>stopper</term> <note>original: "tampon"; a plug, usually of cork, used to seal the head of the flute</note> ends, which is used to block the top of this instrument so that the wind does not escape through **A B**, but is instead forced to descend toward **E D** where it exits when the six holes are stopped. From this, it follows that the length of this flute is measured only from **C** to **E**. Now, I have left the curvature in this figure because it was modeled on one of the best flutes in the world which happened to be curved; for this reason, I mark the size here, which is one foot and 5/8 <note>approximately 53 centimeters based on the old French foot</note>. It measures three inches from **B** to its <term>embouchure</term> <note>original: "emboucheure"; the hole where the player blows</note>. One plays it by placing the lower lip on the edge of the first hole and blowing the wind very gently. From the stopper **C** to the <term>mouth-hole</term> <note>original: "lumiere"</note> **1**, there are only 8 <term>lines</term> <note>original: "lignes"; a traditional measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch</note>. It is bored with an equal thickness throughout its length, which is not the case for all types of <term>pipes</term> <note>original: "Chalumeaux"</note>, as I shall mention elsewhere, and this thickness is eight lines.

The distance from the second hole to the third is 13 1/2 lines; the distances between the 2nd and 7th are almost equal, namely three lines, but those between the 3rd and 4th are a bit wider, and finally, the 5th is 4 lines in diameter. This flute serves as the <term>Soprano</term> <note>original: "Dessus"</note> in ensemble parts, and consequently, the others must be proportionately longer and thicker as they descend lower: for example, the one that descends by an Octave or a Fifteenth must be double or quadruple the size of this one. Their material can be plum wood, cherry, or other woods that are easily bored, but one usually chooses a wood of a beautiful color that takes a fine polish, so that beauty accompanies the goodness of the instrument, and the eyes may in some way share in the pleasure of the ear: they are commonly made of boxwood; they are also very good when made of crystal, glass, or ebony.

As for the range and the <term>fingering chart</term> <note>original: "tablature"</note> of this flute, which can also serve for the Fife (which is entirely similar to it), I have represented it with white and black circles to follow the standard practice. This in no way prevents one from marking it with the small lines of the fingering chart used for the nine-holed flute, or in any other manner one wishes. Now, I have placed each circle opposite each hole so that one knows which holes must be stopped or opened to produce the sounds marked by the notes above them. Each note corresponds to a row of circles, showing that when all holes are stopped, it plays the lowest note, namely the <note>original: "l'VT de G re sol vt"; the note G, referred to here using the traditional Guidonian hexachord system where 'Ut' is the first note of the 'G' hexachord</note> G, and the

...mine <note>original: "re:"; likely completing the word "examine" from the previous page's "exa-"</note>: what happens similarly to the **Fife**, which differs from the **German Flute** only in that it speaks more loudly, its sounds are much more vivid and brilliant, and it is shorter and narrower. It is the specific instrument of the **Swiss** <note>The Swiss were famous for their mercenary infantry, who standardized the use of fife and drum in military maneuvers</note>, and of others who beat the **Drum**, although some play it one way and others another, following different customs and different **fingering charts** <note>original: "tablatures"</note> that the ear and practice can provide. 

However, one does not normally perform all the parts of a musical composition with Fifes as one does with German Flutes, which are tuned to **church pitch** <note>original: "ton de chapelle"; a reference pitch used for sacred and ensemble music, often different from secular or military pitches</note> to perform concerts. And because a **Bass** cannot be made long enough to descend low enough, one uses the **Sackbut** <note>the early form of the trombone</note>, or the **Serpent** <note>a S-shaped bass wind instrument made of wood and leather</note>, or some other Bass to fill the part. For if the German Flute were long enough to play this part, the hands could not easily reach the last holes while blowing into it; though this defect in the Basses of the said Flute can be remedied by several keys, by **doubling them back** <note>original: "rompant ou redoublant"; referring to the practice of "folding" the air column, as seen in the boot joint of a bassoon</note>, as is done with **Bassoons**, which we will discuss later.

<image-desc>A vertical woodcut illustration of a fife (fifre) flute positioned in the right margin. The mouthpiece hole is labeled 'A'. Below it, a section of the head is labeled 'B'. The main body with finger holes is labeled 'C', and the bottom end is labeled 'D'. Along the length of the body, six finger holes are numbered '1' through '6' sequentially from top to bottom.</image-desc>

Now, it is certain that one can add a stop of Fifes to the **Organ** in order to enrich it with a new grace, but it is not possible to replicate the **subtleties of the mouth** <note>original: "gentillesses de la bouche"; referring to delicate nuances of breath and tonguing</note>, the tongue, and the lips with the ordinary bellows of the Organ. I say *ordinary*, because one can add springs to them that will serve to give some new vigor or sweetness to the sounds. But I will speak more fully of Organs in a specific book; meanwhile, players of the Fife and Flutes may invent ways for a single man to play several instruments all at once, as is practiced in **Sicily** and elsewhere; where one blows into two or three Flutes at the same time, which are made of **reeds** <note>original: "cannes"</note>, and whose sounds have certain peculiar charms that imitate those of the voice.

If one had worked as curiously to perfect this species of instrument as has been done with Organs, one might perhaps have discovered the way to play four or five parts from the same breath of the mouth. And if one wished to take the trouble to bore them such that the **Diatonic** genus being on one side, as it is in fact, the **Chromatic** and **Enharmonic** <note>referring to the three "genera" or types of scales in ancient Greek music theory</note> were on the other two sides, one would easily execute all that the Greeks knew, with a small piece of wood. But I leave this research to the **Makers** <note>original: "Facteurs"; instrument builders</note>, as well as the research of the **scale** <note>original: "Diapason"; referring here to the mathematical proportions and measurements of the bore</note> necessary to bore them accurately, although the preceding diagrams show the positions of the Diatonic holes exactly enough to make others in imitation.

Regarding the fingering chart of the Fife, which shows all its tones and the manner of covering its holes to sing all kinds of airs and songs, it does not have as great a **Range** as that of the preceding Flute, for it is only a **Fifteenth** <note>an interval of two octaves</note>, as is seen in the fingering chart that follows.

Now it suffices here to explain all the Hunting Horns which are customarily used, especially since I will speak later of Trumpets. The four preceding figures represent them all, for A B shows the shape of the great Horn, and C D that of the Horn with several coils, though it is not as commonly used as the other. The Horn <note>original: "La Trompe"; here referring to a hunting horn</note> E F, which has only one coil, is the most frequently used; that is why I have included it with its strap <term>Enguicheure: the decorated cord or leather strap used to carry a hunting horn</term> L, M, G, H 1, 2, 3. The other cords G 3 and H 2 hold the Horn in place by means of three rings 1, 2, 3.

N O represents the third Horn, which is ordinarily called the *Huchet* <term>Huchet: a small, curved signal horn used by hunters or woodsmen</term>: and the fifth figure P O shows the *Post Horn*, which is joined to the body with the cord R. It should be noted that these Horns have only two significant parts: namely their *mouthpieces* <term>embouchures: the part of a wind instrument placed against the lips</term> A, C, E, N, which are made of silver, copper, horn, wood, or any other material one wishes; and their *bells* <term>pauillons: the flared end of a brass or wind instrument</term> B, D, F, O. As for the range of their tones, it differs according to the skill and dexterity of the player, for there are some Hunters who give them as much range as the Trumpet, which I will discuss later. The tones used for hunting are described by Fouilloux in the *Book of Venery* <term>Venerie: the traditional art or practice of hunting</term> chapter 43; therefore I do not wish to speak of them here, although one might notice several things that he did not consider. For example: whether the tones (which he uses to call and alert *the Dogs*) are more suitable than others of which the horn is capable. Whether the word *Tran*, which he uses to express the sounds of the Horn, is the best of all those that can be imagined for this subject. Whether this instrument is more suitable for hunting than those that have reeds, like the *Oboes* <note>original: "Haut-bois"</note>, or those of percussion, like Bells or Drums. Whether the sounds of the Horn have more rapport and sympathy with the hearing and imagination of dogs than the sound of other instruments. Whether one can invent instruments whose sounds would make all sorts of wild animals come and be tamed, as some believe—particularly if one called them by the names that Adam gave them <note>Refers to the biblical tradition of Adam naming all creatures in Eden, implying a primal linguistic power over nature</note>. However, in my opinion, there is no sound more suitable for making them come where one wants, or for stopping them, than that which imitates their cries and their voices, as is experienced with the calls <term>apeaux: decoys or whistles that imitate animal sounds</term> for Stags, Boars, Quail, and many other terrestrial and winged animals.

But I leave all these difficulties to speak of the manner in which the Horn is played; this is done by placing the Mouthpiece to the lips, pressing it against them, either by putting it to one of the sides of the mouth, or in the middle. Now, the tip of the tongue must enter the Mouthpiece in order to guide the wind, which is lost if one does not close tightly all the parts of the lips where the Mouthpiece does not touch; from this, it follows that it is difficult to sound this instrument...

After one has positioned the Horn at the mouth, one can play it in three or four manners: namely, by simply imitating the wind of a bellows, as happens with sounds that flow without being animated; and then by moving the lip within the Mouthpiece, which is done in two ways. The first consists of making two sounds with a single stroke or lip movement, and the other depends on as many strokes or lip movements as there are different sounds, which animates the sounds further. Furthermore, one may use the movement of the tongue, in which consists the most excellent manner of sounding the horn <note>original: "trompe"; here used for the hunting horn</note> and all other wind instruments; for when the tongue strikes <note>original: "martele"; literally "hammers"</note> each sound, the instrument imitates the human voice and speech, insofar as it articulates its sounds. This should be noted for all types of instruments with Mouthpieces, and even for others which are more or less susceptible to all these mouth-positions and movements, which can be transferred to Organ pipes by means of several techniques <term>industries: clever mechanical devices or specialized skills</term> that can make their sounds much more agreeable. However, all that pertains to Horns will be even better understood through what I shall say of the Trumpet in the following discourses.

### COROLLARY.

If Hunters wish to have the pleasure of performing Concerts in four or more parts with their Horns, it is quite easy, provided that they know how to produce the correct tones and that they proportion the length and width of their Horns so that they maintain the same ratios as Organ pipes. For example, if the largest Horn is six feet long, it will produce the Fifth <note>original: "Diapente"; the musical interval of a perfect fifth</note> below the one that is 4 feet in length. I shall say elsewhere whether their widths should be in a Three-to-Two ratio <note>original: "Sesquialtere"; a ratio of 3:2, corresponding to the musical fifth</note>. And if one adds a third Horn three feet long, it will produce the Fourth against the second, so that the three will make a perfect Trio and will touch the three principal notes <note>original: "chordes"</note> of the first mode. It would be easy to add three or four others to these to make the other chords. There are several other things concerning Horns which we shall speak of later; I add only that they can be made of crystal, glass, earthenware, stone, etc., and that Makers can add a great many refinements <note>original: "industries"</note> which will make them as much admired as other instruments.

### Fifth Book

we ordinarily use, and which I have named <term>UT</term> <note>The note C, the fundamental or lowest note of the scale</note>, for it descends a whole <term>Octave</term> further, though many <term>Trumpeters</term> do not believe it, because they cannot do it, or because they have never tried.

Now, there is no doubt that the wind [the breath] is pushed and modified differently to produce the second tone than to produce the first, and likewise for the others; and that the one which produces the second has its reflections, or its returns <note>Mersenne refers to what we now call vibrations or frequency</note>, twice as fast as the one which produces the first, as I have demonstrated in the preceding books. This happens by reason of the wind being pushed with more or less violence or speed, and consequently having its returns more or less frequent; so that one must only provide the reason why this greater speed produces the Octave, and the <term>Fifth</term>, etc., for its first and second intervals, rather than another consonance or a dissonance, and why the wind is determined and constrained to make twice as many returns at the second tone of the Trumpet, and three times as many at the third, etc., as at the first, as is seen in the range of its sounds.

Now I say that this happens because all natural agents <note>Physical forces or entities in nature</note> always travel by the shortest and easiest path when they are not hindered, as experienced with heavy bodies that descend toward their center in a straight line, because it is the shortest of all; for every natural thing hastens as much as it can to arrive at its perfection, and serves us as an example to make us embrace the shortest, surest, and easiest path to arrive at our final end: that is to say, charity and the love of God, outside of which one finds only oblique lines. And if nature did not follow the shortest path, it would make useless movements and labor in vain; now, the easiest and shortest path it can follow consists in making the Octave for its first interval, and then the Fifth and the others that follow in its range, as I demonstrate.

It is certain that there is no addition shorter and easier than that which is made from one to one, one to two, one to three, etc. Now, when the Trumpet passes through the intervals I have explained, it does nothing other than add one to one, one to two, etc. It is therefore necessary that it pass through these intervals, unless one prevents it by forcing it against its nature.

The major premise is so evident that it has no need of being proved, unless one wishes to light the Sun at high noon. As for the minor premise, it is very easy to prove, for assuming that the lowest sound—that is to say, the first tone of the Trumpet—is made by a single return or beat of air, if one adds another beat, one will make the Octave; and if one adds yet another beat to the two preceding ones, one makes the third tone of the Trumpet, which is at the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>An interval of an octave plus a fifth</note> from the first, and at the Fifth from the second. And then if one adds a beat to the three preceding ones, one makes the fourth tone, which makes the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>A double octave</note>, or the double Octave with the first, the Octave with the second, and the Fourth with the third. If one adds yet another movement to have the fifth tone of the Trumpet, which is composed of five beats of air made in the same time as the single beat of the first tone, or the two of the second tone, etc., it makes the <term>Major Seventeenth</term> with the first tone, and the <term>Major Third</term> with the fourth. And if one adds another beat to the five preceding ones, one makes the <term>Minor Third</term>. By this, one sees that the progress of nature is a friend to harmony, which it...

One can also provide the reason for these intervals through division, insofar as the <term>Octave</term> is generated by the division of a string into two equal parts, as I have shown in the book on Consonances; and all the other consonances are produced by the second or third <term>bisection</term> <note>The act of dividing something into two equal parts.</note>. That is to say: why does it not add a "return" <note>A "return" refers to a single vibration or oscillation of the air column.</note> to the 6 preceding ones of the 6th tone to make the <term>Sesquisexte</term> <note>The ratio 7:6, an interval slightly smaller than a minor third but larger than a whole tone.</note>, and then the <term>Sesquiseptieme</term> <note>The ratio 8:7, a "septimal" whole tone.</note>? Instead of these, it makes the <term>Fourth</term> again after the sixth tone, or after the fifth interval of the <term>Minor Third</term>, by adding two beats to the six preceding ones.

The other difficulty consists in knowing why it does not always produce an Octave at each jump or interval it makes, given that each of its sounds or tones can be assumed to be unity and a single beat, just as well as the first. The third difficulty is why it sometimes makes a tone lower or higher than the first tone we discussed, instead of making the Octave. I leave aside several other difficulties also encountered in other wind instruments, the solutions for which may be found in the discourses that follow.

*To explain why the Trumpet does not produce the Sesquisexte in its fifth interval, and why it abandons the progression it had followed up to the sixth tone to produce the Fourth, which it had already produced at the third interval.*

Nature prefers to break the sequence of its intervals and its songs rather than pass through an interval that is worth nothing except to wound the ear and the mind. Now, she <note>Mersenne often personifies Nature as "she."</note> prefers to take the trouble of adding two movements, or <term>beats of air</term> <note>Vibrations or pulses that determine the pitch of a note.</note> all at once to create the <term>Fourth</term>, rather than adding only one to create the <term>Sesquisixth</term> <note>The ratio of 6:7, which is a dissonant interval not typically used in traditional Western scales.</note>; this shows that the Fourth does not receive a harmonic division, since nature does not divide it, as she divides the second <term>Octave</term> and the second <term>Fifth</term> into three tones to mark their beginning, their middle, and their end, and consequently the principal <term>cadences</term> of the <term>modes</term>, which have more power over the mind than other strings or other sounds. One can also say that nature, having given the six tones <note>The first six harmonics of the natural series.</note> as her six workdays upon which she rests, imitates her Author <note>God.</note> who rested at the end of six days; and that she occupies herself no further except to show the difference of her first six tones by the division of the Fourth into a <term>major tone</term>, a <term>minor tone</term>, and a <term>major semitone</term>. This is done after having proposed the entire Fourth as the image of the Octave, so that one may know she wishes to divide it into three intervals, just as she has already divided the second Octave into three other intervals. In this way, she still imitates her Author, who contents Himself with showing the distinction and diversity of creatures (the first seeds of which He cast during the six days of Creation) through the different combinations He makes of them at every moment. This He does by Himself immediately, or through the mediation of other creatures, so that one does not grow weary of considering the principles of things, which are too simple to satisfy the imperfection of our senses, which prefer <term>accidents</term> <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities, like color or shape, as opposed to the "substance" or essence of a thing.</note> to substance. It is perhaps for this same reason that Musicians mix tones and semitones among the <term>consonances</term>, for fear that their excessive sweetness might bring us disgust and boredom, and why the <term>Trumpet</term> makes dissonances after consonances.

Furthermore, if she made the <term>Sesquisixth</term> after the <term>Sesquififth</term> <note>The 5:6 ratio, or a minor third.</note>, her beats would serve the <term>Septenary</term> <note>The number seven.</note> number, which can only be divided by unity, to which she cannot return. This is why she leaves this odd number aside as useless to harmony, in order to pass to the number eight, which is the first cube after unity, and which completes the third Octave, acting as the repetition or doubling of the 2nd and 4th sounds. By this, nature shows how much she loves the Octave, which she has reached by the addition of the second beat, instead of stopping at the Sesquisixth by a single beat. Finally, when she beats the air eight times after having beaten it six times, she does the same thing as when she beats it four times after having beaten it three times, especially since one must judge the progress of consonances by the sequence of their <term>radical terms</term> <note>The simplest mathematical expression of a ratio (e.g., 6:8 simplifies to 3:4).</note>.

Now, she creates the major tone after this Fourth by the addition of a single beat, just as she creates the minor: for her tone being composed of eight beats, creates the major tone against the nine beats of the eighth tone, and this 8th tone composed of 9 beats makes the major tone against the 10 beats of her ninth sound. Here it must be noted that all the sounds she chooses are consonances with those that precede them; for example, the ninth sound composed of ten beats creates the Octave with the fifth sound. But if she made the Sesquisixth with her sixth sound, the seventh sound would create no

One can therefore conclude by experience that nature seeks the <term>Octave</term>, and that she does not wish to provide the differences of the consonances until she has reached the Twenty-second <note>An interval spanning three octaves.</note>, arriving at the <term>octonary</term> <note>The number eight; here referring to the eighth harmonic which completes the second octave of the series.</note>, which serves as her boundary. This is because she considers only the <term>solids</term> <note>In a Pythagorean sense, numbers representing three dimensions (cubes), as opposed to points, lines, or surfaces.</note>, without concerning herself with <term>sur-solids</term> or other numbers or quantities that are called <term>dignities</term> in <term>Algebra</term> <note>Historical term for the powers of a number, such as squares, cubes, and beyond.</note>, and which exist more in the imagination of men than in the reality of things. From this it follows that all instruments limit their range by the number eight, and take as their motto, along with all of nature, *No further beyond* <note>original: "Non plus ultra." A famous Latin phrase signifying a limit or peak that cannot be surpassed.</note>. For it must be supposed that ten is worth fifteen, so that 10 1/2 is worth sixteen <note>Mersenne is explaining the mathematical derivation of the 15:16 ratio for the major semitone by adjusting the natural harmonic progression.</note>. This she does in order to provide the third difference of the consonances; for the major semitone is the difference between the <term>Major Third</term> and the <term>Fourth</term>, just as the <term>major tone</term> is the difference between the Fourth and the <term>Fifth</term>, and the <term>minor tone</term> that of the Fifth and the <term>Major Sixth</term>.

Indeed, it is reasonable that the Trumpet divides the Fourth—which it had brought forth in its Sixth interval—in such a way that the final division restores that same Fourth. This cannot happen after the major tone and the minor tone, which it has produced by following its natural progress, unless it produces the major semitone. Now, the Proposition that follows contains yet other difficulties which may serve to understand this one.

## PROPOSITION XIV.

### *Explaining why the Trumpet does not assume each of these tones as the unit, and consequently why it does not always produce an Octave at every interval.*

Since one can assume 2, 4, 8, etc., as easily as one for the first sound of the Trumpet, it seems difficult to know why it does not just as easily produce the Octave, or the Fifth, or any other interval one wishes at the 3rd and 4th interval, etc., as it does at the 1st and 2nd. For its 3rd and 4th sounds, etc., could just as well be assumed as the unit, like the first. Nonetheless, it is easy to explain this difficulty if one wishes to use true suppositions, and those given by nature, without amusing oneself with imaginary ones that have no foundation in the reality of things. For it is certain that the first sound of the Trumpet relates to the second as one relates to two; for the <term>beats of air</term> <note>The vibrations or pulses that constitute a sound's frequency.</note>, which are the first sound, last twice as long as those which are the second—that is to say, the air beats twice in the second sound while it beats a single time in the first sound, as I have proved elsewhere. Thus, if one takes the entire range of the Trumpet for its whole body, one will find it impossible for the first sound to be assumed as anything other than the unit, the second for the binary, the third—

And if one objects that by supposing the first sound for unity, one can imagine a deeper one, which is made by half of unity, and then another made by a quarter, and so on for others following these numbers 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, etc., it must be answered that no sound can be made of a half or a quarter of a <term>beat</term> <note>The author uses "beats" (battemens) to refer to what we now call vibrations or frequency cycles.</note> or return. For one must, at the very least, beat the air once to make a sound; now, one cannot beat it more than once without beating it at least twice, and then three times, etc. But here one still encounters some difficulties in the order of the said sounds, compared to their strength and their weakness. For if nature follows the order of numbers, it seems that the Trumpet should never pass to the <term>Fifth</term> until it has first made the <term>Octave</term>, and that it should never go to the simple or repeated <term>Fourth</term> until it has passed through the Octave and the <term>Twelfth</term>. Now, experience teaches that the Trumpet rises, when one wishes, from its first tone to the last without passing through the middle intervals. For example, one can produce the <term>triple Octave</term> from one to eight in the very first jump, and consequently the Trumpet does not necessarily follow the order of the numbers of which we have spoken. To which I respond that this consideration in no way destroys what I have said of the order of the intervals when one pushes the wind very gently and little by little. This does not prevent one from making larger intervals when one pushes with great violence; for if one gives as much wind to the Trumpet the first time as the third, it is a certain thing that it will rise higher by a Twelfth than its first tone. And if one gives it as much as it receives at the fourth tone, it will rise by a <term>Seventeenth</term>, etc., inasmuch as the later intervals contain the first ones; for the <term>Fifteenth</term> contains the Octave, just as the surface contains the line, and the <term>Twenty-second</term> contains the Octave and the Fifteenth, just as the solid contains the plane and the line.

This is why when the wind is pushed so fast that it beats 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 times at the entry of the <term>mouthpiece</term> <note>original: "bocal." The cup-shaped part of the instrument where the player's lips vibrate.</note>, it rises to the preceding tones. The same thing must be said of the descent of sounds, which is all the greater as one further diminishes the <term>velocity</term> or the number of beats. Now, the reason I have given is not based on the idea that the Trumpet cannot pass from its first tone to the last without passing through those in the middle, but on the fact that it cannot produce smaller intervals than those of which I have spoken.

Nevertheless, there is still a great difficulty that deserves a particular Proposition, namely: how one can increase the sound of the Trumpet...

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*Explaining in what manner one can increase or weaken the strength of each sound of the Trumpet without changing its tone, that is to say, its highness or lowness.*<-

This difficulty can be explained by what I have said concerning the loud and high voice in the book on the Voice, and the difference between the highness and the strength of sounds in the book on Stringed Instruments; for the agitated air never makes a sound higher unless its agitations, or its <term>beats</term> <note>Mersenne uses the word "battemens" (beats) to describe what we now call frequency or vibrations per second.</note>, are faster. From this, one must conclude that the same tone of the Trumpet is always made of the same number of air beats, even though it may be as weak or as strong as one wishes. This is why it must be said that one simply pushes a greater quantity of air, or wind, at the same time when one increases the strength of the tone, and that the movements and beats, or the <term>ebb and flow</term> <note>The original French "flux & reflux" refers to the oscillatory motion of air particles as they vibrate.</note> of the air, are larger, but they are not greater in number. Although it is difficult to explain the manner in which one must push the wind to distinguish between loud sounds and high-pitched sounds with the Trumpet, we may apply to it what has been said regarding the strength and weakness of the sound made by a single string, and the difference between loud and high-pitched voices.

Now, I have demonstrated that a sound is reinforced without changing its tone—that is, without raising it—when one strikes a string harder, because it strikes a greater quantity of air in the same short amount of time that it previously struck a smaller quantity when making a weaker sound. So, the tone of the string, or the Trumpet, cannot change (even if it were increased to infinity) if the number of beats of which it is composed does not increase. Now, this number does not increase as long as one pushes the wind through the same opening of the mouth, or with the same movement of the throat. For it must be noted that the <term>larynx</term> and the <term>glottis</term> <note>The "glottis" is the opening between the vocal folds; Mersenne recognizes that wind players use their throat and mouth to shape the air column.</note> lower and open further when making the first [lower] tones, and that one must narrow these openings to make higher tones, even though those who play instruments do not perceive these changes, because they do not reflect enough on the manner in which they press their lips and push the wind.

But one might object that it follows that one could produce all sorts of intervals with the Trumpet, both high and low, just as one does with the throat, if the tones depended on the different openings of the mouth and the glottis—since we make all sorts of intervals when singing. Furthermore, a bellows can take the place of the mouth and produce all the tones of the Trumpet of which we have spoken, even though it always has the same opening; this is experienced with <term>Organ pipes</term>, some of which rise to the <term>Octave</term> and others to the <term>Twelfth</term> <note>The Octave and the Twelfth (an octave plus a fifth) are the first overtones produced when an organ pipe is "overblown" with increased air pressure.</note> when they are given more weight [pressure]. To this, one may add that the same opening of the mouth and throat produces different tones with the <term>Flageolet</term> <note>A small flute similar to a recorder, popular in the 17th century.</note> and other flutes with holes. From this, it seems one must conclude that the diversity of the Trumpet’s tones, and those of other instruments, does not come solely from the different openings of the throat, or the...

Certainly, these three difficulties are very considerable; for although some maintain that one can make the Trumpet rise through all sorts of steps, both high and low, just like the voice, nevertheless all the experiments I have been able to perform show the contrary. This is despite the fact that I have met someone who descends a Major Third lower than the second sound, instead of descending a full Octave, as I shall describe in the section on the range of the Trumpet. In that range, one still sees two tones below the first, under which there are some who first descend a Minor Third, and then a whole tone; but besides the fact that this is not common, and that these tones are produced with great difficulty, they are of no value. Therefore, no account should be taken of them; we might even leave out the first tone, and consequently the first interval of the Octave, and take the second tone as the first, because it is not used on the Trumpet and is worthless, as I shall say when speaking of its usage.

One can also respond that the preceding reasons would not lose their force even if men were found so skilled that they could produce all the steps of *do, re, mi, fa*, etc. <note>original: "ut, re, mi, fa"</note> from the first tone of the Trumpet, inasmuch as human <term>industry</term> <note>In this context, "industry" refers to the ingenuity, skill, or artificial methods used by a craftsman or performer.</note> can disturb the movements of nature to serve their particular designs, as is experienced in the works of Mechanics.

This is why it can be said that one does not ordinarily produce the lower steps solely through different openings of the lips or the throat; and that after the opening with which one makes the first tone, one cannot open them in such a way as to keep the Trumpet from rising to the Fourth, or some smaller interval. This is because, however little one opens them further, they cannot add less than one return or one <term>beat</term> <note>Mersenne uses "battement" (beat) to describe what we now call frequency or vibrations of air.</note> of air to the beats that determine the preceding sound. So it is necessary to produce the Fifth after the Octave, and then all the other intervals of which I have spoken; unless one uses the same opening of the lips while pushing a different quantity of air with a different force, which can be divided into as many steps as one wishes by weakening or increasing the tone.

One must therefore respond to the first difficulty: that the lips would not produce all sorts of sounds, as they do, if they did not tighten and close in various ways. For the lungs serve as nothing other than bellows, of which the <term>vocal artery</term> <note>original: "l’artere vocale." Mersenne is referring to the trachea or windpipe.</note> is the wind-pipe; the lips, which immediately touch the <term>mouthpiece</term> <note>original: "bocal"</note>, must modify the voice or the wind to produce the low and high sounds. As for bellows, when it has been shown that they can produce all the tones of the Trumpet, we shall easily explain how that is done; yet this should by no means be believed without seeing the experiment, which in my opinion will never be performed. And if it were performed, it would have to be said that the violence of the wind produces a greater number of beats than before, for the speed with which it is pushed can compensate for the narrowing of the channel through which the wind passes. It suffices that the air beats, or is beaten, as many times as is necessary to produce the desired tone; for it does not matter whether it is beaten or whether it beats, just as it does not matter at all whether the Earth or the Sun moves to create the day.

It is true that bellows make organ pipes rise to the Octave and the Twelfth, but I reserve this difficulty for the book on Organs. It is not

### PROPOSITION XVI.

*To explain why the Trumpet and other wind instruments do not always produce the intervals we have spoken of, and why they often produce the semitone or the tone instead of the Octave, the Fifth, or the Twelfth, etc.*

**EXPERIENCE** sometimes shows that the Trumpet rises or falls by a tone from its second sound. This similarly happens to several **Organ** pipes, some of which only rise by a semitone or a tone, beyond which no amount of wind can make them pass; others rise to the Octave or beyond when the wind is forced. This also happens to some **Flutes** and to **Flageolets**, which, with a very soft wind, rise tone by tone up to the **Fifth** before taking their natural tone, as I have experienced; but these sounds are so weak and so poorly defined that it is difficult to judge them.

Now, the principal difficulty consists in knowing how the Trumpet and other instruments change the number of <term>beats</term> <note>The author uses "beats" (battemens) to describe what we now call frequency or vibrations per second.</note> of their first or second sound, etc.—that is to say, 1, 2, or 3 beats into 16 beats when they produce the major semitone, or into nine beats when they rise by a major tone. For it seems necessary to suppose that the first and second sounds are composed of fifteen or eight beats, so that the addition of a single beat creates the interval of a semitone or a tone; this is not possible, since one or two beats cannot be changed into fifteen or eight beats. 

But if one remembers what I have demonstrated in other books—namely, that the second sound of the Trumpet and all others of the same pitch are made by very rapid beats, and that the wind strikes the hole of the <term>mouthpiece</term> <note>Original: "bocal." In this context, it refers to the cup-shaped mouthpiece of the trumpet.</note> at least forty times in the space of one second when it produces the second sound—it is easy to understand how the same sound can be supposed to have eight, nine, ten, fifteen, or more beats when compared to the beats of another sound. This is because forty contains eight, nine, ten, and fifteen times, etc. For if the third sound, for example, is made of forty-five beats in a time equal to that in which the preceding forty were made, there is no doubt that it will form a major tone with the second sound. For I have already said that each beat must be complete to vary the pitch.

Now, to understand this solution, one must take the ratio of the <term>beats</term> <note>In this context, "beats" refers to the frequency of vibrations or pulses of air that determine pitch.</note> in their <term>radical terms</term> <note>The simplest integer ratio used to define a musical interval; for a major tone, this is 9:8.</note>, in order to see if, the first sound being composed of a single beat, one can find another number that creates a tone with it, or if it is entirely necessary that the first sound be composed of eight beats to make the said tone with the second sound. To this I respond that the first sound cannot produce a **major tone** with the second until the wind has struck the <term>mouthpiece</term> <note>original: "bocal"</note> eight times in the first sound, and nine times in the second; and consequently, it may happen that one hears the **Octave** before the tone. For if one takes three Trumpets, or three strings of different lengths—for example, let the first be one foot, the second two, the third eight, and the fourth nine feet—if they are all sounded at the same time, one will hear the Octave before the tone. This is because the Trumpet or string of one foot in length will have struck the air twice, and that of two feet will have struck it once, much sooner than the one of eight feet will have struck it nine times, or the one of nine feet eight times. For the one-foot string strikes it eight times in the same duration that the eight-foot string strikes it only once, and the nine-foot string will not yet have finished its first beat; and consequently, the first two strings will have already produced the Octave four times when the last two have produced the tone only once, since the second string of two feet will have united its four beats four times with the eight of the one-foot string in the same time that the nine-foot string begins to unite its eight beats with the nine of the eight-foot string.

From this, one can also derive reasons to explain why the Trumpet and other instruments produce the Octave as their first interval, and why they seem to have more difficulty, or less inclination, to produce the tone or the semitone, which they do not produce as clearly or as constantly as the Octave. Now, they produce these degrees instead of the said Octave when one does not push the wind strongly enough, though it is difficult to know why they do not produce **Thirds**, the **Fourth**, and the **Fifth** just as well as the tone and the semitone before passing to the Octave. Those who have more leisure or wit than I may find the reason for this in the movements of the wind being pushed, and in the internal shape and construction of the instrument, which are the causes of several particular sounds and several intervals perceived in some instruments though they are not in others.

It is enough to have noted this without it being necessary to detail a thousand small circumstances encountered in the sounds and intervals of each instrument, the reasons for which could not be explained without writing an entire book. This should be reserved for those who have spent their whole lives considering and practicing these instruments; for I do not wish to remain so long speaking of the Trumpet that I forget the others. Therefore, I come to the explanation of its **Diapason** <note>The "Diapason" here refers to the full range or compass of the instrument's natural scale.</note> and its usage.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

*To explain the **Scale** <note>original: "Diapason"</note> of **Trumpets**, that is to say, the different sizes they must have to perform the four parts of Music, & all sorts of Concerts: & the shape & use of the **Mute** <note>original: "Sourdine"</note>.*

There is no doubt that Trumpets descend lower in pitch the longer or wider they are made, and that the ratio of their sounds must follow that of their lengths—provided that no accident occurs to hinder this mutual proportion, which is found in all kinds of instruments. For example, the second sound of a four-foot Trumpet will rise one **Octave** higher than the second sound of an eight-foot one, and all other sounds will rise or fall in the same proportion as the Trumpets are shorter or longer, provided that the wind is blown and distributed proportionally.

From which I conclude that seven different Trumpets are needed to produce the seven sounds that fill the first interval of the Octave, since each Trumpet played in the same manner will produce only one sound. And because the second will be shorter by an eighth part than the first, the third shorter by a ninth part than the second, the fourth shorter by a fifteenth part than the third, and so on for the others up to the seventh, one will produce all the degrees of the Octave: **C, D, E, F, etc.** <note>original: "vt, re, mi, fa, &c."</note> insofar as they will rise tone by tone by conjunct degrees, so that one can sing all sorts of pieces of Music in four parts, both low and high. 

But because it is difficult for several players to tune so perfectly that they can sound their Trumpets while keeping time and with the same force, it would be more expedient to make holes in their branches <note>The "branches" refer to the tubing of the instrument.</note> as is done with the **Serpent** <note>A bass wind instrument shaped like a snake, made of wood and leather.</note>, of which we will speak later; or to adapt them to a keyboard to sound several together, as is done on **Organs**. However, it seems that the wind from bellows is not capable of sounding Trumpets, because it cannot supply the different pressures and movements made by the lips in the **mouthpiece** <note>original: "bocal"</note>, nor the different strikes of the tongue used to give it life. One can also give the Trumpet the form of the **Sackbut** <note>original: "Saquebutte"; the ancestor of the modern trombone, featuring a slide to change pitch.</note>, but I leave those experiments to those who are maintained to please Princes in this exercise, which they can perfect, in order to explain the shape and property of the **Mute**, which is ordinarily made of a piece of wood that is placed in the **bell** <note>original: "pauillon"</note> of the Trumpet, so that it blocks it enough to diminish and dull its sounds.

α, β, γ, δ, ε <note>Greek letters alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, likely referring to a diagram of the mute.</note> show the side that one pushes inside, and ζ <note>zeta</note> signifies the other end, by which one holds it while pushing it into the said bell: although one can use other inventions to diminish and prevent the violence and brilliance of the Trumpet by blocking part of its opening. Now, one uses this Mute when one does not want the Trumpet to be heard from the place where the enemies are, as happens at city sieges, and when one wishes to **break camp** <note>original: "deſloger"</note>. But it is difficult to know by how much the Mute diminishes the sound, for one can only say that it is that much weaker...

...that it is heard from less far away, since one measures the magnitude of the cause by that of its effects, particularly when they are of the same nature as their cause. Now it must be noted that this Mute <note>original: "Sourdine"</note> is pierced all the way through from its mouth α <note>alpha</note> to its foot ζ, η <note>zeta, eta</note>; and that the edges β, γ <note>beta, gamma</note> down to δ, ε <note>delta, epsilon</note> are made very thin and slender, so that they yield a little when they are pushed into the foot of the bell <note>original: "pauillon"</note>. For if it were not hollow and pierced, and if it did not entirely plug the bell, the Trumpet would not be able to sound, because the wind could not escape; so that it serves only to narrow the opening of the bell, and to stifle the sound by means of the neck δ, ε, ζ, η; for one experiences in all kinds of instruments that they ring out <note>original: "esclattent"</note> more in proportion to how much their bells are more 
<margin>2</margin>
open, particularly when this opening begins much higher than the foot of the instrument, as happens with Trumpets, whose opening increases from the last knot until the end; and that they produce sounds that are softer and weaker the more they are narrowed, as one experiences in the different ranks of Organs, where the stopped pipes <note>original: "bouchez"</note> are the softest. From this one can conclude that it is easy to soften the sounds of the Trumpet without using the Mute; although there is no need to change their openings, since those who know how to play to perfection weaken the sound as much as they wish by the mere moderation of the breath; which they dispense with such variety that they imitate the softest Echo, and take away the envy and desire to hear the sweetness of the Lute and other instruments from those who love harmony.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

->*To explain the manner of sounding the Trumpet, and the use it has in War, and elsewhere.*<-

**W**hen one wants to learn to play the Trumpet, it is enough to take the mouthpiece <note>original: "bocal"</note> to get used to making the tones, and to forming the embouchure, insofar as it makes the same intervals as the Trumpet, which serves only to change the qualities of the tones made by the said mouthpiece, and to reinforce them and make them more pleasing and more brilliant: so that everything depends on the embouchure of the mouthpiece: which happens similarly with the mouthpieces <note>original: "bouquins"</note> of Cornets and Serpents. But there are no other precepts for learning to play it than the imitation of those who already know the art, for one must only place the mouthpiece to the mouth in all sorts of ways, sometimes to the side, and then in the middle of the mouth, and press the lips while pushing the wind until one has made the tone that is desired.

Now this instrument is inconvenient in that one is forced to put the edge of the lips into the mouthpiece, which causes them to swell and causes pain: one must also push the tip of the tongue against the edge of the lips, in order to hammer the sounds <note>original: "marteler les sons," referring to sharp articulation</note> and to animate them by the movement of the said tongue, whose different strokes have great effects on the minds of the listeners.

As for the use of Trumpets, they serve in times of peace and war for all sorts of rejoicings and public solemnities, as one...

I shall explain these after noting that there is no doubt that the Trumpets of Moses produced the same intervals as ours. From this, it is easy to conclude how the Priests summoned the people, how they called the Princes, how they celebrated their solemnities, and how they prepared the hearts and minds of the soldiers to go to war, to go to the assault, and to give battle.

Because we find through experience that the fourth tone is the place where man has the most strength, and that it is most suited to animate, I do not doubt at all that they used it just as we do now. Now, the Priests of the ancient Law were charged with sounding the trumpet each time it was necessary to break camp, which was arranged such that the Ark was in the center, and then the Levites stood around the said Ark. Afterwards, the Tribe of Judah was camped to the East <note>original: "Orient"</note>, and had under it the Tribe of Issachar and that of Zebulun. Reuben, with the Tribe of Simeon and Gad, were to the South <note>original: "Midy"</note>, Ephraim to the West <note>original: "Occident"</note>, and Dan to the North <note>original: "Septentrion"</note>. Thus, the first sound of the Trumpet, which was similar to our *Boot and Saddle* <note>original: "Boute-selle," a cavalry signal to prepare the horses</note> and its departure call, made the Tribe of Judah set out. Those who were to the South set out at the second sound, and those of the West and the North set out at the third and fourth sounds, which no doubt lasted long enough to be heard by the whole army—just as occurs now when the *Boot and Saddle* is sounded for the space of a quarter of an hour, or thereabouts, in order to alert all the men-at-arms.

I leave aside the other uses for which God destined the Trumpets, as they are explained clearly enough in the 10th Chapter of Numbers. In that chapter, one must note that the "simple sound" and the "cut" or "diminished" sound mentioned in the seventh Verse can be understood in several ways. For the simple sound consists of striking the same tone several times, as when one sings several white notes <note>likely referring to minims or half-notes</note> on the same line—for example, the F of *F-ut-fa* <note>a term from the Guidonian system of solmization referring to the pitch F</note>. The second manner is practiced like our first and second "Mount" signals <note>original: "à cheual"</note>; for even though the first two notes are diminished <note>shortened in duration</note>, one produces only one same tone, which is why one can call this sound simple, diminished, or cut. But when, in making this diminution, one changes the tone—as happens in the *Boot and Saddle* and the *Charge*—the sound is cut or divided in two ways. Finally, when one makes a pause or a rest between two sounds, as happens at the fourth call of the *Boot and Saddle*, one can say that the sound is divided. This suffices to explain the said Verse in accordance with the practice of war.

As for the notation <note>original: "tablature"</note> of the Trumpet, it is not distinct from that of Music, which is done by notes, though one could make a specific one, like that of the *Musette* <note>a small French bagpipe</note>, which can be used without notes. But it must first be noted that the sounds of both the Trumpet and other instruments have two very significant aspects: namely, their different degrees of low <note>original: "graue"</note> and high <note>original: "aigu"</note>, and those of their strength and vigor. As for the first, they are all marked above the Trumpet that follows, and on its banner. The others have not yet been marked, although one could use the first eight numbers to divide them into eight different de—

# Book Five

One must also consider the timing of each sound, so as to use every kind of movement with the Trumpet, just as one does on the Drum and other instruments. Now, the principal movements, which seem to have the most power over the spirit of soldiers, consist of these metrical feet <note>The symbols 'u' and '-' represent short and long durations in classical poetic meter, here applied to musical rhythm.</note> u ——— u, u u u - u, u u u u u u u - u, and several others like them, each of which lasts one second, which is to say one heartbeat, or thereabouts. They are distinguished on a single tone by their different strengths or speeds; and when they are on different tones, they almost always meet on the third and fourth tones, which form the interval of a Fourth, namely FA, UT <note>UT is the historical name for the note C; the interval between C and F is a perfect fourth.</note>.

But before explaining the foundations of this tablature <note>A form of musical notation indicating instrument fingering or specific signals rather than just pitches.</note>, it must be noted that only six or seven types of tones are used in war; the first is called the *Canalquet* <note>original: "Canalquet," a ceremonial signal used when entering a town</note>, which is used when the army, or one of the regiments, approaches towns through which they pass on the way to sieges or places of battle, in order to alert the inhabitants and make them participants in the joy and hope of achieving victory. The second is called the *Boot and Saddle* <note>original: "Boute-selle"</note>, which is used when one wishes to decamp; and then follows the *Rising of the Boot and Saddle*. Thirdly, they sound *To Horse* <note>original: "A cheval"</note>, and then *To the Standard* <note>original: "à l'estendart"</note>, and *The Charge*. They also sound *The Watch* <note>original: "le Guet"</note>; but all these manners of sounding are most often distinguished only by the measure of time, for they almost always use the Fourth, as is seen in the Proposition that follows.

Now, it would be useless to include here all the types of different measures and movements that can be used in sounding the Trumpet, since I have already provided the science of it in the discourse on the times and measures of Music, and because it is capable of as many different movements as the voice, since it is by means of the voice that one sounds it; for the mouth uses the same breath to sound it as that which forms words. Thus, one can make the Trumpet say everything one wishes, lacking nothing but the articulation and pronunciation of syllables and words. From this, it follows that two or more Trumpeters can easily understand each other from a quarter of a league away, and carry out several discourses that can take the place of speech: although they have nothing unique in this regard, except that they are heard from further away than other instruments, which can similarly be used to hold such discourses as one wishes, as I have said elsewhere.

## PROPOSITION XIX.

### *To explain the tablature and the Trumpet songs used in the military.*

ALTHOUGH musical notes serve as a universal tablature for all sorts of instruments, and although they seem more suited for this subject than any other characters, I nevertheless wish to explain another sort here, so as to use it to mark all the ways of sounding the Trumpet. I suppose, first, that only six tones of the Trumpet are used in the military art, and consequently that one only needs six characters for its tablature, even though one could add six or seven others to mark the other higher tones from which songs are composed.

### On Wind Instruments

Now, of all the characters that one can imagine, I find none more suitable than those of Arithmetic—that is to say, numbers—where the first shall signify the first tone, namely the *ut* of *C sol ut fa* <note>original: "C sol vt fa"; this refers to the note C in the Guidonian hexachord system</note>, which is a <term>Fifth</term> away from the second tone; for the second tone makes the *sol* of *G re sol* <note>The note G</note>. The third tone makes the *fa* <note>In this context, Mersenne is using "fa" to mean the fourth note of the scale relative to G, which is C</note> of *C sol ut fa*, and is an <term>Octave</term> from the first, and consequently a <term>Fourth</term> from the second. The fourth tone makes the *mi* of *E mi la* <note>The note E</note>, and forms a <term>Major Third</term> with the third, a <term>Major Sixth</term> with the second, and a <term>Major Tenth</term> with the first. The fifth tone forms a <term>Minor Third</term> with the fourth, a <term>Fifth</term> with the third, an <term>Octave</term> with the second, and a <term>Twelfth</term> with the first. And finally, the sixth tone forms a <term>Fourth</term> with the fifth, a <term>Minor Sixth</term> with the fourth, an <term>Octave</term> with the third, a <term>Twelfth</term> with the second, and a <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>Two octaves</note> with the first. Thus, the military range of the Trumpet contains the "Great System of the Greeks" <note>A reference to the *Systema Teleion*, the standard multi-octave scale used in ancient Greek music theory</note> and the range of the most excellent voices, as seen in the

I have written the names from the <term>harmonic hand</term> <note>The "Guidonian Hand," a mnemonic device used by medieval and Renaissance musicians to navigate the hexachord system</note> between them, so that everyone may understand the distance from one tone of the Trumpet to another.

This being established, it is very easy to understand that one must repeat each tone as many times as its number is repeated in the <term>tablature</term>. For example, if one repeats the third tone twenty-eight times, as is done when sounding the signal *to horse* <note>original: "à cheval"</note>, one must write the number **three** **28** times, which also serves for the *Cavalquet* <note>original: "Canalquet," a ceremonial signal for entering a town</note>. And if one rises to the fourth tone, one must write **four** as many times as the fourth tone is played, and so on for the others.

But because the greatest part of the grace and pleasure of these Trumpet sounds comes from the timing and the different movements it makes, one must also suppose three kinds of values, or times and measures, within the said numbers that signify the tones. The numbers alone will mark the shortest time, namely the <term>eighth note</term> <note>original: "crochuë"</note>, because it is used more often than the others. The second time, double the preceding one—which corresponds to the <term>quarter note</term> <note>original: "note noire"</note>—shall be marked by a small point similar to an acute accent: for example, if the fourth tone must last a quarter note, it will be written thus, 4' , or with the character used to signify short syllables in this fashion, 4̆ . The third time will be marked with two acute accents placed over the number of the tone, for example on the third tone, as seen here 3'' , or else with a straight line, with which one marks syllables that are long, in this manner 3̄ , etc. This had to be noted so that one may understand the intonations and the movements, or timings, of the Trumpet, and so that one may imitate its sounds with the voice.

Now, since this tablature is so easy, and since songs of joy are sometimes added to the ordinary cries of the Trumpet which rise higher than the six preceding tones—for example, higher by a tone, a Third, etc.—one can also add 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 for the six tones above...

As soon as one has sung or recited one of the trumpet calls, they will know all the others. It is only necessary to note that the commas I have placed after a certain quantity of numbers distinguish the feet, or the movements of this instrument. Furthermore, the dots following the quarter notes in the *Double Cavalquet*, in the *Watch*, in the *Second Charge*, and at the end of *To Horse*, are worth half of the preceding note—that is to say, half of a quarter note, or an eighth note. I leave aside several other things that could be noted regarding the composition of songs for the trumpet, because it is enough to know that one can play all those comprised within the <term>Hexachord</term> <note>original: *Exachorde*; the six-note scale used in medieval and Renaissance music theory.</note>, which is to say the six notes of Music. This is possible because the trumpet can produce all these degrees with all sorts of <term>hammerings</term> <note>original: *martelemens*; a type of rapid ornamental repetition or trill.</note> and <term>diminutions</term> <note>the practice of dividing long notes into many shorter, faster notes.</note>, not to mention the six preceding tones, which can be varied in 720 different ways, as we concluded in the demonstration in the *Book of Songs*.

It must also be noted, before finishing this treatise on the trumpet, that it is customary to explain its sounds by the word *Tarare*, *Tararararare*, etc. This is because the sounds have a certain roughness, which seems better represented by the "canine letter" *r* <note>The letter 'r' was historically called the "canine letter" because its trilled sound resembles a dog's growl.</note> than by any other. This is why we imitate each of its sounds with one of the syllables of this word, repeating the *ra* as many times as the movement, or the <term>rhythmic foot</term>, has sounds. We always begin the first syllable *ta* on the first sound of each foot and end with the last syllable *re* on the final sound.

Now, it is just as easy to use simple numbers for the longest notes—that is, for half notes with or without a stem—as it is for eighth or sixteenth notes. Similarly, one may use numbers marked with one, two, three, or more accents for the brief durations (quarter notes, eighth notes, sixteenth notes, etc.) rather than simple numbers, since it all depends entirely on the player's will. It remains now to show the second figure of the trumpet that I promised, which contains the greatest range of sounds I have been able to test. However, I do not wish to determine whether it is beyond human power to make it go higher or lower. Indeed, some players are found who are so far beyond the reach of others that one cannot believe what they do, or what is said of their skill, unless it is experienced firsthand. This often happens with musical instruments: sometimes the material, construction, and shape contribute something extraordinary, as we see with certain instruments that reach much higher than others despite being of the same size and shape, or which produce a better harmony or different intervals, even though no sense can detect a difference between them and other instruments of the same kind. At other times, this comes from the particular skill of the performers, which I discuss in the specific sections for each instrument; so that...

Now, the first note **UT** <note>The syllable for the note C.</note> marked by **1** signifies the first tone, or the hollowest and deepest of all those that serve for war or for songs: which is also signified by the fifth note at the bottom, which has **11** above it, so that one has here the same range of the Trumpet under the <term>flat clef</term> <note>original: *clef de b mol*; often referring to the F clef or the soft hexachord starting on F.</note>, or of <term>F ut</term> <note>The note F.</note>, to show that its melodies can be related to the first Mode which begins on C, or to the seventh which begins on F.

The second tone of the Trumpet is marked by the second note, and the others by those that follow up to the **13th**, which is the thirteenth tone, or the highest to which it can climb. But the numbers across from the notes at the bottom signify the harmonic intervals through which it passes; for example, the number **11** shows that it descends lower than this tone by an Eleventh, that is to say, by the octave of the Fourth: although one takes this note for the first tone, because the four lower notes marked **9, 4, 2, 1** are not good tones and are worth nothing for singing. It must nevertheless be noted that all those who know how to play this instrument ordinarily descend all at once from this note marked **11** to the note marked **4**, which makes the Octave below; and I have encountered only one who played the three other notes marked **9, 2, and 1**. Be that as it may, it has the range of a Thirty-second, marked on the **17th** or last note—that is to say, it rises to a Fourth above four Octaves. But when one begins at its first military tone of the upper range, it rises only to the Twenty-second, that is to say, up to three Octaves.
