### PROPOSITION XXI.

->Explaining the shape, material, range, and use of the Sackbut, or Harmonic Trumpet.<-

This Trumpet, which is ordinarily called a <term>Sackbut</term> <note>original: "Sacquebute"; the Renaissance and Baroque ancestor of the modern trombone.</note>, is a little different from the military Trumpet, both in its shape and its size, and in its other circumstances. Now, it has first its mouthpiece, or its <term>bocal</term> A, as well as the opening of its bell <note>original: "pavillon"</note> N, similar to that of the other Trumpet: but all its branches are detachable, for the first branch B F, the second F D, and the <term>Tortil</term> <note>A "crook" or coiled piece of tubing used to change the instrument's pitch.</note> G H can be taken apart at their joints F G and H, as can the mouthpiece A, which fits into the branch at point B. Similarly, the three bands C, E, and M are easily disassembled, so that the craftsmen may make them more easily, and so that they might be more portable. But one must principally notice two things in this instrument: namely, that the Crook <note>original: "Tortil"</note> is rarely used, which begins at joint L and ends at joint G; so that the part of the branch N C, that is to say the bell, is usually fitted at joint G, in order to return the Sackbut to its natural pitch. Now, experience teaches that when the Crook is added, it makes the Sackbut descend by a Fourth lower than its natural pitch, in order to play the Bass in concerts made with <term>Oboes</term> <note>original: "Haut-bois"; at this time, these would likely be shawms or early baroque oboes.</note>.

The other thing to be noted concerns the two branches D F, which contain two other interior ones that do not appear except when they are pulled out by means of the bar E, which one pushes down with the hand to make all sorts of tones, because they are pulled out until

...be pleased to explain how the tones are produced by means of the different extensions of this **Sackbut**, provided one understands what I have said of the intervals produced by the **Trumpet** through the different [force of] wind that is given to it.

One therefore easily produces the **Octave**, the **Twelfth**, and the **Fifteenth** <note>These represent the natural harmonic series: the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th harmonics</note> with this instrument without using the slides; which is easy to understand from the sounds of the Trumpet, which it imitates in this regard. But one produces the eight sounds of the **Octave** starting with *sol* <note>The note G</note>, which one intones by placing the two hands one against the other, namely the left on the bar CD, and the right on E. And to play *fa* <note>The note F</note>, one lowers the branches DE, and consequently the right hand, by four fingers' breadth: which is done similarly to sound the other degrees of the Octave, of which the last or lowest tone is made by retracting the branches until the two hands touch, just as they did at the start of the Octave, because the beginnings and ends of all the Octaves are made without the aid of the slides, by the variety of the wind <note>the player's breath and lip tension</note> alone. But one must note that one should hardly touch the mouthpiece <term>bocal</term> <note>The small cup-shaped piece where the player places their lips; in modern terms, the mouthpiece</note> when one wishes to descend very low, and that one must press it as hard as possible against the lips to increase the wind [pressure] when one wishes to rise to the highest tones: a point to be noted for all kinds of instruments with a mouthpiece.

Now, to produce the second Octave while ascending, and to reach as far as the **Fifteenth** <note>A range of two full octaves</note>, one must keep the Sackbut entirely closed to produce the first tone, which will be *UT* <note>The note C</note>, and to produce *RE* <note>D</note>, one must lower the branches by the length of an arm, or thereabouts; but they must be retracted a little to produce *MI* <note>E</note>, and a little more to produce *FA* <note>F</note>. But to produce *SOL* <note>G</note>, one must retract the branches as in the first tone, and then one must lengthen them by half an arm to produce *RE* <note>The high D</note>, and to produce *MI* <note>The high E</note>, which is the penultimate tone of the Fifteenth, one must retract the branches very close to the left hand; and finally to complete the Fifteenth, one must close the Sackbut, with which one descends just as one ascends, throughout the entire extent of the said Fifteenth.

Those who use this instrument can easily experiment to see if it rises as high as the Trumpet, which is why I determine nothing certain on that; I only add that those who use it well can perform <term>diminutions</term> <note>Virtuosic decorative passages where long notes are broken into many fast, shorter notes</note> of sixteen notes to the measure; which occurs similarly on the Trumpet and all other wind instruments. But if one does not use a different manner of <term>embouchure</term> <note>The position and use of the lips, tongue, and teeth in playing a wind instrument</note> for the Sackbut than for the Trumpet, it imitates the sounds of the said Trumpet, which is considered faulty and inept for **Consorts** <note>Ensembles of instruments; the sackbut was valued for its ability to blend with voices and other instruments, unlike the more "martial" sounding trumpet</note>. As for the manner of the embouchure, it must be learned through experience, as it is almost impossible to make it understood perfectly through discourse alone, without finding much difficulty in practice: which always happens in the arts consisting of action and movement, and which seem to have practice for their end and their perfection. Nevertheless, I shall explain the different manners of embouchure in the discourse on the **Cornett** <term>Cornet à bouquin</term> <note>A curved wooden instrument with finger holes and a small mouthpiece, very popular in the 17th century</note>, so that nothing may be found wanting in this treatise.

## PROPOSITION XXII.

### *To explain the form of the Cornett <term>Cornet à bouquin</term>, its material, its construction, its range, and its use.*

I have already said elsewhere that I do not amuse myself by searching for the origin of words <note>original: "dictions"</note>, which is most often unknown or useless, especially since the understanding of instruments does not depend on their names, and it is a matter of indifference whether to name them by the letters of our alphabet or to impose any other name one wishes.

Now, I begin this Proposition with the **Treble Cornett** <term>le Dessus des Cornets</term>, which is represented by **A C** with its seven holes, even though many do not use the seventh, which they judge superfluous and useless, because they give the same range to the Cornett with six holes as others do with seven. The letters **A** and **E** show the **mouthpiece** <term>bouquin</term>, which is demonstrated as one sees in figure **A B**, which represents it separately, and which is used for learning how to form the embouchure <term>emboucher</term> <note>The specific way a player applies their lips to the mouthpiece to produce sound</note>, as I have said in the discourse on the Trumpet.

As for the **Tenor Cornett** <term>la Taille des Cornets</term>, it is entirely similar to the Treble; for it has nothing added but one hole, which descends lower, and which opens by means of the key **a**, which is covered by the box **βy**. This is why I have only included the bottom end of this Tenor,

...third parts, of which the seventh opens with the key **d**, which is covered by its box, etc. But this figure is not proportioned to the others, for it represents a **Bass** <term>Basse</term> four feet long, with a range of an Octave or a Ninth, whereas the **Treble** <term>Dessus</term> is only one foot in length. I provide the very exact measurements here because it is well-made and more commonly used than the other parts, specifically because it is used in vocal concerts and with the Organ to play the Treble part, which is ravishing when one knows how to play it to perfection, like the Sieur Quiclet <note>A renowned cornett player of the period often cited by Mersenne</note>.

I say, then, first that its range is a Sixteenth <note>A range of two octaves</note>, as one sees by the notes below, from which it is easy to conclude all that can be done with this instrument. Secondly, that there are only three inches from **C** <note>the bell/bottom</note> to the middle of the sixth hole, and ten inches from **A** <note>the mouthpiece end</note> to the middle of the first hole. Thirdly, that the distances between the holes are thirteen lines <note>A "line" is a historical measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch</note>, except for the distance from the 3rd to the 4th hole, which is seventeen lines. The diameter of each hole is four lines, and that of the bottom of the mouthpiece <term>bouquin</term> is only one line; this is partly why the sound of the Cornett is so brilliant <term>éclatant</term>, for its bore constantly widens little by little until the bell **C**, whose diameter is one inch—though it widens more noticeably from the mouthpiece to the first hole than from there to the bell. But it must be noted that the Spanish <note>original: "Espagnols"</note> also put a hole in the back, thirteen lines higher than the first hole; and that there are straight Cornetts made of a single piece of wood, whereas those that are curved are made of two pieces of service-wood <term>cormier</term>, plum-wood, or other well-seasoned wood. I wanted to note this so that those who make this instrument observe the proportions I have mentioned as the best of all.

Now, it is customary to cover Cornetts with leather <note>usually black thin leather or parchment</note> in order to preserve them longer, otherwise they would spoil too easily due to their delicacy; though this covering does not make them sound better. As for the quality of the sound it produces, it is similar to the brilliance of a sunbeam appearing in the shadow or in the darkness, when it is heard among the voices in Cathedral churches or in Chapels.

### PROPOSITION XXIII.

#### To explain other forms of Cornetts, and the manner of playing them to perfection, with an example in five parts.

The Cornett <term>Cornet à bouquin</term> can be blown in three or four ways, of which the first and easiest, which is called *flowing* <term>coulante</term> or *mute* <term>muette</term>, is done simply with the wind, as happens with Organ pipes.

The second is done with the tongue and the lip, and pronounces *Tatarararararara* to descend or to ascend an entire Octave in divisions <term>diminution</term> <note>Rapid melodic passages or ornaments</note>, as one sees in these examples.

The fourth [method of articulation] is done with the lip, but one must give only one lip-stroke for two notes, as seen in this example. This technique can be used with any type of embouchure and serves to show in how many ways one can vary the playing of the **Cornett**. However, it should be noted that the instrument is placed in the right side of the mouth by those who are right-handed, and in the left side by the left-handed, although some are found who play on the right, the left, and in the middle of the mouth quite easily.

->Musical notation illustrating articulation: **Tataa**, **taataa**, **Ta ta**, and **Taa taa**<-

Now, one performs divisions <term>diminutions</term> <note>the practice of breaking long notes into many fast, decorative notes</note> on the **Cornett** to the point of playing thirty-two notes to a measure when playing in perfection. In the past, the cadence <term>Cadence</term> <note>here referring to a trill or ornamental finish</note> was made with "hammerings" <term>martelemens</term>, which are expressed by **Tara tara, tara, ta**, as seen in these two examples.

->Example 1: **Taratara** — Example 2: **tarata**<-

The second type of cadence is made by a trill <term>tremblement</term> of the fingers on eighth notes, and by a "redoubling" <term>redoublement</term> on sixteenth notes. But this trill is performed with the breath alone <note>meaning without a hard tongue strike for every note</note>, so that the cadence is sweeter and more pleasing, imitating the human voice and the most excellent methods of singing. It is for this reason that those who play the **Cornett** perfectly soften its sound as much as they can, as it is naturally a bit harsh. And because this instrument should play music almost entirely in divisions, it is necessary for anyone who wishes to learn to play it to know how to compose and to be a good musician, so that they may perform the flourishes <term>fredons</term> and divisions appropriately. Now, he who has the embouchure of the **Cornett** under his command can ascend two tones higher than the fingering chart <term>tablature</term> I have provided, as is experienced when it is in the hands of **Sieur Quiclet**, who gave me the preceding examples.

One can soften the sound of the **Cornett** so much that it is heard no more than that of a **Flute** <note>likely referring to a recorder or transverse flute</note>. It can be played in all sorts of tones and semitones, provided that one has a good enough ear; and one can begin the scale (*ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*) at every hole. Consequently, the fingering chart only serves to show the range of the instrument and does not oblige one to always call it **UT** (C) when all the holes are closed. This is easy to understand, since any sound can be designated by one of the six notes.

**Cornetts** can be made of ivory, and of a wood called **citron sandalwood** <term>sandal cytrin</term>, which is fragrant, as well as all other sorts of wood, like other wind instruments. But we must now discuss what pertains to the **Serpent**, since it is the true **Bass** of the **Cornetts**.

### PROPOSITION XXIV.

->To explain the figure, the construction, the range, and the use of the Serpent, which normally serves as the Bass in Music.<-

Musicians have invented several instruments to blend with voices, and to supply the defect of those who sing the Bass and the Treble, for singers who have sufficiently deep Bass voices are very rare; this is why one uses the **Bassoon**, the **Sackbut** <term>Sacquebute</term> <note>an early form of the trombone</note>, and the **Serpent**, just as one uses the **Cornett** to supply the Treble parts, which are not usually good. Now this instrument is named the **Serpent** because of its shape, which has folds like the animal bearing that name, so that the length it would have, if it were entirely straight, does not cause inconvenience; for it is at least six feet long, and the one from which this figure was taken is six feet and thirteen lines long, without including the length of the **crook** <term>bocal</term>, which is half a foot long. Now, it can be made of brass, and of all other sorts of metals, although it is usually made of **walnut wood**, which is only half a line thick, or some other wood suitable for this; and then it is covered in leather, like the Cornett, to reinforce it. And because it is customary to hold it and carry it by the first fold, which begins at **A**, it is reinforced beneath the leather with **ox sinews**, for fear that it might break. It is made of two pieces, which are then glued together; and for this purpose one takes a beam, or a very thick plank, which is hollowed out into a half-cylinder, and when the two half-cylinders are made, they are applied one upon the other to make the Serpent. **A** shows the hole of the Serpent, into which the crook **ζ θ** is fitted, which is composed of two parts, namely the crook **α β γ δ**, and its neck, or its tail **θ**. **α β δ** represents the **mouthpiece** **ζ**, whose hole **ε** is smaller than that of the head of the Serpent **A**, in order to compress the air.

Now the Serpent has six holes, by means of which one gives it the range of a **seventeenth**, as seen in the notes on the side. But it must be noted that it is divided into three parts, of which the middle one con-

# Of Wind Instruments.

<margin>fol.</margin>...one produces the Fifth and the Octave without passing through the intermediate steps, and without covering or uncovering the holes, as I have already stated. <note>This refers to "overblowing," a technique where a player uses breath pressure to jump to higher notes in the harmonic series without changing their finger position.</note>

Now, this instrument is capable of sustaining twenty of the strongest voices, yet it is so easy to play that a fifteen-year-old child can sound it as loudly as a thirty-year-old man. And one can so soften its sound that it becomes suitable to join the voices of soft chamber music, imitating their delicacies and <term>diminutions</term><note>Fast, ornamental runs where long notes are "divided" into many shorter, decorative notes.</note>, which it can perform at thirty-two notes to the measure—though these should be avoided in multi-part music, because one must simply sound what is in the part one undertakes to sing. Only the descent of the Octave is permitted, as seen here:

<image-desc>A musical score fragment on a five-line staff with an alto clef (C-clef on the middle line), showing a descending scale of eight notes followed by several musical intervals.</image-desc>

As for the <term>embouchure</term><note>The way a player applies their mouth to the mouthpiece of a wind instrument.</note> of the Serpent, one uses the same technique as for the Trumpets and the Trombones, or the <term>Sackbuts</term><note>The ancestor of the modern trombone, known for its telescopic slide.</note>, which are believed to be older than Serpents.

One produces the same intervals with the <term>bocal</term><note>The curved metal neck or "crook" that connects the mouthpiece to the body of the instrument.</note> $\alpha\beta\gamma$ alone as with the entire Serpent, as happens with other <term>mouthpiece instruments</term><note>original: "instrumens à bouquin." This refers to instruments like the cornetto or serpent that use a small cup-shaped mouthpiece similar to a trumpet.</note>. From this, one can conclude that these tones depend more on the manner in which the air is pushed than on the length of the instrument or the opening of the holes. This must be noted regarding the Serpent if one wishes to find why only a single tone is produced between the 4th and 3rd holes, even though they are much further apart than the others. This similarly occurs in several Flutes, where all the intervals do not follow the distance of the holes, as I shall show in the Proposition that follows, which explains the other characteristics of the Serpent. The piece of horn, silver, ivory, or tin $\theta$, which fits into the Serpent, is called the *Pipe*, at the top of which the bocal $\alpha\beta\delta\gamma$ is also fitted.

### PROPOSITION XXV.

->*Explaining the <term>Diapason</term><note>In this context, the "diapason" refers to the physical proportions and scaling of the instrument's construction.</note> of Serpents, Trumpets, and Sackbuts; that is to say, by how much they must be lengthened or shortened to descend or ascend by a tone, or by any other interval desired; and why the distance from the 4th to the 3rd hole only makes it rise by one tone, even though it is larger than that of the other holes.*<-

It seems that the irregular spacing of the Serpent's holes makes its scaling more difficult than that of other instruments. For even though the second hole is only two inches from the first, and the third from the second, the third is a foot away from the fourth—that is to say, six times further—even though it only produces a whole tone like the others. This is very remarkable, and the reason for it is very difficult to explain. This occurrence does not happen because of the instrument's curve; even if these two holes were measured by a perpendicular line, they would still be half a foot apart, which is still three times further than the others. The same thing would happen on Serpents that were perfectly straight, as can be demonstrated by the distance between the fourth and third holes of the Tenor Oboe <note>original: "Taille des Haut-bois"</note>, which we will discuss later, and by Organ Flutes.

which always make the same sound, whether they are bent and folded in all sorts of ways, or made perfectly straight—just like the finger-holes of the recorders, of which we have already spoken.

Now, it is difficult to give the reason for this phenomenon, unless one draws it from the different management of the wind that the mouth adapts and determines for each sound. In this way, the body of the instrument serves only to multiply and fortify the sounds, even though one does not perceive this "determination" of the wind without the presence of the instrument. This is despite the fact that practitioners assert they push the wind in the same way to play the tone of the fourth hole as they do for the third.

As for the <term>Diapason</term><note>In this context, "diapason" refers to the "scaling" or the precise set of measurements and proportions used to determine the pitch and hole placement of an instrument.</note> of Serpents and all other instruments with a <term>cup-mouthpiece</term><note>original: "bocal". While "bocal" usually refers to the metal crook of a bassoon, here the author uses it to group instruments like the serpent and trumpet that use a cup-shaped mouthpiece.</note>, no one has found it to my knowledge. I have not performed enough experiments to provide it in any way other than the scaling used for Organs, where the length of the pipes follows exactly the <term>harmonic ratios</term><note>Mathematical proportions (like 2:1 for an octave) that govern musical intervals.</note> of each interval. Thus, there is no need for any calculation for the different lengths and measures of Serpents or Trumpets (which can play the four or five different parts of a concert) other than that of the preceding table. In that table, one sees that if the Serpent, which has 80 parts, produces the **D** <gloss>re sol</gloss><note>A reference to the "Guidonian Hand" or hexachord system, identifying the note D by its position in different scales.</note> shown opposite it, one must make it longer by an eighth part—that is to say, 90 parts—to make it descend by one whole tone. The same follows for the others: if one wants it to descend an Octave lower, it must be 160 parts; conversely, it should be only forty parts to rise to the Octave above. If this proportion is not found to be exact, it is necessary to find another through experiment.

Now, if the harmonic ratio corresponds to practice—as I believe it does, just as it does in Organ pipes—it is easy to create whatever Consorts one wishes with Trumpets of different lengths, and to fill the intervals of the longest one. For example, one can fill the first interval of the Fifth (from C to G) with the three notes *re, mi, fa*, if one makes three Trumpets: one shorter than the first by an eighth part, the next shorter than the previous by a tenth part, and finally a third shorter than that one by a sixteenth part, as is easily concluded from the preceding table.

But it should be noted that the makers have three or four dozen cardboard templates cut into semi-circles that gradually increase in size, in order to widen the bore or the channel of the Serpent little by little. The instrument is made of two pieces, like <term>Cornetts</term><note>The "cornetto" or "zink," a woodwind instrument with a trumpet-like mouthpiece, usually made of wood covered in leather.</note>, which are glued together after they have been hollowed out. Furthermore, a single experience in manufacturing the Serpent is enough to instruct the <term>master theorist</term><note>original: "Periodicien". This likely refers to a specialist in proportions or cycles.</note>, who will afterwards provide the true scaling and all the ratios of this instrument.

# Book Five

The **blowpipe** <note>original: "porte-vent"</note> **A C**, which is represented by **B β γ**, is hidden inside the skin, and it has a **valve** <note>original: "soupape"</note> **α**, so that it closes the hole through which the wind has passed, for fear that it might escape and be lost while the player takes a breath; for the air must only exit through the aforementioned **pipes** <note>original: "Chalumeaux"</note>. The largest of these, which is called the **great drone** <note>original: "grand bourdon"</note>, is composed of three pieces that fit into one another: namely **P O**, **O N**, and **N L**. Attached to this is the part **L M**, which holds the **reed** <note>original: "anche"</note> **μ χ**. This reed is made of a piece of cane, as I have already said. This must be considered carefully here, because it contributes more to the sound than the other parts; for the sounds are made by the beating of its **tongue** <note>original: "languette"</note> **λ**, which serves as its cover, such that the number of its beats determines the low or high pitch of the sound, as I shall prove in the book on **Organs**.

However, one can make this great drone all of one piece; they are usually made of several pieces only so that they can be carried more conveniently when disassembled, and so that they are not so difficult to bore. This is why it breaks at its joints **O** and **N**, where the parts fit into one another by means of sockets. In place of metal fittings, one uses hemp or thread that is twisted around the parts that fit together, so that they fill the cavities of the drone so completely that the wind cannot escape except through its foot **P**. The **small drone** <note>original: "petit bourdon"</note> **H K** also breaks at **I**, and fits into the concave wooden block **D**, which also receives the **chanter** <note>original: "Chalumeau"</note> **E F G**. And because one cannot see the end of the small drone that enters into **D**, I have represented it outside the bag in figure **H ι θ**, just as I have shown the end of the chanter **E F G** in figure **E ζ δ**. From this, one sees that this instrument is composed of three reeds, for which the blocks **M**, **C**, and **D** serve as cases; for they extend as far into the skin as the said reeds, in order to keep them whole and protected. Now, the skin is sewn from underneath, and is tied over the blocks **M**, **C**, and **D** so tightly that no wind can be lost.

As for the manner in which one plays this instrument, it is quite particular: for one places the great drone upon the left shoulder while inflating the skin with the breath from the mouth, blowing through the hole **A** of the blowpipe **B A**. However, one can be relieved of this labor, as is done now when playing the **Royal Bagpipe** <note>original: "Cornemuse Royale"</note> and the **Musette**, as I shall show when speaking of those instruments, especially since the swelling of the cheeks causes a deformity of the face.

Now, as soon as the skin is inflated, it is placed under the left arm, which presses it to force the wind out through **P**, **K**, and **F G**. Then, one plays the holes of the chanter **E G**, closing and opening them to make all sorts of sounds, which is done with the fingers of both hands, so that the person playing this instrument is entirely occupied. As for the size of the **Shawm** <note>original: "Chalemie"</note> upon which this figure was based, the great drone is two and a half feet long, including the reed **μ χ**, which is two and a half inches long. The slit, and consequently the tongue **λ**, is two inches long and four lines <note>A "line" is an old measurement, about 1/12th of an inch.</note> wide. The small drone is one foot long, including the reed **η**, which is two inches long.

The blowpipe is six inches long, not including **B β**, which holds the valve, though one can make it whatever length one wishes. The chanter is thirteen inches long, of which the reed **δ ζ** with the block **E** that keeps it enclosed is two and a half inches. Its eight holes are all visible, except the first,

The first [hole], because it is at the back opposite **E**, which is three inches and <note>symbol</note> away from the top of the **reed** <note>original: "anche"</note> <note>symbol</note>. But there is only <note>symbol</note> of an inch from this first hole to the second; from the second to the third, and from the third to the fourth, there are ten **lines** <note>A "line" is a historical measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch</note>, and the others are separated by an inch, and are nearly all of the same size. ## PROPOSITION XXVII.

->*Explain the tuning, the range, and the tablature of the bagpipe, along with everything*<-
->*concerning its use.*<-

The **great drone** <note>original: "gros Bourdon"</note> of this **bagpipe** <note>original: "Cornemuſe"</note> sounds an octave below the **small drone**, which is similarly an octave below the **chanter** <note>original: "Chalumeau"</note> when all its holes are closed, and a **fifteenth** <note>two octaves</note> below when they are open. Thus, it has a range of three octaves, as can be seen in the notes marked beside the preceding figure, which serve as its **tablature** <note>a system of notation showing finger positions</note>; for the first note at the bottom represents the sound of the great drone, the second that of the small drone, and the nine others signify those of the chanter, which are produced by means of its holes. Now, one plays this chanter in two ways: namely, by simply blowing through the hole **A**, or through the reed <note>symbol</note> when the chanter is pulled out of the skin, and by "speaking"—that is to say, by moving the tongue as if one were speaking at the same time as pushing the wind while covering the said reed, as I shall describe more fully in the treatise on the **Musette** <note>a small, bellows-blown bagpipe popular in French courtly circles</note>. This makes the sound of this instrument much more agreeable, more "fluttered" <note>original: "fueillé," likely referring to a rapid tonguing or ornamentation</note>, and more vigorous.

One can ascend even a third higher than the **twenty-second** <note>three octaves</note> by increasing the wind pressure, which is why I have marked it with the notes. But since shepherds do not lack reason or spirit, and since some are found capable enough to understand the ratios of the **intervals** <note>the distance between two pitches</note> they use when sounding their bagpipe, their **flageolet** <note>a small flute</note>, and other instruments familiar to them, I include here the **harmonic table** of this range to assist them. For they deserve that one works for them, since they had the honor of being the first notified of the **Nativity** of the Son of God by the music of the Angels.

Now, one can mark the first tone of the great drone as **C-sol-ut-fa** <note>Middle C in the hexachord system</note>, as I have done in the notes, instead of **G-re-sol** <note>the G below middle C</note>, which I use in this tablature; this is of no consequence, since I have demonstrated in the discourses on the three genres of music that one can sing all kinds of pieces...

It is easy to mark this range by B-flat <note>original: "b mol"</note> by placing the semitone between A <note>A mi la re</note> and B-flat <note>B fa</note>, instead of the whole tone that is between A <note>A mi</note> and B-natural <note>♮ mi</note>. However, one must simultaneously use the number 66 for B-flat, instead of 64, if one wishes to make a perfect **minor Third** <term>A "just" or "pure" minor third is a frequency ratio of 6:5, common in older tuning systems before modern equal temperament</term> starting from the G <note>G re sol</note> at 80. Furthermore, if there were a major tone from this G to A, as would happen if G were marked at 81, it would be necessary to mark B-flat as 67 1/2, and consequently the first two G's as 162 and 324. Music, by beginning with whichever letter one wishes.

The first G marks the tone of the **great drone** <note>original: "gros bourdon"</note>, the second that of the small one, and the third those of the **chanter** <note>original: "Chalumeau"</note>, which are played one after the other by opening the holes up to the final A <note>A mi la re</note>, which sounds "open"—that is to say, when all holes are uncovered. For one can say that wind instruments sound "open" <note>original: "à vuide"</note> when one does not touch the holes at all, just as one says a string is sounded "open" when one does not touch the neck, even though wind instruments produce their highest sounds this way, and strings produce their lowest. This is because strings are shortened by the pressure of the fingers on the frets, just as flutes are shortened by the opening of their holes.

And if a shepherd happens to have an ear good enough to perceive that the minor Third is not perfectly "just" from G to B-flat, he can make the G or the B "movable," in order to lower the G by a **comma** <term>A comma is a very small musical interval, the difference between two slightly different tuning calculations for the same note</term>, by which the said Third is diminished, or to raise the B by a comma for the same reason. I provide remedies for this in several ways in the *Book of Organs*, from which one can take everything that might be desired here.

It is therefore easy to conclude that standard musical notes suffice for the **tablature** <note>Tablature is a system of notation that tells the player where to put their fingers rather than which pitch to play</note> of this instrument. One can also use the tablature that serves the **Musette** <note>A smaller, more refined bellows-blown bagpipe</note>, which I will discuss later, or that of the **Flageolet** <note>A small woodwind instrument similar to a recorder</note>.

As for the observations one can make regarding this instrument, they nearly all pertain to the **reeds** <note>original: "anches"</note>, which produce different sounds according to the different openings given to them. For example, the reed of the chanter descends lower by a Third or a Fourth when it is opened further. And when...

If one blows the wind very gently into the said chanter <note>original: "Chalumeau"</note> with the mouth, it descends by an octave lower than its natural tone; and one can even manage the wind so that it will rise through the steps *do, re, mi, fa,* <note>original: "ut, re, mi, fa"</note> etc., as I have experimented, even if one does not use the holes at all. ### PROPOSITION XXVIII.

### *To explain the figure, construction, and parts of the Musette and the Tornebout.*

When one has heard the Musette <term>A sophisticated, bellows-blown bagpipe popular in the French court, known for its soft, sweet tone</term> in the hands of those who play it to perfection, such as Mr. des Touches <note>Philibert Des Touches was a celebrated court musician</note>, one of the King's Oboeists, it must be admitted that it is not inferior to other instruments, and that there is a singular pleasure in hearing it. Now, it has almost all the same parts as the preceding Bagpipe; namely the skin <note>the bag</note> *A B*, which is inflated with the bellows *GF*, which is passed through the right or left arm by means of the attachment marked by *H*. The letter *I* shows the place where the bellows attaches to the skin, which I have also marked with *R* in the bellows *S T V*, which is shown in a larger volume. But the drone <note>original: "bourdon"</note> *K L*, which also enters the skin, is greatly different from that of the Bagpipe, as one sees in the one I have detached and placed in a larger volume, namely *K M*, on which one sees four reeds, which are marked separately, in order to see how they fit into the upper plate *M N O*.

As for the lower plate *I*, it shows the five locations of the concavities of the cylinder, or of the drone *MK*, which one opens and closes with five pieces of wood, ivory, or other material, four of which are seen at the four *L*s, and the other is behind.

These are opened and closed with the thumb of the left hand by means of the small key D, upon which the thumb is placed to uncover the said hole in the bulb.

<image-desc>Three detailed woodcut diagrams of woodwind instrument components. The other Chalumeau A F, which is on the right hand, has its last three holes doubled, as is the 4th; and holes 12, 14, 15, and 16 are closed by means of the keys D, B, and E. Its reed is represented to the side by A B, and the thirteenth hole, which is dotted, indicates that it is on the back. This is similar to the twelfth hole of the first pipe A B E F, which is on the left hand and is double, as can be seen at the two outlets of its foot <note>original: "pate"</note> E F. In this arrangement, reed A produces only the tones of the holes on the left, just as reed B produces those on the right. The thirteenth hole has its own key D, because the fingers cannot reach to close it. This should be noted for all types of keys, as I mentioned in the discussion of the Recorder <note>original: "Fluſte douce"</note>. Now, the casing A B, which is on the right side of this double Chalumeau, serves to cover both reeds, for all Chalumeaux of the Musette must be played "covered." They possess much more grace and vigor when blown by the mouth than when they are attached to the skin bag, because one can articulate their sounds by means of the tongue, as I have remarked when speaking of other instruments; this cannot be done with the wind from the bellows or the bag. I will omit several other ways in which Musette Chalumeaux can be made, because it is enough to show what is currently in use, and because we shall speak of them again in the discussion of the Sourdetine <term>Sourdetine: a "little mute," likely referring to the Neapolitan musette, known for its soft, quiet sound</term>, or Musette of Naples, and because it is easy to imagine an infinite variety of them.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

->*To explain the range, the tablature, and the use of the Musette.*<-

The ordinary **range** <term>Range: "estenduë," the full span of notes from lowest to highest</term> of the **Treble** <term>Treble: "Dessus," the highest-pitched instrument in a family</term> Musette is a tenth, an eleventh, or a twelfth, depending on the number of holes and keys that are placed upon it; the same applies to the **Tenor** <term>Tenor: "Taille," the middle-low voice</term> and the **Alto** <term>Alto: "Haute-contre," the middle-high voice</term>, which have a shape similar to that of the Treble. Now, the notes of the Treble which are sung by **flat** <note>original: "b mol," referring to the hexachord containing B-flat</note> show the range of each part; and the five notes that follow, each of which has its own clef, signify the five different tones of the **Drone** <term>Drone: "Bourdon," the pipes that produce constant background pitches</term>, with which it plays all the parts. For the first note, which has the **F-ut-fa** <note>The F or Bass clef; in this context, the pitch F</note> clef, plays the Bass; the second plays the Tenor, and the third the Alto; and the other two that follow serve to transpose the tone of the Musette to a fourth from **B-fa-mi** <note>The pitch B; "B-fa" is B-flat and "B-mi" is B-natural in the Guidonian system</note>.

From this, it is easy to know which songs can be played with the Musette, which is seen even more clearly in its **tablature** <term>Tablature: a system of notation using numbers or letters to indicate finger positions rather than pitches</term>, which is written by numbers or by notes. Here is the one used by **Le Vacher** <note>Jean Vacher was a famous 17th-century maker of musettes</note>, who makes this instrument and teaches how to play it.

<image-desc>The page contains four lines of musical notation grouped into two pairs. It is marked by **naturals** <note>original: "♯ quarré," literally "square B," used for natural signs</note> and by **flats** <note>original: "♭ mol"</note>, so that one may play every sort of music with the Musette, as with other instruments. ### PROPOSITION XXX.

->*Explaining the form, parts, construction, range, and use of the Sourdeline, or Italian Musette.*<-

EVEN though this Musette is not in use in France, I nevertheless wish to describe and explain it, so that our instrument makers <note>original: "Facteurs," specifically refers to builders of organs or woodwinds</note> may be able to make similar ones. It is held that Jean Baptiste Riva, Dom Iulio, and Vincenze are its inventors. Now, I have fitted the skin bag A B similar to those of our Musettes, instead of a kidskin <note>leather from a young goat</note> which the Italians use, which is long like a cylinder. The bellows M serves to inflate it by means of the leather channel L K I, which serves as a wind-gate <term>Wind-gate: "porte-vent," the tube that carries air from the bellows into the bag</term>: N O is the strap, or fastener, through which one passes the left or right arm, depending on which side the bellows is applied. But before explaining all its pipes <term>Pipes: "Chalumeaux," the various sounding tubes, including melodic chanters and drones</term>,

<image-desc>Detailed woodcut illustration of two types of Italian bagpipes. The primary instrument, the Sourdeline, features a large bag (A, B) connected to a set of bellows (M) by a tube (L, K, I) and has multiple complexly turned wooden pipes (A, F, G, H, C, Q) with various keys and holes. A shoulder strap (N, O) is attached to the bag. A small inset (P, R) shows a detail of a pipe socket. To the left, a smaller, simpler bagpipe (S, T, V) is depicted with three pipes labeled Z, T, V, Y, and X.</image-desc>

it must be noted that the Italians have another small Musette represented by S T V, which has two pipes: namely Z T, whose range is a ninth <note>an interval spanning nine scale steps</note> and which has the key Z; and V, which only produces the five notes of the Fifth <note>an interval of five scale steps</note> by means of its five holes. The middle pipe Y X serves as a Drone <term>Drone: "Bourdon," a pipe that produces a continuous, unchanging pitch to accompany the melody</term> and has no holes; it can be lengthened by the joint Y, where it detaches, for part X fits into Y, as is the case with the drones of Bagpipes <term>Bagpipes: "Cornemuses," generally referring to the louder, rustic folk pipes</term> and Shawms <note>original: "Chalemies," early double-reed instruments, ancestors of the oboe</note>. The skin bag is attached to the stock <note>original: "boëte," the wooden socket where pipes meet the bag</note> S, just as it is on the stock or neck D of the Sourdeline A F G H, to which I now return; it is called the *Organine* and *Sampogne* <note>The Italian Zampogna</note>, and has a fingering system <note>original: "tablature"</note> similar to that of our Musette. Now, this one has four pipes, because I have added the fourth...

h k H, which the Duke of Bracciano <note>Paolo Giordano II Orsini (1591–1656), a patron of the arts and music who significantly improved the Sourdeline's design.</note> invented, so that one can play all sorts of songs in four parts: for only three pipes were used before this invention, such that the second pipe D G did not end at G, but went back up to k, and had all the keys of the branch h k.

Now this fourth pipe has no holes or keys from D to h, and serves only to carry the wind to the holes covered by the keys seen on h k and K C. The pipe <term>Pipe: "Chalumeau," referring here to one of the melodic chanters of the bagpipe</term> D G had fifteen keys to cover its fifteen holes when it curved back to k, since it included those of the fourth pipe h k; but it now has only eight or ten, as seen in this figure; and the fourth has just as many, so that they have a range of a Fifteenth <note>A range of two full octaves</note>. Here it must be noted that these pipes produce all the semitones, like an Organ; and consequently they must have twenty-four keys to produce two octaves, since they sound by "closed play," which is to say they make no sound except in proportion to the keys being lifted.

As for the two other pipes on the right and left, they have some of their holes open and others closed by keys: the one for the right hand, namely F, has six open, and the one for the left, E, has four: but F has six keys for its six other holes, and E has only four; that is to say F has twelve holes and E has nine, by which it is easy to judge their range. The third pipe had a range of only a Twelfth <note>An octave plus a fifth</note> when it was alone, and produced the notes that follow, of which the first is the sound of the pipe entirely closed; the second represents the sound made by the first hole by means of the first key lifted, and the others signify the other sounds made by all the keys up to the last one at the top of the pipe.

->Range of the 3rd Pipe of the Sampogne.<-

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing a sequence of eleven notes rising in pitch. The notes are written in a historical mensural style with diamond and square shapes. The title above it indicates it represents the range of the third pipe of the Sampogne.</image-desc>

But the fourth pipe K H, which I have added, descends a Fifth lower by means of its keys, in order to play the Bass. And because the said keys are difficult to understand on the pipes, I have placed their diagrams separately, as seen at the letters $\alpha$ $\beta$ $\delta$ $\mu$, etc. $\beta$ shows the end of one of the large keys that plugs the hole; but a small piece of sheepskin is glued onto it, so that it plugs the said hole more precisely: the other end serves the finger, which lowers it by pressing the small spring $\delta$ to uncover the hole.

The other small pieces, such as $\alpha$ $\upsilon$ $\lambda$, and $\rho$ show the other springs, or the places on the pipes where the keys are attached: so that there remains only the neck of this instrument P R to explain, which is grafted into the skin bag A, so that the four reeds <term>Reeds: "anches," the vibrating tongues (likely double reeds in this case) that produce the sound</term> which make the four pipes speak are enclosed, so that dust or other accidents cannot alter them. The Italians also place a very fine crepe over the reeds to prevent the hair of the goatskin they use from falling inside. This instrument can serve as a portative organ, but after it has made its lowest sound while entirely closed—and the wind can only escape through the hole of the foot <note>original: "pate," the bottom opening of the pipe</note>—one must plug this hole when lifting the keys to make the other sounds; otherwise, the pipe "horns" <note>original: "corne," meaning it produces a harsh, discordant, or unintended drone-like sound</note> and spoils the play. I leave aside several refinements that can be found on this instrument, because practice and experience will teach more than all the discourse that could be made of it.

## PROPOSITION XXXI.

### Explaining the form, the range, the fingering chart, the tuning, and the use of the large Oboes.

IT must be noted that there are two kinds of <term>Oboes: From the French "Haut-bois," literally "high-wood" or "loud-wood," referring to its piercing tone.</term> in use in France: namely those of Poitou <note>Poitou is a province in western France; these instruments were often associated with rural festivals and the "Grand Écurie" of the King.</note>, the illustration of which I will provide in the thirty-second Proposition, and those simply called Oboes, whose form is almost similar to the large <term>Recorders: Referred to in the text as "Fluſtes douces" (sweet flutes) or "English flutes."</term> that I explained in the 8th Proposition. Now, these instruments have

The first eight numbers show the arrangement of the eight holes, which are closed to create the range of sounds; for nine and ten serve only to provide air to the sounds, and to shorten the **Treble**, whose foot <note>Original: "pate," referring to the flared bell at the bottom of the instrument.</note> descends and widens from the ninth hole, which is double, as is the tenth, for they each have one opposite <insert>an vent-hole on each side</insert>, as happens with the **Tenor** <note>Original: "Taille," the melodic middle voice.</note> and the **Alto** <note>Original: "Haute-contre."</note>. As for the **Tenor**, it descends lower

a fifth lower than the **Treble** <note>Original: "Deſſus," the highest-pitched instrument in the set.</note> when it is sounded "open"—that is to say, with all holes open. However, it only has seven holes that are closed by the fingers, the seventh of which is hidden under the box **I K M N**. This box is pierced with several small holes, both for decoration and to allow the air exiting the seventh hole to escape, as well as to hide the spring of the key which serves to close this hole. Now, this spring appears in the figure next to it, which shows the entire key exposed: it is held at θ <note>The Greek letter theta.</note> by means of two small branches that pass through the two holes ι <note>iota</note> and κ <note>kappa</note>. **L** shows that the body of the <term>Tenor: Original: "Taille," the mid-range instrument of the family.</term> is flattened throughout this opening, so as to more easily house the key. The letters ν <note>nu</note> and ο <note>omicron</note> show the small plate, or piece of brass, whose end, ρ <note>rho</note>, rises by means of the handle υ <note>upsilon</note>. This handle is raised by lowering the key with the little finger of the right hand, which touches one of the branches of the key **H**, while the fourth finger closes the sixth hole. This plate is held by the iron wire π ρ <note>pi rho</note>, which enters and is embedded in the wood at points ϖ <note>omega</note> and ρ; so that the plate ν ο, which closes the hole, moves on this wire like an axis. This had to be noted once and for all, so that one may know what the keys are used for and how they move the springs. There are also four blades to note, through which the iron wire passes, of which two form part of the blade that closes the hole, and two others which are parallel to them, and which are close to ζ <note>zeta</note> and ο, but the perspective could not show them because they nearly touch each other, so that it is necessary to see them in person to understand them.

Now, the reed of this Tenor is similar to that of the Treble, as seen in **A B**; but it is grafted onto the small copper tube β <note>beta</note> at point δ <note>delta</note>. It is then covered with a piece of wood represented by β α γ ζ <note>beta alpha gamma zeta</note>, which the <term>instrument makers: Original: "Facteurs."</term> call the <term>Pirouette: A wooden lip-rest or cap that surrounds the reed, allowing the player to press their lips against it for better control and to reduce fatigue.</term>, which fits into the top of this instrument **F G**, as seen in **C D E**. Thus, **A C D F G O P** represents the Tenor in its entirety, and in its perfection, as it is when played. The eighth hole only serves to provide venting on both sides. However, it must be noted that the holes of these instruments are drilled at an angle, so that they meet the internal bore at a different location than where they appear on the outside. I have indicated this by the white space of the holes: for example, the white of the first hole of the Tenor shows that it slants toward the reed, and that of the second that it moves toward the third, and so on for the others. This is practiced in all large instruments, so that the exterior holes are close enough to one another to be reached by the fingers, while the internal openings in the hollow bore are far enough apart to create the correct musical intervals for the tones.

Now, it must be noted that the holes are spaced differently from one another, for the fourth is as far from the third as the third is from the first, or the fourth from the sixth; and the seventh is almost as far from the sixth as the fourth is from the second, even though the difference in their pitch is the same. This occurs in most other instruments with finger holes, as I have already noted elsewhere.

I must here add the exact dimensions of these two parts, so that those who wish to make them may know the proportions that must be observed. The Treble is two feet long from **B** to **C**, and nine inches from the ninth hole to **D**; and because it can be said that its length ends at the ninth hole, it is only one and a half feet long. As for the other holes, they maintain almost the same distance, except for the eighth, which is separated from the fifth by twenty lines: but its **reed** <note>Original: "anche."</note> A B extends it further by two inches.

The **Tenor** <term>Taille: The mid-range member of the oboe or shawm family.</term> is two feet, four and a half inches long, including its **pirouette** <note>The pirouette is a wooden lip-rest that surrounds the reed, characteristic of the shawm family.</note> A G, which is two inches and five lines long. Let us now see the shape and proportions of the **Bass** B M N, which differs in several ways from the Tenor; for it is so long that the mouth cannot reach the top. This is why a **brass pipe** <note>Original: "canal de cuiure." Known today as a bocal or crook.</note> A B is used, at the end of which a reed is attached at point A for blowing. Now, this brass pipe descends as low as is necessary for the convenience of the person playing this part; but I have already spoken of this in the explanation of the **Recorders** <note>Original: "Fluſtes douces."</note>. This Bass is five feet from B to M N, and has eleven holes which are marked by as many numbers, of which four—namely 8, 9, 10, and 11—are hidden under their **boxes** <note>Original: "boettes." These are fontanelles, or perforated wooden sleeves used to protect the delicate keywork.</note> G H I K L. Thus, the box G H I K has three keys, and I L, which is called the **pocket** <note>Original: "la poche."</note>, has only one, which covers the eleventh hole located opposite its number, just as the three holes of the large box are opposite numbers 8, 9, and 10. And because the four **springs** <note>Original: "reſſorts."</note> are made like those of the Tenor, there is no need to explain them: one must only note that the key covers the eighth hole, D the ninth, E the tenth, and I the eleventh.

As for the range of the **Oboes** <note>Original: "Haut-bois." In this era, the term referred to the louder, keyed shawms used in ensembles.</note>, each part—for example, the **Treble** <note>Original: "Deſſus."</note>—reaches a **Fifteenth** <note>An interval of two octaves.</note>. For after one has played as many natural tones as there are holes, one begins others again, which are more forced and higher-pitched, by **increasing the wind** <note>Original: "redoublant le vent." This refers to the technique of overblowing to reach a higher register.</note>, as I said when explaining the other instruments that have this same property.

*Explaining the shape, size, range, and use of Bassoons, Fagots, Courtaux, and Rackets.*

The seventh hole shows the place where the two holes C and D meet to be continued; this is why it is covered with another box similar to BCD, for fear that the wind be lost, which must be carried from the reed A to the eleventh hole where it exits: so that the air travels down and back up.

There are also six holes in this instrument, namely three on the right side for those who play right-handed, and three on the left side for left-handed players; they are marked by alpha, gamma, and epsilon <note>Original: "α γ & ε."</note>, and by beta, delta, and zeta <note>Original: "β δ & ζ."</note>: but one must stop one set or the other with wax, while using the three on the other side, which are stopped by laying down the same fingers with which one stops the middle holes of the instrument, which are the closest to these added holes that are made of small pieces of wood, which are called *Tetines* <note>Literal translation: "Teats" or "nipples." The final instrument is named the *Cervelat* <term>Cervelat: Also known as a Rackett or Sausage Bassoon. Finally, there are ten inches from the tenth to the eleventh, and from this eleventh until the foot <note>Original: "pate" (paw or foot), referring to the flared end-piece of the instrument.</note>—that is to say, until B—there are fourteen inches. However, it must be noted that the hole with which the Bassoon is bored throughout its length—that is to say, its internal bore <term>canal: the hollow passage through which the air travels; its shape determines the instrument's tone and pitch.</term>—is narrow at the beginning and goes on widening until the end. There remains only the Rackett <term>Ceruelat: A Renaissance woodwind instrument, also known as a "sausage bassoon," featuring a very long bore folded many times within a small cylinder to produce deep bass notes.</term> to be explained, of which the upper base has eight holes of the same size that pierce this instrument throughout its length. In such a way, the lower base also has eight holes, which nevertheless form only a single continuous bore; thus, the Harmonic Rackett goes as low as an instrument that would be eight times as long—that is to say, one that would be three and a half feet long, or thereabouts. This is why the holes must be arranged on this cylinder as one sees here, in order to reach the bore in the proper places to produce the tones of this instrument. The reed <note>Original: "anche."</note> marked A is in the middle of the eight preceding holes, which are covered by a brass <note>Original: "laton" (latten), a copper alloy similar to brass.</note> plate or a box <note>Original: "boëtte." This refers to the decorative perforated cap that often protects the reed on a rackett.</note>, as seen at D, and which are plugged with small pieces of parchment, or wood, or such other material as one wishes, so that they are all continuous and form but a single bore.

As for the arrangement of the holes, it is marked by the fourteen numbers that are upon it, of which the first signifies the 1st hole, and the 2 the second hole, and so on for the others until the fourteenth. But it must be noted that those which appear white and are dotted are behind, and they cannot be seen from the same view as those that are black and are in front—namely 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 (which are close to one another only on the exterior, for as for the interior, they are as far apart as the others, because one is bored diagonally upwards and the other downwards); six and seven, which have four holes, even though they only make two sounds, because the two at the top meet in the same place in the concavity of the bore, as do the two below; and finally 8, 9, and 10. But the 11, 12, 13, and 14 are on the other side, and the 15 makes the lowest sound of all when it is closed and all the others remain closed. The first one opened <note>Original: "debouclé."</note> makes the highest sound. Thus, this Rackett has the range of a Fifteenth <note>An interval of two octaves.</note>, of which one makes every step by closing all the holes one after the other. This is done all the more easily as they are closer to one another, because one can close two, three, or four with a single finger. Now, the wind exits and is lost through the four holes that are at the bottom on the right hand without any number, and through another hole which is in the lower base.

# PROPOSITION XXXIII.

### Further explaining the Oboes, along with the other preceding instruments, and the musical parts they can express.

I wish to display all these instruments on the same plate, as they belong to the same ensemble <note>original: "Concert," referring to a consort of instruments</note>, so that it may serve the mind and the hand of those who wish to make similar instruments. A $\alpha \omega$ <note>$\alpha$ (alpha) and $\omega$ (omega)</note> shows the Bass in its true proportion: the first hole is marked $\delta$ <note>delta</note>, and with an $o$, which signifies that it is on the back: two, three, and four show the locations of the fontanelle <term>boëtte: a protective wooden sleeve covering the keys of large woodwinds</term> marked BF, opposite which are found the second, third, and fourth holes. CD show the back keys, which cover the first hole hidden in the cover GH <note>the fontanelle or "pocket"</note> opposite H: so that this Bass has four keys. The other holes are marked by their numbers up to the tenth. The brass crook <term>cuiuret: the curved metal tube that holds the reed</term> marked $\alpha \zeta$ <note>alpha zeta</note> has its reed $\zeta$ <note>zeta</note>, through which one blows into the instrument.

As for the Tenor <term>Taille: the melodic tenor voice or instrument</term> marked I M, it has only seven holes and one key, and is played through its pirouette <term>piroüette: a wooden lip-rest used on shawms to support the player's embouchure</term> marked XI, as is also done with the Soprano <note>original: "dessus"</note> marked NO. The Rackett <term>Cervelat: literally "sausage," a compact instrument with many internal bores to produce a deep sound</term> marked $\delta \delta$ shows its holes on both the front and the back, because those on the right side show the distance and arrangement they have between them on the side that cannot be seen. As for the Dulcian <note>original: "Fagot," a precursor to the modern bassoon</note> or the Bassoon PS, it has three keys that I have placed to the side, even though they are on the back, so that one can see that the first hole is opposite the holes of the cover $\alpha z$, and the second is opposite the cover XY. Now, the same finger opens two keys by means of the two ends ZY. Similarly, the finger that covers the seventh hole also uncovers the third hole by pressing on the end V of the key TV.

As for the Kortholt <term>Courtaut: a short-bodied, double-bore woodwind</term> marked $\beta \gamma$ <note>beta gamma</note>, I have explained all its holes in the other figure, so it is only necessary here to observe that the holes on the right side signify the locations on the back where they are placed. The reed $\rho \sigma \tau$ <note>rho sigma tau</note> shows the manner in which they are usually prepared; for $\rho$ signifies the very thin canes <note>original: "roseaux"</note> from which it is composed. $\sigma \tau$ is the brass staple <note>cuiuret</note> onto which they are tied with waxed thread, or thread that has been dampened, so that it better seals the sides of the canes and prevents the air blown into the top of the reed from escaping; and then more thread is wound around the end of the staple $\tau$, so that it fits tightly into the pipes, or shawms <term>chalumeaux: the main body or pipe of the instrument</term>, and so that the air cannot escape between the staple and the pipe.

As for their music, it is appropriate for large assemblies, such as for Ballets (even though Violins are now used in their place), for weddings, for village festivals, and for other public rejoicings, because of the great noise they make and the grand harmony they provide; for they have the loudest and most forceful sound of all instruments, except for the Trumpet. But the example that follows will make their nature better understood than a longer discourse. It should only be noted that the Sackbut <term>Sacquebute: an early form of the trombone</term> is used to play the baritone <note>original: "basse Taille"</note> part.

## COROLLARY.

Theseus Ambrosius, a Doctor from Pavia, describes another species of <term>Fagot: an early, complex reed instrument often associated with the origins of the bassoon</term> from page 33 to 37 of his *Introduction to the Syriac and Armenian Languages*, providing an illustration on page 179. He attributes its invention to his father-in-law, Afranius, who could find no craftsman in all of Germany capable of constructing it; consequently, he employed the skill of Giambattista Ravilio of Ferrara, who completed the instrument for him. However, there is no need to include its illustration here, both because it can be seen in Theseus’s book and because it can be understood if one understands the illustrations of the preceding instruments—particularly those of the <term>Sourdeline: a highly complex Italian bagpipe with many keys</term> and the <term>Bassoons: the lower-pitched members of the woodwind family</term>—inasmuch as this *Fagot* contains nothing more than what they do.

It should only be noted that it is composed of two bassoon-like pipes, whose holes are closed by springs (keys) that one opens with the fingers, like those I mentioned in the explanation of the previous instruments. Furthermore, it uses two bellows, or rather two skins, one of which is fitted to a bellows like that of the <term>Musette: a small, bellows-blown bagpipe popular in French courtly music</term> or the Sourdeline, which is placed under the right arm; the other is similar to the skin of the aforementioned Musettes, serving to send wind into the *Fagot*, which does not sound at all unless one opens its keys, as is the case with the Sourdeline, which can be categorized among the *Fagots*.

Now, it is not necessary to search for the origin of this word, which Theseus attempts to derive from <term>phago: to eat</term> <note>original: "φάγω"</note>, especially since the origins of the names given to instruments have not been sufficiently recorded. One might say the name was taken from our French word <term>Fagot: a bundle of sticks</term>, because it consists of two or more flutes bound or "faggoted" together, as seen in the two preceding examples I have explained and illustrated. It is very easy to add skins and bellows to them to avoid the labor of distributing wind from the lungs, and to give them a range of a twenty-second (three octaves), as with the *Fagot* of Afranius, or a twenty-ninth (four octaves), like the keyboards of virginals and organs, which can be used to play several *Fagots* and Musettes simultaneously.

## PROPOSITION XXXIV.

### *To explain the Bagpipe and the Oboes of Poitou, including their size, use, and proportions.*

This <term>Bagpipe: specifically the "Cornemuse de Poitou," a traditional French instrument</term> differs from the <term>Shawm: a loud, double-reed instrument</term> <note>original: "Chalemie"</note> which I discussed in the 25th Proposition, only in that it has no small <term>Drone: a pipe that produces a continuous sustained pitch</term> <note>original: "Bourdon"</note>. It is blown through the blowpipe **Z**, and has the large drone **Y** like the other, but its <term>Chanter: the pipe on which the melody is played</term> <note>original: "Chalumeau"</note> **R V** has eight holes, the first of which is closed with a key covered by its fontanelle (protective box).

## PROPOSITION XXXV.

### *To explain all the other instruments that use wind to sound, and particularly those of the Indies.*

It is certain that one can create an infinite variety of wind instruments, just as with stringed ones, although they can all be reduced to those of which we have spoken, and those we will treat in the book on Organs. One could relate to this type of instrument the various caverns, wells, and other subterranean places which sometimes produce harmonious sounds, and at other times confused, horrible, and terrifying noises. Some have also remarked upon statues that made strange noises when certain winds blew, and birds made of bronze that each sang their own <term>warbling: the song or chirping of birds</term>; this is what <note>original: "Luit-prand"</note> Liutprand <note>Liutprand of Cremona (c. 920–972) was a diplomat and historian who described mechanical wonders in Constantinople.</note> says he saw in Constantinople at the Court of the Emperor Constantine, son of Leo; which Cassiodorus asserts was made by Boethius; and which seems to have happened with the statue of Muscovy named <note>original: "Sclata Baba"</note> Sclata Baba <note>Likely "Zlata Baba," the "Golden Old Woman," a legendary idol described by early travelers to Russia.</note>, whose trumpets and other instruments made a continual noise by means of the winds that blew and entered inside. I leave aside all the deceptions of Oracles and Idols, which were carried out by means of pipes, channels, and winds. And we often experience how all kinds of great winds produce such a great multitude of sounds and different noises—depending on the rocks, walls, window openings, and other places they strike and encounter—that there are no instruments they do not imitate; so much so that one often believes they hear the cry of children, or the song of birds, the concert of Viols, the beat of Drums, etc., although it is only the wind alone making all these noises. But since it is not within our liberty or our power to use it at our discretion, as we do with other instruments, I shall speak of it no further.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an exotic wind instrument labeled 'F B' consisting of five parallel pipes of different lengths held together. The top ends are marked with 'F' and the rounded bottom ends are marked with 'B'. Small horizontal mouthpiece components across the pipes are labeled 'C' and 'P'. To the right of the main instrument is a separate detailed drawing of one such mouthpiece component, labeled 'E P'.</image-desc>

As for the instruments of the Indians, I represent here only one, namely **F B**, which they make of canes or reeds. I show it in this figure, which was sent to me from the rare cabinet of Mr. Claude Menestrier by Mr. Giovanni Battista Doni, Gentleman and Secretary to the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberini. It seems that the holes **F F** determine the pitch of the sounds of each <term>reed-pipe: a simple wind instrument made from a stalk</term>, although the tongues **C P**—similar to the one figured separately at **E P**—make me doubt this; this is easily known by seeing this instrument in the aforementioned cabinet. Now, this instrument is almost similar to our Organs, and can produce an excellent concert of flutes, which a single man could play by means of a skin similar to that of the <term>Musette: a small French bagpipe</term>. I leave aside all that concerns <term>bird-calls: whistles used to lure birds</term>, which are used to catch birds by <term>luring: the practice of mimicking bird sounds to attract them</term> and to imitate their songs, especially since they are no different from the reeds of the Organ, which we will speak of later, or those seen in the instruments of this book.

# BOOK SIX
## ON ORGANS.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

#### TO EXPLAIN THE FIGURE, AND THE *parts of Organ Cabinets, with everything belonging to them.*

Since I have explained all the wind instruments, of which the organ is like a summary <note>The author views the organ as an "epitome" or "abridgment" because it incorporates the principles of all other wind instruments into a single machine.</note>, it is reasonable to consider its form and composition. For many believe it to be the most excellent and perfect of all instruments, as much because of the great variety of its stops as for the equality and accuracy of its sounds. I will therefore treat everything belonging to it in this sixth book, which I begin with an explanation of the figure of an Organ Cabinet that can be moved wherever one wishes, and which is called *portative* <note>original: "portatif"</note>, so that one may have a general knowledge of all its parts before explaining them in detail. I hope the readers' minds will be prepared for the attention necessary for this treatise, due to several difficulties encountered therein, the greatest of which seems to me to be understanding the use of all the parts shown by the various figures I present.

Now, the architecture of this cabinet is represented by *A B C D*, for the organ pipes need this cabinet like a case to be supported and kept in the same state and position. The thickness *C N*, which runs the length of this cabinet, shows the place where the wind is first received, which is called the <term>windchest: the airtight box (le secret) that holds pressurized air before it is released into the pipes</term>. In front of this is placed a board lined with sheepskin, which closes this chest very tightly so that the wind cannot escape; but this board must be secured with wedges or otherwise, lest the wind pushed by the bellows knock it to the ground. 

The top of this chest is covered inside with small pieces of wood called <term>pallets: valves (souz-papes or souz-tapes) that control the flow of air from the windchest to the pipes</term>—as if one were saying "under-stoppers"—because they plug the <term>grooves: the internal channels (rainures) that carry air to the foot of each pipe</term> to make them sound when the keys of the keyboard are depressed. This can be seen at the ninth key of the first row: when it is lowered, it causes the pallet directly underneath to lower by means of a small rod, the top end of which is under the key and the bottom of which rests on the pallet. This rod is called a <term>sticker: a mechanical linkage (pilotis) that transmits motion from the key to the pallet</term>; each key has its own sticker which passes through holes made in the board *N*, and each sticker has its own pallet.

Now, there is a <term>Regal: a small organ stop consisting of reed pipes (une Regale)</term> in this cabinet, which is seen between the stickers opposite *S*. However, one only sees the end of the body of each pipe because they enter deep into the cabinet to meet the wind, which enters their reeds and exits through the ends seen on the outside. As for the keyboard *K L*, it has two rows of keys, like that of the <term>spinet: a small harpsichord-like instrument (l'Epinette)</term>, but there is no...

The board **E F** is named the *windchest* <note>original: "sommier"; while the previous page mentioned the "secret" as the air compartment, the "sommier" or soundboard is the upper part where the pipes actually stand.</note>, because it carries the feet of the pipes, which rest upon it by entering slightly into the holes with which it is bored, according to the size of each foot and the quantity of wind that must enter into the pipes. The other board **G H**, which is called the *Rackboard* <note>original: "Tamis," literally meaning "sieve" or "screen" due to its many holes.</note>, serves only to hold the pipes upright, and to prevent them from shaking or moving out of their place.

Now I have included several types of pipes in this Cabinet so that one may see the difference; for besides the *Regal* <note>A reed stop with a distinctive, buzzing tone, often used to mimic the human voice.</note>, or the "human voices" <note>original: "voix humaines"</note>, which are at the bottom un...

# On Organs.

Looking at the keys of the keyboard <note>original: "marches du clauier"</note> and the facade pipes <note>original: "tuyaux de la monstre," referring to the decorative pipes displayed in the front of the case</note> which stand on either side of the principal—the largest pipe marked with a **1**—one can see two square pipes on the left side marked with three stars. The first of these has a single fold, and the second has three. This is to demonstrate the method used to house pipes when the Case <note>original: "Cabinet"</note> or the available space is not large enough to contain them at their full length, unless they are folded twice or several times. This folding in no way prevents them from producing the same tone. The first star on the second square pipe shows its first fold, and the second star shows the second. As for the stars on the right side, the first shows the shape that the Trumpet pipes <note>original: "tuyaux de la Trompette"</note> have at the top, for they widen to imitate the sounds of the military trumpet; however, I will speak more fully later about all the types of pipes. The second star shows how chimney pipes <note>original: "tuyaux à cheminée," which are capped pipes with a small open tube on top</note> are made, and so on.

The rest of the Case, moving upward, explains the bellows system <note>original: "soufflerie"</note>. **T** shows the hole of one of the bellows, which has a valve <note>original: "souz-pape"</note>; this valve closes the bellows after the air has entered. Now, the bellows system of organs found in churches is composed of several bellows, but these small Cases only have two. These can be made in two ways: one is commonly used in those that only open from one side, forming a triangle shape when opening; the other uses bellows called *lantern bellows* <note>original: "à lanterne"</note> because the upper board rises equally on both sides and always remains parallel to the lower board, just as happens with lanterns made of folded paper. The bellows of this Case are of the lantern type, as seen in bellows **ε δ**, which is fully open, while **V** shows the other one closed.

The two pieces of wood marked by **Y** serve to support the cross-branch, which is marked with two **z**’s. This may be made of wood or iron, but it must rest on the two pivots hidden under the two **Y**’s so that it turns easily by the movement of the wood **ζ η**. This wood is attached to the said rotating branch at point **Z**, which causes the bellows **δ ε** to rise when the rope **ι η** is pulled. When the rope **ζ θ** is pulled, the bellows **V** opens, while the other closes by its own movement, driven by the weight placed upon it.

It is so easy to understand that the rope **β δ** attached to the loop **δ** raises the bellows **δ ε** by the tilting of the branch **β γ**, and that the rope **γ** attached to the loop **ε** raises the bellows **V**, that there is no need to explain it further. I will omit several other ways that can be used to open the bellows according to their different arrangements, in order to explain what remains in this Case—specifically the six pieces of iron marked with numbers **1, 2, 3, 4, 5,** and **6** beside the keyboard. The first and sixth are slightly turned over to show that these six iron pins serve to open and close the registers <note>original: "Registres"</note> or the pipe stops <note>original: "jeux"</note>, for each stop has its own key. One must therefore conclude that this Case has six kinds of stops, since it has six registers or six keys. However, the registers—which are similar to the slats used by roofers and are pierced with as many holes as there are pipes in each stop—cannot be understood without seeing a diagram of them. For this reason, I am reserving that explanation for another place. It is only necessary to note here that the registers usually open the stops when they are raised and close them when they are lowered, though the opposite is just as easy to arrange.
