Now, one must always suppose that the plane of the boards and the <term>windchests</term> <note>original: "sommiers"</note> of the cases is wide enough to support all the ranks of pipes <note>original: "jeux"</note> that are there: for example, that the width, which is not visible here and which supports the pipes, is equal to the length **C D**, so that no one is deceived by the perspective.

As for the pieces of wood marked on either side by **S**, they hold the six keys, which may be called <term>Registers</term> <note>original: "Regiſtres," often called sliders in modern organ building</note>, because they are attached to the ends of the sliders that block or unblock the holes through which the wind enters the foot of the pipes.

The four other small ends located between **S** and **C**, and the two between **S** and **D**, show the ends of the six registers, each of which is attached to the end of its key by means of a small nail or a peg, as seen at the bottom of the second key, which is attached to the end of the second register; this one extends to the left so that it may be noticed more easily. It is not necessary to explain the difference between the ranks and their sounds, nor several other particularities of this case, especially since I shall treat extensively everything that can be known of both the largest and the smallest organs in the other Propositions.

## PROPOSITION II.

->*To explain the construction of the Organ, and all its parts.*<-

There are two sorts of parts in organs: those that serve necessity and others that serve ornament. Now, the necessary parts can be related to the pipes and the wind, for provided that the wind makes the pipes speak well, the Organ has what is necessary for it. But because the wind must enter in a certain manner according to the will of the organists, to create all sorts of songs in one or several parts, the keys of the <term>keyboard</term> <note>original: "Clauier"</note> are also necessary, and consequently all the accompanying parts, which I shall speak of later.

The other parts which serve as ornament consist of the <term>case</term> <note>original: "buffet"</note> and all the elegances with which they are embellished. But here we must particularly consider the construction of the Organ, of which one of the principal pieces is called the <term>frame</term> <note>original: "Chaſſis"</note> by some, because one fits inside it the board of the windchest upon which the pipes are placed. The sides of this frame are three inches high and one and a half inches thick; within it, one applies a bottom of one inch thickness, which must be glued to the said sides. Some make the windchest with springs <note>original: "sommier à reſſort"</note> for the largest ranks of the organ, such as when they make a sixteen-foot pipe for the <term>facade</term> <note>original: "monſtre," the decorative front pipes</note>, because they are too large for the sliding registers of medium-sized organs.

Now, the builders take a large table of very dry, very smooth oak wood, without cracks, and of the thickness of a joist <note>original: "eſpaiſſeur de membrure"</note>, for fear that its size might cause it to warp. After this table has been prepared, one applies upon it wooden <term>ribs</term> <note>original: "Tringles"</note> of the same thickness, which are spaced two fingers apart from each other to make room for the <term>channels</term> <note>original: "cranes, ou graueures"</note>. They thus make forty-eight of these, which some call bars, and which are glued...

[it] upon the said table, some of which are joined by dovetails <note>original: "à queue"</note> which are fitted into the edges of the frame to prevent them from warping: and for this reason they are made of very dry and soft oak, so that they might form the forty-eight grooves <note>original: "reineures"</note> that carry the wind to the pipes. And because the wind must be very steady, they fill them with very clear glue, which is made to flow equally from one side to the other to fill the small cavities and the pores of the wood: and for this purpose, they smooth the glue with brushes, or else they glue paper into the grooves with English glue <note>A high-quality hide or fish glue prized in the 17th century for its strength and clarity.</note>.

But before gluing the said bars, one must measure the places for the pipes on the windchest <term>sommier</term>, and ensure that the holes for their positions are all located in the middle along the strips <note>original: "tringles"</note>: and then one must make other holes to the right of the others in the channels <term>graveures</term>. Now, one must also glue "hairy leather" <note>likely rough-side-out sheepskin or suede used for gaskets</note> over the channels <note>original: "cranes"</note>, and when it is dry, they must be pierced with a hot iron.

This being done, one prepares pieces of wood the width of an inch or two, or thereabouts, of which the widest serve as <term>Toe Boards</term> <note>original: "Chappes," the boards the pipes actually sit on</note>, and the narrowest serve as <term>Sliders</term> <note>original: "Regiſtres," the moving parts that open or close a rank of pipes</note>, which are attached together on the windchest—that is to say, on the top of the bottom of the frame—with pegs, so that they may all be easily pierced opposite one another, either with braces <note>original: "vieil-brequins"</note> or with hot irons, to have forty-eight holes for each stop <note>original: "ieu"</note>, which has only a single hole in each channel for each of its pipes: so that if there are twenty or thirty stops, each groove must have twenty or thirty holes; so that the forty-eight holes of the same stop are found in the same line on the windchest, upon which all its pipes are placed.

When the Toe Boards and the Sliders have been pierced like the grooves and the windchest, they are removed, in order to fit the Sliders between the windchest and the toe board so that they have free movement to close and to open—that is to say, to block and unblock the holes of the grooves—so that the wind passes to all the feet of the pipes placed on the holes of the toe boards, which are attached with screws or nails to the strips that are beside the Sliders, so that these Sliders glide easily underneath without lifting, and without being able to shift from one side or the other.

But because it is too difficult to understand this construction without figures, I provide those that follow, of which the first **T V** signifies the Frame, or the underside of the windchest; **Y** shows the channels, grooves, or channels open. **X** represents them covered with pieces of sheepskin. As for the strips, which are two or three lines thick, they appear in the other figure from **S** to **T**, and **V X**, upon which the Toe Board **Z Z** must rest, so that the Sliders **I**, **L**, **N**, **P** move underneath by means of an iron that is placed in their mortises, which are at the end of said Sliders after their last holes. Now, their movement must not be longer than half of the interval from one hole to another, because it is made only to open and close the holes of the [various] sizes, as is seen at **G** and **H**.

One also sees how the <term>Slider</term> <note>original: *Registre*; a perforated strip of wood that slides to align or misalign with the pipe holes to turn a stop on or off</note> **C** is drawn from above the <term>Windchest</term> <note>original: *sommier*; the pressurized box that holds the air for the pipes</note>, although it is drawn too far here, as it should only be moved by the width of one of the holes; but this figure was designed to represent the holes of the windchest, which are re-drilled with hot irons for fear that the <term>brace-drills</term> <note>original: *vieils-brequins*; hand-cranked drilling tools</note> (which were first used) might leave behind small particles of wood. The inside of this board must be covered with sheepskin, which is folded over its edges, the better to prevent the wind from escaping.

It should also be noted that the <term>trackers</term> <note>original: *pilotis*; also called *tirans* or pull-downs</note>, or rods, which appear in the third figure under the <term>keys</term> <note>original: *marches*; referring here to the levers of the pedalboard or keyboard</note> **H** & **I**, and one of which—namely **G I**—causes the first valve to lower, are attached at one end to the key and at the other to the head of the valve by means of a brass wire. This wire hooks into a small brass eyelet fixed into the valve; this is sufficient, in my opinion, to explain the construction of the principal parts of the Organ, or at least to inspire a desire to see these parts in ordinary Organs.

As for the <term>Blowing Plant</term> <note>original: *soufflerie*; the system of bellows providing air</note>, it is usually composed of five <term>Bellows</term> <note>original: *soufflets*</note> six feet long by four feet wide, each of which must have two <term>Intake Valves</term> <note>original: *lunettes*; literally "spectacles," named for their double-opening shape</note> four inches high by two wide; because if they only had one, it would be too large to draw air in, and its valve could not open easily. Another valve must also be placed in the nozzle of each bellow so that it does not suck air from its neighbor, and so that it remains closed while the others are inflating; otherwise, the wind from one will cause the other to swell. The *Wind-trunk* <note>original: *Porte-vent*</note> which begins at the nozzles must be thicker at the spot where the <term>Tremulant</term> <note>original: *Tremblant*; a mechanical device that creates a pulsating effect in the sound</note> is placed, which we will discuss later.

Now there are several things to note regarding the bellows, particularly that they have five folds and twelve ribs of oak wood on each side, whose glued joints are covered with vellum. Furthermore, they close by themselves in less than a quarter of an hour, even if the Organ is well-sealed and all the valves remain closed. From this, the <term>Builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*; organ builders</note> infer that the wind passes through the wood or the leather, and that the valves of the intake or the nozzle cannot be closed so tightly that the wind does not pass through and escape. To this, some add that they have experimented and found that compressed air passes through wood half a foot thick. I leave aside all that belongs to the different <term>Stops</term> <note>original: *ieux* (jeux); sets of pipes of a specific tonal quality</note> and pipes of the Organ, as I speak of them in the other Propositions.

## PROPOSITION III.

->*To determine in how many ways all the organ stops can be joined together, and how many different composite stops can be made.*<-

I have demonstrated in the *Book on Songs* <note>original: *liure des Chants*</note> how much every number of things can be varied, whether they are taken two by two, three by three, four by four, etc., or whether they are all put together. From this, it is easy to conclude that one can vary the 22 stops of the Organ in 231 ways, if they are taken and joined only two by two; that they vary 1,540 times when putting them three by three, and that they can be diversified in 26,334 ways if they are put five by five—that is to say, if five are put together, as

However, one may consult the table in the said book of Chants, which shows the number of all the stops from a single one up to those composed of twenty-two stops; for it is sufficient here to explain those that are in common use, both because many of the possible combinations are not pleasing and have a poor effect, and because it is easy to invent many others by experimenting on the keyboard or by considering which ones harmonize best together.

Now, the principal of the composite registrations is called the <term>Plain-jeu</term>, which is composed of seven or eight simple stops, namely: the <term>Montre</term> <note>original: *Monstre*; the "show pipes" that stand in the front of the organ case, usually of the principal scale</note>, the <term>Bourdon</term> <note>A stopped pipe that sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length</note> of sixteen and of eight feet, the eight-foot open stop, the <term>Prestant</term> <note>A 4-foot principal stop</note>, the <term>Doublette</term> <note>A 2-foot principal stop</note>, the <term>Fourniture</term> <note>A mixture stop that adds brilliance by having multiple pipes sound for each key</note>, the <term>Cymbale</term>, and the <term>Tierce</term> <note>A stop that sounds the interval of a seventeenth (the third) above the fundamental</note>. For example, the seven letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, which are across from the Plain-jeu, signify that it is composed of the seven stops I have just mentioned. ### PROPOSITION IV.

*To explain the proportion of length to width of Organ pipes, and the practice used by Organ builders in making them.*

It must first be noted that organ pipes are composed of two parts: namely, the body and the foot, as seen in these two figures, one of which represents the pipe laid out flat, and the other represents it as a cylinder. The body of the pipe is encompassed by AD in both, and the foot by CK. For when <term>Organ builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs d'Orgue*</note> make the pipes, they roll out a sheet or plate of tin, such as AB, CD, IK, from which they cut and separate CDIK to make the foot, which is of whatever size one wishes, as its only purpose is to carry the wind up to the <term>tongue</term> <note>original: *languette*; the vibrating part of a reed pipe or the internal structure of a flue pipe</note> GH to make the pipe speak. As for the proportion that must be kept between the length and the width of the pipe’s body, it is not so precise nor so indivisible that it cannot vary; for some give 1/2 of its length to its width, and others give it a third, or a quarter of the same length.

It is sufficient that they speak clearly, sweetly, and uniformly; and experience shows that open pipes can speak even if they are much wider than they are long, for they always speak when they are cut down little by little until the opening of the pipe, which the Builders call the **mouth**. Now, when I say that the Builders give a quarter of the length to the width, and consequently that the height of the pipe is four times its width, this width must be understood as the pipe laid out in the form of a parallelogram, like BC, and not the diameter of the same pipe when reduced to a cylinder, which is <term>sub-triple</term> <note>Meaning the diameter is approximately one-third of the circumference (the width of the flat sheet).</note> of the said width.

It must also be noted that the Builders use a wooden roller, which one might call the mold of the pipe, to roll the sheet of lead upon, in order to join and solder B with A, and D with C, and to reduce it into a cylinder. And because the top of the foot must be of the same width as the body, it must be cut upon the same body, as seen at CD, which represents the section, so as to resolder it afterward with the said body, or rather with the tongue that is between the body and the foot.

Finally, it must be noted that there are two sorts of pipes, some of which are open, like those of which I have spoken, and others are closed at the top with a plate of lead, or tin, or a piece of wood, or other...

material. To which can be added <term>spindle pipes</term> <note>original: *tuyaux à fuseau*; pipes that taper toward the top</note> and <term>chimney pipes</term> <note>original: *tuyaux à cheminée*; stopped pipes with a small open tube or "chimney" protruding from the cap</note>, which are partly open and partly closed. But the height of <term>stopped pipes</term> <note>original: *tuyaux bouchez*; pipes with a plug or cap at the top</note> does not have as great a proportion to their width as the height of open ones, since the wind that is pushed into the closed pipes travels a double path <note>An acoustic principle: in a stopped pipe, the sound wave must travel to the top and back down, making the pipe sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length</note>, even though they can be four times taller than they are wide. In any case, it matters very little what proportion they are made in, provided that they speak well; but since this depends on the skill and wit of the <term>Organ builder</term> <note>original: *Facteur*</note>, and since one finds those who make pipes speak even when the height is five or six times the width, it is not necessary to explain this more fully. As for <term>Reed pipes</term> <note>original: *tuyaux à Anches*</note>, I shall speak of them after having explained the proportion of the mouth and the <term>tongues</term> <note>original: *languettes*; here referring to the internal structural plate or the lips of the pipe mouth</note> of the pipes.

### PROPOSITION V.

*To determine what the width and height of the mouth of the pipes should be, and the width and thickness of the tongues.*

The preceding figures show the proportion that must be observed for the mouth of the pipes, of which the length—measured in the middle of the plate from G to H—is the fourth part of the width CD when the pipes are stopped; this is why Organ builders divide it into four equal parts, so as to take one for the length or height of the mouth. This they do by cutting the piece that covered the opening GEHF. Now, GE or HF shows that the height of the

the mouth must be a quarter of its width: so that the division into four equal parts is very frequent in the making of <term>Organs</term> <note>original: *fabrique des Orgues*</note>, as well as in the harmony of <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>referring to the ancient Greek philosopher's mathematical ratios for musical intervals</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled with letters A at the apex, H and I on an upper horizontal line, F and G on a middle line, and D and E on a lower line, with B and C at the base. Lines radiate from the apex A to the base, dividing it into five equal sections. This diagram is used as a scale for determining the widths of organ pipe mouths.</image-desc>

But the width of the mouth of open pipes should only be the fifth part of the width of the pipe body: and because it is difficult to take this fifth part for the smallest pipes, one can use a triangle for this purpose, whose base being divided into five equal parts, the lines drawn from said base to the summit will give the opening of the mouth of the smallest pipes. For example, if one supposes that the width of the largest pipe is equal to the line B C, it is a certain thing that the width of its mouth will be equal to the line D E: and that the pipe which is an <term>Octave</term> higher will have the width of its mouth equal to the line F G, because the width of its body will be equal to the line H I: so that one will find the widths of all the pipe mouths by applying their widths to those of this triangle, which contains an infinity of different widths that one can apply by raising them from B C up to the summit A; for these six lines will always divide the width of each pipe into five equal parts, and the small middle triangle D A E will always mark the width of the mouths used for open pipes. As for the <term>stopped pipes</term> <note>original: *bouchez*</note>, one does not need a triangle, because the width of their mouth contains a quarter of their width, and consequently supposes a division into four equal parts, which is very easy: although one could accommodate this division into whatever triangle one wishes, like the preceding one.

<image-desc>A technical diagram showing the cross-section of an organ pipe foot. A circle, representing the pipe body, is labeled with points N, O, P, G, and H. Inside, the 'languette' (tongue or languid) is marked by points L and M. Below the circle, a tapered cone representing the foot ends in an opening labeled I and K.</image-desc>

As for the <term>languids</term> <note>original: *languettes*; the horizontal plate inside a flue pipe that directs the air stream</note>, they serve as a tongue for the mouth of the pipes, for they cut and split the wind: their width N H is equal to the base of the pipes, which they cover entirely, except at the place of the mouth, which gives free entry to the wind that is pushed through the opening of the <term>pipe foot</term> <note>original: *pied du tuyau*</note>, which is marked here by I K. But the thickness of the languids, that is to say L G, or M H, must be one-third of the height of the mouth, and its cut, or its slope, must be made as a <term>bevel</term> <note>original: *bizeau* or *tallus*</note>: so that the plane of this thickness inclines by about twenty-two degrees, or a quarter of a right angle, toward the body.

Now this cut must be made cleanly, so that the pipe speaks well; and the material of the languid must be composed of one part of fine <term>tin</term> to four of <term>lead</term>: for example, if one takes five pounds of tin, one must put twenty pounds of lead. If the pipes could receive the wind conveniently enough without their feet, their bodies would suffice with the languid: but because they are necessary to dispense the wind to the great number of pipes that are in Organs, it is necessary to explain them by this figure L M I K, which forms an inverted cone, whose base is that of the pipe body, or the languid; as for the summit of this Cone, it is truncated, in order to have the hole I K, which carries the wind from the bellows to the languid: this is why one can call it the <term>wind-carrier</term> <note>original: *porte-vent*</note>, although this name is given to another part of the Organ.

These feet may be of whatever length one desires; for it is sufficient that they support their pipes, and that they enter into the holes of the <term>toe board</term> <note>original: *chappe*; the upper board of the windchest where the pipes stand</note>, from which they draw the wind, and that they fill them so precisely that the said wind cannot escape. Their material can be lead, wood, or whatever metal one wishes, although it is easier and more appropriate to make the feet of the same material as the bodies, because of their join which is made upon the said body, of which P N O Q represents a part. One can also make <term>Organ</term> pipes of glass, cardboard, quills, and wax, which sound as well as those of wood or tin, as is seen by experience: but all this will be better understood by the Proposition that follows.

### PROPOSITION VI.

**To explain the manner of casting, forging, and flattening the lead and tin to make the pipes; of soldering them, and of composing the solder.**

ONE of the most necessary things for the construction of the Organ consists in melting and casting the lead: and for this purpose, one must have a table that is very straight in every direction, which has its level very true; and then it must be given a little slope according to how thick one wishes to make the <term>metal alloy</term> <note>original: *eſtoffe*; specifically the lead-tin mixture used for pipe making</note>. Now, <term>de Caus</term> <note>Salomon de Caus (1576–1626), an influential engineer and architect</note> has included a figure in his work *The Reasons of Moving Forces* <note>original: *forces mouuantes*</note>, where he treats the Organ, which shows this method so clearly that it is not necessary to speak of it here. He also gives the figure of a mill suitable for flattening and smoothing the sheets of lead, without it being necessary to forge them, for they are made as thin and delicate as one wishes by bringing together the two rollers, or cylinders of iron, or steel, or other material. It is in this manner that gold-drawers flatten gold and silver wire to make <term>purl</term> <note>original: *Canetille*; coiled wire used for gold embroidery</note>, and that one could flatten, smooth, and polish sheets of silver and copper to make Organ pipes, which would perhaps have other properties than those of lead and tin.

Regarding the solder and the manner of soldering the pipes, it must be noted that the metal alloy is composed of a twelfth part of tin to the lead: and that it must be forged very smoothly on a polished anvil like those of the <term>Pewterers</term> <note>original: *Eſtamiers*; craftsmen specializing in tin and lead alloys</note>. Now, after all the pipes are cut, each of them is taken separately, and before rolling it on the <term>mandrel</term> <note>original: *moule*; a wooden form used to shape the pipe</note>, one rubs the sides of the pipe with chalk thinned with a little water and glue, and for this purpose, this mixture is heated slightly. This being done, one begins to bend the side of the pipe that is to be on the inside along the length of the mandrel, upon which it is rolled. Afterward, it is beaten all around the said mandrel with a very flat and sufficiently long ruler. And then the body of the pipe is removed from the mandrel, so that there remains about the width of a quill between the ends that must join one another, in order to rub them with the previous mixture; and after it is dry, one takes a small knife with a very fine point, which is adjusted in the hand in such a way that the length of the knife passes over the thumb, and its handle is between the little finger and the fourth. And then one lightly places the point, supported by the thumb, on the edge of each side, and by sliding from one end to the other, one scrapes each side so,

so that being joined together they form a sort of little gullet, or a small gutter. Now, after having scraped it, one takes a candle end to rub it, so that the solder might flow better. The solder is made from one pound of lead, one pound of fine tin, and a quarter-pound of <term>bismuth</term> <note>original: *eſtain de glace*; literally "ice-tin," a term for bismuth or a similar crystalline metal used to lower the melting point of the solder</note> for lead pipes. However, one uses two pounds of fine tin, one pound of lead, and a quarter-pound of bismuth for tin pipes; though this mixture depends on the judgment and the will of the <term>Organ Builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*</note>. To this, it must be added that to solder the pipes well, one must put a little solder at both ends before making it flow all along the seam, in order to secure both sides of the body and to straighten and adjust them against one another.

And for this purpose, the hand must hold the soldering iron very straight, or at least let it lean very little over the pipe, and the width of the tip should go across the straight line of the pipe—that is to say, all along the joint. As for the foot of the pipe, it is soldered to the body after the <term>languid</term> <note>original: *languette*; the internal horizontal plate that directs wind across the mouth</note> has been secured against the said body, and after they have been rubbed all around with the preceding mixture, scraped, and rubbed with tallow, just like the body. Now, one must first secure the foot and the body by the two sides, by placing the end of the body against one’s chest <note>original: *eſtomach*</note> and letting a drop of solder fall to hold them both in place. And then one must take the body in the left hand and the iron in the right, so that having dipped the tip of the said iron into the solder, one places it on the body, which the left hand moves by turning until one reaches the other side.

But the iron must be very hot, without however being red, for fear that it might burn the solder and melt the pipe. It must also be quite thick and end by tapering at the tip used for soldering, the width of which should be equal to that of the little finger, and the thickness to that of a <term>double</term> <note>original: *double*; a small French coin</note>, rounded in the manner of a burnisher. Now, after having heated it, it must be rubbed on a tile upon which there is some rosin with a little solder, in order to tin the tip well. Afterward, it must be wiped well with a wet and wrung-out cloth to remove any ashes or rosin that might have remained there; and finally, when one takes the solder with the tip of the said iron, it must be diluted in candle tallow placed in a very clean spot, so as to be able to round the solder on the pipes; for it is in this that the Builders place the perfection of their soldering. And then one must wash the pipes well with hot water; and finally, they must be dried and rubbed with a warm cloth.

### PROPOSITION VII.

->*To explain what is unique about stopped pipes and chimney pipes.*<-

Stopped pipes have the same parts as open ones, from which they differ in two things: namely, in that they are closed at the end, either by a plate of lead or tin that is soldered on, or attached with wax or other glue at the end of the pipe, or by a piece of wood called the <term>Stopper</term> <note>original: *Tampon*</note>; and then in that one attaches <term>ears</term> <note>original: *oreilles*</note> to the sides of the mouth. These are for tuning them, because in proportion to how much one shades the opening by bending the said ears over it, the pipes lower their sound by as much as a half-tone or a quarter-tone.

As for the proportion of their length to their width, they are made three times longer than they are wide, though they are long enough when the length is a <term>double sesquitierce</term> <note>original: *double ſeſquitierce*; a ratio of 7:3</note> of the width—that is to say, as seven is to three—or when it is a <term>double superbipartient three</term> <note>original: *double ſurbipartisſante trois*; a ratio of 8:3</note>—that is to say, as eight is to three. When the pipes are small, their length can be equal to their width, so that the sheet or plate from which their body is made is square.

The <term>chimney pipes</term> <note>original: *tuyaux à cheminée*; pipes with a small cylinder protruding from the cap to modify the tone</note> are no different from the preceding ones except that a small cylinder is added to the end, which is similar to a small chimney. Its circumference is one-fourth that of the pipe, and its height is half of that same circumference; consequently, the height of the chimney is double its own circumference, though these proportions are not so necessary that they cannot be changed in a thousand ways. There are still other pipes made in the shape of a spindle, and others that are wider at the top than at the bottom, in order to make them imitate <term>Cornets</term> and <term>Trumpets</term>. But it is enough to remark that one can give an infinite number of different shapes to pipes, both open and stopped, following the various inventions of geometry. For example, they can be made from parts of a parabola, a hyperbola, or an ellipse, from which <term>organ builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> can derive new graces for the harmony. However, I wanted to note the ordinary shapes that builders give to all sorts of pipes, so that one may know what is standard practice. When the pipes are made of wood, they are made square by taking four boards in the shape of four parallelograms and gluing them together with strong glue. One of these is cut into a <term>bevel</term> <note>original: *bizeau*</note> to form the mouth and the <term>languid</term> <note>original: *languette*; the internal block that helps produce the sound</note> of the pipe, though they can all be made round in the shape of cylinders by means of a lathe, as one makes flageolets and flutes. Usually, oak or <term>deal</term> <note>original: *bois blanc*; literally "white wood," often referring to fir or pine</note> is used, though any other sort of wood may be used, such as boxwood, cedar, etc.

### PROPOSITION VIII.

->*To explain the material, the proportion, and the manufacture of reed pipes, and everything belonging to them.*<-

These pipes are very different from the preceding ones, both in their form and their material; therefore, it is necessary to explain their manufacture, their material, their shape, and their proportion. As for the shape, it consists principally of two parts: one is a hollow or concave half-cylinder, and the other is a very thin and slender blade called the *Tongue* <note>original: *Languette*</note>, which covers the concavity of the half-cylinder that some call the <term>Shallot</term> <note>original: *L’eſchalotte*</note>. Now, the material of both is usually <term>brass</term> <note>original: *leton*; a copper-zinc alloy</note>, although they can be made of gold, silver, steel, etc., particularly the half-cylinder. For the cover called the *Tongue* cannot be made of tin or other metals that are too soft, because they cannot strike the air hard enough or fast enough to produce pleasant sounds that are as bright and robust as desired. This is why brass tongues are used; they must be forged very evenly, filed very straight, and well-placed, for <term>annealed brass</term> <note>original: *leton recuit*</note> that has not been re-forged is worthless for these tongues.

The shallot represents the mouth or the palate, and the cover serves as its ton-

After one has made the <term>shallot</term> <note>original: *echalotte*; the small metal tube or "reed" that serves as the foundation for the vibrating part of the pipe</note> **α β γ**, it is covered with the <term>tongue</term> <note>original: *languette*; the thin, flexible metal strip that beats against the shallot to produce sound</note> **δ ε**, which is equal to it in size: and then it is inserted into a larger cylinder of wood, or of another material, such as **λ κ μ ν**, which is called the <term>Block</term> <note>original: *Noyau*; the heavy plug that sits in the boot of the pipe and holds the reed assembly in place</note>, and which is drilled to the same size as the shallot, so that it enters inside with its tongue, by which it is covered: and because it must be held firm, and remain motionless inside the block, one pushes in the small wooden wedge **ζ**, which

...has the same shape as the half-cylinder to fill half of the hole.

As for the other end of the <term>tongue</term> <note>original: *languette*; the thin, vibrating metal strip of the reed</note>, namely **δ**, it must be free to move with more or less force and speed, according to the sound it must produce and the length allowed to it; for it is shortened as much as one desires by means of a wire made of iron or <term>brass</term> <note>original: *laton*</note> that passes through the small hole **10** made in the <term>block</term> <note>original: *noyau*; the lead or metal plug that holds the reed assembly in the pipe</note>. In this block, the wire must be held firmly enough so that it cannot be raised or lowered without force, so that it always keeps the tongue in the same state as the <term>builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> set it, until it becomes necessary to move this wire and make it descend or ascend to tune the reed pipes. Those seen here are called *Regals*, or *human voices*, because they imitate them.

This iron wire is called the *movement*, the *spring*, or the *rudder*, and is bent at the end, as seen at letters **ζ η**, in order to press the tongue against its body, and to close or open it as much as is necessary to make the pipe "speak," and to bring the Regals into tune. For the more the reed is "open"—that is to say, the farther the head of the iron wire **η ζ** is from the tip of the tongue **δ**—the lower the sound of the reed becomes, because it beats the wind or the air more slowly. Conversely, the closer the head of the same iron is to **δ**, the higher the sound, because the part of the tongue that beats the air (the part from **ζ** to **δ**) is shorter, and consequently it makes its vibrations more quickly. Just as the movement of a lever is slower as it is larger, so the movement of the tongue, which is similar to that of a spring, is more sluggish as it is larger; for the cycles of larger bodies customarily last longer.

Now, this spring of the reed, which some call the <term>tuning wire</term> <note>original: *Rasette*</note>, serves to raise or lower its pitch, and to tighten or loosen it, just as the tuning pins or hammers serve to stretch or loosen strings. It can make the tongue rise through all the intervals of an octave, just as the bridge of a <term>monochord</term> <note>an ancient single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals</note> or the pins of other instruments make the strings rise in pitch. Thus, the spring **η θ** can be called a "movable bridge," and the reed can serve as a monochord.

I have also shown the block of this reed separately, so that one may better understand the two openings, of which **λ π** is the one into which the top of the reed is fitted. Thus, nothing is left to be desired that is not found here, where I have also placed two figures on the left side to show the construction and beauty of the <term>Regals</term>, reeds, or *human voices*. These are made of silver or brass, and their spring can pass through the two small holes of the block as in the first examples, or through the first opening of the block and then back through a hole made in the body of the reed, as seen at point **i** of the first of the small Regals (whose body is **i, c**, and the spring is **g, e, f**). This spring holds much more firmly on the first than on the second Regal, because of the tension the end of the spring undergoes when passing through hole **i**.

As for the two tongues of these two Regals, they are shown in two ways, like those of the other two reeds: namely, fully face-on and from the side, so that one may see how they open while "speaking." But it must be noted that they are all shown here in their natural size, and that the smallest are in unison with an open eight-foot pipe—that is to say, at <term>chapel pitch</term> <note>original: *ton de Chappelle*; the standard pitch used for church music in the 17th century</note>—and the largest are in unison with pipes of sixteen or twenty-four feet.

feet, although they cannot speak well if one does not add bodies proportioned to their thickness and length; from these, the <term>reeds</term> <note>original: *anches*; here referring to the complete reed assembly</note> receive several names according to the difference of their sounds, for the simple reeds are almost indifferent to all sorts of sounds, and are modified and determined by the different shape or size of the bodies that are added to them.

For if their bodies are much wider at the top than at the bottom, they are called *Trumpets*, or *Clarions*, because they imitate the sound of those instruments; and if they are longer without widening at the top, they are called *Cromornes*. But it is not necessary to observe as exact a proportion between the reeds as between the other pipes, for the reason that a single reed can serve several tones. From this it follows that <term>builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*; organ builders or instrument makers</note> do not make every reed of a different size, even though they must produce different tones, and they make the same thickness and length serve four or five tones, just as makers of <term>Spinnets</term> <note>original: *Epinettes*; a small type of harpsichord</note> make the same thickness of string serve four or five different sounds that follow one another immediately.

Nevertheless, their harmony would be more agreeable and more natural if each reed kept the proportion of its interval and of the tone it has, for nothing is ever better than when it is in its just proportion and size, and when the sense perfectly corresponds to reason, and the sensible to the intellectual. Now, since human voices are made of these <term>tongues</term> <note>original: *languettes*; the vibrating metal strips</note>, and they make the organs so accomplished, everything belonging to them must be added.

As for the bodies of the Reeds, it must be noted that the largest <term>Trumpet</term> <note>original: *Trompette*</note> is eight feet long, two feet wide at the top, and half a foot at the bottom; upon which it is so easy to create a <term>scale</term> <note>original: *Diapason*; the chart of measurements for a rank of pipes</note> that it is not necessary to speak of it. The <term>Cromorne</term> <note>original: *Cromorne*; a reed stop imitating the woodwind instrument of the same name</note> is four feet long and is completely straight, except that about four inches from the end, a second <term>horn</term> <note>original: *Cornet*; here referring to a section of the resonator</note> four inches long is added; it is one foot wide at the top and half a foot at the bottom. The <term>Human Voice</term> <note>original: *Voix humaine*</note> is a horn of two feet: its true body is half a foot, of which it has two-thirds the width at the top, and half as much at the bottom. The <term>box</term> <note>original: *Boëtte*; a cap or resonator chamber</note> which is soldered to the end is two inches long and is equal in width to the end of the preceding horn.

The horn of the last pipe of the Human Voice is only three and a half inches long, with half an inch in the box, of which it has two-thirds at the top and half as much at the bottom, like the preceding one. From this, it is easy to determine the method of making its scale, for one must only draw a line of six inches to represent the large horn, and one of three and a half inches for the smallest, in order to divide the rest into fifteen parts, as we have done above for the reeds. And then one can make another similar division to cut the boxes for the ends of the horns, to which they are equal in width; this will be understood even more clearly in the Proposition that follows, in which the <term>practice of builders</term> <note>original: *Facteurs*; organ builders or makers</note> is seen.

### PROPOSITION X.

->*To explain the scale, construction, and all the parts of the Human Voice [pipes] of the Organ.*<-

ALTHOUGH organ reeds do not express the Human Voice as well as parrots, who laugh and speak so perfectly that there is almost no way to discern them from the speech or laughter of men, they nonetheless imitate the voice so closely that many are deceived by them. They so greatly surpass all other pipes that the harmony of others loses its luster in the presence of the Human Voice, just as the stars lose their light in the brightness of the Sun. This is why I add this Proposition to explain more particularly the method of making them and all their parts, which are six in number. The body A F must first be considered, which is composed of two parts: one of which is of equal width, namely A B C D, and the other B D F E, which decreases toward the bottom end.

The shallot I L M is the third piece, upon which is placed the <term>tongue</term> <note>original: *languette*</note> N, which creates the sound when pressed against the shallot. The <term>block</term> <note>original: *noyau*</note> F G is the fifth part, which is soldered to the narrowest end of the Human Voice pipe. The iron wire *b h* is the sixth part, which passes through the Human Voice pipe; now it

It should be noted that eight of them are made to the same length, as seen in the figure. And when this proportion is applied to the Reeds, they can serve for all kinds of reed stops, provided they do not exceed the pitch of a stopped four-foot pipe, which corresponds to the natural pitch of men's voices.

## PROPOSITION XI.

->Explaining in how many ways one can raise or lower the pitch or the sound of organ pipes *and of the reeds without changing their lengths or widths, and which tuning tools the builders use.*<-

I have already said in the previous Proposition that the Reeds rise or fall in pitch by the movement of their springs or tuning wires <note>original: *rasettes*</note>. However, one can also make them lower in pitch without moving the wire by placing small pieces of wax on different parts of the tongues <note>The thin metal vibrating strips</note>, which move more slowly the more they are weighted; from this, it happens that the sound of the Reeds becomes softer and more pleasant.

As for the other pipes, if they are open, they are made to rise in pitch in two ways: namely by increasing the height of their mouth or their windway <note>original: *lumiere*; the narrow gap where the air escapes to hit the lip</note>, and by opening them further at the top end, from which one also sometimes cuts a piece to decrease the length until they are in tune. But they are made to lower in pitch by narrowing them at the same end, or by putting a little wax on the top of the mouth to decrease its size.

Now, the builders <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> use small hollow cones to tune these pipes; they decrease the width by capping them with the said cone, pressing down until they are narrow enough and descend to the pitch they ought to have.

-> [Image: A diagram of two tuning cones. On the left, a double-ended tool with cones A-B-C-D and F-G-H connected by rod I. On the right, a single tuning cone A-D.] <-

the first **A B C D** serves to narrow the top of the open pipes: but so that the hand has more strength, one grasps the second **F H G** to push and turn the first upon the said pipes: and when one wants to widen them, one grasps the first to push the second into the same pipes with a greater force and more ease: and for this purpose they are joined together with a bar of whatever material one wishes, which is soldered at points **D** and **E** with the two Tuning Cones: though one also often uses a single Tuning Cone, such as the one seen all alone.

Now, these Tuning Cones are ordinarily made of **brass** <note>original: *laton*</note>, so that they might be stronger and of longer duration, and so that the surface of the pipes yields to their exterior or interior surfaces, such that they narrow or widen as much as the tools do. And because there are several thicknesses of pipes, the **Organ Builders** <term>Facteurs: the historical term for makers of organs or other complex instruments</term> have need of several sorts of Tuning Cones, some of which serve for the smallest pipes, and others for the largest. But when the pipes are **stopped** <note>that is, closed at the top</note>, these Tuning Cones cannot serve; this is why one solders small strips of lead to the two sides of their mouths, in order to lower them down to make the tone lower, or to raise them up to make them rise to more acute sounds. The Builders call them **ears** <note>original: *oreilles*</note>, as if they were listening to see if the pipes are in tune: and when they are lowered, they say that one **shades the light** <note>original: *ombrage la lumiere*; the "light" refers to the opening or "mouth" of the pipe where the sound is produced</note>. One also uses small pieces of wax for the same purpose when the pipes have no ears, as happens with wooden pipes, at the end of which one often puts **stoppers** <note>original: *tampons*</note> that one pushes as far as one wants toward their mouth, until they have been put in tune. And so that they plug the pipe more precisely, they are covered with a piece of **sheepskin** <note>original: *cuir de mouton*</note>, which prevents the wind from being lost between the internal surface of the pipe and the stopper. But all these manners used to tune the pipes serve only to make them rise or fall by a quarter-tone or a half-tone; this is why expert Builders usually cut them so precisely that they are no further from their true tuning than a half-tone.

One can also make the pipes rise in pitch by widening the hole of their **feet**, which gives them a stronger wind, and make them descend by diminishing the wind through the reduction of the same hole: but I shall speak of the change of sounds made by the change of wind in another place, although what I have said in the book on **Wind Instruments**, and particularly in the treatise on the **Trumpet**, may satisfy all that one could desire here.

## PROPOSITION XII.

->*To determine if one can make an Organ that has all its pipes of the same height; that is to say, if the sole difference in their widths can produce the range of four Octaves that are usually found on the Organ: and to show in what ratio their widths must be to produce such sounds and intervals as one desires.*<-

---

This Proposition is very remarkable, especially since many believe that if one makes a pipe twice as wide, it will descend as low in pitch as when it is twice as long, because it is of the same size—for if you fill them both with air or water, they will hold as much as one another. From this, it would follow that a pipe double in width or thickness would descend by an **Octave**, just like a pipe that is double in length, so that the ratio of harmonic intervals would follow that of the widths or thicknesses of pipes of the same height: which is contrary to experience and to truth. For from several pipes of the same height that I had made specifically, whose base diameters are in the same proportion as these numbers 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, I have always observed that the one with double the diameter descends only by a **Minor Third** lower than the one that is half the diameter, except that the slenderest of all, being half the size of the one immediately following it, rises only by one **tone** <note>In music theory, a "tone" or "whole step" is a standard interval, such as the distance between C and D.</note>.

Now I wish to set down here the length and thickness of the pipes I used, so that if others encounter different intervals in smaller or larger pipes, they may have the opportunity to seek the reason for it. As for the length, they are all half a **Royal foot** <note>original: *pied de Roy*; a pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 32.5 cm. Half a foot is about 16 cm.</note>; and the diameter of the base of the slenderest is only three **lines** <note>original: *lignes*; a historical unit of measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch.</note>. The second is half an inch, or six lines, for it is double the preceding one. The third is one inch, the fourth is two, and the fifth is a little more than four: so that the diameters of these five pipes always follow the geometric progression of two to one, following the preceding numbers. From this, it follows that the diameter of the largest is sixteen times that of the slenderest, and that its base—and consequently its void, or its capacity, and its surface, both convex and concave—is in the same ratio to the slenderest as 256 to 1. 

Let us now see their sounds and their intervals; the smallest rises only one tone higher than the second, whose diameter is double. But the third, which has a diameter double that of the second, descends a **Minor Third** lower than the second, and consequently creates a **Fourth** <note>A musical interval spanning four degrees of a scale, such as C to F.</note> with the first. But before continuing the doubling ratio, it must be noted that a pipe whose diameter is to the diameter of the preceding one as the diagonal of a square is to its side <note>original: *diametre du quarré à son costé*; this refers to the ratio of the square root of 2, or approximately 1.414:1.</note>, descends lower by one tone; I leave the consideration of this for now so as not to interrupt the order of the five pipes whose diameters are in double ratio to one another.

I add only that the diameter of this pipe is the **proportional mean** between the diameter of the preceding one and the one following, whose diameter is double that of the third. Now, this fourth pipe descends a **Minor Third** lower than the third; and consequently, it creates a **Tritone** <note>An interval of three whole tones, historically known as the "Devil's interval" for its dissonance.</note> with the second pipe, and an **Augmented Fifth** <note>original: *Quinte superfluë*; an interval a half-step larger than a perfect fifth.</note> with the first.

The fifth pipe descends even lower than the fourth by a...

But when it follows the proportion according to the width of the pipe, it produces only a **Seventh** with the thinnest one; consequently, one would have to increase its diameter by two inches to produce a perfect **Octave**, so that its diameter would be half a **Royal Foot** <note>The *pied de Roy* (Royal Foot) was a standard French unit of length before the metric system, measuring approximately 32.5 centimeters or 12.8 inches.</note>, which is to say twenty-four times larger than that of the thinnest pipe. It is therefore certain that the width of the pipes cannot compensate for their lengths, since it is not possible to descend or ascend as far as the **Octave** using pipes of the same height, as experiments show. For the length of the thinnest pipe being half a foot, and consequently eight times its width, it can hardly "speak" <note>In organ building, a pipe is said to "speak" when it produces a clear, stable musical tone.</note>; the same occurs with the largest pipe, whose width is twelve and a half inches, or thereabouts, and the diameter is four inches; and if it were six inches, it would be equal to its height and could not speak at all, since the four-inch pipe already has great difficulty sounding. Thus, one can say that the thinnest and the widest pipes represent the two absolute extremes, and that the **Octave** marks the limit of the capacity of their widths and diameters.

## COROLLARY.

It must be particularly noted in these experiments that the first two pipes (the thinnest ones) do not maintain the same <term>ratios</term> <note>original: "raisons"; here meaning the mathematical proportions between the physical size and the resulting pitch.</note> between their sounds as the larger ones do. Since the second pipe is double the size of the first, it descends only by one **tone** and not by a **Minor Third**, for which a reason must be found. This makes me doubt whether pipes even larger than those I tested would produce a **Minor Third**, or some smaller or larger interval, assuming they could speak at all. In any case, the base of pipes of the same height must be in a quadruple ratio, and their diameters in a double ratio, to produce a **Minor Third**—which can be made into a **Major Third** by blowing harder into one than the other. Now, having explained what pertains to the width of the pipes, we must see what happens with their different lengths, so that we may consider these concave cylinders in every possible way, just as we did with the solid copper cylinders in the second book on movements, where one can see the different sounds made by cylinders of different thicknesses when they are all of the same height.

<meta>catchword: PROPOSITION</meta>

<summary>The author concludes that increasing the diameter of an organ pipe does not lower the pitch as much as increasing its length, proving that width cannot substitute for height in organ construction. He notes that physical extremes in pipe width eventually prevent the pipe from producing any sound at all.</summary>

# On Organs.

### PROPOSITION XIII.

->*To determine in what ratio the lengths of pipes of the same width must be in order to produce the required sounds and intervals: and whether one can make an Organ, all of whose pipes are of the same width.*<-

Since human reason alone cannot find the proportions of bodies and sounds—as I showed in the second book on motions, where one sees that cylinders of the same width and different lengths do not produce sounds that maintain the same ratio among themselves as their lengths—for example, that a pipe which is double in length does not produce the **Octave**, as many believe; we must again consult experience <note>In this context, "experience" (experience) refers to a scientific experiment.</note> here, in order to observe that sounds do not follow the ratio of the length of pipes of the same width either. However, they come close, particularly with small pipes; for a pipe half a foot long, with a diameter of three lines <note>A "line" (ligne) was a traditional French unit of length equal to 1/12th of an inch, or about 2.25 millimeters.</note>, comes so close to the **Octave** of a pipe half its length that it is difficult to notice by how much it is too weak. But having conducted the experiment on larger pipes that "speak" <note>In organ building, a pipe is said to "speak" when it produces a clear, stable musical tone.</note> better, I have noticed that there is usually a difference of a half-tone, or nearly a full tone, before the pipe double in length produces the **Octave**. Nevertheless, if one cuts off different parts of the same pipe according to the ratios of musical intervals—for example, if one removes an eighth part, it rises by a **Tone**; if one removes a fourth part, it rises by a **Fourth**; if one removes two-fifths, it rises to a **Fifth**, or very nearly so.

As for the second part of the Proposition, it is certain that all the pipes of the Organ cannot be of the same width, even though they have a much greater range of sound than pipes of the same length but different widths. This is because a pipe differing only in its length can rise by two or three **Octaves**. For example, of two pipes four lines in diameter, one of which is triple the length of the other, the shorter one rises higher by an **Eleventh**, and not a **Twelfth**, as it should if the sounds followed the length of the pipes. And yet, it must be nearly four times shorter to produce the said **Twelfth**, for it only rises to the **minor Sixth**, or at most the **major Sixth** above the **Octave**—that is to say, to the **Thirteenth**—while being four times shorter.

Being five times shorter, it produces the **Fifteenth**. Being six times shorter, it produces the **major Sixteenth**. Being seven times shorter, it produces the **major Seventeenth**. Being eight times shorter, it produces the **Nineteenth**, beyond which one can no longer distinguish the high pitch of its sounds. But because these two pipes are perhaps too slender to rely on these experiments—and because the largest, being twenty-four times the diameter of its base, has difficulty speaking, and similarly, the small one eight times shorter no longer speaks well—I have conducted other experiments on larger, better-proportioned pipes.

Having therefore taken a pipe double the width of the previous one—that is to say, with a diameter of half an inch and a length of half a foot (from which it follows that its length is four times its width, or twelve times its diameter)—and having shortened it by one-ninth, it rises a tone higher and con-

...consequently it produces the **Unison** with the pipe that is half its thickness. <note>Mersenne uses the term "sub-double" (souz-double) to refer to a 1:2 ratio.</note>

If this same pipe is shortened by one inch—that is to say, by a sixth part—it rises by a **Major Third**, even though it should only rise by a **Minor Third** (which follows the ratio of six to five) if the decrease in pitch followed the decrease in length. Thus, the interval of the sounds increases more here than it ought to, whereas it did not increase enough in the previous experiments. Nevertheless, it still produces the same **Third** somewhat more accurately when it is shortened by a fifth part. For this reason, I believe it produces the **Minor Third** instead when it is only shortened by a sixth part, given that other experiments show the sounds of this pipe follow the ratios of these shortenings: for having shortened it by a quarter, it produces the **Fourth**; being shortened by a third, it produces the **Fifth**. But being shortened by half, it does not produce the **Octave** unless one shortens it by a further two lines <note>A "line" (ligne) was a traditional French unit of length equal to 1/12th of an inch, or about 2.25 millimeters.</note>, which make up the eighteenth part of a quarter-foot.

By shortening it by two-thirds, so that it is only two inches long, it rises to the **Major Tenth**, whereas it should rise to the **Twelfth**, since its length is to that of a half-foot as one is to three. Shortened by three-quarters—that is, being to the half-foot as one is to four—it produces the **Twelfth**, and still speaks <note>In organ building, a pipe is said to "speak" when it produces a clear, stable musical tone.</note> very well, which did not happen with the pipe that was half as slender, as I have already remarked.

Shortened by 5/6ths—that is, having only one inch left, it produces the **Fifteenth** <note>The "Fifteenth" (quinzième) is an interval of two octaves.</note> compared to the six-inch pipe; but one must give it a great deal of "wind" <note>Air pressure provided by the bellows.</note> to make it speak, and its height is then only twice its diameter. But if it is shortened further, its sounds are no longer of any value. For example, if it is shortened by a quarter of what remains (that is, by three lines), it seems to rise by one tone above the **Fifteenth**. Finally, if it is shortened so much that its height is equal to the diameter of its base, it no longer speaks.

Now, one can conclude from this whole discourse that pipes of the same thickness cannot produce all the tones of one of the Organ stops, and that they can produce at most the **Fifteenth**, which is worthless because the sound is too shrill, and cannot be produced by the wind from the bellows, which must be steady. Instead, the wind required to make shortened pipes rise to the **Fifteenth** is very violent, and similar to that by which one makes a single pipe rise to the **Fifteenth** without shortening it—as I shall explain after speaking of the different lengths of pipes joined to their different thicknesses. From this, we shall derive the method for making the **Diapason** <note>In this context, the "Diapason" refers to the "scaling" or the measurement chart used by organ builders to determine the proportions of pipes for a rank.</note> of Organs for the Builders.

### PROPOSITION XIV.

->*To explain the ratio that pipes must have between their lengths and their widths to produce all the steps of one or several Octaves: and to provide a very accurate Scaling Chart.*<-

Since experience has shown us that pipes must be of different lengths and thicknesses to produce all the sounds of the Organ, we must join these two dimensions together in order to have sounds that are proportioned both in their pitch and in their sweetness and harmony.

# Regarding Organs.

Let us now see what ratio the lengths and widths ought to have. Regarding this, I have found through experiment that when the lengths of two pipes are in a double ratio <note>original: "raison double," meaning a 2:1 ratio</note>, it is not enough for their widths to be in the same ratio as the diagonal is to the side of a square <note>This refers to the ratio of √2:1, often used in geometric scaling.</note>, which is half of the double ratio. This is because when that occurs, the longer pipe does not produce the **Octave** unless it is more than double in height. For example, I have two pipes: the shorter is half a foot long and eleven lines in diameter; the one that is sixteen lines in diameter cannot produce a perfect **Octave** below it unless it is more than double in length by a third of an inch, which makes four lines. <note>A "line" (ligne) is 1/12th of an inch.</note> This third of an inch would almost suffice to make it produce the same **Octave** even if it were only eleven lines in diameter; thus, thickness serves very little to lower the pitch, as we have already remarked. However, pipes produce exactly the interval one desires if their heights and widths have the same ratio as the said interval. For example, if one gives twenty-two lines in diameter to a pipe one foot high, it will produce a perfect **Octave** with a pipe half a foot high whose diameter is eleven lines. From this, it follows that if we consider the pipes as solid cylinders, they must be in the tripled ratio <note>The ratio of their volumes (cubed).</note> of the ratio of the intervals, which represent the roots and the simple length of the pipes, just as the doubled ratio of the said intervals represents the cylindrical surfaces of the pipes.

Now, it is easy to calculate the **Cubes** of all the pipes, for one must only triple the radical terms of the ratios of each interval, as Mr. Cornu has done in the following table. The first column represents the length, and consequently the width of the pipes, and the second represents the solidity—that is to say, the capacity of their internal void.

The second pipe, which produces the **Octave**, is 1/2 foot long, and is measured from the second C to "o." Here it must be noted that the measurement of each pipe is found more easily when it produces a better **consonance** <note>A "consonance" is a musical interval that sounds stable and pleasant to the ear.</note> and a more excellent harmony with the first. From this, it follows that one finds the pipe that rises to the **Octave** more easily than any other.

In the second place, one finds the pipe that produces the **Fifth**, or **G re sol** <note>These compound names (G re sol, F ut, etc.) are part of the "hexachord" system used in the Renaissance and Baroque to name notes based on their position in different scales.</note>, by dividing the entire line into three equal parts, two of which give the **G re sol**; thus, one need only leave one-third of the line from the first C to the G. In the same way, one must leave 1/4 of the same line to have the pipe **F**, which produces the **Fourth**. Next, one must leave a 1/5 part to have the **E mi la**, which produces the **Major Third**; and 1/6 to have the upper accidental <note>original: "feinte"</note> of **E mi la**, which produces the **Minor Third** against the first C. But to have the **Minor Sixth**, that is to say, the pipe of the upper accidental of **A mi la re**, one must leave 3/8 of the entire line divided into eight parts, and 2/5 of the same line divided into five parts to have the pipe **A mi la re**, or the **Major Sixth**.

All the other pipes are found similarly by means of the **Consonances**; for the **B fa si** is found by dividing the pipe **F** into four parts, three of which give the pipe **B**, which produces a **Fourth** with **F**. And if one divides the **G** into five equal parts, four of them give the **B natural** <note>original: "# mi"</note>, which produces a **Major Third** with **G**. It is easy to find all the other accidentals by the same **Consonances**; for if one divides **E** into five equal parts and adds one of these parts from **E** toward **C**, one will have the upper accidental of the first **C**, which produces a **Minor Third** with **E**.

If one further wishes to have the **Major Third** above against **A**, one must divide **A** into five parts, four of which give a new accidental above, and eight similar parts taken on the entire line give it below. Now, we have not yet found the pipe **D la re sol**, which is the second **Diatonic** <note>The second note of the natural scale.</note>, which can be found in several ways; for if one divides the pipe **A** into two parts and adds one of these parts toward the first **C**, one will have the pipe **D**. This is also found by dividing **F** into five equal parts, to which if one adds one more, one will have the same **D**. It is also found by dividing the entire line into nine or ten parts, for once one of these parts is removed, one has one or the other of the **D la re sol** notes, which produce the **major tone** or the **minor tone** with **C**. <note>The author is referencing the "Just Intonation" system where there are two different sizes of whole steps (9:8 and 10:9 ratios).</note>

Finally, one will have the accidental of **F** <note>F-sharp.</note> if one divides **D** into six parts, five of which will give the said accidental, which produces a **Major Third** below against **D**. Consequently, one will have the thirteen keys of the ordinary keyboard <note>original: "clauier"</note>, and the thirteen pipes of the **Register** <note>A "Register" or stop is a full set of pipes of a particular sound quality.</note>, or the rank of an open or stopped half-foot pipe. ...several other ways that one can use by means of **consonances** <note>In music theory, a consonance is an interval that sounds stable and harmonious, such as a Perfect Fifth or a Major Third.</note> to find the same pipes, in order to explain the second method, which begins with the smallest intervals, whereas the first method began with the largest. One first finds the first **accidental** <note>original: "feinte." In early music, this referred to the "feigned" or chromatic notes, typically the black keys on a keyboard.</note> of C by dividing the said C—that is to say, the largest pipe or the longest line—into twenty-five equal parts, of which one is left out or removed to obtain the said accidental. And if one wants the second accidental of C, which is often necessary to create just consonances, one must divide C into sixteen parts and remove one to mark the second accidental, which creates the **minor semitone** <note>A "semitone" is a half-step; Mersenne is distinguishing between two different sizes of half-steps used in older tuning systems.</note> or the **major semitone** with the said C, against which the first accidental creates the minor semitone.

One obtains the pipe for D by dividing C into ten parts, of which one is removed, for the 9/10ths give the first D, which creates a **minor tone** <note>A "tone" is a whole step. In "just intonation," there are two types of whole steps: the "major tone" (ratio 9:8) and the "minor tone" (ratio 10:9).</note> against C, with which the second D makes a **major tone**. However, one must divide the C into nine parts and remove one to have this second D, which is distant from the other by a **comma** <note>A "comma" is a very small interval, roughly 1/9th of a whole tone, representing the mathematical difference between different ways of calculating the same note.</note>. If one wishes to have two accidentals for D similar to the two accidentals for C, one must divide this second D as one divided the C: namely, into twenty-five parts to obtain the accidental of twenty-four, and into sixteen to obtain that of fifteen. And then one must divide the first D into nine parts, or the second into ten, to obtain the pipe for E, by removing 1/9th or 1/10th part. And the **E mi la** <note>A specific name for the note E in the hexachord system.</note> divided into sixteen parts, of which one is removed, gives fifteen for F; from this, one will have two accidentals by dividing it as C was divided into twenty-five and sixteen parts, for twenty-four will give the first accidental and fifteen its second. But it will give eight parts for G when it has been divided into nine parts; and G being divided like C or D, it will give its two accidentals (against which it will make the major and minor semitones) and the pipe for A, against which it makes a minor tone. And A being divided into sixteen parts, the fifteen give B; and if it is divided into nine, the eight give the **B-sharp** <note>original: "#"</note>, which being divided into sixteen parts, the fifteen give the final pipe C, which creates the **Octave** above the first C.

From this, it appears that **Builders** <note>original: "Facteurs," referring to organ builders or instrument makers.</note> do not need a greater knowledge to make their **Scale** <note>original: "Diapason." In this context, it refers to a measuring rule or proportional guide for pipe dimensions.</note> and their pipes very accurately, even though all the pipes I have mentioned are not sufficient to provide all the just consonances against every **key** <note>original: "marche," referring to the physical keys of the keyboard.</note>, and one might still desire some other accidental for this purpose. This is why I am adding another scale so universal that one could desire nothing more, unless one wishes to proceed to infinity. But it must be noted that the preceding figure is a little different from the description I have made of the last scale, or of the second method I explained; for the two accidentals between F and G differ only by a comma, and the B is double like the D, for the reasons I explained from the fourth to the seventh Proposition of the third book of **Genera** <note>Referring to the "Musical Genera," a classical Greek concept of dividing the scale into different types of intervals (Diatonic, Chromatic, Enharmonic).</note>; this in no way prevents one from understanding what I have said.

As for the number 3600, which signifies that the largest pipe being divided into that many parts, the other pipes have the parts that remain, I explained it in the same place; from this, one can conclude that it is the smallest of all those numbers that can represent the nineteen pipes, or the nineteen sounds of the Octave, which has all its consonances perfect, and where I have shown the use of this scale.

### PROPOSITION XV.

*Explain all types of **scales**, **canons**, or harmonic rules that can be used to perfect Organs.*

I have already explained several types of **diapasons** <term>diapason: here referring to a standardized scale or a rule of proportions used to determine the length and diameter of pipes</term> in the book on Dissonances and stringed instruments, but the following table contains everything that can reasonably be desired on this subject, without it being necessary for **organ builders** <note>original: "Facteurs"</note> to know anything else. Now, this table contains eleven columns, which show the length and width of the pipes, the first of which shows the thirteen degrees of the **tempered scale** <note>original: "Diapason temperé." This refers to a tuning system, such as equal temperament, where the octave is divided into twelve equal or nearly equal semitones.</note>; which has its twelve equal, or nearly equal, semitones. But it must be noted that the line **a** represents a pipe one foot long, and that one must only double, triple, or quadruple its intervals to have pipes of two, three, or four feet, or multiply it by sixteen, twenty-four, or thirty-two, to have the largest ones that can be used.

This first column is divided into twelve intervals, or thirteen degrees, each of which has its particular number, so that the eleven numbers between 1000 and 500 represent the eleven **mean proportionals** <note>In mathematics, these are the values found between two extremes in a geometric progression; in music, they are used to divide the octave into equal parts.</note>, of which I spoke in the treatise on the Luth, and elsewhere.

The second and third columns contain another **temperament** <note>A system of tuning that slightly adjusts pure intervals so that instruments can play in multiple keys without sounding out of tune.</note> which also similarly has thirteen degrees in the third column, following the ideas of **Salinas** <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a Spanish music theorist who proposed various systems of "mean-tone" temperament.</note>: but because he draws this temperament from his Octave of twenty-five degrees, he places twenty degrees there, namely the thirteen from this third column, and the seven from the second, which are marked by simple **sharps** <note>original: "dieſes"</note>, each of which has a letter, which refers to the **Diatonic** <note>The standard seven-note scale (like the white keys on a piano).</note> letter that follows or precedes it. But I will speak of temperaments in another Proposition.

As for the fourth and fifth columns, they show the thirteen pipes in their perfection, and without temperament <note>This refers to "Just Intonation," where intervals are based on pure mathematical ratios (like 3:2 for a fifth) rather than being adjusted or "tempered."</note> according to the discourse of the preceding Proposition. But the fourth column contains the four entire Octaves, that is to say, the entire keyboard of the Organ: and has thirteen degrees in the first Octave, and fourteen in the second, so that one may see the degree, or the step, that is missing from the said keyboard of ordinary Organs. The third Octave has only the eight Diatonic degrees by **B-flat** <note>original: "b mol"</note>, and the fourth contains them by **B-natural** <note>original: "X quarre," a reference to the "square B" (B-quadratum) used in early notation to signify B-natural.</note>. I have placed these four Octaves in this column so that it may serve as a **scale** <note>original: "Diapaſon"</note> for Organists and Builders, who cannot fail by following it exactly; this is why I have placed the numbers for each degree of these four Octaves in the fifth column, the first of which has all its numbers as whole numbers; but the others have some of theirs which are fractions, which one can avoid by taking the numbers of the first Octave for those of the fourth, and by increasing those of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th, as it is easy to conclude.

The sixth and seventh columns contain the nineteen pipes of the perfect scale, or of the Octave, which comprises the three **genres** <note>The three classifications of Greek music: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note>, of which I have spoken amply in the third book on Genres, and because the thirteen degrees, or letters of the fourth column belong to this Octave, they
