# Book Six

...are not repeated in the sixth column, so that one may more easily notice that the letters and degrees of this sixth column supplement what is missing in the fourth, which lacks six degrees. But because the seventh column does not include all the consonances of the <term>perfect Diapason of Salinas<note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590) was a Spanish music theorist; "Diapason" here refers to a complete octave scale.</note></term>, which has twenty-five degrees or twenty-five pipes in the octave, and since this one still lacks two degrees, as I have shown elsewhere, I wish to propose here the most perfect Diapason of all those given up to now. This is the one contained in the eighth and ninth columns; for the eighth contains thirteen degrees unique to itself (of which the octave in the sixth and seventh columns is deprived), since it has thirty-two degrees, sounds, steps, or pipes in its octave, each of which follows the precision of harmonic numbers.

Now, I will not dwell on the explanation of this eighth and ninth column, especially since I provide a specific discourse on it in the treatise on Keyboards. I will only say that the tenth column contains all the names of the 31 intervals of this Diapason, from which the <term>Builders<note>original: "Facteurs" — refers to organ builders or instrument makers.</note></term> can take the exact measurement of all sorts of one-foot pipes, or those that are smaller or larger; they can similarly do this using the other columns. It may also be noted in favor of Salinas that the Diapason of the 9th and 10th columns differs from his only by the seven degrees that I add to it: namely, in the accidental <note>original: "feinte" — a term for the chromatic keys or sharps/flats.</note> C#, at the first E, and at the first F, at the first G, at the second G#, at the first A, and at the first ♯ <note>The author uses 'X' and '♯' to denote sharpened notes used to find perfect harmonies not available in simpler systems.</note>, which serve to find certain consonances not found in his system.

As for the width of the pipes, it is easy to understand, because it suffices to know that the sheets or plates of tin, lead, or other material must be the 4th, 5th, or 6th part of the height of the pipes; for this is not so strictly determined that it is not permissible to make them a little wider or narrower, according to the convenience of the location or the will of the Builder, as I have already said. Now, I have marked the fourth and the sixth part of the said height for the width of the pipes in this figure, as seen in the eleventh column; for α β contains the sixth part of the height of the pipe α γ, and α φ contains a quarter of it; so that α φ γ ψ show the width and the length of the tin plate from which a one-foot open pipe is made. Similarly, ζ σ υ show the sheet from which the last pipe of the first octave is made, when its width is a quarter of its height, and when it is only a sixth part, its sheet is marked by ζ η γ θ.

The width of the plate λ η μ shows the first pipe of the third octave, and ι ζ γ o shows the first of the fourth octave, which is only three inches high. But it is so easy to know the width of all the other pipes, if one understands what I have said about these, that it is not necessary to speak of them further. This is why I leave this discourse to focus on the <term>temperament of the Organ<note>The specific way the notes are tuned to balance the purity of intervals.</note></term> that is used in all the organs of Europe, so that Builders may be ignorant of nothing that belongs to their art.

On Organs.

### PROPOSITION XVI.

*Explaining the easiest and most perfect **Diapason** <note>In this context, "Diapason" refers to a complete musical scale or the standard measurement for a set of pipes.</note> for Organs imaginable, when using **temperament**, and when only thirteen or twenty keys are desired for each Octave; and consequently providing the method for perfectly tuning ordinary Organs: wherein one sees the explanation of the second and third columns of the preceding table.*

Since I have shown that the keyboard and the Scale, which contain the **Diatonic genre** <note>The standard musical scale consisting of seven notes (five whole tones and two semitones).</note> as it is currently used in its perfection, have 32, 27, 25, or at least 19 keys or degrees for each Octave, and that ordinary Keyboards of both Organs and **Spinets** <note>A smaller, rectangular stringed keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note> only have thirteen, it follows that they cannot be perfectly in tune, since one wishes to find in them everything that is in the nineteen degrees of the perfect keyboard.

This is why one is forced to increase or decrease most of the intervals, both dissonant and consonant: and because one cannot maintain the difference between the **minor whole tone** and the **major whole tone** <note>In "just intonation," there are two different sizes of whole steps: the major tone (9:8 ratio) and the minor tone (10:9). Tuning systems usually try to reconcile these.</note>, they are made equal, so that there is no difference between the whole tones of the Organ. For this reason, the major tone is decreased by half a **comma** <note>A "comma" is a tiny musical interval, the small difference between two notes that should theoretically be the same.</note>, and the minor is increased: from which it results that the **major Thirds** remain in their perfection, for the interval of the major Third being divided proportionally, one has two equal whole tones, of which one is increased as much as the other is decreased.

And because the Octave is always perfect, and the **minor Sixth** completes the Octave with the major Third, it follows that this Sixth has its correct proportion. I will leave aside several dissonant intervals, which are also in their correct tuning—for example, the **augmented Fifth**, which is composed of two major Thirds, and the **diminished Fourth**, which exceeds the major Third by one **diesis** <note>original: "dieſe" — a very small musical interval, roughly a quarter-tone or the difference between a major and minor semitone.</note>, which also remains in its correct tuning—to explain the alteration of the other **Consonances**, the smallest of which is the **minor Third**. This is decreased by a fourth part of a comma, insofar as it is composed of a major tone and a major semitone when it is in its perfection; now, the major tone is decreased by a half-comma, and the major semitone is increased by a quarter of the same comma, for the reason that it is composed of the minor semitone, which is increased in this **temperament** <note>The practice of slightly "mistuning" intervals so that a keyboard instrument sounds acceptable in multiple keys.</note> by the said quarter of a comma, and the Diesis, which suffers no alteration, and consequently the minor Third is too small by this quarter of a comma.

The Fifth is also too weak [flat] by a quarter of a comma, since it is composed of the two Thirds; and the Fourth is too strong [sharp] by the same quarter, since it forms the Octave with the Fifth. Finally, the **major Sixth** is too strong by this same quarter, since it completes the Octave with the minor Third, which is too weak by this quarter: from which it is easy to conclude that it is enough to know by how much one weakens the Fifth and the minor Third to know by how much the other Consonances increase. I leave aside the discords or Dissonances that suffer alteration—for example, the **Tritone**, which is too weak by half a comma, and the **false Fifth** [diminished fifth], which is increased by as much since it completes the Octave—because it matters very little that the Dissonances be altered, since one does not perceive it as easily as with the consonan—

seventh composed of two Fourths is too sharp by half a comma, while the

Now, if one understands what I have just explained, it will be very easy to describe the
**Diapason** <note>The full range or scale of an instrument.</note> of perfect temperament, as can be seen in the second and
third columns of the preceding table; for the chromatic **c**, that is to say

is separated from it by a minor semitone; and because the enharmonic
accidental which follows, and which is marked with **d**, is separated by only one **diesis** <note>A very small interval, smaller than a semitone, found in enharmonic scales.</note> from the chromatic **c**, and because the Diesis must have its just proportion, the said
**d** must be raised by a quarter of a comma. And then the first **D** of the perfect system must be raised, and the second lowered by half a comma, in order to make only one out of the
two. But because it is much easier to mark the tempered Diapason

major Thirds, since they are just; from which it happens that the **E** *mi la* of the tempered Diapason is that of the perfect Diapason, since it makes a
just major Third with **C**, which it still has when ascending.

The two **#** <note>Sharp symbols.</note> of these two Diapasons also agree, insofar as **G** makes
a major Third with them. But because one cannot use this temperament
unless one places twenty keys, or degrees, in each Octave of the Keyboard,
as can be seen in the thirty-third Chapter of the third book

that which I showed in the treatise on the **Lute**, by means of which all
the semitones of the Octave are equal: although it is better to leave the
major Thirds just, which are divided into four equal semitones by the
invention of three **mean proportionals** <note>A mathematical method used to divide a musical interval into perfectly equal smaller steps.</note>; one can also divide the Fourth into five equal semitones, but because one must find four mean
proportionals for this subject, and six would be needed to divide the
Fifth into seven equal semitones, it is better to divide the major Third
as I have said, because three mean proportionals are found
geometrically and easily: which similarly happens to the minor Sixth,
which is divided into eight equal semitones by the invention of 7 mean
proportionals: so that one can say that the major Third and the
minor Sixth have a great privilege, and that they serve this temperament more than the Fourth or the Fifth; that is why they are rewarded with an accuracy that equals that of the Octave.

But all these temperaments are of no use for the construction of the Organ,
insofar as the pipes that are made according to just proportion approach so
closely to the said temperament, that the same pipes made for the
perfect Organ can serve for the imperfect, or ordinary one, because they are
not separated by more than a quarter of a comma from one another: now this quarter is
nearly 160 to 161, so that if one divides the perfect pipe into 160 parts,
the imperfect one must only be decreased or increased by one part;
which is hardly perceptible in the smallest pipes: but if the pipe were sixteen feet long,
one would have to add an inch and a half to the pipe, which would be the minor tone at the bottom; and...

The Corollaries that follow contain several other things belonging to these temperaments, and serve to explain the columns of the preceding table.

## COROLLARY I.

One can see in the small column, which is between the third and the fourth, by how much each degree of the tempered **Diapason** <note>The full range or scale of an instrument; here refers to the octave.</note> is distant from the degrees of the perfect scale, by means of the two lines of each degree of the one and the other, which terminate on the said column: for example, that the tempered D is higher by a quarter of a **comma** <note>A tiny musical interval representing the difference between two notes in different tuning systems; roughly 1/9th of a whole tone.</note> than the just D, and so on for the others; this can help **Organ Builders**, if they prefer to work by science rather than by routine.

## PROPOSITION XVII.

### Explaining the different solders that can be used for the manufacture of organ pipes.

AFTER the sheets or plates of tin and lead have been cut to the length and width of which we have spoken, one takes wooden cylinders of the same thickness that the pipes must be, in order to roll and join the said plates upon them. But since glue or solder is necessary for this, it must be noted that there are several kinds of glues, cements, and solders, according to the different materials from which one makes the pipes—whether round, square, or of another shape. For if they are made of four pieces of wood, as they are usually made to produce **recorders** <note>original: *Flustes douces*; literally "soft flutes," referring to the internal duct flutes like the recorder family.</note>, it is necessary to use the strong glue of **Joiners** <note>original: *Menuisiers*; craftsmen specializing in fine woodworking and furniture.</note> to join them in a square shape or a parallelepiped. They can also be made in a triangle from three wooden boards, like the **Tromba Marina** <note>original: *Trompette marine*; a tall, triangular-bodied, single-stringed instrument played with a bow, known for its trumpet-like sound.</note>, of which I spoke in the fourth book on stringed instruments.

One can also use fish glue, which is called *Ichthyocolla* <note>original: *Ictyocolle*; derived from the Greek *ichthys* (fish) and *kolla* (glue).</note>, or that which is used by those who **turn wood** <note>original: *tournent en l'air*; refers to the craft of wood-turning on a lathe where the piece is held in place to be shaped.</note> to attach pieces of wood, glass, crystal, copper, or other materials they wish to turn. And if the pipes are made of cardboard, one can use **Spanish wax** <note>A type of sealing wax traditionally used for documents.</note> or the ordinary glue used for the paper of window frames. I leave aside several types of mortars and cements used to bind stones together, as it is not the custom to make Organ pipes out of plaster, clay, stone, nor any other such material, though it could be done: for one could form twenty or thirty thousand pipes within great rocks, by means of several subterranean channels that would carry the wind to stone pipes, and the bellows necessary for this purpose could be raised and opened with mill wheels or other engines which are quite capable of the task.

I also leave aside **ferrumination** <note>A Latin-derived term for the process of welding or soldering iron.</note>, of which **Vigenère** <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and scholar.</note> spoke in his [translation of the] *Images* of **Philostratus** <note>A work describing a collection of ancient paintings.</note>, as pipes are not usually made of iron or steel. I will only note that the Latins gave the name *Ferrumination* to every kind of soldering, because different pieces of iron take hold of and bind themselves together very easily when they are reddened and hammered; and this solder is the strongest and hardest of all. This is perhaps what taught how to make cement with brick and glass powder, and with coal, lime, and sand, among which are mixed scales, powder, ore, or the **Crocus of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus martis*; a Latin term for iron oxide (rust) used in alchemy and as a pigment.</note>—so called by the **Chemists** because it is the color of saffron tending towards blood. Now, iron has this property by reason of its viscous and sticky fluid. I have reported this so that if the curious wish to make stone pipes, they may use this kind of cement, which is the best and strongest of all.

As for the solders used to make pipes of tin, copper,

of brass, <note>Catchword: *de laton,*</note>

of brass, or of silver, they are made of two parts lead, and one part bismuth <note>original: *estain de glace*; literally "glass tin," a term often used in this period for bismuth or a brittle tin alloy</note> over three parts pure tin, or of one part pure tin over an equal amount of lead, so that the solder may be softer and more manageable; although each artisan may add more or less lead or tin according to the hardness he desires, and the work to which he wishes to apply it. But **Goldsmiths** <note>original: *Orfeures*</note> have regulated their solders better than other workers, for they usually divide them into four species or degrees, of which the strongest is at 8—that is to say, they put 1/8 of copper or brass over seven parts of silver. The second is at six, when they put 1/6 of brass in it; the third is at a quarter, and the 4th at a third, which is the weakest and softest of all the solders used to bind silver to silver, and to copper or brass, and iron to copper, brass, and gold; this is why it is suitable for soldering Organ pipes, which can be made of all these materials.

Now, it is at the discretion of the artisans and **Organ builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> to divide these solders into eight degrees, of which the first has 1/8 brass to seven of silver; the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th degrees having 1/7, 1/6, 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, and 1/1, or 2/1 of brass, although it is more appropriate to keep to ordinary practice; which often contains that which is most certain and best in each art, by reason of long experience and continual usage, which has taught truth and utility. If someone wishes to make pipes of gold, he can still use four other kinds of solder, namely that of eight, which is the strongest of all, for it is made of one part silver and copper over seven parts of gold; the second has only 1/6 copper; the third 1/4, and the fourth or weakest 1/3, or 1/2.

It is not necessary to add the other kinds of glues, gums, pastes, and mastics used for gluing paper, cardboard, and pieces of marble that one cements together, nor the manner of amalgamating and joining all sorts of bodies with one another, insofar as that serves nothing for our subject, and since **Organ builders** can learn it from the artisans who use them, if they are curious enough to experiment with the diversity of sounds that can be produced by pipes of all kinds of material, from which they can draw many secrets for harmony. Now, the great diversity of glues and solders deserves an entire book, from which one would draw very particular insights for **Natural Philosophy** <note>original: *Physique*; in the 17th century, this referred to the study of the physical world and its materials</note>, for the small particles of earth and water, which join and mix together to compose stones, metals, and plants, are only bound by different kinds of glue, which are made by the various "cookings" <note>original: *cuissons*; referring to the natural heat or transformative processes within the earth</note> of water, which hardens more or less according to the different degrees of nature's distillations <note>original: *coctions*</note>, which is so subtle in her art and her works that it is not possible for us to discover her procedures and secrets.

Nevertheless, if one wishes to learn some quite notable details of this, one must read the admirable discourses that <term>Bernard Palissy</term> <note>Bernard Palissy (c. 1510–1589) was a famous French Huguenot potter, hydraulics engineer, and natural philosopher known for his scientific observations of the natural world.</note> has made on waters and fountains, both natural and artificial, and on metals, salts, salt marshes, stones, and earths; and what some others have written following the observations they have made. But I shall speak further of metals, and the manner of melting them, in another place, from which the Builders may draw utility and pleasure.

Sixth Book

## PROPOSITION XVIII.

### *To determine if pipes made of a hard metal, or of a more compact material, are in unison when they are of the same size, and if different shapes cause them to change their sound.*

If experience did not teach us that all pipes of the same size are in unison <note>Unison: sounding at the exact same pitch.</note>, even though the material of one be lead or tin, and that of the others be iron, wood, charcoal, wax, feather quills, etc., it would be difficult to believe; although the sound of those made of a softer material—for example, wood or wax—produces sounds that are softer and less brilliant. Now, the **Organ builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> can easily observe what different thicknesses and different materials of the pipes contribute to the quality of their sounds, which is why I do not dwell upon it here.

As for the different shapes of pipes, Mr. Cornu, a very skillful Surveyor, has discovered through experiment that two pipes of the same height, one of which is cylindrical and the other a parallelepiped <note>A three-dimensional shape with six faces that are parallelograms; here, a rectangular or square tube.</note>, are in unison when the side of the parallelepiped (or square) is eight parts and the diameter of the base of the cylindrical pipe is nine. From this, he infers that these two bodies are equal to one another. To this he adds that having made three lead bodies—namely, a sphere and two cubes—and having given fourteen parts to both the diameter of the sphere and the side of the cube (after having extracted the cube root of 1437 1/3, which is slightly less than 11 1/3), he noticed that the cube with a side of 11 1/3 weighs less than the sphere by one-third of the said sphere; that is to say, when the sphere weighs three pounds, the cube weighs only two (this cube weighed three pounds and six ounces). But the cube which has 12 1/4 for its side was found to be of equal weight with the sphere, from which he draws several conclusions, of which I speak elsewhere.

## PROPOSITION XXIX.

### *To explain the different intervals or degrees created by different Organ pipes when they are given different amounts of wind.*

EXPERIENCE teaches us that organ pipes which are voiced—or into which wind is sent by the stronger or weaker pressure of the bellows—produce different sounds. For there are some that rise higher by a semitone than their natural and ordinary sound, and others rise higher by a Fifth, an Octave, a Twelfth, or a Fifteenth, as happens with Flutes and Trumpets (of which I have already spoken when I explained the reasons for these leaps, or intervals). But it is difficult to explain why all pipes do not produce the same intervals, as all Trumpets do. I have found through experiment that open pipes, both large and small, rise to the Octave as soon as one pushes the wind a bit stronger than usual, without them being able to rise to the Third, the Fourth, or the Fifth; and that those which are stopped <note>original: *bouchez*; pipes that are closed at the top, which sounds an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note> always rise to the Fifth, or the Twelfth.

Now, the Builders can assist Philosophy <note>In this period, "Philosophy" (specifically Natural Philosophy) referred to what we now call science.</note> by drawing up a catalogue of the...

It also discusses "overblowing," where increasing wind pressure causes pipes to jump to higher harmonic intervals like the octave or twelfth.</summary>

I will say only this here: it is necessary for the number of pulses <note>original: *percussions*; referring to the frequency of air vibrations</note> with which the wind strikes the languid <note>the flat internal plate of the pipe</note> of the pipe to be double the number of pulses of its natural tone to make it rise by an Octave. Consequently, the number of wind pulses is tripled when the pipe rises to the Twelfth <note>an octave plus a fifth</note>, as is easy to conclude from what I have demonstrated in other books.

I have experimented that open pipes which are very short, such as those where the width is equal to the height, cannot rise above their natural tone, or they do so with difficulty; and that they rise easily when their length is four or five times their width. Pipes whose mouth is too high also cannot "octave" <note>overblow to produce the octave harmonic</note>; and some have noted that reed pipes <note>pipes using a vibrating metal tongue</note> often rise to the Major Third when one tries to make them take their natural tone. I have a pipe whose height is eight times its width which rises first to the Octave with a stronger wind, and then makes the Twelfth by doubling the wind, and finally rises even to the Fifteenth <note>the double octave</note>: it is three lines <note>a historical measurement; one line is about 2.25mm</note> in diameter and half a foot in height. It is easy to test all other heights and observe all the differences brought about by different widths and the height of the mouths and flues <note>original: *lumieres*; the narrow slit where the air escapes to hit the lip</note>.

## PROPOSITION XX.

### *To determine the properties of each organ stop, and why one does not perceive the dissonances that Organists make while playing.*

Since pipes differ in size and material, there is no doubt that they have different tones and sounds which affect the hearing and the mind in various ways. Stopped pipes <note>pipes capped at the top, which sound an octave lower than open pipes of the same length</note> speak more softly than open ones, because the wind exiting through the flue of the pipe does not strike their languid as strongly as that of open pipes. This is because the wind entering the mouth meets the wind returning from inside the pipe, which weakens the force of the air entering; for the wind that goes to strike the end or bottom of the pipe is forced to exit back through the same mouth by which it entered, as it has no other exit.

As for wooden pipes, they are softer than those made of tin because wood is softer or has more pores. However, it is difficult to explain the quality of the sounds of each stop <note>a "stop" or *jeu* is a full set of pipes of a specific timbre</note> unless we compare them to other instruments whose sound they imitate—for example, German Flutes <note>the transverse flute, held horizontally</note>, Cornets <note>the Cornett or *Zink*, a wooden instrument with a trumpet-style mouthpiece</note>, Trumpets, etc. For the greatest part of our knowledge is founded upon the comparison we make between one thing and another. This is why one cannot understand this Proposition if one has not heard the aforementioned instruments, since objects do not enter the understanding unless they have first entered through the senses. It suffices here to say that organ stops can imitate all other wind instruments, and perhaps some of those that use strings, such as the Viol and the Lyre.

As for the second part of this Proposition, it is easier to under-

the Treble, which forms a Third with the Bass, is always distant by a Major Third at every pipe. Consequently, if one supposes that the three notes of the Bass are the three sounds of the largest stop, and that the three notes of the Treble are the three pipes of the smaller stop, it follows that the first note of the Bass makes a Major Third with the first of the Treble, and likewise for the others that ascend. Therefore, if one holds firm on the first key <note>original: *marche*</note> of the Bass while playing the second of the Treble, one creates an Augmented Fifth <note>original: *Quinte superfluë*</note>; and if one plays the third of the Treble, one will create a Seventh.

It is easy to show the same thing regarding Ninths and several other Dissonances that one is constrained to make on the Organ, even though they are not ordinarily perceived. This astonishes those who recognize the slightest Dissonances in concerts of voices and other instruments, though they are much more imperfect than the Organ regarding their temperament <note>the system of tuning or "tempering" intervals</note>. But the reason for this phenomenon must be taken from the weakness of the smaller pipes, whose sounds appear almost not at all among the larger stops, because their sounds hide, stifle, and swallow the others, just as the light of the Sun hides that of candles. And if the voices that make Consonances <note>harmonious intervals like octaves or fifths</note> were as strong in relation to those making Dissonances as the large pipes are to the smaller ones of which we speak here, one would perceive them no better than on the Organ. The same must be concluded for other instruments; for whenever an effect is so violent that it fills the capacity of the senses and organs, we can no longer feel the lesser effects that occur or accompany the powerful impression of the other.

Now it is certain that the six notes *C, D, E, F, G, A* <note>original: *vt, re, mi, fa, sol, la*</note> can sometimes be found upon a single key, so that all the Dissonances accompany all the Consonances. This would be very bad and unbearable if the discordant sounds were strong enough to be heard and noticed. This does not prevent these small stops from making the harmony fuller and more massive, or solid, for they give luster to the pipes that are the Unisons and Octaves, which seem to have too much sweetness to be agreeable if one does not mix in sounds that possess something of the tart <note>original: *aigre*</note>, the biting, and the shrill, which make the harmony better tasted. In this harmony, it is enough that the Consonances predominate and that they so preoccupy the ear that it does not lose the idea of them through the presence of Dissonances.

mixture of two, three, or several stops, which are called compound stops, for I have already spoken of them; but rather of those that depend on a specific shape and a particular harmony of the pipes. Now, it is certain that it is easy to add new forms of pipes, for they can be made triangular, or in a helix <note>original: *helice*; a spiral or screw-like shape</note>, and one can add one or several cavities of all sorts of sizes to ordinary pipes, which will cause them to change their sound. I leave aside several other inventions with which Organ Builders <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> can enrich the stops of the organ: for example, if one puts small sheepskins as thin as those of onions at the ends of the pipes to block them, or if one makes several holes in the body of the pipe that are covered by the said skins, one will hear a unique harmony, which can be further varied by the difference in the movements given to the wind.

As for the "human voices" of the organ, which are called Regals <note>original: *Regales*; a type of reed stop known for its nasal, buzzing quality intended to mimic the human voice</note>, they can be perfected by removing what is most harsh and disagreeable about them. However, because the study of these varieties depends in part on experiments and the hands of the Builders, it is enough to mention them here to open the way for several new inventions. One can also join all sorts of wind instruments to ordinary Organs—for example, all sorts of Musettes <note>a type of small bagpipe popular in the French court</note> and Oboes—and even stringed instruments and percussion instruments. These will produce very specialized harmonies by means of several wheels and other springs, the invention of which is quite easy, for it depends only on hydraulics <note>the science of water-powered machinery, often used in this era to automate musical instruments</note> and other parts of Mechanics. From these, one can derive secrets advantageous enough to make organ pipes "speak," and to make them pronounce all sorts of syllables, and consequently all sorts of words. But this work consists of so many springs and different movements that it requires the spirit, the labor, and the life of several men; that is why I leave the care and invention of it to posterity, in order to begin the discourse on keyboards, which form one of the principal parts of the Organ and contain all the science of Organists.

## PROPOSITION XXII.

->*To explain the science of the Organ Keyboard, and how many keys it must have to*<-
->*include the perfection of the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic genera.*<-

The knowledge of the Organ Keyboard depends on the sequence of its degrees, for one must know the ratios of the intervals encountered within the Octave of the organ to play the keys <note>original: *marches*</note> that produce the Consonances and Dissonances, in order to express one’s musical intent and the dignity of the subject. Now, the ordinary keyboard—both of the great Organs used in Churches and of the cabinets <note>small chamber organs</note> used in private rooms—has thirteen keys in each Octave, and is in no way different from that of the Spinets <note>original: *Epinettes*; a small, plucked keyboard instrument</note> which I spoke of in the book on stringed instruments. That is why there is no need to include it here, except to please Organists and Builders, who will more easily be able to compare the new keyboards I am providing with the ordinary keyboard, in order to see and supply what is missing to achieve all the chords and intervals in their proper proportion.

From this accidental to **G** <note>original: *G re sol*</note>, there is a mean semitone; thus it happens that **E** makes a minor third against **G**, which in turn makes a just Fourth and Fifth against **C** and **D**.

Here it must be noted that this Third exceeds the just Third by a **comma** <term>comma: a tiny musical interval, in this context the minor comma or diesis</term> minor, and that the diminished Third is smaller than the just one by a major comma; but I have explained all these degrees elsewhere, and I shall speak of them again in the Proposition that follows.

## PROPOSITION XXIII. ##

->*Determining whether it is expedient to change the ordinary Organ Keyboards, and in what the use of the perfect Keyboard consists: where one sees the explanation of the Keyboard of twenty-seven and thirty-two keys.*<-

If the observation of laws depended on the intervals of Music, and if they were the cause of changes in morals and good customs, as it seems the Ancients <note>Referring to Greek philosophers like Plato and Aristotle, who believed specific musical modes could influence character and political stability</note> believed, one would have reason to doubt whether it is expedient, or whether it is permitted to add new keys to Organ Keyboards; since we read that they banished those who added new strings to instruments. But experience has not yet shown us that this increase in strings or keys <note>original: *marches*</note> is prejudicial to the state or to morals, and the **Makers** <note>original: *Facteurs*; organ builders</note> have already added several accidentals <note>original: *feintes*; literally "feints," referring to the black keys or accidentals</note>—

added to the keyboards, which are outside the degrees of the harmonic scale of Guido of Arezzo <note>original: *Guy Aretin*; the 11th-century monk who developed the precursor to modern musical notation and the "hexachord" scale system</note>, for they divide the Octave into twelve semitones by means of thirteen keys <note>original: *marches*; here referring to the physical keys of the instrument</note>.

In any case, the change from worse to better, by which much is gained—such as that of ordinary keyboards—must not be blamed, provided one does not also blame those who, to embellish songs and airs for one or more voices, add several flats <note>original: *b mols*</note> and other accidentals that are outside the ordinary letters of music. Thus, augmented keyboards should not be considered extraordinary, since they do nothing other than what voices do, and they only bring harmony to the perfection that the mind and the ear desire.

Now it is certain that these keyboards should be preferred over the ancient ones, since they contain a great multitude of **consonances** <term>Consonances: intervals that sound harmonious and stable to the ear, such as the fifth or the major third</term> and other intervals in their proper tuning, and they imitate the voice more perfectly. For it matters not at all if the difficulty of playing them is greater, as one should not begrudge the effort, nor flee the labor that leads to perfection. To this I add that one will play them as easily as the others once the hands are accustomed to them, because they follow the infallible laws of reason, and there is no need for artifice to hide their imperfection—as happens with ordinary keyboards—since they have none, as is seen in the last two keyboards of the preceding Proposition, in which all consonances are very precise and without any **temperament** <term>Temperament: a system of tuning that slightly adjusts pure mathematical intervals to allow instruments to play in multiple keys without sounding dissonant</term>.

Now, besides the 729 cells and the twenty-seven preceding columns, the square also contains another column on the right hand, which shows the twenty-seven degrees, and two at the bottom, the first of which is similar to the preceding one, and the last of which divides the **Keyboard** into three types of steps. The lowest of these show the **Diatonic** degrees <note>the standard seven-note scale like C, D, E, F, G, A, B</note> found in the cells of the square directly opposite them; the second ones moving upward signify the **Chromatic** degrees or steps; and the third ones show the **Enharmonic** degrees. Thus, it would not be necessary to add the figure of the keyboard, were it not that I desire to make the understanding of it so easy for **Organists** and **Instrument makers** <note>original: *Facteurs*; specifically those who build organs or harpsichords</note> that they find no difficulty in it.

It is for this reason that I place the letters and harmonic numbers on the steps, so that the imagination does not labor at all, and so that the hands may follow it as easily as a shadow follows the body. As for the explanation of the symbols of the **Planets** and the numbers within the 729 cells, it follows the keyboard, in which it leaves no difficulty. Now, I have not marked the numbers on the 8th nor on the 17th step—that is to say, on the second **E** and on the second **G**—so that one may see the two steps missing from the Scale of Salinas <note>Francisco de Salinas (1513–1590), a famous Spanish music theorist</note>, in whose favor I began the square with **E-mi-la** <note>the note E in the system of solmization</note>, just as he begins his perfect System, or his Octave of twenty-five degrees.

If one wishes to begin the preceding square with C <note>original: *C sol vt fa*; the standard Guidonian name for the note C</note>, it must be started at its ninth degree; and if one wishes to begin the Keyboard with E <note>original: *E mi la*; the note E</note>, it must similarly be started at the ninth step of the preceding Keyboard, which is to say by the number 60,000. Now, it is so easy to begin at whatever degree one wishes that it is not necessary to speak further of it.

As for the utility that can be drawn from this Keyboard, it is very great, for it shows very exactly the intervals of the three genres of Music <note>Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic</note>, and gives a greater light to harmony than all that the Greeks and Latins have written of it. Consequently, if one teaches Music and the manner of singing to children by means of its steps, they will be able to understand the most subtle reasons for all sorts of compositions and concerts in a very short time, and sing Enharmonic <note>the most complex musical genre involving tiny microtonal intervals</note> melodies as easily as Chromatic and Diatonic ones. I leave aside several other uses which **Organists** may discover for themselves if they use this Keyboard, upon which they will perform many beautiful passages and graces that they cannot find on ordinary Keyboards.

## COROLLARY I.

One may begin Keyboards with G <note>original: *G re sol vt*</note>, as Guido d'Arezzo <note>original: *Aretin*</note> did in the **Harmonic Hand**; or with D <note>original: *D la re sol*</note>, as Heinrich Glarean <note>a famous Swiss theorist</note> did, following the Greeks, who began their systems and their modes with the *Lowest Added Note* <note>original: *Proslambanomenos*</note>; or with F <note>original: *F vt fa*</note>, as was done in the past on the Organ; or with E <note>original: *E mi la*</note> like the most ancient Musicians, who began their <term>tetrachords</term> <note>a scale of four notes</note> with the *Lowest of the Low* <note>original: *hypate hypaton*</note>, and with the interval of a semitone. For nature has prescribed no boundaries for the beginning of Music, and art has no other authority than that given to it by the human spirit or by custom.

## COROLLARY II.

It is easy to know the <term>Consonances</term> <note>intervals that sound pleasing and stable</note> that are added to this Keyboard, of which that of Salinas was deprived; but since they cannot be found perfectly in tune on either one without the relation of the <term>comma</term> <note>a tiny mathematical discrepancy in tuning, roughly 1/9th of a whole tone</note>, one must yet add five steps in order to have thirty-two degrees in each **Octave**. These correspond to the eighth, ninth, and tenth columns of the table of <term>Diapasons</term> <note>here referring to the range of the octave and its divisions</note>, which I explained in the eleventh and twelfth Propositions of this book. Then, one could reasonably desire nothing more in the Diatonic genre, unless one wishes to extend it to infinity.

->*A most perfect Keyboard of 32 steps to the Octave with its Harmonic numbers.*<-

I therefore present once again this new Keyboard of thirty-two steps, which produces all the Consonances of the one with nineteen or twenty-seven steps, but without the relationship of the **comma** <note>a very small musical interval representing the tiny difference between certain notes in various tuning systems</note>, which seems disagreeable in the others. Now, the steps added to this Keyboard are easy to notice—namely the second E, the second F, the second G, the second A, and the second # <note>sharp</note>; all of these create the interval of a comma with those that precede them. However, the numbers written above them can replace any discourse one might make on this subject; it is therefore enough to consider them in this final Keyboard, where the smaller numbers next to the letters signify only the number and the rank of the steps, which the **Builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*; refers to organ builders or instrument makers</note> may arrange as they please.

### PROPOSITION XXIV.

->*To explain the manner in which sound is produced in organ pipes.*<-

It is easy to explain how the wind is carried into all sorts of pipes, since one can see the movement of the **bellows**, which force it to enter through the foot of said pipes up to their mouth. Having arrived there, it is distributed into two parts, one of which exits outside, and the other enters inside the body of the pipe. However, it is difficult to know if more enters than exits, and by how much, even though the path leading into the pipe, being more open than the one leading out, seems to show that a greater quantity enters than that which is lost. Now, one might say that more enters as the path is wider; but it is even more difficult to explain how sound is produced in the pipe. For although the wind strikes the **languid** <note>original: *languette*; in a flue pipe, this is the flat plate inside the mouth that directs the air</note>, by which it is divided, the body of the pipe nevertheless contributes greatly to the sound, of which it changes the depth <note>original: *graue*; low pitch</note> and other qualities. Nonetheless, one may conclude that the languid is the primary cause, since the pipe does not "speak" when it is poorly made, or when the mouth is too high, or when one places a piece of linen or cloth over the **upper lip**; yet it speaks in whatever form it is placed, provided that its languid remains in its position and is in no way altered. For even if one trims the body so much that it is only an inch high, instead of the foot it was before, this pipe will still speak.

Certainly, it seems one cannot attribute the cause of the sound to anything other than the cutting edge of the languid, which is made in a **slope** <note>original: *tallus*; a bevel or incline</note>, and the upper lip of the mouth, which cleave, cut, or divide the air pushed with violence. For the wind that makes the pipes speak is nothing other than air agitated by the meeting of these two bodies, which are sharp enough and hard enough to cleave it and make it sound. Thus, one can say that the difference in the bodies serves only to modify the sound and to determine it to certain degrees of low and high, soft and weak, strong and harsh, and so on.

For the sound is lower <note>original: *graue*</note> as the body of the pipe is larger, for the reason that the "beats" of the wind cannot be as frequent, since it encounters a larger cylinder of air that it must push out of the pipe, or which it must shake before producing the sound, or while producing it—even though one does not find a corresponding increase in difficulty, and it does not seem to require a force proportionately greater to create the sounds, as the pipes [grow larger]...

<summary>Mersenne introduces a 32-key keyboard that eliminates "comma" tuning discrepancies and begins a scientific inquiry into organ pipe acoustics, identifying the languid and upper lip as the primary sources of sound.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into acoustics and organ pipe construction, specifically comparing the physics of open versus stopped pipes and beginning a new proposition on why these instruments go out of tune.</meta>

<page-num>359</page-num>
<header>of Organs.</header>

are larger. But I will speak more fully of this force in the other Propositions. It is only necessary here to remark that by making two pipes sound, one of which is double the length of the other, one vibrates twice as much air when the longer one speaks, from which it follows that its movement is twice as slow: this must also be concluded for all types of sizes in proportion to the cylinders, or the prisms, and the cubes of air that must be moved or driven out.

As for **stopped pipes** <note>original: *tuyaux bouchez*; pipes with a cap on the end, which lowers the pitch by an octave compared to an open pipe of the same length</note>, even though one does not vibrate a greater volume of air when making one speak of the same height as an open pipe, one nevertheless makes the wind, or the air, travel twice as far as in the open one. From this it happens that the stopped pipe descends as low as an open pipe twice its length. Thus, one can say that the wind which strikes or touches the bottom of the stopped pipe reflects back upon the wind that follows, hindering its speed; for it delays its movement, just as the waves of the sea delay those coming from the opposite side, or as the **South wind** <note>original: *vent du Midy*</note> is delayed by that which blows from the **North** <note>original: *du Septentrion*</note>. This can also be compared to the different passions and reasons by which man is so agitated that he often cannot resolve himself, nor choose any path among all those he proposes to himself, because the different motives that push him—just as waves push a ship—find themselves in equilibrium. And as the two contrary movements of the stopped pipe produce a third movement which renders the sound sweeter and more harmonious, in the same way it happens that the different movements that strike the mind are the cause of it being reduced to a certain temperament that distances it from the two extremes, which are ordinarily vicious, as is taught in **Moral Philosophy** <note>A reference to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," where virtue is found in the balance between two extremes</note>. But the pipe cannot speak when one stops it with cloth, or with other porous and soft bodies, because the wind is dampened upon meeting things that are soft like linen, cotton, and silk, and enters inside them instead of reflecting back to the **mouth** <note>original: *bouche*</note> or to the **windway** <note>original: *lumiere*; the narrow slit through which the wind passes to strike the lip of the pipe</note> of the pipe.

### PROPOSITION XXV.

->*To explain why organ stops go out of tune, and which stops are most subject to going out of tune.*<-

It is not as easy to explain why pipes go out of tune as it is to say why stringed instruments do not hold their tuning, because pipes do not swell like strings, which become tighter when humid weather follows dry. Nevertheless, the principal cause of the discord of pipes must be taken from the air, which is more or less coarse and humid; for all bodies are diversely affected by the different dispositions of the air, as is experienced every day. And because the winds condense and compress it, or rarefy and dilate it, it happens that the pipes feel the effects just as other bodies do.

Furthermore, rust and dust, which accompany the wind from the bellows, and other filth can alter the pipes, whose material can also sag and change shape. Moreover, the hole at the **foot** of the pipes sometimes closes too much, so that it receives too little wind; and the bellows, the **windchest** <note>original: *layette*; the box that holds the pressurized air for the pipes</note>
<sig>Hh ij</sig>

<summary>This page explains the physics of stopped organ pipes, comparing their acoustic properties to human moral equilibrium, and begins an inquiry into why environmental factors like humidity and dust cause organs to go out of tune.</summary>
<keywords>stopped pipes, acoustics, reflection of sound, moral philosophy, organ tuning, humidity, bellows, windchest, pipe maintenance</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on why organ pipes go out of tune, focusing on mechanical leaks and the specific vulnerabilities of reed pipes, before transitioning into a philosophical and technical examination of wind pressure.</meta>

<page-num>360</page-num>
<header>Book Sixth</header>

...and the other parts that contain the wind are not always well-sealed, and lose so much air that they do not distribute enough to each stop and each pipe. Discord can also arise from the **valves** <note>original: *soupapes*; the internal flaps that allow air into the pipes when a key is pressed</note>, which do not sufficiently unblock the holes of the **windchest** <note>original: *sommier*; the pressurized box that holds the air for the pipes</note> and the **registers** <note>original: *registres*; the sliders that turn stops on or off</note>, or from the **pipe-shades** <note>original: *chappes*</note>, and several other circumstances which are often difficult to remedy.

As for the stops that are most prone to going out of tune, it is noted that these are the **reeds** <note>original: *anches*; pipes that produce sound via a vibrating metal tongue rather than a whistle-like labium</note>, for example the **regals** <note>a small, portable reed organ stop with a buzzy tone</note>, or **human voices** <note>original: *voix humaines*; a reed stop intended to mimic the sound of a choir</note>, and the **trumpets**. This is because they easily become loose, either due to their **tuning wires** <note>original: *rasettes*; the sliding wires used to adjust the length of the vibrating reed</note> or the movements used to close and open them, or because they grow weary of "beating the air" and lose their strength—much like any spring that is kept under tension for too long or too often. It may also be because **verdigris** <note>a green pigment or crust caused by the oxidation of copper or brass</note>, which forms against the copper or brass, alters the movement of the **tongues** <note>original: *languettes*; the thin strips of metal that vibrate to produce sound in a reed pipe</note>. However, humidity is almost the sole cause that makes the pipes **go sharp** <note>original: *monter*; to rise in pitch</note>, because it narrows the interior as if one were adding a crust, or it weights down their moving tongues as if one had placed a piece of wax upon them.

### PROPOSITION XXVI.

*To determine whether more wind is needed to make large pipes speak than to make the smaller ones speak, and in what manner the Organ Builders measure the wind.*

One of the greatest difficulties in building **Organs** consists in distributing the wind to the pipes and managing it so wisely that each one receives only as much as it needs to take its natural tone. In this, the **Builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*; the master craftsmen of the instrument</note> must imitate **Divine Providence**, which has so distributed the degrees of being to each creature that it has only as much as it needs to hold the rank God has given it, and to produce the particular "tone" that helps compose the great harmony of the Universe. In this harmony, each created being plays a part different from the others and is similar to one of the pipes, which would remain forever silent and useless if the wind did not enter it—just as all creatures would be not only useless, but would not exist at all, if God did not communicate to them the spirit and the being that makes them subsist.

Indeed, each person can consider themselves as a pipe that continually receives Divine graces (which are sometimes represented by the wind) and should simultaneously accuse themselves of ingratitude toward God every time they fail to relate all that they are, all they do, and all they can to the glory of Him from whom they hold everything they have. For such a person does the same thing as an organ pipe that refuses to speak, even though it receives enough wind. Now, it seems that more wind is required to make the largest pipes speak than the smallest; this is why the openings at the feet of the former are larger than those of the latter. However, it is difficult to determine if the size of these holes should be in the exact same ratio as the size of the pipes—that is, if the hole in the foot carrying a pipe double or quadruple in length must also be double or quadruple in size. But one can measure the force of the wind in order to give as much as is necessary to each pipe...

->On Organs.<-

or to weaken it, and to reinforce it according to the given ratio. This is what the **organ builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*; the master craftsmen who design and construct organs</note> do by means of a **wind-trunk** <note>original: *porte-vent*; a conduit or channel that carries pressurized air from the bellows to the pipes</note> which they place under the feet of the largest pipes, where they leave it once they have confirmed through experimentation that the pipes speak clearly and that their tone is neither too weak nor too strong.

I leave aside several other methods that can be used to measure the force of the wind, such as windmills and wheels, which can be so arranged and graduated that they will show all the degrees of the force of the winds, as I remark elsewhere. For it suffices here to say that the quantity of wind entering pipes of different sizes follows the opening of the **feet** <note>the bottom part of the pipe where the air enters; the size of the hole at the tip—the "toe hole"—regulates the air flow</note> through which it enters, and that it must be made larger for large pipes than for small ones, as the builders practice. And if the proportion of these openings is similar to that of the length or width of the pipes, it is easy to open their feet exactly as required, without it being necessary to experiment to see if the pipes will speak well with such and such a quantity of wind. Nevertheless, many builders say it often happens that large pipes speak with less wind than smaller ones, particularly when their **mouth** <note>the horizontal opening in the front of the pipe where the sound is generated</note> is very low, for they require more wind when it is higher.

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

*Explaining why large pipes make lower sounds than smaller ones.*

If one understands what I have said of **low pitch** <note>original: *graue*</note> and **high pitch** <note>original: *aigu*</note> in other places, it is not difficult to understand why the largest pipes have lower, deeper, and more hollow sounds; for the air that strikes their **tongues** <note>original: *languettes*; the vibrating part of the pipe, either a metal reed or the air-stream at the mouth</note>, and the movement that shakes the cylinder of air they contain within their bodies, is slower than that of smaller pipes, whose interior air does not resist the exterior air by which it is driven as much as that of the larger pipes does.

Now, one can compare the small ripples of air that strike the tongues to the waves of the sea and rivers, or to the leaps and bubbles made by water when it encounters pebbles or other obstacles; for waves are accustomed to being in greater multitude when the obstacles are smaller, but said waves are smaller in return. Thus, their frequency is as much less as they are larger, when they are pushed by an equal force. Some believe that the waves beating against ships in the most orderly seas create a harmony, and that the tenth wave, which is called the **Tenth Wave** <note>original: *Decumanus*; a Latin term for the "great wave," as Romans believed every tenth wave was significantly larger</note>, makes the lowest sound of all because it is the largest. However, it is very difficult to make this observation, both because of the difficulty in noting the pitch of each wave—which is so dull and low that it surpasses the reach of the ear—and because I have often experimented and found that the tenth wave is not the largest. Furthermore, there is nothing sufficiently regulated or known in the sequence of waves occurring at the harbors of our French seas to derive from them any sensible or intellectual harmony.

Whatever the case may be, I do not doubt that there exists some order and proportion of speed and slowness, and likewise of size, among the waves, just as there is among the beats of the **pulse** <note>original: *poux*; an archaic spelling of *pouls*</note>, and the inhalations and exhalations of animals; but I believe that our knowledge of it is no less...

<header>Sixth Book</header>

hidden, as the reason for the **flow and ebb** <note>original: *flux & reflux*; referring to the tides</note> of the sea; this is why I return to the wind that makes the pipes speak, and whose tremors or shocks occur more slowly as a greater quantity [of wind] is pushed with equal force. This is easier to explain in **reed pipes** <note>original: *tuyaux à anches*; pipes where sound is produced by a vibrating metal tongue</note> than in others, because their **tongues** <note>original: *languettes*; the vibrating part of the reed</note> move, while those of the others remain motionless.

Now, they move more slowly the more they are open, and faster the more they are closed, because they have less force and more distance to travel when they are longer, for they are subject to the laws of the **lever**, which I have discussed elsewhere. From this, it follows that they produce **lower sounds** <note>original: *sons graves*</note> when they are longer than when they are shorter, and they cover less distance in the same amount of time, because they strike the air more slowly; just as it happens that a lever, or the spoke of a wheel, and all other things that follow their proportion, descend more slowly as they are longer—that is to say, as they have more path or space to travel.

The twentieth Proposition sheds further light on this one, which is why it is not necessary to extend this discourse; for what one might desire regarding the proportion of the returns of the tongues has been explained elsewhere.

## PROPOSITION XXVIII.

->*To explain why two or more pipes tremble while speaking together when they are not in tune, and how the **drum stop** is made on the Organ.*<-

It is certain that two pipes sounding at the same time make each other tremble when they do not form perfect **consonances** <note>musical intervals that sound stable or "in tune" to the ear</note>; for if one holds two or more pipes that are even slightly distant from **unison**, they make the hands that hold them tremble, and when they are perfectly in unison, they no longer tremble. This is the opposite of what happens with strings, which make each other tremble more noticeably the better they are in tune, and which tremble less as they are further from consonances, as I have demonstrated in the book on stringed instruments. 

But it is difficult to find the reason for this difference, which causes pipes that are only a **semitone** or a quarter-tone apart to produce a buzzing or **beating of air** <note>the acoustic phenomenon where two slightly different frequencies interfere, creating a pulsing volume</note> similar to the beats of a drum when they sound together. Indeed, one notices ten very audible beats of air in the space of one second; this happens with large pipes as well as slender ones. This prevents us from saying that the number of air vibrations, which make the two different sounds, is the cause of these tremors; for it seems that one should notice a much greater number [of beats] between pipes forming a semitone than between those forming a whole tone. Nevertheless, the **drum stop** <note>original: *jeu du tambour*; a special effect where two low-pitched pipes are tuned slightly apart to create a rhythmic thumping like a drum roll</note> does not produce a greater number of beats between smaller intervals than between larger ones, as is experienced with pipes at the semitone of 16 to 15, or that of 25 to 24, or the **diesis** <note>a very small musical interval, here 128:125</note> of 128 to 125, or the **comma** <note>a minute interval representing the difference between two nearly identical notes, here 81:80</note> of 81 to 80. For since these movements do not agree or unite except at the 15th, 24th, or 80th strike, it seems that one should notice fifteen, or twenty—

# of Organs.
Hh iiij

...four beats in the **drum stop** <note>original: *jeu du tambour*; an organ stop that mimics the sound of a drum by using two pipes tuned slightly apart to create acoustic interference</note> which is made with two pipes that produce a **major or minor semitone** <note>original: *demiton maieur, ou mineur*</note>, and 125 or 80 beats in that made by pipes separated by a **diesis** <note>original: *diese*; a very small musical interval</note> or a **comma** <note>original: *comma*; a tiny interval representing the difference between two notes that are theoretically the same but differ slightly due to tuning systems</note>, at the same time that one hears eight or nine beats from pipes producing the whole tone—which does not happen. Regarding this, it is appropriate to note that **organ builders** <note>original: *Facteurs*</note> must take care that others do not prevent them from tuning when they are adjusting their Organs, especially when it is time to put them in tune to deliver them to those who commissioned their construction. For if someone makes a sound a **quarter-tone** <note>original: *quart de ton*</note> lower than the pipes, they will always tremble, so that the builder will find them discordant even though they are in tune with each other. The Lute and other stringed instruments could also hinder the tuning of the pipes; this is why the builder must remove everything that might interfere with him, so that he does not waste time and does not expose himself to the mockery of those who are more knowledgeable than he is.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

->*To explain the manner and method of tuning Organs, both in pure and tempered systems.*<-

Everything we have said until now is of almost no use for the practice of Organs if they are not in tune; this is why it is necessary to explain all possible methods, or at least the best ways used to tune all the stops of the Organ. On this subject, it must first be noted that one needs a good ear to judge **consonances** <note>original: *Consonances*; intervals that sound harmonious together</note> and to recognize if they are **pure** <note>original: *iustes*; notes tuned to perfect mathematical ratios</note>. This would only be unnecessary if one could cut all the pipes so perfectly, and adjust the wind so equally and with such skill, that all the pipes were in tune without needing to use the ears to tune them. This would always happen if one observed all the proportions and circumstances I have spoken of in this book—if the physical material followed the precision of the mind, and if manual operation perfectly matched the science. But since this surpasses human industry, as we cannot foresee the great multitude of circumstances that accompany the lead, tin, wood, and other materials from which pipes are made—and which even occur within the air itself—I assume that ears are entirely necessary for tuning the pipes.

In the second place, it must be noted that the ear perceives the imperfection of Consonances more easily than that of **dissonances** <note>original: *Dissonances*; clashing or unstable musical intervals</note>, just as perfection is further removed from imperfection than imperfection is from itself (though this Proposition is not without many difficulties that deserve other discussions). From this, it follows that one tunes by Consonances rather than by Dissonances; it is for this same reason that one chooses the most pleasing and easiest to understand, as I will say later.

Finally, one begins tuning with the middle keys rather than with the first or last, because the sounds in the middle of the Organ are better proportioned and more suited to the voice and the ear than those at the beginning or the end, which are too low or too high to notice their differences with enough accuracy.

This must be observed in all other judgments, which are all made—

# Sixth Book

...days with more assurance, when the things being judged have more harmony and relationship with the capacity of the senses; by which means the truth of objects enters the mind and lodges in the understanding, which comprehends each thing all the more easily and perfectly as the application of the external senses is stronger and more perfect.

It is for this reason that one begins the tuning with the second **C-sol-ut-fa** <note>Middle C</note>, or by the second **F-ut-fa** <note>The F below middle C</note>, which serve as a base or foundation for the ear; although one could start with any other letter or key one wishes: for example, with **D-la-re-sol** <note>D</note> or **E-mi-la** <note>E</note>; and those whose voice or ear is proportioned to deeper or higher sounds may begin with the first or the last **C-sol-ut-fa**. But it is sufficient to explain the easiest and most frequent method, upon which it is easy to invent several others. Now, I explain it first through ordinary musical notes, and then through discourse. As for the notes, I put them all under the **F-ut-fa** clef <note>The bass clef</note>, so that the sequence of the tuning is better understood. Because the Octaves must be **just** <note>perfectly in tune, with no "beating"</note> and the Fifths **weak** <note>slightly flattened or "tempered," a common practice in keyboard tuning to allow music to be played in different keys</note>, I use two characters to show on which side the weakness and justness lie. The first is a comma curved upwards, as seen here ᴗ; since it is already in use to signify short syllables <note>In poetic meter</note>, it can similarly be applied to weak and diminished intervals. But this other character —, consisting of a straight line and signifying long syllables, will show just intervals. One may also add the character made of two straight lines in this fashion Λ, to signify intervals that are **strong** <note>widened or sharp</note>—for example, Fourths, which are always as much larger and stronger as the Fifths are smaller or weaker.

The first line of notes shows the tuning of the principal keys, which are called **Diatonic** <note>The natural notes, typically the white keys on a modern piano</note>; and the second shows the tuning of the other keys, which are called **feints** <note>original: *feintes*; a term for the accidentals or "black keys"</note> or **chromatic**, because they provide the semitones in all parts of the keyboard, dividing each whole tone into two parts.

### PROPOSITION XXX.

->*To determine if one can supplement the accuracy and goodness of the ear by some science and artifice, and if one can tune the Organ without using the sense of hearing.*<-

If the ear is good enough to recognize the <term>unison</term> <note>two notes sounding at the exact same pitch</note> of a string with a pipe, one can tune the Organ by means of stringed instruments; but since one cannot know if the Organ pipes are in unison with the strings (unless one uses the ear, or the <term>tremblings</term> <note>known today as "beats," these are the audible pulses created when two sounds are slightly out of tune</note> they make when they are at the unison or the Octave of said pipes), and there is no other way to tune the Organ through the intervention of said strings than by noting if they agree with the pipes, we must see if there is any other way to tune Organs.

### Regarding Organs.

...octave, or the **Fifth**, and they do not vibrate <note>The author uses the term "trembler" (to tremble) to describe the physical phenomenon of acoustic "beats," where two slightly different frequencies interfere with one another.</note> at all when they are tuned perfectly; so that if one could know the number of vibrations they make when one diminishes their tuning to make them tempered as they should be, one could tune them, because one would diminish their accuracy until they produced that specific number of vibrations. For if they must vibrate twenty times within the space of a measure <note>Likely referring to a standard time unit, such as the beat of a pulse or a pendulum.</note> to be perfectly tempered, it would only be necessary to observe this number to put them in tune. But one must experiment with how many times the pipes—or the air being pushed or enclosed within them—vibrate at every distance from the **unison** and other consonances, if one wishes to know the universal method for tuning the Organ.

And if one can recognize these vibrations, or beats, without the ear, it would not be necessary for tuning the Organ; for if it were required (for example) that the pipes beat ten times in a second to create the tempered **Fifth**, one would be certain that the Organ was in tune when all the **Fifths** beat ten times, and the ear would not be needed for this purpose, provided the hands holding or touching the pipes could note the said number of beats through the sense of touch.

Now, this consideration of beats serves not only to recognize the tuning and the temperament of the Organ, but also as the object of an excellent scientific inquiry <note>original: "ſpeculation"</note>, which consists of searching for the causes of this beating, which differs according to whether the pipes are more or less distant from the consonances; for they beat differently when they are a <term>diesis</term> <note>A very small musical interval, smaller than a semitone.</note> away from the unison than when they are a major second away, and an equal distance from the **Fifth** does not make them beat in the same way as that of the **Unison**. From this, it follows that one must consider these distances in as many ways as there are consonances; for as for dissonances, they make the pipes beat and vibrate even when they are in their "just" <note>Perfectly mathematical or "pure" intervals.</note> intervals: though one might consider whether they make them vibrate more or less when they are just than when they are tempered.

One can also examine if the pipes making the tempered **Fifth** vibrate as strongly as the strings that are at the unison with said pipes, when one sounds one of the said strings to make the other vibrate, and several other things that one can imagine on this subject. But whatever one might say, it is certain that the ear is necessary to hear these vibrations, just as it is necessary to hear sound, for touch is not delicate enough to note the number of these vibrations, given that the pipes must be placed on their <term>registers</term> <note>The wind-chest or the mechanism that distributes air to specific sets of pipes.</note> when they are tuned, in order to give them a more equal wind than that of the mouth: and consequently, one cannot hold them in one's hands to note the number of beats in the air. Now, if one could cut the pipes so accurately, and give them such equal wind, that they were in tune upon being placed on the registers without any need to trim them or touch them with the <term>tuning tool</term> <note>original: "accordoir," a metal cone used to slightly flare or compress the top of a pipe to adjust its pitch.</note>, the ear would not be necessary for tuning; but it is very difficult to make pipes so accurately that one does not need to touch them at all to widen, narrow, shorten, or alter them—whether one uses temperament or keeps them "just" according to harmonic ratios—insofar as it is too difficult to observe all the proportions of the mouths, the <term>languids</term> <note>original: "languettes," the internal flat plate of an organ pipe that directs air against the lip to create sound.</note>, and the opening of the feet, and...

<meta>catchword: tes les (indicating the next page begins with "toutes les" / "all the")</meta>

The author concludes that while beats follow mathematical laws, the human ear remains essential for tuning because the sense of touch is insufficient and pipes must be tuned while fixed in place.</summary>

<page-num>368</page-num>

->Book Sixth<-

that the material of the different pipes is not similar: added to which, small pipes proportioned exactly like the large ones do not produce the same intervals, as I remarked when speaking of those that are of equal height and different width.

And then experience shows that a pipe which is at **unison**, or at the **Octave** on its <term>windchest</term> <note>original: "ſommier"; the pressurized box of air upon which organ pipes stand.</note>, often changes its tone by touching it lightly, and even without touching it at all: so that having made two or several pipes of the same thickness, length, shape, and material, it may happen that they will not be found at **unison** on the **windchest**. One should not be astonished by this, since we cannot even be certain if two pipes, or any two other bodies, are of the same length and the same thickness, for we cannot discern the hundred-thousandth part of a line, or of an inch.

This is why it is not necessary for <term>Builders</term> <note>original: "Facteurs"; specifically makers of musical instruments like organs or harpsichords.</note> to be perfectly exact in the cutting of their pipes, since it is necessary that they adjust them either by cropping them, or by widening and narrowing them with their <term>tuning cones</term> <note>original: "accordoirs"; metal tools used to flare the tops of pipes open or closed to change the pitch.</note>: although it is very appropriate that they make them in a tripled ratio of the interval of the sounds they are meant to produce, so that they may make better-proportioned tones, and more full and rich. But there is no need to warn them of this, since we experience that they often crop several pipes by an entire foot, or by several inches, to bring them into tune.

## COROLLARY I.

Since the strings of the <term>Lute</term> and other instruments sound without being touched when someone sings at their **unison**, or at their **Octave**, as I have experienced, and as the sound of the pipes is similar to the voice, I have no doubt that it will make the same strings tremble and sound. These can serve to know when the pipes are in tune, for if one stretches several strings on a soundboard of a **Lute**, or on a <term>Monochord</term> <note>A scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure musical intervals.</note>, or on a <term>Spinet</term> <note>original: "Epinette"; a small, wing-shaped keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note>, and one gives them the tuning desired for the **Organ**, each pipe will be in tune when each string that corresponds to it resonates or trembles: which would perhaps succeed even better if one attached the strings to the pipes, or if one joined to them some spring that communicated with the said strings.

## COROLLARY II.

The <term>Builders</term> who have a learned and delicate ear judge that the **Fifths** are tempered as they should be, and that they are sufficiently diminished, when they beat so little that one has quite a bit of difficulty noticing the beat; and that the **Unisons** and the **Octaves** are accurate without any diminution when one no longer perceives any beat at all: which experience will make much more easily understood than a longer discourse. I add only that voices singing with the **Organ** can put the pipes out of tune, for if they are not accurate, and they fail even slightly to be at the **unison** of the pipes, they will make them tremble: so that those who hear them beating will judge that they are not in tune. I leave aside a thousand other accidents that can happen to **Organs** both from the wind and from several other circumstances that the **Builders** may observe.
