## PROPOSITION XXXI.

*To explain all the stops, both simple and compound, of the most complete and largest organs being built today.*

ALTHOUGH I have already spoken of the different <term>stops</term> <note>original: "jeux"; the sets of pipes of a particular color or pitch controlled by a single knob.</note> of the organ, nonetheless this Proposition will supply what might have been omitted; for it contains the greatest multitude of stops that the most excellent <term>Builders</term> <note>original: "Facteurs"</note> put into the largest organs in Europe—even though future ages may add many others, since the imagination of men has not yet reached its limits in this subject.

Now, I shall mark each stop with letters of the alphabet, so that they may serve to help understand the "compound" stops which I will add after the "simple" stops. The first of these, which belongs to the <term>Great Organ</term> <note>original: "grand jeu"; the main, loudest division of the instrument.</note>—of which we shall speak first—is called the **Montre**.

->Table of the Simple Stops of Large Organs.<-

A **The Montre** <note>original: "Montre," meaning "show" or "display"; these are the large, polished pipes standing in the front of the organ case.</note>, of which the largest pipe is sixteen feet long and open; consequently, the last pipe, which forms a <term>Twenty-ninth</term> <note>An interval of four octaves.</note> with the first, is only one foot long. They are all made of tin.

B **The Bourdon** is eight feet long and stopped <note>original: "bouchez"; a pipe with a cap on the end, which makes it sound an octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.</note>, and is made of wood or <term>metal alloy</term> <note>original: "estoffe"; usually a mixture of lead and tin.</note>. It plays at <term>unison</term> with the Montre, but it is softer because it is stopped.

C **The other Bourdon** is four feet stopped, or eight feet open in the fashion of a flute; it is an octave above the previous ones, and can be of tin or wood.

D **The Prestant** is four feet long and open, at a <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>Two octaves higher.</note> from the Montre, or two feet stopped; it is so named because it serves to regulate the pitch of the organ, as it is proportioned to the human voice.

E **The Doublette** is two feet open, at a <term>Twenty-second</term> <note>Three octaves higher.</note> from the Montre.

F **The Flageolet** is one foot open, and is at a Twenty-ninth from the Montre; it should naturally be played alone with the 4-foot stopped pipe.

G **The Nazard** is about five and one-third feet, and is stopped or has a "chimney"; it is at a <term>Twelfth</term> from the Montre and is made of lead.

H **Another Nazard** at the octave of the previous one, of about two and two-thirds feet, stopped or with a chimney.

I **The German Flute** <note>original: "Fleute d'Allemand"; a transverse flute stop.</note> is four feet long and has a <term>chimney</term> <note>original: "cheminée"; a small tube protruding from the cap of a stopped pipe, giving it a bright, hollow tone.</note>, which is to say its body has two thicknesses. The first begins at the mouth of the pipe and ends at a third of the length, where it has the thickness of a stopped pipe of the same length; the chimney comprises the other two-thirds of the length, with the thickness of a two-foot open pipe. Now, if one makes this Flute four feet long, the first third of the body will be four inches in diameter, and the other two-thirds made as a chimney will be two inches in diameter.

L **The Tierce** is about one foot and seven inches open, and is at a <term>Third</term> <note>Specifically a Major Third relative to the fundamental harmonics.</note> of <term>Middle C</term> <note>original: "C sol"; a note in the hexachord system corresponding to C.</note> of two feet open.

M **The Fourniture** <note>A "mixture" stop where multiple pipes sound for every single key pressed.</note> has four pipes per key, of which the first is nearly one and a half feet open, the second is one foot at Middle C, the third is eight [inches]...

And if one wants six pipes per key, one adds **C** of two feet, and **G** of four inches.

S **The Clarion** <note>original: "Cleron"</note> is four feet, at the Octave of the Trumpet, and widens just like it.

T **The Crumhorn** <note>original: "Cromhorne"; a reed stop intended to imitate the buzzing sound of the Renaissance woodwind instrument of the same name.</note> is four feet, in <term>unison</term> with the Trumpet: it is four feet from the <term>block</term> <note>original: "noyau"; the part of a reed pipe that holds the tongue and shallot.</note> to the end, of which the first half-foot widens up to five inches, and then it continues straight, having a diameter of one and a half inches.

V **The Human Voice** <note>original: "Voix Humaine"; a short-resonator reed stop designed to imitate the sound of a choir.</note> is half-a-foot, in unison with the Trumpet.

X **The Pedal** is eight feet, stopped.

Y **The Pedal Trumpet** is eight feet.

Z **The Pedal Flute** is four feet, stopped.

### *Simple Stops of the Positive.*

The small Organ that is usually placed at the base of the large one, and which the Organists have behind them when they play, or when they look at the keyboard of the Great Organ, is usually called the **Positive** <note>Also known as the "Chair Organ" because of its position behind the organist's bench.</note>: it uses the same bellows, the same wind, and the same keyboard. ### COROLLARY.

It must be remarked that the <term>Tremulant</term> <note>original: "Tremblant"; a mechanical device that modulates the air pressure to create a vibrating effect.</note> is not a specific stop [of pipes], and that it is nothing other than a movable board attached within the wind-trunk in such a way that it is raised when the pipes should not tremble while speaking, and lowered when one wants it to make the wind tremble. This is easy to conceive by striking one's lips with the hand while pronouncing a vowel—for example, *a* or *o*. However, many people reject this trembling as a disagreeable noise, of which I shall speak later.

As for the simple stops, for which I have not specified the material, they can be made of lead, tin, or wood. Now, I do not believe that the Ancients had musical instruments so large, so diverse in their stops, and so perfect as our **Organs** are. Every day new inventions are added to them, such as new stops to imitate the **Nightingale** and other birds. Some even seek a way to add a **Viol** stop by means of several unisons, although it is more appropriate to add a **Spinet** stop, as do those who use small cabinets <note>Likely referring to "Claviorgana," hybrid instruments combining a keyboard string instrument with a small organ.</note> where the same keyboard makes the pipes and the strings speak at the same time in unison or at the octave. This produces a very sweet harmony because the pipes are very soft and blend so perfectly with the strings (made of brass or gut) that one has difficulty distinguishing them. If one adds the Viol stop, which many are trying to adapt to the Spinet, it seems there would be nothing left to desire in the Organ, unless it were for its pipes to be made to sound vowels and syllables; however, it seems one must not hope for this, given the great difficulty encountered therein.

### PROPOSITION XXXII.

->*To show how many compound stops can be made on the Organ: wherein one sees the manner of combining, grouping by threes, grouping by fours, etc.*<-

I have provided the method for finding how many ways any number of things can be varied when they are taken one by one, two by two, three by three, etc., in the sixteenth Proposition of the *Book on Songs*. For example, if one takes the twenty-two preceding stops of the **Great Organ**, one will know how many times they can be varied when taken two by two, or three by three, etc. If you multiply 22 by 21, and then the product by 20, and so on until you have as many ranks of numbers as you wish to take stops. For instance, if you want to make all the <term>compound stops</term> <note>original: "jeux compoſez"; registrations created by pulling multiple stop knobs simultaneously.</note> of two or three simple stops: 22 multiplied by 21 will give 462 compound stops made of two simple stops. If one then multiplies 462 by 20, one will have 9,240 different stops composed of three simple stops. Those who wish to know how many stops there will be composed of four, five, or six simple stops will find the required numbers by multiplying 9,240 by 19, and then that product by 18, and so on. But because this number is so great that the life of an Organist is not long enough to use them all, I...

### COROLLARY I.

Since one can use all these stops in all these ways—supposing they harmonize well together, as can happen, particularly if they are made for that purpose, and since organists already join seven of them in the <term>Plein Jeu</term> <note>The "Full Rank," a registration that uses the principal pipes of the organ to create a bright, majestic sound.</note> and in the full <term>Cornet</term> <note>A compound organ stop that mimics the sound of a cornett (a reed-like wind instrument), made of several pipes sounding different harmonics.</note>, as seen in the twenty-seventh Proposition—it is certain that they can play 255 different combinations on a small organ of eight stops. This can easily be known by means of a <term>doubling geometric progression</term> <note>A mathematical sequence where each number is double the last: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128.</note> starting with unity, the sum of which (when the next number is taken and one is subtracted) gives this same total. For if one adds 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128—which is done by taking the next number in the progression, namely 256 [and subtracting one]—one will have the said number of stop combinations. This can easily be applied to all other sorts of numbers without any labor by means of the tables I have given in the *Book of Melodies*, from which organists and other musicians can draw an infinity of secrets for their art without it being necessary to specify them; for they will receive more satisfaction by contributing something of their own ingenuity.

### COROLLARY II.

The consideration of all the different organ stops, both simple and compound, is not unworthy of fine minds, who can draw from them specific knowledge to perfect or to begin a philosophy founded on the different experiences of the ear, the eye, and the other senses. For example, the <term>Nazard</term> stop—composed of two pipes that are at a <term>Fifth</term>, a <term>Twelfth</term>, or a <term>Nineteenth</term> from one another—imitates those who speak through their nose and has a "nasal" quality because of these two sounds. This will give occasion to investigate why vibrations, of which one strikes three or six times in the same period that the other strikes once or twice, produce this nasal sound more than those of the <term>Fifteenth</term> <note>An interval of two octaves (a ratio of 4:1).</note>, where one strikes four times while the other strikes only once, etc. And because there is no stop that does not have some effect different from the other stops, one has as many subjects for reasoning as there are different stops in the Organ. Just as the different rays of light, being gathered together, produce very different heats and visions, the...

When the Cornet stop (which is set to play across the whole keyboard without being divided, provided there are two keyboards in the Organ) is mixed with the **Tremulant** and with the **Clarion**, it makes a most excellent stop which imitates the **Oboes** rather than the wooden cornett. I leave aside all the considerations that can be drawn from all the other compositions of organ stops, because they would require an entire volume.

### COROLLARY III.

If one counts all the pipes of the Organ along with those of its <term>Positive</term> <note>original: "Positif"; a smaller, secondary organ case, often located behind the organist's back or as a separate division of the main instrument.</note>, of which I spoke in the twenty-seventh Proposition, one will find at least two thousand, which make as much noise as if 2,000 men were singing. Yet there are men to be found who can, all by themselves, make all the sounds of these pipes one after another; for I have heard those who so perfectly counterfeit the stops of the Tremulant, the Flageolet, the Larigot, the Trumpet, etc.—either by pressing some comb, leaf, or other thing against their lips, or without such artifice—that it is difficult to distinguish them from the stops of the Organ.

### COROLLARY IV.

The **Bird-calls** <note>original: "Apeaux"; decoys or whistles used by hunters.</note> which are used to call birds, Stags, Foxes, etc., are nothing other than reeds similar to those of the Organ, or of other wind instruments that use reeds. These have different effects according to the small boxes that enclose them, the consideration of which can serve to augment Organs with new stops, either by means of the different sizes and shapes of the said boxes, or by the different configuration of the reeds, which can be made to pronounce vowels and some consonants. ### PROPOSITION XXVIII.

**Explain the different force of weights that press upon the bellows, according to the different inclinations of their lids.**

ALTHOUGH the same weight always presses equally upon <term>lantern bellows</term> <note>A lantern bellows uses a vertical, cylindrical, or pleated design that collapses uniformly, maintaining more consistent pressure than a hinged triangular bellows.</note>, the figure of which is seen in the first Proposition where I explain the layout of Organ Cabinets, it nevertheless seems that it weighs and presses very unequally upon ordinary bellows represented by the triangle **A B C**. For it is certain that the weight placed at point **C** presses the lid **C A** to lower it toward its line, or toward its horizontal plane **A B**, along the perpendicular **C I**, and that **C A** being lowered to **D**, the weight **C** presses **A D** along the perpendicular **D H**. Thus, the force, or the heaviness of the weight **C** at point **C** is to the force of the weight **C** at point **D**, as the line **A I** is to the line **A H**; that is to say, it weighs twice as much at **D** as it does at **C**, if **A H** is double **A I**, as I have

<image-desc>A geometric diagram representing the mechanics of a bellows lid. It features a right-angled triangle labeled A, B, C, where AC is the inclined lid and AB is the horizontal base. A vertical dashed line CI drops from C to the base. Additional points D, E, and F are marked along the lid AC to show different stages of its descent toward point B. Vertical dashed lines also drop from these points to the base, meeting at points H and G, illustrating the changing leverage and force distribution as the lid closes.</image-desc>

demonstrated in the discourse on the <term>lever</term> <note>The author treats the bellows lid as a lever where the hinge (A) acts as the fulcrum.</note>, whose support one can imagine to be at **A**. This being established, the weight will have more force at **E** than at **D**, and at **F** than at **E**, following the proportion of the lines **A H**, **A G**, and **A B**.

To this one can add the reason of the different inclinations of the plane, for the weight always weighs less on those less inclined toward the horizon, as we have shown in the eighth and tenth Proposition of the second book on <term>Movements</term> <note>original: "Mouuemens"; likely referring to Mersenne's work on mechanics and the physics of falling bodies.</note>. From this, it follows that less force is required to support the weight on **A D** than on **A C**, and that no force is needed to support it on **A B**. I leave aside several other considerations—for example, how much greater the impact of a weight falling from a given height would be on **A D** than on **A C**—in order to explain in what manner the <term>wind</term> <note>In organ building, "the wind" refers to the pressurized air stored in the bellows and windchest.</note>, which fills the open bellows **A C B**, exits from within. For since the weight has less force on **C A** than on **A D**, or on **A F**, it seems that less wind should come out during the descent from **C** to **D** than during that from **D** to **B**, since there is a <term>volume of air</term> <note>original: "solide d'air"; literally a "solid of air," a geometric term for the three-dimensional space inside the bellows.</note> in **A C D** which is double the volume in **A D B**, and since **C** presses less than **D**—that is to say, there is less force and more resistance. This nevertheless does not happen, inasmuch as if the wind were pushed less at the beginning of the descent than at the end, the sound of the pipes would be altered <note>If the air pressure fluctuated significantly as the bellows closed, the pipes would change pitch or "waver," losing their steady tone.</note>, which does not happen. From this one concludes that the wind exits equally, and consequently that one must not here consider the ratios of the different levers, or of the different inclination of the planes. And if there is any notable difference in the wind, it is at the end from **F** down to **B**, because so little remains that it is not capable of providing what is necessary for the pipes.

<header>of Organs.</header>

But this defect is remedied by the other bellows that accompanies it, because it is full when the other is empty, and the <term>wind-chest</term> <note>Original: "layette." In an organ, this is the box that holds pressurized air before it is distributed to the pipes.</note> being full of wind prevents the weight from descending too quickly. Furthermore, once the bellows is filled, the wind naturally tends to exit, just as it does in a balloon filled with air. There are also very skilled men who maintain that the weight, which is usually encased in the bellows of several <term>cabinet organs</term> <note>Small, portable pipe organs intended for domestic use rather than large churches.</note>, does not weigh more at one inclination than at another. It may also happen that no more wind will exit from a stronger pressure than from a lesser one, for it will not yield to a pressure that is too sudden and too violent, just as water does not yield to blows that are too quick and violent; hence it happens that water reflects and rejects cannonballs and musket balls, or stones that one fires or throws into it.

There are still several things to consider in the movement of bellows: for example, whether they lower by tiny jumps so imperceptible that they seem to make a continuous movement—as some believe regarding the natural motion of stones falling toward their center <note>A reference to the Aristotelian and early modern debates on whether motion and acceleration were continuous or composed of discrete "instants."</note>—and whether they draw in air for fear of a vacuum, or by the pressure of the surrounding air which forces the neighboring air to enter. However, it is enough to have proposed these difficulties to induce fine minds to research many others, and to provide the solution to these. One can also determine in what proportion the weights must be increased when the bellows are made two, three, four, five, or six times larger; how much more difficult it is to lift the lid of one bellows compared to another according to a given ratio when they are not loaded with any weight and their boards are of equal heaviness; how the wind can exit when they are raised and they fall back by themselves without the aid of any weight; how much easier it is to lift them when their <term>intake valves</term> <note>Original: "lunettes" (literally "spectacles"). These are the circular openings or clack-valves that allow air into the bellows.</note> are double or triple in width rather than half or a third; and how much more easily the wind exits, and with how much less pressure, when their <term>nozzle</term> <note>Original: "mufle" (literally "snout"). The outlet through which the air is forced into the wind-trunk.</note> is wider in a given ratio. This can similarly be applied to the different pressures of water and the different openings through which it exits, in order to compare the movements and resistances of these two elements, which serve to make the Organs and all their mechanisms play. It is not necessary to point out that the end of the bellows **C** does not rise in a straight line, since the arc of the circumference **B F C** shows its path, and the height to which they are usually raised—that is, at an angle of sixty degrees, which constitutes each angle of an equilateral triangle. Thus, one can consider **A C** as the leg of a compass describing the arc of the circle **B D C** from the center **A**.

Since the Organ without bellows is like a body without a soul, we must teach the manner of constructing them in order to complete this treatise; and for this subject, we will first explain their size and their number according to the instruments for which they are intended. Secondly, we will see

that which concerns the <term>wind-trunk</term> <note>Original: "porte-vent." This is the large wooden pipe or conduit that carries compressed air from the bellows to the wind-chest.</note> which serves as a conduit to carry the wind to the reservoir; and then we shall speak of the <term>tremulant</term> <note>Original: "Tremblant." A mechanical device in an organ that causes the wind supply to fluctuate, creating a vibrato or "trembling" effect in the sound.</note> which is ordinarily placed in the wind-trunk to make the sound more agreeable. Now, one must first choose good, well-dried oak wood to make the <term>bellows</term> <note>Original: "soufflets."</note>, so that it does not warp after it has been put to use. As for their size, it must be proportioned to that of the Organ; for example, if the Organ is of sixteen feet—which is one of the largest made at present—and if it is furnished with the diversity of all the <term>stops</term> <note>Original: "ieux" (modern French: "jeux"). The different sets or ranks of pipes that produce distinct sounds.</note> now in use, of which I have spoken previously, there must be at least four bellows, each six feet long and four feet wide. Each should be weighted with sixty pounds, so that the wind is pushed with enough force to make the **Trumpets**, the **Pedals**, and the other stops speak promptly. And if one adds a **Positive** <note>A smaller, secondary organ case, often placed behind the organist’s back or as a separate division of the main instrument.</note> in proportion to the Great Organ, and if the same wind must serve both, one must add one or two bellows similar to the others, so that they may supply the need when the others are emptying.

Upon which it should be noted that when the Organ is furnished with many bellows, there is much less effort required to raise them often, and the wind is more steady; for even if two bellows provide as much air as several, they nevertheless do not distribute the wind as equally and they descend much faster. One can easily determine the number and size of the bellows for smaller Organs; for example, if it is an eight-foot organ, two bellows are sufficient, provided it has no separate Pedals—for there are some Organs where the Pedal keyboard only pulls down the keys of the other manual—but when they are separate, at least three bellows are needed to provide the necessary wind.

Now, having chosen the proper wood, it must be well-joined, glued, and pegged, and internal bars must be well-nailed so that if the wood tries to warp, it is prevented by this means. This being done, it will be given the necessary length and width; and then one must cut a <term>vent</term> <note>Original: "soupirail." An intake hole.</note> into the bottom board, which is to say a square hole. After lining it all around with leather, a <term>check-valve</term> <note>Original: "soupape."</note> of fairly thick wood is applied over it, lined with very soft leather, so that when the <term>ribs</term> <note>Original: "eclisses." The folding wooden sections that form the sides of the bellows.</note> of the bellows are raised, the valve draws in wind until the bellows is allowed to descend; for then it closes, so that the wind can only exit through the conduit that carries the wind to the <term>wind-chest</term> <note>Original: "sommier." The wooden box upon which the pipes stand and which distributes the air to them.</note>. After having properly fitted the valve, a small leather strap is added over it, one end of which is glued to the valve and the other to the bellows, for fear that if the bellows is accidentally overturned, the valve—not being secured—might also flip over; for it would be very difficult to repair. One can also add a small iron handle over the valve, which will prevent it from opening more than necessary; but the square hole must be large enough so that it draws in wind quickly: for example, the hole for the aforementioned bellows of six feet long can be half a foot long and four inches wide. As for the folds of the bellows, they are made of several small boards of very thin and slender wood, which are rubbed with glue to attach the leather to them; and for the folds at the end, they are made of other small boards proportioned to the bottom of the bellows. However, the sight and inspection of the bellows of an Organ will teach more than words, which is why I shall dwell on it no further.

Now, having applied the top of the bellows of the same size as the bottom, one must leave an opening at the end of the bellows where there is a <term>valve</term> <note>Original: "soupape." A device that allows air to flow in only one direction.</note>. This valve does not need a piece of leather to be held in place like the other, because it does not lie flat like the first; rather, it is suspended in such a way that it opens when the bellows provides the wind, and it closes on the inside when the bellows is raised. This valve must close so precisely that the wind from one of the bellows cannot pass into the other; otherwise, the wind cannot be as steady as required. Those who place this valve inside the <term>wind-trunk</term> <note>Original: "porte-vent." The conduit that carries air from the bellows to the wind-chest.</note> must connect one end of said wind-trunk to each bellows, lest the wind be obstructed by the valves that meet there. It should be noted that larger valves are better, because they provide the wind more effectively; however, the size of the wind-trunk and the <term>reservoir</term> <note>Original: "reserue." A storage area for pressurized air to ensure a steady supply.</note> should not be excessive, for fear that the wind might not be compressed enough to produce a good effect. For example, the reservoir and the wind-trunk of a sixteen-foot Organ are eight inches wide on the inside, and four or five inches high; and if the Organ is only eight feet, these must be reduced by a third or so, and so on for others in proportion. And if it is only four feet, as the **Positive** organs usually are, the wind-trunk may be five inches wide and three inches high.

# PROPOSITION XXXV.

### Explaining the shape, weight, and other circumstances of the Tremulant.

THE **Tremulant** <note>Original: "Tremblant." A mechanical device that causes the air supply to fluctuate, creating a vibrato effect.</note> belongs to the wind-trunk, in which it is enclosed; for this reason, it is called a "closed-wind tremulant." This is the type used nowadays because it is more pleasant and does not beat the air as harshly or as quickly as the "open-wind" (or "lost-wind") tremulant used in the past, as can still be seen in old Organs.

Now, the closed-wind Tremulant is nothing more than a valve lined with three or four layers of leather, which is suspended at a slight tilt and supported on a small square of wood hollowed out in the middle, which is only half an inch high all around. The edges of this square are also lined with leather, lest the valve beating against it should make too much noise or strike too harshly. But it is only attached at the top against this square, so that it may open and close freely. This square must also be arranged at an angle, so that the bottom is toward the outside and the top is toward the bellows, so that the wind finds the passage more free upon entering the wind-trunk; for if the square were perpendicular to the wind-trunk, the wind—already interrupted by the valve attached there—could not supply the organ stops one wished to play. This can be avoided by giving a slope of an inch and a half to the square, which some call the <term>lunette</term> <note>A bracket or frame, named for its resemblance to a small moon or spectacles.</note>. Now, one must place a wire made of iron or <term>brass</term> <note>Original: "leton" (modern French: laiton).</note>, hooked in the manner of a chest handle, upon the Tremulant. Its two points should be fixed on the top of the valve so that the handle runs its full length, and so that it is raised and curved two inches higher than the bottom of said valve, so that the lead weight of the Tremulant is attached to the end of said handle or ring so that it is suspended in the air. But it should be noted that one makes it beat more or less quickly follow-

adjusting the weight attached to it, for it beats faster when it has more weight, and more slowly when it has less. The skill of the **Organ-builder** <term>Facteur: the craftsman who designs and constructs the organ</term> consists in tempering it in such a way that it beats neither too fast nor too slowly; for if it is too sluggish, it will no longer serve any purpose when several keys are pressed after pulling three or four stops. It beats as it should when it beats eight times within the space of a measure lasting two seconds of an hour.

As for the size of the **Tremulant** <term>Tremblant: a mechanical device that causes the air to pulsate, creating a vibrato effect</term>, it is not strictly fixed, though it succeeds better the larger it is; and because the **wind-trunks** <term>porte-vents: the large wooden pipes that carry air from the bellows to the pipes</term> are usually a little too flat to house it, one adds a small casing that projects out of the **wind-trunk** at the site of the **Tremulant**. This is done so that it may be longer than the height of the **wind-trunk**; since the width of the trunk is four or five inches, it is good for the **Tremulant** to be three and a half or four inches wide, and half a foot long. It should also be noted that it is appropriate to make two grooves on both sides of this frame which is added to the **wind-trunk**, in order to have a sliding board or a "tail" piece. This board, being lined with leather and fitting against the frame (also lined with leather), seals the wind and provides a means to inspect the **Tremulant** when it becomes necessary to adjust it.

When the **wind-trunk** is half a foot wide, the **Tremulant** should be five inches wide and seven or eight inches long, so that it is always about one-third longer than it is wide. The other sort of **Tremulant** differs from the previous one only in that it is applied to the outside of the **wind-trunk** over a frame, or a straight window, or one that slants like the previous one; but one must place another valve in the **wind-trunk** so that, when closed, it prevents the wind from going to the **Tremulant** except when it is opened.

Now, this **Tremulant** <note>This likely refers to the "strong tremulant" (tremblant fort), which vents air out of the system, whereas the first type is the "mild tremulant" (tremblant doux) which operates inside the trunk.</note> beats more firmly than the other, and beats just as fast with several stops as with a single one, so that it should be added to the Organ if one desires to hear all the varieties that arise from different **Tremulants** (even though this one is not as pleasant as the other). After all, the pleasure of harmony consists particularly in diversity, which admits dissonances just as well as chords. Finally, it should be noted that one will have a perfect **Tremulant** if it does not alter the pitch of the pipes too much (as happens when it does not have enough of an opening, or when the wind is lost elsewhere) and if it beats in such a way that it imitates the trembling of voices in the Organ stops. It is all the better the closer it is to the **wind-chest** <term>sommier: the wooden box upon which the organ pipes stand and which distributes the air</term>, where the wind does not make it beat too quickly.

### PROPOSITION XXXVI.

->*To explain how one must construct Organ stops to pronounce vowels, consonants, syllables, and words.*<-

It is first of all certain that only **reed pipes** <term>tuyaux à anches: pipes that produce sound via a vibrating metal tongue rather than a whistle-like flue</term> can serve to pronounce vowels, consonants, and syllables, as experience teaches. Secondly, that the said pipes can do this because we find through experience that **bird calls** <term>apeaux: mechanical whistles or decoys used by hunters to mimic birds</term> make syllables so similar to those of birds that they fly toward them and are lured and caught by means of this imitation. This similarly happens with stags, foxes, and several other wild beasts, whose belling, yelping, and

# of Organs.

the other sounds with **reeds** <term>anches: the vibrating metal tongues in certain organ pipes that produce a characteristic "reedy" sound</term>, which are made longer or shorter according to the highness of the sounds and the voices one wishes to represent. But it must be noted that the shaping and modification of the sound is done primarily by the different shapes of the pipe's body, and not by that of the **tongues** <term>languettes: the thin strips of brass that vibrate against the shallot</term> or the **shallots** <term>eschalotes: the tube upon which the tongue beats</term>, which must always be of the same fashion, although one can make the tongue thicker or thinner.

Now, the body of the pipe can be altered in several ways, either by placing some spring inside that strikes the air with different movements, or simply by placing the hand over the top of its casing (which we discussed in the tenth Proposition) and removing it at the same time the sound of the pipe begins to form; for this positioning and lifting of the fingers, or the hand, causes the reed to pronounce the syllables *vé* and *fé*, and not *vé* and *fè* <note>The author is distinguishing between the closed 'é' and the open 'è' sounds in French phonetics</note>, because the reed pronounces the "great ê," which is between *a* and *e*, and which can be called a "feminine *a*" or a "masculine *e*," unless one prefers to make it a new vowel. From this comes the fact that the **Human Voice** <term>Voix Humaines: an organ stop designed to imitate the sound of a human choir</term> stops on Organs seem to bleat like sheep, or like calves.

When one closes both hands over the same end of the pipe body so that they taper in the manner of a cone, the vowel *U* is produced; this shows that one must give the same shape to the end of the pipe as to the lips to make them pronounce the same syllables. The vowel *o* is heard when the hands are closed in a circle, just as when one closes a pipe that is widened like a Trumpet and pierced with 3 or 4 holes. The vowel *a* is made by the same widening of an open body, pierced with as many holes: regarding this, one may see the forty-third Proposition of the *Book of the Voice* <note>Likely referring to another section of Mersenne’s "Harmonie Universelle" where he analyzes human speech</note>, where I explain the movements of the tongue and lips that make vowels and consonants, in order to place springs in the body of the pipe to imitate these movements.

I leave the research of consonants to the skilled **Organ-builders** <term>Facteurs: the master craftsmen who design and build organs</term>, who can easily find them through experimentation with various pipe bodies, some ending in a cone, others in funnels shaped like a sheath, and in all other necessary fashions, by adding certain springs inside or over the opening of the body. These will create the consonants at the same time the reed begins to sound and pronounce its vowel. For each consonant is only heard at the same moment the vowel begins: so that one cannot know if a consonant has been pronounced, or only the vowel, even if the same sound continues, if one has not heard the beginning of the pronunciation. For example, one cannot know if a man sings *ba, ca, da*, or *fa*, etc., when one hears only his voice on *a* and was not there at the start of the pronunciation; so it seems that consonants are nothing other than a certain circumstance of the vowels.

Now, it would suffice to find pipes that make the syllables, and consequently the words of the **Holy** <note>original: "Sanctus"</note> or the **Lamb of God** <note>original: "Agnus Dei"</note>, so that they could be sung in four parts on the Organ within the span of an **Octave** <term>Octaue: the interval of eight notes, or the basic set of thirteen chromatic keys</term>. For there being only seventeen different syllables in the **Lamb of God** <note>original: "Agnus Dei"</note>, etc., the thirteen pipes of the Octave would suffice to sing it in four parts; these must be multiplied by seventeen to have two hundred twenty-one pipes that make all the syllables of the said **Lamb of God** <note>Agnus</note> with each key of this Octave, by means of which one could sing the **Lamb of God** <note>Agnus</note> in more than ten thousand different ways.

<header>Book Six</header>

It must nevertheless be noted that syllables which begin with one consonant and end with another—such as the syllables *car*, *nous*, *par*, etc.—are the most difficult; this is why the reed needs two springs for this purpose, one of which strikes the edges of the pipe body at the beginning, and the other at the end of the pronunciation. This is enough to inspire clever minds and engineers to make pipes pronounce every syllable, and consequently, all sorts of speech. However, it would require several pipes in unison to pronounce different syllables on the same tone; for example, it would take four pipes to pronounce the word "Truth" <note>original: *Veritatem*</note>.

### PROPOSITION XXXVII.

->*Explaining the manner of inspecting Organs and recognizing the faults of the Builders, where it will be seen how the defects of the Organ can be repaired.*<-

I am not speaking here of the organ case, the proportion and beauty of which must be judged by architects and joiners, but only of all the parts that contribute to the goodness and perfection of an Organ. This perfection consists in the absence of defects that may be encountered, which we can reduce to eight; four are of great consequence, and four others can be remedied. First and most particularly, one must observe during the inspection of an Organ if, when all its stops are closed, there is any pipe that **ciphers** <term>corne: a fault where a pipe sounds unintentionally because air is leaking into it</term> when each key of the keyboard is touched. Now, this defect is very great and comes from the **slider** <term>registre: a movable strip of wood that turns a stop on or off by aligning holes</term> being pulled too far, or not far enough, or not sitting flush against its **upperboard** <term>chappe: the top wooden plate of the windchest where the pipes are seated</term>. This can be corrected by striking a few hammer blows on its nails to make it tighter. However, one must also watch if, when the stops are pulled, any pipe ciphers even when no key is touched; for then, one must look into the air reservoir of the **windchest** <term>sommier: the heart of the organ, a wooden box that distributes pressurized air to the pipes</term> to see if this fault comes from some dirt caught between the **pallet** <term>soupape: the valve that opens to let air into a specific note's channel</term> and the windchest, or if the said pallet, not being straight, does not seal well against the windchest, or if, being placed to the side, it does not entirely cover the **channel** <term>reineure: the internal groove in the windchest that carries air to all the pipes of a single note</term>.

In the second place, one must check every key of the keyboard, after having pulled the first stop—which is called the **Prestant** <term>Prestant: the Principal 4' stop, used as the foundation for tuning the rest of the organ</term> (upon which all other stops must be regulated as their foundation)—to see if, when making one key speak, there is any "borrowing" from its neighbor. This defect is one of the greatest and most disagreeable that can be found in an Organ because it creates dissonances at every moment. Furthermore, it is more difficult to remedy than the previous ones, as it can proceed from three causes. The first is when the channel has an opening, however small it may be, so that the air given to it passes through and enters the one next to it; this can be avoided if, when making the Organ, one lines the insides of the channels with parchment. The second cause can come from the top of the channels, over which leather is usually glued; if it is not well-glued in all places, it allows air to pass from one channel to another. The third cause can come from the **upperboard**, which does not sit perfectly level on its slider, from which it happens that air escapes from one of the holes and slips between them so much that it causes the other nearby pipes to cipher. This can easily be avoided in the construction of the windchest, for if...

apply small wooden strips over each groove, placing them into two small slots made on each side of the groove; if one then glues the ordinary leather over them, it will be impossible for any **borrowing** <term>emprunt: a defect where air leaks from one channel to another, causing pipes to sound weakly or out of tune</term> to occur there.

In the third place, the bellows must be constructed in such a way that they do not falter and are equal in force; that is to say, the wind from one must not communicate with the other. When this vice occurs, the **flap valve** <term>languette: a leather hinge or valve</term> of the bellows' nozzle does not sit tightly upon the square of the wind-trunk or upon the nozzle where it is placed; this can only be avoided by ungluing the bellows. As for the equality of the wind it must provide, it may fail for two reasons: the first comes from the inequality of the weights placed upon the two bellows; but it is easy to correct this defect by increasing or decreasing one of the weights until the wind is equal. The second reason is taken from the construction of the bellows and is of very great importance; this happens when they push their wind with more force at the beginning when they are raised than at the end, such that it is almost impossible to tune the Organ. Now, this defect appears in two ways: one is when the wind steadily decreases in force, which proceeds from the **ribs** <term>écliſſes: the folding wooden sides of the bellows</term> not being free; the other is when the wind is equal in certain places and moves by jolts in others, because the ribs strike against one another as they descend. One can only remedy these defects by breaking the bellows apart to rebuild them anew.

In the fourth place, one must consider if the pipes of the *Prestant* <note>The Prestant, or Principal, is the foundation stop of the organ, usually an open metal stop that sounds at 4-foot pitch.</note> are equal in strength, for this equality is one of the greatest ornaments of the Organ, just as inequality is very disagreeable. This is noticed when one encounters strong pipes and weak pipes within the same stop. This proceeds sometimes from the fashioning of the pipe, which is difficult to remedy, and at other times from the opening of the pipe foot, or from the **languid** <term>languette: the horizontal plate inside the pipe mouth that directs air</term>, which is also sometimes too pressed or beaten down; this is easy to remedy with the point of a knife.

In the fifth place, it is necessary to have a skilled Organist to inspect the tuning of the *Prestant*, not so much to play it as to have a good ear. For just as the foundation of a building must be well secured or one cannot hope for much fruit from it, if the first stop—which is the foundation of the others—is not well tuned, one can expect nothing from the others but a perpetual beating, which will be so harsh to the ear that it would be much better not to use such Organs at all.

Now, this inspection will be done exactly by seeing if the Fifths of the following notes are tempered: namely from *C* to *g*, from *D* to *a*, from *E* to *B* <note>original: *♯* (natural/sharp sign)</note>, from *F* to *c*, from *G* to *d*, and from *A* to *e*. These notes or keys are the principals of the **Diatonic** genus <note>The standard musical scale of seven notes</note>; one must check if these Fifths are a bit weakened and lower than their perfect purity. And then one must see the same thing on the **accidentals** <note>original: *feintes* (the "faked" or black keys)</note>, by taking the Fifths from *B* <note>original: *♯*</note> to *F-sharp* <note>original: *xf*</note>, from *F-sharp* to *C-sharp* <note>original: *cx*</note>, and from *C-sharp* to *G-sharp* <note>original: *gx*</note>. And for the two that remain, one must take *f* and descend to *B-flat* <note>original: *b*</note>, and from *B-flat* descending to *E-flat* <note>original: *ex*</note>; it is necessary that *E-flat* be a bit higher than its perfect pitch. For by this means, one will have all the required Consonances: namely the Thirds and Sixths, both major and minor. Having found this within the span of one Octave, it will be necessary to follow each key by the Octave to the top of the Keyboard.

In the sixth place, one must see if every stop responds to the *Prestant* for the tun—

In the seventh place, one must consider whether the **soundboard** <term>sommier: the heart of the organ where pressurized air is distributed to the pipes</term> and the **rollerboards** <term>abbregez: the mechanical linkage that transmits the touch of a key to the valve beneath a distant pipe</term> are well-made; this will be known regarding the soundboard by seeing the arrangement of the pipes placed upon it, and particularly if the **upperboards** <term>chappes: the planks that hold the pipes in place</term> and the **sliders** <term>registres: the sliding strips of wood used to turn stops on and off</term> fit together well, if they slide easily, and if the wind reservoir is so well-sealed that no wind escapes except when opening the **pallets** <term>soupapes: the valves that let air into the pipes when a key is pressed</term>; and finally if the **access panel** <term>regard: a small opening for inspecting the internal valves</term> is appropriately made for visiting the pallets and for remedying them if by chance some dirt gets caught there. As for the rollerboards, one will know if they are well-made when the keyboard is not sluggish in giving wind to the pipes, when it closes easily, and when it is not necessary to depress the keys very deeply.

In the eighth and final place, one must see if the bellows are well-sealed, and if the wind is not lost too much: which can be remedied by gluing small pieces of leather to the places where the wind escapes. But if the wind from the bellows is too slack and too weak, without however being heard to escape, this arises because the **builders** <term>facteurs: organ builders</term> have not rubbed the wood with glue on the inside, and the wind passes through its pores. One can also see if the **Tremulant** <term>tremblant: a device that causes the air to pulse, creating a vibrato effect</term> located in the wind trunk is perfect—that is to say, if it does not beat too harshly, as happens when it is not sufficiently lined with leather, or if it beats too quickly; which must be remedied by decreasing the weight attached to it: and if it does not alter [the pitch] too much, that is, if the pipes do not lose too much of their force when it is drawn: which would result from it being too small, not having enough of an opening to supply the stops that are drawn. As for the **reed stops** <term>jeux d'anches: stops that produce sound via a vibrating metal tongue rather than a whistle</term>, it suffices to observe if they speak promptly and clearly. Now, after having spoken of the inspection of Organs, and assuming they are in tune and that nothing is lacking in their construction, I wish to add a new Theory of Music, in which one will have the proper numbers to divide the **scale** <term>diapason: here referring to the mathematical proportions of the octave</term> of Organs into twelve equal semitones, of which I have already spoken in the fifteenth Proposition, and several other things which will show the excellence of the mind of him who invented them.

twelve equal semitones, namely the minor Third, the major Third, and the Fourth, and their complements <note>In music theory, a complement is the interval that completes an octave; for example, a Fourth and a Fifth together make an Octave</note>, which are the major Sixth, the minor Sixth, and the Fifth.

In the third place, that all harmony is generated from different and non-contiguous sounds, which are so commensurable among themselves that one can contain the other, and that they are joined by a common bond. Because sounds are produced by physical bodies, we must seek the reason for this in solids <note>Three-dimensional shapes</note>, and not in planes <note>Two-dimensional shapes</note> or in lines. From this, he concludes that the union of sounds creates harmony through the equality of the unison, or through the resemblance of other intervals. This being established, he supposes that the Octave is a **harmonic cube** <note>The author treats the octave as a cube with a side of 12 units, representing the 12 semitones. Therefore, the "volume" of an octave is 12 x 12 x 12 = 1,728</note>, upon which all harmony is founded, such that it must have as many harmonic intervals as there are similar cubes which can be joined together by means of another, or of several middle cubes; this is because one cube is similar to another cube, and the cube which is their difference is also similar to them, or contains similar ones.

Now, the minor Third contains three intervals, and its complement contains nine. The whole cube of the Octave, which has twelve intervals, is 1,728; the cube of the minor Third <note>3 x 3 x 3</note> is 27, that of its complement <note>9 x 9 x 9</note> is 729, and the sum of the two is 756. Their difference from the cube of the Octave is 972, which contains 36 cubes of the Ditone <term>Ditone: A major third, literally "two tones"</term>, just as the major Sixth contains 64 cubes of the minor Third. Consequently, these cubes agree with that of the Octave, and are joined by similar cubes. The entire Octave contains 64 cubes of the minor Third, and two cubes of the Sixth, plus ten cubes of the Sesquiditone <term>Sesquiditone: A minor third, literally "one and a half tones"</term>.

The major Third has four intervals, and the minor Sixth, which is its complement, contains eight. The cube of the Ditone is 64 <note>4 x 4 x 4</note>, and that of the minor Sixth is 512 <note>8 x 8 x 8</note>, which together make 576. Thus, 1,152 is the difference between their cubes and the cube of the Octave. This difference contains 18 cubes of the Ditone, just as the minor Sixth contains 8, and the entire Octave contains 27—or three cubes of the minor Sixth, plus three cubes of the Ditone.

In the fourth place, one must proceed differently for the Fourth and the Fifth, because their ratio is not composed of cubes, but of **plinths** <note>Rectangular blocks</note> or **parallelepipeds** <note>A six-sided solid where every face is a parallelogram</note>. For the solid rectangle of the Fourth is 720, and that of the Fifth is 1,008, the sum of which makes the cube of the Octave, 1,728. The solid rectangle of the Fourth is different from the plinth of the Octave—that is to say, by 288—and they have eight as their common measure. Consequently, the plinth of the Fourth is equal to 90 cubes, and that of the Fifth to 126 cubes. But the cube of the Octave is equal to 216 cubes <note>216 is 6 x 6 x 6, which is an eighth of the 1,728 cube</note>; and consequently, these two plinths are composed of equal cubes which make up that of the Octave. Now, these two Consonances are the most perfect, since they divide the cube of the Octave into two equal solid rectangles, and they have the first cube for their common measure.

As for the other consonances, besides the two cubes, they consider three solid rectangles which are drawn from the division of a cube into two similar cubes. From this, he concludes that union, and consequently harmony, is preserved when the division is not multiplied, and that it is destroyed when it increases.

As for the Tritone <term>Tritone: An unstable musical interval spanning three whole tones</term>, it contains six intervals, the complement of which is another Tritone. The cube of both the one and the other is 216 <note>6 x 6 x 6</note>, and the sum of the two, namely 432, leaves a difference from the cube of the Octave of 1,296, which contains six cubes...

<page-num>387</page-num>
<header>on Organs</header>

of the **Tritone** <note>An interval of three whole tones, known for its restless or "unstable" sound</note>; and the entire Octave contains eight cubes of the Tritone <note>Mathematically, if the Octave is 12 units and the Tritone is 6, then 6 cubed is 216, and 12 cubed is 1,728. 1,728 divided by 216 equals exactly 8</note>. But this interval is not harmonic, even though it can be resolved into equal cubes that are commensurable with one another, because there is no difference between them, and one cannot contain the other; from this it happens that no union of sounds is created by the reception of both, but rather a disagreeable collision. For harmony requires that the Octave contains the largest interval, and that the larger contains the lesser, so that there may be a commensurable distance between them. It must nevertheless be noted that harmony allows for the commensurability of the Tritone's cubes by means of a slight "touching" <note>likely referring to a passing tone or a quick resolution</note>, through which one passes toward a perfect harmony.

The Second, or the whole tone, has two intervals <note>semitones</note>, of which eight is the cube; the Seventh, which is its complement, has ten, and its cube is 1,000. The sum of these cubes makes 1,008, and their difference from the cube of the Octave is 720, which contains 90 cubes of the tone. The Seventh contains 125 cubes of the tone. The Octave contains all the cubes of the Seventh, plus 9. But it cannot be called harmony, even though the Octave contains the Seventh and the Second, because both of their sounds are contiguous to the extremities of the Octave, and they clash—though differently than in the Tritone, where the collision happens in the middle of the Octave; now, this collision is the reason these sounds are disagreeable to the ear.

## PROPOSITION XXXIX.

->*To determine whether the ancients had Organs, and to note what is missing from this treatise.*<-

It is not difficult to respond to this difficulty, since Vitruvius describes this instrument in the thirteenth chapter of his tenth book <note>Vitruvius was a Roman architect; he described the "hydraulis" or water organ</note>; and the Emperor Julian wrote an epigram in its praise, which I have placed at the beginning of the Latin book on Organs. Additionally, Master Naudé <note>Gabriel Naudé (1600–1653), a famous French librarian and scholar</note> sent me from the garden of the Mattei, Roman Lords, the figure of a small organ cabinet, whose bellows are similar to those used to light a fire; they are raised by a man who stands behind the cabinet, and the keyboard is touched by a woman. The inscription that follows is beneath the said cabinet:

> <note>original Latin: "LAPISIVS C. F. SCAPTIA CAPITOLINVS EX TESTAMENTO FIERI MONVMEN. IVSSIT ARBITRATVM HEREDVM MEORVM SIBI ET SVIS."</note>
> LAPISIUS, SON OF GAIUS, OF THE SCAPTIAN TRIBE, CAPITOLINUS, ORDERED BY HIS WILL THAT THIS MONUMENT BE MADE AT THE DISCRETION OF HIS HEIRS FOR HIMSELF AND HIS FAMILY.

From this, antiquarians may surmise what they can, for it is enough that I have provided the practice of our own century, which far surpasses everything that antiquity shows us on this subject.

We also have the 28th Epistle written to Dardanus in the fourth volume of Saint Jerome <note>This letter, *Dardanus*, is now considered "Pseudo-Jerome," a medieval forgery that described imaginary instruments</note> (which cannot be attributed to that excellent man, for it is full of barbarisms), in which the author describes an Organ that had twelve bellows and fifteen pipes, and whose windchest <term>layette: the box that holds the pressurized air for the pipes</term> was made of two elephant skins. To this he adds that this Organ made as much noise as thunder, that it could be heard from more than a thousand paces, and that there was one in Jerusalem that could be heard from the Mount of Olives. He describes yet other instruments that can be seen in the same Epistle. Now, if one imagines that these two elephant skins were sewn together like those—

pipes of the **Musettes** <note>A type of small bagpipe or woodwind pipe</note>, and that twelve bellows were used to inflate them, one could say that this Organ was a species of **Bagpipe**. Be that as it may, we do not read that the Ancients had all the diversity of stops that are found in our Organs.

I now add several things that have not been noted before, the first of which consists of making an Organ so light that anyone can carry it as easily as a **Violin** or a **Lute**. This will be possible if one uses four **Recorders** <note>original: "Fleurtes douces"</note>, each having the range of the organ keyboard; for one could open and close their holes by means of small springs lined with leather, as I have already shown in the fifth book on instruments when I spoke of the **Sourdelline** <note>A complex, bellows-blown Italian bagpipe</note>, or **Musette of Naples**, in the thirtieth Proposition; and because they can be cut in several places, one can assemble them and fit them into as small a space as the **Rackett** <note>original: "Ceruelat," a compact Renaissance woodwind where the bore folds back on itself many times</note>, or one of the smaller **Bassoons**, which I treated in the said book.

As for the **windchest** <term>fommier: the pressurized box that holds the air and distributes it to the pipes</term>, it is enough that it has four holes to receive the four heads of the four Recorders; I leave the rest to the discretion of the **Builders** <note>original: "Facteurs," specifically instrument makers</note>, who may use a small drum or **barrel** <note>An early reference to a mechanical "barrel organ" mechanism</note>, which will perform the **diminutions** <note>Rapid melodic passages or ornaments</note> and cadences more accurately and quickly than the fingers of the most skillful Organists. Thus, the same movement of the barrel will raise the bellows and open the **pallets** <note>original: "foupapes," the valves that let air into the pipes</note> and the keys of all the holes of the Recorders. These holes can be made in such great number on four Recorders that each **Octave** will have nineteen sounds to allow the three genres of Music <note>Referring to the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales of Greek theory</note> to be heard in their perfection; now, it would be easier to adapt these Recorders to the Lute or the **Viol** than other organ pipes.

The second thing concerns the proportion that Builders observe for the **Scaling** <term>Diapafon: here referring to the ratio of a pipe's diameter to its length</term> of the pipes. For although I have given a great multitude of scalings, nevertheless, ordinary Builders give different proportions to the pipes depending on the place where they are to be set, the convenience of the windchests, and the strength or sweetness they wish to give to their stops. For this purpose, they make the **mouth** <note>The opening where the air hits the lip to produce sound</note> or the **flue** <note>original: "lumiere"</note> higher or wider; for example, pipes speak more softly the smaller their mouth is, and louder the higher and more open it is.

As for the smallest pipes of the highest Octave, they make them thicker than their length requires when following the proportion of the largest pipes, so that they speak better and have more body. For example, they make their width equal to their length, so that the **tin plate** from which they are made is square, whereas it should be four times longer than it is wide if it followed the proportion of the four-foot or eight-foot pipes. They also make the mouth of these small pipes larger than the others in proportion, so that their sounds may be more **bright** and lively; for they give to the mouth only a fifth part of the length of the pipes in the lowest Octave, but they give a fourth part to those of the second Octave, a third and a half to those of the third, and a third or almost half to those of the last Octave, so that they may be better heard. And because the sound of the large pipes would be too corpulent if they were twice as thick as those an octave above them, they make them less wide, without it being necessary to observe any rule other than that...

which pleases them, and which is convenient for them for placing the pipes on the **windchest** <term>sommier: the pressurized box that holds the air and distributes it to the pipes</term>, and for making them produce a harmony that is more or less coarse, or delicate. But they keep them a little longer in compensation; as I noted in the thirteenth and fourteenth *Propositions*: now one can see in the twelfth what different widths contribute to pipes of equal height.

The third thing concerns the **beats** <note>acoustic interference heard as a pulsing sound when two notes are slightly out of tune</note> of pipes that are not perfectly in tune, which I discuss in the thirtieth *Proposition*; to which I add that large pipes do not beat as fast as smaller ones, even if their tuning is equally imperfect, and that both beat faster the further they are from perfect tuning. For example, a pipe that is off by a **semitone** <note>original: "demiton," the smallest interval in common scales, like the distance between E and F</note> beats faster than one that is only off by a **comma** <note>original: "comma," a tiny musical interval used in mathematical tuning theory, much smaller than a semitone</note>, and one off by a comma beats faster than one off by only a quarter of a comma, which is the exact displacement of the tempered and weakened **Fifth**: so that if one uses the second **Octave** of the *Prestant* <note>a standard 4-foot principal stop on the organ</note>, or some other stop proportioned to the voice of the one who tunes, one can easily put all sorts of Organs and stops in tune, even if one does not have a precise and delicate ear. For example, if one observes once and for all that the two-foot pipes of the *Prestant* beat only once in the time of one second of an hour when they are well tempered, one will be certain that pipes of the same size of the *Prestant* in other Organs must beat once in the said second to be in tune. One can also observe how much faster or slower the half-foot or eight-foot pipes of the same stop beat compared to the preceding ones.

And if the sound of pipes is made by as many beats, or vibrations of air, as that of strings at **unison**, as is certain, one can say that pipes beat more slowly as they descend lower; for example, they beat half as fast when they descend by an **Octave**: and similarly that pipes that are off by only a comma beat more slowly than those off by a semitone, because the vibrations of the two sounds that create the comma take longer to join together. That is to say, if the semitone is a ratio of 16 to 15, and the comma is 81 to 80, the beat of the comma will be slower because the terms of its ratio are larger than those of the ratio of the semitone; and consequently, this semitone will beat at least four times in the same time that the comma beats once: because 81 contains 16 more than four times, from which it is easy to state the number of beats of each pipe. I leave aside several conclusions that can be deduced from this speculation, for example, that one can perceive the beats of large pipes separated by a whole tone, even though the beats of smaller pipes, which are also separated by a tone, cannot be heard; as much as the latter, being too fast—as happens when they occur 12 or 24 times in the space of a second—the former will occur only three or six times in the pipes that descend lower by two or three Octaves, so that one will distinguish the beating of sixteen-foot pipes, even though one cannot discern that of four-foot or two-foot pipes.

The fourth concerns the distribution of wind in the pipes, of which I speak in the twenty-sixth *Proposition*, which seems marvelous in this

that the large pipes speak <note>in organ building, "speaking" refers to the pipe producing its sound</note> more easily and with less wind than the smaller ones; this happens because they have lower and narrower mouths, and the hole at their feet is much smaller in proportion than the small pipes. But if their mouths were proportional—that is, if the mouth of a sixteen-foot pipe were sixteen times higher and wider than that of a one-foot pipe, and the opening at the foot of the former were sixteen times larger than the opening at the foot of the latter—it would perhaps require sixteen times as much wind. Thus, **organ builders** <term>Facteurs: the master craftsmen who design and construct organs</term> remedy this by diminishing the mouths and the foot-holes, just as they do with the thickness of the pipes while increasing their length. This deserves consideration for use in hydraulics and the distribution of water.

The fifth point concerns the birds that can be added to Organs, whose figures can be seen in the *Moving Forces* <note>Salomon de Caus’s 1615 treatise *Les Raisons des forces mouvantes*, which described mechanical inventions</note> of de Caus, Problems 22 and 23. However, the visual shape of the birds serves no purpose, as their song is produced by pipes hidden within the machinery, just as the decoys for deer, foxes, ducks, etc., are hidden in their boxes. Now, this ingenuity can be used to make a tree appear entirely covered in birds, each of which will have its own warbling by means of wind, water, wind-trunks, and various pipes.

The sixth point provides a very easy way to make a pipe, or a flute, that can play each **genus of Music** <note>In classical music theory, the three "genera" are Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic, each using different types of intervals</note> separately from the others. For if one slits the pipe from its mouth <note>original: "lumière," the opening where the air hits the lip of the pipe</note> to its foot—that is, from top to bottom—and fits a piece of leather around the flute so that it can be turned in whichever direction one wishes, it will exactly seal the slit of the flute. This will produce **Diatonic** <note>the standard seven-note scale, like the white keys on a piano</note> intervals when one turns the holes in the leather over the said slit (the leather having been pierced with as many holes as there are on a **flageolet** <term>Flageollet: a small, high-pitched flute with four holes in front and two for the thumbs</term>). And when one aligns the other holes made on the second side according to the **Chromatic** <note>the scale consisting of all twelve semitones</note> intervals, one will hear that genus. And when the third side of the leather, pierced with the holes necessary to sing by **Enharmonic** <note>a system using microtones or quarter-tones, rare in Western music after the Greeks but of great interest to Renaissance theorists</note> intervals, is placed over the slit, one will hear this third genus, by closing and opening the holes according to the art. This would likewise happen if one pierces one side of the leather with as many holes as are needed to play all the degrees of the "mixed" genus of the three, of which I speak in the book on the genera of Music.

Now, he who possesses such a Flute will be able to say that he carries all harmony in his hand, that he has it in his power, and that he knows the true **Diapason** <term>Diapason: here meaning the standard measurement or scale of the instrument</term> of the flageolet and of all sorts of wind instruments.

## PROPOSITION XL.

->*Explaining the Tablature of the Organ, and the greatest speed at which pieces of Music can be played on the Keyboard; where one sees music composed by the King.*<-

SEVERAL authors have provided **tablature** <term>Tablature: a system of musical notation using letters or symbols instead of notes on a staff</term> for Organs in various ways. But it would be necessary to have several specific symbols to mark the places for <term>mordents</term> <note>original: *martelemens*; rapid alternations between a note and the one below it</note>, <term>trills</term> <note>original: *tremblemens*</note>, <term>beats</term> <note>original: *battemens*</note>, and other <term>ornaments</term> <note>original: *gentillesses*; literally "niceties," referring to the elegant decorative flourishes added by a performer</note> with which this excellent Organist enriches his playing when he touches the <term>keyboard</term> <note>original: *Clauier*</note>. These symbols will be available when Sieur Ballard <note>Pierre Ballard was the sole royal printer for music in Paris, holding a monopoly on music printing during this period.</note> prints his <term>tablature</term> <note>In this context, a collection of written-out musical scores for keyboard.</note>, and those of others who play the Organ and the <term>Spinet</term> <note>A small, plucked keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note> perfectly. It remains now to explain the manner of playing the Organ, and how children should begin to place their hands on the keyboard to perform all sorts of chords and <term>fugues</term>—both <term>legato</term> <note>original: *liées*; smooth and connected</note> and <term>staccato</term> <note>original: *deliées*; detached or quick</note>—and to show how one must compose all types of pieces for the Organ. Regarding the first point, it is very difficult to understand it without the guidance of Masters; on this, one must note that there are some who teach so poorly how to place the hands on the keys that their students have as much or more trouble forgetting what they were badly taught than in becoming accustomed to the beautiful touch of an excellent Master. Such a master must be chosen from the very beginning in order to acquire the good grace and fine posture which makes Sieur de la Barre <note>Pierre de la Barre (1592–1656), a renowned court musician and organist to the King.</note>, and those he takes the trouble to teach and who are formed by his hand, incomparable. This should also be noted for all other kinds of instruments, which have all the more grace the more delicately, cleanly, and skillfully they are played.

Regarding the second point, I have spoken quite amply of <term>Composition</term> in an entire book, without there being any need to repeat it here—though one might note several details that are specific only to the Organ and other keyboard instruments. But it is better to reserve everything that can be said about this for Monsieur Raquette <note>Charles Racquet (c. 1597–1664), the organist of Notre-Dame de Paris and one of the most famous musicians of his era.</note>, organist of Notre-Dame de Paris and a most excellent Composer. He will be able to provide a treatise on Composition more perfect than any yet seen, whenever he pleases, in which he will distinguish what is unique to vocal music, and what it has more or less of than Organ music; what is better on the Organ than on the <term>Harpsichord</term> <note>original: *Clauecin*</note>; and what succeeds better on these than on the <term>Lute</term>, and so on. One can, however, observe that an Organist is all the more excellent when he makes the <term>plainchant</term> <note>The traditional, monophonic chant of the Church, often used as the foundation (cantus firmus) for organ improvisations.</note> or the subject better heard, when he makes the other parts of the <term>Counterpoint</term> sing better, and when he performs the <term>Cadences</term> <note>The concluding phrases or "musical punctuation" of a section.</note> better.

Some place great value on those who can create three or four hundred measures of good <term>figured counterpoint</term> <note>An elaborate melodic line played against a simpler theme.</note> against an <term>organ point</term> <note>original: *point d'Orgue*; a long, sustained note in the bass, similar to a drone.</note>; others value those who have great speed and lightness of hand, as happens when they play thirty-two notes in a <term>binary meter</term> <note>A time signature based on groups of two or four beats.</note> that lasts only one second <note>original: *seconde minute*</note>; and others, finally, value those who perform a very great number of <term>passages</term>, <term>diminutions</term> <note>A technique where long notes are broken down into many fast, shorter notes.</note>, and variations against whatever subject might be given to them. To this, one may add that those who play with a beautiful movement and good grace, and who are precise in their timing, are the most perfect of all—particularly if they possess all that has been noted above, and if they know how to use <term>Chromatic</term> steps as perfectly as <term>Diatonic</term> ones.

# PROPOSITION XLI.

## Explaining all the <term>Diminutions</term> <note>Also known as "divisions," these are rapid melodic passages where a single long note is broken down into many smaller, faster notes to decorate a melody.</note> that can be performed on the Organ or on the Spinet.

I have already spoken of diminutions in the book on stringed instruments, and I gave an example of those performed on the <term>Treble Violins</term> <note>The "Dessus de Violon," roughly equivalent to the modern violin.</note> in the seventh Proposition of the fourth book. However, since the Organ is considered the most perfect of all instruments, it deserves a specific example from the same hand as the person who set the preceding song into <term>tablature</term> <note>In this context, a written-out musical score for keyboard.</note>. In this example, one can see what each hand can, or should, do while the other is occupied with <term>passages</term> <note>Rapid scales or ornamental runs.</note>; for an excellent Organist must have two equal hands, both in speed and lightness, to execute everything that might be proposed to him.

Here it should be noted that one can find more assistance on the Organ than on other instruments; for example, one can weight down two or three <term>keys</term> <note>original: *marches*; literally "steps," referring here to the physical keys of the keyboard or pedals.</note> with small pieces of lead to create just as many sustained notes and <term>drones</term> <note>original: *bourdons*</note> while both hands are busy performing variations and diminutions. In this way, a single man can perform concerts spanning four <term>octaves</term> on each <term>stop</term> <note>original: *jeu*; a specific set of pipes controlled by a knob.</note>. And because the range of all the stops taken together spans at least eight octaves in large Organs—that is to say, a <term>Fiftieth</term> <note>A musical interval spanning fifty scale degrees, or eight octaves. Mersenne calculates the ratio as 128 to 1.</note>, the ratio of which is 128 to 1, as I showed in the fortieth Proposition of the book on Consonances—he will perform concerts of more than eight octaves. This is possible because he can sustain the sound of as many pipes as he wishes by means of small springs that will hold down the lower keys and the <term>pedals</term> <note>Keys played with the feet.</note> which are usually played with the feet, while the hands touch the <term>keyboard</term> <note>original: *clauier*</note>. Furthermore, there is a way to use one or several <term>barrels</term> <note>original: *barillets*; pinned cylinders used in mechanical organs to play music automatically.</note> to supply whatever else is desired, though it is much more agreeable to see the entire performance depend solely on the hands of the Organist. Their skill possesses a dexterity that is difficult to replicate through artifice, regardless of what springs one might adapt to the instrument.

I am therefore including here what the most skillful and fastest hands can execute, so that this example may serve as an ideal for the perfection of a "fine touch." This is understood much better by seeing excellent Masters play than by any discourse one could make about it. It should be noted that this piece of tablature contains only the first two measures of the preceding air—that is, the melody used for these words: *Tu crois ô beau Soleil* <note>"You believe, O beautiful Sun," a popular song of the period.</note>. The right hand begins these two measures in simple <term>eighth notes</term> <note>original: *crochuës*</note> while the left hand holds steady; then the left hand does the same as the right. After this, the right hand begins again to play sixteen notes to the measure, which the left hand also does in its turn. Then the right hand plays 32 to the measure, followed by the left. Finally, the right hand plays 64 to the measure, with which the left finishes these examples.

On this point, it must first be noted that these last two lines of Diminution are only marked with notes of thirty-two to the measure, like the ones before them, whereas they ought to be sixty-four to the measure. This is why a fourth bar must be added to the stems so they become <term>sixty-fourth notes</term> <note>original: *quadruples crochuës*</note>, as the music printing shops do not yet possess these specific notes. Secondly, the time of each measure does not last...
