# PROPOSITION XLII.

->*To investigate why the stopped pipe produces two different sounds at the same time, which together form a Twelfth.*<-

We have spoken of the different sounds made by the same string at the same time when it is touched, in the eleventh Proposition of the fourth book of *String Instruments*, and we shall speak of it again in the *Book of Bells*; but it suffices for now to explain the phenomenon of this species of pipe that we call <term>stopped</term> <note>Pipes that are capped at the top. They sound an octave lower than open pipes of the same length and produce a different harmonic profile.</note>, which I mentioned previously. For I have not noticed that open pipes—whether they have a simple mouth, like those of the <term>Prestant</term> <note>The principal "4-foot" stop of the organ, which provides the foundation for the chorus.</note>, or have <term>reeds</term>, like the Trumpets and Human Voices—produce two sounds at once, despite any trial I have made. I say, then, that stopped pipes, such as <term>Recorders</term> <note>original: "Fleutes douces." While this can refer to the instrument, here it refers to the organ stop that mimics its soft, mellow tone.</note>, often produce two sounds at the same time, which are a <term>Twelfth</term> <note>An interval spanning an octave plus a fifth (twelve scale steps). In modern physics, this corresponds to the third harmonic, which is characteristic of stopped pipes.</note> apart, as I have pointed out to the best organists; although this does not happen, or at...

...is not perceived by the ear in all stopped pipes; for example, one does not notice it in the smallest pipes, but rather in the largest or medium-sized ones.

I leave it to the builders <note>original: "Facteurs" — specifically organ builders.</note>, or rather to the philosophers <note>In this period, "natural philosophers" were what we now call scientists.</note> to determine if this double sound demonstrates the imperfection or the perfection of the pipe; for since there are many that do not produce it, although they are of the same size as those that do, it seems that this cannot happen unless some are more perfect than others. And although one might admit that strings or bells which produce several sounds together more distinctly are more excellent than others, one might doubt whether the same judgment should be made regarding pipes. Be that as it may, the principal sound of the stopped pipe is the lowest, the strongest, and the most natural, while the other is higher and weaker. But it is as difficult to explain the reason for it as it is easy to experience it: for how can the wind, or the air, which makes the natural sound, make the second sound, since it must make one return in making the former, and three in making the latter? <note>Mersenne is observing that the "Twelfth" (the 3rd harmonic) vibrates three times for every one vibration of the fundamental tone.</note> And although one might say that the three vibrations are not made precisely at the same time, but so immediately after that the ear is not capable of perceiving the interval of time, nonetheless the difficulty remains: namely, why the air makes exactly three returns after one, rather than four or another number. For the reason I deduced in the *Treatise on the Trumpet* in the fifth book—namely, that three follows two more naturally and immediately than one—seems to contradict this phenomenon, unless one says that first there are two tremors of air against one, which make the Octave (which is not noticed because of the great resemblance it has to the Unison), and then one can say that one hears the Fifth, and not the Twelfth, and consequently that the three beats of air of the high sound immediately follow the two of the low sound. Indeed, the ear is often mistaken in taking the Twelfth for the Fifth, because they resemble each other. <note>A "Twelfth" is an Octave plus a Fifth; Mersenne is theorizing about the mathematical ratios of these intervals.</note> Now, the great conformity of all bodies that make noise with these pipes can help to find the reason for this experience, for one almost always perceives the Fifth, or its replica <note>The "replica" of the Fifth is the Twelfth.</note>, in all sounds of all sorts of bodies. And some assert that they have noticed in several churches that the voices of the singers <note>original: "Chantres."</note> produce one of these Fifths, whether they are produced by some sort of echo or otherwise; so that the vocal artery <note>The larynx or windpipe.</note> imitates the stopped pipe; which I have nonetheless not been able to observe.

Now, this experience being assumed, I say that small returns of air occur within each large return of the same air, with which they have the same ratio as the two sounds of the Twelfth, or the Fifth; and consequently that each part of air, whose movement lasts a moment in making the low sound, still undergoes within itself some sort of tremor or shivering similar to that of vibrating bells, or of water that shivers in a glass when one makes it ring by pressing a finger upon its rim, and that the air is agitated three times by these little shocks while it makes each of its larger returns.

The same thing can be said of all the other sounds of a touched string, for each smaller vibration can still be divided into other smaller ones: which will be easily understood if one moves the hand from right to left and from left to right in such a way that at each back and forth of one foot...

while one makes other lesser movements by making the same hand tremble in different ways, whether the strings, or the other bodies touched and struck, receive these different vibrations within themselves, or whether they are only in the air, or whether they are in both, or whether they occur in the ear, or in the imagination—which, being corporeal <note>Mersenne follows the 17th-century view that the "imagination" was a physical faculty of the brain capable of being physically agitated by sensory input.</note>, is capable of all these agitations. To this one may add that changing colors, which represent several at the same time, are similar to these sounds that affect the air and other bodies almost as light does; this is why I have several times compared these two qualities together in the *Book of Sounds* and elsewhere. But if one could find a way to see and count these second, third, etc., vibrations, as I have done for the first ones, one would speak more exactly about this difficulty. I do not believe this to be impossible, since experience shows that one can make sensible in several ways that which seems imperceptible; for example, the eight feet and the hair of mites, and the ten legs of tiny mites <note>original: "cirons" — these are microscopic mites; they were a favorite subject for early microscopists to prove the existence of a world beyond the naked eye.</note> are seen clearly and distinctly with small convexo-concave lenses <note>An early reference to the microscope.</note>, and the vibrations of the smallest strings become sensible and countable by means of those of the largest.

### COROLLARY I.

When the stopped pipe produces its two sounds at the same time, it confounds and mixes together what other stopped pipes distinguish; for if one gives a stronger wind to one of these pipes, it leaves its natural tone and rises to the Twelfth, as I have pointed out to several people; whereas open pipes rise to the Octave, as I said in the 29th Proposition; this can further serve the preceding reasons. Now, if one could observe the number of vibrations made by water when some instrument sounds within it, that could perhaps serve to determine how much denser or heavier it is than air; but I have spoken more amply of this difficulty in the *Book of Sounds* and elsewhere.

### COROLLARY II.

Those who imagine with Democritus and Epicurus that the entire Universe is composed of atoms <note>Atomism was the philosophical theory that the world is made of tiny, indivisible particles. Mersenne was often skeptical of using it as a total explanation for physics.</note> believe that the different sounds of the same string, or of the same pipe, are made by their various movements: for example, that three atoms move or collide when one hears the high-pitched sound of the Twelfth, while only one moves to make the low-pitched sound, or that there are some that move three times faster than others. But it would be necessary to explain how a single breath constrains some to move three times, and why this does not happen to all pipes, both stopped and open, and a thousand other things that I find very difficult in the speculation of atoms, as well as in other ways of philosophizing. It must also be noted that some Organists create stops <note>original: "jeux" — refers to the different sets of pipes or "ranks" in an organ.</note> where the same pipes have both the sounds we have just spoken of; and that it is perhaps not impossible to make some that have the two sounds of the Octave, the Fourth, the Third, etc. Now, one must make their mouth very low <note>term: mouth <gloss>the opening in an organ pipe where the wind hits the lip to create sound; "low" refers to the 'cut-up' or height of this opening.</gloss></term> when one wants them to produce the Twelfth.

# PROPOSITION XLIII.

## *Explaining the thickness of the pipes used in the largest organs, and the width of their mouths according to the practice of organ builders.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the proportions of organ pipe widths relative to their lengths. A vertical line segment represents the length of the pipes, with points labeled A (top), D (middle), F (further down), and B (bottom). From points A, D, and F, horizontal line segments extend to the right, ending at points C, E, and G respectively. These horizontal segments represent the widths (largeurs) of pipes of 16, 8, and 4 feet in length. The segments AC, DE, and FG show that width does not decrease linearly with length; rather, DE is the side of a square with diagonal AC, and FG is the side of a square with diagonal DE.</image-desc>

ALTHOUGH I have already spoken of pipes in several places, and gave the proportions for their length in the fourteenth and fifteenth Propositions—where I set down their heights in various ways—it is nevertheless necessary to add this discourse to explain their thicknesses and their widths, even though these are not as strictly regulated as their lengths. For some <term>builders</term> <note>original: "Facteurs" — the specialist craftsmen who design and build organs.</note> give only a sixth part of the height of a sixteen-foot pipe to its width, and others give it a fifth part. Now, once this is established, they easily find the width of the others; for by setting this first and largest width as the diagonal of a square, they take its side for the width of the pipe eight feet high, which produces the higher <term>octave</term>; and then they use this side as the diagonal of another square, whose side serves as the width for the pipe four feet long, which produces the second octave, and so on for the others. 

So, if we suppose that pipe AB is sixteen feet long, and its width is AC, the width of the pipe halved in length, DB, will be greater than half of AC; for it will be DE, which is the side of the square whose diagonal is AC. Similarly, FG, which is the side of the square whose diagonal is DE, is the width of pipe FB, and so on for the others. By this, one sees that pipes do not decrease in width in the same proportion as their lengths; otherwise DE would only be half of AC, whereas FG is exactly half of AC. Consequently, the pipe FB, being one-fourth the length of pipe AB, is only half the width. That is to say, if pipe AB were sixteen feet long and two feet eight inches wide, the pipe of four feet long, FB, would be one foot and four inches wide. Now, although the line AB in the diagram is only half a foot long, it is easy to imagine it thirty-two times longer for a pipe sixteen feet high.

From this, it is easy to conclude that pipes are relatively wider and thicker as they decrease more in length, and that their widths or thicknesses are <term>incommensurable</term> <note>In geometry, this means they cannot be compared by a simple whole-number ratio, similar to the relationship between the side and the diagonal of a square (the square root of two).</note> with one another, like the diagonals and sides of squares. However, the builders—who do not require such great precision—apply their own measurements to them, and do not always observe these exact thicknesses, which they manage according to the place where the pipes must speak; for example, they make them thicker when they want them to speak more loudly.

As for the width of the <term>mouths</term> <note>The "mouth" is the rectangular opening on the front of an organ pipe where the air hits the lip to produce sound.</note>, they also maintain different proportions in different pipes; for they take up a fifth part of the thickness in the largest pipes, a fourth in the following ones, and a third 

<summary>Mersenne explains the geometric scaling used by organ builders to determine the width and mouth size of pipes, noting that width decreases more slowly than length to maintain sound quality.</summary>
<keywords>organ building, pipe scaling, geometry, octaves, acoustics, proportions</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Book Six, transitioning from the mathematical proportions of organ pipes to the practical art of "voicing" and the imitation of orchestral instruments, followed by a more detailed structural breakdown of the organ's windchest.</meta>

<page-num>399</page-num>
<header>of Organs.</header>

and a half in the smallest: which must be noted to supplement what was said in the fifth Proposition, where it is not necessary for the thickness of the <term>languid</term> <note>original: "láguette" — the flat plate inside an organ pipe that directs air against the lip to produce sound.</note> described there to be a third of the height of the mouth; for it does not matter so long as it splits the wind well to make the pipe speak. Now, I do not believe there is any better way to make pipes speak as one wishes—that is to say, softly, or harshly, etc.—than by imitating the different Flutes, Recorders, Oboes, etc., of which we spoke in the fifth book; for if one makes those of the Organ of the same height and width, and they imitate their mouths, they will produce the same effects. From this it follows that skilled <term>builders</term> <note>original: "Facteurs" — the master craftsmen of instruments.</note> invent new stops every day by imitating all sorts of instruments. Thus, it is highly likely they can counterfeit the sound of Viols, since the new <term>Spinets</term> <note>original: "Epinettes" — early harpsichord-like keyboard instruments.</note> which can be made to sustain notes as long as one likes, like the Organ, by means of wheels or bows upon which the strings are lowered by the movement of the keys, so closely imitate Organ pipes that it is difficult to distinguish them from a distance. This shows that the Sounds of all kinds of instruments are all made in the same manner—that is to say, by a multitude of air vibrations. From this it comes that the noise made by doors turning on their hinges, and carts on their axles, is often so similar to the cry of animals, or the sound of Flutes and other instruments, that it is almost impossible to distinguish them. This happens similarly with the doors of Churches and other very spacious buildings, whose doors make noises perfectly similar to musket shots and other pieces of artillery when they are closed with speed and force.

## PROPOSITION XLIV.

->*To explain the Construction and the parts of a large Organ, and of a small Cabinet organ; wherein one will see distinctly and clearly what is more confusedly and obscurely presented in the second Proposition.*<-

IT is certain that distinction brings great clarity, and that when one thinks to explain many different things in the same place by mixing them together, they often remain obscured and confused, as happens with wine and water when they are mixed. This is what happened in our second Proposition, which speaks sometimes of the parts of a large Organ, and then of those of a small one. That is why this one will serve as its explanation, and will provide everything one could desire on this subject. For example, when I said that the <term>toe boards</term> <note>original: "chappes" — the upper planks of the windchest.</note> and the <term>sliders</term> <note>original: "registres" — the moveable strips of wood that allow air to reach specific ranks of pipes.</note> of the <term>windchest</term> <note>original: "sommier" — the "heart" of the organ, a wooden box that distributes pressurized air to the pipes.</note> are two and a half inches wide, this must not be understood for large Organs, whose toe boards are sometimes a foot wide depending on what the size of their stops requires, but only for a small Cabinet Organ, upon which the design of the entire construction was based. This is why we must here speak more clearly and distinctly of the entire construction of this instrument, without dwelling much on what is easiest. And because the windchest is the principal part of the Organ—of which it is the body, in which, upon which, or around which all the other parts necessary to animate it are applied—we shall begin with its construction.

# Book Six

<page-num>400</page-num>
<header>Book Six</header>

One must therefore first consider the size of the Organ, as well as the multitude and size of its <term>stops</term> <note>original: "jeux" — a set of pipes of the same timbre.</note>, to determine the size of its <term>windchest</term> <note>original: "Sommier" — the wooden box that distributes pressurized air to the pipes.</note>, which depends upon them. For example, when one wishes to build an eight-foot Organ—such as those commonly found in churches where there is only a single <term>organ case</term> <note>original: "Buffet d’Orgues" — the decorative wooden exterior of the instrument.</note>—one can make the windchest five or six feet long, according to the judgment and will of the <term>builder</term> <note>original: "Facteur"</note>. Some find the space for their stops more easily on a four-foot windchest than others do on one of five feet; for this reason, I do not limit the size so strictly that the ingenuity of the builders cannot reduce it. I say, nevertheless, that the windchest of small <term>chamber organs</term> <note>original: "Cabinets"</note> is usually two and a half or three feet long. As for the width, it is determined according to the number of stops one wishes to place there. For instance, if there were four stops, the largest of which was a two-foot <term>stopped</term> <note>original: "bouchez" — pipes capped at the top to produce a sound an octave lower than their length suggests.</note> pipe, and if one wished to leave room for the <term>keyboard</term> <note>original: "Clauier"</note> on the same windchest, it would be enough to give it a width of fourteen inches, of which four inches would serve to place the keyboard and the remainder for the span of the four stops. And if one were to add several small stops, such as the <term>Cymbale</term> <note>A high-pitched mixture stop.</note> and the <term>Regals</term> <note>original: "Regales" — a reed stop with a metallic, buzzing quality.</note>, one would add four inches to the width, so that its total width would be one and a half feet.

Organs of four-foot stopped pipes usually have a windchest five or at most six feet long. And if they have a <term>Prestant</term> <note>A 4-foot principal stop.</note> in the <term>facade</term> <note>original: "Montre" — the visible pipes displayed in the front of the case.</note>, the <term>upperboard</term> <note>original: "Chappe" — the board on which the pipes sit.</note> of this stop must be very narrow, because it does not carry its pipes directly, but only the <term>conveyances</term> <note>original: "Porte-vents" — tubes that carry wind from the chest to the facade pipes.</note> that give wind to the facade. Thus, it would be in vain to make its upperboard wider than necessary. Now, if besides these two stops one adds the <term>Doublette</term> <note>A 2-foot principal stop.</note> of two feet, the <term>Nazard</term> <note>A mutation stop sounding a twelfth above the fundamental.</note> of about three feet, the <term>Flajollet</term> <note>A small, high-pitched flute stop.</note> of one foot, the <term>Fourniture</term> <note>A mixture stop providing brilliance.</note> with <term>three ranks</term> <note>original: "trois sur marche" — referring to three pipes sounding for every single key pressed.</note>, the <term>Cymbale</term> with <term>two ranks</term> <note>original: "deux sur marche"</note>, the <term>Trompette</term> <note>Trumpet.</note>, the <term>Cromhorne</term> <note>A reed stop named after the medieval woodwind instrument.</note>, and the <term>Voix Humaine</term> <note>Vox Humana, a reed stop meant to imitate the human voice.</note> with a <term>Cornet</term> <note>A powerful multi-rank stop used for soloing.</note>, it will suffice to give three feet or thereabouts to the width of the windchest.

Regarding sixteen-foot Organs, it must be noted that they are usually built with two windchests, because the length of a single one would be excessive. These chests provide wind to one another by means of a lead <term>wind trunk</term> <note>original: "Portevent"</note> of substantial size, which runs from one to the other. They are placed at the two ends of the Organ so that a space is left in the middle to find room for the longest pipes, or as a "reserve" space, in order to be able to tune the stops more freely from all sides. Otherwise, the length required by such an instrument would prevent the wood from being planed as accurately as is necessary if the windchest were made of a single piece. Furthermore, it must be noted that if one adds <term>Pedals</term> to this Organ, as is usually done, it is necessary to add two specific windchests at the two extremities of the Organ case, so that the first pipe is on the right hand, the second on the left, the third on the right, the fourth on the left, and so on for the others. If a Cornet is added, a separate windchest is required, which is usually placed behind the facade and attached against the case. Strictly speaking, it is not a true windchest, as it lacks all the standard parts, but is rather an assembly of <term>grooved wind conductors</term> <note>original: "Porte-vents de Reyneures" — channels carved into wood to route wind.</note> within the same piece of wood, to which the wind is communicated by other lead conveyances coming from the main windchest. This is why the upperboard reserved...

<header>on Organs.</header>

for the said <term>Cornet</term> <note>A powerful solo stop composed of several ranks of pipes, often mounted on its own small windchest.</note> must be very narrow, given that it only needs to contain the <term>wind trunks</term> <note>original: "Porte-vents" — the pipes or channels that carry air from the main windchest to the Cornet's pipes.</note>.

As for the width of the <term>windchests</term> <note>original: "sommiers"</note> of a sixteen-foot Organ, they are usually made four and a half feet wide, or thereabouts, because of the multitude of its <term>stops</term> <note>original: "jeux"</note>, which I have explained in the 3rd and 31st Propositions. I come now to the construction of the windchest, and for this subject I assume the Organ consists of a four-foot <term>stopped</term> pipe <note>original: "bouchez" — pipes capped at the top</note>, and a four-foot open pipe in the <term>facade</term> <note>original: "Montre" — the decorative pipes displayed in the front of the organ case.</note>, and that one also wishes to place there the **Nazard**, the **Doublette**, the **Flageolet**, the **Fourniture** (with three pipes per note), the **Cymbale** (with two), the **Trumpet**, the **Crumhorn**, the **Vox Humana**, and the **Cornet**—that is to say, eleven stops. One must take Oak wood an inch and a half thick, very dry and very clean, which is five or six feet long, and assemble all the pieces with good glue and with dowels, putting two bars with <term>tenon and mortise</term> joints at the two ends. Having thus assembled the wood, one must give it three feet in width, and after having planed it smooth on both sides, one must apply <term>slats</term> <note>original: "tringles"</note>, or bars, as wide as necessary following the size of the <term>channels</term> <note>original: "reyneures" — the internal grooves that direct air to specific notes.</note>, and an inch and a half high; so that being glued and doweled onto the <term>table</term> of the windchest, they reach a thickness of three inches along with it.

Now, these must be placed across the table throughout the entire width, so that they are perpendicular to the length of the table. As for the distance that should be between the slats, it depends on the discretion of the <term>Builder</term> <note>original: "Facteur"</note>, who must regulate himself according to how the pipes must be arranged, so that the smallest are found in the middle, and the large ones go alternately to one side and the other: this is why the channels will be larger in the places of the largest pipes, and smaller in the places where the smallest are found. But care must be taken that the smallest channel has no less than a third of an inch of empty space in width; for as for the height of the void, it is equal in all the channels, because the slats that enclose them are of the same height. Now, the place for all the pipes must have been determined, and consequently, as many holes must be made in the windchest as there are to be pipes, so that each slat is beside the holes that belong to each channel, as one can see in the figures of the third Proposition.

The channels having been thus arranged, one must apply two bars of wood all along each side of the width of the said table, so that by joining against the ends of the other slats, they complete the channels; at the bottom of these, it is appropriate to glue small strips of parchment, which join against the table and against the bars; so that if they happen to come unglued in any place, one avoids by this means the <term>leakage</term> <note>original: "l’emprunt" — literally "borrowing," referring to air leaking from one channel to another, causing unintended notes to sound.</note> that could occur there. After these channels are made, one must apply to the two ends of the table two pieces of wood half a foot wide, which two ends will be <term>rabbeted</term> <note>original: "fueillez" — a step-shaped cut made in the edge of the wood to form a joint.</note> to half their thickness, that is to say, an inch and a half, in order to nail and glue the said pieces of wood on top.

Afterward, one must apply a bottom of the same thickness, and eight inches wide, which will be the same length as the table, and will be supported on the two ends of the two aforementioned pieces of wood, to which it must also be nailed and glued, after one has notched the pieces of wood to the thickness of the said bottom, until, being applied to this <term>rabbet</term> <note>original: "fueilleure"</note>, it is flush and level.

# Book Six

at the edges of the said pieces of wood: so that a hollow of about four inches in height is created between the table and the bottom, for the reservoir of wind, which we will discuss later.

Once all this is done, one must apply a good, very furry sheepskin leather—thick enough and the softest one can encounter—over the grooves, beginning from the end of the table (which must be at the front of the <term>windchest</term> <note>original: "sommier" — the pressurized box that holds the air for the organ pipes.</note>), extending to a width of eight inches. This is done so that, being thus glued, it aligns point-for-point with the bottom; it should be glued before the said bottom is attached to avoid the difficulty of glueing it afterward. Once this leather is glued along the entire length of the windchest to a width of eight inches and is quite dry, it must be cut from the inside of the grooves, starting from their ends up to four inches wide. 

Then, one must prepare as many <term>valves</term> <note>original: "soupapes" — also known as pallets, these are the wooden flaps that open to allow air into the channels of a specific note.</note> as there are keys on the <term>Keyboard</term> <note>original: "Clauier"</note>: these valves are nothing more than small wooden slats, lined with very furry leather, which are applied over the part of the grooves where the leather was cut. This is so that by opening one of these valves, the wind slides along the <term>groove</term> <note>original: "reyneure" — the internal channel that directs air to all the pipes for a single note.</note> to make the pipes speak by means of the <term>registers</term> <note>original: "registres" — the sliders that allow the organist to engage or disengage specific sets of pipes.</note>, which we will discuss later.

Now, since the leather is cut four inches over the grooves, it follows that each valve must be about half a foot long, so that it overlaps slightly—that is, it extends beyond the open end of the groove. As for the width, the wider it is, the better, so that after covering the groove it extends on either side nearly to the middle of the <term>bars</term> <note>original: "barreaux" — the wooden dividers that separate one note's air channel from the next.</note> that form the said grooves, as can be seen in the third figure of the second Proposition. One must then prepare small wooden slats half an inch or two-thirds of an inch thick; after cutting them to length and width, they must be planed down along their length into a <term>bevel</term> <note>original: "biseau" — a slanted or chamfered edge.</note> on each side, so that there remains only a width of one <term>line</term> <note>A traditional French unit of measurement, roughly 2.25 millimeters or about 1/12th of an inch.</note> at the top of the valve, upon which the spring is applied to close the valve. 

It is easy to determine the width of all the valves by driving <term>brass</term> <note>original: "Iaton," likely a misspelling of "laiton" (brass).</note> pins an inch high into the middle of all the bars; one must also place two of these pins on each bar, located opposite the two parts of the leather cut over the grooves. Thus, with the valves being made the width of the spaces between the pins, each may open and close freely over its groove between the said pins. The valves are attached to the grooves by means of leather strips, with the furry side left on the outside; they are glued by the back after being scraped on the flat of the valve, so that about an inch of length remains at the end to form the back of the valve.

But before glueing the leather, one must bevel both ends of the valves, so that the back end is at least twice as long as the front, for reasons we will explain later. Finally, one glues the tails of the valves onto the leather of the grooves, so that the front end of the valve overlaps the end of the groove by only two lines. Then one trims a strip of leather with a knife, making it very thin and three inches wide, to glue it along the tails of the valves, so that half its width is firmly glued to all the bevels at the back of the valves, and the other half on the end

# Of Organs.

the leather tails, which are already glued onto the <term>windchest</term><note>original: "sommier" — the central pressurized air box of the organ.</note>. But after the said strip is dry, the leather between the bevels of the <term>valves</term><note>original: "soupapes" — also known as pallets; these wooden flaps open to let air into the pipes.</note> must be notched so that they open and close freely. Some also apply a small wooden rail that runs all along the back of the said valves and is nailed to the windchest; this is a good practice, as it prevents the valves from shifting backward.

Once this is done, a rail the length of the windchest must be applied over the back of all the valves. Opposite each valve, points will be marked on the rail where saw-cuts will be made, thin enough to hold the end of each spring. This rail should be two inches high and two-thirds of an inch thick; after making all the saw-cuts, it must be attached and pegged to the bottom board we previously mentioned. However, the saw-cuts must face outward, and the rail should be positioned only an inch and a half or two inches from the front of the bottom.

After all these things, the bottom will be fixed to the two pieces of wood at the two ends of the windchest table. One must then make as many <term>brass</term><note>original: "laton"</note> springs as there are valves; these will be shaped and arranged as seen in the penultimate figure of the second Proposition. One end of the spring, which is slightly curved, bears down on the first third of the valve's length, while the other end is secured in its saw-cut on the rail above the valves. Afterward, a board the length of the windchest must be placed at the back of the valves, reaching from the windchest to the bottom, and should be two-thirds of an inch thick. This is attached using a <term>rabbet</term><note>original: "fueilleure" — a step-shaped groove cut into the edge of a piece of wood to allow another piece to fit into it.</note> or otherwise according to the will and skill of the <term>organ builder</term><note>original: "Facteur"</note>; but it must be lined with leather all around with leather strips so that it is perfectly airtight and the wind cannot escape. The same must be done at the front of the windchest with a board of the same fashion, which will be lined with leather and set into four rabbets made around this <term>chest</term><note>original: "quaisse" — refers to the wind chamber itself.</note>, which must likewise be lined with leather on the inside. However, this front board should not be glued with leather strips all around like the previous one, because it must be able to be removed and replaced to clean the chest and the valves whenever some debris has entered. It is therefore enough that it closes the said chest very snugly and is held in place with three or four iron hooks or by other means.

As for the hole where the <term>wind trunk</term><note>original: "Porte-vent" — the large duct that carries air from the bellows to the windchest.</note> terminates, it is usually made in the back board, and is given a length of two and a half feet and a height of three inches. One must also pierce the bottom with as many holes as there are valves, directly opposite them, so that after passing <term>brass wires</term> through these holes and hooking them to the front of each valve by means of small staples, buckles, or rings nailed there, one can open them at will. But for fear that the wind might escape through all these small holes, one makes as many small leather cones or <term>pouches</term><note>original: "pochettes" — often called "purses" in modern organ building; these flexible leather seals allow the wire to move while keeping the air pressure inside.</note>, the ends of which are well glued. Now, after glueing the wide part of the said cones over each hole, each brass wire is passed through, and having hooked it to each valve, all the said pouches are tightened at the top of their cones against the brass wire with thick thread, tying them so tightly that the wind cannot escape.

After all this, the back of the <term>grooves</term><note>original: "reyneures" — the internal channels that lead to the pipes.</note> must be covered with a leather that one...

Let us now look at the <term>Toe Boards</term><note>original: "Chappes" — the top boards where the pipes sit.</note> and the <term>Sliders</term><note>original: "Registres" — the moving strips of wood that turn stops on or off.</note>, and the order that must be kept for placing the <term>stops</term><note>original: "jeux" — the different sets of pipes.</note>. It must be noted that this order must be arranged before applying the channels, because one cannot drill the holes until the design is finalized; this is why I shall speak a bit more about the <term>windchest</term><note>original: "sommier"</note>. Having then taken a table one and a half inches thick and three feet wide, the Toe Board of the <term>Prestant</term><note>A 4-foot principal stop, often placed in the front.</note> in the <term>Montre</term><note>The "Display" or facade pipes visible to the audience.</note> will be two and a half inches wide, because there is nothing upon it but the <term>conveyance tubes</term><note>original: "Porte-vents" — lead tubes that carry air to pipes not standing directly on the windchest.</note> which provide wind to the pipes of the facade. After which follows the <term>Bourdon</term><note>A stopped flute stop.</note> of four-foot stopped pipes, which has a toe board half a foot wide. Then one makes the toe board for the <term>Cornet</term><note>A multi-rank stop that produces a bold, soloistic sound.</note>, which is only a "half-stop" beginning at the <term>accidental</term><note>original: "feinte" — refers to the black keys or sharps/flats.</note> of C-sharp in the middle of the <term>keyboard</term><note>original: "Clauier"</note> toward the treble; this toe board is only two inches wide. That of the <term>Nazard</term><note>A mutation stop providing a nasal tone, usually a 2 2/3' pitch.</note>, of three feet open and one and a half feet stopped, is five and a half inches wide. The <term>Doublette</term><note>A 2-foot principal stop.</note> of two feet open is placed on the following Toe Board, which is three inches wide. The <term>Flajollet</term><note>A high-pitched flute stop.</note> of one foot open will have its toe board three inches wide, and the toe board of the <term>Fourniture</term><note>A "Mixture" stop that adds brilliance by playing several high-pitched pipes for every one note.</note>—which has three pipes per <term>note</term><note>original: "marche" — literally the 'step' or key press.</note>, of which we spoke in the thirty-first Proposition in the treatise on the Choir Organ—is four inches. The Toe Board of the <term>Cymbale</term><note>A higher-pitched mixture stop.</note>, which is placed next with two pipes per note, is three inches wide; that of the <term>Trompette</term><note>Trumpet — a powerful reed stop.</note> is four, and that of the <term>Cromhorne</term><note>Crumhorn — a reed stop with a buzzy, medieval character.</note> and the <term>Voix Humaine</term><note>Vox Humana — a reed stop intended to imitate the human voice.</note> is three; so that all these Toe Boards together make up the width of the windchest.

Now, all the stops of an organ of this size must have their pipes arranged in this manner, so that they are easy to tune. But it should be noted that what has been said of four-foot organs can easily be applied to the largest ones of sixteen feet, whose Toe Boards shall have whatever width the <term>Builder</term><note>original: "Facteur" — the organ maker.</note> desires; though it must be noted that they do not widen in the same proportion as the length of the windchest, which serves to put many pipes in the same row. And when two pipes cannot fit together on the Toe Boards arranged as we have said, one must be placed in a spot that does not inconvenience the others, and set it upon a small piece of square, thick wood, in which a hole must be made to fit the foot of the pipe; and another hole on the side, meeting the first, so as to carry wind to the pipe by means of a lead <term>conveyance tube</term><note>original: "Porte-vent"</note> which comes from the hole in the Toe Board—where the pipe should have been placed—to the aforementioned hole made in the side of the wooden block. Now the pipes of the facade take their wind in this manner, that is to say <term>by off-chesting</term><note>original: "par poste" — a technique for supplying wind to pipes located away from their primary air source.</note>, and are not usually placed directly on the main windchest like the others; this is why a small slider is made under each foot of the large pipes, acting as a Register.

One uses this invention to avoid the excessive width of the Toe Boards; but it should only be used when necessary, for the pipes should be placed as much as possible over the holes of the windchest, although the other way of giving them wind hardly alters their sound at all. # About Organs.

pipes, and the *windchest* <term>in the style of drawers</term><note>French: "en façon de layettes." This refers to a construction where the windchest is built like a shallow box with dividers, similar to a chest of drawers.</note>; they are commonly called *sliding registers*, as seen in the second and the last figures of the second Proposition.

After having drilled all the holes on the table of the *windchest*, as I have said in the same place, and after having determined the width of the *toe boards*, one must apply between each distance of the stops small *rules* or *bars* of wood of the same thickness as the aforementioned *registers*, and place them on the *windchest* in such a way that they separate the holes of one stop from those of another, as can be seen in the same figures. These *rules*, or *rods*, are spaced about two inches apart for the width of the *registers*: now, they must be applied to the *windchest* so that the edges of the width of each *toe board* fall exactly in the middle of each *rule*, except for the two last *toe boards*, which are at the outer edges of the *windchest's* width; for these must rest entirely upon their *rods* or *rules*, which must be glued and pegged onto the table.

The *registers* must fill the intervals between these *rods* so that they slide easily between them when pulled from one side or the other; and they must be of the same thickness as the said *rods* throughout. Then, having fixed them in their places on the table of the *windchest* with iron points so that they do not move at all, and having placed the *toe boards* on top, one must drill through them all together through all the holes of the table, as if they were but a single board, so that these holes meet exactly opposite one another to give a free passage to the wind when the stops are opened.

This being done, the *toe boards* are removed in order to adjust the *registers* so that they do not stick more than is necessary. This is executed by taking each *register* one after the other and placing it on the *windchest* so that its holes are opposite those of the chest; and then one must nail an iron point at one end, so that it does not exceed the thickness of the *register*. A slot, or mortise, is then made in the *register* with a chisel suitable for that purpose, so that the *register* slides on the point of the nail. Thus, when pulled to one side, all the holes are open, and when pushed back by the distance—which is half the distance from one hole to the next—the holes of the *register* are no longer opposite those of the *windchest*. Consequently, the wind entering the channels finds no holes to exit when one strikes the keys of the *keyboard* to make the stops speak that are opened by means of the pulled *registers*. But they must be lined with sheepskin on the side that slides upon the *windchest*, so that the hairy side of this leather touches the table of the *windchest*. The same must be practiced on the side of the *toe boards* that rests on the *registers*, so that their sliding is made more easily, and so that one has a well-sealed *organ*.

All this being done with sufficient precision, one must pass a red-hot iron rod through each hole, so that it is pierced very cleanly without any wood particles remaining, as often happens with the drillings of an old <term>brace</term><note>French: "brequin" (vilebrequin), a hand-operated tool used for boring holes.</note>. And then one must fix the *toe boards* over the *registers* and nail them onto the small *rules*, which are called *rods*, or attach them with *screws*; which is much better, since by their means one can tighten or loosen the *toe boards* as much as one wishes, until the *registers* pull easily and they seal well against the said *toe boards*. # Sixth Book

above the rods must be lined with leather, just like the **registers** <term>sliders</term>, so that as they slide they are flush and at the same height, and so that the **toe boards** <term>upper boards</term> rest evenly on both of them.

I will omit another style of **windchest**, which is called a **spring chest** <note>original: "à Ressorts"</note>, and which is still seen in some ancient organs; this is because it involves much more clutter and difficulty than the ordinary kind with **sliding registers**, and it is longer to make and of greater cost. Furthermore, it is a waste of time to use difficult inventions when easier and more useful ones are available. As for the manufacture of the **pipes**, I have spoken quite fully of their lengths in the 31st Proposition, where I placed them according to the order in which they must be positioned. As for their thickness, or width, it is adjusted according to the different churches where they are placed: for example, if the buildings are "dull" <note>acoustically dry or non-resonant</note>, the pipes must be stronger, and consequently wider; and if they ring out and resonate, creating a good echo, they can be made thinner. It suffices to note that once the pipes are cut to length, following one or another of our systems or **diapasons** <term>scaling charts</term>, and having given the first or largest pipe whatever thickness one desires for the **stopped pipes**, one will then find the thickness for the first **open pipe**, to which one gives a portion less than the stopped ones. For example, if the first **C** <note>original: "C sol"</note> of two feet, when stopped, has a thickness equal to a third of its length, the two-foot pipe being open will have a thickness of only a quarter of its length; and if the stopped pipe has only a fourth part, the open one will have only a fifth, and so on. However, it is always appropriate to make the **cymbals** <note>mixture stops</note> thin, and to make the one-foot open **flajolets** thick, which is likewise observed for the **cornet**. The width of the **mouth** of the pipes is taken from the width of the said pipes; for example, one must divide the width of the stopped pipes into four equal parts, and place one of these parts exactly in the middle. But as for its height, one must only note that if the pipes are very wide, the height must be less than usual; although this cannot be determined so precisely as to make a general rule. Furthermore, it is always good to make the height quite small, because after the pipe is finished, it can be increased very easily until the pipe speaks as it should, according to the will of the **organ builder** <note>original: "Facteur"</note>. Nevertheless, when a stopped pipe has a width slightly more than a third of its height, its mouth usually has a height equal to a quarter of its width; and for open pipes, a fifth part. Now, one must not dwell on the height of these mouths, but only on their width, which is entirely necessary for the making of a good pipe.

Having found the width of the first pipe suitable for the place where the organ is to sound (which depends solely on experience, which can be as varied as the layout of different places), it is easy to find the thickness of all the others by dividing the width of the first into two parts; for the **diagonal** of the square made from one of these parts will give the width of the pipe an **octave** above. In this way, the line drawn through the points of the width of these two pipes will give the width of all the others, as I showed in the preceding Proposition. From this, it follows that the width of this second pipe will be the **mean proportional** <note>a geometric average</note> between that of the first; and the width of the third pipe, which will be the second octave above, will have half that of the first; and consequently, the width of the second will divide the **double ratio** <note>original: "raison double," referring to the 2:1 ratio of the octave</note>.

Therefore, I come to the reed pipes, which I explain so clearly in the ninth and tenth **Propositions** that it is only necessary to remark that the old method by which their **shallots** <note>the metal tubes in a reed pipe that the tongue beats against</note> were formerly cut is almost no longer in use, because they are now stamped in cast molds. As for the bellows, the **Tremulants**, the manner of melting lead for the pipes, their soldering, and all the other things concerning the construction of **Organs**, I have spoken of them previously without need for repetition. Therefore, I conclude this **Proposition** with the **Rollerboard** <term>abrégé</term>, which has not yet been explained. But because it cannot be well expressed by discourse alone, and as it is easy enough to understand by merely seeing common **Organs** that have **rollerboards**, I will say only that they were invented so that each key of the **keyboard**, which is only two feet long, corresponds to each **pallet** <note>the valve inside the windchest that lets air into the pipes</note> of the windchests, which are four, five, or six feet long. This is done by means of several wooden bars that are somewhat round <note>the rollers</note>, and which have two iron wire points at the two ends, which serve as pivots for them to turn; for these two points are placed into two small wooden pegs <note>studs or blocks</note> in which each bar turns freely. When one wishes to make a **key action** <note>original: "marche"</note> pull, one must put a peg at the end of the bar that is under the said key, and another peg at the other end of the same bar, which is opposite the pallet it must open. For this purpose, a small wooden rod <note>a tracker or sticker</note> is attached to the end over the key, to which it is permanently held; and then, to the peg at the end of the bar opposite the pallet, the brass wire is attached—which we previously said was attached to the pallet inside the windchest—so that when the key of the **keyboard** is depressed, the rod attached to it moves the bar, which pulls the pallet attached to the small wooden peg at the end of said bar. From this, it happens that a key of the **keyboard** often makes a pipe speak that is very far away. But the bars must be so well adjusted that they turn very easily in their pegs, so that the **keyboard** is easy to play and the pipes respond promptly. I leave aside everything else that can be imagined on this subject, because a single glance will make one understand more than what could be written in entire volumes.

<header>Book Six</header>

Mean proportionals are among the most important subjects; I wish here to add a means of finding them geometrically, since it depends on a single **Parabola**, and because it was discovered by one of the most excellent minds in the world, whose modesty is so great and so extraordinary that he does not wish to be named. I would have included here only the construction he gave me, had it not been that Mr. de **Roberval**, a most excellent geometer and Professor of Mathematics at the **Royal College of France** <note>Now known as the Collège de France, a prestigious research institution in Paris</note>, promptly provided the demonstration. This already gave me reason to include it in the second proposition of my **Latin book on Bells** <note>original: "liure Latin des Cloches"; referring to Mersenne's *Harmonicorum libri* (1636)</note>; but it will be better placed here because the diagram I am using corresponds more precisely to the discourse than the one in the aforementioned book, which is missing a few lines. Thus, the reader will find here what I did not wish to provide in the seventh proposition of the second book of **Instruments**, where I explain various geometric and mechanical ways to find eleven, 23, etc., mean proportionals between two given values, in order to divide the **Octave** <term>Diapason</term> into twelve semitones and into twenty-four diesis, or quarter-tones.

## PROPOSITION XLV.

->*Between two given unequal straight lines, find two mean continued proportionals, in order to divide the Organ Octave into twelve equal semitones.*<-

This construction is, in my opinion, the simplest of all those invented until now for the solution of this problem, upon which depends the famous **doubling of the cube** <note>A classic geometric problem: given the edge of a cube, find the edge of a second cube whose volume is double that of the first</note>. This problem has been much sought after by both ancient and modern geometers, such that in the commentaries of **Eutocius** on **Archimedes**, one finds eleven of the most renowned authors among the ancients—not including those of our own time—who have given a demonstration of it. Some used **solid loci** <term>lieux solides</term> <note>Geometric solutions involving conic sections like parabolas</note>, such as **Menaechmus**; others used **linear loci**, such as **Nicomedes**, **Diocles**, and our own **Viète**; and others used **complex motions** <term>mouuemens impliquez</term>, such as **Plato**, **Archytas**, **Philo of Byzantium**, **Pappus**, and **Sporus**; or by descriptions of circles by **trial and error** <note>original: "à taſtons"</note>, such as **Heron** and **Apollonius**. I set aside a great number of others who, instead of demonstrations, gave us only **paralogisms** <note>illogical or fallacious arguments</note>. Now, as the ancients (according to the report of **Pappus**) esteemed it a great error to resolve by solid or linear loci a problem which by its nature could be resolved by **plane loci** alone; I similarly estimate that the error is no less to resolve by linear loci, or by complex motions, or by trial-and-error descriptions, a problem which by its nature can be resolved by solid loci. For since among these "loci" the order is such that those we call "plane" are the simplest—namely the straight line and the circumference of the circle, the description of which **Euclid** asks to be granted him at the beginning of his *Elements*—these are followed by solid loci, which take their origin from the section of a conical surface, generated by a straight line and the circumference of a circle. These solid loci are the **Parabola**, the **Ellipse**, and the **Hyperbola**. These are followed by the loci called "linear," most often generated by two complex motions, such as **Conchoids**, **Spirals**,

<sig>Mm iii</sig>

**Quadratrices** <note>A complex curve used for squaring the circle or trisecting angles</note>, and an infinity of others, the description of which is usually nearly impossible: it seems reasonable that every Problem which can be resolved by **plane loci** <note>Geometric solutions using only straight lines and circles</note> should be resolved by plane loci; and that which, being unable to be resolved by plane loci alone, can be resolved by **solid loci** <note>Solutions involving conic sections like parabolas or hyperbolas</note> alone, or mixed with plane loci, must be resolved by solid loci alone, or mixed with plane loci. Finally, when a Problem is of such a nature that it cannot be resolved by plane or solid loci, then it is permitted to resolve it by **linear loci** <note>Higher-order "mechanical" curves</note> alone, or mixed with plane and solid loci—provided, however, that one makes use of plane loci as much as possible, and the others as little as possible. A construction in which only one solid locus enters, the rest being plane, is more esteemed than one in which two solid loci enter, since, in imitation of nature, we must do everything by the simplest means.

For this consideration, in the solution of the Problem at hand—which has not yet been able to be resolved by plane loci alone—I cannot approve of any other constructions among all the ancient ones except those of **Menaechmus** <note>original: "Menechinus"; a 4th-century BCE Greek mathematician</note>, who gives two: one by means of a **parabola**, a **hyperbola**, and the straight line; the other by means of two parabolas and the straight line. But I value even more the one which follows, which is achieved by means of a single parabola, the circle, and the straight line, and was recently invented by a man of rank and merit, who, by his rare wit, is one of the greatest ornaments of our France <note>This refers to René Descartes; Mersenne was a key correspondent and promoter of Descartes's mathematical work</note>. It is true that he gave us only the construction; but it was not difficult to find the demonstration, both of which are as follows.

Let two unequal straight lines be given, **M** and **N**, of which **M** is the lesser; and between the two, it is required to find two **mean continued proportionals** <term>Two values $x$ and $y$ that satisfy the ratio $M:x = x:y = y:N$</term>. Let **AE** and **EH** be two straight lines perpendicular to each other, of which **AE** is equal to **M**, and **EH** equal to **N**. Let **AE** be cut into two equal parts at point **B**, from which the perpendicular **BC** is raised on the same side as **EH**, and equal to half of the same **EH**. Let the line **CA** also be drawn; and from center **C** and with the distance **CA**, let a circle be described, the circumference of which will pass through points **A**, **H**, and **E**, which is easy to demonstrate. Then, taking the line **AE** (given by position) for the axis of a parabola, and the length of the same **AE** for the **latus rectum** <note>original: "costé droit"; the chord through the focus of a conic section perpendicular to the major axis</note>, let the parabola **AGD** be described, intersecting the line **EH** at point **G**, and the circumference of the circle at point **D**. Now it is a clear thing that the parabola intersects line **EH** perpendicular to the axis **AE**. That it also intersects the circumference of the circle between points **E** and **H** is proved thus: because the line **EG**, by the nature of the parabola, is equal to the latus rectum **AE**, which **AE** is lesser, by supposition, than **EH**; therefore **EG** is lesser than **EH**. And point **G**, which is on the parabola, is inside the circle; therefore the parabola passes into the circle between points **E** and **H**. And since the parabola extends infinitely, while the circle is finite, it will exit and intersect the circumference at point **D** between **E** and **H**. From point **D** onto the extended axis **AE**, let the perpendicular **DI** be dropped. I say that **DI** and **AI** are the two mean proportionals that were requested. For let line **CD** be drawn, and **CF** perpendicular to **ID**, which **CF** will fall either between **I** and **D**, or at point **D**, or on **ID** extended beyond point **D**. Let us say it falls between **I** and **D**; for this case being demonstrated, the two...

Similarly, by the same seventh Proposition of the second book of Euclid, the squares AI and AB are equal to the square of BI (or CF) and to twice the rectangle IAB—or to the single rectangle IAE. That is to say, the squares AI and AB are equal to the square CF and the rectangle IAE. Let equals then be added to equals: specifically, add the two squares DI and BC to the two squares AI and AB; and the square DF with its rectangle formed by DI and N to the square CF and its rectangle IAE. Then the four squares DI, BC, AI, and AB will be equal to the two squares DF and CF, and to the two rectangles—one of which is formed by DI and N, and the other being IAE. But of these four squares, the two CB and AB are equal to the single square AC <note>By the Pythagorean theorem, as they form the sides of a right triangle.</note>; and on the other side, the two DF and CF are equal to the single square CD. And AC is equal to CD because they are radii of the same **circle**. Let these equal squares AC and CD therefore be removed, and there will remain the two squares DI and AI on one side, equal to the two rectangles formed by DI and N, and by IAE on the other side. But the square DI is equal to the rectangle IAE because of the **parabola**, of which AE is the **latus rectum** <term>latus rectum</term> <note>Also called the "parameter," this is a fixed line segment that defines the specific curvature of a parabola; in this construction, the square of a horizontal distance from the axis equals the vertical distance multiplied by this parameter.</note>. But AI is to ID as ID is to the latus rectum AE (or M), because of the parabola. But of the first three, the two AB and BC are equal to the single AC, which is equal to CD. Therefore, let the squares AC and CD be removed from both sides; there will remain only the square AI equal to the two squares ID and BC; which in this case being equal, the square AI will be double the square ID, or the square of BC. But the double of the square of BC, or ID, is equal to the rectangle formed by ID and N, because N is double BC, or ID. Therefore, the square of AI is equal to the rectangle formed by ID and N; from which it follows that the three lines N, AI, and ID are proportional. And the three lines AI, ID and AE (or M) also being proportional because of the parabola, the four lines N, AI, ID, and M will be continually proportional, which is what was required. And since it has been proved that the square of AI is double the square of ID, it appears that the four lines are continually double in power of one another; and that N will be eightfold in power of M. In the third case, when the perpendicular CF falls upon ID extended beyond D—which happens when the greater given extreme is more than eightfold in power of the lesser—the demonstration is exactly as in the first case, without changing a single letter or a single word; except that then, of the two points where the line ID cuts the circumference of the circle, point D is the one closest to point I, whereas in the first case it is the furthest from the same point I.

### I. NOTICE.

It should be noted that when the two given extremes are, in length or in power, as a cube number to a cube number, then the problem is plane; because the lines are continually between them in length or in power as the sides of the cube numbers. These numbers and sides being given, their ratio is given, and therefore the continual ratio of the lines is also given; and thus, the first being given, the second will be, and the third. For example, if the given extremes are between them as 27 to 8, the first will be to the second as 3 to 2, or as 27 to 18; and the second to the third also as 3 to 2, or as 18 to 12. Similarly, if the extremes are between them as 8 to the square root of 27; the first will be to the second as 2 to the square root of 3, or as 8 to the square root of 48; and the second will be to the third again as 2 to the square root of 3, or as the square root of 48 to 6, and so on for the others.

We have therefore found between two given straight lines, two other straight lines in continual proportion by means of a single parabola, the circle, and the straight line. We also have, by the same means, the trisection of the angle; the section of the sphere by a plane into two...

### II. ADVISORY.

If there are any organ builders, or makers of other instruments, or any other artisans who despise this manner of dividing the necks of the **Lute**, the **Viol**, etc., or the **Diapason**, and who believe they can do better by practice alone and by the goodness of their ear than by all the methods we have prescribed until now, we do not prevent them from following what pleases them; but we can assure them that they will never fail by following the ways we have explained in several places in this work.

As for the most reliable practices, it is appropriate to consult the best builders, such as **Valeran**, **Le Pescheur**, and several others, who have made the majority of the organs that are now seen in churches, and from whom one can learn everything that is missing in this treatise. To this, we will perhaps add a **Fugue**, which contains everything that can be done on ordinary organs; but if one wishes to use the keyboards that contain the three **Genres of Music** in their perfection <note>The three genres refer to the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales of classical Greek theory, which Mersenne sought to revive in modern tuning.</note>, of which I have spoken at great length in several places, one will find several passages and traits as excellent as they are rare; additionally, the accuracy of the intervals, both <term>consonant</term> and <term>dissonant</term>, will bring new graces to the music. Now, I desire that the forty-fourth Proposition be read along with the first and second Propositions, so that they may mutually assist one another, as well as the Preface of this book, which serves for the understanding of this Treatise.

# BOOK SEVEN
## ON INSTRUMENTS OF PERCUSSION.

-> PROPOSITION I. <-

> *To determine the number of instruments of percussion, and which is the most excellent.*

All bodies that make a noise and produce a perceptible sound when they are struck can be ranked among the instruments of percussion. Consequently, stringed instruments could be included in this book, since one strikes them with the finger, a quill, or otherwise; but because this striking is so light that it should rather be called a simple touch, or a simple pulling, than a striking or a percussion, we ordinarily distinguish those that are struck with a hammer or a stick from those that are touched differently. This is why I give them a separate book. This in no way prevents one from arranging them in another order: for the order I have proposed for myself is not so precise nor so exact that it cannot be changed. For example, one could place the **Psaltery** <note>A stringed instrument of the zither family, often played by plucking or, as Mersenne notes here, by striking the strings with small hammers or sticks.</note>, which I treated in the book on stringed instruments, with these ones, insofar as one strikes its strings with a stick, just as one strikes the bars of the **wood regals** <note>In this context, Mersenne refers to a "claquebois" or an early form of xylophone, rather than the reed organ also known as a regal.</note>.

But be that as it may, I treat here only the instruments of percussion that are in use, and particularly bells and other similar vessels, castanets, cymbals, drums, and the **jew's harps** <note>original: "Trompettes, que quelques-vns appellent Rebubes." While "trompette" usually means trumpet, here Mersenne refers to the *guimbarde* or jew's harp, which was sometimes called a "trompe" or "rebube" in 17th-century France.</note>, which some call *Rebubes*, of which I could also have treated in the other books.

Now, all other instruments of percussion can be related to these: for one finds the tones of metals, stones, and all sorts of wood in the same manner as those of the castanets and the **regals**. But because it seems that bells are the most excellent of all these instruments—as much by reason of their material and their manufacture as by their sounds and their utility—they occupy the largest part of this treatise, which I begin with them. Even though I began the others with the least significant instruments, I do this so that the diversity of the order may produce the same effect in the minds of the readers as the diversity of sounds does in the ear of the listeners. This does not prevent one from starting to read this book with the Propositions that treat the lesser instruments of percussion.

-> PROPOSITION II. <-

> *To explain the invention, the antiquity, the names, and the blessing of bells.*

One almost always has trouble and difficulty in identifying the first inventors of the arts and things that serve for the pleasure or the utility of men; either our predecessors were so negligent that they left us no trace of them, or they were ignorant of letters and knew neither how to read nor write, as we now experience among the **Canadians** and other **savages** <note>Mersenne uses these terms in the 17th-century sense to refer to the Indigenous peoples of North America (specifically New France), noting their oral rather than written traditions.</note>.

# BOOK SEVEN

From this it follows that we do not know with great certainty the Inventor of the Cannon, or of Printing, and that there is doubt concerning the inventor of wheeled Clocks and Sun-dials, of telescopes, of the use of the magnet, of glass, and of several other things, among which we can place bells. For it is not known if the first was made at *Nola*, where *Saint Paulinus* <note>Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431 AD) is traditionally credited with introducing bells into Christian worship.</note> was Bishop, and from which bells were called *Nolæ*; and *Campanæ*, because *Nola* is in the Campania region of Italy. This is why *Polydore Vergil* <note>An Italian humanist historian (c. 1470–1555) who wrote "On the Inventors of Things."</note> and those who followed him were mistaken when they said that *Pope Sabinian*, who succeeded *Saint Gregory*, was the Inventor of bells; for *Saint Jerome*, a contemporary of *Saint Paulinus*, speaks of a bell in the thirty-fifth chapter of the rule for Nuns.

From this it is easy to conjecture that these saints are not the Inventors of bells, and that they only introduced them into Temples. For *Lucian of Samosata*, who lived in the first century, speaks of a clock that sounded; and *Suetonius* and *Dio* call bells <note>original: "tintinnabula"</note> "little tinklers" in the *Life of Augustus*; and *Ovid* and *Tibullus* name them "bronzes," "basins," "kettles," etc. <note>original: "æra, pelues lebetes"</note> of which *Strabo* and *Polybius*, who lived two hundred years before our Savior, also spoke. Furthermore, *Josephus* asserts that the Jews used them in the third book of his *Antiquities*, chapters eight and eleven, where he calls the bell a <term>κώδων<gloss>bell (kōdōn)</gloss></term>.

Now they have several names, of which I have already reported some, and the others are: *Petafus*, *Æramentum*, *Crotalum*, *Signum*, *Cloca*, etc. The first is taken from the shape of a hat <note>The *petasos* was a wide-brimmed hat worn by ancient Greeks, resembling the flare of a bell.</note>, just as *tintinnabulum* comes from the "tin tin" sound they make when ringing. The second is taken from their material, which is copper <note>original: "æramentum," referring to bronze or copper-work</note>. The third is used by *Dante* and *Ariosto*. The fourth is taken from the "signal" <note>original: "signum"</note> that is made with bells, of which *Ivo of Chartres*, *Burchard*, and the *Decree* speak in the first distinction of *On Consecration*, chapter fifty. The fifth is a German or old Gallic word <note>The word *cloca* is the root for both the French *cloche* and the English *clock* or *cloak* (from the bell-shape).</note>, for it is found in the Capitularies of *Charlemagne*.

It is from there that our name *Cloches* [Bells] comes; regarding which one can read the twenty-second chapter of the first book that *Duarenus* <note>François Douaren (1509–1559), a noted French legal scholar.</note> wrote on the Ceremonies of the Church.

As for the term *Nola*, *Quintilian* uses it in the last chapter of his eighth book when he brings up the Proverb "A bell in the bedroom" <note>original: "Nola in cubiculo"</note>, which *Rhodigin* explains as referring to one who talks too much in a room and in private, but who becomes mute when it is necessary to speak in public. But I leave all these names behind in order to speak of their *Blessing*, which the people call *Baptism*, because they are washed.

Now this Blessing is very ancient, for *Alcuin* <note>A leading scholar and teacher at the Carolingian court (c. 735–804 AD).</note>, a disciple of *Bede* and tutor to *Charlemagne* who lived in the year 770, speaks of it as a thing that had long been in use. This can be proved by the blessing found in the *Roman Order*, which is very ancient, and whose Author is unknown. Here is the form used to bless it:

> *Lord, let this Bell be sanctified and consecrated in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.* To which are added several Prayers before and after these words, washing it outside and inside with holy water, and making seven crosses upon it with the oil of the sick, and four inside with the Chrism, as is seen in the *Roman Pontifical* <note>The liturgical book containing the rites performed by bishops.</note>.

Where it must be noted that these Ceremonies were instituted by the authority

Now when they are blessed, it is customary to give them a name in honor of some saint, as is seen with the bells of Notre-Dame in Paris, the largest of which is named *Mary*, and its companion *Jacqueline*; the great bell of Saint John Lateran, which John XIII named *John the Baptist*, according to Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Italian cardinal and historian.</note> in the year 968, or thereabouts, when this ceremony was instituted; the great bell of Notre-Dame in Rouen, which is called *George*, whose size I will give in the third Proposition; and those hanging in the towers and steeples of all Churches.

As for the Pagans, they use bells to signify the hour of baths, markets, the escort of criminals led to execution, and the death of someone, so that shadows and specters might move away, as Ovid remarks in the fifth book of the *Fasti* <note>A Latin poem by Ovid that serves as a poetic calendar of Roman festivals and customs.</note>:

> And asks the shadow to leave his house.

and for several other things according to their will, for everything depends on the institution of men.

It is held that the Turks have forbidden bells to the Christians of Greece, who use a wooden board (which they call a <term>symandre<gloss>semantron</gloss></term>, to which they attach small mallets) or a blade of iron which they call <term>holy iron<gloss>hagiosideron</gloss></term> <note>original: "ἁγιοσίδηρον"</note>, which they strike with hammer blows to call the people to prayer.

# PROPOSITION III.

->*To explain of what size and of what material bells can be made; what is the best material of all, and why the sound of large bells is deeper than that of small ones.*<-

EVEN though the mind, which reaches out toward the infinite, can imagine bells as large as the sky, nonetheless art cannot equal thought, for it is restricted by material and by the weakness of the artisan; the whole world does not contain enough metal to make such bells. And even if the Founders had enough material, it would be impossible for them to handle a bell of ten or twelve million pounds, for all machines would break before being able to move them.

But because there are Artisans and Engineers who have better minds than others, it is difficult to determine the largest bell that can be made; for although the great bell of Notre-Dame of Rouen weighs thirty-three thousand pounds, according to these Latin verses,

> I myself am she who is to be revered for my sound as great as the Thunderer <note>original: "Tonanti," referring to Jupiter or God as the Thunderer.</note>,
> First glory must be given to my author:
> For with thirty-three thousand weight of bronze <note>original: "ter & denis cum ternis millibus æris"</note>
> He offered these dedicated gifts to the true God.

or thirty-six thousand, according to the French verses which are also upon it, with the year 1501, during the reign of Louis XII.
