Nonetheless, one could make bells whose diameter would be double or quadruple that of this one, which would weigh 320,000 or 2,560,000 pounds. Now, the clapper of the Rouen bell weighs 710 pounds, and its circumference taken at the rim is thirty feet—that is to say, it has a diameter of ten feet, if one believes the person who wrote the *Antiquities of Rouen*. But if one prefers to follow the truth of the experience I had in the presence of <term>Mr. Titelouze<note>Jehan Titelouze (c. 1563–1633) was a famous French organist and composer at Rouen Cathedral, often called the "founder of the French organ school."</note></term>, Canon and Organist of the same Church, its diameter is only eight and a half feet, or thereabouts.

This shows that one should not grant too much belief to those who write about the antiquity of cities, inasmuch as they often rely on the reports of others, as other historians do. From this it comes that many despise the study of History, for which one usually has no greater assurance than the authority of those who wrote it at the same time it occurred. Now, we often experience that the writers of the time, who compose the history they were able to see with their own eyes, are full of lies, whether because they believe too lightly in common rumor, or because they do not examine things judiciously enough. I leave aside several other bells whose size is quite notable, such as the great bell of Rennes, of which it is said the diameter is nine feet; that of Arras, which weighs more than seventeen thousand pounds, and which is named *White* <note>original: "Alba"</note> or *Desired* <note>original: "Desiderata"</note> according to the report of Ferolus in his *Chronicle of Flanders*, page 530, which was recast in the year 1464; the great bell of Saint John of Lyon, which weighs 28,000 pounds; the great bell of Notre-Dame de Paris, whose diameter is seven and a half feet and which weighs 24,000 pounds, according to what is said; the great bell of Saint Martin of Tours, which weighs 25,000 pounds; and the one that was formerly at Mende, whose clapper is held to weigh 2,200 pounds—from which it is easy to conclude that it could have weighed 88,000 pounds, which does not seem credible to me. Whatever the case may be, if the hand could follow the spirit, and if created nature had enough matter, one could make bells of all sorts of sizes, the material of which could be gold, silver, copper, brass, bronze, tin, iron, lead, and the mixture of two or more of these metals, stone, etc. But because one ordinarily seeks what is useful, they are made of copper mixed with fine tin rather than other metals, for the reason that this material is long-lasting and sounds the best of all those that do not cost more, or because it melts and is worked more easily.

Now, experience shows that the best material should be composed of three, four, or five parts of pure copper, or <term>rosette copper<note>High-quality refined copper, often appearing as reddish discs or "roses" after the refining process.</note></term>, to one part of tin from Cornwall or England; for Founders put twenty pounds of tin for every hundred pounds of copper. However, this practice allows for great variation, as clockmakers put a third of tin into their <term>chiming bells<note>original: "timbres," referring to the small stationary bells struck by hammers in a clock mechanism.</note></term>, which makes them very resonant; and other founders put more tin into their bells when they want them to have a more excellent sound. Nevertheless, one must proceed with judgment in this matter, for if one puts in too much tin, they are liable to break, and if one puts in too little, they imitate the sound of cauldrons. Some mix in a little <term>bismuth<note>original: "estain de glace." Historically, this term referred to bismuth or a specific hard tin alloy used to improve the flow of the metal or the brightness of the sound.</note></term>—for example, a 20th part—in order to melt the copper more easily, but I leave this industriousness, and

# On percussion instruments.

a thousand other small details they might use, in order to explain the last part of this Proposition, which consists in knowing why large bells have lower sounds than small ones: this is easy to resolve by means of the Principles I have established in the other books. For what happens to bells is the same as what is experienced with <term>lute strings<note>Strings made of gut used on the lute, a popular Renaissance and Baroque string instrument.</note></term>, which strike the air all the more slowly as they are longer, or thicker, and less stretched; so that all parts of the bell, or the entire bells, have more or fewer vibrations depending on whether they are smaller or larger.

Now, I will explain the proportion they must have to make whatever chord one desires in the seventh Proposition, in which I will speak again of these tremblings, the greatest number of which can be attributed to the greater tension of the bell; for one can say that it is all the more "stretched" as it has a higher sound, following the analogy it has with strings.

But one must notice two kinds of turns and returns in the movement of bells: one of which is visible, and occurs when they are swung, and go from one side to the other like a stick, or a weight hanging from a nail, which moves freely at the other end, of which I have spoken quite extensively in the third book on Movements.

The other kind of returns, or tremblings, is nothing other than the <term>vibration<note>The original French uses "fremissement," meaning a shivering or quivering motion.</note></term> of all the parts of the bell, which one perceives by putting a hand or finger upon it; now, the first returns (the swinging) do not make the bell sound, but only the second (the vibrations), by means of the <term>clapper<note>original: "batant"</note></term>, or the hammer with which it is struck, as one experiences by stifling the sound, when one prevents this vibration in different ways—for example, by touching the bell with a piece of cloth, or by squeezing its rim with the hand. Wherein one may notice that there is almost nothing easier than to excite this vibration, for one can hardly touch the largest bells with the tip of a finger, or with the head of a pin, without hearing their sound: which shows the ease of movement of all the parts of a bell.

---

### PROPOSITION IV.

#### *Explaining all the parts of a bell, and the proportion they must keep between them to make pleasant tones.*

It is difficult for a figure to represent all the proportions of a bell, because of the different thicknesses it must have in various places; that is why I use discourse to make it understood. I say then, first, that the <term>Founders<note>The craftsmen who cast metal bells.</note></term> take the measure of all the parts of the bell based on the thickness of its rim, which they make thicker at the spot where the clapper strikes as the bell gets larger: so that their <term>scale<note>original: "diapason"</note></term>, or their <term>gauge<note>original: "brochette," literally a small spit or rod used for measuring proportions.</note></term>, of which I speak later, is nothing other than the knowledge of the thickness of the rims.

Now, they give fifteen "rims" to the width, or the diameter of the bell; for example, if the rim is one foot thick, the bell must be 15 feet wide from rim to rim: but the height of the bell, which is taken from the rim up to the place where it begins to vault, is only twelve rims. From this, it is easy to conclude that the width of the bell is <term>sesquiquartal<note>A ratio of 5:4 (15:12). In music theory, this mathematical ratio corresponds to the interval of a Major Third.</note></term> to its height, which provides the ratio of the **Major Third**.

As for the small belts, D E and F G, they can be called *mouldings* <note>Original: "cordons," literally "cords."</note>, which serve only as ornament. ### PROPOSITION V.

->*To explain the exterior and interior shape of a bell, and the proportions of all its parts.*<-

<term>Bell-founders<note>Original: "Fondeurs."</note></term> guide themselves by the thickness of each bell to describe its lines and shape; and they divide this thickness into three equal parts, which they call *units* <note>Original: "corps," literally "bodies." A relative unit of measurement used in bell-founding based on the thickness of the sound-bow.</note>; then they draw a straight line which contains the height of the bell they wish to make; they divide it into twelve equal parts, which represent the twelve rims, or thicknesses of the bell, for its height is twelve times its greatest thickness.

This line and its twelve parts serve as their guide and rule for giving different thicknesses to the various parts of the bell; for the place which is opposite the sixth part of the said line has only 1 and 1/2 or 2/3 units of thickness; that which is opposite the third part has two units, and the top of the bell has only one, except for the crown, which has 1 and 1/4.

Now, all these thicknesses are found by means of the lines that one describes in this manner. The line A B divided into twelve parts represents the height of the bell, which is taken from the edge of its rim A to B, where it begins to curve to close; but the first stroke, or the first part of the circle which gives the thickness of the bell, is a part of

## On Percussion Instruments

circle, which must be described with a compass opening of thirty parts, each being equal to the twelfth part of the line AB. Thus, one must find the center of the circle to describe the arc BD, and to obtain the shape of this part of the bell, both inside and out. This center is easily found by marking the center point using two small segments of a circle described to the right of points D and B, serving as two centers, with the compass set to thirty parts; however, the page of this book is not large enough to contain these thirty parts.

The second line, or the segment of the second circle DE, which completes the length of the bell, has its center twelve parts away—that is, the length of the line AB. This is found by opening the compass to the length of line AB and placing one of its feet on D and then on E, while using the other foot to mark two small intersecting arcs. The center is taken at the point of their intersection, and the line DE is then drawn to complete the interior shape of the bell.

As for the exterior, it is formed by another line described with a compass opening of seven parts, though some practitioners open it to nine parts.

But since all these lines assume that one has point D, where the *waist* <note>original: "fausseure." The middle, inward-curving section of the bell's profile.</note> of the bell begins, it should be noted that this point is found by drawing a perpendicular line marking the middle, though one may describe it half a rim lower. Once this line is drawn, one must measure one and a half rims to find point D.

It is therefore evident that the thickness of the bell increases unequally from D to E, and that it does not change from D to B.

As for the *crown* <note>original: "cerveau," literally "brain." The flat or slightly domed top of the bell.</note> of the bell, it is seven and a half rims wide; that is to say, its width is half the maximum width of the bell, measured from rim to rim. The center of the circular line that gives shape to the crown is found by opening the compass to eight parts, or eight rims, placing one foot of the compass at point A—which is called the *lip* <note>original: "pince," literally "pincer." The sharp outer edge of the bell's mouth.</note> of the bell—and the other at point B.

The thickness of this crown must be one *body* <note>original: "corps." A technical unit of measure in bell-founding.</note>, which is to say one-third of a rim; it is enclosed by the exterior and interior lines of the crown, which are drawn by keeping the same compass foot on the intersection of the two previous circles. However, the opening used to draw the exterior must be decreased by one-third of a rim to draw the interior.

The *ridge* <note>original: "onde," literally "wave."</note> R L, which sits upon the crown, is one and a half rims away from point B and is about one "body" thick; the handles are attached to this ridge.

Regarding the *foot* <note>original: "patte." The flared bottom section of the bell.</note> or the rim of the bell E G A, its thickness must be taken at point E (where the first part of line AB ends), upon which the perpendicular line EG is drawn, equal to EA. Thus, EG provides the greatest thickness of the bell and determines the spot where the clapper must strike.

Book Seven

# PROPOSITION VI.

## *Explain how metals melt and dissolve with or without fire, which are the easiest and most difficult to melt, and how they are generated in the earth.*

Experience shows that lead melts the most easily of all, and then tin, which can be called a species of lead <note>In early modern science, tin was often categorized alongside lead, sometimes called "white lead" (plumbum album) to distinguish it from "black lead" (plumbum nigrum).</note>; but it is more difficult to melt the other metals, for example, copper and silver. There is no doubt that every metal can be dissolved without using fire, as is observed with <term>aqua regia</term> <note>original: "eaux regales." A powerful mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids.</note> and <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "eaux fortes." Nitric acid, used to separate precious metals.</note>, which dissolve gold, silver, iron, etc.

But this dissolution is greatly different from fusion (melting), and cannot serve the Founders who cast in molds; that is why I shall speak of it no further here.

As for fusion, that of pure copper, or <term>rosette</term> <note>Refined copper that takes on a reddish, rose-like hue.</note>, is so difficult that it is very hard to cast it in a mold to make bells unless one mixes in some other metal or mineral to aid its melting. For example, fine tin, or "tin of glass" <note>original: "estain de glace." Likely referring to bismuth, which was used to lower the melting point of alloys and increase their fluidity.</note>, or borax, which is also used to melt gold and iron. Now, if one wishes to know more, one must consult the Founders and perform several experiments on this subject, both with sulfur—which melts red-hot iron by its touch alone and has an admirable power over all metals—and with antimony and other minerals; from which one can draw enough knowledge to establish a particular science.

As for their generation, it usually occurs underground, as is experienced in mines; and if we believe Palissy <note>Bernard Palissy (c. 1510–1589), a famous French potter and natural philosopher known for his theories on geology and water.</note>, who treats this subject in his book on the nature of waters and metals, it is nothing other than a certain "congealing water," which is enclosed and contained by common water. He proves this by salt, saltpeter, and crystal, which are formed by the virtue of this interior water, which serves as the matter for precious stones and for everything created by congelation—both in animals and in plants, whose seed is nothing other than a congealed water or a salt—as well as in metals, minerals, and <term>marcasites</term> <note>A term then used to describe various sulfide minerals or metallic ores with a bright luster.</note>. I leave aside a thousand highly significant things that can be seen in that Author; additionally, one has the books of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), whose work *De Re Metallica* was the standard text on mining and metallurgy for centuries.</note>, which treat metals and mines very extensively.

->PROPOSITION VII.<-

*Determine the proportion that the thicknesses of bells must maintain to make all kinds of chords and music: and consequently what the Diapason, the rule, or the Gauge, which the Founders use.*

It must be supposed that one already has a bell well made according to the proportions of which I spoke in the fourth and fifth Propositions, for one must have a particular knowledge to cast a bell that makes whatever sound one wishes, and which serves as the foundation for the others; just as one must assume the tone of one of the strings of the <term>Spinet</term> <note>original: "Epinette." A small keyboard instrument where strings are plucked; here used as a reference for tuning.</note>, or of other instruments, to tune the others.

Now the Founders have a custom of decreasing the width of all the bells that follow the largest (which they use as the foundation of their chords) by one and a half "edges" <note>original: "bord." In bell-founding, the "edge" or "lip" thickness is the standard unit of measurement used to determine all other dimensions of the bell.</note> for each: so that if the largest has fifteen edges in its diameter, the second will have thirteen 1/2: the third twelve, the fourth ten 1/2: the fifth nine, and so on for the others.

But I wish here to provide the practice of an entire chord, following the method of one of the most excellent Founders of this time, and then I shall show the best manner of all those possible.

The table that follows contains the said practice: for the first column shows the eight tones, or the eight notes made by the eight bells: the second shows their diameters, the third their thicknesses, and the fourth their weights. Now the largest bell is at the beginning of the column, because it is the foundation of the chord, although one could begin with the smallest, or with such other bell as one might wish, as I shall say later.

But the Measuring Stick <note>original: "Brochette," a specialized tool used by bell-casters.</note>, or the Scale <note>original: "Diapason"</note> which they use to find the size and the weight of their bells will make the proportion we are discussing here better understood than any particular example.

Now they mark the different thicknesses of the bells on a small cylinder of wood or brass, which they call a *staff*, *skewer*, or *scale*: this they do by dividing the said cylinder lengthwise by four lines, upon which they mark the different thicknesses with points, as seen in this figure A C B H, which shows the circumference of the cylinder laid out flat.

But it must be noted that the first thickness, which is from A to I, serves as the foundation for the others, and that it signifies that the bell, whose rim has this thickness, weighs twenty-five pounds. The second thickness is on the second line, and is taken from D up to fifty. The third is taken on the third line from F to 100, and the fourth on the fourth line from B to 200: in such a way that one always goes from the first to the fourth line by crossing over, and then one returns to the first line to get the thickness of the fifth bell, which is taken from A up to the number 300, to signify the weight of this fifth bell. By this, one sees that the thickness gives the weight, and the weight gives the thickness.

Now, one could mark all these thicknesses and weights on a single line. But because this scale of the Founders is not accurate, and it is not reasonable that we remain in this imperfection—since we seek the perfection of everything belonging to Music and all its instruments—it is necessary here to describe the manner of making Measuring Sticks, or Scales for bells, which form their rims and their thicknesses so accurately that nothing can be added to them, and so that the Founders never fail to give perfect tunings <note>original: "accords"</note> to all the bells they undertake: which

But I wish here to explain the general method of making whatever <term>Diapason</term> one wishes: for the Founders <note>Bell-casters or smiths.</note> only go by guesswork when they have bells to cast that are heavier, thicker, and larger than those marked on their <term>Brochettes</term>, which they cannot increase because they do not know their construction through a certain and infallible science that I explain here.

To find the weight of the second bell of which I spoke—when it creates a <term>major tone</term> <note>A "major tone" is the musical interval of a whole step, defined by the ratio 9:8.</note> with the first—one must triple the ratio of nine to eight. That is to say, one must cube nine and eight to obtain their cubed numbers, 729 and 512; for the weight of the second bell is to the weight of the first as 729 is to 512. Therefore, one must find a number which relates to twenty-five (the weight of the first bell) as 729 relates to 512. This is found by the <term>rule of three</term> <note>The "rule of three" is a method of finding a fourth proportional value; in modern terms, solving for x in a/b = c/x.</note>, by saying: if 512 gives 729, how much does twenty-five give? The result will be 35 and 105/512.

I wish to give another example that is easier to understand, assuming that one wants to make bells an <term>octave</term> apart from the first, where the thickness of the rim will be double that of the first, since the ratio of the octave is two to one. However, the weight of the larger bell will be to the weight of the smaller as eight is to one. Consequently, it will weigh two hundred pounds, since the smaller weighs twenty-five; for the ratio of twenty-five to fifty <note>The author uses "fifty" here likely referring to a measurement of thickness or diameter, which when "tripled" (cubed) results in the weight ratio.</note>—that is to say, the tripled ratio of the octave—gives two hundred for the weight of the said bell, which would be the eighth in a set of eight bells.

For the cube of fifty—which is 125,000—when divided by 15,625—which is the cube of twenty-five—gives two hundred. One will always find the same result for all other bells if this method is used, by means of which one can find the thickness and weight of all sorts of bells, however large they may be, even unto infinity.

For example, let us suppose that the rim of the bell which weighs 200 pounds is 2 inches thick, and that the Founders wish to make a <term>Brochette</term> <note>A "brochette" in bell-founding is a measuring gauge or rod used to mark the dimensions of the bell mold.</note> that goes up to a thickness of 4 feet. I say that the bell whose thickness is 4 feet will be to the first bell (which weighs 200 pounds) as 24 to one in terms of thickness, since 4 feet contains forty-eight inches. Consequently, it will weigh 2,764,800 pounds, as seen by the tripled ratio of 200 to 4,800, which are in the same ratio as twenty-four and one. For the tripled ratio of twenty-four to one gives the ratio of 13,824 to one; so one must find a number that is to two hundred as 13,824 is to one, which is 2,764,800. This shows the weight of the bell whose thickness at the rim is four feet.

But one can reduce this <term>Diapason</term> <note>A master scale.</note> of bells to a single line to make it more portable, as seen in line A B, which shows the thickness of thirty-nine <note>The text says "trente-neuf" (39), though the accompanying diagram only labels up to 30.</note> bells, where the largest is taken from A to 30, the second from A to twenty-nine, and so on for the others down to that of A to one.

Let us now see the different widths, or the diameters of the bells, so that there is nothing concerning them that the Founders do not understand perfectly, and so that they may reform their <term>campanary scales</term> <note>Specific measurement rules used by bell-makers.</note> and the proportions they give to the diameters or widths of the bells. It is these errors that cause them to fail in tuning them, often forcing them to recast the bells at their own cost and expense; this brings them great prejudice and sometimes ruins them completely.

The previous <term>diapason</term> <note>In this context, a "diapason" refers to a standardized scale or ruler used by craftsmen to determine proportions.</note> used by Founders is greatly flawed, for they assign sixteen <term>lines</term> <note>A "line" (French: *ligne*) is a traditional unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch, or approximately 2.25 mm.</note> to the rim of a two-hundred-pound bell. From this it follows that the bell they mark as weighing two hundred pounds must actually weigh 298 pounds, <gloss>186/211</gloss> assuming that the first bell, whose rim is only seven lines thick, weighs twenty-five pounds, as they claim.

## PROPOSITION VIII.

### *To explain the Diapason, or the Bell-Scale used by Founders for the sizing of bells.*

This Proposition will provide Founders with more knowledge than they could acquire through sixty years of practice alone, and will disabuse them of the method they currently use to find the tones of all sorts of bells, and to make the <term>cores</term> <note>The "core" (*noyau*) is the inner part of the mold, while the "cope" (*chappe*) is the outer cover; the metal is poured between them.</note> and the copes which they use for casting.

Now, they usually begin with the largest bell when marking their sizes, and take its diameter as the foundation—for example, the diameter AB (which is half a <term>King’s foot</term> <note>The "King's foot" (*pied de Roy*) was the standard French unit of length before the metric system, roughly 32.5 cm.</note>, which can be doubled as many times as necessary to represent the width of the bells one wishes to cast). This they first divide into ten equal parts, of which they give nine to the second bell BC; then they divide the diameter BC into ten other parts, of which they take nine again for the third bell BD, so that these three bells produce the notes *UT*, *RE*, *MI* <note>These are the traditional names for the first three notes of a scale: C, D, and E.</note>.

As for the fourth bell, which must create a semitone with the third to complete the <term>Fourth</term> <note>A "Fourth" is a musical interval spanning four notes of a scale (e.g., C to F).</note> by sounding the *FA*, they find its diameter by dividing the ninth part of the second bell (that is, DC) into five equal parts. They then carry three of these from D to E, so that BE gives the diameter of the fourth bell; or alternatively, they divide AC into three parts, placing two of them from D to E.

They also divide the diameter of this fourth bell BE into ten parts, and take AF, which contains nine parts, for the fifth bell which makes the *sol*, and the <term>Fifth</term> <note>A "Fifth" is a musical interval spanning five notes (e.g., C to G).</note> with the first. They continue in the same manner by dividing BF into ten parts, of which nine give the sixth bell BG; which being divided into ten parts, gives BG <note>The original text repeats "BG" here, likely a printer's error for the next point in the geometric progression.</note> for the seventh; and finally they divide GH into five parts, of which they transfer three from H to I, in order to mark the diameter BI of their eighth or last bell, which should form the <term>octave</term> with the first.

But this practice is not good, because the first two whole tones do not make a perfect <term>major Third</term>, since two minor tones are too small by a <term>comma</term> <note>A "comma" is a tiny mathematical discrepancy in tuning, specifically the difference between a major whole tone (9:8) and a minor whole tone (10:9).</note>, as I have demonstrated elsewhere; the same error occurs with the fourth and fifth bells.

Furthermore, the semitone from D to E is not in its proper proportion—which is sixteen to fifteen—but is instead forty to thirty-seven. For if one divides DC into five parts, CB is divided into forty-five, from which one removes three units (that is, from CD) which are transferred from D to E; consequently, AE is no longer worth more than thirty-seven. From this it is easy to conclude that the first bell does not make

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*Determine if the Founders should make the minor tone or the major tone between bells, when there are to be only two.*<-

The <term>Founders</term> <note>Bell-casters or makers.</note> always make the tuning of DO, RE, or LA, SOL <note>original: "VT, RE, ou de LA, SOL". Mersenne uses the hexachord system; DO-RE and LA-SOL are both "whole step" intervals.</note> when they cast only two bells which are not meant to be accompanied by another, or by several: and because the tone can be major or minor between RE, DO, and LA, SOL, it is not useless to examine which it should be. Upon which I say that it does not matter at all, and that it is only the third bell, or the others, which compel one to make the major tone rather than the minor in certain places, as I have demonstrated in the *Book of Dissonances and Genres*.

From this, it is easy to conclude that there is a great difference between considering a thing all alone and comparing it with others, which often causes it to lose its goodness and value, or at least robs it of grace and pleasantness, as one can observe in many things: from which it also happens that what seems bad or disagreeable when joined to other things appears excellent when one views it separately.

Nevertheless, if one considers the birth and the origin of these two tones, one

...one will prefer the major tone to the minor, both because it comes from the difference between the first two consonances that all the ancients recognized—namely, the <term>Fifth</term> and the <term>Fourth</term>—and because its mathematical ratio is greater, and these sounds unite more often, as one can easily conclude from the *Book of Consonances* and the *Book of Dissonances*.

To this one can add that Pythagoras, Plato, and several other ancients admitted only the major tone, and that it is firmer and more powerful than the minor tone by reason of its larger interval. Furthermore, the <term>Diatonic Genre</term> <note>The standard musical scale of seven notes per octave.</note> took its name from this interval, which the octave contains five times; for although we now use the minor tone, nevertheless we only place two of them in the octave, which has three major tones; so that this tone always dominates in Music, and it is better to use it than the minor tone when one is in no way constrained by other intervals. This is why one can conclude that <term>Founders</term> <note>Craftspeople who cast metal objects, in this case, bells.</note> must divide the diameter of their largest bell into nine parts and give eight of them to the second, when they have only two bells to cast and to tune to the chord they call <term>UT ✶ RE</term> <note>The first two notes of the traditional musical scale, equivalent to C and D.</note>; even though this is rather a discord if one considers their two sounds at the same time, for they do not join nor unite together except at every ninth vibration or shivering of the second bell, or every eighth of the first. In contrast, even the smallest of the simple chords must unite its movements and vibrations at every fifth shivering of the largest bell.

### PROPOSITION X.

*The edge, or the thickness of a bell being given, to find its size, its weight, and its heaviness; or its size being given, to give its thickness; similarly, one of the preceding things being given, to give the tone of the bell, and that tone being given, to find its weight and its size.*

**T**his Proposition is as agreeable and useful as it seems difficult, but if one understands what I have already explained, one will find it very easy: For since we know that the diameter of every bell contains fifteen of its <term>edges</term> <note>original: "bords". In bell founding, the "edge" or "thickness" of the metal at its widest point serves as the basic unit of measurement for all other dimensions.</note> and that its height has twelve, as soon as one knows the edge of all sorts of bells, one will know their diameters and their heights.

Similarly, when one has noted the edge or the diameter of a bell and its weight, one will know the weight of all others. For example, if the bell whose edge is seven <term>lines</term> <note>A historical unit of measurement, roughly 2.25 millimeters or 1/12th of an inch.</note> weighs twenty-five pounds, the one that has an edge of fourteen lines will weigh two hundred pounds, if it is well-made like the other; and if this does not match, the Founders will have failed. One will find the same thing when the edge of the bell has eight, nine, ten, or eleven lines, or two, three, four, five, and six feet, for the cubed ratios of the edges will always give the ratio of the weights.

But it is more difficult to know the edge, or the thickness, and the size of a bell when one only knows its weight; for one must divide the given weight of the bell whose edge is unknown by the weight of the bell whose edge is known, and then one must extract the <term>cube root</term> of the quotient, which will give the edge or thickness that one seeks. This is to be understood for weight that is greater than the one we know: for

For example, if one wants to know the thickness of the **brim** <note>The "bord" or "brim" refers to the thickness of the metal at the part of the bell where the clapper strikes; this measurement is the standard unit for all other bell proportions.</note> and the size of a bell that weighs 40,000 pounds, like the one at Notre-Dame de Rouen, one must divide 40,000 by twenty-five; this gives 1,600 as the quotient, the **cube root** of which is between eleven and twelve. Consequently, we know that the brim of the 40,000-pound bell is at least eleven times larger than that of the bell weighing twenty-five pounds. Since that brim is seven **lines** <term>A "line" (ligne) is a historical unit of measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch.</term> as I have said, the brim of the other will be more than seventy-seven lines and less than eighty-four lines.

But it is easy to determine this brim much more precisely, because one can approach the cube root of numbers that do not have a perfect one so closely that it will not lack a hundred-thousandth part of a line; thus one obtains the true brim and thickness of the bell for which the weight is known. For example, one can take 11 1/4, or 11 1/12, etc., which signify eleven times seven lines—that is to say, seventy-seven lines plus the fraction—which makes it a little larger than a half-foot, for 7/10 of seven lines is worth almost half an inch.

Now, it is easy to practice with several other examples from which one will gain **insight**; for instance, if one supposes that seven lines of brim result in a weight of twenty-five pounds, one will find that a brim of eight lines results in a weight of thirty-seven <gloss>109/141</gloss>.

The same method must also be used when one wants to find the brim of a smaller bell by its weight, assuming the knowledge of the brim of a larger one. For example, if one supposes that 1,600 pounds gives a brim of twenty-eight lines, one will find that twenty-five pounds gives a brim of seven lines, which is to say a brim four times smaller than the other.

As for the **tone** of the bell, for which the size, brim, or weight are given, one must assume that the tone of some bell—either larger or smaller than the one whose tone is being sought—is already known. This being assumed, it is easy to know the tone of all the others. For example, if the tone of the twenty-five-pound bell has two hundred **degrees of pitch** <note>The author uses "degrees of sharpness" (degrez d’aigu) as a conceptual measure of frequency or pitch height.</note>, the two-hundred-pound bell will have only one hundred degrees; for the tone of the twenty-five-pound bell has the same ratio to the tone of the two-hundred-pound bell as the brim of the former has to the brim of the latter. Now, the brim of the former is **half** <note>original: "sous-double"</note> the brim of the latter, from which it follows that the tone of the smaller is half the tone of the larger.

One must conclude the same for all other bells, since their tones are in the same ratio as their brims and their diameters; and because one finds the brims and the diameters by the weights, one will know the said tones when the brims or diameters are known.

Similarly, if the tone of a bell is known, one will know its brim, its diameter, and its weight. For if one supposes that the tone of another bell is known, and that the brim or weight of that bell is also known, one will find the weight or size of the other. For example, if the tone or sound of the bell whose size and weight are unknown is double the tone of the one that weighs twenty-five pounds and has a brim of seven lines—and consequently a diameter of eight and a half inches, since the diameter contains fifteen brims—the other bell which makes the **octave below** <note>original: "l’octaue en bas"</note> (that is to say, which has a tone double the other) will have a brim of fourteen lines and a diameter of seventeen and a half inches, and will weigh two hundred pounds. All other examples confirm this speculation.

But so that it may be better understood, it must be noted that one can divide the tone or sound of each bell into as many parts or degrees as one wishes, just as I have divided that of the strings, whose vibrations being...

known values can serve to regulate the pitch of bells, so that one may know how many vibrations <note>The author uses the term "tremblemens" to describe what we now call frequency or cycles per second (Hertz).</note> compose the sound of the bell being considered.

Now, everyone can take the lowest pitch of their voice as a rule for others, just as I take the pitch of forty <note>original: "quarante"</note> for the pitch to which my voice can descend, because the string that makes a unison with my voice vibrates forty times in the span of one second. But if one cannot remember a certain pitch of the voice, one can use a hollowed key, a **flageolet** <term>A small flute-like wind instrument popular in the 17th century.</term>, an organ pipe, or whatever device one wishes to aid the memory.

And then one can always have recourse to the string, for which the number of vibrations made in a given time will represent whatever pitch one desires.

I wish here to give an example taken from the bells of our house in Paris, of which the largest of the four—which produce the four sounds of the **Fourth** <note>The interval of a "Fourth" consists of four notes; here the author identifies them by the traditional solfège syllables: *ut, re, mi, fa* (equivalent to C, D, E, F).</note>, *ut, re, mi, fa*—has the pitch or sound of one hundred and sixty vibrations, insofar as the string making a unison with the *ut* of this Fourth (that is to say, with the pitch of the largest bell) vibrates one hundred and sixty times in the space of one second.

Now, this bell weighs 278 pounds, and has a diameter of one foot, ten and a half inches; consequently, if one wants to know how much a bell weighs that descends lower by a **Fifteenth** <note>An interval of a "Fifteenth" is two full octaves. In terms of frequency, this means the vibrations are four times slower.</note>, and which has a pitch quadruple the other pitch (that is to say, four times deeper), one must multiply 278 by sixty-four, insofar as the **triple ratio** <note>The "triple ratio" refers to the cube of the ratio (4³ = 64). In geometry and physics of the time, doubling the size of a three-dimensional object increases its volume/weight by eightfold (2³), and quadrupling it increases it by sixty-fourfold (4³).</note> of four to one is sixty-four to one; and one will find that the bell, which descends as low as my voice, must weigh 17,792 pounds, if it is made according to the proportions of the preceding one.

This must always be observed before making any judgment on the weight of a bell by the knowledge of its pitch; for if it is of another shape than the bell upon which the foundation was taken—for example, if it is only fourteen **brims** <note>As established on the previous page, the "brim" (bord) or thickness of the metal is the standard unit of measurement for bell-making.</note> wide, or if it is fifteen high, whereas the foundation was taken from one that is twelve brims high and fifteen wide, or if it was made using different **compass strokes** <note>French: "traits de compas." This refers to the geometric curves drawn by the founder to determine the bell's profile.</note> than those I have spoken of—one will be mistaken.

But if one has followed the same rules, and the bells are of the same material, and the casting was equally good, one will in no way fail to find the weight by the sound, and the sound by the weight.

## PROPOSITION XI.

### Explaining how one can find the size, or the volume, and the weight of a bell by means of water.

WHEN we speak of finding the size of a bell, this can be understood as the size of its diameter, its surface area, or its **volume** <note>original: "solidité." In this period, "solidity" was often used to mean three-dimensional volume or the space occupied by a solid body.</note>. Now, we have already shown the means of finding the diameter and the other dimensions that correspond to simple lines. However, because the lines used to trace the mold of a bell are composed of three or four different circumferences, we do not yet have a way to express their length using straight lines; consequently, we do not know how to measure the surface of a bell, since it depends on those parts of the circumferences that give it its shape. This is why I do not dwell on the measurement of the surface. Nevertheless, if one assumes the size of the surface of one bell, it is very easy to find geometrically the surface of all others, whether larger or smaller; for if they are larger, they will be in a **duplicate ratio** <note>A mathematical term meaning the ratio of the squares (e.g., if the diameter doubles, the surface area increases by four, or 2²).</note> of the diameter of the bell whose surface is known and the diameter of the larger ones. For example, if the surface of a hundred-and-twenty-pound bell is one foot, that of a bell with double the diameter will be four feet, because if we suppose the smaller bell has a diameter of one, the larger will have four: now, the ratio of one to two, when doubled <note>i.e., squared</note>, produces the ratio of one to four. Thus, if one takes the trouble to measure the surface of one bell—for example, one weighing twenty-five pounds—one will know the surface, both internal and external, of all possible bells, provided they maintain the same proportion between their parts.

But it seems one cannot measure this surface more easily than by covering it with pieces of paper, parchment, lead, or another material that does not stretch; for these pieces, once measured, will give the surface area quite precisely. This will serve as a foundation for finding all the others, and for knowing how much paper, or cloth, etc., is needed to cover them, and consequently to know the size of the concave surface of the air or water that surrounds them.

As for the **volume** <note>original: "solidité"</note>, it is easier to find, whether by standard scales or by the **steelyard** <term>A portable balance with a short arm for the load and a long graduated arm for a moving counterweight, here called a "Romaine" or "Crochet" (Hook).</term> (which some call the Hook), or by means of water.

->### Book Seven<-

...of which I speak here particularly; for if one submerges the bell in a vessel full of water, wine, or another liquid, the water that comes out of the vessel will be equal to the size, or the **volume** <note>original: "solidité." In early scientific writing, this refers to the three-dimensional space or cubic volume of an object.</note> of the bell: that is to say, if the water reduced to a cube has a side of four feet, the bell reduced into a cubic mass will yield a cube of sixty-four feet, because the content, or the solid of the cube, is in a **triple ratio** <note>original: "raison triplee." This is the historical term for the third power or cubing (x³), as 4 times 4 times 4 equals 64.</note> of its sides.

And if one fears that the water will bulge at the rim, and that as much as the volume of the bell will not come out, one can pass a ruler over the rims, in order to strike off the excess and the swelling of the water.

One can also know the volume or size of the bell without filling the vessel, provided that one puts water in it up to the height of the bell; for the **tap** <note>original: "robinet." A small valve or spigot used to control the flow of liquid.</note> that one will place level with the top of the said bell, being opened, and the bell being plunged and sunken into the water, the water that comes out through the tap will be equal to the size or volume of the bell.

Now this tap is easier and more exact than the other way, because it prevents the water from being lost, and it gives as much leisure as one wants to have the water conveniently and to measure it several times and in several ways.

The reason for this **Mechanical practice** <term>Mechanics in the 17th century often referred to the practical application of mathematical principles to physical objects.</term> is taken from the fact that there always rises a quantity of water, or other liquid, equal to the quantity of the body that descends into it; for no movement would occur if as much metal did not descend as water rises, because nature, which loses nothing on one side that it does not gain just as much on the other, is similar to scales which lower one of their basins as much as they raise the other, so that all things keep the **equilibrium** <note>A fundamental concept in early physics; here referring to the balance and displacement of fluids according to natural law.</note> that God has given them.

But it must be noted that one should plunge the bell, or other hollow and concave vessels, by beginning to sink them by the handles, so that the inside being filled with water no longer has any air: for if some part of air still remains in the concavity of the bell, the water that it makes come out will be equal to the size of the solid composed of the bell's metal and the air it encloses.

Now the consideration of air requires a particular discourse, by reason of its rarefaction and condensation, and its weight and lightness: that is why I do not speak of it here, where it is only a question of water, which can still serve in another way to find the size of the bell, without it being necessary to sink it into the water.

But because the practice of it is more subtle than the preceding one, its foundation must be explained, which consists in knowing that the body that one sinks into the water can be considered in two ways: First, insofar as it is heavier than the water in which it sinks: Second, insofar as it is lighter, though it descends a little into the water: Now in whatever manner one takes it, it always weighs less in water than in air: and it weighs as much less in water than in air as another volume of this body and of the water approaches closer to equilibrium; from this comes the fact that bodies which are of the same weight as water do not weigh at all in water, and that they stay in the same place where one puts them **between two waters** <note>original: "entre deux eaux." A phrase describing neutral buoyancy, where an object neither sinks to the bottom nor floats on the surface.</note>.

From which it follows that the body placed in water weighs half as much as in air, when an equal mass of water is twice as heavy as the body, and

...that the said body weighs less in water than in air by only a twentieth, or a hundredth part, when an equal mass of water is less heavy than the said body by only a twentieth, or a hundredth part.

This being established, I say that one will know the size, or the **volume** <note>original: "solidité." In this period, this refers to the three-dimensional space an object occupies.</note> of the bell, once its weight is known, if one takes a piece of the metal from which the bell was made and weighs it in water (of which the weight is known). For one will then know by how much a mass of water equal to that of the metal is larger than that of the said metal; and consequently, by how much the bell, when reduced to a cubic mass, is smaller than a cube made of water that weighs as much as the bell.

For example, if one wants to know the size of a bell that weighs twenty-five **pounds** <term>liures: The "livre parisis" or Paris pound, roughly 490 grams.</term>, and the metal it is made of is to water as nine is to one—that is to say, it takes nine times as much water as metal to weigh the same—one must take nine times as much water by volume as the piece of metal. And because the weight of the bell is known, one will know how many times it is heavier than the piece of metal that was used; for example, if the piece of metal weighs one ounce, the bell will weigh four hundred ounces. Now, these four hundred ounces take up nine times less space than an equal weight of water: so that one only needs to know the size of three thousand six hundred ounces of water to know the size of the twenty-five pound bell, which is nine times smaller.

Now, it is easy to reduce the said water into a square shape by means of a vessel made for this purpose, in order to take a ninth part of it for the similar square of metal; or to find the side of the cube it forms, if one assumes the experiment which shows that a **cubic foot** <term>pied cube: Based on the "pied du Roi," approximately 32.48 cm.</term> of fresh water weighs seventy-two pounds. From this, one can conclude that a cube of water weighing twenty-five pounds (like the bell) has a side of eight **inches** <term>pouces: 1/12 of a foot.</term>, five **lines** <term>lignes: 1/12 of an inch, roughly 2.25 mm.</term>, <gloss>16/25</gloss>.

And because the metal is nine times heavier than water, the twenty-five pounds of which the bell is composed make a cube whose side is forty-eight lines and <gloss>3441/5408</gloss>.

By this, one can determine the size of all bells whose weight is known; for example, that of the great bell of Rouen, which, when reduced to a mass, forms a cube whose side is three feet, eleven inches, five lines, and <gloss>8/43</gloss>, assuming it weighs forty thousand pounds; for a cubic foot of copper weighs six hundred forty-eight pounds.

But I will speak further on the manner of finding the size of a bell whose weight is given in another place, and of finding the difference in weight between copper, brass, and other metals in the twenty-sixth Proposition.

## PROPOSITION XII.

->Determine if one can know how much tin, copper, or other metal<-
->is in all sorts of bells, and if the Founders, or other artisans who<-

# Book Seven

to discover the theft of the **Goldsmith** <note>This refers to the famous story of Archimedes and the crown of King Hiero II, where Archimedes discovered how to detect if silver had been substituted for gold by measuring water displacement.</note>, who had mixed silver into a crown that was supposed to be of fine gold.

But it must be assumed that there are only two kinds of metals in the bell, for if there were three types, one could not discover the quantity of each metal, because one can compose two or more bodies from three metals mixed indifferently that will be equal in weight and in size.

And because it is customary to compose the metal of bells from **copper** and **tin**, I now assume that one wishes to know how much there is of one and the other in a given bell, without being permitted to melt it down or break it.

Now, for this purpose, one must take three bodies of the same weight, of which the first is of copper, the second of tin, and the third composed of the two, following the mixture and composition of which the bell is made. And then one must take three bodies of water equal in size to the three bodies of metal, in order to find how much copper and tin are in the proposed bell in this manner, for the sake of which I assume that **A** represents the copper, **B** the metal

->A B D<-
->G F H<-

composed of copper and tin, and **D** the tin; and that the three bodies of water equal to the three preceding ones are **G**, **F**, and **H**, so that **G** is equal in size to **A**, **F** to **B**, and **H** to **D**.

This being established, **Marin Gethalde** <note>Marino Ghetaldi (1568–1626), a scientist from Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik) and a friend of Galileo. His book *Promotus Archimedes* (Archimedes Furthered), published in 1603, refined methods for determining the weights of mixed metals.</note> demonstrates in the tenth Theorem of his *Archimedes Furthered*, that when of three equally heavy bodies, the first and the third are of different sizes, and the second is composed of the one and the other, and one has three bodies of water of the same volume as the three bodies of metal: as the difference in the weight of the two bodies of water (which are equal to the first and the third metal bodies) is to the weight of the second metal body, so the difference of the weights of the first and the second water bodies is to the weight of the part of the second metal body which is of the same kind as the third metal body; and consequently, that the difference of the weights of the second and the third body of water has the same ratio with the weight of the part that is of the same kind as the first metal body.

But the example that follows will make this difficulty easier to understand.

And for this purpose, I assume that the bell weighs two hundred pounds, and that its metal is composed of four-fifths copper and one-fifth tin—that is to say, forty pounds of tin and one hundred and sixty pounds of copper; and I say that it will displace a greater quantity of water than if it were made entirely of copper, and that it will displace all the more as it contains more tin, because copper is to water as nine to one, and tin is to the same water as eight to one <note>This means copper is 9 times denser than water, and tin is 8 times denser than water.</note>: this is why the bell, if it were made entirely of tin, would only displace or cause to rise eight times its own volume of water, and if it were of copper, it would cause nine times as much to rise.

From which it must be concluded that it will displace that much less water when it has 1/5 tin, because this fifth is a larger volume than a fifth of copper; and consequently, that it will displace twenty-two and 7/9 pounds of water when it is mixed with tin, and that if it is all copper it will only displace twenty-two and 2/9 pounds; but if the bell weighs only twenty-five pounds, it will displace two and 7/9 pounds of water when it has 1/5 tin; if it is all...

## PROPOSITION XIII.

### To determine if bells can be made that float on water, or on other liquids.

IT is certain that no body sinks in water unless it is heavier than the water; and that if it is forced down, it returns to the surface as soon as the force has ceased. It is also certain that the water which rises due to the descent of a weight cannot be heavier than the weight itself, otherwise the weaker would overcome the stronger. In the third place, it is certain that a floating body always sinks until the water that is equal in size to the submerged part is as heavy as the entire body: for example, if a body sinks halfway, and it contains two cubic feet, one cubic foot of water will weigh as much as the whole of said body.

This being established, I say that if one makes a bell of which a part, being submerged, displaces a weight of water equal to the entire bell, it will float on the water: that is to say, if the submerged part weighs two hundred pounds, and the entire bell weighs three hundred pounds, the water equal in size to the submerged part will weigh four hundred pounds <note>The author is illustrating the principle that the potential buoyancy—the weight of the water the object *could* displace—must exceed the object's weight.</note>; the reason for which is that the lighter cannot occupy the place of the heavier, and that nature always maintains the equilibrium in which it exists.

But because the bells which are ordinarily used are always much heavier than an equal volume of water, they cannot float; although if one wishes to change their proportions, and particularly their thickness, it would be easy to make them of all sorts of metals that would float. This will happen whenever they are lighter than the same volume of water as they occupy, including their empty space: for example, if the bell weighs four hundred pounds, and the water which can fill it—that is, the water equal to its internal void—weighs four hundred and one pounds, the bell placed on the water will float. This will always happen when the water equal in size to the submerged part is as heavy as the entire bell. From this, one can easily conclude in what manner one must adapt plates of gold, lead, and other metals to make them float on water, and how one can make boats from them without any danger of sinking.

For if one makes a bell, or boats of gold, which contain twenty times more space than if they were reduced to solid cubes <note>This refers to making the metal very thin so that the hollow interior creates a large volume relative to the weight of the metal.</note>, they will float; and if those of silver have eleven times more space, those of lead thirteen times, those of copper nine times, and those of tin eight times, they will float likewise. But these spaces must be understood to include both the solid material of these vessels and the void they contain: for if one only took the solid material, its volume never changes regardless of the shape one might give it.

Now, one can apply everything I have said about water to other liquids, whether

whether they weigh more or less. Regarding the difference in waters, it is certain that solid bodies sink less in heavier waters, such as seawater, which I discuss elsewhere. This is why ships that are out of danger on the open sea may perish in ports where the water is fresh, because fresh water is lighter than seawater.

->COROLLARY.<-

First, it must be noted that the air filling metal vessels—for example, cauldrons that do not sink and float on the water—is not the reason they do not sink or why they float. The same thing would happen if there were no air at all and they were empty <note>The author is referring to a vacuum, suggesting that the shape and displacement, not the presence of air inside, create the buoyancy.</note>; the true cause of this phenomenon lies in the equilibrium <term>equilibrium: here referring to the balance between the weight of the object and the upward force (buoyancy) of the displaced water</term> which we have already discussed.

Second, regarding two bodies of the same weight in air, the larger one would, it seems, be the heavier in a vacuum, since neither would have any support in said vacuum, whereas the larger one receives more support from the air than the smaller one does. This is similar to how, between two bodies of equal weight in water, the one with the larger volume weighs more when moved into the air. Now, it would be easy to find the weight of air equal to said body if one could weigh it in a vacuum.

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*To determine by how much bells of all kinds of metals must be larger or smaller than one another to produce a unison, or any harmony and interval that one may desire.*<-

It is easy to find by how much the bells, of which we spoke in the preceding Proposition, must be smaller or larger than one another to produce a unison, or all kinds of intervals—both consonant and dissonant—if one knows the proportions they must maintain when they are of the same material in order to rise or fall to all kinds of tones. Because I have already shown what these proportions must be, one must only remember them here, beginning with the unison. This unison will be produced by all the preceding bells if one increases the diameters of those that have the lower or higher sound in the same ratio as their sounds are lower or higher, provided that the same ratio is observed in the other dimensions of the <term>bells</term> or <term>chimes</term>.

For example, if one wants to put <term>bismuth</term><note>original: "eſtain de glace," literally "ice-tin," a period term for bismuth due to its crystalline structure.</note> in unison with common tin, following the notes of the fourth table of the fourteenth Proposition, one must decrease the diameter of the <term>bismuth</term> chime, or increase that of the common tin bell, until that of the common tin is in a <term>sesquitertian</term><note>A ratio of 4:3, often used to define the interval of a perfect fourth.</note> ratio to that of the <term>bismuth</term>—that is to say, one has four parts and the other three.

It is easy to put all the other chimes in unison by increasing the diameters of the higher-pitched ones, or by decreasing those of the lower-pitched ones, in the same ratio as the numbers corresponding to the lower sounds are larger or smaller than those corresponding to the higher sounds.

If one wishes to follow the first table of the preceding Proposition, in which I listed all the consonances and dissonances made by the <term>chime metal</term> with other metals, the radical numbers of the intervals they produce when sounding will serve to put them in unison, as seen in the following table.

This table has three columns, of which the first and the third represent the third table of the fourteenth Proposition, and the second shows what remains of the string of the monochord. For example, when the bridge is placed under one hundred forty-nine, which gives the unison for common tin, two hundred eleven parts of the string remain on the other side.

Now, with the bells being in unison, it is easy to set them to whatever tuning you wish by using the <term>rule of three</term><note>A mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known values based on proportions.</note>, and by ensuring that the diameter of the lower or higher bell is increased or decreased according to the ratio of the <term>consonance</term><note>A harmonious musical interval.</note> that is desired. For example, if the diameter of the brass chime has nine parts and that of the copper chime has eight to produce a unison, and one wants to raise the brass chime to a <term>Fifth</term><note>A musical interval encompassing five notes of a scale (e.g., C to G).</note>, one must take its diameter and make it relate to the diameter being sought as three is to two—this results in a diameter of six for the brass chime, which produces the Fifth above.

But if one wants it to produce the Fifth below, the diameter would be thirteen and a half. If one raises the copper to a Fifth (with the brass diameter remaining at nine), its diameter must be five and one-third; and if one lowers it a Fifth, its diameter will have twelve parts. The same method must be used to find other intervals. One can also raise or lower them to any desired tuning without first putting them in unison, by adding or subtracting from their diameters as many parts as the harmonic ratios require. For example, assuming that lead produces a <term>Fourth</term> with common tin, if one wants to raise the tin to a Fifth, its diameter must be decreased in a <term>sesquioctave</term><note>The ratio of 9:8, which corresponds to a whole tone.</note> ratio. For this purpose, I suppose it to be twelve parts, so as to find a number that relates to twelve as nine relates to eight—which is ten and two-thirds. If one lowers it to a Fifth, its diameter will be thirteen and a half.

It is so easy to find all the other intervals between the other chimes that there is no need to explain it at greater length. It must only be noted that the chimes I used were cast in sand in the very same mold; even so, this did not prevent their edges from having different thicknesses. From this, it follows that they would slightly change the tones I have explained if all their edges and other parts were made to be of the same thickness, whether by means of a <term>lathe</term> or otherwise.

Now, this difference occurs because metals that are simple and without mixture are much more difficult to melt than those that are mixed; for example, pure copper, which is called *rosette* <note>Pure copper, so called because of its reddish color after being refined.</note>, is so difficult to melt for casting in a mold that one of the most skillful Founders in Paris lost several <term>chimes</term><note>original: "timbres," referring to stationary clock bells.</note> which turned out imperfectly before casting a good one. The same thing happens with fine gold and silver, which are much more difficult to melt than when they are mixed and alloyed with other metals; this is why gold is alloyed with silver, and silver with copper, in order to use them and work them more easily. Now, I shall explain the quality of the metals from which I made the twelve chimes in the Proposition that follows.

Because the casting of gold is more difficult than that of lead, which flows much better and fills the mold more perfectly, it happens that the gold bell is less thick in all its parts.

To this one may add other accidents of casting, which cause small voids to form within the thickness of certain metals—which one might call <term>air bubbles</term><note>original: "vents," literally 'winds' or 'gases' trapped in the cooling metal.</note>—which render them less heavy.

<header>Of percussion instruments.</header>

Now, one can say how much thinner the <term>bell</term><note>original: "timbre," referring here to the physical object of the clock bell or chime.</note> made of gold is than one of lead, since the true proportion of their weights is known, as I will explain later; and if it is of an equal size on the exterior, one can determine the size and the number of its <term>air bubbles</term><note>original: "souffleures," which are small holes or voids formed in metal during the casting process.</note>.

But since these experiments cannot serve to determine the proportion of weights, they will at least serve to warn those who wish to perform them that one must foresee and prevent all accidents that might hinder the truth, and which most often render experiments useless or less exact; I remark on this so that my own findings bring no prejudice to anyone.

As for the manner of knowing the difference in the weights of each metal by means of water, it is easy enough, though it is very subtle; for the weight of a metal is greater as the weight it has in the air differs less from that which it has in the water. For example, if one metal weighs only one-third less in water than in air, and another weighs half as much less, the former will weigh one-sixth more than the latter, provided they are both of the same size. The reason for this is taken from the fact that bodies plunged into water cause a volume of water to rise equal to their own size, from which it follows that they are less heavy in water by the weight of the water they displace. For example, gold is less heavy in water than in air by one-nineteenth part, because a quantity of water equal to the gold weighs 19 times less than the gold. Thus, the force it has to descend toward the center of the earth being nineteen degrees in the air, it has only eighteen degrees of force to descend in the water, because it employs one degree of its force to lift and displace a volume of water as large as itself. This can be applied to all other sorts of bodies heavier than water, and to all other sorts of liquids, such as wine, oil, etc., whose weights are found precisely by those of the bodies that one plunges and weighs within them; for the weight they have in the air decreases more or less in other liquids than it does in water, according to whether they are lighter or heavier than water.

Now, it is not necessary that the metals whose weights one wishes to know by means of water be of the same volume, for one can perform the experiment with pieces of metal of all sizes: for example, one can use <term>quarter-crowns</term><note>original: "quarts d'escus," a French silver coin.</note>, <term>tokens</term><note>original: "jettons," metal counters used for calculation.</note>, <term>pistoles</term><note>original: "pistoles," gold coins.</note>, etc. But one must have very accurate scales to make the experiments certain, and arrange them so that the two basins are in balance; then one must attach the pieces of metal to a <term>horsehair</term><note>original: "crin de cheval," used because it is strong, thin, and does not absorb much water.</note> hanging from one of the basins, and plunge them into the water after they have been weighed in the air, in order to see how much less each weighs in the water than in the air, and to conclude what difference there is between the weights of all sorts of metals, or other bodies that are more or less heavy than water.

But one must note the weight of the water in order to compare it with the weight of all sorts of bodies heavier than it, and to create tables similar to the one that follows, in which one sees the weight of sixteen bodies, whose differences are easy to observe.

Now, anyone can perform private experiments to satisfy their mind and to confirm this Proposition and many others that may be devised. However, it must be noted that no metal sinks to the bottom unless it is compact enough to "split" the water. For example, the leaves of gold commonly used for gilding and <term>illumination</term><note>The art of decorating manuscripts with gold and bright colors.</note> cannot sink to the bottom of the water when they are spread out; and if they are forced down by strength, they return to the surface. This happens similarly to all other metals. From this, several difficulties may arise in the manner of weighing them in water or in other liquids.

### COROLLARY I.

One may consult the Preface of the book that Monsieur <term>Petit</term><note>Pierre Petit (1598–1677), a French mathematician and physicist who wrote on the "proportional compass" and hydrostatics.</note> wrote regarding his work on the use of the proportional compass. From this, he infers that water is to tin as 1,843 grains are to 12,984—that is to say, a little more than one to seven; and to silver as 225 is to 2,304, or a little more than one to ten. ### COROLLARY II.

It should be noted that the pound <note>original: "liure."</note> I have used is that of the <term>Paris Mark</term><note>The "Marc de Paris" was the standard system of weights in France before the metric system.</note> weight, which contains sixteen ounces; the ounce contains eight <term>gros</term><note>A unit of weight equivalent to a drachm or dram.</note>; the *gros* contains three <term>deniers</term><note>A unit of weight equivalent to a scruple.</note>; and the *denier* twenty-four grains. Thus, the *gros* weighs 72 grains, the ounce 576, and the pound 9,216. And if one wishes to compare the Roman pound—composed of 6,912 grains and divided into twelve ounces—to ours, it equals only eleven of our ounces, such that one hundred of ours make 145 of those of Rome. From this, it is easy to conclude that the grains used in Rome are not of the same weight as ours. Now, Monsieur Petit used scales so precise that the sixteenth part of a grain would tip them.

## COROLLARY III.

If one wishes to begin experiments with fine gold, in order to know the weights of other metals and all other bodies, I have found that a ball of gold—the axis or diameter of which is five and a half lines <note>A "line" is a historical unit of length, approximately 2.25 millimeters or 1/12th of an inch.</note>—weighs 321 1/2 grains, and that a lead ball of the same size weighs 193 grains. However, it must be noted that it is appropriate to use small pieces of paper to mark the parts of a grain, particularly when it is divided into twelve, sixteen, thirty-two, or sixty-four parts. This is because sixteenth and thirty-second parts made of brass <note>original: "laton"</note> are too difficult to handle and are not felt easily enough; hence it happens that one often searches for them, even while they are between one's fingers, without being able to feel them or let them go. A cubic foot of gold, following the preceding ball, weighs three hundred thirty-seven and a half pounds.

## COROLLARY IV.

Having weighed the aforementioned ball of fine gold in water, using the very accurate scales of Monsieur de Roberval <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675) was a renowned French mathematician and physicist who invented the "Roberval Balance."</note>, I found that the weight of this gold is to that of water of equal volume as 18 3/4 to one. From this, I conclude that Gethalde <note>Marino Ghetaldi (1568–1626), a Ragusan scientist whose work *Promotus Archimedis* dealt with the specific weights of various substances.</note> and others who found the ratio of 19 to one used water lighter than ours from the spring of Rungis <note>The Rungis spring supplied Paris with water via an aqueduct; its water was considered a standard for purity at the time.</note>, and that one may follow the experiments of the said Gethalde without further trouble. Now, I have provided the tables he made of the weights of all the bodies he weighed in air and in water in the fourth and fifth articles of the twenty-third question of our *Commentaries on Genesis* <note>original: "Commentaires sur la Genese." This refers to Mersenne’s own encyclopedic work, *Quaestiones celeberrimae in Genesim* (1623).</note>.

As for lead, I found it is to water as 11 1/3 to one: so that one can regulate the weight of all other bodies based on gold and lead.

## COROLLARY V.

Those who wish to test weights must have scales so accurate that an eighth or sixteenth part of a grain makes them tip, like those we have used. As for different weights, one must use a Pile <note>Probably a "Pile de Charlemagne," a standard set of nested weights.</note>, a pound, or a half-pound in marc weight <note>The "poids de marc" was the traditional French weight system prior to the metric system.</note>, and have a quantity of grains and halves, quarters, and eighths of grains. For although in necessity one can use four weights following a triple progression—namely of one, three, nine, and twenty-seven—to weigh from one up to forty, and up to one hundred twenty-one by adding the following terms of the same progression (namely eighty-one), and by adding two hundred forty-three, up to three hundred sixty-four <note>This refers to a mathematical puzzle: by placing weights in either scale pan, one can measure any weight up to the sum of the progression.</note>, because the last number of the progression that keeps the triple ratio (starting with unity) contains twice the preceding numbers plus one; nevertheless, the manner and the ordina<unclear>ry</unclear> series of weights starting with the half-dram, the dram, the quarter-ounce, etc., are much more convenient and the only ones suitable for use.

# PROPOSITION XVII.

->*To explain the manner of producing different sounds with the same bell, or the same glass, and whether one can determine the quantity of water, wine, or other liquids they contain by the sound they produce.*<-

It is certain that those who are accustomed to handling glasses can produce all sorts of consonances <note>Harmonious combinations of notes.</note> and dissonances, whether with a single glass or with several, as is experienced when one makes a glass descend to the octave by filling it with water or wine. But Aristotle says in the 50th Problem of the 19th Section <note>Referring to the *Problems* attributed to Aristotle, a collection of questions on various scientific and philosophical topics.</note>, that two barrels, of which one is empty and the other half full, produce an octave, a claim which we shall examine further below.

Certainly, if the sounds of the glass, of bells, and of all other vessels follow the ratio of the different quantities of water or wine that are put into them, one can know how much water or wine there is in all types of glasses, or how much is needed to fill them, without seeing the glass, provided that one hears its sound; and consequently, one can add water or remove it, which will have such a ratio as one desires with the water necessary to fill it.

One can similarly put as much water in a glass as was there before, even if it has <unclear>not</unclear> been measured, nor weighed, nor seen; for the ear will easily judge the same quantity by the same sound, or how much more or less there is than before by the difference in the sounds.

I leave aside several other things that can be discovered by means of the sounds of all types of vessels, which deserve our examination of this Proposition, in order to determine the proportion that the different empty spaces of a glass must have to produce such a difference of sounds as one wishes, and to derive from it a great multitude of uses according to each person's will.

Now, before determining what can be said on this subject, I wish to explain the experiments I have conducted, especially as they must serve as the foundation for this entire discourse.

I say then, first of all, that glasses never have a sharper <note>Higher in pitch.</note> sound than when they are empty, which seems likely to happen because their parts vibrate <note>original: "fremissent"</note> and move more quickly; and that their sounds become deeper <term>graue (lower in pitch)</term> in proportion as one fills them with water or other liquids, until, being filled, they descend to the octave of their sounds when empty. This shows that one should <unclear>not</unclear> believe too lightly what one reads in several authors—for example, what Aristotle says in the preceding Problem, namely that the barrel which is half full rises to the octave of the empty one which is equal to it; for since that does not happen with glasses, it seems it should <unclear>not</unclear> happen with barrels, of which I shall speak later.

Experience thus shows that water makes them lower in tone, but this lowering does not exactly follow the proportion of the parts of water put into the glasses; for I have experimented that by dividing the water, which must fill a glass three and a half inches in height and width, into six equal parts, the first part being put in the glass makes it descend only by an enharmonic or chromatic <term>diesis (a very small musical interval, often less than a semitone)</term>; that the second part makes it descend by a tone; the third by a minor third; the fourth by a tone; the fifth by a
