# Of percussion instruments.

<note>This page begins mid-sentence, continuing a list of musical intervals produced by adding liquid.</note> ...tone: and the sixth by a minor third; and when these six parts of water almost fill the glass, its sound is nearly an octave lower than the tone it produces when empty: and if it is full to the brim, the pitch descends by a major ninth.

But it must be noted that I used my finger, running it along the rim of the glass, to observe its tones; for when one strikes the bowl of the glass with a finger or some other object, the sound is not as distinct, and it is difficult to identify the tone because it is composed of a number of sounds that interfere with one another.

It should also be noted that when the rim of the glass is pressed <note>Meaning rubbed with a damp finger to create a "singing" glass effect.</note>, as I have said, it often produces two sounds at the same time—one being a major third, a fourth, or a twelfth from the other—and one must take the lowest as the natural tone. It also sometimes produces three sounds, the highest of which is an octave or a fifteenth from the lowest. Although this is not so well-regulated that one could establish a science of it, for it sometimes produces other sounds—for example, the fourth and the sixth—which are difficult to notice because they are too high-pitched and too inconsistent, and they do not hold steady enough.

The same occurs with sounds made by striking the body or the bowl of the glass, which almost always produces several different sounds depending on where it is struck. Now, one of the best signs one can use to recognize the sound that should be taken when pressing the rim is observed in the water, which ripples and creates small disturbances <note>original: "boüillons"</note> in the glass. This usually only happens after wetting the finger and cleaning the rim of the glass, for the water does not normally ripple so noticeably when the glass makes other sounds, even if one presses the finger much harder.

When the glass is empty or full, the deepest sound it makes with the finger on the rim is a twelfth, an eleventh, a sixth, a fifth, a fourth, or a third lower than the sound it makes while rippling—that is to say, the higher sound. This happens similarly when water is added.

A crystal glass eight inches high and three wide, when full of water, descends to the ninth of the sound it makes when empty. And if one divides the water that fills it into three equal parts, the first part only makes it descend by one tone, but the second makes it descend by a fifth, and the third part by a fourth.

From which it is easy to conclude that it is not possible to judge the quantity of liquid contained in glasses by the difference in their sounds, since they are not all uniform, and one can only say that they produce deeper sounds when they are fuller, without being able to determine the genus or species of their proportion.

When the water filling the same glass is divided into six equal parts, the first only makes it descend by a diesis <note>original: "Dieſe." In early music theory, a diesis is a very small interval, smaller than a semitone.</note>, the second by a minor third, and the third by a major third.

This being established, it suffices to conclude that no general rule can be made for the proportion of liquids and sounds, and each person must be content with individual experiments; although something general might be established for glasses of the same material and the same shape.

I have observed that water, wine, and oil produce the same effect in glasses, which are in unison <note>Produce the same pitch.</note> when an equal quantity of one of these liquids is placed in them:

<header>Book Seven</header>

...and that the crystal glass I used sometimes leaves its natural tone with certain quantities of water to take another a twelfth higher.

As for other vessels, such as bells and metal mortars, they do not maintain the same proportion as glasses, for mortars, when full of water, descend only by a [whole] tone, and bells only by a major third. It is easy to conduct experiments on all other types of objects; therefore, I only add that their sounds maintain a different proportion when they are immersed in water than when they are merely filled with water while in the air. For the bell that descends only by a major third when filled with water in the air, when it is so submerged in water that it remains empty <note>Meaning the bell is lowered into a pool of water but its interior remains filled with air.</note>, produces the major third; and when it is full of water <insert>and submerged</insert>, it produces the tritone—that is to say, being full of water and sunken in water, it descends one tone lower than when it is only full of air in the water. But all these experiments need to be refined with different bells, and I have often remarked that bells submerged in water descend by a major tenth, unless the senses are deceived by taking this repetition <note>In music theory, a "repetition" (replique) refers to an interval plus an octave; a tenth is a third plus an octave.</note> for a major third; which I wished to note so that no one thinks I am contradicting other experiments regarding this tenth, and so that the difficulty of these observations is considered, and consequently, that one may be grateful to those who provide us with exact ones.

Now, although it is easy to explain why glasses lower their pitch in proportion to how much they are filled with water—because it is certain that the glass, or the air struck by the glass, does not vibrate <note>The author uses "tremble," which in a modern acoustic context describes the frequency of vibration.</note> as quickly when it is full of water as when it is empty, and that this decrease in vibrations comes from the resistance it receives from the water touching the inner surface of its bowl—nevertheless, it is difficult to show the relationship of the empty and full glass to a short and long string, or thin and thick ones. For in what manner can one say that the string, shorter by half (which creates the octave above), is represented by the empty glass, and that the full glass represents the string of double length? And if it is said that the empty glass represents a <term>chorde: a vibrating musical string</term> whose length is the entire circumference of the rim, and whose thickness or diameter is the height of the glass, and that the same string length always remains while its thickness or diameter decreases because of the water put inside, it follows that the water should make the pitch rise, whereas it actually makes it descend. And if one says the opposite—namely, that the height of the water determines the thickness of the string—the glass ought to lower by more than two or three octaves, since the height of the glass being half a foot makes for a string whose diameter is half a foot; now, this diameter being reduced by half makes strings descend by an octave, and when it is only as one to four, eight, or sixteen, it makes them descend by two, three, or four octaves, as I have demonstrated elsewhere; this does not happen with the glass, which never descends more than an octave, or a ninth or thereabouts, even when it is completely full.

Kepler <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), the astronomer who also wrote extensively on the "Harmony of the World" and musical proportions.</note> maintains that the rim of the glass is like a string that becomes longer as the empty space in the glass diminishes, because a string that loses thickness seems to become longer; but I have shown that a string rises in pitch in proportion as its diameter decreases, and that it never descends lower because of this reduction.

# On percussion instruments.

But the immediate reason for this phenomenon is that an empty glass vibrates twice as fast as when it is full: so that the water inhibits half the freedom of its vibration; this does not happen to bells, whose vibration is only inhibited by a fourth part, when they descend only by a major third by means of the water that fills them.

As for Aristotle’s barrels <note>Aristotle discussed the sounds of empty and full vessels in his *Problems*, suggesting that pitch varies with the volume of air.</note>, upon which he based the octave on what happens with flutes, we must examine the truth of the matter: and for this purpose I include here what empty flutes do compared to those that are half-full of water.

When an organ pipe is plunged into water, as soon as it touches it, it descends to a seventh or an octave from the sound it makes before touching it, and raises its pitch in proportion to how much deeper it is submerged in the water; and when it is submerged to the midpoint, and consequently is half-full of water, it descends yet another tone lower than the empty pipe, with which it makes a unison when it is submerged about an eighth part above the midpoint: and consequently it is not true that the empty pipe descends to the octave of the same pipe when half-full.

Now, the pipe I used is five inches and five lines <note>A "line" (ligne) is an archaic measurement equal to 1/12th of an inch.</note> long, and seven lines in diameter; although it is not necessary to note this size, because the same thing happens to all others, as well as to flageolets and nine-holed flutes <note>original: "flustes à neuf trous"; this typically refers to a recorder.</note>; so that there is no wind instrument that supports Aristotle's reasoning, since all experiments prove the contrary of what he says: the reason for which is easy to give, since the wind pushed into a flute half-full of water has as much distance to travel as that which is pushed into an empty flute; from this it follows that they produce a unison.

But we must not dwell so much on the foundation he took that we fail to consider the experiment which may be true, even if he did not give the true reason for it; for it seems that the empty barrel should produce a thicker and lower sound than when it is half-full, and that the water should make it rise to the octave, since the air in the empty space is double that of the half-full space; this similarly occurs when one half-fills a flute that is closed at the foot <note>Referring to "stopped" pipes, where the end is blocked.</note>: for the water makes it rise to the octave, or very nearly so, insofar as it shortens its void by half: which does not happen to those that are open, which I mentioned and upon which I performed the previous experiments, because their void being shortened by half, like that of closed flutes, the wind still has as much distance to travel as in the empty flutes, as I have already said: so that Aristotle chose his reasoning well if he intended to speak of closed pipes.

Now it must be noted that there is a great difference between lower sounds and duller <note>original: "sourds", meaning muffled or less resonant.</note> sounds, for the dullest sounds can be much higher in pitch than the clearest ones; therefore it does not follow that the sound of one barrel is lower than that of another, even if it is duller and weaker. It must also be noted that it is difficult to give a certain judgment on the low or high pitch of sounds produced by barrels, because they are not well enough articulated, and they are not suited to the harmony <note>In this context, "harmony" refers to the musical system or scales used in the author's time.</note> we use: although part of this difficulty can be resolved by using several barrels of different sizes, whose sounds compared together allow one to discern the low and high pitch of each, as happens with instruments made of sticks <note>Likely referring to a percussion instrument like a xylophone or "sticcado-pastrole".</note>, and with the soundboards of lutes and viols when they are compared together.

He also distinguishes between the clarity of a sound and its actual musical pitch when evaluating resonant objects like barrels.</summary>

# Seventh Book

But it must be observed that the experiment with these **barrels** can be understood in two ways: for one can make them sound when they are open, or when they are closed, as happens with barrels that are full or half-full of wine. As for those that are open, it is difficult to determine their pitch, especially since they resonate very little—though some people put their head inside to make them resonate while speaking—because the air, being free, does not offer as much resistance as that which is enclosed, as is experienced with drums.

Regardless, if the barrels correspond to <term>organ pipes|The author is comparing the resonance of the air inside a barrel to the standing waves in an organ pipe</term>, the water that fills them halfway should make them rise to the **Octave**, because they are then similar to a pipe shortened by half. But if their tones are produced like those of glasses, they descend lower when full or half-full than when empty of water. It is simply necessary to verify the experiment, and one will know the number of <term>vibrations|The original text uses "tremblemens" (tremblings), an early term for frequency or acoustic oscillations</term> of the barrel whether full, half-full, or empty; the same must be concluded for all other bodies whose percussion creates a sound, and for which one knows the number of vibrations, or those of the air by means of the said sound.

### PROPOSITION XVIII.

#### *Explaining why one and the same Bell makes several different sounds at the same time.*

The same thing happens to large **Bells** as to the thick strings of instruments: namely, that they produce three or four sounds at the same time. For besides their own natural pitch, which is the strongest, they produce the **Octave**, the **Major Tenth**, and the **Twelfth**; so that if the first sound, which is natural to them, has a value of two, the second is four, the third is five, and the fourth is six <note>These numbers (2, 4, 5, 6) represent the harmonic series. In modern music theory, these are the fundamental, the first overtone (octave), the third overtone (major tenth), and the second overtone (twelfth).</note>.

But the **Major Tenth** is heard more commonly than the **Twelfth**, and these intervals are not so strictly regulated in all sorts of Bells that one does not occasionally hear the **Eleventh**—that is, the <term>repeated Fourth|A musical interval consisting of an octave plus a fourth</term>—instead of the Tenth in the sounds of some Bells. The reason for this is difficult to find, unless one says that the different parts of the Bell vibrate differently, and that the vibrations of those parts that move faster are to the vibrations of those that move more slowly as four, five, or six is to two. Or, perhaps these different tones come from the different parts or portions of the spheres that compose the Bell; for one of its parts is described by a <term>compass opening|The geometric setting used by bell-founders to design the curve or 'profile' of the bell</term> of thirty parts, and the other by an opening of twelve. Now, twelve is to thirty as two is to five: from which it follows that the Bell must produce the **Major Tenth** when it is made according to these openings, and when it does not, it follows other proportions.

As for the **Octave**, it could be related to the smallest opening of the compass, which has seven parts to describe the two portions of the Bell of which we have spoken; but it would need to be opened to only six parts to create the Octave with its opening of twelve parts, or be opened to fifteen parts to correspond to the opening of thirty parts.

Certainly, it is very difficult to give a reason for this phenomenon which is not subject to any rebuttal; for if one says that the natural tone of the Bell, which is the deepest of all, divides into two equal parts, and then that one of these parts divides again into two other halves to produce the three or four sounds of which I have spoken, it seems that one should not admit this reason,

## PROPOSITION XIX.

->*Explaining how the sound of Bells is made, and that of all other percussion instruments.*<-

This Proposition is quite universal, given that the majority of bodies produce no sound unless they are struck; now, when they are struck, they tremble, as one experiences by placing a hand on the rim of Bells that are ringing, and which shiver after having been struck by the clapper or the hand. I leave aside for now other bodies—for example stones, rocks, wood, etc.—the vibrations of which will be easy to explain once one has understood those of Bells and other similar bodies. This shivering of Bells is caused by the disturbance of their parts, which imprint a similar movement on the air by which they are surrounded, and on the <term>auditory spirits|In early modern science, "spirits" were thought to be subtle fluids that carried sensory information through the nerves to the brain</term>, which carry the impression of the sounds or vibrations to the <term>common sense|The "sensus communis," a theoretical faculty of the mind where all sensory inputs were integrated</term> and to the understanding.

But it is difficult to explain how the said shivering occurs without the Bells breaking; for if all their parts move when they tremble, some must yield to others. For example, those touching the exterior or interior surface must leave their place so that those neighboring them may follow, and so that they find spaces in which to move and tremble; and consequently, all the parts must change location as often as the Bell trembles while sounding.

To this end, the air-filled pores, which are believed to exist within bodies, can be useful; for each part of the Bell can move by filling the pore that touches it. But it is difficult to know what constrains it to return many times to its place, and to float back and forth for as long as the sound lasts. Furthermore, it would follow from this hypothesis that Bells would produce very different sounds if their materials were more or less porous than others. For example, one that had twice as many pores, or pores twice as large, would have a sound twice as strong or weak, and twice as low or high; for it takes twice as much time to move in a pore of four parts as in one that has only two parts, or in the space of four pores than in the space of two pores.

The same must be said of the movement of the air particles that fill the said pores, and which cannot tremble or shiver unless they change place, whether by <term>rarefying and condensing|The process of air becoming less or more dense, which characterizes the physical nature of sound waves</term>, or otherwise. But before entering further into this difficulty, it must be noted that the shivering is not...

not distinct from the trembling, and that the trembling is not different from the back-and-forth movements made by the strings of instruments, which I have spoken of elsewhere, even though they are not called tremblings unless they are very fast and frequent. For example, if a string moves as slowly as the <term>pulse|The original text uses "poux," an archaic spelling of "pouls" (pulse). 17th-century scientists often used the heartbeat as a standard unit of time</term>, and it only makes 4,000 cycles and returns in an hour—as happens with strings one hundred feet long—one does not say that it trembles. One would, however, say this of human limbs—for example, the head or the hand—if they moved as fast as the pulse and went here and there in a reciprocal movement, which is experienced by those afflicted with the trembling of the nerves and muscles.

From this it is easy to conclude that all movements of solid and hard bodies, which occur through back-and-forth cycles related to the <term>spring|The term "ressort" refers to the elastic property of a material that allows it to return to its original shape after being deformed</term>, are types of tremblings and shiverings, even though we only give this name to those that happen very quickly—for example, to those that occur twenty or thirty times in the space of a second, or while the pulse and the heart beat once, and generally speaking to all those that are so fast that they cannot be counted.

This is also noticed in the tremblings or changes of place made by the water in a pot that is beginning to heat up; for one does not ordinarily say that it shivers or trembles until it moves so quickly, and its parts <term>crackle|The French "petillent" suggests the tiny, rapid agitation or sparkling movement of the water's surface</term> so minutely, that one can no longer notice the number and the shape of their movements. This happens shortly before the water begins to boil, and I have reported this so that one may more easily conceive the manner in which Bells shiver while ringing.

We see the same thing again in glasses, the rims of which one rubs by sliding and pressing a finger upon them; for the water inside testifies by its tremblings and its leaping that the air surrounding it, and the parts of the glass touching it, are shivering and have similar movements. For no body moves unless it is moved from elsewhere, and it has no other kind of movement than that which preceded it in the other bodies on which it depends, when they are capable of it.

Those who believe that all bodies have a great multitude of small empty spaces, like <term>Hero|Hero of Alexandria (1st century AD), a mathematician and engineer who studied vacuums and air pressure</term> and the disciples of <term>Democritus|An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe is made of tiny, indivisible "atoms" and void</term>, and that all things are composed of atoms of different shapes, can easily explain the shivering of Bells. For when they are struck, their atoms are moved and leap by changing place and occupying the spaces of the small voids; then they return several times to their ordinary <term>alignment|The French "assiette" refers to the stable, resting position or configuration of the particles</term> and return to the said voids until they come to rest. But the main difficulty always remains: namely, why they return to their alignment. For it is not enough to say that it is natural to them, and that every thing has the power and the faculty to return to its own place when it is removed from it by violence—as we experience with heavy bodies that always tend downward and return to their center as soon as the violence ceases. To this, one responds that atoms are indifferent to all sorts of places, and that movement is as natural to them as rest is contrary to them.

Furthermore, one must find the cause that constrains them to return to their alignment; for since movement is natural to them, and they can just as easily move in one direction as another, they must be constrained by some agent

exterior [force] to return to where they started. Now, it seems one cannot encounter other agents than the air that repels them, or the little hooks and crochets of the other <term>atoms|In 17th-century physics, "atoms" referred to the smallest constituent particles of matter, often imagined as having specific geometric shapes and hooks to hold them together</term> of the Bell, which pull them back into their ordinary position, just as it happens that one link of a chain pulls another link, and as the fibers and filaments of an <term>intestine|Referring to gut strings made from animal intestines</term>, or a cord, pull the other fibers.

One can also imagine that since the whole world is filled with solid bodies or atoms, it happens that the parts of the Bell, being forced in their shimmering, are immediately repelled by the atoms of the air that surround the Bell, and which cannot yield to their trembling without all of nature suffering and enduring some sort of excessive pressure. But since nature is capable of being pressed during the shimmering, it is difficult to know why it does not last forever, and why all of nature does not grow accustomed to this pressure, as happens when <term>springs|French: "ressorts." This refers to the elastic property of the material</term> grow accustomed to remaining in the place where they were put by force, when they stay there for a long time. For example, if one keeps a bow bent, or leaves the string of a Lute stretched for a long time, they contract a "habit" that makes them remain in the same state where violence led them, even though that violence is no longer there and has ceased entirely.

Now, this "habit" is nothing other than the loosening of the fibers, hooks, or other bonds and attachments of the spring, or the breaking and loss of some body that made the spring work.

If the metal of the Bell were only composed of atoms that perfectly fill space—namely, equilateral triangles, squares, and hexagons, or an infinity of irregular figures that can do the same—they could not tremble or shimmer, and consequently they would make no sound. This is why it is necessary that they have other shapes—for example, circular, octahedron, rhomboid, elliptical, etc.—so that the little <term>voids|The author argues that for movement to occur within a solid, there must be tiny empty spaces between the particles</term> serve as space for the movement of the said atoms. The same must be said of tetrahedral atoms, and of cubes joined to octahedrons, and of an infinity of irregular bodies, since they fill solid spaces just as the equilateral triangle, the square, and the hexagon fill surfaces or planes.

One can also consider whether the parts that shimmer have a certain center of gravity common to the whole body they compose, which constrains them to return to their place, and several other things that can provide entry to this difficulty. In effect, the continuity of the parts can be compared to the force of the center, or to <term>magnetic virtue|The invisible force that pulls things together, similar to gravity or magnetism</term>, for it always pulls back all the said parts until it is broken.

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the parts of the Bell tremble as many times as the strings with which they are in <term>Unison|When two sounds have the same pitch and frequency</term>, and that the parts of bodies that have a higher pitch tremble faster than those of bodies that have a deeper pitch. From this, one can infer how much more or less quickly the parts of each metal tremble than others. But it is difficult to know why the parts of a large Bell tremble more slowly than those of a smaller one when the sound of the larger one is deeper or lower—considering that the parts of the larger one tremble faster when its sound is higher. This happens when the larger Bell is also thicker; for the thickness being greater, the pitch rises higher, as I have said elsewhere.

## PROPOSITION XX.

### *To determine from what distance the sound of Bells can be heard, and if it can be as loud as the noise of thunder.*

THIS Proposition is very difficult, because of the difficulty of the experiments that must be performed to know from what distance each Bell can be heard; it is held that the great Bell of Saint-Jean de Lyon, which weighs 28,000 pounds and has a clapper of 700 pounds, can be heard from three <term>leagues|A league was a common unit of distance, roughly equal to the distance a person could walk in an hour, approximately 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers</term>; and that the great Bell of Notre-Dame de Rouen, whose size and weight I gave in the third Proposition, can be heard from a place called La Bouille <note>La Bouille is a village situated on a bend of the Seine, roughly 15-20 kilometers downstream from Rouen</note>, which is to say, from five leagues away.

But the main difficulty consists in knowing by how much one Bell must be larger than another to be heard twice, thrice, or four times as far, and of what size it must be made to be heard from a given distance. If the distances followed the ratio of the sizes, it would be quite easy to know everything that could be said about the strength and the reach of sounds, for the Bell that has double, triple, or quadruple the diameter would be heard twice, thrice, or four times as far as the one that is its sub-double, sub-triple, or sub-quadruple; and the Bell that would be heard twice as far would be eightfold in size and weight compared to the one heard half as far, just as the <term>sphere of activity|In early modern physics, this refers to the three-dimensional space through which a force or sound extends its influence</term> of the air affected by the sound of the latter would be one-eighth of the volume of the air affected by the former.

But so many difficulties are encountered in the air that it is not possible to entirely satisfy this Proposition. In this matter, it must be noted that I mean for one to strike two or more Bells of different sizes proportionally—that is, the one that is twice as large must be struck twice as hard—when one wishes to know if it is heard twice as far; otherwise, it is certain that the smaller one can be struck so hard, and the larger one so weakly, that the former will be heard from much further than the latter. Furthermore, one must consider whether the bell with double the diameter should instead be struck four or eight times harder, by reason of its quadruple surface area or its eightfold <term>solidity|In this context, "solidity" refers to the volume or mass of the object</term>, rather than only twice as hard by reason of its diameter being double.

Experience, which is not too difficult, can serve to solve this doubt, for one often has Bells in the same tower, some of which are doubles or <term>sesquialteran|A sesquialteran ratio is 3:2, often used in music and geometry to describe proportions</term> of the others, so that one can move different distances away and mark the limit or the extent of the sphere of activity of the smaller and larger Bells. For example, if the one that is only two feet in diameter is heard from one league, and the one that is four feet from two leagues, and then the one that is eight feet from four leagues, there is no doubt that the distances will have the same ratio as their diameters, and that the solidity of the spheres of activity will have the same ratio as the size and weight of the Bells. For if the said Bells ring at the same time and the listeners are on the same side and on the same plain, one can say that the air is disposed equally enough for the truth of the experiment, especially since it is not necessary here to use mathematical precision, nor to consider the proportion of the <term>tangent lines of sound|A reference to the geometric way sound waves were imagined to radiate from a central point</term>.

Now, one of the greatest difficulties of the experiment consists in the proportion of the strikes, or the percussions, of two or several Bells; it is especially difficult to know if one strikes a large Bell as hard as a small one in proportion to its size, because it has not yet been determined what size the <term>clapper|The "battant" or clapper is the swinging part inside a bell that strikes the internal wall to produce sound</term> of a Bell should be to strike it exactly as required to make it ring perfectly. For even though one gives a pound and a half of clapper to a Bell of ten pounds, it does not follow that the clapper of a Bell of twenty pounds must weigh three pounds; and indeed the <term>Founders|Artisans who cast bells from molten metal</term> make it only two pounds, and that of a Bell double in diameter, six and a half pounds. <note>In bell casting, doubling the diameter usually results in a bell eight times heavier in volume, yet the clapper weight does not scale linearly to prevent the bell from cracking.</note>

It would therefore be necessary to know what weight the clapper of each Bell should be so that they were all struck proportionally, even though one might use the same hammer for this purpose by striking one of the Bells harder and the other more weakly. But it is hardly less difficult to know how to proportion the two blows, or the two strikes, so that one is double—or in whatever ratio one wishes—of the other, than to determine how much larger one of the hammers must be than the other to have two similar strikes. For even if one lets the hammer fall from one foot high, and then from two feet upon the same or different Bells, it does not follow that the blow is twice as strong; for since I have demonstrated elsewhere that the hammer which falls from two feet high goes faster at the second foot than at the first, and that it does so three times faster than the first, it seems one must conclude that the hammer falling from two feet high strikes three or four times harder than when it falls only from one foot.

...is led up to point L, it weighs its full weight, since point A does not support it at all, whereas it supports it entirely at point B; so one must conclude that it is all the more difficult to hold and stop it at each point of the quarter-circle B L, as it is less supported by point A.

This is why, when it is set in motion and moved by means of one or several ropes attached to wheels or other pieces of wood that hold the Bell attached by its <term>handles|original: "anses"; the loops at the top of a bell used for suspension</term>, one has all the more trouble moving it from B to O than from B to D, because the line A N is longer than A P. This can be understood by imagining that K L is a lever, or the beam of a <term>steelyard balance|original: "Romaine"; a weighing scale with unequal arms</term>, for if one applies force at point K, it will support the weight of the Bell much more easily at point L than at point N, because the ratio of K P to P A is greater than that of K N to N A.

I leave aside the consideration of different inclinations of the plane, of which I spoke in the second and third books of *Movements* and elsewhere, and whose reasons follow those of the lever when they are well understood, in order to speak of the <term>momentum|original: "impression"; the force or impulse imparted to the object</term> that gives the swing to the Bell: for since it weighs more the closer it approaches point L, following the different points from which one imagines it is supported along the line A L, one must conclude that it requires a greater momentum to move from O to L than in any other part of the quarter-circle; though it should be noted that the weight increases more from B to D than from D to O, and from D to O than from O to L, and consequently it is not necessary to add as much force or momentum to lead it from O to L as to lead it from D to O, as is easy to demonstrate by the reasons drawn from points P, N, and L.

For the momentum that makes it go as far as O diminishes the difficulty of making it rise to L, because one only needs to add as much new momentum as the line N L adds weight to the line A N. But when one begins to set the Bell in motion to move it to D, one has the entire weight A P to surmount; to which one adds the weight P N when moving it to O. From this, it is easy to conclude the different degrees of difficulty one experiences while ringing, particularly if one joins the consideration of momentum to that of weight.

As for the manner of hanging Bells to make them easy to ring, several methods are used, and particularly a thick piece of wood called the *<term>Headstock|original: "Mouton"; the heavy wooden yoke from which the bell hangs</term>*, into which the handles of the bell are fitted. I leave aside the machines suitable for hoisting bells to the top of Towers and Belfries, because they deserve special Treatises: it suffices to say that <term>blocks|original: "mouffles"; sets of pulleys</term> with several pulleys joined to a <term>windlass|original: "tour"</term>, or to a double or triple <term>worm gear|original: "viz sans fin"; literally "endless screw"</term>, are capable of easily lifting the largest bells that can be made. Regarding this, one may note the method I have been told was used in Germany, placing <term>petards|small explosive charges</term> under the branch of the lever that turned the axle of the windlass and its wheel: so that each petard caused the handle of the lever to rise to a certain height until the bell was raised; but it is necessary that the lever be of a material so strong that it cannot break. One could also use one or several screws similar to those of <term>presses|such as wine or paper presses</term>, the force of which depends on the inclination of the planes, of which one...

...one will possess the science, if one reads the *Treatise on Mechanics* that I have placed at the end of the third book of *Movements*, as noted in the sixth Corollary of the first Proposition.

### COROLLARY I.

One will find the demonstration of the different forces necessary to hold the proposed bell at points D and O, or at any other point of the quarter-circle <note>The "quarter-circle" refers to the 90-degree arc a bell travels from a vertical hanging position to a horizontal "set" position.</note> that one might wish, in the second Corollary of the first Proposition of the aforementioned *Treatise on Mechanics*. This treatise provides great insight into several things we have proposed in this work, even for creating a machine capable of pulling or lifting the greatest resistances, forces, or weights that one might need. As for the manner of hanging bells so that they are very easy to ring, that depends on the carpentry, which must be perfectly straight so that the bell is in <term>equilibrium|original: "equilibre"; a state of balance where the bell can swing with minimal effort</term>.

### COROLLARY II.

One can use different types of balances to weigh large Bells of thirty or forty thousand pounds—though one must not imagine that they can be so precise that a single <term>grain|a historical unit of weight, approximately 0.05 grams</term> would make them tip, as happens with the small scales used to weigh diamonds and to test gold carats. For the beam of the balance presses upon its <term>pivot|original: "appuy"</term> all the more as it is heavier and as the weights attached to its two ends are greater. 

Thus, if a single grain is needed to break the equilibrium of small <term>hand-scales|original: "trebuchets"; highly sensitive scales for small items</term> which are only capable of carrying one or two pounds, several grains will be required to break it for balances that support three or four thousand pounds. However, it is unlikely that one must multiply said grains in the same proportion as one increases the size of the scales or weighs heavier loads; otherwise, it would take 3,000 grains (that is to say, more than five pounds) to tip a balance carrying three thousand pounds. But one must consult experience on this subject; and meanwhile, see the *Treatise on the Balance* written by <note>Johannes Buteo (c. 1492–1572), also known as Jean Borrel, a French mathematician who wrote extensively on geometry and mechanical instruments.</note> Buteo, in which he shows the way to construct <term>steelyard balances|original: "Romaines"; a scale where a single weight is moved along a graduated arm</term>, to weigh great burdens, and to make <term>nested weights|original: "Piles"; a set of weights designed to fit inside one another, often called Nuremberg piles</term> which contain all sorts of weights—for example, the pound, the half-pound, the ounce, the half-ounce, etc.—which follow a doubling ratio. 

Regarding this, it must be noted that those who sell balances do not adjust them well, and those who desire to be exact in their observations must have the patience to adjust them such that 576 grains weigh exactly one ounce, and that each grain counterbalances the other. Now, although there is usually less error in experiments performed on a large scale when one applies every kind of diligence, nevertheless, others performed on a small scale can often be more exact, by reason of the great care applied to them, the high precision of the small hand-scales made for the purpose, and the ease of the operation.

### PROPOSITION XXIII.

->*To explain the natural and miraculous properties of Bells.*<-

It is certain that Bells possess no natural properties other than those arising from the various movements they impress upon the air, the stirrings of which allow us to perceive everything intended to be signified by the sound of the Bells. Now, it is held that this sound can be so violent and powerful that it will cause wine to surge in cellars and cause children to perish in their mothers' wombs—claims similarly made regarding thunder. To this, it is added that sounds dissipate clouds and thunder; hence why Bells are rung when it thunders. For although many maintain that this effect depends upon the blessing of the Bells <note>The "blessing" or "baptism" of a bell is a formal consecration ceremony in the Catholic Church intended to set the instrument apart for sacred use.</note>, which is used to dedicate them to the service of Churches and to release them from profane use—and consequently that the effect is supernatural—nevertheless, others believe it is natural, by reason of the shaking of the air, which drives away the lightning bolt by sending it elsewhere or by dissipating it. For since sound consists of the beating of the air, one can attribute as many effects to it as to the movement of the air.

Juan Quiñones, a Spaniard, wrote a discourse on the Bell of Velilla in Zaragoza <note>The "Campana de Velilla" is a famous legendary bell in Spain said to ring by itself as an omen of disaster.</note>, which often rings all by itself without anyone being able to prevent it. He cites several authors to confirm what he says of it, namely Vairus in the second book of *Charms*, chapter 14; Torreblanca, and several others, such as Zurita in the 14th book, chapter 27, of his *Annals*; Guadalajara in the first part of the *Expulsion of the Moriscos*; Martín Carrillo in the fifth book of his *Annals*; Lanuza in the third book of the *History of Aragon*, etc.

He says that this Bell has two Crucifixes raised in relief <note>original: "releuez en bosse"; a sculptural technique where the figures stand out from the surface.</note>, one of which is to the East and the other to the West, and that it rings all by itself when the Ecclesiastical or Political State is threatened by some notable accident. This occurs in such a way that its clapper strikes the side from which the evil is to come—that is, from the East, the South, the West, or the North. The Church is named Saint Nicholas because he is its Patron. As for the times it has rung, he notes the years 1435; 1485; 1527; 1558, when Charles V <note>Holy Roman Emperor (1500–1558).</note> died; 1568; 1578, at the death of Sebastian, King of Portugal, in the Battle of Alcázar; and finally the year 1601, from the thirteenth until the thirtieth of June. Roccha speaks of several other Bells that often ring all by themselves when someone is about to die, or when something extraordinary happens, in the 7th chapter of his treatise on Bells. In this work, he explains the hours at which it is customary to ring the bells and the reasons for which they are rung, as can be seen from the fourteenth to the twenty-fifth chapters of his Commentary. In these, he shows that Bells have succeeded the Trumpets of the Jews <note>A reference to the *shofar* or silver trumpets described in the Old Testament used to gather the congregation.</note>, for they are used to alert the people of the hours when they must pray to God, whether in private—as happens three times a day when the *Ave Maria* <note>original: "Aue Maria"; also known as the Angelus, a prayer recited in the morning, at noon, and in the evening.</note> is rung in the morning, at noon, and in the evening—so as to remember that the Son of God was upon the Cross toward the evening, that He rose in the morning, and that He ascended to Heaven toward noon, as Saint Augustine and Saint Jerome note in the explanation of the 54th Psalm; or because the Angel saluted the Virgin in the morning, as Saint Athanasius says in the discourse...

Now, it would be in equally poor taste to investigate whether bells can ring on their own, and whether what is reported about the bell of Velilla <note>The "Campana de Velilla" was a famous Spanish bell rumored to ring spontaneously as an omen.</note> could proceed from the influence of the Stars, under the pretext that there is a correspondence and sympathy between superior and inferior bodies. There is no need to read what is written by de la Torre, de Moura, and several other Theologians and Philosophers against these reveries and these dreams of the Arabs and the Chaldeans <note>The author is dismissing astrological and occult explanations common in Middle Eastern and ancient traditions.</note>.

Nevertheless, one may see what Doctor Quiñones says against this opinion, and his investigation into the reasons people have imagined to explain the ringing of this Bell. For example, some claim it occurs because of one of the coins for which Judas sold our Lord, which was thrown into the metal of the Bell when it was cast; or because the verse of the Cumaean Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were ancient prophetesses; the Cumaean Sibyl was one of the most famous in the Roman world.</note>, *Christ the King comes in peace, and God was made man* <note>original: "Christus Rex venit in pace, & Deus homo factus est"</note>, is written around the Crosses engraved on said bell, so that it might predict future events like the Sibyl. I leave aside several other things said about the Bell in certain Benedictine Monasteries, which is accustomed to ring all by itself when one of them is about to die, because I have no certain account of it—along with many other things that could be added to this treatise on Bells—in order to finish the discourse on other instruments of Percussion.

...usually they are tied to the thumb of the right or left hand, and joined in such a way that their concave sides are placed one over the other like two small plates: although they must be left a little open toward their edges **CDEF**, so that they can be made to strike against each other with the middle finger, or with the ring finger, which is most commonly used.

They can be made of plum wood, beech, and all other sorts of resonant wood, like the <term>Regals</term> <note>original: "Regales"; here referring to a "regale de bois" or wooden xylophone, rather than the reed organ of the same name</note> of which I spoke in the 26th Proposition of the third book, and they harmonize with all kinds of instruments, though they are most often joined with the **Guitar**: for even though they produce several dissonances, these are not noticed because of the great difference between the quality of their sound and that of stringed instruments. The elegance of the **Castanets** depends on the hand of the player, and particularly on the movement, the cadences, the passages, and the <term>diminutions</term> <note>The division of long notes into many fast, short notes; a form of melodic ornamentation.</note> or shakes, which are performed so quickly that it is impossible to count the beats, unless one uses a precaution, which consists in observing the measure and the cadence. This leads us to judge that the most skilled players beat the Castanets eight or nine times within the span of a single measure, or a single pulse-beat, which lasts one second; so that one performs almost as many diminutions on this instrument as on the **Spinet**, and on others whose speed surpasses the imagination.

All the bone clappers and small sticks of wood, or other material, that are held between the fingers or otherwise, and which are handled so dexterously and so fast, and with such well-regulated cadences that it is almost impossible to explain them, can be compared to the Castanets and the Regals: but they cannot be so expressed by figures <note>illustrations</note> that one might understand the skill and the movements involved; this is why I come now to the **Cymbals**, for as for the songs or the movements of the Castanets, they will be understood through the discourse I shall make regarding the beats of the **Drum**.

If the **Rabbis** had given us the figure of the Cymbals of which so much is spoken in Holy Scripture, I would compare it with the one now in use among us, in order to determine if they were more suited to providing the pleasure and jubilation mentioned in the last Psalm <note>Psalm 150:5, "Praise him upon the loud cymbals: praise him upon the high sounding cymbals."</note> than our own, of which **A B C** represents the form, which makes an equilateral triangle. this shell **A I**, or **E K** is almost equal to its width **L K**, or **A C**, which shows at once the width of the skin <note>the drumhead</note>, with which the shell is covered, and which is tightened over it by means of the hoops <note>original: "cercles"</note> **A C** and **I K**, to which are attached **K G**, **L G**, and **I G**, which serve to tighten or loosen and unbind the skin; for when one raises the knots <note>these are the leather sliders or "buffs" used to adjust tension on a rope-tension drum</note> marked by the letter **G** up to the hoop **A D C**, one loosens the skin **A B C D**; and when one lowers them to the hole **H**, one tightens it. It is for this reason that each knot embraces two cords, and that they are made to slide in order to raise or lower the tone <note>pitch</note> of the Drums. They are usually made of sheepskin, like the parchments **A B E D** and **A B C D**, or of the same material as the cords **K G**, which can be made of hemp...

# Seventh Book

...copper, or liver-colored leather; the Makers call them *tugs* <note>original: "tirans"; these are the sliding leather buffs used to tighten the tension ropes</note>. But it must be noted that everyone who believes that Drum drumheads <note>original: "parchemins"</note> are made of donkey skins is gravely mistaken, for they are made only of sheepskin, though they are chosen a bit stronger and thicker for large Drums so that they last longer.

I have here depicted the Drum in two ways, so that one may see the parchment, or the skin **A B C D**, upon which one strikes, or which one beats with the sticks **A C B**, and the one underneath which is supported by the cord **A B**, which crosses through the diameter, and which is called the *snare* <term>timbre: a cord stretched across the bottom head of a drum to create a rattling sound</term> of the Drum. This snare is made of two cords, or a single cord doubled; and when it has crossed the skin, it is passed through a hole so as to be secured with a peg which appears near the letter **E**, and which tapers like a spigot <note>original: "faucet", referring to a conical wooden tap</note>, so that the snare is tightened as the said peg is pushed. This also raises or lowers the pitch of the Drum, depending on whether one pulls or pushes it. Now it should be noted that the shell <note>original: "quaiffe", modern: "caisse"</note> of the Drum is sometimes made square, and that it can be made triangular, and in all sorts of other shapes.

The hoops that hold the skin on the shell, namely **A B C** and **L I K**, are called *counter-hoops* <note>original: "vergettes"</note>, which can be made of wood or whatever metal one wishes; it does not matter, provided they grip and tighten the edges of the skins as they should.

As for the thickness and size of the sticks, they must be proportional to the size of the Drum, like the clappers of Bells; for if they are too large or too small, the skins do not produce a good sound.

### PROPOSITION XXVII.

*To explain what size Drums must be, and what proportion they must maintain to produce whatever musical chord one desires.*

**I** have seen no Drums that produced musical chords except those that I had made specifically, which show that their heights and widths must maintain the same ratio as bells do to produce the same intervals: for example, if one wants four Drums to produce these four notes,

<image-desc>A fragment of a musical staff showing four notes in an ascending pattern: G, A, B, C (Ut, Re, Mi, Fa in the context of the description).</image-desc>

their heights must maintain the ratio of these numbers 4, 5, 6, 8; that is to say, if the Drum that makes the *ut* <note>The note C</note> is thirty inches high, the one that makes the second note must be twenty-four inches, or two Royal feet <term>pied de Roy: the "King's foot," a pre-revolutionary French unit of length equal to approximately 32.5 cm</term>, the 3rd which makes the 3rd note must be twenty inches, and the 4th which rises to the Octave must be fifteen inches in height. It is easy to follow the same method to make the other degrees, as one sees in the System that follows, and which serves as a *Diapason* <term>diapason: here meaning a fundamental scale or standard of measurement</term> for all kinds of Drums: and for this subject I suppose that the largest Drum is two feet wide, for they are not made larger than that: Secondly, that the last, or the eighth, is only one foot in width and height, and that it rises to the Octave of the first, as experience teaches.

Now, this being established, I say that the numbers which follow mark exactly the width and the height of the eight Drums that make the degrees of the Octave.

| I | II | III |
|---|---|---|
| 8 FA | 1 | 90 |
| 7 MI | 1 1/15 | 96 |
| 6 RE | 1 1/5 | 108 |
| 5 SOL | 1 1/4 | 120 |
| 4 FA | 1 1/2 | 135 |
| 3 MI | 1 3/5 | 144 |
| 2 RE | 1 4/5 | 162 |
| 1 UT | 2 | 180 |

But it must be noted that the first column contains the deduction, or the order of the voices <note>The solfège syllables</note>; the second contains the measurements reduced into parts of feet; and the third contains the harmonic numbers, which one can apply to whatever measurement one wishes. This serves those who do not wish to use fractions, or broken numbers, which make one observe that there is an infinite distance between one and two, as between God and His creatures, since there is an infinity of numbers in between, just as there is an infinity of possible creatures between God and nothingness.

It must also be noted that the largest skins that can be found to put on the shells <note>original: "quaisses", referring to the drum body or frame</note> are only two and a half feet wide, and consequently that one is forced to restrict oneself to this size when one wishes to perform several musical parts with Drums, which...

# On percussion instruments.

[one] may easily tune them by means of slip knots, which make the pitch rise or fall, as I have stated. However, one must have a good ear, and use industry and judgment to notice their tones, and by how much some are deeper <note>original: "graues"</note> or higher <note>original: "aigus"</note> than others: for it would be difficult to determine the pitch of a single Drum; this is why it is necessary to have three, four, or five of different sizes, so that they may serve one another, and that by the relationship or connection they have together, one may judge the high and low pitches of them all.

Now it is appropriate to warn the Reader of the Fable of the wolf skin, which many believe has the power to deafen the skin of a sheep or ewe when they are beaten upon a drum <note>original: "quaisse," referring to the drum body or shell</note> at the same time; for one never makes Drum-skins from wolf skin, which is entirely unsuitable and useless for this purpose, as the Makers <term>Facteurs: instrument makers</term> and the most expert witnesses maintain, who hold that it is not possible to prepare this kind of skin as it should be for Drums: so that one may be certain that those Authors who take this fable for a true history care little for the truth, which we have no reason to receive from them before having examined it.

## PROPOSITION XXVIII.

### *To explain the Tablature of Drums, and their different beats.*

It is certain that one can perform as many kinds of movements on the Drum as on other instruments, and that one can as easily beat it 16, 24, or 32 times within the space of one musical measure, just as one sings a similar number of notes: from which it is easy to conclude that one can make whatever movement one desires while beating the Drum, as is experienced in the various beats <note>original: "batteries," meaning rhythmic patterns or "rudiments"</note> of all those who play it in peace or in war, of which some use the spondee, others the iamb, the anapest, and the fourth species of Paeons, etc. <note>These terms refer to classical poetic meters used here to describe rhythmic patterns: a spondee is two long beats, an iamb is a short followed by a long, etc.</note> so that one may use the consideration of different movements to see if they show the genius, the inclination, and the temperament of different nations.

But because not everyone understands Rhythmics or Metrics, it is necessary to use a tablature that can be understood very easily, and to describe all the movements, or all the beats, that can be used on Drums. Those who compose songs for fifes are accustomed to using musical notes to signify the beats of the Drum that accompanies them, as Thoinet Arbeau did in his *Orchesography* <note>Thoinet Arbeau (1519–1595) wrote *Orchésographie*, a famous manual on dance and drum rhythms</note>, where he uses three kinds of notes for this subject: namely minims <note>original: "blanches à queue," literally white notes with stems</note>, which usually serve for binary half-measures; crotchets <note>original: "noires," literally black notes</note>; and quavers <note>original: "crochuës," literally hooked notes</note>. Now, he uses the syllable *Tan* under the minim; and under the two crotchets, which have the same value as the minim, he places the word *tere*: but he uses the syllable *fre* under the four quavers, which are worth as much as the two crotchets, because the beating that follows the speed of the quavers cannot be explained with the voice unless it holds steady while pronouncing *fre*, or *re*, which only makes the consonant R heard.

One may use such other syllables as one wishes to express the sounds of the Drum, for example *ton, ton*, or *plan plan*, instead of *tan*; of

# Seventh Book

...*trelan* instead of *tere*, and *tirelirelirelirelan* instead of *fre*, for one can make the sounds of Drums and Bells say whatever one wishes. It is easy to mark all kinds of beats <note>original: "batteries"</note> using ordinary musical notes—for example, the **French March**, the **Diane** <note>the morning reveille</note>, the **Chamade** <note>a signal for parley or surrender</note>, the **Assembly**, etc.—and similarly all the beats of other nations. This can also be done without musical notes, by using the characters used to mark long and short syllables; for the character of the long syllable - will signify the preceding *tan* or *tou*, and this sign for the short ◡ will serve for the *tere* or the *trelan*. And if one wishes to mark eighth notes <note>original: "crochuës"</note>, one could use the sign of the acute accent ', or any other sign one wishes. For example, the march of the Swiss can be expressed in this manner, and in a thousand other similar ways: ◡ ◡ --, ◡ ◡ --, etc., since they use the foot called the *Minor Ionic*, which they call *Colintampon* <note>an onomatopoeic Swiss-German term for their specific drum rhythm</note>.

Those who are curious to know the English, Dutch, Spanish, and German beats, etc., can mark them with these same characters, and many other new ones that can be invented according to the different changes that different timings can undergo when mixed with one another. For example, the timing of this Ionic foot can be changed in five ways, as seen here: -- ◡ ◡, - ◡ - ◡, ◡ - ◡ -, -- ◡ ◡, ◡ ◡ --. But it is enough to have shown the great number of movements that come from the mixture of notes of different value, of which I spoke in the *Book of Songs*, without it being necessary to repeat it here.

Now, before leaving this Proposition, it must first be noted that some beat the Drum so quickly that the mind or the imagination cannot comprehend the multitude of blows that fall upon the skin like a very violent hail. Among these, the Drummers who beat the drum <term>quaisse: the body or shell of the drum</term> to perfection sometimes strike with so much violence that its noise imitates that of muskets or cannons, and one marvels how a simple parchment can endure such great blows without bursting. Secondly, these great blows, which far exceed the strength of the others, serve to mark and distinguish the measures, and to finish the cadences. One also sometimes strikes the skin near the edges, but most often in the middle, which distinguishes the sounds slightly by making them clearer or fuller.

And when one beats the skin with violence, if one places a hand on the bottom skin, one feels as many blows as the number of times struck, and one cannot keep the hand there; this shows the agitation and movement of the air, which follows the movement of the sticks <note>original: "bastons"</note>.

But besides this movement, there must be another which forms the tone <note>pitch</note> of the Drum by the frequency of its vibrations <note>original: "tours & retours"</note>, as I have said of the tone or sound of other instruments; so that one can know the said number when one knows the depth or height of the tone, which is always equal in terms of its pitch <note>original: "qualité d'aigu"</note>, whether one beats the skin gently or with violence, provided it always has the same tension; unless one says that the air is more tense when one strikes harder, because it is more compressed, although the string <note>referring to the snare or the metaphorical "string" of air</note> does not sensibly produce a higher tone when it is more strained by striking it harder than by touching it feebly.

<header>On percussion instruments.</header>

### COROLLARY I.

Since we experience that the drum, thunder, and the trumpet have a greater effect on the spirit or the senses than the sound of other instruments, it is easy to conclude that the great effects of Music, or of other sounds, can only occur by means of great movements made by a large volume of air, or that violence must compensate for the lack of air when there is only a small amount of air producing the noise.

I leave aside several uses that can be drawn from drums; for example, that soldiers can use them to measure the height of towers and walls, the width of moats, etc.; or to know, by the movement of <term>dice placed upon them</term><note>A common 17th-century military tactic: placing dice on a drumhead; if the dice vibrated or moved, it signaled that enemy "miners" were digging tunnels or "mines" nearby.</note>, if mines are being dug, and the noises made two or three leagues around, more or less. One can also relate to this sort of instrument everything that makes similar noises, such as those of the musket, the cannon, and those made by the doors of Churches and other places, whose echoing imitates the sound of <term>arquebuses</term><note>An early type of long-gun or portable firearm.</note> so closely that it is almost impossible to discern them.

### COROLLARY II.

If I had had musical type at my disposal, I would have included here all the <term>beats of the French drum</term><note>original: "bateries du tambour François"</note>, namely the **entrance** (both simple and double), the **march**, the **assembly**, the **double march**, the **ban**, the **reveille** <note>original: "diane"</note>, the **parley** <note>original: "chamade"</note>, the **alarm**, and would have explained what the **round stick**, **broken stick**, and **mixed stick** are. I will only say that the beating of the **round stick** occurs when the two sticks strike each stroke one after the other; that of the **broken stick** occurs when each hand strikes two strokes in succession; and the beating of the **mixed stick** occurs when one beats sometimes once with each hand, and sometimes twice. As for the **retreat**, the two sticks strike both together. If anyone desires to see all these beats expressed in musical notes, I shall show them to him.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

->*To explain the construction of composite Instruments.*<-

After having explained the simple harmonic instruments, it is necessary to say something about the **composite** ones, which would deserve a book of their own if it were not easy enough to imagine their manufacture by comparing all those of which we have spoken. Now, they can first be composed of those with <term>gut and brass strings</term><note>Lutes typically used gut strings, while instruments like the spinet or harpsichord often used metal; combining them would create a unique timbre.</note>, as would happen if one strung a **Lute** with these two kinds of strings.

In the second place, one can place **Spinet** strings under the soundboard of the **Lute**, which will be played with keys similar to those of the Spinet, located between the ordinary frets of the Lute, so that the same fingers can touch both when desired.

In the third place, the same keys of the Spinet, placed on the neck of the Lute, can play an **Organ** composed of three sorts of stops, of which the...

The pipes will be made of feathers, or of wood, so that the <term>Lute</term><note>A plucked string instrument with a rounded body, popular throughout the Renaissance and Baroque.</note> will contain everything that one can imagine as excellent in harmony; particularly if one also adds a set of <term>chimes</term><note>original: "timbres"; referring to a set of small bells or metal plates.</note>, which the same keys, or others, could cause to sound; and if one desires pipes that pronounce the five vowels, and several others, and even the consonants—and consequently syllables and words—besides what we have already spoken of in the *Treatise on the Organ*, we will perhaps give the entire practice of it in another place.

One can apply to the <term>Viol</term><note>The Viola da Gamba family of bowed instruments.</note> and other simple instruments everything I have said of the Lute. I add only that it is now so easy to adapt the sets of Viols to the <term>Spinet</term><note>A smaller, often wing-shaped keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</note>, by means of an <term>endless bow</term><note>A mechanical device, often a continuous loop of material, used to bow strings automatically via a keyboard.</note>, made of vellum or other material, and to make them represent the stops of the Organs, that there is no need to explain their construction.

Upon which I wish to advise the <term>instrument makers</term><note>original: "facteurs"</note> that it is not appropriate for them to waste time making wheels similar to those of <term>Hurdy-gurdies</term><note>original: "Vielles"; an instrument that produces sound by a crank-turned wheel rubbing against strings.</note> to put the viol-set into the Spinet, since the endless bow is easier and succeeds much better.

I leave aside the <term>beats</term>, the <term>trills</term>, and the <term>hammerings</term><note>original: "batemens, les tremblemens, & les martelemens"; these refer to various 17th-century musical ornaments and articulations.</note>, and the other graces of which I spoke in the *Treatise on the Lute*, which one can adapt to the said viol-set, and a thousand other things that one can add to these Treatises; for example, that there is a way to set the Lute to such a tone and tuning that it will have as much or more range than the Spinet, even though it has only ten courses of strings; that one can string it in such a way that it will not be necessary to use the left hand, and which will be played entirely on open strings like the Harp; and that one can finally—contrary to what I had formerly imagined—make instruments that supplement church singing, and which pronounce all sorts of words, although the difficulty is too great, by reason of the great expense and time that would be necessary to make these <term>talking machines</term>.

### PROPOSITION XXX.

*To explain the contents of the excellent Treatise on the Genres and the Modes, written by Monsieur Doni, Secretary of the Sacred Consistory.*

Since I do not wish to omit anything that can serve Music, it is reasonable that I show the excellence of the book that Master <term>Jean Baptiste Doni</term><note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), an Italian music theorist known for his studies of ancient Greek music.</note> has recently given us in Italian, in which he makes us hope for great things for the restoration of all that belongs to the ancient Music of the Greeks. Now I remark here only what pertains most to my subject, so that everyone may go read the rest at its source, and that he may be prayed to favor the public with everything he has prepared in favor of harmony; for example, his <term>Amphichord</term>, which he wished to name the **Barberini Lyre**, by reason that he dedicates the Treatise to the great Cardinal Barberini, most worthy nephew of His Holiness, and to whom every science, and particularly harmony, will be as long indebted as lasts the excellent account he had made and printed in Rome of the heroic actions of **St. Alexis**, whose life is expressed by excellent voices.

He promises us still a book on Scenic or Recitative Music, the manner of singing Latin verses, the true pronunciation of that language, and several other Treatises whose names are seen in the 15th chapter of his book.

<page-num>59</page-num>
<header># Of percussion instruments.</header>

Now, he <note>Referring to Giovanni Battista Doni, a contemporary music theorist.</note> remarks in the 10th chapter that <term>Hesychastic music</term><note>original: "Muſique Heſychaſtique"; from the Greek for "stillness," referring to music that is calm, grave, and moderate.</note>, which is grave and moderate, is suited to the <term>Dorian Mode</term><note>In this period, the Dorian mode was often associated with dignity and solemnity.</note>; the <term>Diastaltic</term><note>original: "Diaſtaltique"; music that is stirring, majestic, or energetic.</note> for the <term>Phrygian Mode</term>, because it is more lively and vigorous; and the <term>Systaltic</term><note>original: "Syſtaltique"; music that is mournful, humble, or contracting.</note>, filled with sadness, for the <term>Lydian Mode</term>. Upon this, it must be noted that he calls the fifth of our ordinary modes the Dorian Mode (which I call the Lydian on page 182 of the third book of *Genres*), as can be seen in his 7th chapter, where he places the said mode in <term>E-mi-la</term><note>The note E.</note>, just as the Phrygian is in <term>D-re-sol</term><note>The note D.</note>. One may see his reasons there, for I wish to add nothing to what I have said in the 17th Proposition, where I believe I have demonstrated clearly enough the opinion of <term>Ptolemy</term><note>Claudius Ptolemy, the ancient Greek astronomer and music theorist whose work was being rediscovered.</note> regarding the Modes.

He adds that the <term>Organ</term> can serve to express each mode because of the great number of its stops, of which the one made of tin is suited to the Dorian; and that the others—composed of pipes wider or narrower at the top than at the bottom, closed or open—are also specialized. For example, the narrowest are suited to the Phrygian, and the widest to the Lydian. Furthermore, he says that pipes which imitate <term>recorders</term><note>original: "fleutes douces"</note> are good for expressing the Dorian; those that imitate the <term>fife</term> and the <term>flageolet</term><note>A small high-pitched flute.</note> for the Phrygian; and the <term>cornett</term> and the pipes that make the sound of the <term>German flute</term><note>The transverse flute, as opposed to the recorder.</note> for the Lydian. Boxwood is suitable for making the Dorian pipes; <term>regals</term><note>A small, portable reed organ with a buzzy sound.</note> are good for the Lydian, and brass pipes for the Phrygian. And if one uses a <term>Harpsichord</term><note>original: "Clauecin"</note> to express each mode, besides the fact that the strings can be longer or shorter, and more or less tensioned, and struck closer to or further from the bridges, they can also be of different materials—such as gold, silver, brass, steel, and gut—so that those with the sound of the <term>Harp</term> serve the Dorian, those with the sound of the <term>Cittern</term><note>A wire-strung instrument with a bright, twangy tone.</note> the Phrygian, and those of the ordinary <term>Spinet</term> or the <term>Lute</term> the Lydian, etc. But I have treated all the different stops of the Organ and all types of strings so amply in the preceding books on instruments that it seems not much more can be added. That is why I come to what he says of his "Harmonic Division" <note>original: "diuiſion Harmonique"</note> suitable for the restoration of the Tones and Modes of the ancients in the sixth, ninth, eleventh, and twelfth chapters, and of the tuning of the "Perfect Organ" in the thirteenth. I say first that the division I explained in the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh Propositions of the third book of *Genres* encompasses his own and serves to understand it perfectly, just as the keyboards in the twenty-second and twenty-third Propositions of the *Book of Organs* contain and demonstrate what he describes in the eleventh chapter—where he desires that the rows of keys be distinguished by woods of different colors to avoid confusion; for example, that some be white, others black, red, yellow, etc.

I say in the second place, that his entire book deserves to be read in its entirety, both to know wherein lies the difference between the tones and modes of the Greeks and what is lacking in modern music, and to learn the meaning of several Greek terms belonging to this Art, as seen in his discourse <note>original: "diſcours de la perfection de la Melodie"</note> *On the Perfection of Melody*. Now, I wish to finish this book with the praises of men who have been illustrious in Music, among whom the Author of this excellent *Treatise on Tones and Modes* <note>original: "Traité des Tons & des Modes"; likely referring to Doni's *Compendio del trattato de' generi e de' modi della musica*.</note> holds one of the primary ranks—which I would have him hold if his great modesty did not prevent me, and if his praise did not deserve a better pen than mine.

He concludes by praising Doni's scholarship and the importance of understanding Greek musical terminology.</summary>

## NOTICE.

Although the scope of Music is extremely far removed from that of Geometry and the other most sublime sciences, it is nonetheless capable of several quite subtle inventions, as is easy to conclude from all the considerations I have touched upon in the preceding books. Now, if one compares the sound of strings to that of pipes and flutes, and if one encounters a stringed instrument that so disguises its sounds that it is almost impossible to distinguish them from those of wind instruments, one will perhaps have one of the most remarkable effects of nature and of Art. This occurs with the Harpsichord, which can so effectively play a <term>Concert of Viols</term><note>A "consort" or ensemble of stringed instruments from the viola da gamba family, known for their resonant, vocal quality.</note> that one cannot distinguish it from an Organ performance, even though different ways of playing it allow it to imitate both Viols and the Organ.

Many have worked on the invention of this instrument, in Germany and Italy as well as in France, and I have seen some in foreign countries with wheels upon which the strings sounded <note>This refers to instruments like the hurdy-gurdy or the "geigenwerk," where a rotating wheel acts as a continuous bow.</note>. But as for the bow, which many have imagined without being able to put it into practice due to the great difficulties encountered, I have not known anyone to have used it—at least in France—until now, when Pierre Hubaut invented a way to use it so easily that it is perhaps impossible to make it simpler. This is due both to the simple motion that moves the bow endlessly and to the flexibility it leaves in the instrument, whether for lengthening or shortening notes, and for other very significant circumstances, such as adding as much sweetness, <term>vibrato</term><note>original: "tremblemens"</note>, <term>trills</term><note>original: "martelemens"</note>, sustained notes, <term>appoggiaturas</term><note>original: "appuis"; melodic "leanings" or ornaments where a note is delayed.</note>, and other ornaments and enrichments as one could wish. He has similarly invented pipes that pronounce the five vowels, and is capable of adding the pronunciation of consonants and syllables. Now, if syllables are added, they will be able to pronounce anything one desires without the need to touch them, since one or more barrels <note>Mechanical cylinders used in early automated instruments like music boxes.</note> can take the place of a human hand.

But because these two instruments are difficult to carry, it is easy to place the three <term>Genres</term><note>The three types of Greek scales: Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic.</note> of Music upon the neck of the Lute; for the <term>Enharmonic</term> steps will have their frets just as well as the <term>Chromatic</term> ones, since <term>geometric means</term><note>original: "moyennes proportionnelles"; a mathematical method used to calculate the exact placement of frets for tuning.</note> provide everything necessary for this subject. On this point, it must be noted that the Enharmonic frets can be played by means of the left-hand thumb by pushing small springs, as I will show to those who wish to use them. And if some desire to know the manner of playing an entire Concert of Viols in four, five, and six parts upon the <term>Spinet</term><note>A smaller, rectangular or wing-shaped member of the harpsichord family.</note>, I will give them the model for it, as well as for the talking Organs. Now, after having spoken of all kinds of instruments, it is reasonable to offer all their sounds to Him who is their Author, so that harmony is not ungrateful, and that it returns honor to Him from whom it has received everything it has, offering Him the conclusion of the 150 Psalms as a sacrifice of eternal praise, namely:

->LET EVERY SPIRIT PRAISE THE LORD.<-
<note>original: "OMNIS SPIRITVS LAVDET DOMINVM." From Psalm 150:6.</note>
