# PROPOSITION XXXI.

## To give the Eulogies of illustrious men in the Theory and Practice of Music.

THIS Proposition will serve as the beginning of a proper volume on the lives and <term>Eulogies</term><note>In this context, "eulogies" (éloges) refers to commemorative biographies or tributes praising the achievements of notable figures.</note> of those who have excelled in the Theory and in the Practice of Music, for everyone will be able to provide the portrait and the most remarkable actions of those they have known. For example, the Italians who know the life of <term>Gioseffo Zarlino</term><note>A celebrated Italian theorist (1517–1590) whose works established the foundations of modern counterpoint.</note>, and the Spaniards who know that of Salinas, will be able to write their lives, and so on for others. And if one had the portraits of <term>Jubal</term><note>A biblical figure mentioned in Genesis 4:21 as the "father of all who play the harp and flute."</note>, in whose favor I raised the great question of Music regarding the 21st verse of the 4th chapter of Genesis, and those of Orpheus, Timothy, and others celebrated by Antiquity, one could join them with those who seem to have restored Music within the last hundred or two hundred years. For example, with those of <term>Adrian the Elder</term><note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the founder of the Venetian School, whose complex polyphony influenced generations.</note>, whose work served as a model for the greatest Masters in composition; for it is held that Eustache du Caurroy drew a good portion of the Art of his <term>counterpoint</term><note>The relationship between voices that are harmonically interdependent yet independent in rhythm and contour.</note> from him.

But <term>Orlando</term><note>Orlande de Lassus (c. 1532–1594), one of the most prolific and influential composers of the late Renaissance.</note> was one of the first to provide the greatest quantity of all sorts of compositions, which can be found at the shop of Mr. Ballard, Printer of the King’s Music; namely, five books of <term>Motets</term><note>Sacred polyphonic choral works.</note> for 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, and 12 parts; three books of miscellanies of songs in several parts; twelve motets and as many fantasies for two parts; 22 Masses for 4, 5, 6, and 8 parts, which are still often sung in Cathedral Churches and others; two books of the eight tones of the <term>Magnificat</term><note>A canticle also known as the Song of Mary, frequently set to music for vespers.</note> for four parts, and one for five. The Lessons of Job, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah for four and five parts; the 7 Penitential Psalms for 3, 4, and 5 parts, and several other pieces of Music printed in other countries.

<term>Claude Le Jeune</term><note>A primary representative of the "musique mesurée" style, which attempted to adapt the rhythms of ancient Greek and Latin poetry to music.</note>, who lived at the same time as du Caurroy, particularly succeeded in providing beautiful melodies for the text he used, and employed a variety of movements that make his Music cheerful; this is why it is in great use in ordinary <term>Consorts of Viols</term><note>Ensembles of stringed instruments of the viol family.</note> and for voices.

He left two books of miscellanies of songs, the twelve modes on the Psalms, the twelve modes on the <term>Octonaires</term><note>Eight-line poems, specifically "Octonaires de la vanité et inconstance du monde."</note>, the Psalms in <term>measured verse</term><note>Verses written using the quantitative meter of classical poetry rather than simple rhyme and accent.</note> based on the words of Baïf, the 150 Psalms in simple counterpoint, the 150 Psalms in three parts, and one Mass. But among all the French who have applied themselves to this Art, it seems that du Caurroy carries off the prize for the great harmony of his composition and of his rich counterpoint, as can be seen in his two books of Motets, in the miscellany of Songs and <term>Noëls</term><note>Traditional French Christmas carols.</note>, in his fantasies, and in his three Masses for four voices and the one for five; this is why I have used his compositions in simple counterpoint in the 4th book on composition, as so many lessons to teach how to compose.

Now, since all the Composers of France hold him as their Master, I believe they will take pleasure in singing the following <term>Canon</term><note>A piece where multiple voices sing the same melody starting at different times.</note> in six parts in his honor, since he composed it for the deceased, and it has not yet been printed.

Now, I include here only the <term>Eulogy</term><note>A commemorative biographical tribute.</note> of <term>Jacques Mauduit</term><note>A French composer (1557–1627) known for his involvement in the Academy of Poetry and Music and his innovative polyphony.</note>, because I knew him more intimately than any other, and because I observed very singular virtues in his life. I do this so that he may be imitated, and to encourage those who are witnesses to the virtues of other excellent musicians to provide their lives, their praises, their portraits, and their works. In this way, we may render to virtue what it deserves, following the exhortation made to us by the Book of <term>Ecclesiasticus</term><note>Also known as the Wisdom of Sirach, a book of the Bible containing ethical teachings.</note> in the 44th chapter, with these words: "Let us praise men of renown," <note>original: "Laudemus viros gloriosos"</note> after which one may add, "searching out musical melodies through their skill, and reciting the verses of the scriptures" <note>original: "In peritia sua requirentes modos musicos, & narrantes carmina scripturarum."</note>.

As for other musicians, those who are the heirs of their knowledge and their resources may write their praises if they see fit—for example, that of <term>Guédron</term><note>Pierre Guédron (c. 1570–1620), a seminal figure in the development of the French "air de cour."</note>, who gave the start to <term>learned airs</term><note>Sophisticated vocal compositions (airs savants) that moved away from simple folk melodies toward more complex, expressive forms.</note> by joining beautiful movement to melody.

### Eulogy of Jacques Mauduit, excellent Musician.

<image-desc>A circular portrait of Jacques Mauduit, a man with a beard and a formal ruff collar. The portrait is enclosed in a border with the inscription: "Jacques Mauduit of Paris, Father of Music" <note>original Latin: "IACOBVS MAVDVIT PARI. MVSICÆ PATER"</note>. Below the portrait is a short poem:

"Here is a new Amphion <note>A legendary figure in Greek mythology who moved stones with the music of his lyre.</note>, a new Apollo heard by the French, having restored the melody of songs and of strings. The painter barely captures the eyes, barely the dignity of the brow: who can capture a spirit so refined by the Aonian arts <note>The arts of the Muses.</note>?"

-> By La Rechmaillee. <-
-> 1633. <-
Mathous made this. Eggerich Hilchene painted this.</image-desc>

JACQUES Mauduit, born of a noble family, was born in Paris on September 16, 1557, and was baptized at the font of Saint-Landry. His childhood was instructed in the Catholic faith of his ancestors, and his youth was happily spent in the study of the humanities and philosophy. He then made several journeys, notably to Italy, from where he returned learned in the language [Italian], to which he added Spanish and several others from the North <note>Likely referring to Flemish or German dialects.</note>; these, along with the languages he had learned at college <note>Latin and Greek.</note>, he used for the understanding of great authors. His subtle and curious mind left no science untouched upon which he could not discourse relevantly, without excluding mechanics.

He devoted himself particularly and with such great care to music, with no other help than books, and perfected himself so much in all its genres that France, during his lifetime, honored him with the title FATHER OF MUSIC—and with good reason, because he alone as if sired beautiful music in France through the excellence of several works and concerts composed for voices and all sorts of harmonic instruments, which had not been practiced there before him, or at least not so perfectly. It was there that people of all ranks were seen practicing very willingly under the precision of his beat <note>Refers to Mauduit's role as a conductor or "master of the measure."</note>. His merit earned him a place in the illustrious Academy of the learned Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf, who founded the Academy of Poetry and Music in 1570 to reunite the two arts.</note>, which Charles IX, protector of Parnassus, usually honored with his royal presence, and whose laws I have described on page 1683 of my *Commentaries on Genesis* <note>original: "Commentaires sur la Genese"; referring to the author Marin Mersenne's own 1623 work.</note>. Now, so many poets who flourished then seemed to produce their refinements only to make them live through the melodies of Mauduit.

The first piece that revealed the profound science of his harmonies was the Requiem Mass, which he set to music and had sung at the service of his friend Ronsard <note>Pierre de Ronsard (1524–1585), the preeminent poet of the French Renaissance.</note>, in the famous assembly of the Chapel of the College of Boncourt, where the great du Perron <note>Jacques-Davy du Perron, a cardinal and famed orator.</note> was admired for the funeral oration of this prodigious genius of poetry.

This Mass was later celebrated under his direction in the Petit Saint-Antoine, on the anniversary of the death of the invincible Henry the Great <note>King Henry IV of France.</note>; and for the third and last time, his eldest son Louis Mauduit had it performed on the anniversary of the author's own death.

# Seventh Book

...his father, in our Church of the Place Royale <note>The Church of Saint-Louis-des-Jésuites, now Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis in Paris.</note>, where I had the honor of offering the holy Sacrifice to God for the intention of this excellent personage, all with the applause of a very great crowd of people.

After the composition of this Mass, this great Musician composed that inimitable work for the three days of Tenebrae <term>Tenebrae: A religious service held during the last three days of Holy Week, characterized by the gradual extinguishing of candles to symbolize the darkness of the Passion.</term> of Holy Week, which he had sung until the end of his life in the same Church of Saint-Antoine, to the general satisfaction of all the listeners. He held such a reputation among musicians that nothing opposed the order he established; he arranged his performers with such symmetry of seating that his direction made the music succeed marvelously. He had an ear so true and so delicate that he usually noticed a single mistuned string among a great number of instruments playing together; without mistake, he would go to adjust it even before the player had noticed it.

We still have from him a great number of Masses, Vespers, Hymns, Motets, Fantasies, Songs, and other pieces, which the storms of the age <note>A reference to the political and religious turmoil of the French Wars of Religion.</note> will deprive of light for a time. He never wished to engage in the intrigues of the Court, though several times invited to do so by the highest powers, in order to live his life peacefully and honorably in his father's office as Keeper of the Petitions of the Palace <term>Garde du dépôt des Requêtes du Palais: A legal administrative position responsible for managing judicial filings.</term>, which he seemed to exercise only to serve everyone. He was cheerful and of ample stature, with a handsome face, a sweet temperament, pleasant conversation, chestnut hair, and was slightly balding. He was nearsighted, though it was not apparent because he read without glasses at a normal distance; however, he could not recognize a face from one side of the street to the other. He had a fortunate memory, such that he remembered the carriage, gestures, and gait of those he had seen, which meant he was never mistaken when meeting them; he would approach or greet them from quite a distance, his memory making up for the defect of his eyes. He never drank wine, never swore, never angered anyone, and all who knew him cherished and loved him.

He was devoted to God, faithful to the King, humble to the Great, courteous to his equals, kind to inferiors, helpful to the poor, and ready and prompt for those who needed his aid.

He welcomed the needy who possessed some skill with a frankness and assistance that treated them as his own children. Finally, a long succession of virtues recommended him to his Fatherland and carried his reputation even beyond Europe. It would be necessary to exceed the bounds of a Eulogy if I wished to detail his merits, but I leave that task to those more capable of presenting his life, and contenting myself with treating the part concerning our subject, I conclude with two of his actions, as pious as they were generous. The first was when, at the capture of the suburbs of Paris, he hazardously left the city, ran to the home of Baïf <note>Jean-Antoine de Baïf (1532–1589), a poet and co-founder of the Académie de Poésie et de Musique.</note>, his intimate friend who had recently died, and through the victorious soldiers, he carried away the unpublished works of this learned man, miraculously saving them from such disorder and looting as one can imagine.

The second was no less remarkable, when during the siege of Paris he saved the *Twelve Modes* of Claudin le Jeune <note>Claude Le Jeune (c. 1530–1600), the most influential composer of the "measured music" style.</note>, who was fleeing through the Saint-Denis gate, and other works that were not yet printed, so that all those who now use them in their Concerts, are entire-

# On Percussion Instruments. 65

...largely indebted to our Mauduit, who stayed the arm of the Sergeant as he was throwing them into the guardhouse fire. Because Mauduit was a man of the Law and recognized as an expert in Music, he easily persuaded the soldiery to hand everything over into his hands. He allowed them to sacrifice to their zeal the "Huguenot and seditious confession of faith" by Claudin <note>Claude Le Jeune (c. 1530–1600), a famous Huguenot composer whose works were nearly lost during the Siege of Paris.</note>, signed by his own hand and railing against the League <term>The Catholic League: A militant faction that sought to eradicate Protestantism in France.</term>. This document was nothing less, in that moment, than his death warrant—and his end would surely have been swift had Jacques Mauduit not been there. Mauduit made them understand that he would decipher this music and would know within a few hours if there were anything within it contrary to the service of the city. For this reason, he requested the prisoner be handed over to be confronted, which they granted him based on his integrity and the favor of the Captain, his friend. Accompanied by several guards who escorted him to a place of safety, he settled this affair very skillfully. It was in this way that the work of these two personages was saved by a third, of whom it can be said that he gave it the final touch and was its second father.

On August 21, 1627, at the age of seventy, he passed away from a hepatic flux <note>A historical term for a liver ailment or severe dysentery.</note> in his house in Paris, on the Street of the Jews, in the parish of Saint-Gervais. He is buried there in the chapel of Saint-Eutrope, leaving to his dear companion four boys and four girls, to whom—with me present—he gave his blessing. He offered an exhortation as worthy of himself as of his family and of those gathered, who saw him pass away in a Christian manner: with his soul soaring, constant despite the pains of his body, and peacefully in the total rest of his conscience. This followed his receiving with every kind of reverence the precious Viaticum <term>Viaticum: The final Holy Communion given to a person who is dying.</term> and the last Sacrament of the Church, in which he was born, lived, and died.

Now, although I have provided some pieces of music of his fashioning in the thirteenth article of the 57th question on Genesis—namely, *In His Sacred Temple* <note>original: "En son temple sacré"; a setting of Psalm 150.</note>, etc., which ravishes the listeners when it is well sung with voices and instruments, and *Judge the Right* <note>original: "Iuge le droit"; a setting of Psalm 43.</note>, and several others—I wish to add here the final part of the Mass of which I spoke previously. This is so that one may experience the sweetness of his manner of composing and the power of a very simple music when sung with devotion, and so that those who cherished him during his life may sing it for his intention; for the Church has particularly ordained its text and subject for invoking divine mercy on behalf of the deceased.

We hope that the entire Mass, the Office for the three days of Holy Week, and several other compositions he made will soon see the light of day, along with the *Treatises on Rhythm* and on the *Manner of making measured verse* <term>Vers mesurés: A style of poetry that uses the long and short syllables of Ancient Greek and Latin meters, which Mauduit helped adapt to the French language.</term> of all kinds in our language, to give a particular virtue and energy to the melody, which his eldest son has prepared. As for the praises of Adrian the Elder <note>Adrian Willaert (c. 1490–1562), the influential founder of the Venetian school of music.</note>, whose works served in part as an inspiration to du Caurroy, and those of other excellent composers—not only from Germany and the Low Countries, but also from Italy, among whom are placed Lucas Marenzio, Frescobaldi <note>original: "Fresco Baldi"</note>, Claudio Monteverdi <note>original: "Claude Montenerde"</note>, and several others—I leave that care to those who knew them. And if one wished to speak of our own who live now, Monsieur Boesset <note>Antoine Boësset, a master of the "air de cour."</note>, Superintendent of the King's Music; Monsieur Fremart, Master of that of Notre-Dame de Paris; Sieur Bouzignac, and several others, would deserve particular praise for the excellence of their Art.

F iij

## NOTICE.

Lord Louis Mauduit, Prior of Saint Martin of Bretheucourt—who had the portrait engraved that is seen at the beginning of his father's Eulogy, as lifelike as he was able—would deserve a particular Eulogy himself. This is as much for his virtues and the perfections of his excellent spirit as for several other reasons that his modesty prevents me from including here. However, I will content myself for the present by adding the Paraphrase he made of the learned Creed of Saint Athanasius <note>A statement of Christian belief focusing on the Trinity and the nature of Christ, traditionally attributed to the 4th-century bishop Athanasius.</note>, by which one will easily judge his ability and what may be expected of him in the future. This is done so that musicians and others who do not understand Latin may learn from these verses what they must believe regarding the mysteries of our faith to be saved.

# THE CREED OF ST. ATHANASIUS. <note>The Symbole de S. Athanase, also known as the Quicunque Vult, is a statement of Christian belief focused on the Trinity and Christology. Here it is presented in French verse.</note>

Whoever among mortals is driven by the desire
To lay the foundations of an eternal life;
And to save, while floating upon the worldly sea,
His fragile vessel from the abyss of hell; <note>The poet uses the common Renaissance metaphor of the human soul as a ship navigating a dangerous sea.</note>
He must first apply his care
To follow the beacon of the Catholic faith:
The route where its light safely leads us,
Let each person take good care not to be led astray;
One must maintain oneself there with an inviolable path;
To stumble therein but once is a damnable crime,

<meta>This page continues from the previous page's conclusion of Jacques Mauduit’s Requiem. It transitions into a French poetic paraphrase of the Athanasian Creed (traditionally known by its Latin opening, *Quicunque Vult*). This creed is a concise statement of Christian belief, specifically focusing on the nature of the Trinity.</meta>

And he who would renounce his course
Shall perish forever without hope of help.
The catholic faith <note>original: "catholique foy." In this historical context, "catholic" refers to the "universal" or "whole" Christian faith as shared by the institutional church before the divisions of the Reformation.</note> that I propose here to you,
And which must be constantly held above all things,
Is that we worship within the Trinity
One God, but of this God the most simple Unity,
And that with one same heart we show reverence
To this Trinity under a single essence;
Without confounding, however, with a confused judgment,
The persons <note>In Christian theology, "persons" (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) are distinct identities within the one Godhead, not to be confused with one another.</note> whom one must clearly distinguish
Without taking one for the other, or further separating
The substance <note>The "substance" or "essence" is the fundamental nature of God that remains undivided even though there are three persons.</note> of the three whom alone one adores:
The person of the Father belongs to the Father alone;
The person of the Son belongs to the Son alone;
The Holy Spirit has his own, thus very clearly
One can notice all three are distinct;
But these three have only one Divinity;
Possessing the same glory, and the same majesty:
Such as the Father is in all things, the Son is the same;
The Holy Spirit to both in every point relates,
And all three agreeing through similar effects,
Just equality never leaves them.
The Father is <term>uncreated: existing eternally without being made or brought into being</term>; the Son follows his nature;
The Holy Spirit is not a creature any more than they.
The Father is infinite; the Son is just the same;
And as both are, the Holy Spirit is also;
And the Father, and the Son have such an essence
As that of the Spirit, which is to say, eternal;
Each is eternal, and yet one must not
Believe in more than one eternal, it is wrong to say three;
Just as three uncreated beings are not spoken of, in the same way
Three infinites cannot be claimed without blasphemy.
The Father is almighty; the Son is just as much;
Almighty is also the Holy Spirit, and yet
There is but one Almighty, for all-mightiness
Is not divided into a triple essence.
Thus the Father is God; the Son is God, and like them...

*The Holy Spirit is God, and yet there are not three Gods.*
*But one unique God, as it must be recognized*
*That the Father is Lord, and the Son is also;*
*The Holy Spirit the same, and to believe absolutely*
*That these persons make only one Lord:*
*As the Christian faith strictly commands*
*To believe in truth that each person*
*Is perfectly God, perfectly Lord;*
*In the same way, it forbids the heart from holding*
*The false opinion that would suggest*
*Three Gods, or three Lords in this triune number.* <note>original: "nombre ternaire." This refers to the Trinity, emphasizing that while there are three "persons," they do not constitute three separate deities.</note>
*The Father, independent to the supreme degree,*
*Is neither made nor created, nor begotten by any:*
*The Son can be said to be begotten of the Father alone,*
*Not made, nor created: The Holy Spirit, who draws*
*His glorious being from both the Father and the Son,*
*Is neither begotten, nor made, nor created, but rather*
*His person proceeds equally from the two.* <note>The phrase "proceeds from the Father and the Son" refers to the *Filioque* doctrine, a key theological point in Western Christianity defining the relationship of the Holy Spirit to the other members of the Trinity.</note>
*Thus the Trinity does not possess three Fathers;*
*Three Sons no more than he shall be included there;*

*A single Father, a single Son, a single Spirit reigns there:*
*If one must debate it, let it never be taught*

*As for equality, the Christian must deny*
*That anything there is greater, or anything is lesser,*
*But one must boldly join these persons*
*Under one eternity, under similar knowledge,*
*Under equal greatness, and under the same power:*
*So that one must carefully learn in all things,*
*As we have previously made understood,*
*To serve the Unity within the Trinity,*
*And this Trinity within the same Unity.*
*Therefore, he who desires the happy path of future salvation,*
*This is what he must believe concerning the Trinity.*
*Furthermore, one must confess an <term>incarnate: the central Christian belief that God took on human flesh and became man in the person of Jesus</term> Jesus,*
*Son of God, the God-man, the man born on earth.*

## An Essay on the Moral Lessons Drawn from Pure Mathematics

If one wished to create a Christian Euclid, one could begin with his first definition, which states that *a point is that which has no part*, and say that it applies better to God than to any other thing; for there is nothing but Him that does not have parts, since even the Angels have "metaphysical parts," for they are composed of acts and powers, of essence and existence and subsistence, and of substance and accidents. <note>These are Scholastic philosophical terms: "Act and Power" refers to the distinction between what a being actually is and its potential to change; "Substance and Accident" distinguishes the core essence of a thing from its external qualities.</note> But God is the only and true <term>metaphysical point</term>, which has no parts. The three degrees of being—that which simply grows, that which feels, and that which reasons and understands—depend no less on this point than the three kinds of quantity <note>The three dimensions: length, width, and depth</note> depend on the geometric point. Just as the solid is the perfection and the end of the surface and the line, so too the degree of reason is the fruit and the end of the vegetative and sensitive being.

And although the point has no part, it is the only thing of consequence in every kind of quantity, which is but a nothingness without it; for if one removes all the points from quantity, it must necessarily perish. This has led many to conclude that quantity is composed of points, and that every quantity has an infinite number of them. From this it follows that some infinities are larger than others in a given ratio, so that they are comparable in as many ways as finite things; this is why propositions founded on <term>incommensurability</term> <note>A mathematical term for lengths that cannot be measured by the same whole unit, such as the side and the diagonal of a square</note> remain entirely valid.

Now, if one considers creatures in their origin, it is difficult to imagine them with any perfection, subsistence, or reality distinct from God; from this it may happen that one imagines there is no other perfection in creatures than that of God, just as one imagines there is nothing else in quantity but points. And if one cannot comprehend the latter, the former is even more difficult, so that one may say on this subject with the Psalmist, *deep calls unto deep*. <note>original Latin: "abyssus abyssum invocat"; a reference to Psalm 42:7, often used to describe the overwhelming nature of divine mysteries.</note>

Be that as it may, the intelligible or "archetype" world, as it exists in the divine ideas, is not different from the divine being; but the great difficulty consists in knowing how He rendered it visible and subjected it to time and place. On this, one may note the definition that Aesculapius sent to King Ammon: *out of all things being one, and being one all things*, <note>original Greek: "ἐξ πάντα ὄντα τὸν ἕna, κ' ἕna ὄνta τὰ πάνta"</note> meaning that all things are but one, namely in the idea of God.

The second definition teaches that *the line is the flow or the movement of the point*. Now, if the Contemplatives <note>Religious mystics or those dedicated to deep prayer</note> considered attentively how the line depends on the point, into which it can return by a movement equal and contrary to the preceding one, they would see almost nothing in themselves but God alone, into whom they would return voluntarily by annihilating themselves—just like the line that leaves its exterior to sink into the interior of the point, which is its source and its origin.

One can also imagine that God, like an infinitely luminous point, sent out all creatures like so many rays, via straight lines; and that it is only imperfection and malice that curves them and makes them follow a thousand paths far from rectitude. Or if one supposes that they are...

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of geometry as a spiritual allegory. Having established God as the "metaphysical point" on the previous page, the author now expands this metaphor to include circles, straight lines, and the logical principles of Euclid to explain the soul's relationship with the Divine and the nature of the Trinity.</meta>

...similar to the circumferences of a circle when they emerge from His power as effects, so that He may imprint upon them the character of the sphere to which He is compared. When it is said that He is a sphere whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere, one can say that they [souls] leave their cycles and their circles when they do not acknowledge their Author, and instead follow the straight line, which always moves away from its beginning without ever being able to return to it. From this, one concludes that straight movement is almost useless to the world in comparison to circular movement; although some believe that the infinite straight line and its straight movement agree with infinite circular movement.

I leave aside the other definitions, which are very easy to moralize, like the two previous ones, in order to add several other examples taken from common notions and Propositions.

The first common notion shows that *things which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other*; this serves theologians to prove the equality of the three Divine Persons, each of whom is equal to—or rather, the same thing as—God. One can say that the force of all types of <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two shared premises; for example: All men are mortal, Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal.</note> and reasoning depends on this, even though they are composed of three different terms, because the distinction refers to and is resolved in the last resort into unity, identity, or equality. This is why the first Propositions of Euclid begin with the consideration of equality, upon which all sorts of <term>analysis</term> <note>The process of breaking down a complex problem into its simplest parts; in 17th-century mathematics, this often referred to algebra or the method of discovery.</note> are founded. Indeed, if one wishes to compare every creature with every geometric figure, one will find that there cannot be a greater number of one than the other. This is easy to prove by the figures inscribed in or circumscribed around a circle, which are infinite in potential, even though the circle evidently contains them all—perhaps even actually—just as God contains all creatures. Thus, one can say that just as the point always remains while the figures pass away, God does not change at all, even though creatures, like so many figures, alter and change, following this verse:

> *the form of this world is passing away*, <note>original Latin: "præterit figura mundi huius"</note>

while we profess the opposite when speaking of God, who is the true permanent *now* <note>original: "nunc permanent," a philosophical term for an eternal present that does not move or change.</note> and the <term>metaphysical point</term>,

> *but you are the same, and your years will not fail*: <note>original Latin: "tu autem idem ipse es, & anni tui non deficient"</note>

it is therefore into this point that we must strive to return as often as possible, with perpetual attention to the inspirations by which He draws us to Himself, as if with so many harmonies, to make us taste the sweetness of His concert, following this verse:

> *taste and see that the Lord is good*; <note>original Latin: "gustate, & videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus"</note>

it is this true Orpheus <note>In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a musician whose music was so beautiful it could charm animals and move stones. Here, the author uses him as a symbol for Christ or God calling the soul.</note> who draws us so powerfully by sounds that are heard only within and in the spirit, such that nothing remains but to say:

> *I will sing and I will understand in the perfect way, when you come to me.* <note>original Latin: "psallam & intelligam in via immaculata, quando venies ad me"</note>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut header ornament featuring symmetrical patterns of stylized flowers, scrolling leaves, and intertwined vines.</image-desc>

### BOOK
# ON THE UTILITY OF HARMONY,
## and other branches of Mathematics.

Since there are very few people who do not value utility more than beauty and nobility, and since one does not always approve of the thoughts of the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato</note> or other philosophers—who were distressed to see the theory of science reduced to mechanics <term>mechanics: the practical application of mathematical principles to physical objects or machines</term> and practice, because they imagined that applying them to matter caused them to lose their purity—I wish to conform to the advice of the former group. I do this partly because experience, when subjected to the senses and justified in every way, greatly confirms the truth of the sciences against the opinion of those who believe they are nothing more than fantasies of the human mind with nothing but uncertainty for their foundation. I also do this because true Religion consists not only in the contemplation of divine mysteries, but also in the practice of virtues and in a great number of very useful actions by which the truly faithful comfort and help one another. It is for this reason that I add this book to the preceding ones, so that it may serve as a kind of instruction to those who wish to use Harmony and the other considerations we have proposed, whether for their own personal comfort or to help those whose salvation they seek to ensure.

### FIRST PROPOSITION.

->*There is almost no art, science, or profession to which harmony and the preceding books cannot be of service.*<-

Those who take the trouble to read all our discourses will not need this proposition, since they will encounter a great number of uses that I have shown in several Propositions and Corollaries <note>logical consequences or supplementary proofs</note> of each book; and those who are content to read only this book can use it like a table <note>a table of contents or index</note> to find what pleases them most. Now, it is easy to prove that Harmony is useful to all the sciences when taking it in the full scope of our treatises. For example, several things occur in Geometry in which the ratios of consonances <term>consonances: musical intervals that sound harmonious and stable</term> are seen, as I show in the 9th Theorem of the 2nd book of the treatise on *Universal Harmony*. Similarly, the 3rd, 10th, and 11th Theorems show what Mechanics have in common with Harmony, just as the others from the 5th to the 9th teach almost everything belonging to Astronomy, in order to make understood what it has of the harmonious—particularly if one adds the 2nd part of the 13th Theorem, in which I explain all that Plato wrote that is most excellent regarding Harmony. Furthermore, if the same thing happens to the motions of bodies lighter than water when they rise through water as happens to weights that descend through air—namely, that they descend just as fast as one another, or at least that the difference is not noticeable over a distance of one hundred feet or more, even if some are 12 times heavier than others of the same volume—one cannot entirely resolve this difficulty by comparing these motions. This is why it is good to use all the methods I have provided in the other aforementioned places, so that by confronting all the experiments with one another, one may see if they correspond, in what ways they are similar or different, and so that one can justify or correct some by means of others.

It must nevertheless be noted that some estimate that air is a supremely light body in nature, and that it cannot be made lighter by any sort of <term>rarefaction</term><note>The process of making a substance less dense, such as heating air so it expands.</note> that one can imagine, just as they believe that earth taken in its purity (which gold approaches very closely) is supremely heavy, without it being possible to become heavier by any sort of <term>condensation</term>.

Be that as it may, it is enough to weigh the air we breathe and compare it to the weight of our water; for although it is full of vapors and exhalations, it does not fail to be greatly different from water. As for air taken in its greatest purity, when someone provides it to us, we shall weigh it just as we would weigh all sorts of bodies in a <term>vacuum</term><note>The author refers to the *vuide* (void), a major subject of debate among 17th-century scientists like Pascal and Mersenne.</note>, if one could be produced; by which means we would know the weight of the air, in which they would weigh less than in a vacuum by the weight that an amount of air equal in volume to the said bodies would have, just as it happens now that they weigh less in water than in air by the weight of the water that is equal to them in size.

Now, one must hold warm cloths around the bladders, tubes, or other vessels used to contain the <term>spirits of wine</term><note>original: "eau de vie." Historically, this referred to distilled alcohol, often used in experiments because of its volatile nature.</note> or another rarefied liquor, to prevent the coldness of the surrounding air from making the vapors thicken so much that they turn back into water. This must be done until one has very accurately weighed the bladder or the other vessels filled with the said vapors. Upon which it must also be noted that it is not necessary for them to turn into air to be as light as it, since we always see that the smoke rising above chimneys is lighter, even though it does not convert into air, and that it falls back down after being cooled and re-condensed.

Given the size of this volume and comparing it with the water from the aeolipile, it will show how many feet or inches of vapor or air are required to weigh as much as an inch of water.

### Of the Utility of Harmony.

[Light rays] were compared to those of sounds throughout the first book, and particularly in the 25th Proposition, and the effects of Echoes and mirrors that I explained in the 28th Prop. of the same book and elsewhere, in order to elevate the spirits of their listeners to the knowledge of the **Father of Lights** <note>original: "Pere des lumieres," a reference to James 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights."</note>, and to facilitate their understanding of the divine rays with which he enlightens our understandings and warms our wills. Now, one can say that the Father, being like the center of the Divinity, begets his Son by the reflection of the entire sphere of knowable things, who is nevertheless but one and the same thing with him, just as the luminous point sending all its rays from the center to the circumference of a concave spherical mirror generates another equal point of light, which returns to the preceding point and remains there as if by a <term>circum-incession</term> <note>original: "circon-incession"; also known by the Greek term perichoresis, this refers to the mutual indwelling and interpenetration of the three persons of the Holy Trinity.</note>; so that it is a light of light, which would happen to the Sun if it were at the center of the world, and if the starry sky, the <term>Primum Mobile</term> <note>The "First Moved" sphere, which in traditional geocentric astronomy was the outermost sphere of the universe that carried all others.</note>, or the **Empyrean** <note>The highest heaven, traditionally believed to be a realm of pure fire and light where God dwells.</note> were solid and polished, for all the light that fell upon that mirror would return into the same Sun.

But other types of mirrors, for example the **Elliptical** and the **Parabolic**, show how we ought to use all creatures for the glory of God: for as the Ellipse, which some call an Oval, sends back all the rays from one of its <term>foci</term> <note>original: "foyers." In geometry, these are the two central points of an ellipse; any ray starting at one focus and reflecting off the edge will pass through the other.</note> to the other, as I have demonstrated in the 28th Prop. of the first book and in the book on the voice; in the same way, the knowledge of all creatures, and of everything we consider, must reflect upon the will in such a way that it has as much fire of love to love God and neighbor as the understanding has light to know, so that these two faculties are like the two centers, or foci, which bear the resemblance of God, and that they use creatures only as an **Elliptical mirror**, to relate everything they have and everything they can do to the goodness of God.

One can add that one must not amuse oneself only with the "bark" or outer shell of creatures by considering only their exterior, as do the pure **Geometers**, who have only quantity as the sole object of their speculation, for fear that this exterior study scatters the rays of the spirit, just as the convex or exterior of the Ellipse scatters the rays of light that tend toward one of its foci, and prevents them from reflecting upon the will to warm it; whereas if the interior of creatures is considered—that is to say, the contemplation of their internal virtues and their depths (the mechanisms of which cannot be understood if one does not consider the acting power of God)—it causes the light of the understanding to reflect upon the will, which would burn incessantly with the love of sovereign beauty and goodness if all the rays that strike the spirit were reflected upon it. Furthermore, the convex of the Ellipse can still serve this purpose, because it scatters the rays that come from or seem to come from one of its foci in such a way that it sends them back as if they were returning to the other, toward which they all tend; for it is good to turn away sometimes from contemplation and to pass its rays to the will, so that it may employ itself entirely with more energy and efficacy in the love of God.

Preachers can also use these figures to express the mysteries of the Faith; for example, to show that it is easy to believe that the body of the Savior can be contained under every particle of the consecrated **Host**...

And if one adds that this luminous point sends its rays over the entire surface, and that it seems almost to reproduce itself as many times as there are parts and points in said surface—that is to say, an infinite number of times—one will have a means of explaining how one and the same body can be in several places. Now, what I have said of light can be applied to colors, to the <term>representative species</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy and optics, "species" were the forms or images emitted by objects that traveled through the air to the senses.</note> of objects, to heat, and to sounds, without there being any need to give other examples than those in the aforementioned places, or which can be deduced from them.

The equality of parallel rays reduced to a point within the interior of the parabola, and the parallelism occurring on its exterior by rays tending toward its focus, can further provide a great multitude of thoughts to explain how everything that comes from God tends equally to his glory, and with what equality we must view and receive everything that comes from his hand.

Keen minds will also be able to conclude from the 29th proposition of the *Book of Sounds* that lenses, where one side has a hyperbolic convexity and the other is a straight plane, refract parallel rays in such a way that they reunite and converge all at a single point, and consequently that rays falling from a point onto said surface change from diverging to parallel; and if one knows how to adapt all the other <term>sections</term> <note>The author refers to "conic sections," the geometric curves (circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas) produced by intersecting a cone with a plane.</note> to lenses and other <term>diaphanes</term> <note>A technical term for transparent substances, such as glass, water, or air, through which light or sound can pass.</note>, one will know how to change the shape of the rays in as many ways as one does with the same opaque sections we have spoken of. Moreover, one can combine <term>diaphanes</term> with opaque materials and compose several types of instruments to serve the eye, and to burn in whatever place one wishes: for example, a convex hyperbolic <term>diaphane</term> placed near the focus of one of the preceding opaque mirrors will change their diverging rays into parallel ones.

They may also use these sections for the convenience of their voices, which they will greatly assist if they have the backs of the **pulpits** <note>original: "chaires," the elevated seats or desks from which a priest or orator speaks.</note> where they preach made in the shape of a hyperbola, with the internal focus toward the location of their mouth; for all the sound rays that strike the sides of the hyperbola will reflect toward their listeners. However, if the back of the pulpit were made so that there were three niches—namely one on each side and another in the middle—in the shape of parabolas, whose foci met toward the location of the mouth, the words would be heard much more clearly by the listeners facing said niches, who would receive the parallel rays from them.

Second, it teaches at what pitch one should begin the oration, or each <term>period</term> <note>In classical rhetoric, a "period" is a complete, well-rounded sentence consisting of several clauses.</note> of it, and how much one must raise or lower the voice at each encounter.

In the third place, how one must strengthen or weaken it, and hasten or slow it, according to the different subjects treated and the different movements one desires to impress upon the minds of the audience.

Fourthly, it teaches how to create the intervals appropriate for each passion, and how to bend the voice in all sorts of ways, in order to excite joy, sadness, anger, hatred, and other <term>affections</term> <note>The "affections" were the various emotional states that a speaker or musician sought to evoke in their audience through specific technical means.</note> that serve to lead the listener to follow the speaker's intention.

In the fifth place, it serves to design the vaults and arrange all sorts of spaces that aid the voice, making it clear and distinct. This is why speakers should dictate the architecture of places destined for eloquence, in order to draw the great advantages that can result when they are built according to the laws of harmony.

As for the first point, it is easy to determine how many syllables one should pronounce in a one-hour sermon, for experience teaches that the fastest pronunciation should only be seven syllables in one second, such as these: *I will bless the Lord* <note>original: "Benedicam Dominum"</note>, and consequently that one can, at most, pronounce only 25,200 syllables loudly enough to be heard clearly and distinctly by the audience—that is to say, 26 pages similar to those in this book. But it is much more fitting to speak more slowly, though one should not use too great a delay; for example, one should pronounce at most three times more slowly, so that a one-hour sermon has at least 8,400 syllables, which can serve to remind the Preacher to present and dedicate his tongue, his lungs, his heart, and his mind as many times to the One whose will he announces. And if he wishes to choose the middle pronunciation between the two preceding ones, it will be the best received and the most pleasant—though he should take the liberty of hastening or slowing his pronunciation according to the profit he perceives his listeners are gaining from it, since it is intended for them. For this purpose, he may recite three or four periods of his discourse in the presence of one of his friends, who will use a <term>seconds-clock</term> <note>A clock capable of measuring seconds; a relatively new precision tool for timing speech in the 17th century.</note> to advise him on the timing of the best pronunciation; for it is certain that those who speak too quickly, or too slowly, bear very little fruit in their preaching.

The second point is even more difficult to observe than the first, because many give a good tempo to their words but lack the inflection of the voice to make the necessary transitions from period to period, and do not adopt the best tone for their voices in the places where it should be strongest and most robust. Now, to achieve this practice, one must learn a sermon, or part of it, in order to recite it in the presence of a friend who has the freedom to make the voice take the proper tone, and to make the speaker restart the periods and movements of the voice until it has become accustomed to the necessary inflections to express all sorts of passions. But one must not imagine that the singer who performs all sorts of intervals while singing can do them just as easily while speaking; for such a person does them...

Preachers will benefit from reading the Treatise written by Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric (c. 60 BC–after 7 BC) who wrote "On the Arrangement of Words."</note> on the manner in which one must follow the dictions in orations, for he shows that the beauty of harangues <note>Formal, lengthy speeches delivered to a crowd.</note> depends on harmony, rhythm <note>original: "nombre," referring to the "number" or poetic meter of the prose</note>, and the mutation of words; and he notes that the <term>Diapente</term> <note>The musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> is the ordinary interval through which the voice moves in harangues; but it must always keep the long or short time of the syllables, whereas in Music they are so subjected to modulation that one can lengthen short syllables or shorten long ones, as I prove by the verses Euripides has Electra sing in the *Orestes*, namely: "Silence, silence, light step of the sandal," <note>original: "Σίγα σίγα, λευκὸν ἴχνος ἀρβύλης"</note> etc., of which the first three words are sung on the same note.

He also shows the nature of each vowel and each consonant, so that the orator may choose the softest ones to express subjects of peace and agreeable things, and the harshest to explain vehement passions and the affairs of war: so that the 43rd and 50th Propositions of the book on the voice, where I have treated these letters, can be greatly aided by the discourse of Halicarnassus. This can further serve to teach those who try to restore the manner of singing Greek and Latin Odes: that among the long syllables there are some longer than others, and among the short, some shorter than others, as I have shown in the Treatise on Rhythm <note>original: "Rythmique"</note>, of which he speaks next to teach which "feet" or movements Orators and others should use, particularly examining the styles of Thucydides, Demosthenes, Homer, Plato, and Isocrates. Now, whatever intervals the ancient Orators used, it is certain that a Preacher’s voice has an entire <term>octave</term> <note>A series of eight notes occupying the interval between (and including) two notes, one having twice or half the frequency of vibration of the other.</note> for its range, and that the accent of anger can rise suddenly by an octave, although it usually ends at the Diapente. But all these intervals must be examined before using them, especially since what is good for one voice is worth nothing for another.

And when the Preacher has noticed the best tone of his voice, and the intervals that succeed best for him in expressing all kinds of passions and <term>affections</term> <note>The emotional states or "movements of the soul" that a speaker aims to evoke.</note>, it will be easy for him to prepare a small hollow staff in which there will be a <term>monochord</term> <note>A scientific and musical instrument with a single string, used here as a pitch pipe or tuning reference.</note> using wind or a string, by means of which he will adjust his voice to all sorts of tones, and will make such intervals as he wishes very exactly, without any of the listeners being able to perceive this instrument, if it is made according to the skill seen in the <term>cervelat</term> <note>Also known as a rackett; a Renaissance woodwind instrument with a very compact, folded bore.</note> of the 32nd Proposition of the 5th book on Instruments, or following the little organ of 4 pipes in the 39th Proposition of the 6th book. He can also use a small cylinder of brass or silver, whether hollow or solid, for the same purpose, or whatever he pleases, since our Treatises teach the harmony and tone of all kinds of bodies.

The 3rd point is of no less consequence than the two preceding ones, for the strengthening and increasing of the voice often has great power over the listeners when the subject requires it: whereas if the orator increases...

I could here report a great multitude of thoughts and comparisons between sounds—and everything that constitutes Music—and light, or spiritual and divine things. Preachers could use these in a thousand types of encounters and subjects as advantageously and usefully as any other thing. To this, one can join the 6th, 7th, and 8th Propositions, along with several others whose <term>corollaries</term> <note>A logical consequence or a small additional inference following a proved proposition.</note> are full of many moral applications.

-># Of the Utility of Harmony.<-

## I. ADVICE.

Many Preachers imagine that the mathematical sciences are of no use to preaching, particularly those called "pure" sciences <note>In the 17th century, "pure" mathematics referred to abstract studies like geometry and arithmetic, as opposed to "mixed" mathematics like music, optics, or astronomy.</note> which are abstracted from physical matter. But even if there were nothing but the high regard in which such men are held when it is seen that they solidly master the most subtle sciences—and the good reputation they enjoy among all the learned—they would have no reason to despise these studies. Indeed, there is no better way to make preaching greatly fruitful than to acquire a reputation for being ignorant of nothing that can be known, while simultaneously holding the Gospel, true Religion, and divine worship in such high esteem that one entirely despises the sciences in comparison to piety. In this way, all listeners, of whatever status they may be, will be much more easily moved to believe what such Preachers say and to imitate what they do, rather than when they judge the speaker to be ignorant or poorly educated. Furthermore, the most subtle sciences will provide them with a thousand inventions <note>original: "inuentions" — in rhetoric, the "discovery" or "invention" of valid arguments.</note> to persuade toward virtue, and will strengthen their judgment in all sorts of encounters. 

Indeed, a Preacher who knows what I have just described, yet nonetheless places a hundred times more value on the practice of Religion and on the honor and respect due to holy things, would easily persuade those who love the sciences and apply themselves entirely to them of the excellence of Religion. Such listeners would judge that Religion is far more excellent than the sciences, since the Preacher holds it in such high regard that he despises all else by comparison.

For there can be no doubt that such a man has understood and tasted the pleasure and beauty of the sciences, since he knows them all to perfection. As for those Preachers who do not know them and who speak ill of them, those listeners who are not naturally inclined toward piety might imagine that they blame the sciences only because they are ignorant, and that they value prayer more only because they have never tasted the pleasure of the sciences. Therefore, it is always more profitable for both the Preacher and his audience if he is learned and has at least some introduction to all the sciences. As for the vanity that might be feared, it easily vanishes when the learned see how much they remain ignorant of and what they cannot possibly know; and when they remember the contentment found in remaining in the sweet presence of God—adoring Him and annihilating oneself before Him, as nothingness before the All—and subjecting oneself for eternity to His holy will.

### III. ADVICE.

It is appropriate to note that I have included all the moral lessons found in a large part of the Propositions of this entire work specifically for the benefit of Preachers. With even a little industry, they can use Harmony not only to embellish and enrich their preaching, but also to structure the Octaves <note>A period of eight days following a major church festival.</note> of the Holy Sacrament, Advent, and entire Lents. For example, the 8 sounds of the Diapason <note>The interval of an octave, which contains the eight primary notes of a scale.</note> or the 8 tones of the Church can provide the subject for the sermons of an octave, which serves as an inscription for several psalms.

Now, it is easy to apply the 8 beatitudes to the 8 tones or modes of the Church—which can be seen at the end of the 6th book on Genres and Modes in our Latin book—and to join them with the first or last 8 strings of the Harp of David. To these I have matched the names of God and the degrees of being on page 1705 of our *Commentaries on Genesis*. Thus, one may adapt each tone to whatever one wishes far more advantageously than Georgius Venetus <note>Francesco Zorzi (1489–1540), a Venetian friar whose work "De Harmonia Mundi" attempted to explain the universe through musical proportions.</note> did in his *Harmony of the World*, which he divided by canticles. This is because of the greater knowledge I provide regarding the Modes, both in the aforementioned commentaries starting on page 1666, and in the 16th, 17th, and 18th Propositions of the 3rd book on Genres and Modes, and often elsewhere. Furthermore, if one knows how to skillfully use all the considerations regarding French verse that I have placed starting on page 1854 of the aforementioned Commentaries, one will entrance the listeners by reason of the perpetual enthusiasm and harmonic transport they contain.

Transitions or passages from one consonance <note>A combination of notes that sound pleasant or stable together.</note> to another, using the four types of movement found in the book on Composition, are suitable for explaining the ways of passing from one virtue to another, and from nature to grace. The proportion by which the speed of natural movements increases, or that of violent movements decreases, teaches how one can advance from virtue to virtue. The intervals produced by the trumpet can serve to explain the sounds of that trumpet which will call everyone to the final judgment. ### IV. ADMONITION.

Harmony, which cannot exist without the proportion of three different parts or voices, is very well suited to help one conceive of the necessity of the three persons in the Blessed Trinity; and the sequence of chords that follow one another in Duos, Trios, etc., in the book on composition, can help in understanding the admirable order and sequence of the works of God. But all the Propositions that follow, particularly the 3rd and 5th, will serve them as much as this one, about which there is no need to advise those who know how to profit from all kinds of truths.

In these, he says that one can reach the knowledge of everything that can be known by means of numbers, which make us understand intellectual things. Furthermore, I desire that Preachers be able to judge these *Conclusions*, and that they know enough to show everything in them that is true or false; for I see no reason why they should be forced to follow the opinion of this author, as there is only the light of divine faith, or demonstration <note>In a 17th-century context, "demonstration" means a logical or mathematical proof.</note>, to which one must surrender. Now, if I undertook to show the falsehood of his *Conclusions*, it would suffice to produce several excellent truths that Mathematicians have found in physical things, and to place here the 9th and 10th, where he asserts that **Abbot Joachim** <note>Joachim of Fiore, a 12th-century mystic known for his prophetic theories regarding the ages of the world.</note> used only formal numbers in his prophecies, and that there is no better way to acquire natural prophecy.

### V. NOTICE.

When preachers wish to elevate their spirits to something great and sublime, to prepare themselves to speak to listeners who habitually engage in very high-minded thoughts, or to console themselves, I advise them to read the 2nd and 3rd books of *On Free Will*, as well as *On True Religion*, *On Order*, and *On the Blessed Life*: the 3rd, 52nd, 56th, 57th, 85th, and 151st epistles of Saint Augustine, and many others that each may choose and read at their leisure—for example, the 12th, where he teaches how one must pray. Now, when preachers draw powerful motives and pressing moral lessons from the purest **Geometry**, from **Algebra**, and from all other branches, they will demonstrate their excellence and industry. This is especially true since many believe these subjects are no more suited for such a task than a pebble or a rock is for yielding honey and oil. He who does this skillfully can say that God has given him possession of a mountainous land full of rocks, like that of the Israelites, of which it is spoken in the 32nd chapter of Deuteronomy: *He set him upon the high places of the earth* <note>original: "Constituit eum super excelsam terram"</note>, so that he may draw from it all the spiritual profits that can console and strengthen his spirit and that of his listeners, in accordance with what follows in the same verse: *That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone* <note>original: "Vt fugeret mel de petra, oleúmque de saxo durissimo." Regarding this, I say first that if they know how to use the abridgment I had printed for them of the principal parts of Mathematics, titled *Mathematical Synopsis* <note>Original Latin: *Synopsis Mathematica*.</note>, they could choose for one of their sermons some Proposition from Euclid; for the second, a proposition from Archimedes; for the 3rd, one from Apollonius; for the 4th, one from Serenus, or Menelaus, or Maurolico <note>The author lists famous ancient and Renaissance mathematicians: Apollonius of Perga (conics), Serenus of Antinoöpolis (cylinders), Menelaus of Alexandria (spherical geometry), and Francesco Maurolico (optics and geometry).</note>; for the 5th, one from **Optics**; for the 6th, one from **Catoptrics** <note>The study of light reflection and mirrors.</note>; for the 7th, one from **Dioptrics** <note>The study of light refraction through lenses.</note>; for the 8th, one from **Perspective**; for the 9th, one from **Parallaxes**; for the 10th, one regarding the center of gravity of the universe; for the eleventh, one regarding the center of solids; for the 12th, one regarding the line of direction; for the 13th, one regarding the balance; for the 14th, one regarding oblique weights; for the 15th, one or several of the wonders of the circle; for the 16th, one regarding machines; and for the 17th, one from **Hydrostatics**. And each day one can always use the same text: "That he might suck honey out of the rock, and oil out of the hardest stone" <note>Original Latin: *Vt sugeret mel de petra, oleúmque de saxo durissimo*, a reference to Deuteronomy 32:13.</note>, as the subject of each sermon, for I have provided all these Treatises in the aforementioned Abridgment.

And if, instead of using all these parts, one is content to take just one—for example, **Mechanics**—**Isorropics** <note>The science of equal weights or equilibrium.</note> will provide the invention and the conduct of the first preaching; **Centrobatics** <note>The study of centers of gravity.</note> for the 2nd; **Zygostatics** <note>The science of weighing and scales.</note> for the 3rd; **Mochlostatics** <note>The science of levers.</note> for the 4th; **Trochilostatics** <note>The science of pulleys and wheels.</note> for the 5th; **Sphenostatics** <note>The science of wedges.</note> for the 6th; **Cochleostatics** <note>The science of screws.</note> for the 7th; **Hydrostatics** for the 8th; **Aerostatics** for the 9th; **Pyrotechnics** <note>Here referring to the mechanical application of fire or artillery.</note> for the 10th; **Automatics** for the 11th; **Polymechanostatics** <note>The study of combined or complex machines.</note> and **Poliorcetics** <note>The art of conducting sieges.</note> for the 12th; and so with the others. The same can also be said of **Optics** alone, or **Catoptrics**, etc., each of which is capable of furnishing more material and thoughts than are needed not only for one sermon, but for an entire Advent. For example, one can use the 12 properties of flat or concave mirrors for as many points of a sermon, for Holy Scripture will easily furnish 12 moralities to apply to these properties. I am persuaded that Preachers will have exhausted their wits before they have used all the circumstances and aids that can be drawn from mirrors. To this they can add the inventions of the 55th question on *Genesis*, and what is at the end of the *Notes* I made on the problems of Venetus <note>Francesco Zorzi, known as "the Venetian," a friar whose work "De Harmonia Mundi" sought to harmonize philosophy and theology through music and numbers.</note>. Now, if they accustom themselves to this use, and if they give themselves the leisure to reason for themselves, they will find a thousand kinds of inventions, which they will enrich more and more, and in this manner ensure that what has seemed useless until now for divine and moral things will serve more advantageously than any other science, as is easy to conclude from all I have said, and by the Proposition which follows further in favor of Preachers.

## VI. ADMONITION.

Those who love moral lessons drawn from Mathematics will find much to satisfy them in the works of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa <note>A 15th-century German philosopher and mathematician famous for his theory of "learned ignorance," which suggests that the more we know, the more we realize our ignorance of the divine.</note>, both in his book *On Learned Ignorance* <note>Original Latin: *De docta ignorantia*.</note> and in his other treatises. Meanwhile, I shall prepare for them a method for using the most subtle thoughts of all the sciences—provided I see that they have made use of those in this book and others. This is not as difficult as many imagine, proof of which can be seen in this Proposition and the two that follow. They will also find several moral lessons in the works of William of Auvergne <note>Original: *Guilielmus Parisiensis*, a 13th-century Bishop of Paris and philosopher.</note> which he draws from Mathematics; his *Divine Rhetoric* and other treatises are very useful for Preachers.

## III. PROPOSITION.

->*To demonstrate the use of Mathematics for the benefit of Preachers, and the way to draw motifs of humility from all the sciences.*<-

There are a thousand things in the mysteries of the Faith that seem impossible to Pagans, and to those who have no other light than 그 of Peripatetic Philosophy <note>The philosophy of Aristotle and his followers, which dominated medieval and early modern universities.</note>. But the Preacher who wishes to use Mathematics to clarify the difficulties of our mysteries, and everything he treats in his sermons, will have very great advantages. For if it is a question of comparing the finite to the infinite to explain the union of the two natures <note>The human and divine natures of Christ.</note> in one divine person, he will easily show that an infinite movement can occur within a finite space; that the smallest circle in the world travels as much distance as the largest circle imaginable with every turn they make; that one can give a very small quantity which, being decreased unto infinity, will always remain larger than another quantity that is increased unto infinity; that one can pass from one extremity to the other without passing through the middle, etc.—as I show in the fourth book of *The Truth of the Sciences*, chapters 11 and 12. Now, I give one particular example among a million that are easy to propose; and for this subject, I suppose one wishes to give a Sermon on Saint Francis of Paola, Founder of my Order <note>The Order of Minims, known for their extreme humility and asceticism.</note>, and that one takes the 30th verse of the 29th chapter of Ecclesiasticus <note>Also known as the Book of Sirach.</note> for the theme, namely, *Let the least please thee as if it were great, etc.* <note>Original Latin: *Minimum pro magno placeat tibi, &c.* This verse encourages contentment with one's lot, whether small or large.</note>

One can first show the excellence of small things, and of the "Minims" <note>A clever pun: "Minime" in Latin means "the least," and it is also the name of Mersenne’s religious order (the Minims).</note> of all nature and all sciences. Just as the wise man prefers his four "little things" in the 30th chapter of Proverbs, verse 24 <note>The verse mentions four things on earth that are small but exceedingly wise: ants, rock hyraxes, locusts, and lizards.</note>, likewise one can take four points to divide the preaching into four considerations or parts. Namely: the Mathematical point, which is the "minim" <term>minim: the smallest possible unit</term> of Geometry, though it is the most powerful; for it generates everything, since its "flow" creates the line, and through the line the plane, and then the solid body through the movement of the surface. This is similar to how God generates His Son through the action of the understanding—which one can conceive of as the first divine movement, or rather as the first emanation, for the thought of "movement" is too coarse for divine things.

The Father with the Son produce the Holy Spirit, just as the point with the line produce the surface; so that the appearance of the Holy Spirit can be conceived as the "surface" of the Divinity. And all three produce the world, just as the point, the line, and the surface generate the body by their three movements. This world is no longer indivisible like its causes; and if one...

...compare God to the center of a circle, one will find three distinct things, namely the plane or surface of the circle, its circumference, and the center at which they meet, in such a way that they reduce to the same center when they return to where they began; this can be compared to the Trinity of divine persons.

Now if one compares this *minimal point* <term>Original: *minime*. Here, the author uses a play on words: a "minim" is the smallest unit in geometry (a point) or music, and it is also the name of his religious order, the Minims.</term>, or this point, to humility, one will show that this virtue achieves or obtains the greatest things in the world. For example, the *Incarnation* occurred through the humility of the Virgin, "Because he hath regarded the humility of his handmaid, etc." <note>Original Latin: *Quia respexit humilitatem ancillae suae*. From the Magnificat, Luke 1:48.</note>. And just as the point extends to infinity through the production of bodies, so does humility rise to the infinity of God, which it joins to man through the union called *Hypostatic* <note>The "Hypostatic Union" is the theological term describing how the divine and human natures are joined in the single person of Jesus Christ.</note>. One can further say in some manner that humility honors the *essence* of God and pays Him a particular homage, because it makes use of nothingness—which is more opposed to the divine being than the point is to quantity—so that it can be called the greatest or smallest *minimal point* of all. For it reduces all human pride and everything created to nothingness when it compares infinite being to the finite. It is easy to propose several other *minima*; for example, the instant, or the moment, of which time seems to be composed or dependent, though it is indivisible. For the flow or movement of the moment creates all time, however long; and when it does not flow, and remains in perpetual rest, it constitutes eternity. Thus, that which is *minimal* becomes infinite in greatness.

I add that God is as indivisible as a point, even though He fills heaven and earth; but my thoughts overwhelm me on this subject which cannot be exhausted. This is why I come to the *arithmetic minimum*, namely unity <term>The number one (1), viewed here as the source of all other numbers.</term>, which produces all numbers. And what appears far stranger is that numbers are nothing other than unity counted several times and, as it were, folded back into itself. This can provide such a great number of excellent thoughts for conceiving and explaining the unity of God and His attributes that entire volumes are no more capable of containing them than they are the properties of all possible numbers. So, if Preachers study the prerogatives of unity, they will be able to say, "But one thing is necessary" <note>Original Latin: *Porrò vnum est necessarium*. From the Gospel of Luke 10:42, where Jesus speaks to Martha.</note>, and will never need any other study to give as many sermons as they wish, whether by taking a type of union or unity for each, or the properties of some number, which has nothing it does not draw from unity, just as the creature does from the Creator. Unity can also be considered as the source of the infinite number of parts into which every quantity is divisible, however small it may be. This is why many admit infinity in number, even while they deny it in quantity, because the infinity of parts is actually in every quantity, even though it is not divided; thus there is nothing in the world that does not bear witness to the infinity of divine perfections.

The third *minimal point* could be the center of gravity of every body, upon which a good part of Mathematics is founded; for example, the part of Mechanics named *Centrobaryc* <term>The study of centers of gravity.</term>, and then *Isorropic* <term>The study of weights in equilibrium or balance.</term>. And because if there are light things in the world, they also have their center of lightness, and all the force of Mechanics is considered to proceed as if from a center, and has its line of direction (as is demonstrated in the treatise on Mechanics), it is easy to compare the different properties of these centers and directions to those of the heart and the spirit of man, following...

One will find many ways here to explain the limits of the simple creature, the limits of our Lord in terms of His humanity, and the absolute immensity in terms of His Divinity. Now, it is very easy to derive humility from all the sciences to satisfy the second part of this Proposition. So it is that we are as little knowledgeable in this matter as if it were happening in someone else, outside of ourselves.
