...so that it is infinite both on the side of A and that of B, if one takes away the part

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment representing the concept of infinity and its parts. At the left end is the letter 'A' and at the right end is the letter 'B'. In the middle of the segment, two vertical tick marks define a smaller portion labeled 'C' and 'D'.</image-desc>

C D, it will be finite at C and at D, so that the subtraction of a finite part would make finite that which was infinite, even though it still remains infinite toward A and B. And if one says that the part CD, or any other one chooses, is only an **aliquant part** <note>In historical mathematics, an "aliquant part" is a magnitude that does not divide a larger whole evenly (like 3 is to 7), as opposed to an "aliquot part" which is an exact divisor (like 2 is to 6).</note>, which does not diminish the whole, and not an **aliquot part**, or that it is not a part *of* the infinite, but only *within* the infinite, the judgment of those who embrace only the truth seems to have difficulty and reluctance in granting this distinction of parts. And even if they were to admit it, it does not satisfy them; for whether the line C D, being replicated and repeated an infinity of times, can make an infinite line, or whether it cannot, everything that one can imagine as most reasonable seems at one moment to destroy the infinite, and at another the finite. For if this line is not composed of an infinity of parts equal to C D, or to any other line one chooses, how is it a "whole" in relation to its parts? And if it is composed of bounded parts, how can it be infinite? Since that which is finite can never become infinite. 

From this comes the view of some who say that an infinite line has no parts at all, from which it follows that it is indivisible; so that a sovereignly great quantity—that is to say, the infinite—takes on the nature of a **point**, and is like an infinite point, just as the eternity of God is indivisible, like His immensity, and sovereign greatness has the same properties as sovereign smallness. 

Thus we see that Mathematics considers only finite quantity, which limits the reach of the human spirit, without the spirit being able to penetrate, or even consider, the infinite without becoming entangled in a thousand contradictions from which it cannot extricate itself, any more than a bird caught in **birdlime** <note>A sticky substance smeared on branches to trap birds; a common metaphor for being hopelessly stuck.</note> or in a snare and net. This is why many deny that there can be any other infinite than God, who surpasses every sort of contradiction; and consequently, they argue that the world could not have existed from all eternity, and that the created spirit, though blessed in Heaven, will not be able to comprehend the infinity of God—otherwise, it would follow that the spirit itself would be infinite. Thus infinity seems to necessarily include indivisibility, incomprehensibility, and independence; this is why all the parts that can be cut away from the infinite line would be parts *within* the infinite, rather than *of* the infinite. 

There are others who, making every line composed of an infinity of points, say that there are some infinities larger than others, according to a given ratio, whether **effable or ineffable** <note>Ratios that can be expressed as whole numbers (effable) or those that are irrational (ineffable).</note>. And although we consider only finite quantity, the mind still finds itself halted when it sees that the smallest line—for example, C D—has as many parts as A D, since one can draw an infinity of lines across both; by which some strive to prove that a very small circle is equal to a very large one, and that both are divisible into an infinity of parts. In this way, that which is finite is also infinite. This is found just as much in light and in other qualities divisible to infinity as it is in lines; from which one can conclude that everything that exists bears a **divine character**, which bears witness to the absolute infinity of the Creator. This shows that the jurisdiction of the human spirit lies between these two kinds of infinity, without being able to extend it to one side or the other, and that the spirit has marvelous reasons to humble itself when it considers its lack of light and its ignorance, which is so...

...so great that it <note>The human mind.</note> understands nothing in perfection, and that it is blind in the midst of the first principles which serve as an Alphabet to nature; added to which, it knows so little of finite things that there is nothing in the world, in whatever way one might take it, of which it does not ignore far more than it knows. This is so easy to demonstrate by examining all the objects of the senses, and the ways in which the spirit (or its spiritual faculties, or the bodily ones like sight and hearing) receives its images and impressions, that we may say nothing is so fitting for man as to show and to know that he knows nothing, properly speaking, and according to the conditions and properties of a perfect science. I would never be finished if I undertook a catalogue of everything ignored by the best minds in the world; and it is enough that Preachers use the first thing that comes to mind to convince their listeners of an appalling ignorance, in order to plant humility so deeply in their spirits that they never have the boldness to become proud, and that they have no other greater care than to serve God by adoring and loving Him, until He strips them of the ignorance that accompanies them now, to clothe them instead in the light of glory. Hope puts these excellent words of Psalm 35 into our mouths:

> You shall make them drink from the river of your pleasure; for with You is the fountain of life, and in Your light we shall see light. <note>Original Latin: *Torrente voluptatis potabis eos; quoniam apud te est fons vitæ, & in lumine tuo videbimus lumen.* (Psalm 36:8-9 in modern numbering).</note>

### PROPOSITION IV.

->To explain how Harmony can serve the spiritual life, prayer,<-
->and contemplation.<-

There are certain people who blame or despise the sciences, particularly all branches of Mathematics, under the pretext of piety, which they imagine the sciences oppose or harm because they do not understand them. To such people one can apply the words of Saint Jude: *They blaspheme whatever they do not know.* <note>Original Latin: *Quacumque ignorant, blasphemant.* (Jude 1:10).</note> But since it is certain that there are no worse judges than the ignorant, one must not dwell on them, unless one wishes to maintain at the same time that one must abandon or despise the stages of nature, as if they were repugnant or harmful to those of grace or glory.

It seems to me that those who wish to banish the sciences from the religious life act almost like Julian the Apostate <note>A 4th-century Roman Emperor who attempted to suppress Christianity; he famously forbade Christians from teaching or studying classical rhetoric and philosophy.</note>, who wanted to forbid study to Christians so that, being destitute of the light of the sciences, they would become so stupid that they could not defend themselves against the attacks of the pagans, nor respond to their objections. I freely admit that I am not of this opinion, and that if devout persons knew all the sciences in perfection—for example, if a member of a Religious Order <note>Mersenne uses "Religieux" here to refer to a monk or friar, likely including himself as a member of the Order of Minims.</note> knew Philosophy as well as or better than Plato and Aristotle, and Geometry as well as Euclid, Archimedes, and Apollonius of Perga <note>Pergæus refers to Apollonius of Perga, a Greek mathematician known for his work on conic sections.</note>—he would have great advantages for raising himself to God and for drawing spiritual profit from a thousand things of which the ignorant are incapable. For it is not enough to say that God gives more light and devotion in a single moment to an ignorant soul (whom one characterizes as simple and kind) than all the sciences can bring in a thousand years; this is because the learned are no less susceptible to this same favor from God when they resign themselves entirely to His will and use their knowledge for His honor and glory.

...added to which, they are not so subject to the illusions of the evil spirit, and to false and simulated devotion, as others are; and they are much more capable of discerning in what consists the solidity of the spiritual life, for which the subtle thoughts of the most abstruse sciences can serve as a kind of preparation or disposition. This is not to say that one cannot abuse the sciences, which can inflate a poorly formed mind that does not possess them as it ought: but one must not blame good things under the pretext of their abuse, which one should only correct. Let us see then now if one can draw spiritual profit from Harmony, even though it seems, perhaps, not so sublime as the other sciences; and believing that God is no less the God of sciences than of grace—*for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him thoughts are weighed* <note>original Latin: "Deus scientiarum Dominus, & ipsi præparantur cogitationes." A reference to 1 Samuel 2:3.</note>—let us prepare our souls and our thoughts for Him through the concert of virtues, the Harmony of which can be seen in Plato, when he marks the principal consonances within the faculties of the soul.

I shall not repeat what is seen in the discourse on Unison, nor in several propositions of the first book on Consonances, and others, which contain several thoughts suited for devotion; I add only some new considerations drawn from the preceding sections. I say that one can be inflamed with divine love by the comparison of the glowing fire produced by parallel rays in a parabolic, hyperbolic, or elliptical focus <term>foyer: the mathematical "focus" of a curve where rays of light or sound converge</term>, since all the thoughts we have of creatures, of the sciences, or of divine perfections, reflecting upon the will, are capable of making it say: *While I was musing, the fire burned* <note>original Latin: "In meditatione mea exardescet ignis." From Psalm 39:3.</note>. And this fire is as powerful for making one despise gold and silver, and everything that can deprive us of grace, just as the fire of a parabolic focus is capable of calcining these metals, melting them, and burning everything that opposes it.

And if, instead of God complaining of His people when He says, *I became a proverb to them* <note>original Latin: "Factus sum illis in parabolam." From Psalm 69:11. If I wished to expand upon showing the spiritual profit that can be drawn from the different reflections of light, of sounds, and of their concurrence, divergence, and parallelism, an entire volume would be needed. But it suffices to have brought a sample of it to give cause to spiritual persons—to whom it belongs to judge all things, as Saint Paul teaches: *But he that is spiritual judgeth all things* <note>original Latin: "Spiritualis autem iudicat omnia." From 1 Corinthians 2:15.</note>—to make all sciences useful, and to sanctify them by the good use they shall make of them. There is, in my opinion, nothing in the world that can raise us so easily to God as that which is already intellectual, and which seems to most closely neighbor the Angels—as can be shown by a thousand Geometric demonstrations, which so greatly surpass the reach of the imagination that it is almost impossible to express it. If one can explain divine things with some kind of report and particular satisfaction, perhaps it cannot be executed more happily than through the light of Mathematics. ### I. ADMONITION.

The intention of this discourse is not to suggest that the sciences are absolutely necessary for the spiritual life, since we experience that many who have no knowledge of them cultivate piety and are mirrors of virtue. Rather, it serves only to show that those who know them—in whatever perfection one might imagine—have great advantages if they wish to avail themselves of them, given that God is accustomed to accommodate Himself to the capacity of the spirits who adore Him in spirit and in truth. Thus, excellent Geometers and Analysts are much to be blamed if they let slip the opportunity they have to draw spiritual profit from the lights God has given them, and if they allow themselves to vanish into their own thoughts without eternally adoring and ardently loving Him who is their source and origin.

Furthermore, when Saint Paul said that Philosophy deceives and seduces, he meant that which is vain and useless—that is, which does not take truth as its basis, such as the genealogy of the Gods, and the rules of Judicial Astrology <term>Iudiciaire: Judicial astrology, the practice of predicting human affairs or the future based on the stars, which was often viewed with suspicion or condemned by the Church.</term>. But that which has no other foundation or goal than truth cannot be reprehensible, since this truth is the image of Eternal Truth. And when he considers that he knows nothing but Christ crucified, this must be understood prudently: in that he valued no other knowledge compared to that of the Cross, to which he referred all others, just as all Christians must refer all their sciences to it, in order to animate them with the spirit of grace that makes us the children of God.

To this, one may add that to know all the sciences is, in some way, to know Jesus Christ, since He contains the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God—"In whom are the treasures of wisdom and of the knowledge of God" <note>original Latin: *In quo funt thesauri fapientiæ & fcientiæ Dei*. From Colossians 2:3.</note>—of which our own knowledge is like a small ray reflecting its origin. Thus, the most learned can say, in some way, that they enter deeper than others into the treasures of Jesus Christ; and the science of Mechanics, which teaches them how to move the earth and all the elements, and to make the whole sea weigh but a single pound, and Catoptrics <term>Catoptrique: The branch of optics dealing with reflection and mirrors.</term>, which teaches how to do whatever one wishes with light and sounds, etc., makes them participants in His power.

### III. NOTICE.

Saint Augustine clearly demonstrates the utility of Geometry in his book *On the Quantity of the Soul*, by explaining the equilateral triangle, the square, the rhombus, the point, length, width, and height, in order to compel the reader to admit that the rational soul is indivisible and immaterial. Likewise, Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian.</note> would not have been able to understand or explain Aristotle if he had not known what the <term>squaring of the circle</term> <note>The ancient mathematical challenge of constructing a square with the same area as a given circle.</note> consists of, nor the <term>gnomon</term> <note>In geometry, the part of a parallelogram remaining after a similar smaller parallelogram has been taken from one of its corners.</note>, nor the incommensurability of the diagonal of a square with its side. Nor would he have known why it is necessary that the three angles of any rectilinear triangle be equal to two right angles. I leave aside many other propositions that were necessary for him to write his commentaries, though we do not read that this knowledge caused him to abandon or diminish his devotion. Now, one must not imagine that Mathematics so inflates those who possess it that it fills them with presumption; on the contrary, if it falls into a well-formed mind, it removes every cause for pride, by reason of the great multitude of things it reveals that we do not know, and by the great presumption or simplicity of many which it uncovers, when its light compels them to admit that they do not

In the second place, the irradiations of light, and of all the <term>species</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "species" refers to the sensory images or "likenesses" that objects transmit through the air to the eye or ear.</note> that objects send and spread into the air, can help us conceive how all the **Angels**, and all the bodies of the blessed, can be found in the same place and in the same point. This is both because a single indivisible ray exiting from an object situated in a point suffices for such an eye, and because in glory the body is as prompt in its functions as the spirit is in its own. It no longer needs any other help to see all that is physical and visible than that by which it was raised to its happiness, just as the understanding needs only the **light of glory** to perform all its functions. Now, what I have said of the rays of light and species can be applied to those of **sounds**, which extend and meet in the same points of the air, upon which they imprint all kinds of noises and words.

In the third place, the **perpendicular line** can serve as a Master in the spiritual life as well as in **Geometry** and in all parts of **Mechanics**, to explain all the **virtues**, which consist between two opposing vices. For as nothing can subsist in all of nature without the perpendicular, likewise virtue is not significant if it does not stand "at plumb"—that is, equally distant from one and the other vicious extremity. As soon as the will inclines more toward one of the two, it makes an **obtuse angle** on one side and an **acute** one on the other, toward which it leans more. And just as there are an infinity of acute angles from the line parallel to the horizon up to the perpendicular—which makes the **right angle**, which is most perfect and at the **Arithmetic mean** between the two sides of the parallel upon which it is raised—likewise there are an infinity of degrees from one of the vices up to the perfection of virtue considered in a sovereign degree and in its perfect rectitude. > Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you forever and ever. <note>original: "Beati qui habitant in domo tua Domine, in fæcula fæculorum laudabunt te." (Psalm 84:4)</note>

### V. PROPOSITION.

->*Explaining through figures what has been said in discourse: whereby one will understand all that is necessary for this subject.*<-

Since all **Preachers** have perhaps not studied Geometry enough to understand the preceding discourses, which I have made particularly for their benefit, I place here the necessary figures to remove every kind of difficulty for them, and to facilitate for them the preceding moral lessons, or to give them the means to create an infinity of others.

[A geometric diagram showing a system of parabolic reflection. A large parabola (BAC) has an axis AD and a focal point E. Now, all parallel rays—for example, OL and FA—which fall upon the concave surface of the parabola BAC, reflect to the <term>focus</term> <note>In optics, the "focus" (or *foyer* in French) is the point where rays of light meet after reflecting off a curved mirror.</note> E, so that all the rays that fall perpendicularly upon the <term>ordinate</term> <note>A vertical coordinate line in a geometric graph.</note> BC, composed of their incidence and their reflection, are equal: for example, the ray OLK is equal to the ray GDE, and so with the others. Now, this parallel redirection by the convex surface of the smaller parabola occurs for the same reason that each ray coming from outside toward the focus E—for example, the ray NL—is reflected along the line LM parallel to QD, or DKG. From this, it is easy to conclude what I explained on page 62 of the *Book of Sounds*: namely, that the fire and light produced by the rays OGF, etc., near the focus E, can be so reflected and transported toward PQ that they will be almost as vivid and vigorous at 3 or 4 <term>leagues</term> <note>A league is an old unit of distance, roughly 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note> from the focus E as they are on the convex surface of the smaller parabola HK. And if instead of light one receives the rays of objects OGF, etc., the eye placed in some spot between AQ will see them very large and very clearly.

Now the first property relevant to my subject consists in the fact that all rays falling upon the polished concave of the hyperbola E I C in such a way that, if they were not obstructed, they would all go to join and unite at the exterior focus A, are reflected instead to the interior focus H, as one sees in X V, which returns from V to H, instead of going to A. This can be explained by the 4th figure preceding, of which the 6th part Q O suffices for burning; for its chord <term>chord<gloss>a straight line segment whose endpoints both lie on a circular arc</gloss></term> is the side of a hexagon, as one sees in the 6th figure. Because spherical burning mirrors have almost the same property as parabolic ones, he could have joined two circles together, just as we have joined the two parabolas of the first and second figure, to burn the ships at one hundred or two hundred paces from the walls of Syracuse, wherever the Sun happened to be on the horizon; for it is easy to direct and send the parallel rays P Q, or E Q to whatever place one wishes by the application of a straight or plane mirror, as I have said in other places. It is almost impossible to cast the sixth part of a sphere that would be large enough to burn all on its own from so far away; and if one takes only 4 or 5 degrees of the said sphere, whose axis must be at least 400 paces to burn at one hundred paces, this portion will not be sensibly different from a plane mirror, or a straight line, even though the diameter of its concave is more than 178 paces. This would happen similarly with parabolic mirrors; so it is entirely necessary that he used two or several mirrors joined together. However, the nature of incombustible material, and whether its polish could resist the flame and the heat of the focal points, always leaves me with some suspicion regarding the truth of the history. One would receive it with more assurance if he had been able to join and arrange such a great multitude of plane mirrors in a machine that they sent enough rays to burn the ships. Whatever the case may be, it suffices that the moral analogies of the Preachers be founded in the truth of the subject, that they bear fruit in the minds of their listeners, and that those for whom it suffices to preach to themselves may draw consolation and light by applying to themselves some of the preceding properties.

### FIRST COROLLARY.

It is evident by what we have said in this Proposition that the rays of light can be changed into all sorts of figures by means of mirrors and diaphanes <term>diaphanes<gloss>transparent substances, such as glass, through which light is transmitted</gloss></term>, since the Parabola changes them from parallel to concurrent when they fall upon its concave surface and reflect into its focus; and from divergent to parallel when the flame is in the said focus. Likewise, its convex surface changes the divergent rays (which nevertheless tend toward the same focus, and for this reason can be called Concurrent) into parallel, and consequently parallel into divergent, so that the convex produces an effect contrary to the concave, as one sees in the preceding figures.

--- Page 729 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on geometric optics and conic sections, moving from the legend of Archimedes' burning mirrors to the specific properties of hyperbolas and ellipses, and finally to their application in acoustics as described by Vitruvius.</meta>

->Of the Utility of Harmony.<-

The concave side of the **hyperbola** <term>hyperbola<gloss>a type of smooth curve lying in a plane, defined by its geometric properties or by the section of a cone</gloss></term> reunites all rays tending toward its exterior **focus** <term>focus<gloss>a fixed point used in defining a conic section; in optics, the point where rays converge</gloss></term> into its interior focus. When a flame is placed within it, its rays are spread by the concave glass, and those that were already spreading out (divergent) are made even more so. Because its convex side has opposite effects, it spreads the rays coming from the internal focus and changes those converging toward its internal focus into rays converging toward the external one; in this way, it delays or prolongs the convergence, which is otherwise hastened and shortened by the concave side.

The elliptical convex serves only to spread the rays in such a way that a ray tending toward one of its foci is reflected so that it goes toward the opposite focus. This is similar to what happens when a ray produced in one of these foci is sent back to the other by its concave side, and consequently is changed from spreading out (divergent) to meeting at a point (convergent). Now, if one combines these different sections and their foci, the results will be prodigious: for example, **burning mirrors** of infinite power, and **telescopes** <note>original: "lunettes de longue vûe"</note> of infinite range. A portion of 20 degrees or so of a well-polished concave sphere will produce nearly the same effect as a **parabola** <term>parabola<gloss>a mirror curve that reflects all incoming parallel light rays to a single focal point</gloss></term> of the same size, for all the rays will join between the 4th and 5th part of the axis. Those who wish to know the manner of describing all these sections will find it from the 23rd to the 30th Proposition of the book *The Voice* <note>Likely referring to a section of the author's own work on acoustics and optics.</note>, to which one can add those explained by the Reverend Father Baptiste the Jesuate <note>Bonaventura Cavalieri (1598–1647), a member of the Jesuate order and a mathematician who wrote "Lo Specchio Ustorio" (The Burning Mirror) in 1632.</note>, Professor of Mathematics at Bologna, from the 41st chapter of his *The Burning Mirror* <note>original: "Spechio Vſtorio"</note>.

### COROLLARY II.

It is evident that all speculations regarding nature and Mathematics proceed from equality, as has been seen in the effects of mirrors; for parallelism, convergence, and the spreading of rays depend on the equality of angles. To this, one may add the method of creating a circle or a straight line of fire and light, and all other sorts of glowing and burning figures by means of the parabola and other sections. If these are carried and moved in such a way that their axes remain parallel to that of the Sun, their foci will burn continuously while tracing all sorts of figures—provided they are not incompatible with the parallelism of the axes. If one adds different mirrors together according to the possibilities of the art, one can create all kinds of burning shapes.

### COROLLARY III.

The preceding sections can serve to explain the **theater vases** <note>These were bronze or clay resonators placed in ancient theaters to amplify and improve the sound of the actors' voices.</note> mentioned by **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect of the 1st century BCE.</note> in the 5th chapter of his 5th book. Regarding this, Father Baptiste remarks that the hyperbolic figure is best suited for reflecting the voice to the listeners, and that these vases must be placed in small chambers or niches. They should be elevated slightly above their rims and open at the top, so the voice enters them to strike the walls of the small chambers; reflecting several times against the sides of the vases and the cells, the voice resonates like the sound of **Lutes** and other instruments.

Now, I do not wish to waste time describing these vases according to the imagination of many others, which can serve at most as a conjecture; for it

->### Of the Utility of Harmony. ###<-

...it is enough to know the proportion that the aforementioned vases must have, in order to make the **consonances** <term>consonance<gloss>a combination of notes that are pleasant or "stable" to the ear</gloss></term> resound by the sound of the voices of those who recite on the stage. This proportion is in no way different from that of bells, which make the same consonances; that is why I do not speak of it here, nor of the **intervals of Aristoxenus** <note>Aristoxenus was a Greek philosopher and music theorist who argued that musical intervals should be judged by the ear rather than mathematical ratios alone.</note>, of which I have treated very amply in the second book on **Stringed Instruments**, and in the book on **Genres**; from which one can easily conclude that **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a 1st-century BC Roman architect whose work "De architectura" describes placing bronze vessels in theaters to amplify sound.</note> did not understand the laws of Harmony. Otherwise, he would not have said that the theater vases must make several **fourths** <term>fourth<gloss>a musical interval spanning four notes of a scale; in ratios, it is 4:3</gloss></term> or **tetrachords** <term>tetrachord<gloss>a scale of four notes, the basis of ancient Greek music systems</gloss></term> in succession, since the extreme sounds of two or more fourths produce very disagreeable **dissonances**. I demonstrate this by these three numbers: **9, 12, and 16**, which contain two **sesquitertial ratios** <term>sesquitertial ratio<gloss>the ratio of 4 to 3, which defines the musical interval of a perfect fourth</gloss></term>, and consequently two tetrachords; for 9 is to 12 as 3 is to 4, just as 12 is to 16. So, 9 and 16 contain two fourths and make a **minor seventh** which wounds the ear marvelously. Instead, it should have been said that the vases must be so arranged that the first makes a **fifth** <term>fifth<gloss>a musical interval of five notes, considered highly stable and harmonious; a 3:2 ratio</gloss></term> with the second, and the second a fourth with the third, and so on, in order to create good effects that contain Harmony to satisfy the listeners.

As for the size of the vases, assuming they have a similar shape—for example, a cubic one—if the side of the largest is 3 feet, that of the second must have been 2 feet to produce the fifth. Consequently, the surface area of the first must have been to that of the second as 9 is to 4, and the empty space (or the solid volume to the solid volume) as 27 to 8. This is so easy to conclude from the demonstrations in our preceding books that it is not appropriate to stop any longer on this subject.

Now, as for the sounds of these vases, it is difficult for them to be loud enough to make their consonances heard by the audience when they are struck only by voices. We experience this with the barrels which he says were used in villages instead of bronze vases to avoid the expense. For whether they are made of potter's clay or wood, one never hears the consonances for which they are prepared when it is only the voice that touches them. They serve, at most, only to reflect the voice to make it louder and more intelligible—much like the body of a **lute** or other instruments, which, by making several reflections of the sound, preserve it longer and make it stronger. It is for this reason that one places **sparrow pots** <note>original: "pots à moineau"; these were acoustic jars built into the masonry of church vaults, thought to improve resonance, though they resembled bird-nesting pots.</note> or other hollow vessels in or upon the vaults of churches to help the voices of those who sing. For a voice is not as strong in an open field or in the open air as in an enclosed place where the walls reflect the voice and prevent it from being lost.

Those who have understood the **mixed genre** (composed of the three types: **Diatonic**, **Chromatic**, and **Enharmonic**, which I explained in the 13th Proposition of the book on **Musical Genres**) will perfectly understand all that Vitruvius reports of Music. They will easily conclude that the arrangement of his 13 vases placed around the theater is not good, since it generates **sevenths** and **fourteenths**, etc., whereas they should only produce consonances. Thus, if one uses 13 vases as he says—of which the six on the **right side** <note>original: "dextre"</note> are in unison with those on the **left side** <note>original: "seneſtre"</note>—the first jars must make a **major third** with the second, the second a **minor third** with the third, the third a **fourth** with the fourth, the fourth a **major third** with the fifth, and

...the 5 with the 6 make the **minor third** <term>minor third<gloss>a musical interval consisting of three semitones; expressed by the ratio 6:5</gloss></term>, so that these 6 pairs of vases ascend to the **Twelfth** <term>twelfth<gloss>an interval spanning an octave plus a fifth; ratio 3:1</gloss></term>, and then the 13th vase will be the **Fourth** <term>fourth<gloss>an interval of five semitones; ratio 4:3</gloss></term> with the 6, or the **double octave** <note>original: "Disdiapason"</note> with the first, so that all their sounds will have among them the same ratio as these numbers: 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16. Or, if one prefers to follow the natural order of **consonances** <term>consonance<gloss>a combination of notes that sound pleasant and stable together</gloss></term>, as the trumpet does in its intervals, one will have the sounds 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, which make up the range of the **triple octave** <note>original: "Trisdiapason"</note>, which is called the **Twenty-second**.

As for the size of the vases, it matters very little what it may be, provided that their homologous or similar sides are in the same ratio as the aforementioned numbers, although their sounds become deeper and more corporeal, or more massive, when they are larger. Now, one can imitate the shape of bells and large **timbres** <term>timbre<gloss>here referring to a stationary bell or a hemispherical gong</gloss></term> which widen almost hyperbolically, or that of the parabola, the ellipse, or the circle. Father Baptista <note>Likely Giambattista della Porta, an Italian polymath whose works on "Natural Magic" included studies on acoustics and optics.</note> proposes cells in the form of ellipses both in length and width, of which one of the **foci** <term>focus<gloss>in geometry, one of the two central points of an ellipse; sound produced at one focus reflects directly to the other</gloss></term> is located near the place where those who speak or sing on the stage are positioned; and the other within the small chambers or niches of the said vases, so that the focus of the ellipse and the interior focus of the hyperbolic vases meet at the same point, and that the mouths of these vases be turned upwards. For the voice of the actors, produced at the focus of the ellipse located on the stage, will spread out and strike the elliptical concave of the chambers, and will be gathered in the internal focus of the hyperbola, from where, reflecting once again by meeting the concave surface of the vases, it will spread out to all the necessary places to reach all the listeners. Whereas if they were parabolic, only the listeners parallel to its concavity would hear the voice; and if they were elliptical, only a single person would hear the voice, albeit more clearly. But being hyperbolic, the listeners can have 13 reflections from the 13 vases, under which **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, 1st-century BC Roman architect.</note> teaches that one must place wedges, so that being raised in the air, they resonate better: though it seems they would resonate even better if they were attached and suspended like bells.

Certainly, in whatever ways one might arrange these vases, I believe that the method now used in Italy is the best and most excellent when performing tragedies; this consists of the harmony of an **Organ** or a **Theorbo** <term>theorbo<gloss>a large, long-necked lute with additional bass strings, used to accompany singers</gloss></term>, which perpetually accompanies the voices of the actors, in order to make the primary consonances with their voices, and to render them harmonious and more agreeable. Now, it is easy to experiment with empty barrels to see the effect of these vases, which will not be found so great that one would wish to prefer them to the aforementioned instruments; so that Vitruvius's imagination now seems useless to me, whether it succeeded in his time, or whether he was content merely to make the project and design for it.

-> COROLLARY V. <-

**S**ince all Music regards the **unison** <term>unison<gloss>two or more musical parts sounding the same pitch</gloss></term> as its source and origin, following our discourses in the first book of *Consonances*, and since all sciences must serve our salvation, it is reasonable that those who have read this work, or who understand its reasons, should imitate the manner one takes to bring strings or voices down to unison. This consists of abandoning all differences and varieties to arrive at equality; for example, when one descends from the **octave** <note>The interval of an eighth.</note> to the unison—that is to say, from 2 to 1—one can pass through a continuous movement, and consequently through an infinity of degrees, intervals, and ratios that are found between 1 and 2. Or, one may pass only through 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7 different movements, just as one can pass through several degrees from the state of imperfection represented by the **binary** <note>In the Pythagorean tradition, the number 2 (the binary) represents division, duality, and the material world, whereas 1 represents God and unity.</note> where we are, by gradually leaving behind the differences of time, place, and the various motives of our actions which are not conforming to the will of God, to reduce ourselves to unity, and to break the veil that prevents us from recognizing and feeling the effects of the promise of our Savior described in Saint John chapter 14 by these words:
> *On that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you* <note>original Latin: "In illo die vos cognoscetis, quia ego sum in Patre meo, & vos in me, & ego in vobis"</note>,
which can be understood through the comparison of the unison, the source and father of the octave, in which the consonances are contained. Furthermore, Jesus Christ testifies in the 17th chapter that he desires the Faithful to make so perfect a unison of their wills with his, that he made this prayer to his Father:
> *Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be one, just as we are.* <note>original Latin: "Pater sancte, serua eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint vnum, sicut & nos."</note>

# Of the utility of Harmony. #

...I have given in the books on *Instruments*. Soldiers can still draw several benefits from the first three books of *Movements*, both natural and violent <note>In 17th-century physics, "natural movement" referred to gravity (falling), while "violent movement" referred to motion caused by an external force, like a shot.</note>: for example, they will know at what speed they must walk and turn to avoid the strike of arquebus <term>arquebus<gloss>an early type of portable long gun</gloss></term> balls or cannonballs after they have seen the flash, assuming they know the distance of the place from which the shot is fired. They will easily explain why the balls should not travel further toward the West than toward the East, even though one supposes that the earth moves and rotates in 24 hours from West to East; and why, being fired perpendicularly to the horizon, they must nonetheless fall back to the same place from which they were fired, whatever daily and annual motion the earth might have <note>This refers to the ongoing scientific debates of the time regarding the rotation of the Earth and its effect on falling objects.</note>. They will know the manner of firing the cannon by the force of Harmony, and according to what ratio the speed of musket balls and other missiles diminishes. To which I add that some estimate that the curved line of the **dead range** <term>dead range<gloss>original: "portée morte" — the trajectory of a projectile after it has lost its initial horizontal momentum and begins to fall</gloss></term> almost forms the figure of a **parabola**, because the natural weight of the ball pulls it toward the center in equal times by straight lines which are in the same ratio as the odd numbers, by which we have explained the speed of natural movements; for example, if the ball drops by one inch in the first interval of its dead range, it will drop by 3, 5, 7, 9, etc., in the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th intervals. 

Although others estimate that the said curvature describes a **hyperbolic** line, which Gunners can test by placing 7 or 8 cloths, or other bodies easy to pierce, all along the said range; for the distance of the holes to the horizontal line will determine the said curve. Now, perhaps Divine Wisdom used these sorts of lines that arise from the sections of the cone of which I have spoken to adjust the shapes and mechanisms that serve the eye and the ear; for there is a great appearance that the convex of the crystalline humor <note>The lens of the eye.</note> is hyperbolic, or that it has chosen the most advantageous figure of all to create clear and distinct vision. There are many other things that Gunners can observe—for example, how much deeper <note>original: "graues" — meaning lower in pitch</note> the whistling of cannonballs is than those of musket balls in their dead range, in order to notice the proportion of the size of the cannonballs and bullets in relation to their sounds.

I said "in their dead range" because one does not hear the whistling of arquebus balls in their straight line from **point-blank** <term>point-blank<gloss>original: "blanc en blanc" — a shot fired directly at a target without calculating for the drop of the projectile</gloss></term>, at least when one's ear is close to the place where they pass, even if they are hollow, as I have experimented several times; and I could not even hear them when the ball had already traveled more than 300 **toises** <term>toise<gloss>an old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.39 feet</gloss></term>. Now, if these whistlings are in the same ratio as the diameter of the balls, one will know their size, and consequently their weight, by their whistling, just as happens with bells, strings, and pipes, whose sounds indicate their dimensions, as I have demonstrated in the books on *Instruments*.

As for the speed of the movement of cannonballs and bullets, whether in their point-blank range or in their dead range, they can know it if they notice the speed of one of the parts of its movement, because it diminishes in the duplicate ratio of the times; for example, if half of the point-blank range lasts one second, or one beat of the pulse, and that half-range is 37 **toises**, and the movement lasts ten seconds, the ball will travel 51 **toises** in the second beat of...

He first remarks that the **Imperial cannon** of the Netherlands—which is 12 feet long, has a **caliber** (or mouth diameter) of 7 inches, a bore length of 16 "mouths" <note>This refers to the ratio of the barrel length to the diameter of the bore.</note>, and a ball of 42 to 44 pounds—carries 280 **geometric paces** from target to target, or at a level, and 653 in its **dead range** <term>dead range<gloss>original: "portée morte" — the point where the ball's momentum is exhausted and it falls to the ground</gloss></term>; and that it carries **point-blank** <term>point-blank<gloss>original: "de point en blanc" — the range at which a projectile can be fired directly at a target without accounting for gravity's pull</gloss></term> in its range of 45 degrees (that is, at the 6th point), 1160 paces, and 2800 in its dead range.

Secondly, he finds the length of the point-blank range by means of a **quadrant** <note>original: "quart de cercle" — an instrument for measuring angles of elevation</note> divided into 6 equal parts; he says that if the ball, being fired at the first point, travels the length of the line that **subtends** <note>original: "ſouſtend" — the chord of an arc in geometry</note> the first part of said quadrant, then it travels the chord of its 2 parts at the 2nd point of the cannon's elevation; at the 3rd point it travels the chord of 3 parts, and so on for the others up to the 6th point (that is, at an elevation of 45 degrees), where the ball travels the line that subtends the entire quarter of the circle.

### I. NOTICE.

There are so many things in our Treatises that can serve Engineers and the military that it is difficult to explain them without writing an entire book. For example: they can use the <term>echo<gloss>the author suggests using the time delay of a returning sound to calculate distance</gloss></term> to measure the moats of a city, the width of a pond, or a river, etc.; and use the speed of sound to know how far they are from the enemy, as is easily concluded by the 21st Proposition of the 3rd book of Motions. Soldiers will know, through the second book of Motions, the time necessary to avoid stones that are dropped or thrown against them from the tops of walls or elsewhere. ### III. NOTICE.

After having rectified the trials of the perpendicular flight of the ball which rises high by the force of gunpowder, I have found that it falls back so far from the place where one fires the <term>musket<gloss>a heavy, long-barreled muzzle-loading gun</gloss></term> or the <term>arquebus<gloss>an early form of portable firearm, lighter than a musket</gloss></term>, that it is no longer surprising if one does not hear it fall by day or night. Now, I find by the calculation made according to the proportion that weights keep in the speed of their falls—which I discussed in the 2nd and 3rd book of *Motions*, and in this one—that the ball rose 338 toises, because it employed 26 seconds from its exit from the arquebus until its return. However, it did not rise so high with every shot, for I sometimes found only 284 toises and a time of 24 seconds; and when we fired with <term>lead shot<gloss>original: "dragée," small pellets rather than a single solid ball</gloss></term>, it went and returned in the time of 12 seconds, and consequently it only rose 72 toises.

As for the great range of 45 degrees, we found it hardly greater than the perpendicular, namely from 330 to 360 toises, so that those who say that this great range is 9, 10, or 11 times greater than the horizontal <term>point-blank<gloss>original: "de blanc en blanc," referring to a shot fired level toward a target</gloss></term> range, like Ufano and the others who treat the Art of Artillery, are very far from our experiments; unless the wind, which was against us, decreased this range by two-thirds. I wished to remark upon this so that those who have the opportunity may conduct these experiments in calm weather, and as exactly as they can; or if I do them, I will provide notice.

### VIII. PROPOSITION.

->*Explaining several paradoxes of the speed of motions, for the benefit of Masters and Generals of Artillery, and of Engineers.*<-

When one fires cannonballs, musket balls, arrows, or other missiles perpendicularly upward, it is certain that if they fall back, their total descent lasts no longer than their entire ascent; that is to say, they descend in a time equal to that which they employ to rise. For example, arrows, rods, fireworks, <term>bolts<gloss>original: "matras," a type of arrow with a heavy, blunt head</gloss></term>, stones, etc., which one throws perpendicularly upward, and which employ 5, 6, or 7 seconds to rise, employ just as many to descend; which happens similarly even if the shot is not perfectly perpendicular. Thus, it is very probable that a ball fired at an angle of 45 degrees takes as long to fall from the point of its greatest height as it took to rise, as the experiments show. But the paradox of this phenomenon consists particularly in the fact that the descending missile has almost

no force compared to that which it has while ascending, even though it descends at the same time—the reason for which is very difficult to find. For experience does not show that an arrow which rises slows its movement so significantly toward the end that it is slower than the corresponding movement of the fall, which always seems to increase in the same ratio as the <term>violent motion<gloss>A term from Aristotelian physics referring to motion caused by an external force, such as a bow or gunpowder, as opposed to "natural motion" caused by gravity</gloss></term> under consideration decreases. Thus, if a ball or an arrow began to descend from the top of a tower at the same moment that another was fired from an <term>arquebus<gloss>An early type of long-gun or portable firearm</gloss></term> to travel exactly to the top of said tower, the first would reach the ground at the same moment the second reached the top of the tower.

The second paradox consists in the fact that it seems an arrow moves much more slowly while descending the last ten <term>toises<gloss>A French unit of length roughly equal to 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet</gloss></term> than when it first leaves the bow; for it starts so quickly that it is almost invisible, whereas at the end it seems to travel so slowly that one could catch it with the hand without being injured, even though its entire descent is as fast as its ascent. This would lead one to judge that the last toises of violent motion are as much slower than the first toises of <term>natural motion<gloss>The movement of an object toward its "natural place," such as a heavy object falling toward the center of the Earth</gloss></term>, as the first stages of violent motion are faster than the last stages of natural motion. However, the experience of the eye does not seem to correspond to this balance of slowness and speed between the first natural toises and the last violent ones. In my opinion, the air being split and struck perpendicularly while ascending brings no more resistance, nor consequently more force to the blow, than when it is struck while descending. Therefore, one cannot find the reason for the lack of impact in the fall there, any more than in the fact that it is natural. Indeed, I know no reason for it, unless one takes it from the lesser speed of the final parts of natural motion, which may be much slower than the first parts of violent motion—even though the entire fall occurs in a time equal to the ascent, as shown by all sorts of experiments both in a perpendicular line and on all sorts of planes inclined to the horizon. But the light of experience does not show clearly enough that the first parts of the fall are faster than the last parts of the ascent, and consequently whether the speed of violent motions decreases in the same ratio as that of natural motions increases; I leave the determination of this to those who can conduct experiments exact enough to conclude what must be held as truth.

I add only a few observations I have made regarding arrows shot from bows, having been unable to do the same with balls from a <term>musket<gloss>A heavy infantry firearm</gloss></term>, a pistol, or a <term>wall gun<gloss>original: "arquebuse à croc"; a very heavy arquebus supported by a hook or rest, used in fortifications</gloss></term>. This is because, of several shots fired perpendicularly upward both by day and by night, I could neither hear nor see the balls fall back, nor where they landed at their greatest range at 45 degrees.

As for arrows, one that rises 32 toises perpendicularly takes 4 seconds to ascend and just as many to descend. Thus, if it follows the speed of its fall, it travels 14 toises in the first <term>second<gloss>original: "seconde minute"; the author is using the early terminology for divisions of a minute</gloss></term> upon leaving the bow, then 10 toises in the second second, 6 in the third, and 2 in the fourth; since heavy bodies falling from 34 toises in 4 seconds travel two toises in the first second of their fall, 6 in the second, 10 in the third, and 14 in the fourth.

### PROPOSITION IX.

->*To demonstrate that Kings and all the greatest Powers of the earth can*<-
->*derive utility from our Harmonic Treatises, wherein one sees several*<-
->*observations on Sounds and Echoes.*<-

If all men knew and loved God as they ought, and as they are able, I do not doubt that they could use our Treatises and our experiments very advantageously, and particularly those concerning motion; since Monarchs, for example, can use the speed of sounds to learn news of everything that happens across the entire surface of the earth in a very short time, as I demonstrate in this fashion.

It is first certain that a sound, whether loud or soft, of whatever kind it may be—for example, that of the voice, or of a pistol, or a musket, etc.—whether against a headwind or with a favorable one, travels through the air at an equal speed, as we have experimented several times very exactly. <note>Modern physics shows that wind speed actually does affect the speed of sound relative to a stationary observer, though the author’s experiments led him to believe otherwise</note>. Secondly, that it travels 230 <term>toises</term> in the time of one second, as we have similarly observed both on great mountains and in the park avenues of <term>Monsieur de Verderonne<gloss>Referring to the estate or gardens of Claude de L’Aubespine, Marquis de Verderonne, where the author conducted acoustic experiments</gloss></term>, and elsewhere. From this, it follows that sound will not take 30 hours to travel around the earth, as I had said in the first corollary of the 21st Proposition of the 3rd book of *Movements*, because I was speaking there only of the speed of sounds reflected by echoes; but having found that the speed of direct sounds is much greater—since they travel 230 toises in the same time that the sounds of an echo only travel 162—it must be concluded that sound can travel all around the earth in 21 hours and 5 minutes, and consequently, if there were "voice posts" <note>Relay stations for shouting or signaling</note> or other sounds in suitable places, one could learn...

The direct voice covers 115 toises in half a second, therefore it covers 80 in less time, since 80 is nearly one and a half times in 115, for 120 is <term>sesquialter<gloss>A ratio of 3:2</gloss></term> of 80. This is why those who wish to create echoes of 14 syllables must place the reflecting surface 160 toises away, which will take two seconds to respond to a syllable pronounced in the seventh part of a second. However, I do not wish to conclude the cause of this delay so firmly that I am not ready to accept a better reason, as I am with all the other difficulties of which I have spoken.

## COROLLARY.

If sound-posts were established from Rome to Paris, one could have news every hour of everything happening there; for sound does not take even 55 minutes to travel 300 <term>leagues<gloss>A "lieue" or league varied, but was typically about 2.5 to 3 miles (4 to 4.8 km)</gloss></term>, whereas no horse, or other animal, nor even any bird, can go from one of these places to the other in three hours—even if they flew as fast as an <term>arquebus<gloss>An early type of long-gun or musket</gloss></term> ball at point-blank range. Such a ball would take at least three hours to make this journey, even assuming it maintained its initial speed, for it only covers those first hundred toises in a second and a half, as I have remarked elsewhere; consequently, it would only cover one league in 37 seconds.

...after the three parts of a concert, all the others are nothing but replicas; and each virtue is like a particular string of the soul, whose harmony chases away passions and vices, just as the sound of David’s harp chased away demons. <note>A reference to the Biblical story in 1 Samuel 16, where David plays the lyre to soothe King Saul’s troubled spirit.</note> And if one wishes to apply the 18 strings of the 3 genres, <note>In 17th-century music theory, the "three genres" usually refer to the Diatonic, Chromatic, and Enharmonic scales inherited from Greek antiquity.</note> which are explained very clearly in the 13th Proposition of the Book of Genres, it is easy to compare them to the exercises of the 3 kinds of life—namely the active, mixed, and contemplative—each of which can be divided into 15 or 18 parts, or exercises, so that each one corresponds to each string; or into 5 considerations, to be accommodated to the 5 types of Tetrachords. Now, the ill effects of dissonances, and the displeasure they bring to the hearing, can let us conceive of the disorder that passions and vices bring into life, so that there is nothing in all of Harmony that does not serve morality, whether to show the Harmonic, Arithmetic, and Geometric middle <note>In this context, the "middle" or "mean" refers to the classical concept of the Golden Mean or the mathematical proportions used to define "virtue" as a balance between extremes.</note> of each virtue, or for anything else one can imagine.

If it were permitted to take the same liberty that Plato, Ptolemy, and several others have given themselves in the relationships they have made between sounds, consonances, and Genres, and the soul, its faculties, and everything concerning it, we would have the subject of an entire volume; for they say that sound carries the idea and the affection of the one who sings into the depths of the listeners' minds, which they believe to be the link between the soul and the body, and that it ravishes them with an inexplicable pleasure. Thus, if consonances were mixed with as much artifice as flavors, or that which charms the sense of touch, Apollo would have much more power over them than Bacchus or Venus. <note>Apollo represents order, reason, and music, while Bacchus represents wine/excess and Venus represents lust/physical pleasure.</note> Now, Ptolemy compares the simplicity of the Octave to the understanding, or to the rational life, in the 4th chapter of his 3rd book; the <term>Diapente<gloss>The musical interval of a Fifth</gloss></term> to the sensitive life; and the <term>Diatessaron<gloss>The musical interval of a Fourth</gloss></term> to the vegetative life, because the Fifth is closer to the octave than the Fourth, just as the sensitive life is closer to the rational than the vegetative is. He further compares the three types of Fourth to the 3 stages of the vegetative life—namely to its beginning, its vigor, and its decline—but I would prefer to compare them to its 3 functions—namely to engender, to increase, and to preserve, or to attract, to retain, and to reject. He compares the four types of <term>Diapente</term> to the four principal faculties of the sensitive soul, which consist of seeing, hearing, smelling, and tasting; and the 7 species of Octave to those of the rational soul—namely to imagination, intellect, memory, the cogitative power, opinion, reason, and science. I leave the rest of his chapter for one to read, so that one may judge if the reasons for the number of virtues, which he accommodates to reason, the irascible, and the concupiscible, <note>These are the three parts of the soul in Platonic and Aristotelian philosophy: the rational, the spirited (anger/courage), and the appetitive (desire).</note> are sufficient to compare them to the <term>Diapason<gloss>The musical interval of an Octave</gloss></term>, the <term>Diapente</term>, and the <term>Diatessaron</term>.

But I have explained all this so particularly in the 13th Theorem of the 1st book and in the 16th of the 1st book of the treatise on *Universal Harmony*, printed under the name of <term>Sermes<note>Anagram for Marin Mersenne.</note></term>, that it is not necessary to speak of it further. To this one may add the 27th, 28th, and 29th chapters of the abridgment made by Marsilio Ficino of Plato's *Timaeus*. I will only remark that the large intervals that ascend and then descend—as happens when one ascends by a minor Sixth and descends by a semitone—excite sadness and tears, particularly if the meter is binary and heavy, for triple meter excites joy. I say, then, that the knowledge of Harmony serves to judge the lawsuits that may arise between the parishioners or the **Churchwardens** <note>Lay members of a parish administration who managed church property and finances.</note> of a church and the **organ builders**; the latter claiming that his organ is perfect and that they are obliged to accept it, and the former contesting that it is not in proper condition. **Judges** will also profit from the reading of this work to judge the disputes that can occur between two or more **Music Masters**; for example, if the King gave the leadership of his **Chapel** <note>The "Chapelle Royale," the group of musicians and singers who performed for the King’s religious services.</note>, or of all his Music, to the most learned musician in France, and it was a question of sending Commissioners to preside over their competition, they will easily judge their knowledge. They will be able to interrogate them themselves and see, by two or three questions and difficulties they propose to them, who is the most skillful; and consequently, they will judge equitably without favor, and without there being any possibility of appeal, since they will know the science of Music much better than the competitors, if they read and understand our Treatises. For one must not imagine that the hope of 15 or 20 thousand livres of income, which the said Masters can acquire in a short time in this position, is not capable of inciting a lawsuit.

This science can also help **Presidents** and other officials who open the sessions of the Palace <note>The *Palais de Justice*, the seat of the high courts.</note> or their Chambers, or who deliver **harangues** <note>Formal, oratorial speeches.</note> before the King, because the beauty, the precision, the fine order, and the other circumstances of Harmony will provide them with a thousand beautiful thoughts to begin their subject, and often win the good graces of the King, who so dearly cherishes the beauty of this Art that it is difficult for the inventions and comparisons drawn from it not to be agreeable to him. I leave aside a thousand other uses that they will apply themselves to whatever they please while reading each Treatise, or whichever one pleases them most. They will also regulate all the disputes that may arise between **bell-founders**, since they will be able to know the weight of bells by their sounds, and vice versa, as I demonstrate in the book on Bells.

## PROPOSITION XI.

->*To consider ratio in all its kinds, and to explain the terms*<-
->*necessary to understand them.*<-

The relationship, or the habit that two things have together, is called **Ratio** <term>original: "Raison"; in 17th-century mathematics, this term specifically refers to the relationship between two quantities.</term> by Geometers, and because things are either equal or unequal, they establish two types of ratios. One is that of **equality**, which is explained by two equal numbers, such as 2 and 2. Now, this ratio forms its own category, or rather it has no category, since it has no subspecies; so that it may be compared to God, who is above all genus and every species.

But the category of **inequality** is divided into two other subordinate categories, namely the ratio of **major inequality** and **minor inequality**, each of which has five species. For when that which is greater surpasses the lesser in such a way that it contains it several times without anything remaining—as it happens that 2 contains one twice, and three contains it 3 times, and so on to infinity—this ratio is called **Multiple**, and it contains an infinity of individuals, namely the **double** ratio, the **triple**, the **hundredfold**, the **thousandfold**, etc. And when the smaller thing is the **antecedent** of the ratio, it is **sub-multiple**. This must be noted once and for all: the ratio of minor inequality differs from the **major** only in that one must add the syllable or preposition **sub** <note>original: "souz"</note> before the name of the major inequality ratios. It must also be noted that the first term of the ratio, or the comparison, is called the **Antecedent**, and the second is the **Consequent**, although they can be named more simply the **First** and **Second**.

The second species of ratio is called **Superparticular** <note>original: "Surparticuliere"; a ratio where the greater term contains the smaller term once, plus one "aliquot" (even) part of it.</note>, because its greater extreme contains the lesser once, and additionally one of its aliquot parts. For example, 3 contains 2 plus half of 2; and 4 contains 3 plus a third of three. This is why the name of each individual of this ratio is taken from that aliquot part. From this, it follows that we say the ratio of 3 to 2 is **Sesquialter**, or **as much and a half**, because the aliquot part is a half; and that of 4 to 3 is **sesquitertian**, or **as much and a third**, because the aliquot part is a third, and so on to infinity, since a whole has an infinity of aliquot parts. And if one puts the smaller term first to serve as the antecedent of the ratio, one adds **sub**; for example, that of 3 to 4 is **sub-sesquitertian**.

The third species is called **Superpartient**, because its larger term contains the smaller once, plus two or more of its aliquot parts, such as two-thirds, three-quarters, etc., which cannot form a single aliquot part of the smaller term. For example, 5 contains 3 plus two-thirds of the same 3; this is why we call the ratio of 5 to 3 **superbipartient three**, or **superpartient two-thirds**, so that the aliquot parts are expressed after the word **superpartient**.

The 4th species is nothing other than the first joined to the second, as when one compares 5 to 2; for 5 contains 2 twice, plus half of 2. This is why this ratio <term>Raison; the relationship between two numbers or quantities.</term> takes its name from both the *multiple* and the *superparticular*, and is called **Double-sesquialter** <note>A ratio of 5:2. In music, this represents a compound interval of an octave plus a fifth (a twelfth).</note>. If 2 is the first term, we say **sub-double-sesquialter**, and so on for the others.

The 5th species is composed of the first and the third, as seen when comparing 8 to 3, for 8 contains 3 twice, plus two-thirds; this is why it is called **Double-superpartient-two-thirds**: or **sub-double**, if 3 is placed in the first position. Now, all these species of ratios are called <term>Rational</term>, because their terms are in the same relationship as numbers to numbers, where unity <note>The number 1.</note> always serves as the common measure. But there is another kind of ratio called <term>Irrational</term>, such as that of the diagonal of a square to its side <note>The square root of 2; a value that cannot be expressed as a simple fraction of two whole numbers.</note>, of which we will speak after having explained what concerns the rational ones.

I say then, first, that if one divides the greater term of a ratio by the lesser, one will have the *denomination*, or the name of that ratio, and consequently one will know it by its extremes: for example, if one divides 16 by 2, the quotient 8 shows that these two numbers, 16 and 2, are in an octuple ratio. If one divides 3 by 2, one and a half gives their ratio of "as much and a half" <note>This is the literal translation of the Latin *sesquialtera*.</note>; just as dividing 8 by 3, one has 2 and <gloss>⅔</gloss> for the name of the ratio **double superpartient two-thirds**.

In the second place, if one divides the greater term by the name of the ratio, one will have the lesser term; and if one multiplies the lesser, one will have the greater. Thus, it suffices to know one of the terms of a given ratio to find the other: for example, 6 being given for the double ratio, one gets three by dividing it by 2 (which names the double ratio); and if one has 4 for the sub-double ratio, 2 multiplied by 4 gives 8.

In the 3rd place, if one multiplies the extremes by whatever number one wishes, the products will always be in the same ratio as the extremes: for example, if one multiplies the terms 3 and 2 by 4, one will have 12 and 8 in a sesquialter ratio, and so on for the others. Finally, one finds the <term>radical terms</term> <note>These are what we today call "lowest terms"—the smallest whole numbers that represent a specific ratio.</note> of each ratio in the following manner. The denominator of the ratio and unity give those of the multiple; for example, 2 (which is the denominator of the double) and 1. The denominator of the <term>aliquot part</term> <note>A factor or part that divides a number exactly without a remainder.</note> and the number greater by one give those of the superparticular ratio, as seen in the sesquialter of 3 to 2, of which 2 is the denominator. The denominator of the aliquot parts and the number composed of the numerator and the denominator give those of the superpartient ratio: for example, 3 is the denominator of the surbipartient-three, and the numerator is 2; which, when added to the denominator, gives 5. The lesser term always remains in the particular multiples and superparticulars, as seen from 5 to 2, which is double sesquialter, and from 8 to 3, which is double surbipartient three: from which it follows that the radical terms of each ratio do not share any aliquot part except for unity.

As for the generation of ratios, one obtains multiples by multiplying the numbers that follow naturally by the denominator of the first multiple—namely by 2, if one wants to have all the double ratios, or by 3 to generate all the triples; as one sees...

### XII. PROPOSITION.

->To explain incommensurable or irrational quantities and ratios.<-

Those who are not accustomed to the terms of geometry are astonished by what is called an *irrational* ratio; and those who know only numbers have difficulty imagining it, especially since there are no numbers that are not **rational**, because they all have unity as their **common measure**. But when one considers lines and their **powers** <note>In this context, "power" refers to the square of a line's length.</note>, one encounters an infinity of **irrational** relationships. For one can take as many lines as one wishes that are **commensurable** and **incommensurable** in length and in power to any other proposed line, which is called *rational* because it is known, and its parts can be explained by numbers if one wishes.

But one must first consider the **incommensurability** of two terms between themselves before mixing in this "rational" line. We shall do this using lines, though it can in some way be applied to motion and time. I say first, then, that lines which cannot be measured by a common linear measure are **incommensurable in length**, as happens with the **diagonal of a square** compared to its side. For if one divides the diagonal by the side, and the side by the remainder of the diagonal, and so on consecutively, one will never encounter two equal parts, and one will always exceed the other by an incommensurable part; this also happens to the line composed of the diagonal and the side.

As for lines that are incommensurable not only in length, like the preceding ones, but also in power, there is likewise an infinity of them. For example, the **mean proportional** between the side and the diagonal has no common measure, whether in length or in power; it is

to say that its **square** is not at all commensurable to the squares of the **diameter** <note>In 17th-century geometry, the "diameter" of a square refers to what we now call the diagonal.</note> and of the side (the former being double the latter), for the square of a line or a number is its **power**. Now, it is so evident that there are **irrational ratios**—that is to say, those that cannot be expressed by numbers <note>Meaning they cannot be written as a ratio of two integers, like the square root of 2.</note>—that it is not necessary to prove it. For example, the two equal ratios that compose a **double ratio** <note>The Octave (2:1).</note>, or by which it is divided by the **mean proportional**, are irrational. The same occurs with the 6 or 12 ratios that divide it into 6 equal **tones** or 12 equal **semitones**, of which we have spoken in the 1st, 2nd, and 4th books on String Instruments. This double ratio and its division are found in the square, where the diameter is the mean proportional between the two lines that are in a double ratio. And if one describes a smaller triangle on half the diameter of the preceding square, so that its side serves as its diameter, it is certain that the large diameter will be double the smaller one; consequently, the large diameter, its side, and the side of the smaller one will be three **continually proportional** lines. The middle line will divide the ratio of the two extremes into two halves of the double ratio. From this, it follows that the ratio of the diameter to the side is half of the double ratio; it often happens that the whole can be expressed by numbers, even though they cannot explain its half, if one takes the divided ratio as a whole and the dividing ratios as its parts.

Now, just as the mean between the diameter and the side is incommensurable to them in power—because there is the same ratio of the square of the diameter to that of the mean as there is from that same diameter to the side—similarly, all other means between the said mean and the diameter (or the side) are always incommensurable in power. If one wishes to know everything pertaining to lines (both commensurable and rational, and incommensurable and irrational) and to squares and rational or irrational planes, one must read the 10th book of **Euclid** <note>Euclid’s *Elements*, Book X, is the classical Greek foundation for studying irrational numbers.</note>, for it is not appropriate to include it here. Therefore, I come to the explanation of the ratios that are necessary both to Musicians and to all those who make a profession of reasoning and contemplating the works of the **Creator**, who has made everything in **number, weight, and measure** <note>original: "en nombre, en poids, & en mesure." A reference to the biblical Book of the Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note>—that is to say, in proportion—though it is very difficult to find their exact terms and progression.

Now, all knowledge of ratios consists of numbering, continuing or composing, adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing them. Thus, the preceding Proposition can be compared to Arithmetical notation, and those that follow to the Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, and Division of Numbers. Consequently, this Treatise is the **Arithmetic of Ratios**, which I have previously provided in the 5th Latin book of *Dissonances* <note>Referring to Mersenne's own *Harmonici Libri* (1636), specifically the section *De Dissonantiis*.</note>. But because few Musicians understand that language—even though many of them have fine minds—I am explaining them here in **French** for their benefit.
