## PROPOSITION XII.

### *To continue, add, subtract, multiply, and divide ratios.*

#### Continuation of Ratios.

->*A given ratio is continued by ensuring the consequent <note>In a ratio like 4:6, the first number is the antecedent and the second is the consequent.</note> has the same ratio to another term as the antecedent has to said consequent.*<-

This method seems more difficult in its terminology than in its operation, which depends entirely on the **rule of three** <note>A mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known values, based on proportions (if a/b = c/x, then x = bc/a).</note>, as I show in the ratio of 4 to 6, where the antecedent is 4 and the consequent is 6. For if 4 gives 6, it is evident that 6 will give 9, because 9 exceeds 6 by half of 6, just as 6 exceeds 4 by half of 4. That is to say, the ratio of 6 to 9 is **sub-sesquialter** <note>original: "souzsesquialtere"; a ratio of 2:3, or 1 to 1.5.</note>, just like that of 4 to 6. And if one begins the ratio with 9, one will find that there is the same ratio from 9 to 6 as from 6 to 4, and that both are **sesquialter** <note>original: "sesquialtere"; a ratio of 3:2.</note>. Now, this operation has an infinite number of uses, as is easy to conclude from much of what I have said in various places, from all the examples found in books of arithmetic, and from all the solutions for triangles that depend upon it.

I will provide just one example from **Physics** to demonstrate its practice. It is certain that every kind of sound <note>original: "bruit"</note> travels 230 **toises** <note>An old French unit of length, approximately 6.4 feet or 1.95 meters.</note> in one second; one may then know how many toises it travels in one minute of an hour. For this purpose, one must say: if 1 gives me 230, how much will 60 (that is, one minute) give me? This is found by providing a third number that is to 60 as 230 is to 1; which one obtains by multiplying 230 by 60, namely 13,800 toises, which is to say, nearly 5 and a half **leagues** <note>original: "lieuës"; a league was roughly 2.5 miles or 4 kilometers.</note>.

Now, this first rule serves to find the terms of a **consonance** <note>A harmonious musical interval.</note>, or of a doubled, tripled, or quadrupled **dissonance**, and so on to infinity. It also serves to disabuse those **Practitioners** <note>Referring here to practical musicians or performers who may lack theoretical mathematical training.</note> who believe that the consonances they call **repliques** <note>original: "repliques"; octave repetitions of an interval.</note> or repetitions are simply doubled. For example, they believe that the **Twelfth** <note>original: "Douziesme"</note>, whose ratio is 1 to 3, is nothing other than a doubled **Fifth** <note>original: "Quinte"</note>. From this it would follow that if the ratio of 2 to 3 were doubled, it would be 1 to 3, whereas it is actually 4 to 9, as I have shown above. For the ratio of 1 to 3 is actually composed of the ratio of 1 to 2 <note>An octave.</note> and that of 3 to 2 <note>A fifth.</note>.

Finally, this Proposition is very useful for doubling and tripling all sorts of ratios in order to determine the ratio of **planes** <note>Two-dimensional surfaces.</note> and **solids** <note>Three-dimensional volumes.</note>. For example, when one wants to know the ratio of two squares whose sides are in a sesquialter ratio of 3 to 2, this ratio being doubled (as seen above) shows that said squares are in the same ratio to each other as 9 is to 4. And if one wishes to go further to find the ratio of **cubes** whose sides are as 3 to 2, one must continue the ratio further to find a number that is to 4 as 2 is to 3—that is, a number in a sub-sesquialter ratio to 4—and one will have 2 2/3. Thus, the sequence 9, 6, 4, 2 2/3 (or, to avoid the fraction, 27, 18, 12, 8) contains three continued sesquialter ratios, and consequently three **Fifths**, or a tripled Fifth, whose extremes 27 and 8 show the ratio of cubes that have 3 and 2 for their sides. One can continue ratios in this same fashion to infinity...

...which is of little use in Music, because two or more doubled, tripled, and continued chords <note>In this context, "chords" refers to the mathematical intervals or ratios themselves.</note>, as many as one might wish, are worth nothing and always create dissonances, with the sole exception of the Octave. ### PROPOSITION XIII.

> *The addition of ratios is performed by multiplying the antecedent of one of the ratios by the antecedent of the other, and the consequent by the consequent; for the products resulting from these multiplications contain a ratio composed of the two added ratios.*

One must write these numbers so that the antecedent <note>The first number in a ratio.</note> of one ratio is opposite the antecedent of the other, and the consequent <note>The second number in a ratio.</note> opposite the consequent, in this manner \*. And after having drawn a line beneath, one must multiply 4 by 3 to get 12, which is placed beneath the antecedents, and then 3 by 2 to get 6, which is placed beneath the consequents,

And if one wishes to add one or more other ratios to the ratio of 12 to 6, it is best to first reduce it to its radical terms—namely to 2 and 1—and then add whatever other ratio is desired in the same manner as we did before, without it being necessary to give further examples. I only add that this addition of ratios is necessary for Musicians who desire to prove the truth of their positions; for how will they prove that the **sesquioctave** <note>The ratio 9:8, representing a Major Tone.</note> and the **sesquinuefiesme** <note>The ratio 10:9, representing a Minor Tone.</note> of the major and minor tone create the **Diton** <note>A Major Third (literally "two tones").</note>, or that the minor tone joined to the minor Third makes the Fourth, if they cannot add said ratios?

### PROPOSITION XV.

->*One will multiply the given ratio if one takes the powers of the antecedent and the consequent to the degree determined by the multiplier.*<-

This will be easily understood by the examples that follow: let us suppose then that one wishes to multiply the ratio <unclear>as</unclear> 3 to 2, and consequently the **Fifth**, and because multiplication goes on to infinity, that it must only be doubled and tripled: the squares of its antecedent 3 and of its consequent 2 will give 9 and 4 for the doubled ratio; and the cubes of the same antecedent and consequent will give the tripled ratio of 27 to 8; just as the **squared-square** <note>The fourth power ($x^4$).</note> of the same antecedent and consequent will give the quadrupled ratio of 81 to 16, and so on for the others to infinity, according as one raises the powers to the squared-cube <note>Fifth power ($x^5$).</note>, cube-cube <note>Sixth power ($x^6$).</note>, squared-squared-cube <note>Seventh power ($x^7$).</note>, etc. So that if the multiplier is 2, one must only square the antecedents and the consequents of the ratios; if it is 3, 4, 5, or 6, etc., one must cube them, square-square them, square-cube them, etc. But one rarely passes beyond cubes, because the rest consists more in the imagination than in nature, which contents itself with cubes <note>A reference to the three dimensions of physical space.</note>. Upon which one should remark that there is nothing more useful in all of **Geometry** than this multiplication of ratios, joined to their division (of which we shall speak later), as it is easy to conclude from all that we have said of the speed of descending weights, which is in a doubled ratio <note>In modern terms, the distance an object falls is proportional to the square of the time ($d \propto t^2$).</note> of the times, and through the entire treatise on Bells, pipes, and other Instruments: so that the knowledge of ratios is entirely necessary to understand the greatest part of our discourses.

### PROPOSITION XVI.

->*One divides the given ratio by taking the roots of the antecedent and the consequent to the degree determined by the divisor.*<-

This Proposition can be called the inverse of the preceding one, because it uses <term>roots</term> <note>The author uses the word "roots" or "sides" (original: *racines* or *coſtez*) to describe the base value which, when multiplied by itself, produces a square or cube.</note>, or the sides of the powers, whereas the previous one used the powers themselves. Now, we call the roots "sides" because they produce geometric figures when they are multiplied by themselves or by other numbers. This will be easily understood by the following example: if one wants to divide the ratio of 27 to 8 by 3, it is certain that 3 represents the third order—that is to say, the side, or the **cubic root**. Consequently, one must take the two cubic roots of 27 and 8, which are 3 and 2, to divide the ratio of 27 to 8. This resulting ratio of 3 to 2 is contained within the ratio of 27 to 8 three times, as I demonstrate with these numbers: 27, 18, 12, 8. For the <term>sesquialter ratio</term> <note>The ratio of 3:2, which produces the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</note> exists between 27 and 18, between 18 and 12, and between 12 and 8. Thus, the ratio of 27 to 8 is the triple of the ratio of 27 to 18 (or 3 to 2), just as 8 to 27 is the sub-triple of 2 to 3.

Now, this division of ratios is **Geometric**, because of the equality of the ratios it contains. However, **Arithmetic** division only considers the equality of the distance of its middle term, which must always be equally distant from the extreme terms. This occurs in the arithmetic division of the <term>double ratio</term> <note>The ratio of 2:1.</note> of the **octave**, expressed as 2, 3, 4. Here it is good to remark that the product of this middle term is always greater by one unit than the product of the extremes; for 3 times 3 makes 9, which surpasses the product of 4 times 2 (which is 8) by one. In contrast, the product or the square of the **Geometric** middle is equal to the rectangle, or the product, of the two extremes.

As for **Harmonic** division, it is of so little consequence in the true theory of Music that there is no need to add to what I have said from the 34th Proposition of the first book of *Consonances* up to the 40th; in the 6th Proposition of the 3rd book of *Dissonances*; and on the 3rd page of the Preface to the book of *Consonances*. And if one wishes to see a longer discourse, it will be found in the 5th Latin book of *Dissonances* <note>original: "5. liure Latin des Diſſonances," referring to the Latin version of his musical treatise, *Harmonicorum Libri*.</note>, from the 22nd to the 40th Proposition.

### NOTICE.

Those who wish to delve deeper into these ratios, in order to use all the types of reasoning employed by Geometers when they compare the <term>antecedent</term> <note>The first number in a ratio.</note> to the antecedent and the <term>consequent</term> <note>The second number in a ratio.</note> to the consequent by **alternate** ratio; let them take the consequent as the antecedent to compare it to the antecedent as if it were the consequent, by **inverse** ratio. Let them take the antecedent with the consequent as a single term to compare it to the same consequent, by **composition** of ratio. This is **converse** when one takes the antecedent and the consequent as a single term to compare it to the antecedent; just as it is the contrary when one takes the antecedent to compare it to the antecedent and consequent...

## PROPOSITION XVII.

### *To explain the preceding operations on ratios, both by lines and by numbers.*

The following manner for adding and subtracting ratios was given by Mr. de Beaugrand <note>Jean de Beaugrand (c. 1584–1640), a French mathematician and rival of Descartes.</note>, a very subtle Geometer, in the 12th Proposition of his *Geostatics*, which I add to the preceding Propositions so that one may see the demonstration of all the operations I have explained. I say, firstly, that one will compose <note>In this context, "composing" ratios means multiplying them together, which in musical terms corresponds to adding two intervals together.</note> the ratios of AB to BC, and of CD to DE, in this fashion.

**I**f one wishes to know the way to find two or several <term>mean proportionals</term> <note>Middle values that create a continuous geometric proportion between two numbers (e.g., finding the 'steps' between two notes).</note>—for example, finding 5, 6, 7, etc., means—between two other given numbers, in order to divide their ratio into as many equal ratios as one desires, beyond what can be concluded from the 5th, 7th, 8th, and 9th books of the *Elements*, one will find the method in the 21st chapter of the *Algebra* of Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a highly influential Jesuit mathematician.</note>. ### PROPOSITION XVIII.

*If heavy bodies become lighter as they approach the center of the earth, to investigate what the reason for this is.*

If a heavy body, for example, a lead ball weighing one pound, becomes lighter the closer it approaches the center of the earth; and if it weighs nothing at all when it reaches said center—as Mr. de Beaugrand <note>Jean de Beaugrand (c. 1584–1640) was a French mathematician and rival of Descartes; his work *Geostatics* (1636) argued that weight decreases as one approaches the Earth's center.</note> concludes in his *Geostatics*, where he maintains that the weight of every body diminishes in the same ratio as it approaches the center of the earth, and even that the entire earth itself has no weight—one might imagine that it would be quite easy to move it to another location with little force, and that the great machines of Archimedes <note>Archimedes famously claimed that with a long enough lever and a place to stand, he could move the world.</note> are not necessary for this purpose. It would also seem possible to infer that weights falling toward the center would not always increase their speed until reaching the center, in the same proportion as they increase it when falling from 147 feet high (as we stated in the 2nd book of *Motions* <note>Referring to the author's previous work on the physics of falling bodies.</note> and elsewhere); rather, they would slow their movement until coming to rest at the center of the earth, beyond which they would not pass. This is unless we consider the counter-example of balls attached to a cord, which often pass beyond their center or their line of direction before coming to rest, as I have said in the same book—though one might argue that this center is not like that of the earth, and that the ball only rests there by force, being unable to fall according to its natural inclination.

Now, if weights diminish according to the preceding ratio, one can say that this diminution occurs because of the attraction of all parts of the earth, which has two hemispheres, one pulling from one side and the other from the other. For example, let the diameter <margin>A | B | C <image-desc>A vertical line diagram positioned in the right margin, with the letter A at the top, B in the middle, and C at the bottom, illustrating the diameter of the Earth and its center as described in the text.</image-desc></margin> of the earth be A C, and the center be B. When the weight A is at point A, it is attracted by the whole earth A C; but when it has descended to B, it will be equally attracted from both sides by the two hemispheres B A and B C, and consequently, it will be unable to move toward one side or the other. Regardless, it seems it is not within human power to demonstrate whether the earth is so easy to move and transport to whatever place in the air one wishes—requiring only the overcoming of the resistance of the surrounding air—or if it is so firm and stable in the place God has given it that it cannot be shaken by any created force.

However, since Mr. Fermat <note>Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665), the famous lawyer and mathematician, who corresponded frequently with the author on these physical paradoxes.</note>, Counselor to the Parliament of Toulouse and a most excellent geometer, has given me the reasoning he developed regarding the varying heaviness of weights as they approach the center: if this position is true, one could designate a place in the air where a weight of one pound would weigh only a grain <note>A "grain" was a very small unit of weight, roughly 0.065 grams. There were 9,216 grains in a French "livre" (pound).</note>. This would happen when the ratio of the two distances from the center to the weight is the same as one to 9,216, for there are that many grains in a pound. Consequently, a weight that weighs one pound on the earth's surface would weigh only one grain if it were only 310 toises <note>A "toise" is an old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet.</note> from the center of the earth; and if the weight were only one toise away, it would weigh only the 310th part of a grain. I wish to share his thoughts on this subject with the public.

F

Which he demonstrates in this fashion: let C be the center of the earth, and CA the radius, upon which point B is taken; at this point, the attached weight is to the power R as AC is to CB. C will then be the center of gravity of the body composed of the two weights B and D; this is why, if one removes power R from point A, weights B and D will remain in equilibrium, since the line BA has no weight <note>The author assumes an idealized "weightless" rod for the sake of the geometric proof.</note>. And if one places a weight at A that pulls downward, equal to the power R which pulls upward, it is the same as if one removed power R from point A, since the weight pulls down as much as the power lifts up.

Let this weight then be placed at A; thus, the body composed of power R placed at A (pulling upward), the weight at A (pulling downward), and weights B and D, will remain in equilibrium. Now, since weight D is equal to weight B, and the line CD is equal to line CB, then AC is to CB as AC is to CD, and as weight B is to power R placed at A, so weight D is to the weight placed at A that pulls downward (which is assumed equal to power R). Now, as AC is to CB, so weight B is to power R placed at A; therefore, as AC is to CD, so weight D is to the weight placed at A. Consequently, the weight placed at A will be in equilibrium with weight D, since the distances are in <term>inverse proportion</term> <note>original: "proportion reciproque." This is the law of the lever: weight times distance must be equal on both sides.</note> to the weights. But if one removes weights that are in equilibrium from other weights that are also in equilibrium, those that remain will still be in equilibrium. Therefore, if from the equilibrium formed by power R placed at A (pulling upward), the weight placed at A (pulling downward), and weights B and D, one removes the equilibrium formed by weights A and D, those that remain will stay in equilibrium.

Indeed, if one considers the weights attached to a balance beam <note>original: "fleau de balance"</note>, whose support is the center of the earth, the demonstration seems convincing: but because two heavy bodies that are not joined by any beam, and which do not depend on each other at all, do not form a single body, or a single mass of which one could take the center of gravity, I do not see the force of this demonstration. This is because if one imagines two heavy bodies in the air, which are not held by anything—for example, bodies A and B—I do not see why they should be considered as if they were conjoined and united together by means of some line that goes from A to the center of the earth C. Consequently, it seems that there is nothing to prevent weight B from weighing as much at point B (or at another point taken between B and C) as it weighs at A; although I hope that the one who first proposed this proposition <note>The author is likely referring to Jean de Beaugrand, whose work "Geostatics" (1636) claimed that weight decreases as an object approaches the center of the Earth.</note> will give us such satisfaction on this subject that no more difficulty will be found, as he promises in his *Geostatics*.

Those who consider a particular center of gravity in each part of a proposed body, and who give a particular inclination to each point of said body to descend to the center of heavy bodies (which is supposed to be the same as that of the earth), prove by another way—which seems better to me—that weights become lighter, or weigh less, as they approach said center, but not in the same proportion as they approach it. For example, if a weight were raised from the surface of the earth to the Moon, it would weigh more, but it would not be by a quarter; whereas in the other opinion <note>Referencing the theory that weight changes in direct proportion to distance.</note> it would weigh 60 times more, if the Moon is 60 times as far from us as the distance from here to the center of the earth. 

But because the other different weight comes from the different angles made by each point of the proposed body (by reason of the straight line by which it wants to descend to the center of the earth) with the line that crosses the center of gravity of said body, or which is parallel to it, it follows that if the weight is considered as a point—that is to say, if one considers a point that has weight—it will always have the same weight near or far from the center of the earth. This does not happen in the other opinion, in which this point becomes lighter in the same ratio as it approaches the center, just as the heavy body does. Now, one can understand the force of the reasoning, which gives unequal powers to each point of a proposed weight to descend to the center of the earth, by what has been demonstrated in the *Treatise on Mechanics*, which is at the end of the 3rd book of *Movements* <note>The author refers to his own earlier sections in *Harmonie Universelle* regarding the laws of motion and mechanics.</note>.

I add only that a weight attached and suspended at the end of a string <note>original: "filet"</note>, having no need of any force to be supported in its line of direction other than the said string which supports it, and weighing always more as it is further from this line, seems to conclude that each weight should no longer weigh anything at the center of heavy things, and that it is heavier the further it moves away from it. Whatever the case may be, Preachers <note>In the 17th century, "Natural Philosophy" (science) was often used by clergy to create moral allegories or "moralities" for their sermons.</note> can draw moralities from both opinions; for if weights grow heavier in proportion as they approach their center, as we see indeed that they hasten their course <note>A reference to the acceleration of falling objects.</note>, they will use this to show that the soul moves with more—

Now, the 44-pound ball of the **Imperial Cannon** must take as much time to ascend as it does to descend, if its perpendicular path is 2,392 <term>toises</term> <note>A toise is an old French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet.</note>.

Fourthly, I explain here the easiest method of all those possible for us to find how high each ball, arrow, or other missile rises perpendicularly. This consists simply of holding our **second-hand clock** <note>One of the earliest references to using a pendulum or balanced clock for scientific timing.</note>, or any other kind one wishes, in the hand and counting the number of its beats. Half of this number, when squared, gives the number of <term>toises</term> or feet the missile traveled while ascending or descending. For example, if one finds 30 seconds (or clock beats) from the moment the ball is fired until its fall, one must take half, which is 15. The square of this, 225, shows that the ball descended 225 measures, each of which is equal to the measure or space it covers in the time of one second—that is, 2 toises or 12 feet. This is because a ball of lead or iron, falling from a height of only 12 feet, employs one second in that fall, as I have already remarked in the aforementioned book of *Motions*. From this, it follows that the 225 preceding measures made by the descent of the ball in 15 seconds must be doubled (multiplied by 2) if one wants the path of its fall in toises, or multiplied by 12 if one desires it in feet.

Fifthly, because one might doubt whether some part of the **violent impression** <note>A term from early physics referring to the kinetic energy or "impetus" imparted by the gunpowder.</note> which preceded remains in the descending ball, and whether this part delays its natural fall and by how much; and furthermore, whether it always keeps the same proportion we have spoken of, increasing its speed by the **square of the times** <note>A reference to Galileo’s law of falling bodies: distance is proportional to the square of the time.</note>. It would be appropriate to test this by means of some very high mountains, or coal and charcoal pits. For if the ball or arrow falls back as fast after having been fired as it falls when one simply lets it drop from the hand, the "violent impression" changes nothing. And if it descends the aforementioned 225 measures in 15 seconds, its speed always increases following the proportion we observed up to 147 feet high. Now, the great speed of the descending ball is the reason it has great effects; for **Monsieur Gallé** told me that musket balls pierce copper plates the thickness of two **lines** <note>A "line" is a small unit of measurement, 1/12th of an inch.</note>, or one-sixth part of a **Royal foot**, when they fall back after being fired perpendicularly. We can examine this in this way: It is certain that if the musket ball takes 30 seconds to rise and fall, it will take 15 to descend, and it will rise 450 toises high; consequently, it will cover 29 and a half toises in the last second of its fall, as seen in the table on page 101 of the book of *Motions*. But because this ascent would not be five times the horizontal **point-blank range** <note>The distance a projectile travels in a straight line before gravity causes it to curve significantly.</note>, as shown by our observations (which do not testify that it is more than triple, or at most quadruple), I set it higher in favor of what others who have treated the **Cannon** say. For this subject, I suppose the ball rises perpendicularly 1,152 toises, so that this path is nearly ten times the level point-blank range of the musket, which is held to be 120 toises. From this, it follows that it will employ 48 seconds from its exit from the muzzle until its fall; and taking half, that is, 24 for the time of its fall, it will cover 94 toises in the last second of its fall—that is, it...

In the 6th place, if one reflects on all sorts of movements that occur on planes inclined to the horizon, whether in a straight or curved line, whether the weights roll without being attached or are supported by a rope, one will always find that their <term>natural return</term> <note>In the physics of this period, "natural motion" (falling back to Earth) was contrasted with "violent motion" (being forced upward or outward).</note> occurs in a time equal to that of their **violent movement**; this was enough to conclude the same thing regarding perpendicular motion. From this, one can conclude that there is a certain **equilibrium** in all of nature that one cannot remove, whatever force and industry one might apply, as is experienced in the <term>equilibrium of the Siphon</term> <note>A reference to hydrostatic principles where liquids seek a level balance.</note>, and in all sorts of moving forces which do not allow one to increase force unless one simultaneously increases time. This is also held as an axiom or a maxim in the **spiritual life of Christians**, who approach God all the more as they distance themselves further from creatures; this perhaps caused, in part, an excellent man of our time <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary philosopher or theologian, possibly René Descartes or a prominent Jansenist/Augustinian thinker.</note> to place our **liberty** in the detachment from all sorts of creatures, believing that we are never more free than when we move toward our ultimate end without any reflection or regard for creatures.

In the 7th place, it is appropriate to remark upon the force and the effects of the balls from a **battery cannon**, in order to compare them with the effects it has when it falls perpendicularly. Now, the tests that were made in the presence of **Count Buquoy** <note>Charles Bonaventure de Longueval, Count of Bucquoy (1571–1621), a famous commander in the Thirty Years' War.</note> show that these balls enter 17 or 18 feet into newly made works of earth and <term>fascines</term> <note>Bundles of sticks or brushwood used to reinforce the walls of trenches or fortifications.</note>; and **Master Gallé** <note>Likely an engineer or author of military treatises.</note> assures us that it pierces from 18 to 22 feet into newly moved earth or settled sand: in firm, settled, and fatty earth, from 10 to 14 feet: in beaten and tight clay, from 9 to 12: in dry and hardened potter’s clay, from 7 to 10: in walls of medium-baked brick, or of <term>tuff</term> <note>A porous rock formed from volcanic ash.</note>, pumice stone, etc., from 4 to 6 feet; and in those of hard stone, such as marble, <term>sandstone</term> <note>Original: "grez."</note>, and other stones that share the nature of flint, from 2 to 4 feet, when one fires the 1st species of Cannon from 800 to 1200 feet, which amounts to 150 or 200 of our <term>toises</term> or thereabouts. As for bales of wool, it pierces through 3. I leave aside several other things concerning Cannons, about which one could make a particular philosophy—for example, how much further they fire on land than on sea, being tied and fixed rather than making their recoil, etc.; for as to the 8 shots it can fire per hour, the cost of the powder, and the officers who govern...

# On the Utility of Harmony.

regarding the distances of batteries, and everything concerning the military, several authors have written entire treatises on the subject.

Now, before finishing these notices, I wish to add the observations of Monsieur Gallé, an excellent Engineer and Mathematician, because he has applied more care to this than any other whom I know. Having used a <term>perrier</term> <note>A 'perrier' was a type of stone-throwing mortar or small cannon used in early modern warfare.</note> or mortar, which carried eight-pound iron balls, and whose chamber contained six ounces of musket powder, he found in the year 1622—in the presence of the Sieur Mortagne, General of the Artillery—that its horizontal <term>dead range</term> <note>Original: "portée morte." This refers to the distance the projectile travels until its first impact on level ground, without accounting for subsequent bounces.</note> was 529 feet (each foot equaling approximately 10 and a half <term>lines</term> <note>A 'line' (ligne) is an old unit of measurement equal to 1/12 of an inch.</note> of our <term>King's foot</term> <note>The 'Pied de Roy' was the standard French unit of length, roughly 32.5 cm or 12.8 inches.</note>). After firing twelve other shots from 5 degrees up to 45, he noted that the dead ranges followed the numbers in this table:

| Dead Ranges | |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Degrees** | **Feet** |
| 5 | 960 |
| 10 | 1340 |
| 15 | 1669 |
| 20 | 1949 |
| 25 | 2178 |
| 30 | 2359 |
| 35 | 2490 |
| 40 | 2569 1/2 |
| 45 | 2600 |
| 50 | 2570 |
| 55 | 2491 |
| 60 | 2361 |

Having adjusted the same piece to 85 degrees, he found its range to be 952 feet. As for the other degrees, since he did not test them, I am not including the proportional table he later created from 1 degree up to 90, which I will show to those who desire it.

He also conducted another trial with a <term>quarter-cannon</term> <note>A specific size of artillery piece, typically firing a 12-pound ball.</note>, which deserves consideration; for having raised it 5 feet high above the horizon, like the previous mortar, he found along the Rhine that its horizontal dead range, while preventing its <term>recoil</term>, was 3368 feet, and its greatest range at 45 degrees was 16850 feet—that is to say, about five times greater. The same piece, firing at a level but allowing for recoil, has a range of 2803 feet, which is about one-sixth of the maximum range; thus, the level range without recoil is one-sixth greater than with recoil.

He further observed that the <term>point-blank range</term> <note>Original: "portée de point en blanc." Historically, this was the distance a projectile traveled in a nearly straight line before gravity caused it to drop significantly.</note> of the musket is to its dead range as 4 is to 7; and therefore, the level point-blank range of the same piece, with recoil, is 1605 feet (for 7 is to 4 as 2803 is to 1602), and without recoil, it should reasonably be 1925 feet. Thus, the point-blank range with recoil is to the dead range at 45 degrees without recoil as 1 is to 10 1/2, and the point-blank range without recoil is to the dead range at 45 degrees without recoil as 1 is to 8 3/4. The same piece firing with recoil at 45 degrees carries 15883 feet, so that the horizontal dead range with recoil is to the dead range at 45 degrees with recoil as 1 is to 5 2/3, and the point-blank range with recoil is to the maximum range with recoil as 1 is to 9 4/5.

When I have made the necessary observations to regulate more specifically everything belonging to this subject, I will share them with those who desire them.

# NEW PHYSICAL AND MATHEMATICAL OBSERVATIONS
## First Observation.

->*On the speed of heavy bodies, which descend by their natural motion in air, or in water, and by how much water is heavier than air.*<-

---

Although we have often spoken of the natural movement of bodies descending toward the center of the earth, whether perpendicularly or on inclined planes, it is nevertheless appropriate to add here some remarks in favor of the eleventh Proposition of the second book of *Movements* <note>The author is likely referring to his own earlier work, *Harmonie Universelle* or *Traité des Mouvements*, where he established early rules for mechanics.</note>; the first of which is that it is impossible for heavy bodies to descend in such a way that their speeds follow the ratio of a line divided proportionally, if we follow experimental evidence. This is because if they followed the proportion of a line cut in <term>mean and extreme ratio</term> <note>Now commonly known as the Golden Ratio, where a line is divided such that the ratio of the whole to the larger part is the same as the larger part to the smaller.</note>, they would descend to the center of the earth within the time of one minute of an hour, assuming that their fall covers 3 feet in half a second, as actually happens; and 12 feet in the time of one second. For if 3 is the first term of the said section, 5 will be the second term, 8 the third, and so on, following the fifth column of the table of the said 11th Proposition. Thus, if one continues the numbers, the 34th—which would represent the fall at the 34th second—would be 23,859,617, which contains the number of feet of the said fall, and which surpasses the number of feet in the radius of the earth. The radius is only 17,175,000 feet, or thereabouts—that is to say, 1,145 <term>leagues</term> <note>A 'lieue' or league was a unit of distance; here defined as 15,000 King's feet.</note>, each of which is 15,000 <term>King's feet</term> <note>Original: "pieds de Roy." The standard French unit of length before the metric system, approximately 32.5 cm.</note>. From this it follows that if the fall lasted one minute, and continued to increase its speed following the proportional division of the line, heavy bodies would travel more than seventy thousand times the semi-diameter of the earth, and consequently more distance than there is from here to the stars, whatever distance Copernicus gives them.

Furthermore, if one assumes the first space of the fall to be 3 feet, and the second 5, and one joins these two numbers to make the first term, the weight will descend 8 feet in the first space; but the numbers that follow no longer correspond to the phenomena, and always maintain a different proportion according to the different numbers used for the first term of the progression. This is why the <term>doubled ratio of the times</term> <note>This is an early description of the law of falling bodies ($d \propto t^2$), where the distance (d) is proportional to the square (the "doubled ratio") of the time (t).</note> better demonstrates the speed of falls when the bodies are heavy enough. As for very light objects, such as <term>elder pith</term> <note>Original: "moüelle de sureau." The soft, lightweight spongy tissue found in the center of elderberry stems, often used in early physics experiments to demonstrate air resistance.</note>, which is 193 times lighter than lead, they soon find a point in the air where they cease to accelerate their fall, even though the beginning of their movement is as fast as that of light bodies, or nearly so. But heavier bodies, such as lead, wood, etc., visibly outpace the fall of the said pith after the first or second <term>toise</term> <note>A 'toise' is an old French unit of length roughly equal to 1.949 meters or 6.39 feet.</note>. From this it is easy to conclude that heavier bodies descend faster than light ones, although...

<summary>This page critiques the use of geometric progressions to model gravity, using mathematical proofs to show that such models would result in impossible speeds. Instead, the author advocates for the "doubled ratio of times" (time squared) to describe the acceleration of heavy falling bodies.</summary>

# New Observations

one does not easily perceive this difference in the descent of 147 feet between balls of wood and lead; and they all eventually encounter a point in the air where they no longer accelerate their fall, regardless of their weight <note>The author is describing what we now call terminal velocity—the point where air resistance balances the force of gravity.</note>.

Now, if one finds this location, or this point of equilibrium, in the fall of elderberry pith or cork, one can conclude the point of equilibrium for lead and other bodies whose weight is known. And if one cannot find this point in the air, it will be easy to find it in falls that occur in water, in which movements are slower and can be made in a given ratio; for we have bodies that descend very slowly in water, and others that descend very quickly, such as wax weighted with iron filings or with small pieces of lead. This wax, being made only slightly heavier than water, descends very slowly, while lead descends quite fast.

I add that the progression of the line divided in <term>mean and extreme ratio</term> <note>The Golden Ratio.</note> goes too fast starting from the 6th half-second, in which the lead ball only covers 33 feet, and not 34 according to the sections of the said line. This model moves further and further away from the truth, which also contradicts those who imagined that heavy bodies would take 12 minutes to fall from the earth's surface to its center; an hour and a half to fall from the Moon; and 24 hours to fall from the Sun. For this proportion is repugnant to experiments, which always show that bodies as heavy as metals or wood accelerate their fall according to the <term>square of the times</term> <note>The author uses "raison doublée des temps" (doubled ratio of times), the classical phrasing for a squared relationship, $d \propto t^2$.</note> at our ordinary heights, or according to the <term>versed sines</term> <note>A trigonometric function ($1 - \cos \theta$) used in early calculus and physics to describe oscillating or circular motions.</note> of which I spoke in the 3rd Proposition of the 2nd book of *Movements*.

The second thing worth noting concerns the semi-circumference of which I speak in the same place: for besides what I have shown regarding the <term>helical line</term> along which weights descend according to the imagination of <term>Galileo</term>, an excellent Geometer has demonstrated the properties of this helix. This could serve as an occasion to restore the book of <term>Demetrius</term>, *On Plane Lines* <note>original: "περὶ γραμμῶν ἐπιπέδων"</note>, of which <term>Pappus</term> spoke in the 4th book of his *Collections*. I will only say that he notes there a perpetual ratio of 15 to 8; those who wish to know a greater number of details may hope for them from this excellent person. He has found several other new helices, one of which is perhaps the "admirable" one of <term>Menelaus</term>, in which the first space made by the first revolution is half that of the second; and yet all the other subsequent spaces produced by the other revolutions are equal to that of the second revolution, and consequently equal to each other. I leave aside the other properties, for which he will provide the demonstration when he pleases. One can also see the first observation placed at the end of the table of contents, and what I say regarding the fall of heavy bodies in the 2nd observation.

The 3rd thing concerns the matter of finding the height of towers, or the depth of wells, and everything that can be inferred by the fall of heavy bodies: for one must subtract the time that the sound of the weight takes to travel from the place where it falls to the ear, when one uses sound to know the final moment the fall ended. Although this time is so short at our ordinary heights of fall that it is almost negligible—because if the height is only 23 <term>toises</term> <note>A pre-metric French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet.</note>, sound only takes a tenth of a second to spread through all that space—if the well were...

### Physics & Mathematics.

...a depth of 230 <term>toises</term> <note>A French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet.</note>, sound would take only one second to travel, whereas a weight would take 10 and a half seconds to fall from that height, so that 11 and a half seconds would pass before the noise testified to the fall of 230 toises: but I know of no height from which this experiment could be made.

The fourth point concerns the different speeds of falling weights, which must be greater when they weigh more, even though this difference is not easily perceived at the ordinary heights from which they are let fall, unless they are very different in their heaviness. For example, cork takes three seconds to descend from about 50 feet, from which lead descends in 2 seconds, as does wax similarly, though it is eleven times lighter: and yet cork is barely 4 times lighter than the said wax, or 44 times lighter than lead. A ball of <term>elderberry pith</term> <note>The soft, spongy tissue inside the stem of an elderberry plant, often used in early physics experiments for its extreme lightness.</note> only descends in 5 seconds; it is 193 times lighter than lead; and another body 162 times lighter than wax takes nearly 8 seconds to fall from the said 50 feet of height. I always assume bodies of the same shape and volume, so that no difficulty is created here. Now, these different speeds of the falls of all these bodies, and of several others that I have tested, made me imagine a way to find how much heavier water and all other proposed bodies are than air: which several have desired to know. The reader will therefore see if this method, of which I had already spoken in the books on *Movement* and elsewhere, will satisfy him.

<margin><image-desc>A vertical line with letter labels on its left side. Point A is at the top, point C is approximately one-third of the way down from A, and point B is at the bottom.</image-desc></margin> I say then, in the fifth place, that a body which descends in the air is heavier than the air, and that if one finds a body so little heavy that it descends in the air through an equal space, in an equal time, as the space and time that another sufficiently heavy body descends in water, the ratio of the heaviness of the first body will be to the heaviness of the air as that of the second body is to the heaviness of water. I explain this by the line AB, which represents the height of 2 toises both in water and in air, and I say that if body A, being so light that it takes as much time to descend through the air as far as B as the heavier body C takes to fall in the water from C to B, it must only be as heavy in relation to air as C is in relation to water, since both of these elements hinder the descent of bodies by their resistance and heaviness. Now, I have found a body that descends in the air as slowly as lead does in water, for both descend 4 feet in the time of one second, and 12 feet in the time of 2 seconds; which shows that they no longer maintain the <term>squared ratio of times</term> <note>This refers to the law of falling bodies (distance = 1/2 gt²), where distance is proportional to the square of time. The author notes that resistance causes the body to deviate from this ideal mathematical law.</note>, which always decreases little by little until it meets the point of equality, of which I spoke in the 2nd book of *Movement* and elsewhere.

Having weighed body A which descends in the air, I found that it weighs 4 <term>grains</term> <note>A small unit of weight, historically based on the weight of a single grain of cereal.</note>, and that it is at least 162 times lighter than wax of the same volume and shape: so that if we suppose that water of the same size as wax is heavier by a 21st part, it follows that air, being eleven times lighter than the said body A, is 1,870 times lighter than water, since the lead which descends in the same time and from the same height in water is eleven times heavier than it. This heaviness of air can be confirmed by the observation I made of the slowness of the movements of the circles that form in water when one lets a stone fall into it, or touches it with a stick: for while the diameter of the circles of the air makes 1,380 feet in one second

# New Observations

Now, I am taking the smallest proportion of the weight of water to that of air that can be drawn from my observations; and the Reader will find pleasure in considering and measuring very exactly the speed of the diameter of the said water circles, in order to see if it is even less than I have stated: though it is difficult to know if the motion of the water is communicated through its entire solidity <note>In this context, "solidity" refers to the entire volume or bulk of the liquid.</note> and to its depth, as that of the air does; this must be treated elsewhere, after having conducted the necessary experiments.

It is easy to conclude that if a cubic foot of water weighs 70 and a half pounds, or 649,728 grains, a cubic foot of air will weigh about 360 grains, which is to say 5 <term>gros</term> <note>A unit of weight equal to 1/8 of an ounce, roughly 3.8 grams.</note>; and that it would require a marvelously large mass of air to weigh as much as a cubic foot of water. This is why, if one tries the method of weighing air by means of a box of one cubic foot—of which I spoke in the 17th proposition of the 1st book of *Motion*—with air twice as dense being weighed, one will find that the air twice as rare <note>Meaning "thinner" or less dense.</note> in the other equal box (or the same box weighed with these two kinds of air) will weigh only less than two and a half *gros*. That is to say, there will not be half an ounce of difference between the weights of the two types of air. Consequently, if the scale used to weigh the boxes or other similar vessels is not so precise and delicate that a quarter of an ounce easily tips its balance when loaded with said vessels, the experiment cannot succeed. Now, if this difference in weights is found to be as I have said, the method I have maintained through the descent of weights will be beyond doubt, and so certain that everyone can rely upon it. Several other things will be seen in the Corollaries of this observation which pertain to this proportion of weights; for this reason, I come to

The 5th thing, which is no less difficult than the preceding: namely, in what time each body heavier or lighter than water descends or rises within it, and what its movements and speeds are, according to the different heights and pressures that the water has and exerts in channels of different heights. We must first remark that water does not flow through the holes of channels—for example, through open keys, which are called <term>robinets</term> <note>Original: "robinets." These are faucets, taps, or stopcocks.</note>—in the same ratio as its heights or pressures. That is to say, the water that flows and exits a vessel through the tap, or through a hole placed at the bottom of said vessel, does not exit faster or in greater quantity simply because the channel or vessel is higher, such that there would be the same ratio between height and height as between quantity of water and quantity of water. Experiment shows this: for the height of a vessel being divided into 8 equal parts, each being almost a third of an inch (because the water is 2 inches and 7 <term>lines</term> <note>A "line" is 1/12 of an inch.</note> high), it empties drop by drop through a small hole made at the bottom of the vessel, in the times that follow for each part—the first part being that at the top of the vessel, when the water begins to flow and exit faster. Those who make the channel flow very fast will see if the water maintains the same ratio in its discharge as when it exits drop by drop; and if this is found to be the case, it is certain that the experiment is easier to perform in this way, because drops take more time to exit.

->New Observations<-

...makes the lightest body in the air among all those I have been able to encounter, because its gravity <note>The author uses "gravity" (pesanteur) to mean relative weight or density in this context.</note> has the same ratio to that of the air as the gravity of lead has to that of water, as I have already stated. I further add that it is not a marvelous thing to see bodies of the same kind but of all sorts of sizes—for example, a lead ball of one ounce and another of one hundred pounds—descend through the air and through the water in the same amount of time over an equal distance. This is because they must always displace a portion of water or air, which is equal to them in volume: for example, if one ounce of lead causes one grain of air to rise, one hundred pounds will cause 1,600 grains <note>A "grain" was a traditional unit of weight, approximately 0.06 grams.</note> to rise, and so on for the others; so that the gravity of the air, being equal in volume, always increases in the same ratio as the gravity of bodies of the same kind, regardless of what size they may have.

### COROLLARY I.

It is easy to conclude from the preceding observation that the proportion Galileo <note>Galileo Galilei (1564–1642), who famously theorized that in a vacuum, all bodies fall at the same rate regardless of mass.</note> noticed in the speed of falls is not perpetual, and even that it ends quite soon. Indeed, the body we used shows quite clearly from the 4th second onward that it fails to keep this proportion; for descending one foot in the first half-second, and 4 feet in one second, it only descends 12 feet in 2 seconds, whereas it ought to descend 16 feet according to the rules we gave in the second book of *Motions* <note>original: "Mouuemens"</note>. In that book, most of the calculations assume perpetual proportion, a notion I wish for the reader to dismiss from their imagination following these latest observations. Now, it appears that if the said body, which is only eleven times lighter than air, ceases to accelerate its fall within the first 20 feet of its descent, a similar body of lead will cease to accelerate its own once it has fallen 500,000 feet—that is to say, ten thousand times further, because lead is at least ten thousand times heavier. Thus, if one had a height of 40 <term>leagues</term> <note>A league (lieuë) was roughly 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers; 40 leagues is approximately 120 miles, roughly the height of the atmosphere's denser layers.</note> from which one could drop a lead ball, it would find its point of equilibrium near that place. From this, one can judge other bodies more or less heavy than lead, both in water and in air.

### COROLLARY II.

One can adapt to the air everything that Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), the Greek mathematician who discovered the laws of buoyancy: any object, wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, is buoyed up by a force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.</note> demonstrated regarding water, when he explained the manner of weighing all sorts of heavy bodies by its means, provided that one compares the <term>vacuum</term> <note>original: "vuide"</note> to the "air" of Archimedes, and his "air," or our own, to the "water." For every heavy body in the air is heavier in a vacuum by the total weight of a body of air equal to the said heavy body. For example, a lead ball that weighs 12,000 grains in the air will weigh 12,001 grains in a vacuum—that is to say, one grain or 1/12000th more—if the volume of air equal to the said ball weighs only one grain. From this, one can conclude everything that can be said of other bodies more or less heavy than lead.

### COROLLARY III.

One will easily weigh all other sorts of air, both those down here and that which is near the Sun and the Stars, if it extends that far, provided that one is provided with a notable quantity of it; for the <term>Thermoscope</term> <note>An early instrument, a precursor to the thermometer, that shows changes in temperature through the expansion and contraction of air.</note>...

On this point, one might imagine that if there is nothing but a void <note>The "void" refers to a vacuum. In the 17th century, the existence of a vacuum was a subject of intense debate among scientists like Pascal and Descartes.</note> beyond the middle region of the air <note>The "middle region" refers to a layer of the atmosphere in early meteorological theory; it was believed to be the place where clouds and storms formed.</note>, as some believe, one could say that vapors lighter than air begin to weigh more when they arrive at the surface of the void. There, they encounter a very great cold because there is no longer any substance capable of receiving and maintaining heat, and consequently, that is the highest point to which they can rise.

### COROLLARY IV.

Among several objections that can be proposed against the reasoning regarding the heaviness of these two elements <note>The "two elements" here are air and water.</note>, one can be taken from their different stickiness, glue, and tenacity <term>tenacity (tenacité): a term used here to describe what we now call viscosity or surface tension</term>, which causes water not to yield easily, even though it perhaps does not have as much resistance or weight as that of which we have spoken. However, one can imagine the same thing regarding the tenacity of air, which makes it continuous and bound together like water; added to which, everything one might say about the hardness and other qualities of one of these elements can also be said of the other in proportion—particularly if air is nothing but water that has been graduated, purified, and rarefied almost to a supreme degree.

As for those who believe that it is not the air that has weight, but only the vapor mixed within it, they are, it seems, obliged to show that the air is heavier in summer than in winter, since it then contains more vapors. But the difficulty that follows seems much greater to me; that is why I give it a particular corollary, after having remarked that one can also say that movements or falls are heterogeneous <note>Meaning "of a different kind." The author suggests that the laws governing motion might not be directly comparable to the laws governing weight.</note> to weights, which can prevent one from arguing legitimately from one to the other. On this point, it is easy to notice many things regarding speeds and forces or powers, which deserve a particular treatise.

### COROLLARY V.

One of the greatest difficulties that can be raised against the preceding proportion of the weight of water and air—and even against the method we practiced to find it—consists in the descent of other bodies. These should, it seems, make their falls in a time proportioned to their weights compared to one another, or to that of the air. For example, since elderberry pith <note>The soft, spongy tissue inside the stems of the elder tree, used in early physics experiments for its extreme lightness.</note> is 17 times heavier than the body used as a test for the weight of air, it seems it should fall 17 times faster than the said body; and nevertheless, the speed of the fall of the said pith is only as 5 to 3, or 10 to 5, compared to that of the said body.

Similarly, the fall of lead should be more than a thousand times faster than that of this body, since it is more than a thousand times heavier; and nevertheless, the speed of its fall is only as 5 to 1, since it falls in only 2 seconds, and the said body in 10 seconds. Thus, the speed of falls in no way follows the ratio of the weight of the falling bodies, nor that of their weights compared to the weight of the air.

I leave the search for the solution to this difficulty to those who wish to pursue it.

### COROLLARY VI.

If water or air were bounded by some surface that prevented them from expanding further, and one let a heavy body fall into them, it seems that it would be unable to move and would remain on their surface. This is because it could not descend without displacing or causing a volume of water or air equal to its own volume to rise; and because this volume of water or air has no new place to occupy, it could not rise to make room for the heavy body. The body would thus be constrained to remain on the surface of the air or water, assuming it could not condense <note>Condensation here refers to compression—squeezing the fluid into a smaller space.</note> them as much as the space it must occupy. Thus, if God or an Angel prevented the surface of the sea and rivers from rising and increasing, one could walk upon them without sinking.

Refers to Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a philosopher and scientist who proposed using the time it takes for a float to rise from the seabed to measure depth.</note> touches upon in his treatise on *Static Experiments*, and that Besson <note>original: "Besson." Refers to Jacques Besson (c. 1540–1573), a French engineer. Now, the trial can be conducted in the greatest depths of rivers, wells, and the sea, when it is very calm, by having some instrument similar to the one described by Besson. For by attaching to it a body whose lightness surpasses that of water by as much as the weight of the body descending in the water surpasses the weight of water (by reducing the weight of this body by the full lightness of the light body), one can say that the light body will take as much time to rise as it took to descend with the heavy one. A French unit of length roughly equal to 6.4 feet or 1.9 meters.</note>, etc.—one can draw up tables from them to serve as gauges, compasses, and sounding lines for depths. I add that these light bodies joined to others more heavy can serve to make the said heavy bodies exist in a given ratio with the water, so that they descend into it more or less quickly in a given ratio, provided that the terms of this ratio do not exceed the greatest speed or the greatest slowness of bodies falling in water.

This can also be adapted to bodies descending in the air; for a weight that descends 12 feet in one second will descend more slowly if one causes it to descend on a pulley in such a way that it has a counterweight, the weight of which removes as much of its own weight as one desires. For example, if to a pound <note>original: "livre." The pre-metric French pound was approximately 489 grams.</note> of lead one gives a counterweight of 15 ounces of lead, it will weigh no more than one ounce; and one can give it such a large counterweight that it becomes hardly any heavier than air. However, it is appropriate to experiment with the descents or falls of these counterbalanced weights before concluding whether they maintain the same ratio in the speed and slowness of their falls as bodies whose weight is equal to theirs without the opposition of the counterweight. For example, whether a lead ball weighing 8 ounces, and having a counterweight of 8 ounces minus 4 grains <note>A grain was a small unit of weight; in France, there were 576 grains in an ounce.</note>, will descend in the same time as a body that weighs only 4 grains, etc. Now, this manner of delayed falls by counterweights can serve many purposes both in water and in air; for example, to measure the strength of the power that bodies have to rise or descend, or all the impediments that pneumatic and hydraulic machines may suffer by the encounter of weights and counterweights in all sorts of mediums.

## COROLLARY VIII.

Having cast some lead into sand of the same size as a body weighing 4 grains, which descends at least as quickly in the air as the said lead does in water, I found that it weighs 1,854 times more; and because the grains are too heavy by half a grain or so, one can say that the weight of this body (which I shall show to those who desire to see it) has the same ratio with the weight of lead as the weight of air has to that of water—that is, from 1 to 1,870. And if there is an error, it consists rather in making the air too heavy than too light, for it comes very close, in my opinion, to the ratio of 2,000 to 1.

## Second Observation.

### *On violent motions, and those composed of the natural and the violent.*

I have already spoken of violent motions <note>In the Aristotelian physics of this period, "natural motion" refers to an object's inherent tendency to move toward its "natural place" (like a stone falling to earth), while "violent motion" refers to motion caused by an external force (like a stone being thrown).</note> on pages 222 and 225 of the 3rd book of *Motions*, and in the 6th and 8th Proposition of the book *On Utility*, and elsewhere, where I said that missiles <note>The author uses "missiles" to refer generally to any projectile, such as an arrow or bullet.</note> go faster when leaving the bow, the hand, or the arquebus <note>An early type of portable long gun, common in the 15th through 17th centuries.</note>, than when falling back. Indeed, an arquebus ball that takes 12 seconds <note>original: "secondes minutes." In early modern science, seconds were often called "second minutes" to distinguish them from "first minutes" (standard minutes).</note> to fall covers only 46 fathoms <note>original: "toises." An old French unit of length approximately equal to 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet.</note> in the last second of its fall, whereas it covers nearly a hundred in the first second of its violent motion; so that violent motions do not decrease in the same ratio that natural ones increase, contrary to what I may have said elsewhere.

Upon which it must first be considered that some maintain that the same body can go faster at the moment it leaves the force that moves it, even if it does not go as far: for example, that an arrow shot by a pistol <note>Likely referring to a "pistol-crossbow" or a similar mechanical device rather than a firearm, given the use of "arrow."</note> goes faster at the beginning than when shot by a bow, and yet it does not go as far: so that the different types of impression, impulse, or emission are one of the causes of the difference noticed in the effects.

Regardless, the total perpendicular ascent—and perhaps the oblique ascent—of the missile occurs in a time equal to that of the fall back, like the to-and-fro of a weight attached to the end of a cord <note>A reference to the period of a pendulum.</note>: so that by keeping the proportion of natural falls, one knows how high a cannonball has risen once the time of its violent and natural motion has been observed. For example, if half of this duration is 24 seconds, as happens if the motion of a cannonball lasts twice as long as that of an arquebus ball, it is certain that the said ball will have risen, and consequently descended, 1152 fathoms.

Secondly, one can imagine that the impression given to the missile, whether by the hand, the cannon, or otherwise, is nothing other than a certain kind of heaviness <note>The author is struggling to define "impetus" or momentum using the vocabulary of "weight" (pesanteur).</note> that one gives it toward the direction of aim; and that one cannot throw it higher than the height of the cylinder made by the thrown missile, which can be supported or moved by the same force applied to the said missile. For example, when one throws a lead ball 20 feet high, it seems to be nothing else than if, with a force equal to the weight of the ball, one carried it just as high in a time as much longer than that by which it was thrown, as the force that throws it is greater than the said weight of the ball. So, if the lead ball is half an inch in diameter, and one imagines that in passing through the air it leaves behind a lead cylinder of its own thickness as long as its motion—that is to say, 20 feet—this cylinder will weigh as much as everything that the force which threw the ball upward can support. Now, this thought having found favor with several to whom I communicated it, I have found by experience that one cannot support the said cy- <note>The text cuts off mid-word; it likely continues as "cylinder" on the following page.</note>

I demonstrate this in the following manner:

<image-desc>A diagram representing the path and speed of a falling object. It consists of a vertical dotted line labeled with points. At the top are letters E, A, and D. To the left of the line are vertical columns of numbers: a column of 7s, and two columns showing sequences (1, 3, 5, 7) and (7, 5, 3, 1). If the weight A descends to B in 4 seconds, it is certain that it will travel a path of 16 measures, each of 12 feet—namely, one in the first second, 3 in the second, 5 in the third, and 7 in the fourth, as experience teaches; and that in rising violently from C to D, it will travel 7 measures in the first second, 5 in the second, 3 in the third, and one in the fourth. Now, when the numbers facing each other are joined, they always make 8 for each interval of time, so that if a body descends from A to B by these two types of motion combined, it will travel 8 measures in each second, and consequently it will descend from A to B in 2 seconds—namely, from the top of the towers of **Notre Dame de Paris** <note>The famous cathedral in Paris, used here as a standard height reference.</note> by these two motions joined together, if they are only 32 **toises** <term>Toise: An old French unit of length, approximately 1.949 meters or 6.4 feet.</term> high, as is said. Thus, this movement will always be equal, because the natural motion always increases in the same proportion as the violent motion diminishes. 

But if the violent force does not perish at all, the body will descend much faster; for the natural motion will always be accompanied by 7 degrees of speed from the violent force, as seen from E to F, and consequently it will have 8 degrees of speed in the first second, 10 in the second, 12 in the third, and 14 in the fourth, and will travel 44 measures in 4 seconds, which is to say 88 toises. From this, one can easily conjecture that this movement does not last forever; otherwise, one could throw a stone from almost three times as high as the aforementioned tower to the ground in 4 seconds, if the force with which it is thrown gave it 7 degrees of speed.

## III. Observation.

->*On the speed of direct sounds and reflected sounds, or the Echo, and the means of creating a concert in 4 parts with the Echo.*<-

Although I have spoken of the speed of direct and reflected sounds in several places, these observations can serve to create a concert for 2, 3, or several voices, and those to make known the distance of places where the sound of thunder begins or where a cannon is fired. For having arranged three different locations for Echoes separated from one another by 81 toises, and the four principal voices of the first type of **Octave** <note>The author uses the old solfège syllables: UT (now Do), MI, SOL, FA.</note> UT, MI, SOL, FA being sung, the first Echo will repeat the UT at the same time the voice says MI, the second will repeat the UT while the voice says SOL and the first repeats MI, and the third will repeat its UT at the same...

...time that the voice says **FA**; so that those who perform with the Trumpeter—who plays the four aforementioned cadences of the first mode—will hear Music in 2, 3, and 4 parts. This is because the **UT** <note>The original note for "Do" in the hexachord system.</note> of the 3rd Echo will be heard at the same time as the **MI** of the 2nd, the **SOL** of the first, and the **FA** of the voice; in such a way that one will hear **UT, MI, SOL, FA** all at once. This can only happen at a distance of 324 <term>toises</term> <note>A French unit of length; one toise is approximately 6.4 feet or 1.95 meters.</note>, assuming one wishes to make the concert of these 4 voices last the time of one measure, or one second <note>original: "seconde minute." In this era, a "minute" was the first division of an hour, and a "second minute" was the second division—what we simply call a "second" today.</note>, and that each Echo is distant from the other—that is, the 3rd from the 2nd, and the 2nd from the 1st—by 81 <term>toises</term>, which is the distance from the speaker's location.

But a man's voice is not strong enough to make itself heard from so far away, for it would have to travel 648 <term>toises</term> <note>The total distance for the sound to travel to the farthest wall and back.</note>; that is why one can use the first 4 sounds of the Trumpet, which produce the 4 preceding notes. However, it is so difficult to arrange the locations of these 3 Echos that it borders on the impossible, both because it is very hard to make the 3 sounds meet with the same volume—as they must in concerts—and for several other reasons.

As for direct sounds, since they travel 230 <term>toises</term> in each second, it is certain that if the noise of thunder begins with its fire or its flash, and one marks the seconds that pass between the fire seen and the noise heard, one will know the distance of the thunder. For example, if 10 seconds pass, the location of the thunder will be 2300 <term>toises</term> from the ear, which is to say nearly one league. And when one hears the sound of a cannon from 30 leagues away, such as that of the siege of Dole <note>The Siege of Dole occurred in 1636 during the Thirty Years' War.</note> which was heard in Nevers, it is certain that only 5 and a half minutes have passed since the shots were fired when one hears the noise—that is, about the 10th part of an hour. From this, it is easy to conclude that there is no noise in the world so great that it can be heard an hour after it began, unless it is strong enough to be heard from 300 leagues; and how great must be the strength of the sound of the Trumpet which shall call men throughout the world on the great Day of Judgment.

Now, one of the greatest difficulties regarding sound consists in knowing why that of the Echo—that is, the reflected sound—travels more slowly than the direct sound, according to what I said in the 9th Proposition of the book *The Utility* <note>Referring to "L'Utilité de l'harmonie," a section of Mersenne's "Harmonie universelle" (1636).</note>. Weakness cannot be the cause of this, since it is often stronger than many direct sounds. Some imagine that this slowness comes from the reflecting bodies, which must vibrate anew as many times as there were vibrations required to produce the direct sound; but that does not explain why the delay of the reflected sound multiplies in the same proportion as one moves away from the reflecting wall, as I noted on page 46 of *The Utility*. For, assuming the wall vibrates, it should not delay the sound more from a distance than from nearby when it is of the same tone. This I wish to explain further by the following line **ABC**, in order to give occasion to fine minds to seek the true reason for it.

## IV. Observation.

->On the different sounds that the same voice makes at the same time.<-

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'C' featuring floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>This phenomenon of the voice is as marvelous as that of strings, which I noted in the 9th Proposition of the 4th book on Instruments, which is misnumbered as XI; and this error, having begun after the 4th Proposition, continued until the end of the book: but the table of Propositions placed at the beginning of the volume corrects this fault, and all others.

Now, this experiment of the voice consists of the three different sounds, or tones, that it makes at the same time; this occurs similarly in bells, as I showed in the 18th Proposition of the 7th book on Bells, and in cylinders, and other resonant bodies. These vocal sounds have their natural pitch as their base and origin: for when the voice holds its tone firmly, one hears two other very distinct voices, though very faint, one of which is perpetually at the Twelfth, and the other at the Seventeenth above. In such a way that if the principal or lowest voice is at **C (Ut)** <note>original: "C vt sa." These are the note names from the guidonian hexachord system used in the 17th century.</note>, the second is at **G (Sol)** <note>original: "gre sol."</note>, which is 3 times higher in pitch than the **C (Ut)**, and the third is at **E (Mi)**, which is 5 times higher than the said **C (Ut)**. Consequently, the 3 sounds that correspond to these 3 numbers 1, 3, 5, always accompany each other both in the voice and in all kinds of string and percussion instruments; they are 9 vibrations <note>The author is likely discussing the ratios of frequency: the fundamental (1), the 12th (3), and the 17th (5).</note>, of which the lowest voice provides a single one, the second 3, and the third 5.

Nevertheless, I estimate that the other intermediate sounds, namely 2 and 4, which make the Octave and the Fifteenth with the first, are also produced, for I hear them sometimes, and they are easy to understand on strings; but because I have said several things on this subject in the aforementioned 9th Proposition, I do not wish to repeat them here. I add only that to clearly hear these 3 sounds of the voice, one must be in a place removed from noise, and use the lowest tones of the voice, such as the tones of Organ pipes of 5 or 6 feet which serve for the Bass; for one does not hear this multitude of sounds in high-pitched voices, any more than in very short strings or small bells, whether because the ear does not have the capacity to judge sounds so high, or because in fact they are not produced.

not. Now this diversity of sounds can serve as a solution to the 22nd Proposition of the book on the Voice. I only add that the ear does not always perceive the two high-pitched sounds that accompany the principal voice, but sometimes the one that creates the Twelfth <note>In music theory, a "Twelfth" is an interval consisting of an octave and a fifth; it vibrates three times for every one vibration of the fundamental tone.</note>, and at other times the one that creates the Seventeenth <note>A "Seventeenth" is an interval of two octaves and a major third; it vibrates five times for every one vibration of the fundamental tone.</note>.

Indeed, if the circles or motions of the air made by the string, by the larynx <note>The "voice box" or part of the throat used for singing and speaking.</note>, or by other instruments do not create other circles that overlap with those newly formed in the continuation of the sound—thereby creating the aforementioned small sounds by doubling, tripling, or quintupling their tiny vibrations—one must say that from the first production of the sound until it ceases, the bodies that strike the air (or are struck by it) do not beat it uniformly. Rather, one part beats it in such a way that it trembles faster in relation to that part than in relation to others. For example, while the larynx beats the air to be in unison with a six-foot organ pipe, some of its parts beat it so that its vibrations are three times faster than those of the principal sound (when one hears the Twelfth), and other parts of the same larynx beat it in another way to make it tremble five times in the same period. Nevertheless, a greater number of the larynx's parts make it tremble only once in the same period to produce the principal tone. One might also say that the air, being struck or striking, breaks in several ways, splitting or cleaving some of its parts into 2, then into 3, 4, and 5 parts, etc., just as one experiences with water shimmering in a glass when the rim is pressed with a finger: it breaks into several small bubbles or atoms, some of which move only once while others move 2, 3, 4, or five times, etc.

### V. Observation.

->*On the weight of bodies, according to their different distances from the center of the earth.*<-

<image-desc>A vertical diagram placed to the left of the main text block showing a line AC with marked points. A is at the top, followed by D, then B, and C is at the bottom. Point B is identified in the text as the center of the earth, and D as the midpoint of the line segment AC.</image-desc>
In the 18th Proposition of *The Utility of Harmony* <note>original: "l'Vtilité de l'Harmonie," referring to one of the author's previous treatises on music and physics.</note>, I examine whether the same body becomes lighter as it approaches closer to the center of the earth, as some excellent individuals believe. They use several means to try to demonstrate this; for example, a rigid line holding two weights attached to its two ends, as seen in the diagram. In this, one must suppose that point B is the center of the earth, and that points A and C are two equal weights, such that A is twice as far from B as weight C is. Because it seems that line AC should move until its midpoint D joins with the center B—so that the center of gravity of the total weight AC meets the center of the universe B <note>During this period, the center of the Earth was often theoretically equated with the center of the universe in discussions of gravity.</note>—the weight A should, it seems, descend and press or push weight C until C is as far from B as A is. Consequently, weight A would be heavier than weight C because it is further from the center B. But one can deny that weight A can descend, because being equal to C, it pushes just as strongly; so that it
