it is not necessary that the midpoint of the solid line AC join with B, even if CA were an iron bar or a stick. There are even some who doubt whether the stick AC, descending toward B, would stop there as soon as one of its ends reached B. Furthermore, it is not so certain that every body descends all the way to the center that one could not doubt it, given the great multitude of accidents and circumstances that would have to be examined all along the Earth’s radius before being able to conclude so. 

Now, it will not be out of place to add here a particular observation made regarding the arms of a balance, whose weights are in reciprocal ratio <note>In a "reciprocal ratio," the weight on one side of a scale must increase as the length of the arm on that side decreases to maintain balance.</note> to the length of the said arms, following the positions of Archimedes <note>Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC) was a Greek mathematician who defined the principle of the lever.</note>. This is because he supposes that the cords of balances descend in parallel lines, whereas they actually slant and lean toward the center of the Earth, where they would meet if each were 1,145 leagues long. From this, those who consider the balance more precisely conclude that the weights are in reciprocal ratio to the perpendicular lines drawn from the centers of each weight to the line connecting the center of the Earth and the balance; or in a reciprocal ratio composed of the ratio of the slanting lines and the ratio of the angles made at the center of the Earth by the line joining the centers of the Earth and the balance and the aforementioned slanting lines—that is, the lines of inclination or direction of the weights toward the center of the Earth. Or rather, they are in reciprocal ratio to the perpendicular lines drawn from the center of the balance onto the slanting lines, as Jean Benoist <note>Jean-Baptiste Benoist was a 17th-century mathematician known for his work on mechanics and geometry.</note> does in his third chapter on *Mechanics* <note>original: "Mechaniques"</note>; which many excellent geometers <note>In this period, "geometer" often referred generally to mathematicians.</note> consider to be true.

Now, I do not think one can demonstrate that weights descend exactly to the center, or toward the center of the Earth, since we have no experiences or reasons that could not be satisfied and explained even if they only descended within four or five leagues of the said center. From this one may conclude the uncertainty of Mechanics and other parts of Physics, at least regarding men, who do not know the first principles with enough certainty and clarity; without these, one is not assured of the conclusions. This is why it is easy to draw motives for true humility and remedies against the presumption of all the sciences for those who have penetrated them to their principles. For it is difficult to find a man who could have the least bit of vanity in the world regarding the esteem of his knowledge if he meditates seriously on the first maxims that serve as the foundation for what we call Science. 

So it is that everyone can apply to themselves the second verse of the eighth chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, namely: *If anyone thinks they know something, they do not yet know as they ought to know.* <note>original: "Si quis se existimat scire aliquid, nondum cognovit quemadmodum oporteat eum scire."</note> And although he says in the preceding verse, and often elsewhere, that we know many things; and that in the third verse of the sixth chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians, he says the same thing regarding the being of man as he does of his knowledge: *If anyone thinks they are something, when they are nothing, they deceive themselves* <note>original: "Si quis existimat se esse aliquid, cùm nihil sit, ipse se seducit"</note>, in order to detach men's affection from everything that is not God, and to make them seek the "science of the Saints" <note>A traditional theological term referring to spiritual wisdom and the knowledge of God.</note>, which consists of knowing God and loving him perfectly. Nevertheless, if we take "science" according to the rigor of its definition—which requires certain and evident knowledge of the true, primary, and immediate causes of the effect or conclusions—one can take the first passage from Saint Paul in the literal sense, as well as the second, if one compares the being of the creature to that of the Creator.

## VI. Observation.
### *On Pitch, Cornetts, Flageolets, and Flutes.*

It is certain that the holes of these instruments do not follow the proportions of musical intervals, and that no one has found the theory for the distances that these holes must maintain between one another. However, one may follow the practice noted by Master Gallé <note>Possibly a reference to a contemporary instrument maker or theorist familiar to the author.</note>, namely that the length of each of these instruments being divided into 27 equal parts—from the top of the <term>window<gloss>lumiere; the opening near the mouthpiece where the sound is created</gloss></term> to the end of the <term>foot<gloss>pate; the bottom end of the instrument</gloss></term>—the first hole of the <term>cornett<gloss>a curved wooden wind instrument played with a trumpet-style mouthpiece but having finger holes like a flute</gloss></term>, starting from the foot, should be found at the end of the 5th part, the 2nd at the end of the 7th, the 3rd at the end of the 9th, the 4th at the end of the 11th, the 5th at the end of the 13th, the 6th at the end of the 15th, and the thumb hole at the back in the middle of the 16th and 17th parts. The six holes of the fife, and the first six of the <term>recorder<gloss>fleute douce</gloss></term> follow the same proportion, but the 7th hole of the said recorder is at the end of the 17th part, and the thumb hole at the 18th. As for the <term>flageolet<gloss>a small flute with four holes in the front and two in the back</gloss></term>, its first hole must be in the middle of the 4th and 5th parts, the second (which is at the back) at the end of the 6th and 3/4 part, the 3rd at the 9th part, the 4th at 12 1/3, the 5th at 15 1/4, and the 6th (which is at the back) at 16 1/4 parts. If anyone desires to see these proportions on the instruments themselves, I will show them; nevertheless, they are not so exact or necessary that one cannot change them slightly, because those who play them compensate for many things by covering or narrowing the holes with their fingers or with wax.

## VII. Observation.
### *On the manner of tuning all sorts of instruments without knowing music, and without using one’s hearing, or without the accuracy and goodness of the ear.*

Besides the manner which I explain in the 7th Proposition of the 3rd book on Instruments for tuning stringed instruments without the aid of the ear, one can use another method, the foundations of which are seen in the 5th and 13th Propositions of the first book on <term>Consonances<gloss>the study of harmonious sounds</gloss></term>; namely, the vibration of straws or other light bodies placed upon the strings. For if one tightens them while touching and sounding them until these bodies vibrate very strongly upon the untouched strings—whether on the <term>spinet<gloss>epinette; a small harpsichord</gloss></term>, the lute, or the <term>viol<gloss>viole</gloss></term>, etc.—it is certain that they will be in tune at the unison, the octave, or indeed the twelfth <note>original: "Douziéme"</note>, since the vibration is very small at the fifth and other consonances.

Now, assuming they are all at unison, or at a simple or repeated octave, one can make them go up or down to whatever chord or discord one wishes by means of <term>bridges<gloss>cheualets; movable supports used to change the vibrating length of a string</gloss></term>. For example, if one wants to tune the harpsichord by equal semitones so as to begin the <term>do, re, mi<gloss>vt, re, mi</gloss></term>, etc., on whatever key or <term>accidental<gloss>feinte; the black keys on a keyboard</gloss></term> one wishes, in order to raise or lower all sorts of tones by one or several equal semitones, the bridge applied successively to eleven...

The portions of the string chosen for this purpose, following the 11 <term>mean proportionals<gloss>a mathematical method used to divide an octave into twelve equal parts by finding geometric means</gloss></term>—which I have explained in the 2nd and 6th books of *The Instruments*, and elsewhere—will yield exactly the 12 equal semitones. According to these, one must tune the 11 shorter or thinner strings in unison with the said 12 semitones marked on the string taken as the foundation of the tuning. This is done to tune an entire octave, from which one can very easily tune all the others by means of the octave interval. This [resonance] will cause straws, papers, or other similar objects placed on the untouched strings to vibrate <note>The author is describing sympathetic resonance, where a string vibrates automatically when a note an octave apart is plucked nearby, used here as a tool for precise tuning.</note> as you seek to tune them.

Now, it is easy to quickly find the places on the fundamental string where the <term>bridge<gloss>cheualet; the wooden piece that supports the strings and transmits their vibration to the body of the instrument</gloss></term> must be placed, by using a <term>compass<gloss>compas; here referring to a specialized proportional scale or measuring rule</gloss></term> made of two wooden rules. Upon these rules shall be marked the numbers or lines of the 11 mean proportionals: for when this compass has an opening equal to the said string, its eleven marked points will show the eleven points on the string under which the bridge will produce the 11 equal semitones.

This compass can serve as a <term>universal pitch-standard<gloss>Diapason vniuersel; a reference tool to ensure consistent tuning across different instruments</gloss></term> for all kinds of instruments, and even for cutting organ pipes to a precise length. This applies whether one uses this tuning of equal semitones, or the one common among practitioners on both the organ and the <term>spinet<gloss>Epinette; a small, plucked keyboard instrument similar to a harpsichord</gloss></term>, or if one wishes to practice "just" tuning <note>Just intonation, where intervals are based on whole-number ratios, sounding very pure but making it difficult to change keys.</note> of which I have spoken in several places. Since these tunings are marked on the said compass, they will be just as easy to apply to all kinds of instruments, even though a <term>temperament<gloss>the slight adjustment of intervals away from mathematical purity to allow for playing in different keys</gloss></term> must be used there. This is because usually only 12 keys are used for each octave; consequently, it is impossible to find consonances or other intervals in their perfect purity, except perhaps for some specific song where all the tones and steps have been adjusted to their purity on the strings and keys of the instrument. However, as soon as one wishes to play another air using different sounds, the instrument will no longer be in tune, the reason for which I have given in several places. From this comes the necessity of making all semitones equal on the <term>Viol<gloss>Viole; a bowed, fretted string instrument</gloss></term>, the <term>Lute<gloss>Luth</gloss></term>, etc., in order to play all sorts of pieces upon them.

However, I know of no one but Master Gallé who has adapted this [equal] tuning to the organ and the spinet. Having seen the trial of it, the experience led me to consider the theory I had set down in the 1st and 2nd books of *The Instruments*: namely, that the <term>Fifths<gloss>Quintes</gloss></term> are so little diminished that it is almost impossible to distinguish them from "just" ones. Only the <term>Major Thirds<gloss>Tierces majeures</gloss></term> are too sharp by slightly more than half a <term>comma<gloss>a very small musical interval representing the tiny difference between two notes that are theoretically the same but arrived at by different mathematical paths</gloss></term>. This offends the ears of our practitioners, who are not accustomed to this tuning, so that the difference of this Third—augmented by a one-hundred-and-twenty-seventh part—is large and notable enough to be perceived by the ear and to cause discomfort. The equal semitones have also been judged too small to create pleasant <term>cadences<gloss>the concluding sequence of notes in a musical phrase</gloss></term>, such as those made from *mi* to *fa*; hence they are not pleasing on the minor semitones of the spinet.

As for the Minor Third, it is diminished by 1/111, while the Sixth is increased by the same amount. The Minor Sixth is diminished by 1/127, while the Major Third is increased by that amount. The Fifth is diminished by only 1/444, while the Fourth, which is its complement, is increased. The equal semitone is smaller than the major semitone by 1/142 part—that is to say, by a half-comma, or thereabouts; this also offends the ears of our practitioners.

# New Observations

Some believe they can find the previous agreement of equal semitones by starting *ut, re, mi, fa, etc.* <note>The traditional solfège syllables used to name the notes of the scale.</note> on each key of the **spinet**, either by the number of vibrations or the **beats** <note>The "beat" is an acoustic pulsing heard when two notes are slightly out of tune with each other; as they come closer to a "just" or pure interval, the beating slows down and eventually stops.</note> produced by the **fifth** and other tempered consonances. For example, the **fifth** beats once every second <note>original: "ſeconde minute." In early modern scientific French, this typically refers to a second of time.</note> when the fifth is tempered as it should be, on both the **organ** and the **spinet**; whereas when it is "just," it no longer beats.

Now, I am astonished by the dispute of some excellent **lute** players, who do not believe that the most pleasant **fifth** is in the ratio of 3 to 2, nor that the other consonances are in the terms usually given to them. They think those of their lutes are sweeter and more charming; yet, if they had measured two strings of the same thickness, both good and equal, one of which was 3 feet and the other 2 feet, such that they were stretched by the same force, they would disabuse themselves. They would find that only necessity forces the tempering of fifths—that is, to diminish them and to increase the fourth, and so on for the others. But stubbornness is so particular to certain people, who despise accurate observations before forming their doubts, or who believe in no experiments unless they perform them themselves, that they do not deserve one to work for them or to reason with them.

Additionally, according to the common proverb among practitioners, the **lute** is the **charlatan of music**, because it makes what is bad on good instruments pass for good. Now, the beats that occur roughly every second between the strings and the pipes forming the fifth and other tempered consonances show that they are sweeter when they are "just," for then no beating is heard. On this point, it should be noted that strings and pipes beat faster as their sounds are higher-pitched; the reason for this is easily explained by the number of unions and disunions of the vibrations of the air.

But I am reserving many things worthy of note regarding these beats until I have verified several experiments belonging to this subject. Now, it is certain that if the **organ** and the **spinet** were tempered according to the neck of lutes and viols, the resulting concerts would appear more "just" because of the compatibility of their tunings. But our practitioners are not of the opinion to change the tuning of the spinet to force it into the lute's tuning, for fear of losing the perfection of their **thirds** and their **semitones**, which are among the greatest beauties and varieties of music.

Those who wish to make a portable <term>monochord<gloss>a scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard with a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical relationships between intervals</gloss></term> to tune the **spinet**, the **organ**, and all other instruments, may use the **endless bow** <note>original: "archet ſans fin." Likely a mechanical device such as a wheel or a continuous belt that bows the string, similar to the mechanism of a hurdy-gurdy or a "geigenwerk."</note> of the new invention, which I mention in the General Preface and elsewhere. This is so that the sounds of the strings give the ear leisure to taste and well understand the fifths, the thirds, and the other consonances, whether just or tempered, according to the tuning one wishes to apply to the instruments. For this bow keeps the tone steady on the strings as long as one likes, which so closely imitates the sounds of the organ that it is as easy to tune all its pipes with this monochord as it is the spinet, the lute, etc. One can put 2, 3, or 4 strings in unison on the said monochord, so that...

## IX. Observation.

->*On the practice used by spinet players and organists for tuning.*<-

It is certain that the first **keyboards** <note>original: "Clauiers"</note> had only the 8 sounds and 7 intervals of the **harmonic hand** of **Guido of Arezzo** <note>original: "Guy Aretin." Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033) was a music theorist whose "Guidonian Hand" served as a mnemonic device for singers to find pitches.</note>, following the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, *a*, of which I spoke in the first Proposition of the 6th book on Consonances and often elsewhere. From this, it happened that the **accidentals** <note>original: "feintes," literally "feints." These refer to the raised keys (black keys) which were seen as "faked" or "feigned" versions of the main notes.</note> or **sharps** <note>original: "dieſes"</note> which have since been added have retained the name of the principal keys <note>original: "marches"</note> upon which they depend or which they supplement. For example, the accidental a minor semitone away from *C ut* <note>C</note> is named the accidental of *C sol ut* <note>The note C in the medieval hexachord system</note>, and so with the others marked by the sharp sign in practical musical notation. However, many mark the accidental or the *fa* of *E mi* <note>E</note> by a **flat** <note>original: "bmol"</note>, as well as that of *b fa b mi* <note>B</note>, because these two accidentals have the same properties. As for the accidentals of *F ut* <note>F</note> and *G re* <note>G</note>, they are marked like that of *C ut* <note>C</note>. *D re* <note>D</note> and *A mi la* <note>A</note> have no accidentals a minor semitone away.

Now, some imagine that the first inventors of these accidentals initially tuned all the **fifths** as just <note>pure, or mathematically perfect</note>, or nearly just, following the equal tuning of which I spoke in the previous observation. But as their ears could not tolerate the **major thirds** (which are necessarily too sharp <note>original: "fortes," literally strong or high in pitch</note>, because when all semitones are equal—acting as a middle ground between the major and minor semitones—each semitone is too large to properly transform a minor third into a major one), they tempered the tuning such that they weakened the fifths in order to lower the major thirds, which offended the ear with their excessive harshness. This they did with such skill that they produced twelve fifths so slightly weakened and diminished that they do not offend the ear. The first of these is from the accidental of *E mi* <note>E-sharp/F</note>, which is kept sharp, to that of *B-flat*; the second is from *B-flat* against *F fa* <note>F</note>, and so with the others, which I explained in the 29th Proposition of the book on the **Organ**, where some accidentals are found that must be corrected according to the 2nd Advertisement found at the end of the table of Propositions.

The final fifth is from the accidental of *G re* <note>G-sharp</note> to the *fa* of *E mi* <note>E-flat</note>, where the defect of the tuning is encountered <note>This refers to the "wolf fifth," a notoriously dissonant interval that occurs as a byproduct of certain tuning systems.</note>, as seen in the notes marked at the top of the fi—

...figure of the Spinet in the 3rd book on Instruments, and in the aforementioned Proposition of the book on Organs.

This being established, practitioners—the craftsmen and builders of **Organs** <note>original: "Orgues"</note> and **Spinets** <note>A spinet is a small harpsichord-like instrument.</note>—many of whom cannot tune their own instruments, note two types of semitones (minor and major) on their **keyboards** <note>original: "Clauiers"</note>, in the same places where composers place them in vocal compositions. They also note major tones and superfluous tones, such that they compose the major tone from a major semitone and a minor one, and the superfluous tone <note>An "augmented" tone in modern terminology.</note> from two major semitones. These are found at the two keys that have no **accidental** <note>original: "feinte," referring to the raised black keys on a keyboard.</note>, namely at **D-re** and **A-la** <note>D and A in the solfège system used at the time.</note>, which have the major semitone on both sides; whereas all the other keys have the accidental of the minor semitone to serve chromatic purposes and to change minor thirds and sixths into major ones, and vice versa.

One may call the accidentals that create the minor semitone *dieses* <note>An early term for sharps.</note>, to distinguish them from those that create the major semitone. Now, although practitioners find **equal temperament** <note>original: "l'accord d'égalité," where all semitones are tuned to be exactly the same size.</note> to be very harsh—due to the sharpness of the major thirds and the narrowing of the semitones, which lessens the stability and quality of the **cadences** <note>A melodic or harmonic configuration that creates a sense of resolution.</note> (which are also poor on minor semitones)—they judge it more appropriate to adjust the frets of the **Lute** <note>original: "Luth"</note> and the **Viol** <note>original: "Viole"</note> by means of a **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals mathematically.</note> so that they are in perfect tune with the Spinet, rather than corrupting and destroying their own tuning, whose harmony they find sweeter. And it would not be so difficult to place said frets on the neck of the Lute (either with ivory frets or by using springs hidden inside or beneath the neck) that one could not achieve it. Nevertheless, it would not be a bad thing to retain equal temperament in order to increase the variety of harmony; in a single concert, one might play one piece of music in this tuning joined with ordinary Lutes and Viols, and then another piece in the ordinary tuning of the Spinets, upon which a single man can play up to ten parts with his ten fingers, and continue them by using his feet for the **pedals**, as many **Organists** do who use three or four keyboards.

It seems that practitioners can better tune the Spinet by equal semitones by making the **fifths** <note>original: "Quintes"</note> perfect, rather than by starting the *ut, re, mi* on every key, as I said in the 7th Observation. This is because the accuracy of the fifths forces the major thirds to be sharp; however, after having played said *ut, re, mi, fa* everywhere, it is easy to go over the tuning again to correct any defect that may occur, by making all the fifths so close to perfect that they almost no longer **beat** <note>original: "batent." "Beating" is an acoustic pulse heard when two notes are slightly out of tune with each other.</note>.

## XI. Observation.

->*Concerning the line described by the revolution of a circle on a flat plane.*<-

In the 9th Proposition of the 2nd book on **Movements** <note>Likely referring to the author’s own treatise on mechanics or harmonics.</note>, I had stated that a circle or globe rolling on a horizontal plane and making a full revolution described half of an **Ellipse**. In fact, when the line is described mechanically, as I have said, it approaches so closely to half of an ellipse that it is difficult for the eye to perceive the difference. But when one examines this line geometrically, it is neither an Ellipse, nor a **Helix** <note>original: "Helice"</note>, nor a **Quadratrix** <note>A complex curve used in ancient geometry to square the circle.</note>; rather, it is something in between and can be described in several ways. First, as I said in the aforementioned 9th Proposition. Secondly, by the **versed sines and right sines** <term>Versed sine (1 - cos θ) and right sine (sin θ) are trigonometric functions used here to plot the coordinates of the curve.</term> of the circle describing the line. If one raises the versed sines upon the line described on the horizontal plane by the circumference of the circle (to which it is equal), and applies the right sines to the tops of the versed sines such that they are drawn to the left side and parallel to the plane, the curved line described by the circle will pass through all the ends of the right sines as if through so many points, showing how to describe it. The third way to describe it was found by an excellent **Geometer** <note>A mathematician.</note> by means of a circle divided into as many parts as one wishes through several diameters. When one diameter is opposite the line of the plane, the others are so arranged in relation to that straight line that—for as many straight lines as there are radii described in the circle—when they are applied above or below the line of the plane so that they are parallel and equal to said radii, the ends of these lines mark the places or points through which this curved line, which one may name a **roulette** <note>Now commonly known in mathematics as a cycloid.</note>, must pass.

<summary>This page describes acoustic methods for detecting enemy miners using drums and discusses the geometric properties and construction of the cycloid curve, then called a "roulette."</summary>

--- Page 788 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of geometry and physics from page 24, specifically focusing on the properties of the cycloid curve as discovered by Gilles Personne de Roberval. It then transitions into Observation XII, which critiques historical accounts of Pythagoras’s musical experiments.</meta>

<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>Physics & Mathematics.</header>

Now, among the several properties of this line, the one discovered by **Mr. Roberval** <note>Gilles Personne de Roberval (1602–1675), a French mathematician who studied the cycloid, a curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel.</note> is quite remarkable: namely, that the area contained between the straight line (equal to the circumference of the circle) and the curved line is triple that of the circle which describes the curve. Consequently, anyone who can **square this area** <note>Calculate the "quadrature," or find a square with an equal area.</note>—that is, find a square equal to it—will have squared the circle. Now, other points taken on the circumference of the circle that do not touch the plane describe a portion of this same line; however, each point closer to the center describes a different line, even though its base is equal. Only those points located in the axis of a sphere describe straight lines when one of its great circles rolls along a straight line.

As for circles of different sizes, they always describe a similar curved line when the circumferences of the larger ones have the same ratio to their straight lines as the circumferences of the smaller ones have to their straight lines, and not otherwise. This is what happens with the circles mentioned by **Aristotle in the 25th Mechanical Question** <note>Refers to the "Wheel of Aristotle" paradox, which examines how two concentric circles of different diameters appear to travel the same distance when rolled.</note>, where the larger carries the smaller, or is carried by the smaller. In that case, the curved line made by one is not similar to the curved line made by the other, even though the straight line produced by their rolling is equal, and even though the method of describing them all using the aforementioned sines found by Mr. Roberval serves equally for all. But when the circumference is **half** <note>original: "sous-double"</note> the length of the straight line, the area contained by the straight line and the curve is five times the area of the circle describing said lines. If the straight line is two and a half times larger than the circumference, the area is six times the circle, and so on for the others. In decreasing, if the straight line is less than half the circumference, the area is only double the circle; however, it can never happen that the area is equal to the circle, which it will always exceed, even if one continues to decrease the straight line toward infinity.

## XII. Observation.

->*On the errors of Pythagoras, or of the Historians.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap O featuring a sun with a face rising over a landscape.</image-desc>
One could add a specific book to warn of all the errors that authors have made when speaking of music, both theoretical and practical, in their books. But this is so easily done by those who know the truth of experiments that such a critique would seem useless to me. For example, when **Censorinus** <note>A 3rd-century AD Roman grammarian and author of "De Die Natali."</note> says in the 10th chapter of *The Birthday* that Pythagoras found the **consonances** <note>Harmonious musical intervals like the octave or fifth.</note> and intervals of music using strings of equal length and thickness by stretching them with weights—and that having noted their proportions, he applied them to the intervals of sounds—he is entirely mistaken, as we have shown in the 13th and 14th Propositions of the 3rd book. For the intervals of sounds are in a **sub-duplicate ratio** <note>The ratio of the square roots.</note> of the said weights; the weights are similar to the squares, and the sounds to their sides and roots. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the Greco-Roman polymath who wrote "Harmonics."</note> seems to make the same mistake in the 11th chapter of his 1st book, if he places the same ratio between the tensions as between the weights or the forces that stretch them.

He is also mistaken when he says in the same chapter that Pythagoras, having had flutes made of the same thickness and keeping the same proportion in

## XIII. Observation.
### On Aliquot Parts, the Number 120, and Amicable Numbers.

It is necessary to add to what I said regarding the **aliquot parts** <term>aliquot parts: The "proper divisors" of a number, meaning all the integers that divide into it exactly, excluding the number itself. For example, the aliquot parts of 6 are 1, 2, and 3.</term> of numbers in the tenth remark of the first General Preface, the method for finding the number similar to 120, which I mentioned in the place cited above. One must set down as many numbers in sequence as desired in a double ratio <note>A geometric progression where each number is double the previous (2, 4, 8, etc.).</note>, beginning with 2, such as the numbers A, B, C, D, E, F; from which, if unity is subtracted, the other numbers G, H, I, K, L, M are formed; and to which, if unity is added, the other numbers N, O, P, Q, R, S are formed.

<margin>
**G, H, I, K, L, M.**
1, 3, 7, 15, 31, 63,
**A, B, C, D, E, F.**
2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64,
**N, O, P, Q, R, S.**
3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65.
</margin>
When one of the numbers G, H, I, K, L, M—for example, K—divided by the number N from the last row (four places to the left), produces a prime number, then triple that prime number multiplied by the number from the middle row that immediately precedes K will give the required number. This is seen in 15 divided by 3, which results in 5 (a prime number), the triple of which is 15; multiplied by 8, this makes 120, which is the number we gave in the aforementioned Preface.

The other example is seen in 63; which, divided by 9, produces the prime number 7, the triple of which is 21; multiplied by 32, this makes 672, which is the other required number.

As for the two numbers whose aliquot parts mutually recreate one another <term>amicable numbers: Pairs of numbers where the sum of the divisors of one equals the other number. The most famous pair is 220 and 284.</term>, one must also set down the numbers that follow from 2 in a geometric progression: 2, 4, 8, 16, etc. Then, one must write the triple numbers below them: 6, 12, 24, 48; from which, if unity is subtracted, there remain 5, 11, 23, 47, which must be placed above. Finally, one must multiply 6 by 12, subtracting unity, to get 71; and 12 by 24, minus unity, to produce 287; and 24 by 48, minus unity, to get 1151, which must be arranged as seen here, to infinity.

<margin>
5, 11, 23, 47.
2, 4, 8, 16.
6, 12, 24, 48.
71, 287, 1151.
</margin>
When one of the numbers of the last row, along with its opposite and the preceding number of the first row, are prime numbers, one will find numbers similar to those in question. For example, the number of the last row, 71, and 11 from the first row, and 5 which precedes it, are prime numbers. This being established, if one multiplies 71 by 4, and similarly 5 and 11 by the same 4, one will have the two numbers 284 and 220, whose aliquot parts mutually recreate—

## XIV. Observation.

### *On the multitude of musical instruments, and particularly the new ones.*

The book of instruments by Michael Praetorius <note>Michael Praetorius (c. 1571–1621) was a famous German composer and theorist. His "Syntagma Musicum" is a foundational text for understanding Renaissance and early Baroque instruments.</note>, whose anagram is *Here now is another Orpheus* <note>Original Latin: "Hic iam alter Orpheus."</note>, printed in the year 1619, fell into my hands after I had finished all my books on Harmony. I believe readers will find it agreeable to know the contents of his *Organography* <note>Original: "Organographie." This refers to the second volume of "Syntagma Musicum," which describes musical instruments.</note>, of which I would provide an abridgment here if it were not written in the German language. He provides a brief discourse on each instrument, and then sets down its tuning and range with ordinary notes, clefs, and the letters used in its practice. Secondly, he provides a treatise on all the stops of the Organ, according to the different Organs he saw in Germany. Thirdly, he includes the figures of all sorts of instruments in woodcuts; but the figures I have used seem to me more distinct and better made, though I leave the judgment of this to the readers. He calls the *Pandore* <note>A long-necked, plucked string instrument from the lute family.</note> the *Orpheoreon* and *Penorcon*, and represents the **marine trumpet** with four strings, calling it a *Trumscheit* <note>A tall, stringed instrument played with a bow, known for its buzzy, trumpet-like sound.</note>. As for the other German names, I leave them out because they are not in use among us. He adds several types of ancient Organ keyboards, which are not as well-made as ours, and includes in the 29th, 30th, and 31st plates several figures of Indian instruments, which I have not provided. As for the 32nd, 33rd, and 34th plates, he transcribed them from the book *The Art of Music* by Ottomarus <note>Referring to "Musurgia seu praxis Musicae" (1536) by Ottomar Luscinius.</note>. The 37th and 38th plates represent figures of Organ pipes and their reeds, and the 42nd has some unusual instruments that I have not included. His third volume contains several pieces of music used in France, Germany, and Italy—for example, Airs, Passemezzos, Galliards, etc.—along with many things that serve in the composition of counterpoint, both simple and figured. Finally, he shows the manner of performing concerts with all sorts of instruments. However, I have not seen his fourth volume, in which he says he has included several compositions by good authors, and where he teaches how to play the Organ and the **spinet** <term>spinet: A smaller, rectangular or wing-shaped keyboard instrument of the harpsichord family.</term>, and how to perform cadences and other ornaments of music. The titles of the books by Henricus Baryphonus <note>A German music theorist (1581–1655) known for his work on the mathematical foundations of music.</note>, on page 227 of his third book, are so impressive that they deserve to be sought out by all musicians, because they promise the solution to questions of theoretical and practical music; I do not know if they actually provide them. I omit several new instruments—for example, the Viol that sounds all by itself with an endless bow <note>Likely a reference to a mechanical bowed instrument like the "Geigenwerk," which used rotating wheels to bow the strings.</note>, producing trills and soft effects; the Organ that pronounces vowels and the syllables composed of them, and that which can pronounce syllables containing consonants; and the Viol whose construction Mr. Doni <note>Giovanni Battista Doni (1594–1647), an Italian scholar who attempted to recreate ancient Greek music and invented the "Lyra Barberina."</note> describes on page 30 of his book for playing the tones and modes of the ancients. Many other instruments, simple or composite, may yet be found that have never yet been invented.

# NOTICE.

ALTHOUGH I have spoken quite extensively of the intervals produced by the Trumpet, and have attempted to provide the reasoning for them since the 12th Proposition of the 5th book on Instruments, and in the 18th Proposition of the 2nd Latin book <note>The author refers to his own previous works, likely *Harmonie Universelle* and *Harmonicorum Libri*.</note>, where one sees another very subtle reasoning; nevertheless, it is not out of place to advise of another manner in which this phenomenon might be explained, following the conjecture of an excellent Philosopher <note>Likely René Descartes or Isaac Beeckman, both of whom corresponded with Mersenne regarding the physics of music.</note>. This is done by first supposing that the range of the Trumpet, or of another wind instrument, comprises several Octaves according to the force of the breath that one pushes through, and that each sound is similar to an equal weight. Thus, the first breath, or the softest, corresponds to the first tone, which is the lowest, with which it is as if in equilibrium. The second, stronger breath, being unable to equal the 2nd tone—which is at the Octave of the first—unless it is double in strength, produces the Octave. And the 3rd breath, three times stronger than the first, emptying the air from within the Trumpet once more, makes it rise to the Twelfth <note>An interval of an octave plus a fifth (a 3:1 ratio).</note>, and so on for the others, up to the 6th jump or interval. This interval, which should be from 6 to 7 to follow all the intervals comprised by the numbers that follow naturally, rises to the Fourth, as I said in the 13th Proposition of the 5th book. This interrupts this reasoning, as well as the one I have used, unless it can divide this Fourth into a Sesquisexte <term>the ratio of 7:6</term> and a Sesquiseptième <term>the ratio of 8:7</term>, and so on for the other numbers 10, 12, 13, etc., which must be tested by experiment.

Now, it is enough that our phenomena have been well observed, even if we have perhaps not given the true reasons for them, as can be seen in the first Observation. This is because not everyone admits that the ratio of the weight of water to that of air follows that of falling bodies or circles, inasmuch as many things that are less heavy, or equally heavy, can further hinder the movement that occurs within; and the movement of the heaviest things can be faster. I desire this to be understood for all the other reasons I have used, so that those whom they do not satisfy may be content with the simple observations, and search for the true reasons themselves. I may yet give several other Observations, God willing, once I have justified them; meanwhile, one can place here the 2 others which are at the end of the table of contents. I add only that the person of whom I spoke in the 29th Proposition of the 1st book on the nature of Sound <note>This refers to René Descartes, whose "Dioptrique" was published in 1637.</note> has given his discourse on Dioptrics <term>the study of the refraction of light through lenses</term>, and demonstrated the nature of refractions, so that this book can greatly serve to better understand and enrich what I said in the said Proposition and in the 28th, and similarly in the 5th Proposition on Utility, and elsewhere, when speaking of light. He has similarly given the elliptical and hyperbolic figures of transparent bodies <note>Original: "diafanes." Referring to glass or lenses.</note> suitable for changing the rays of light in all fashions, and for making the best possible telescopes <note>Original: "lunettes de longue & de courte vûe." Literally "glasses for long and short sight."</note>. To which, if Monsieur Mydorge <note>Claude Mydorge (1585–1647), a French mathematician and friend of Descartes.</note> adds his most excellent speculations on light, vision, and all that concerns the said telescopes, nothing more remains to be desired on this subject.

->Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah.<-

# Table of the xix. books of Music.

<margin>
**A.** signifies the 3 books on movements.
**a.** The treatise on mechanics.
**B.** The 2 books on the voice and songs.
**C.** The 6 books on consonances.
**D.** The 6 books on instruments.
**E.** The 7th book on percussion instruments.
**F.** The 8th book on the utility of harmony.
</margin>
I had resolved in the first general Preface not to make a table <note>An index or table of contents.</note> for these books, due to the different restarts that the Printers were forced to mark by repeating the same numbers, signatures, and Alphabets several times, because they lacked musical notes <note>17th-century printing was complex; the printer likely had to send the work to different shops or wait for specialized musical type, causing the page numbering and paper gathering marks (signatures) to become inconsistent.</note>; but the utility derived from Tables is so great, as several learned persons have persuaded me, that their desire and advice have made me change my resolution. But so that this Table may be understood by all, it must be noted that each letter preceding or following the numbers signifies the book in which the subject of the Table is contained: thus **A** signifies the 3 books on movements. **a** the treatise on Mechanics placed at the end. **B** the book on the voice, and that of Songs, **C** the 6 books on Consonances and Composition. **D** the first 6 on instruments. **E** the 7th on percussion instruments, and **F** the 8th on the utility of harmony: so that all subjects found before or after one of these letters, after which no other follows, belong to the book marked by said letter: and if another follows, everything preceding it belongs to it: for example, when one reads at the letter **A**. *Advice for miracles 227. D. for Prosody and Metrics. 431. C.* the letter **D** signifies that the first advice for miracles is in the books on instruments, at page 227, and that the advice for Prosody is in the books on Consonances, page 431, and so on for the others; which had to be noted once and for all, so that there would be no difficulty.

As for the numbers at the top of the pages, they were sometimes incorrectly marked by oversight, and particularly since number 290 of the 5th book on Composition, for the number 191 which follows should be 291: which error continued until 212, which should be 312. and because it was necessary to catch up to the 6th book, we were forced to put only one number on each leaf from 313 until the beginning of the said 6th book. But these errors in numbers, as well as those of the signatures, are of little consequence, because the material and the meaning always follow as they should. Now, before reading these books, besides the errors marked at the end or at the beginning of the Treatises, these must also be corrected. Page 343 of the 5th book on Composition, line 39. read *minor* for *major*, and RE for MI. line 4. R. for V. page on the back of page 313, line 17. after *found*, read *in*. p. 324. l. 40. *As*. p. 325. l. 23. *others*. back page l. 21. erase, and p. 328. l. 21. read *line*. p. 330. l. 19. *stones* for *pieces*. l. 23. *push*.

<meta>This page transitions from the index of "Harmonie Universelle" to a supplementary section where Marin Mersenne discusses physics and mechanics, specifically responding to Galileo Galilei's groundbreaking work on the motion of falling bodies.</meta>

# FIRST OBSERVATION.

Among several observations that deserve a dedicated treatise, I am placing only two here. The first pertains to the natural movements of heavy bodies (which I have discussed in several places in this work) in order to fill the empty pages. I say first, then, that having seen the book that Mr. Galileo wrote on local motion <note>original: "mouvement local," referring to Galileo’s *Two New Sciences* (1638), which revolutionized the study of kinematics</note>, I learned that he had only performed his experiments from 12 Florence fathoms <term>brasse: an old Italian unit of length, roughly 58 centimeters</term>, which do not equal 24 of our Royal feet <term>pied de Roy: the "King's foot," a French unit of length roughly 32.5 centimeters, slightly longer than the modern English foot</term>, whereas I have performed mine from 147 feet high. He notes that the increase in the speed of descending heavy bodies is uniform and equal, because they acquire as many new degrees of speed as the time of their fall increases. For example, the second interval of time adds one degree of speed to that of the first interval; and the 3rd interval adds a degree of speed to the 2nd degree, and so on for the others. Consequently, if the moving body continued its fall with only the degree of speed acquired at the first moment of its fall, it would cover half as much ground as when it descends with the 2nd degree acquired at the 2nd moment and joined to the first degree. This is why it is enough to know the total duration of the fall to know how many degrees of speed the moving body possesses. This being established by the testimony of experience—which I have performed from more than 24 fathoms <term>toise: a unit of length equal to 6 Royal feet, approximately 1.95 meters</term> high in the presence of learned persons who assisted—I set down here his first 8 theorems, which can be deduced from the 7th proposition of our 2nd book on motions, and from the 22nd of the 3rd book.

->The First VIII Theorems of Galileo.<-

**I.** The time in which a moving body covers a given distance is equal to the time in which the same body would cover that same distance with a uniform motion, the speed of which would be half the maximum speed acquired by the body as its motion increases. <note>This is the "Mean Speed Theorem," a fundamental concept in kinematics.</note>

**II.** The distances covered by a falling body in any given times are in the duplicate ratio of the times, or as their squares <note>This describes the law of falling bodies, where distance $d$ is proportional to time squared ($t^2$)</note>. This we have demonstrated in our 2nd book of motions: from which it follows that all the individual spaces covered have the same ratio as the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, etc. So, in the same time that the degrees of speed increase according to the natural order of numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, etc.), the distances traveled in those same intervals increase according to the odd numbers, starting with unity. From this, he concludes that if one takes 2 given distances from the beginning of the fall, made in given times, the times of the falls will be as the 2 aforementioned distances are to the mean proportional distance between those 2 distances, both on inclined planes and in a vertical drop.

**III.** If a moving body falls along an inclined plane and along a vertical line, both having the same height relative to the horizon, the times of the falls will be to each other as the lengths of the said planes.

**IV.** The times of falls on equal planes that are unequally inclined are in the sub-duplicate ratio <note>The "sub-duplicate ratio" refers to the ratio of the square roots.</note> of their heights, taken inversely.

**V.** The ratio of the descents on planes differing in length, inclination, and height is composed of the ratio of their lengths and the sub-duplicate ratio of their heights, taken inversely.

**VI.** If planes are drawn from the top or bottom of a circle to any point on the circumference, the times of the falls on those planes are equal: which we have treated in the 3rd book of motions. From this, it is easy to conclude that the vertical plane and the inclined plane described from the same point, upon which falls occur in equal time, are within the semicircle of which the vertical plane is the diameter: and that the times of falls on planes are equal when the heights of equal parts of those planes are to each other as the length of the same planes.

**VII.** If the heights of two planes are in the duplicate ratio <note>i.e., the ratio of the squares</note> of their lengths, the falls will occur in equal times.

**VIII.** The times of falls that occur on planes cut by the same circle elevated above the horizon, which begin at the top or bottom of the diameter, are equal to the time of the vertical fall that occurs through the diameter: but the times of the fall on planes that do not reach the diameter are shorter; and those of the fall on planes that cut the diameter are longer.

<summary>Mersenne presents and validates Galileo's laws of falling bodies and inclined planes, noting that his own experiments from greater heights (147 feet) confirm these mathematical principles. The page lists eight specific theorems regarding the relationship between time, distance, and speed in uniform acceleration.</summary>
<keywords>Galileo Galilei, kinematics, law of falling bodies, uniform acceleration, inclined planes, units of measurement, Royal feet, Florence fathoms, mean speed theorem</keywords>

--- Page 802 ---
<meta>This page continues Mersenne's engagement with Galileo Galilei’s work, shifting from the physics of falling bodies to the physics of sound and musical intervals (acoustics). He discusses how the mathematical ratios of music can be visually demonstrated through the motion of pendulums and stretched strings.</meta>

## SECOND OBSERVATION.
->On the agreement of consonances <term>consonance: a combination of notes that sound pleasant or stable together</term>, and on the union of the air’s vibrations on the eardrum; and on the manner of measuring pitches by the movements of strings.<-

Although I have explained in several places everything concerning the vibrations <note>original: "reversions," referring to the back-and-forth oscillation of a string</note>, or the returns of the strings that produce sound, and the unions or meetings of their cycles—and consequently of the vibrations of air <note>original: "batemens d'air"</note>, which seem all the sweeter to the ear as they unite more often—it is nevertheless appropriate to remark that Mr. Galileo had the same thought in his book on motion <note>original: "liure du mouuement," referring to Galileo’s *Discorsi* (1638)</note>. There, he adds that strings attached to a nail at the top, having a weight at the other end <note>Mersenne is describing pendulums used to model musical strings</note>, demonstrate the unions of the said vibrations that occur in consonances. For example, if one wishes to represent all the movements or vibrations of the octave <term>diapason: the musical interval of an octave</term> divided into a fifth <term>diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth</term> and a fourth <term>diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term>, which unite or are disjointed, one must take three strings. Their lengths must be in the duplicate ratio <note>original: "raison doublée," meaning the ratio of the squares</note> of the three terms of the said divided octave—namely of 2, 3, and 4, or of 6, 4, 3, which divide the octave arithmetically or harmonically. But because the first arithmetic division is the most natural and most consistent with the truth (as I demonstrated in the 36th proposition of the *Book of Consonances*), I use it here. I say that the ratios of these terms 2, 3, and 4, being squared, give us these three following terms: 4, 9, and 16. These show the lengths of the three strings whose movements unite as many times as those of the three strings of a lute or other instruments that divide the octave into a fifth and a fourth. For a string 16 feet long will make only 2 movements (or vibrations) while the 9-foot string makes 3, and the 4-foot string makes 4. Thus, while this last and shortest string makes 2 movements, the first or longest will make only one; this is why each of its strokes or vibrations will strike at the same time as every second stroke of the other. Thus, there will be no disjointed stroke, properly speaking, because its first movement begins and occurs with the first half of the first vibration of the other, and the second ends with the second part.

As for the 9-foot string, which makes 3 movements in the same time that the 16-foot string makes 2, it only unites its vibrations at every third of its strokes; and because the first of the three begins with the first of the two, and the third ends with the second, one can say there is only the single middle stroke of the three which does not unite at all. These three strokes, being compared to the 4 strokes of the 4-foot string, only unite at the beginning and the end of the said 4 strokes, so that there are 2 disjointed ones. From this, it happens that some hold the fourth <term>diatessaron</term> to be the last or the least of the simple consonances, because it has as much "bad" as "good"—that is to say, as many unions as disunions—as I stated in the very long and difficult 33rd proposition of the *Book of Consonances*. Be that as it may, I wish to give here the lengths of three strings consistent with those I have always used in our observations, which are 3 and a half feet long, and which I use for the longest string. This is because a 16-foot string is too inconvenient, as there are few people who can easily arrange such a height to enjoy the satisfaction of seeing sounds and harmony with their eyes, without using the ear.

I say, then, that the first or longest string being 3 and a half feet, the second will be almost 2 feet (as there is not a line's difference), and the third will be 7 and a half inches. When released, all three will return together at every fourth vibration of the shortest; so that the eye will see the harmonic union. Yet neither the eye nor the mind will see *why* these unions please the ear so greatly, the immediate cause of which is as well hidden from us as other natural effects. Those who have enough height available have here the two types of strings represented in numbers:

| 16 feet | 9 feet | 4 feet |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 3 and ½ feet | 2 feet or thereabouts | 7 and a half inches |

And those who have galleries or other places 60 feet long, and strings of brass or other material of that length, will not need the said suspended strings. For if they stretch three strings horizontally, like those of a spinet, where one is 60 feet long, another 40, and the other 30, at the same time that the 60-foot string makes two vibrations, the 40-foot one will make 3, and the 30-foot one will make 4. Thus, all their vibrations will unite as many times as the shortest string makes 4 vibrations.

<meta>This page continues Mersenne's exploration of acoustics and the laws of motion, specifically connecting the mathematical ratios found in musical intervals (consonances) to the physical behavior of pendulums and falling bodies. He moves from theoretical vibrations to practical measurements of height and even to the rhythmic patterns found in manual labor.</meta>

...just as it happens that the strings of a spinet <term>epinette: a small, plucked keyboard instrument similar to a harpsichord</term>, or other instruments that share the same division of the octave, unite their movements fifteen times in the space of one second, when the lowest pitch is in unison with the great bell of Notre Dame <note>This refers to "Emmanuel," the famous 13-ton Great Bell of Notre Dame Cathedral in Paris</note>. This bell has the pitch of the second G-sol of the 8-foot open pipe of an organ, which is 2 feet and 8 inches in height. For a string tuned in unison with the said bell performs 60 cycles and just as many returns <note>original: "60 tours, & autant de retours"; Mersenne is describing 60 full oscillations per second (60 Hz)</note> in the time of one second.

Now, although I have provided several uses for a string hung from a nail—which can mark seconds or any other interval of time one desires—it can be used in a thousand other circumstances. For example, if one considers the time of a single swing <note>original: "tours"</note> of a string attached to the vault of a church (as happens with the ropes or chains that support lamps, candles, or other weights), or one attached at the top of mine shafts or quarries when one is at the bottom, one can determine the height of those vaults and wells. For if one of the swings lasted for half a minute, the height of the well or the vault—that is to say, the length of the string—would be 477 and a half toises <term>toise: a traditional French unit of length, approximately 1.95 meters or 6.4 feet</term>.

But since we do not have such great heights here from which to conduct this test, let us merely suppose that the swing of the string lasts 4 seconds—that is, the fifteenth part of a minute. It is then certain that the vault will be 56 feet high, measured from the weight of the string, as seen in the table of the 15th proposition of the 2nd book on movements. This table will serve all those who see lamps swaying in churches to determine, by their motion, the height of the vaults or other places where their strings or chains are attached. Similarly, one can know the time of a string's swing if the height from which it is suspended is known, since the heights of suspension (or the lengths of the strings) must be in the square ratio of the times, and consequently the times in the square root ratio <note>original: "raison souz doublée"</note>, or like the roots of the numbers that express the lengths of said strings.

One can also compare the time it takes for heavy bodies to fall from the same places where the strings are attached with the time they take to fall perpendicularly. For example, if the string is 56 feet long, the weight attached to it will complete each of its cycles in 4 seconds. And the same weight falling perpendicularly covers 32 toises in 4 seconds—that is to say, more than three and a half times the length of the string.

But if one takes only a 3-foot string to mark seconds, the time of perpendicular falls, the swings of the suspended string, and its lengths will have an analogy that is easier to understand: for a string 12 feet long will make one swing in the time of 2 seconds, and the weight will fall perpendicularly 12 feet in one second. A string 48 feet long will make one swing in 4 seconds, and the weight will fall perpendicularly 48 feet in 2 seconds. Thus, the weight falling perpendicularly will always have its time of fall be half <note>original: "souz double"</note> the time of each return of a string of the same length as said fall. And if one takes only half of each cycle—that is, the fall alone, or the ascent alone, or the single natural movement, or the single violent movement of the weight attached to the string—these times will be equal to one another. However, one must deduct what I said in the 13th proposition of the 2nd book on movements, which should be read along with the 14th and 15th propositions of the same book, and the 20th of the 3rd book, where several very specific observations can be seen.

Now, one could also compare the union of several other sorts of movements to those of the air and the strings that create musical consonances. For example, that of three or four flails <term>fleaux: manual tools used for threshing grain by striking it</term> with which one beats wheat in the threshing floors. This is why one receives such pleasure from seeing three or four men threshing wheat in Anjou, Maine, and elsewhere, when they coordinate well. The same is true for three or four merchants or carters who create, it seems, all sorts of harmonies with their whips, which they sometimes know how to handle so dexterously that they can knock a pin off the edge of a glass full of water or other liquid without spilling a single drop, as I have been assured.

On this subject, it is worth noting an invention found by a brave gentleman from Dauphiné, which allows a single man to thresh wheat with eight flails by means of a keyboard similar to that of a spinet. I leave aside various other craftsmen who make many kinds of noises and clatterings while working, whose meetings and unions give a kind of satisfaction, while their disunity brings displeasure—just as it happens with the union and disjunction of sounds, which create consonances and dissonances.
